title: Postoperative Wound Discharge After Hip Arthroplasty in Elderly Patients: Hypoalbuminemia, Not Infection, Is the Cause
Postoperative Outcomes of Robotic Versus Conventional Surgery in a Multi-Cancer Cohort: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Evidence on robotic surgery is largely procedure-specific and depends on the comparator. We examined associations with postoperative outcomes, prioritizing colorectal and uterine cancer and distinguishing laparoscopic from open comparators. Methods : This retrospective cohort included 2139 patients undergoing elective surgery for colorectal, uterine, prostate, or renal cancer at a tertiary referral center in 2019-2023. The primary analysis included 1232 colorectal or uterine cancer patients undergoing robotic ( n = 462) or laparoscopic ( n = 770) surgery. Generalized linear models adjusted for age, sex, cancer type, and T category/FIGO stage group; operative time and staffing were added in sensitivity analysis. Absolute differences were estimated by G-computation. The four-cancer pooled analysis was secondary. Results : Robotic surgery was associated with a shorter hospital stay (length-of-stay ratio 0.78; 95% CI 0.73-0.83; adjusted difference 2.34 days), which persisted with operative-time/staffing and calendar-year adjustment. Rehospitalization within 30 days after surgery was higher overall (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.82; 95% CI 1.34-2.47), but differed by cancer: aOR 2.50 (95% CI 1.77-3.53) for colorectal and 0.38 (95% CI 0.16-0.90) for uterine cancer (interaction p Conclusions : Rehospitalization differed in direction between these cancers, indicating that cancer type and comparator selection materially affect inference. These associations do not establish a platform-specific benefit or transferable bed-day savings.

title: Individually Prescribed In-Bed Exergaming Using Nintendo Ring Fit Adventure in Posttransplant Inpatients With Marked Functional Impairment After Intensive Care: Prospective Single-Arm Feasibility Study.
abstract: Background Early rehabilitation is important after transplantation and critical illness, but profound weakness, fatigue, and motivational, psychological, and safety barriers may limit participation. Exergaming may facilitate rehabilitation, but the feasibility of full-body in-bed exergaming in this population remains unclear. Objective We evaluated the feasibility and observed safety of individually prescribed in-bed exergaming using Nintendo Ring Fit Adventure (NFA; Nintendo Co, Ltd) in posttransplant inpatients after intensive care unit (ICU) care. Methods This prospective, single-center, single-arm interventional feasibility study (October 2024-October 2025) enrolled 26 posttransplant adults with prior ICU care and Functional Ambulation Category (FAC) scores ≤3. Participants were referred after ward transfer by transplant-team advanced practice nurses, and the principal investigator confirmed eligibility based on prespecified inclusion and exclusion criteria. Ten individually prescribed, supervised in-bed NFA sessions, each scheduled for 30 minutes, including setup and operation, were planned alongside usual physical therapy. Data were obtained from medical records, standardized session logs, and prespecified clinical and questionnaire assessments. Outcomes included retention; session delivery, completion, and interruptions; exercise-item completion and interruptions; session-terminating adverse events; net exercise time; satisfaction; and exploratory strength, mobility, and health-related quality-of-life changes. Results Participants (mean age 53.0, SD 12.4 y; 14 men) included 23 liver and 3 bilateral lung transplant recipients. Mean ICU stay and mechanical ventilation duration were 24.3 (SD 11.0) days and 21.3 (SD 11.6) days, respectively; median baseline FAC and Medical Research Council Sum Score were 0.5 (IQR 0.0-1.0) and 38.0 (IQR 30.5-42.0), respectively. None had an FAC score above 2. Twenty completed the final assessment (20/26, 76.9%, 95% CI 57.9%-89%). Of 227 delivered sessions, 223 (98.2%, 95% CI 95.8%-100%) were completed. Of 2161 prescribed exercise items, 2072 (95.9%, 95% CI 93.4%-97.9%) were completed. No session-terminating adverse events were observed (0/227, 0%, 95% CI 0%-1.6%). Median within-participant net exercise time increased by 159.0 (IQR 35.5-296.3) seconds from sessions 1 to 10 (95% CI 81.0-284.0; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P P =.004), 2.0 Intensive Care Unit Mobility Scale points (IQR 1.0-4.3; 95% CI 1.0-3.5, P P =.009). Questionnaire responses were favorable. Conclusions Under therapist supervision, the individually prescribed in-bed NFA program showed favorable operational feasibility, with no session-terminating adverse events. By combining the accessibility of a commercial off-the-shelf exergame with individualized exercise prescription, the program extended bedside exergaming to posttransplant inpatients with substantial functional impairment after ICU care who had not achieved independent ambulation.

title: A qualitative exploration of medication discussions in nursing home care conferences.
Interprofessional collaboration in emergency department nursing care for patients with diabetic ketoacidosis: a narrative review.
abstract: Introduction Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is an acute metabolic emergency requiring timely risk recognition, fluid resuscitation, insulin therapy, electrolyte correction, dynamic monitoring, and coordinated care transitions. These interdependent tasks pose substantial challenges to emergency nursing. This narrative review aimed to synthesise current evidence on interprofessional collaboration in emergency DKA nursing and propose a conceptual framework to support coordinated care. Methods A structured narrative review was conducted using literature retrieved from PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and the Web of Science Core Collection from database inception to July 10, 2026. DKA-specific clinical and implementation evidence was integrated with broader literature on interprofessional collaboration, communication, and healthcare implementation. The evidence was synthesised using Donabedian's structure-process-outcome framework. Results Current collaborative approaches include nurse-led standardised pathways, risk-stratified subcutaneous insulin and non-intensive care unit management, collaborative medication management, laboratory and point-of-care monitoring, structured communication, digital decision support, and multidisciplinary discharge planning. Available evidence suggests that standardised collaborative pathways may improve the timeliness and consistency of care, shorten emergency department length of stay, and reduce intensive care resource use. However, evidence evaluating complete interprofessional nursing teams and nursing-sensitive outcomes remains limited. Based on the synthesis, a conceptual closed-loop collaboration framework comprising six interconnected stages was proposed: recognition and activation, shared risk stratification, coordinated monitoring and execution, escalation, care transition, and recurrence prevention. Discussion Effective interprofessional DKA nursing requires shared clinical information, explicit responsibility, timely feedback, and predefined escalation procedures, with emergency nurses serving as continuous information integrators and process coordinators. The proposed framework provides an evidence-informed approach to organising collaborative emergency care. However, it has not been prospectively validated, and further implementation research is required to evaluate its feasibility, safety, and effects on nursing-sensitive and patient outcomes.

title: Standardizing Intensive Care Unit Discharge Through Use of the National Early Warning Score.
National assessment of trauma care system capacity in Ecuador: Evaluating institutional resources and practitioner KAPS domains.
abstract: We evaluated Ecuador's trauma care system capacity by analyzing the discrepancy between hospital infrastructure and the individual dimensions of the Knowledge, Attitudes, Practices, and Safety (KAPS) framework among medical specialists. A nationwide, multicomponent cross-sectional study was conducted (2025-2026), comprising a complete structural audit of 49 eligible public hospitals (Levels II and III) and a KAPS survey of 215 trauma-facing specialists representing 36 institutions (73.5% institutional participation rate). Spatial workflow efficiency was assessed via Emergency Department-to-Computed Tomography (ED-CT) transit distances. Independent multivariable Poisson regression models evaluated each KAPS dimension separately, reporting adjusted Incidence Rate Ratios (IRR)accounting for institutional clustering and professional seniority. The institutional audit revealed significant operational constraints: 51.0% of hospitals lacked 24/7 radiological coverage, and 16.3% experienced CT scanner downtime. Spatial ED-to-CT distances were significantly greater in Level III tertiary centers, reaching up to 300 meters (p = 0.006). Among specialists (N = 215 across 36 hospitals), ecological associations with provincial trauma volume yielded wide confidence intervals spanning the null value across domains (Knowledge: rho = 0.113, 95% CI: -0.39-0.61; Reported Practice: rho = -0.160, 95% CI: -0.66-0.34), reflecting low statistical precision from macro-level aggregation. Dimension-specific multivariable models revealed marked inter-specialty divergence: Emergency Physicians exhibited lower Knowledge (aIRR = 0.61; 95% CI: 0.50-0.74), but higher rate ratios in Reported Practices (aIRR = 1.48; 95% CI: 1.34-1.65), Attitudes (aIRR = 1.12; 95% CI: 1.09-1.16), and Safety (aIRR = 1.18; 95% CI: 1.12-1.25) relative to General Surgery. Ecuador's trauma network exhibits a measurable discrepancy between nominal infrastructure and operational availability. System capacity is constrained by physical architectural barriers and a divergence between practitioners' subjective perceptions and objective decision-making skills. Strategic priorities must include a unified National Trauma Registry, integrated teleradiology, and continuous scenario-based training.

title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the timing of rehabilitation training intervention for recipients of extracorporeal membrane oxygenators.
abstract: Objective To systematically evaluate the effects of early versus delayed rehabilitation training interventions (RTI) on clinical outcomes in patients receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Methods We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled studies, and observational cohort studies comparing early and delayed RTI in patients receiving ECMO. We searched databases including Embase, PubMed, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, China Science and Technology Journal Database, and China Biology Medicine disc from inception to 1 April 2025. Study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers. Outcomes included complications, intensive care unit (ICU) and hospital length of stay (LOS), duration of mechanical ventilation, ECMO duration, and in-hospital mortality. Results Twelve studies (five RCTs, four non-RCTs, and three cohort studies) were included. Compared with delayed RTI, early RTI significantly reduced the risk of complications [risk ratio (RR) = 0.43, 95% CI: 0.26-0.69, P P P = 0.007). No significant differences were found in mechanical ventilation duration (MD = 0.14 days, P = 0.914), ECMO duration (MD = -1.77 days, P = 0.136), or in-hospital mortality (RR = 0.72, P = 0.097). Sensitivity analysis excluding one study demonstrated a greater reduction in hospital LOS significant (MD = -5.82 days, 95% CI: -9.34 to -2.30, P = 0.001), while other outcomes remained unchanged. Conclusions Early RTI is associated with reduced complications and improved recovery outcomes (ICU/hospital stay) in ECMO patients compared with delayed RTI. However, due to the limited number and moderate quality of included studies, these findings should be interpreted with caution. High-quality RCTs are needed to confirm these results. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?ID=CRD420251025533, PROSPERO CRD420251025533.

title: Comorbidity Count Versus the Charlson Comorbidity Index in Predicting Hospital Stay After Hip Fracture in Older Adults: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Background and Objectives : Hip fracture in older adults is associated with high morbidity, and length of hospital stay is the simplest summary of the acute admission. We aimed to identify the clinical factors associated with prolonged hospital stay in older adults admitted with a hip fracture, and to test whether a weighted comorbidity index predicts stay better than a simple count. Materials and Methods : A retrospective cohort of 624 consecutive patients aged 65 years and older with a trochanteric or femoral neck fracture was studied. Length of stay (LOS) was strongly right-skewed (skewness 5.02) and was log-transformed; comparisons used Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis tests and Spearman correlations, with multivariable models fitted on 487 operated patients with complete data. Postoperative stay was analyzed as a secondary outcome because the preoperative interval forms part of the total stay. Results : Median stay was 10 days (IQR 8-13) and median wait for surgery was 4 days (IQR 2-6), with only 25.2% operated on within 48 h. In-hospital mortality was 5.3%. The number of comorbidities was the only patient characteristic consistently associated with stay (rho = 0.119, p = 0.003; 1.4% per comorbidity, p Conclusions : A simple count of active comorbidities was associated with LOS whereas the CCI was not, and the model containing the count fitted modestly better (adjusted R 2 0.385 vs. 0.365; index term non-significant). This hypothesis-generating finding suggests that the comorbidity count, which is available on admission, may serve as a pragmatic screening tool for selecting patients for comprehensive geriatric assessment; its use in place of the CCI would require validation in independent cohorts. The preoperative wait remains the dominant modifiable target, although its effect on total stay is largely structural.

title: Persistent Differences in Reported Inpatient Rehabilitation-Bed Capacity Across 27 European and OECD Countries.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Reported inpatient rehabilitation-bed stocks vary widely across countries, but their trajectories and relationship with population ageing are less clear. We examined convergence and associations with ageing in 27 European and OECD countries during 2000-2023. Methods: We combined Eurostat and OECD data into a 504-country-year panel. Analyses included sigma- and beta-convergence, the Phillips-Sul log-t test and exploratory club clustering. Monte Carlo checks used the actual panel dimensions. Mean-group, common-correlated-effects mean-group, and Driscoll-Kraay models examined associations between bed-capacity growth and changes in older-population shares. Results: Reported capacity ranged from 2.4 to 193.8 beds per 100,000 population in 2023. Panel-wide convergence was rejected, while beta-convergence estimates remained imprecise. Dispersion increased descriptively in the balanced core, but country-bootstrap intervals for its change and trend included zero. Associations between capacity growth and ageing showed no consistent positive pattern. Simulation results distinguished panel-wide testing from less stable club membership in short panels. Conclusions: Reported inpatient rehabilitation-bed capacity followed heterogeneous trajectories across the included countries. Population ageing alone did not explain capacity growth. These findings concern one component of rehabilitation provision and support joint monitoring of inpatient capacity, community services, workforce, and service use.

title: Integrated Rehabilitation, Airway, and Nutritional Nursing is Associated with Short-Term Outcomes in Critically Ill Patients: A Historical Controlled Before-After Study.
abstract: Background This study evaluated the association between an integrated rehabilitation, airway-management, and nutritional nursing protocol and short-term outcomes in critically ill patients. Methods This historical controlled before-after study included 101 adult ICU patients: 58 received conventional nursing and 43 received the integrated protocol. The primary outcome was pulmonary infection within 14 days or before ICU discharge, transfer, or death. Stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles, was used to balance baseline covariates. Weighted risk differences (RDs), risk ratios (RRs), and mean differences (MDs) were estimated with robust variance. Results After weighting, all baseline covariates had absolute standardized mean differences below 0.10. Pulmonary infection occurred in 14.1% of the intervention phase and 24.0% of the control phase after weighting (RD, -9.9 percentage points; 95% CI, -27.6 to 7.8; RR, 0.59; 95% CI, 0.21-1.66). The difference was not statistically significant. Exploratory analyses showed less gastrointestinal bleeding (RD, -16.0 percentage points; 95% CI, -25.1 to -6.9), higher SpO 2 (MD, 2.09%; 95% CI, 0.99-3.19), shorter mechanical ventilation duration (MD, -4.57 days; 95% CI, -5.84 to -3.31), and shorter ICU stay (MD, -7.34 days; 95% CI, -9.11 to -5.57) during the intervention phase. Conclusion The integrated protocol was associated with favorable secondary outcomes, but the reduction in the primary outcome was not statistically significant. Larger prospective studies are required.

title: Perioperative management and challenges of robotic-assisted surgery: a narrative review.
abstract: Over the past two decades, robotic surgical technology has become increasingly widespread worldwide. RAS (robotic-assisted surgery) has attracted surgeons across various specialties with its advantages of high precision, a shorter learning curve, and reduced postoperative pain, while also imposing new requirements on the entire surgical team, including anesthesiologists. The physiological changes and unique complications associated with RAS have brought major challenges for anesthesiologists, who should respond rapidly to patient responses throughout the entire procedure.This review focuses on the potential issues encountered in the perioperative management of RAS, as well as the application of RAS across several specialties and the specific intraoperative management challenges involved.

title: Preliminary Feasibility Implementation of Post-Decompressive Craniectomy 3D-Printed Externally Applied Cranial Orthosis (PEACO) During Inpatient Rehabilitation: A Retrospective Cohort Study Reporting Short-Term Tolerability and Patient/Caregiver-Reported Feedback.
abstract: A minimally monitored clinical protocol demonstrated preliminary short-term feasibility and tolerability: 18/23 (78.3%) fitted patients were confirmed compliant, with 18/20 (90%) respondent compliance and three patients of unknown status, without serious adverse events. Longer follow-up studies are needed to assess sustained compliance throughout the pre-cranioplasty period. Future research should standardise materials and outcome measures to inform clinical practice guidelines. Background/Objectives : 3D-printed externally applied cranial orthosis (PEACO) represents an emerging solution for temporary cranial protection, though evidence remains limited regarding real-world implementation using minimally monitored clinical protocols. Methods : Retrospective cohort study conducted at a 121-bed rehabilitation centre in Singapore (November 2022-November 2025). Adults >21 years, >3 weeks post-DC with healed wounds and available caregivers were included. PEACO devices were individually designed from CT stereotaxis scans using contralateral hemi-cranium mirroring and fabricated using Ultra-durable Resin. Rehabilitation therapists fitted devices using progressive wearing schedules. T0 outcomes (30 min post-fitting) included therapist-observed pain, redness, skin imprints, and pruritus. T1 outcomes (at least 2 weeks post-fitting) included wearing duration, cosmesis ratings (0-10 scale), compliance, and adverse events via digital surveys. Exploratory comparisons using descriptive analysis were performed to compare outcomes from 2021 ( n = 10) and 2025 ( n = 23) cohorts. Results : Twenty-three patients (14 males, median age 56.0 years) were fitted with PEACO at median 67 days post-DC, (13 traumatic brain injury, 10 stroke). At T0, primary reprinting for poor fit was required in 3/23 (13.0%), 18/23 (78.3%) fitted patients were confirmed compliant, 18/20 (90%) were compliant with responder feedback; 2/20 (10.0%) were non-compliant, with three patients of unknown status. At T0, 9/23 (39.1%) had therapist-observed mild, transient adverse events, with no reported wound dehiscence. At T1, among 18 respondents: 16/18 (88.9%) wore PEACO ≤4 h/day, 7/18 (38.9%) reported self-limiting discomfort or transient skin changes at T1, median cosmesis rating was 6.0/10. At T1 assessment, no falls with head impact occurred. Clinical Trials Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07122752.

title: Spatiotemporal Analysis of Hospitalisations and Mortality From Gynaecological Cancers in Ecuador, 2015-2024.
abstract: Purpose To analyse the spatiotemporal patterns of hospitalisations and mortality due to gynaecological cancers in Ecuador (2015-2024), identify provincial geographic disparities, and examine the association between healthcare infrastructure and clustering patterns. Methods This population-based ecological study used INEC hospital discharge and general death records for women with gynaecological cancers (ICD-10: C51-C57) in Ecuador from 2015 to 2024. Age-standardised rates per 100,000 women were calculated by year, cause, age group, and province of residence. K-means clustering was applied separately to hospitalisation and mortality rates to identify provinces with similar temporal trajectories. Global and local Moran's I assessed spatial autocorrelation, and Spearman correlations and Kruskal-Wallis tests examined associations with healthcare infrastructure. Results Between 2015 and 2024, 39,492 hospitalisations and 11,410 deaths were recorded. Cervical cancer accounted for 45.4% of hospitalisations and 42.2% of deaths, followed by ovarian cancer (32.6% and 22.0%). Hospitalisations declined markedly in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Trajectory-based k-means identified three clusters for each outcome. The highest hospitalisation rates were concentrated in the southern provinces, with significant global spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I = 0.48-0.64, all p ≤ 0.002) and a persistent High-High spatial cluster, while the highest mortality occurred in the northern and central Sierra and the Amazon, without consistent spatial autocorrelation. Nine provinces had high mortality, low hospitalisation, and lower bed density (224.9 vs 260.1 per 100,000 women). Bed density was not significantly correlated with hospitalisation (rho = 0.35, p = 0.097) or mortality (rho = -0.27, p = 0.205); bed density did not differ across mortality clusters (p = 0.52). Conclusion The mismatch between hospitalisation and mortality clustering patterns, together with lower healthcare infrastructure in high-mortality provinces, suggests that unequal access to timely care may contribute to excess mortality, although these associations were not statistically significant.

title: Bacterial culture positivity in placental basal plate tissue and associated factors among women with spontaneous preterm births at Mubende Regional Referral Hospital, Uganda: A cross-sectional study.
abstract: Aerobic bacterial culture positivity in placental basal plate tissue and its associated maternal factors remain poorly described in Uganda. This study estimated the prevalence of culture positivity and identified associated factors among women with spontaneous preterm births at Mubende Regional Referral Hospital. We conducted a hospital-based analytical cross-sectional study among 383 women between 15 May and 15 September 2025. Placental basal plate tissue specimens were collected aseptically immediately after delivery and processed for aerobic bacterial culture. Sociodemographic, obstetric and clinical data were obtained using interviewer-administered questionnaires and medical record review. Associations were examined using multivariable logistic regression and reported as adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Positive cultures were identified in 159 women, giving a prevalence of 41.5% (95% CI: 36.5-46.6). Culture positivity was associated with fever (aOR = 11.32, 95% CI: 4.89-26.19), abdominal pain or uterine tenderness (aOR = 9.13, 95% CI: 4.37-19.08), membrane rupture lasting more than 24 hours (aOR = 5.93, 95% CI: 2.08-16.89), HIV infection (aOR = 4.23, 95% CI: 1.21-14.74), urinary tract infection during pregnancy (aOR = 4.20, 95% CI: 2.13-8.27), foul-smelling vaginal discharge (aOR = 3.22, 95% CI: 1.48-6.97), traditional herb use (aOR = 2.19, 95% CI: 1.16-4.13) and no formal education (aOR = 6.97, 95% CI: 1.50-32.46). Earlier gestational age, prolonged labour and primary education were also associated with culture positivity. Positive aerobic placental basal plate cultures were common in this population. These findings support improved recognition and management of maternal infection during antenatal and intrapartum care. However, culture positivity alone cannot distinguish invasive infection from colonization or contamination, and prospective studies are needed to clarify temporal and causal relationships.

title: Development and preliminary validation of a patient-report experience measure of acute oncology: The PREMAC study.
abstract: Background Patients with cancer often experience oncological emergencies requiring immediate care, and the quality of acute oncology (AO) care varies between providers. Patient-reported experience measures (PREMs) are a key tool for quality improvement, but none currently exists for AO. This study developed a prototype PREM, the Patient-Reported Experience Measure for Acute OnCology (PREMAC), and conducted preliminary single-site psychometric testing. Materials and methods A quality assessment framework guided development across three stages. Stage 1 generated a conceptual framework of accessing AO services from a scoping review and interviews with patients and health professionals. Stage 2 developed a prototype questionnaire, with content validity assessed by a Service User Reference Panel (SURP) and face validity tested through cognitive interviews. Stage 3 tested acceptability, feasibility, structural validity and internal consistency at one tertiary cancer centre in southern England. Results Data integration identified ten domains, in the chronological order patients accessing AO experience them: reasons for accessing AO; patient preparedness; accessibility of care; the care environment; competence of care; communication and decision-making; compassionate care; the carer's role; patient anxiety; and service issues including discharge. The 46-item prototype was completed by 171 respondents. Exploratory factor analysis of 18 four-category ordinal items, using polychoric correlations with minimum residual extraction and oblimin rotation (n = 121 complete cases), supported three provisional domains: information, communication, involvement and perceived care quality (α = 0.935); care environment, dignity, trust and safety (α = 0.711); and discharge information and preparedness (α = 0.704). Conclusion PREMAC is the first PREM developed specifically for AO. Preliminary testing indicates the prototype is acceptable and feasible, with early evidence of internal coherence across three provisional domains at a single site. The domain structure and item allocations remain provisional; no total score is recommended. Multisite validation is required before PREMAC could support service comparison or benchmarking.

title: Defensive medicine and advanced imaging overuse in emergency departments: A focused review of imaging stewardship and overcrowding.
abstract: Emergency departments (EDs) are encountering a significant increase in patient volumes, compounded by greater reliance on advanced radiological imaging modalities. This trend is most evident for computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging, with expanding use of emergency ultrasonography in selected pathways. These modalities are essential for time-sensitive diagnosis, triage, and risk stratification. Under diagnostic uncertainty, time pressure, crowding, and medico-legal concern, imaging may exceed evidence-based thresholds. Imaging overuse, also described as overutilization, has been associated with radiology bottlenecks, longer ED turnaround times, higher healthcare costs, and worse overcrowding. It may also expose patients to radiation, contrast-related risks, incidental findings, downstream testing, overdiagnosis, and avoidable financial burden. Excessive imaging demand further increases the workload of radiologists and emergency physicians and may contribute to reporting delays, cognitive fatigue, and burnout. This focused narrative review synthesizes the clinical, behavioral, and system-level drivers of overuse of advanced imaging in EDs, and proposes a conceptual reciprocal-pressure framework linking crowding, diagnostic uncertainty, defensive ordering, and radiology bottlenecks. It also discusses mitigation strategies, including clinical decision rules, computerized clinical decision support, Choosing Wisely initiatives, artificial intelligence-supported tools, shared decision-making, audit and feedback, and multidisciplinary imaging stewardship. The evidence supporting these strategies is heterogeneous, and their reported effects are not equivalent. The aim is to support safer, more efficient, and patient-centered diagnostic workflows in emergency care.

title: In-hospital events and resource utilization associated with percutaneous-based vs. open lumbar fusion, stratified by admission status: a national inpatient sample analysis.
abstract: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) may be associated with a more favorable short-term inpatient profile after lumbar fusion, but whether these associations differ by admission status remains unclear. In this retrospective observational analysis of repeated cross-sectional 2016-2022 National Inpatient Sample (NIS) discharge data, hospitalizations of adults undergoing lumbar fusion were identified and stratified as elective or non-elective. The exposure was defined by the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Procedure Coding System-coded approach as percutaneous-based (percutaneous/percutaneous-endoscopic) vs. open fusion. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression accounted for the NIS's complex design and adjusted for demographics, hospital characteristics, fusion extent, indication/case-mix, and individual Elixhauser comorbidities; formal approach-by-admission interactions were tested. A total of 174,704 hospitalizations met the inclusion criteria. In elective admissions, percutaneous-based fusion was associated with lower odds of blood product transfusion (aOR 0.448, 95% CI 0.311-0.644), acute posthemorrhagic anemia (aOR 0.591, 95% CI 0.475-0.736), and prolonged length of stay (aOR 0.774, 95% CI 0.656-0.914). In non-elective admissions, it was associated with lower odds of acute posthemorrhagic anemia (aOR 0.669, 95% CI 0.491-0.912) and non-home discharge (aOR 0.666, 95% CI 0.502-0.883). Significant approach-by-admission interactions were observed for blood product transfusion ( P = 0.037) and non-home discharge ( P = 0.022). These findings indicate that the short-term association profile of percutaneous-based vs. open lumbar fusion differs across admission settings and specific in-hospital measures.

title: Early sitting within 72 hours in the intensive care unit and post-intensive care outcomes: a multicenter cohort study.
abstract: Background and purpose Early mobilization is recommended in the intensive care unit (ICU), yet clinically meaningful early milestones remain unclear. We investigated whether achievement of sitting within 72 h of ICU admission was associated with post-intensive care outcomes among ICU survivors who underwent rehabilitation. Methods In this multicenter observational cohort study, we included mechanically ventilated adult ICU survivors who underwent rehabilitation. Early sitting was defined as achievement of sitting at the bedside within 72 h after ICU admission. The primary outcome was death or functional decline at 3 months after hospital discharge, assessed using the Kihon Checklist. Prespecified secondary and exploratory outcomes included domain-specific impairments (physical, cognitive, and depressive), hospital readmission, and a composite of readmission or death within 3 months. Overlap propensity score weighting was used to balance baseline covariates. Multiple prespecified sensitivity analyses (48-h alternative definition, landmark analysis, exclusion of never-sitters, adjustment for Day-3 clinical status and rehabilitation dose) and Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) multiplicity adjustment were performed. Results Among 423 patients, 173 achieved early sitting (≤72 h) and 250 did not. After overlap weighting, baseline characteristics were balanced. Early sitting was not associated with the primary outcome (adjusted risk ratio [aRR] 0.94, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.80-1.09; p = 0.401). In exploratory analyses, early sitting was associated with a lower risk of cognitive domain impairment or death (aRR 0.80, 95% CI 0.67-0.97; p = 0.024; BH-adjusted p = 0.096) and of readmission or death (aRR 0.53, 95% CI 0.32-0.88; p = 0.014; BH-adjusted p = 0.027). No individual KCL item showed a clear association after weighting, and the cognitive association was not observed under a stricter definition. Associations with readmission-related outcomes were attenuated after adjustment for Day-3 clinical status. Conclusion Achieving sitting within 72 h of ICU admission was not associated with death or functional decline at 3 months. The exploratory associations with cognitive-functional impairment and readmission-related outcomes may reflect the selection of clinically stable patients for early sitting rather than an effect of sitting itself. These findings support the feasibility of early sitting in clinically stable patients but do not establish early sitting as a therapeutic target; randomized trials are needed.

title: Elective primary total hip arthroplasty in rheumatoid arthritis versus osteoarthritis: in-hospital outcomes from the national inpatient sample, 2016-2021.
journal: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery
abstract: Background Whether coded rheumatoid arthritis (RA) among patients undergoing elective total hip arthroplasty (THA) is associated with excess short-term inpatient morbidity in contemporary U.S. practice remains uncertain. Methods We performed a retrospective cohort study using the National Inpatient Sample (2016-2021). Adults undergoing elective primary THA were identified using ICD-10-CM/PCS codes. The exposure cohort included admissions with coded RA in any diagnosis position. The comparator cohort included admissions with narrow primary hip osteoarthritis (OA) as the principal diagnosis and no RA. Propensity scores were estimated from demographic, socioeconomic, hospital, and comorbidity variables. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) with survey weighting was used for the primary analysis, followed by doubly adjusted regression models that included age and all variables with persistent post-weighting imbalance greater than 0.10 (female sex, osteoporosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic anemia, depression, and race). Additional sensitivity analyses included stricter weight truncation, a restriction analysis, conventional multivariable modeling, and sex-stratified analyses addressing residual sex imbalance. Results A total of 274,582 admissions met eligibility criteria; 274,539 were included in the final analytic cohort after exclusion of 43 records with missing or invalid propensity-weight inputs. The analytic cohort included 7,264 RA admissions and 267,275 OA admissions. In the primary weighted analysis, RA was associated with higher odds of acute blood loss anemia (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.23-1.38), red blood cell transfusion (OR 1.40, 95% CI 1.23-1.60), acute kidney injury (OR 1.47, 95% CI 1.26-1.71), non-home discharge (OR 1.27, 95% CI 1.19-1.36), and a composite hematologic/renal in-hospital complication (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.24-1.39).RA was also associated with slightly longer length of stay (+ 0.14 days, 95% CI + 0.10 to + 0.19) and modestly higher total hospital charges (+$1,018, 95% CI +$89 to +$1,947). Findings were directionally consistent across sensitivity analyses, including stricter weight truncation, restriction to admissions with principal OA plus concomitant RA, and sex-stratified analyses. Conclusions In this contemporary national THA cohort, coded RA was associated with a small but consistent increase in in-hospital complication and resource-utilization burden compared with OA. These findings should be interpreted as adjusted associations rather than causal effects, and the modest effect sizes should not be overstated. They may provide context for perioperative risk assessment and discharge planning among patients with coded RA undergoing elective THA.

title: Evaluation of collection efficiency and safety of a precise distention fluid collection device compared to traditional devices in hysteroscopic surgery.
abstract: Objective This study aims to validate the effectiveness of this device in collecting distension fluid during hysteroscopic surgery, providing a more reliable tool for monitoring fluid outflow. Methods A total of 164 patients scheduled for elective hysteroscopy were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the precision collection group or the control group. The precision collection group utilized a precision distension fluid collection device for hysteroscopic distension fluid collection, while the control group used a conventional collection device. The primary outcome was the hysteroscopic distension fluid collection rate. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of adverse events, operating room cleaning time, and satisfaction levels of surgeons, nurses, and operating room support staff. Results There were no significant differences in baseline patient characteristics or surgical types between the two groups. Compared to the conventional fluid collection device, the precision distension fluid collection device significantly improved the hysteroscopic distension fluid collection rate (95% vs. 48%, P P Conclusion The precision distension fluid collection device effectively enhances the collection rate of hysteroscopic distension fluid, reduces risks associated with improper fluid management, shortens operating room turnover time, and improves the satisfaction of the surgical team. Clinical trial registration https://www.chictr.org.cn, identifier ChiCTR2500101460.

title: Integrating emergency medical services and hospital surge capacity for mass-gathering preparedness: a structured narrative review
Palliative-Oriented Referral and Advanced Vulnerability in Very Old Patients Hospitalised for Acute Heart Failure.
Delayed Presentation of a Traumatic Retroperitoneal Hematoma With Low-Grade Renal Injury After a Low-Speed Electric Scooter Handlebar Impact in a Child: A Case Report.
abstract: Electric scooters (e-scooters) are an increasingly common cause of injury in children, but their capacity to cause occult intra-abdominal injury is under-recognized. We report a seven-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes mellitus who presented to the pediatric emergency department seven days after a witnessed low-speed fall from an electric scooter with a direct handlebar impact to the right abdomen. He was initially asymptomatic, developed right-sided abdominal pain on the second day after injury, and became progressively pale. On arrival, he was hemodynamically stable, with right upper quadrant tenderness and fullness, no peritonism, and no external signs of injury. Bedside sonography showed no free intraperitoneal fluid, but marked anemia prompted contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT), which demonstrated a large right retroperitoneal hematoma extending from the subhepatic region into the right hemipelvis, a right perinephric hematoma, and no active contrast extravasation. Targeted renal Doppler ultrasonography identified a small inferior-pole cortical laceration that was not discernible on computed tomography, and the renal injury was classified as low grade. He received a single red blood cell transfusion, was managed nonoperatively in a pediatric high-dependency unit, and was discharged in stable condition on day 5. This case shows that a low-speed handlebar impact without external signs can cause major retroperitoneal bleeding with a delayed presentation, that unexplained anemia after blunt abdominal trauma warrants cross-sectional imaging despite normal vital signs and negative bedside sonography, and that large retroperitoneal hematomas can be managed nonoperatively in stable children without active extravasation.

title: Clinical, Economic, and System-Level Outcomes of Bariatric Surgery in Adults: Protocol for a Systematic Review.
abstract: Background Obesity affects approximately 880 million adults worldwide and carries substantial health, economic, and social consequences. Although bariatric surgery achieves sustained weight loss and metabolic improvement, existing systematic reviews largely predate 2020 and rarely integrate clinical, economic, and system-level perspectives within a single synthesis. Objective This study aims to identify, critically appraise, and synthesize evidence published between 2020 and 2025 on the clinical effectiveness and economic impact of bariatric surgery in adults with obesity. A secondary, exploratory objective is to address system-level resource utilization, specifically length of stay, preoperative pathway duration, and outpatient care burden. Methods This protocol follows the PRISMA-P (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols) 2015 guidance and is registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO: CRD420261351022). Eligible studies will enroll adults aged 18 years or older with obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m 2 ) undergoing any primary bariatric procedure, including Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB), sleeve gastrectomy (SG), one-anastomosis gastric bypass (OAGB), adjustable gastric banding (LAGB), and biliopancreatic diversion with or without duodenal switch (BPD±DS); revisional procedures are excluded as the index intervention. Eligible designs include randomized controlled trials, cohort, case-control, cross-sectional, and economic evaluation studies published in English. MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science will be searched using predefined, database-tailored strategies; records will be managed in Zotero (Corporation for Digital Scholarship). A single primary reviewer will perform screening, extraction, and risk-of-bias (RoB) assessment, with at least 20% independently duplicated by a second reviewer, weighted toward full-text and included studies. RoB will be assessed with RoB 2 and ROBINS-I (Risk of Bias in Nonrandomized Studies of Interventions); economic evaluations will be appraised for completeness of reporting with the CHEERS (Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards) 2022 statement and for methodological quality with the CHEC (Consensus on Health Economic Criteria) checklist. The primary synthesis will be narrative; meta-analysis will be considered only where prespecified comparability criteria are met. Certainty of evidence will be rated using GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation). Results This protocol describes a review that is currently in progress. Registration with PROSPERO was completed on April 15, 2026, and database searches were run on August 1, 2026, identifying 9400 records. Title-and-abstract screening is scheduled to begin on August 15, 2026. Data extraction and synthesis are expected to be completed by the end of 2026, with publication of the completed review anticipated in the first half of 2027. Conclusions This protocol provides a transparent and reproducible methodology for an integrated, contemporary synthesis of the clinical, economic, and system-level outcomes of bariatric surgery in adults. The findings are intended to inform health policy, resource planning, and future research priorities.

title: A pilot study investigating the clinical and financial impact of a pharmacist discharge service in a hospital setting.
journal: European journal of hospital pharmacy : science and practice

title: Complications and Hospital Resource Utilization Associated with ECMO in COVID-19 ARDS with Acute Kidney Injury: Insights from United States National Inpatient Sample, 2020-2022.
abstract: Background Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common complication of COVID-19-associated acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), yet the impact of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) on outcomes in this high-risk population remains unclear. Methods We performed a retrospective, survey-weighted study using the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) database from 2020-2022 to compare outcomes among adults hospitalized with COVID-19-associated ARDS and AKI managed with invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) alone versus IMV and ECMO. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality, while secondary outcomes included renal replacement therapy (RRT), complications, hospital length of stay (LOS), and healthcare utilization. Results Among 198,395 hospitalizations with COVID-19 ARDS complicated by AKI, 4730 received IMV and ECMO. ECMO use was not associated with statistically significantly lower adjusted in-hospital mortality (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.96, 95% CI 0.81-1.12). However, ECMO was associated with greater odds of RRT, intracranial hemorrhage, disseminated intravascular coagulation, cardiogenic shock, vasopressor use, tracheostomy, acute liver failure, deep vein thrombosis, ischemic stroke and ICU-acquired weakness. ECMO was also associated with longer LOS and higher hospitalization charges. Conclusions Among hospitalizations with COVID-19-associated ARDS and AKI, ECMO was not associated with statistically significantly lower adjusted in-hospital mortality but was associated with markedly higher complication burden, longer hospitalization, and substantially greater healthcare resource utilization.

title: Different rehabilitation destinations: non-clinical factors associated with inpatient rehabilitation versus skilled nursing placement.
abstract: Purpose Examine clinical and non-clinical factors associated with post-acute rehabilitation placement after acute ischemic stroke. Methods 236 adults hospitalized with acute ischemic stroke; independent and community-dwelling before stroke; and discharged to an inpatient rehabilitation facility (IRF; n = 171) or skilled nursing facility (SNF; n = 65). Clinical factors included NIHSS, Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), length of stay (LOS), AM-PAC "6-Clicks," and neglect. Non-clinical factors included demographics and contextual characteristics. Logistic regression was used for associations with discharge location. Results Individuals discharged to IRFs were younger, more likely to cohabitate, and had shorter LOS. Functional status (AM-PAC) and CCI did not differ significantly between groups despite differences in discharge destination. In univariable analyses, younger age, cohabitating marital status, living with family, available assistance, shorter LOS, private insurance, and higher NIHSS were associated with greater odds of IRF discharge. In the multivariable analysis, increasing age (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.91-0.98) and greater comorbidity burden (CCI: OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.73-0.98) were associated with lower odds of IRF discharge. Marital status was not associated with discharge destination after adjustment. Conclusions Among previously independent stroke survivors, discharged to an IRF or SNF increasing age and greater comorbidity burden were associated with lower odds of IRF placement after adjustment. NIHSS and AM-PAC Daily Activities scores were not associated with placement in the adjusted analysis.

title: Implementing an EHR-Integrated Quality and Safety Dashboard to Improve Inpatient Safety: Clinical Usage and Preliminary Outcomes
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Data driven tools are increasingly used to support patient safety and quality improvement, yet evidence on the impact of integrated quality and safety dashboards remains limited. Methods We conducted a pre–post implementation study using interrupted time series analysis to evaluate the impact of an EHR-integrated quality and safety dashboard on clinical processes and patient outcomes, among three general medicine units at a 171-bed community teaching hospital. All adult patients admitted during seven-month pre- and post-implementation periods were included. The primary outcome was the proportion of hospitalizations with at least one adverse event. Secondary and exploratory outcomes included hospital-acquired conditions, adherence to safety-related process measures, and dashboard utilization. Results A total of 9,023 hospitalizations were included (4,640 pre-implementation; 4,383 post - implementation). The proportion of hospitalizations with at least one adverse event was similar pre-implementation (23.15%; 95% CI, 20.96–25.29) and post-implementation (22.97%; 95% CI, 20.86–25.23). CLABSI per 100 patient-days was reduced (aOR 0.47, 95% CI [0.37-0.60]); and exploratory analyses demonstrated decreases in slope for post-discharge venous thromboembolism (aOR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.48–0.91; p =0.01) and hospital-acquired pressure injury (aOR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.48–1.00; p =0.05). Several process measures improved, including code status confirmation, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, delirium screening, chlorhexidine bathing, and fall precautions. Conclusions Implementation of an EHR-integrated quality and safety dashboard was associated with meaningful improvements in multiple care processes and CLABSI but not overall adverse events. These findings highlight the potential of workflow-integrated dashboards to support frontline quality improvement, while underscoring the need for additional measures to improve clinical outcomes.

title: Specialist Palliative Care Service Involvement and Prognostic Factors in Patients Presenting With Acute Limb Ischaemia to Waikato Hospital, Hamilton, New Zealand: A Retrospective Review.
abstract: Background There is significant morbidity and mortality associated with acute limb ischaemia (ALI) and prognostication is complex. Current literature reports underutilisation of specialist palliative care (SPC) and lack of prognostic indicators to guide decision-making and referral. Objective/aim The aim of this study is to review and analyse demographic, clinical and mortality data for a cohort of ALI patients to determine potential prognostic indicators, SPC referral patterns and SPC services received. Method Retrospective clinical record reviews for a cohort of ALI patients referred to the Waikato Hospital Vascular Surgery team in a specified time period. This included laboratory, imaging and death documentation and functional status at baseline and ALI diagnosis. Results One hundred fifty-five ALI patients were identified of whom 140 met the inclusion criteria. A 30-day mortality was 19% and 1-year mortality was 31% for the study cohort. Lactate > 2.2 mmol//L, albumin Conclusion The four independent predictors of mortality could be used to identify ALI patients with a poor prognosis, encourage earlier referral for SPC, support appropriate symptom management and enable discussions on patient priorities.

title: ISO 9001 and JCI preparedness as drivers of quality improvement at a tertiary cardiac care center: a 5-year analysis from Pakistan.
journal: International journal for quality in health care : journal of the International Society for Quality in Health Care
abstract: Background External quality frameworks such as ISO 9001 certification lay the foundation for healthcare quality, patient safety, and operational efficiency, but sustained improvement depends on leadership, a culture of safety, and systems that translate assurance into ongoing learning. Evidence on this transition from low- and middle-income countries, particularly in specialized cardiac care, remains limited. Methods A retrospective longitudinal analysis of quality assurance data from January 2020 to December 2025 was conducted at the Peshawar Institute of Cardiology (PIC-MTI), Pakistan. Independent-samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and Difference-in-Differences (DiD) modeling were applied, with three regional hospitals of similar bed capacity and patient volume serving as a comparison group. Results Following ISO 9001 certification (February 2022), monthly mortality within 48 h declined from 2.8% (SD ± 0.4%) to 1.9% (SD ± 0.3%) (t = 3.21, df = 58, P = .004). Hospital-acquired infections (HAIs) fell from 3.2% to 2.0% (t = 4.15, P = .002), reaching 1.3% by 2025, with zero CLABSIs recorded in the final quarter following the mid-period intensification of the infection-control bundle. Mean length of stay decreased from 6.2 to 4.7 days [ANOVA: F(2,57) = 8.76, P Conclusions ISO 9001 certification, undertaken alongside deliberate investment in leadership, a culture of safety, and structured use of data, is associated with sustained improvements in clinical outcomes and operational efficiency at a resource-limited cardiac care center that has not yet pursued formal Joint Commission International (JCI) accreditation but is using JCI's standards, as one example of an internationally recognized framework, to guide its preparation. The pattern observed here suggests that a learning quality management system, and not any single certificate or accreditation status, is what converts external standards into measurable gains, offering a replicable model for institutions considering how to move from quality assurance toward continual quality improvement.

title: Polypharmacy and Activities of Daily Living in Older Patients Undergoing Cerebrovascular Rehabilitation: An Observational Study Using Japanese Real-World Data.
An Australian Narrative Review of Adoptive Cellular Therapies in Malignancy: Expanding Indications, Referral Pathways and Safety Beyond Specialist Centres.
abstract: Adoptive cellular therapies (ACT), including tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL), T-cell receptor-engineered T (TCR-T) cell and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapies, represent an evolving class of immunotherapies with established efficacy in selected haematological malignancies and emerging applications in solid tumours. Additional platforms under investigation include virus-specific T cells, tumour-associated antigen-specific T cells, natural killer (NK) cell therapies and dendritic cell-based therapies. The therapeutic scope of ACT is expanding beyond oncology into autoimmune and fibrotic diseases, infectious diseases and inherited metabolic and immune disorders, highlighting the broad potential of cellular immunotherapy platforms. In solid tumours, efficacy remains limited by tumour antigen heterogeneity, immunosuppressive tumour micro-environment and impaired immune cell trafficking and persistence. These barriers are driving development of next-generation cellular products and combination strategies. Characteristic immune-mediated toxicities, particularly cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), remain important considerations. Although potentially severe, these toxicities are generally manageable with early recognition, multidisciplinary care and prompt specialist intervention. As ACT indications expand in Australia, clinician familiarity with indications, mechanisms of action and toxicity profiles is essential to support informed patient discussions, appropriate patient selection, timely referral and prompt toxicity recognition and management. Non-oncology specialists have an important role in shared care, including patient identification, referral coordination, monitoring for delayed or late toxicities and provision of ongoing survivorship and supportive care. Achieving equitable national access to ACT will require streamlined health technology assessment processes, coordinated reimbursement and delivery funding models and structured referral networks with cross-institutional collaboration to support the specialised infrastructure required for their delivery.

title: Diagnostic and therapy gaps in BPPV care: a retrospective analysis and feasibility evaluation across a London NHS trust.
abstract: Background Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is the most prevalent cause of peripheral dizziness, yet it remains poorly assessed and treated in acute settings. Despite the availability of validated bedside tools such as the Dix-Hallpike test (DHT) and canal repositioning manoeuvres (CRM) such as the Epley, diagnostic variability is high, neuroimaging is overused, and vestibular suppressants are frequently prescribed. This two-part evaluation characterised BPPV assessment and management across a London NHS Trust and assessed the feasibility of incorporating DHT into an existing AHP-led falls pathway within the emergency department (ED). Methods A two-part evaluation was conducted across a large London NHS teaching hospital. Part 1 comprised a retrospective review of electronic patient records to characterise current BPPV assessment and management practices and identify potential service gaps. Part 2 was a prospective feasibility study evaluating the incorporation of AHP-led DHT screening into routine falls assessments for patients aged ≥65 years presenting to the ED. Results Part 1 identified 128 cases (mean age 63.4 years; 61.7% female). BPPV was the most common discharge diagnosis, 45.3% (95% CI 37.0-53.9%), yet full assessment and treatment were documented in only 14.8% of cases (95% CI 9.7-22.0%). Vestibular suppressants were prescribed in 43.8%, neuroimaging performed in 71.9 and 18.8% left without a definitive diagnosis. Readmission for dizziness within three months occurred in 13.3% (95% CI 8.5-20.2%). Part 2 included 102 patients, 79 with complete records (mean age 84.6 years; 54% female). DHT was completed in 62% (63/102 attempts; 95% CI 52.1-70.6%); BPPV was identified in 8% (95% CI 4.0-14.7%) and all received CRM. No dizziness-related readmissions occurred at three months. Conclusion This evaluation identifies consistent gaps in acute BPPV assessment and management, including overuse of neuroimaging and vestibular suppressants alongside underutilisation of validated bedside tools. Physiotherapy led DHT screening is feasible in a busy ED setting, even in older adults with multiple comorbidities, and the absence of readmissions in this small feasibility cohort is an encouraging finding that warrants evaluation in a larger, controlled cohort.

title: Evaluating the Efficacy of Comprehensive Nursing Care in Improving the Well-Being of Patients With Colon Cancer Who Developed Postoperative Sleep Disorders.
abstract: Background This study aimed to investigate the effect of comprehensive nursing care on the psychological state and related indicators of patients with postoperative sleep disorders after colon cancer surgery. Methods We retrospectively selected 121 patients with sleep disorders who underwent colon cancer resection in our hospital between January 2021 and December 2023. After 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM), 52 patients were included in the routine nursing group and 52 in the comprehensive nursing group. Comprehensive nursing care, as documented in medical records, included psychological nursing, pain management, rehabilitation guidance and social support care. Results Data extracted from medical records and follow-up files showed that the comprehensive nursing group had greater reduction in Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS) and Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) scores after surgery than the routine nursing group ( p p p = 0.080). Improvements in all domains of the Short-Form 36 (SF-36) Health Survey in the comprehensive nursing group were greater than the routine nursing group ( p p Conclusions Comprehensive nursing care is a significant correlated between improved psychological state, rehabilitation-related indicators, quality of life and sleep quality in patients with postoperative sleep disorders after colon cancer surgery.

title: Acceptability and feasibility of the Home Support Needs Assessment in a forensic mental health service: An initial study.
abstract: Introduction Identifying and addressing the support needs of forensic mental health patients in daily life occupations is critical yet complex due to the health comorbidities and environmental restrictions impacting their participation. Occupational therapists support forensic patient recovery by facilitating their performance in daily life occupations required at home and in the community. Standardised assessments of daily living are important for guiding interventions. The Home Support Needs Assessment (HSNA) is a standardised measure identifying unmet support needs in daily life occupations. The aim of this study was to evaluate its initial acceptability and feasibility for occupational therapists' use in a forensic mental health setting. Methods An exploratory convergent, parallel mixed-methods design was used. Semi-structured interviews with five forensic occupational therapists explored their perspectives about using the HSNA in practice. Interview transcripts were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. HSNA data were extracted from 13 patient medical records and summarised using descriptive statistics. Consumer and community involvement There was no consumer and community involvement in this research as the focus of the study was on occupational therapists. Findings Three overarching themes were generated: value of the assessment, informed care planning, and applicability to the environment. The HSNA was found to structure observations, facilitate discussions about daily life occupations, and clarify ongoing support needs. An over-support of some needs emerged as a unique factor of the forensic mental health environment. Some items were viewed as not applicable to the setting. Conclusion The HSNA highlighted that the safety focus of the secure environment inadvertently limited opportunities for patients' involvement in daily life occupations. Acceptability was associated with enabling holistic occupational assessment. Further tailored training may increase overall implementability.

title: Blood Management Strategies in Placenta Accreta Spectrum.
abstract: Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) presents a major challenge in obstetric care because attempted placental separation may result in rapid and life-threatening hemorrhage. As PAS is often suspected before delivery, there is an opportunity to identify correctable risks and prepare for anticipated blood loss. This narrative review examines blood-management strategies throughout the antenatal, intraoperative, and postoperative periods. A targeted narrative search of PubMed and PubMed Central, supplemented by searches of journal and publisher websites, was conducted for literature available through September 2026. Antenatal management focuses on identifying and treating maternal anemia, referring patients to experienced centers, and developing a multidisciplinary delivery plan. Perioperative preparation includes coordination with the transfusion service, timely access to appropriate blood components, clear criteria for activating a major obstetric hemorrhage protocol, and defined responsibilities for each team member. Blood-product preparation should be individualized according to the severity suggested by prenatal imaging and the anticipated anatomical extent of placental invasion, ranging from suspected accreta to increta or percreta. Key intraoperative blood-conservation measures include intraoperative cell salvage and timely administration of tranexamic acid when clinically indicated, particularly during significant hemorrhage. Viscoelastic hemostatic testing, fibrinogen-directed therapy, and selected interventional radiology procedures may also contribute to individualized management. However, evidence supporting these interventions remains inconsistent and is frequently derived from observational studies, expert consensus, or broader obstetric hemorrhage populations rather than PAS-specific randomized trials. Consequently, blood-management plans should reflect the anticipated severity of PAS, the patient's clinical condition, and the expertise and resources available at the treating institution. A structured and individualized approach linking antenatal optimization, multidisciplinary preparation, timely hemorrhage control, and postoperative surveillance may support safer and more efficient care for patients with PAS.

title: Hospital Transfer Decision-Making for Residents with Dementia in Long-Term Care: A Qualitative Study of Interprofessional Perspectives.
abstract: Background : Hospital transfers of residents with dementia may provide them with access to acute diagnosis and treatment but also disrupt their continuity of care, which is essential for residents' stability, safety, and quality of care. The aim of this study was to examine how transfer decisions are produced within the organizational context of long-term dementia care and how they may affect continuity of care. Methods : A qualitative descriptive design was used, supplemented by retrospective referral data. The study was conducted in a 200-bed dementia-specialist long-term care facility. Referral records over three years were reviewed to describe transfer patterns, reasons, and outcomes. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 nurses and 2 physicians. Referral data were analyzed descriptively, and interviews were analyzed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis (RTA). Results : A total of 578 referrals to hospital emergency departments were identified; 34.9% resulted in hospitalization. Three themes were identified: (1) From recognition to authorization, describing interprofessional hierarchy in referral decision-making; (2) When uncertainty becomes risk, describing how limited diagnostic and treatment capacity shifted decisions toward transfer; and (3) Protecting continuity, describing staff concerns about the disruptive effects of transfer. Overall, decisions were shaped by clinical uncertainty, organizational conditions, and continuity-of-care concerns. Conclusions : Transfer decisions for residents with dementia are context-dependent organizational judgments, not solely responses to acute clinical deterioration. Strengthening institutional capacity, decision-support tools, staff training, and advance care planning may help preserve continuity of care, reduce avoidable disruption, and improve resident safety and quality of care.

title: Effects of Adding Incentive Spirometry to Hospital-Based Cardiovascular Rehabilitation on Pulmonary Complications, Hospital Length of Stay, and Clinical-Functional Recovery After Cardiac Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
journal: Physiotherapy research international : the journal for researchers and clinicians in physical therapy
abstract: Background and purpose This study investigated the effects of combining incentive spirometry with cardiac rehabilitation compared with cardiac rehabilitation alone on postoperative pulmonary complications, clinical-functional recovery, and hospital length of stay in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. Methods Randomized controlled trial was conducted from May 2019 to October 2023 in two hospitals, including 46 inpatients undergoing cardiac surgery. Participants were assigned to incentive spirometry plus cardiac rehabilitation or cardiac rehabilitation alone. Both interventions were performed twice daily; spirometry used a volume-oriented device, and rehabilitation followed a seven-step protocol (2-4 METs). Outcomes included postoperative pulmonary complications, functional capacity (6-min walk test), handgrip strength, respiratory muscle function, and length of hospital stay. Results The incentive spirometry associated with cardiac rehabilitation group had a longer extracorporeal circulation time (98 ± 26 min) than the cardiac rehabilitation group (76 ± 1; p = 0.008). Both groups showed a postoperative decline in respiratory muscle strength, and walking distance (MD: -64.37 m; 95% CI: [-24.1; -104.6]; d = 0.71), with no difference in postoperative pulmonary complications and handgrip strength. The incentive spirometry associated with cardiac rehabilitation group did not significantly differ on postoperative hospital stay compared with the cardiac rehabilitation group (MD: -1 day; 95% CI: [-4.71; 2.71]; d = -0.19). Conclusions In this study, no additional benefit was observed with the addition of incentive spirometry to cardiac rehabilitation compared with cardiac rehabilitation alone. No significant differences were detected between groups in postoperative pulmonary complications, hospital length of stay, or clinical-functional recovery among individuals undergoing cardiac surgery. Trial registration Brazilian Registry of Clinical Trials (REBEC) under the number RBR-8tsjf97.

title: Emergency-Care Utilisation During Two Healthcare Crises in South Korea: A Single-Centre Comparison of Calendar-Aligned 32-Week Windows.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Emergency department (ED) attendance may change differently from subsequent hospital utilisation during healthcare disruptions. We compared two historical crisis episodes within one Korean regional emergency medical centre. Methods: Four calendar-aligned 224-day windows before and after the onset of COVID-19 and the 2024 workforce disruption were analysed using episode-by-phase interactions. Modified Poisson models used patient-and-day two-way clustered variance. Less-conditioned and initial-acuity-conditioned models were compared. Daily counts used calendar-lag autocorrelation-consistent variance. Source-data audits, full-period segmented analyses and alternative-baseline sensitivities were added. Results: The windows included 83,998 visits by 66,096 patients after source-data recoding. The ratio of relative changes was 0.73 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.68-0.78) for daily visits, 1.28 (1.19-1.37) for transfer-in presentation and 1.44 (1.33-1.55) for acuity-conditioned ICU admission. EMS arrival increased more during COVID-19, but the corrected physiological composite showed no clear between-episode contrast. ED-origin ICU admissions/day were 9.24 before and 9.67 during the workforce episode; the primary ratio of incidence rate ratios was 1.13 (1.05-1.22), but the prior-calendar-year sensitivity included the null (1.06, 0.97-1.15). Workforce-period mortality associations differed before and after acuity conditioning, with adjusted risk ratios of 1.28 (1.10-1.49) and 1.06 (0.92-1.22), respectively. Conclusions: Attendance contracted more than ED-origin ICU admission volume during the observed workforce episode. These findings describe utilisation, not measured capacity pressure, and depend partly on baseline and adjustment choices. The contribution is a multidimensional approach to utilisation surveillance, not universal crisis-specific effects or evidence of unchanged survival.

title: The Psychological Impact of Hospital Admission on the Elderly: A Prospective Comparative Clinical Audit and Service Evaluation.
abstract: Introduction Hospital admission in older adults can be associated with functional decline, loss of independence, delirium, disruption of routine, and psychological deterioration. Virtual Wards, also described as Hospital-at-Home models, provide acute clinical care in a patient's usual place of residence and may reduce some harms associated with inpatient admission. Although Virtual Wards are commonly evaluated in terms of bed capacity, admission avoidance, and clinical safety, their psychological impact remains less well explored. This audit compared depressive symptoms and self-rated mood in older adults managed in hospital with those treated through a Virtual Ward service. Methods A prospective comparative clinical audit and service evaluation was conducted within the Care of the Elderly directorate at East Cheshire NHS Trust. The audit included 100 patients aged ≥70 years: 50 hospital inpatients and 50 patients managed through Virtual Ward pathways. Eligible patients had received at least five days of inpatient or Virtual Ward care and had broadly comparable medical diagnoses. Patients with severe acute or life-threatening illness, those lacking capacity to participate, and those with communication barriers preventing completion of the assessment tools were excluded. Baseline age, sex, primary diagnosis, and Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) characteristics were compared descriptively between cohorts. Depressive symptoms were assessed using the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15), and self-rated mood was assessed using a five-point mood scale. Exploratory unadjusted between-group comparisons were performed for selected patient-level outcomes. Results Hospital inpatients demonstrated a greater depressive symptom burden than Virtual Ward patients. A GDS-15 score of ≥5 was recorded in 36 (72%) hospital inpatients compared with 15 (30%) Virtual Ward patients, corresponding to an unadjusted odds ratio of 6.00 (95% CI, 2.53-14.24; Fisher's exact p<0.001). Low self-rated mood, defined as a score of 1 or 2, was reported by 19 (38%) hospital inpatients compared with three (6%) Virtual Ward patients, with an unadjusted odds ratio of 9.60 (95% CI, 2.62-35.21; Fisher's exact p<0.001). Conversely, positive mood scores of 4 or 5 were reported by 32 (64%) Virtual Ward patients compared with 16 (32%) hospital inpatients. Baseline age and frailty distributions showed substantial descriptive overlap, although some variation in sex and primary diagnosis was present between cohorts. Conclusion Older adults receiving inpatient care demonstrated a greater burden of depressive symptoms and less positive self-rated mood than those managed through the Virtual Ward service. However, the non-randomised design, potential selection bias, and absence of adjustment for important baseline factors such as cognitive status, functional status, social support, and baseline psychological wellbeing mean that causation cannot be established. The findings should therefore be interpreted as an association between care setting and psychological wellbeing rather than evidence that Virtual Ward care itself improves mood. Further prospective evaluation using comprehensive baseline assessment, adjusted analyses, and post-discharge follow-up is required. Older adults who require hospital admission may also benefit from routine mood assessment and targeted measures to support psychological wellbeing.

title: Anterior ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction Followed by Acute Popliteal Artery Occlusion in a 25-Year-Old Tobacco Smoker with Cannabis Use.

title: A case report of pulmonary embolism following endoscopic cervical discectomy in an elderly patient with cervical disc herniation.
abstract: Rationale Posterior percutaneous endoscopic cervical discectomy (P-PECD) is a minimally invasive procedure for cervical spine disorders. Although it is associated with less surgical trauma and faster postoperative recovery, serious perioperative thromboembolic complications may still occur. Patient concerns A 65-year-old woman with cervical disc herniation, right upper limb pain, and multiple comorbidities underwent posterior percutaneous endoscopic cervical discectomy after unsuccessful conservative treatment. On the 2nd postoperative day, she developed dizziness and decreased oxygen saturation. On the 3rd postoperative day, she complained of chest tightness. Diagnoses Laboratory testing revealed a markedly elevated plasma D-dimer level. Venous color Doppler ultrasound of both lower limbs demonstrated thrombosis in the bilateral calf muscular veins, and computed tomography pulmonary angiography confirmed multiple pulmonary emboli. Interventions The patient received oxygen therapy, continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring, anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin, and other supportive treatments. She was transferred to the intensive care unit for further monitoring and management. Outcomes The patient's respiratory and circulatory status gradually stabilized, and her chest tightness and dizziness resolved. She was subsequently transferred back to the pain ward and discharged in stable condition. Lessons This case highlights that minimally invasive spinal surgery does not eliminate the risk of perioperative venous thromboembolism. Comprehensive preoperative thrombotic risk assessment, individualized perioperative management of antithrombotic therapy, appropriate thromboprophylaxis, early mobilization, and timely recognition and treatment of suspected APE are important for improving perioperative safety.

title: Cross-Sectional Survey of Critical Care Provision in Ministry of Health Hospitals in Zambia.
abstract: Background Critical care is an essential component of universal health care; however, its provision in low- and middle-income countries remains poorly understood. Although Zambia has expanded critical care services over the last 15 years, national evidence regarding workforce capacity, infrastructure and service provision remains limited. Aims To evaluate critical care workforce, service provision and patient case mix across Ministry of Health hospitals in Zambia. Study design A cross-sectional survey was administered across 14 public hospitals with critical care units across Zambia, representing all 10 provinces. Data were collected via an e-survey questionnaire instrument. Descriptive statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS. Ethics approval was obtained prior to the study. Results All hospitals responded (n = 14/14, 100% response rate), accounting for a capacity of 131 critical care beds. Only 28.6% of hospitals had 24-h intensivist coverage, whereas all had registered critical care nurses. Equipment availability varied, with universal access to ventilators and monitors but limited access to syringe pumps and inconsistent availability of functional CT scanners. Over a 7-day period, 121 admissions were recorded, predominantly medical (29%), surgical (24.8%) and trauma-related (19.8%). Paediatric cases accounted for 40% of admissions. Formal admission and discharge protocols were present in fewer than half of the hospitals. Conclusion The study provides the first national overview of public critical care provision in Zambia and provides a snapshot of current provision. The findings highlight urgent areas for capacity strengthening.
