title: Male Sex, Early Postoperative C-Reactive Protein and Prolonged Hospital Stay After Lung Resection in Older Patients: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Background/objectives Older patients make up a growing share of the lung-resection workload, and C-reactive protein measured in the first days after operation is used to judge recovery. Whether the same concentration means the same thing in older men and older women is not established. Methods We analysed 724 lung resections in 716 patients from VitalDB, an open perioperative dataset from a Korean tertiary hospital; 313 (43.2%) were aged 65 years or older. The primary outcome was a postoperative stay of 7 days or longer. Older general surgical patients from the same institution served as an age-matched negative control. Results Among patients aged 65 or older, prolonged stay occurred in 55 of 192 men (28.6%) and 10 of 121 women (8.3%), adjusted odds ratio 3.031 (95% CI 1.425-6.446, p = 0.0040). Median day 1 C-reactive protein was 51.9 mg/L in older men and 27.4 mg/L in older women, adjusted ratio of geometric means 1.825 (1.593-2.090, p = 1.8 × 10 -16 ). C-reactive protein predicted prolonged stay unadjusted (1.594 per doubling, 1.292-1.967) but not once sex entered the model (0.865, 0.691-1.084, p = 0.208), an interval that remains compatible with a modest association in either direction. In 1635 older general surgical patients, neither effect was present (0.863, p = 0.302; 1.238, p = 0.163). The sex-by-age interaction was not significant ( p = 0.519). Conclusions In older patients undergoing lung resection, men mount a larger early inflammatory response than women to comparable operations and are three times as likely to stay a week or longer, an association absent from older general surgical patients at the same institution. In this dataset and with the measured covariates, C-reactive protein on the first postoperative day was not independently associated with prolonged hospital stay after adjustment for sex and the other available factors; with 113 events, this does not establish absence of prognostic value. These data do not derive, validate, or justify sex-specific C-reactive protein thresholds, and none is proposed.

title: Opportunities for age-friendly emergency care: a mixed-methods study of older adult experiences in a Canadian Emergency Department.
Validity of Administrative ICD-10 Diagnosis Codes for Ventricular Arrhythmia and Cardiac Arrest in a French University Hospital.
abstract: Purpose Drug-induced QT interval prolongation increases the risk of ventricular arrhythmias and cardiac arrest. Assessing these outcomes in electronic health databases and evaluating their association with drug exposure requires prior validation of administrative diagnostic codes. This study aimed to evaluate the positive predictive value (PPV) of International Classification of Diseases, 10 th revision (ICD-10) codes for ventricular arrhythmias and cardiac arrest in the French hospital discharge summary database ( Programme de Médicalisation des Systèmes d'Information (PMSI)). Methods In a retrospective validation study, we examined PMSI data recorded at Amiens University Medical Center (Amiens, France). Hospital stays between September 2022 and August 2025 with ICD-10 codes for cardiac arrest (I46.0, I46.9), ventricular tachycardia (I47.2), or ventricular fibrillation/flutter (I49.0) were identified. Events were confirmed by electronic medical record review. PPVs with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. The study design prevented the estimation of sensitivity, specificity, and negative predictive values. Sensitivity analyses were stratified by year, and by type of care unit. Exposure to QT-prolonging medications prior to events was also assessed. Results In a population of 182 patients (median age: 66 years; 75% males; in-hospital mortality rate: 45%), PPVs [95% CI] for all diagnosis codes were high: 0.98 [0.95; 1.00] for cardiac arrest with successful resuscitation, 0.96 [0.79; 1.00] for unspecified cardiac arrest, 0.99 [0.94; 1.00] for ventricular tachycardia, and 0.93 [0.87; 0.97] for ventricular fibrillation/flutter. Sensitivity analyses yielded consistent results. Overall, 49.7% of patients had been exposed to ≥1 QT-prolonging medications prior to a validated event, and 26.5% to ≥2 of these medications concomitantly. Conclusion The high PPVs in PMSI data supports the use of the evaluated ICD-10 codes for outcome identification in pharmacoepidemiological studies of electronic health databases in general, and those investigating QT-prolonging medication use and the risk of serious cardiac events in particular.

title: WIse CHoices in the ICU (WICH-ICU): Protocol and Statistical Analysis Plan for a Stepped-Wedge Cluster Randomized Trial of Choosing Wisely Interventions in Swedish Intensive Care Units.
abstract: Background Healthcare overuse, including unnecessary diagnostic testing and procedures, contributes to patient harm, increased healthcare costs, and resource waste. The Choosing Wisely initiative aims to reduce low-value care through evidence-based recommendations. However, limited evidence exists regarding the safety and effectiveness of implementing Choosing Wisely recommendations in intensive care settings. Methods The WICH-ICU is a registry-based stepped-wedge cluster randomized controlled trial designed to evaluate the implementation of specific Choosing Wisely interventions in Swedish intensive care units (ICUs). The study will include adult patients treated in participating Swedish ICUs. The intervention consists of three parts of the Choosing Wisely recommendations: (1) reduced frequency of arterial blood gas sampling, (2) reduced routine laboratory testing, and (3) reduced routine chest radiography. The primary outcome is 30-day mortality. Secondary outcomes include ICU length of stay, duration of mechanical ventilation (invasive and noninvasive), continuous renal replacement therapy duration, and ICU readmission within 72 h. Intervention data, testing intensity (arterial blood gas samples, laboratory tests, and chest radiographs per patient-day), will be collected through local monitoring, while outcome data will be obtained from the Swedish Intensive Care Registry (SIR). The stepped-wedge design allows each participating ICU to serve as its own control, with randomized timing of intervention implementation. Discussion This study will provide evidence on the safety and effectiveness of implementing Choosing Wisely recommendations in intensive care settings. The stepped-wedge cluster randomized design minimizes contamination while allowing all participating sites to eventually receive the intervention. The results will inform evidence-based de-implementation strategies in critical care. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT07013175.

title: RSV Disease Among Hospitalized Children: Second vs. First Year of Life Multicenter Study.
abstract: Background Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of pediatric hospitalization, yet data on children hospitalized with RSV in their second year of life are limited. Objective To compare clinical characteristics and management practices of children hospitalized with RSV during their second versus first year of life. Methods This retrospective multicenter study included children aged 0-23 months hospitalized with RSV infection across 11 medical centers between 2017 and 2021. We compared demographics, outcomes (length of stay [LOS] > 3 days, and pediatric intensive care unit [PICU] admission), and systemic corticosteroid and antibiotic use between the second and first years of life, adjusting for prematurity, comorbidities, and the COVID-19 pandemic. Results Among 6260 children hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed RSV infection, 1321 (21%) were hospitalized during their second year of life. Compared with first-year admissions, second-year patients had higher rates of prematurity (18.0% vs. 13.4%) and comorbidities (6.3% vs. 2.6%) (both p Conclusions RSV hospitalization in the second year of life carries a significant burden, with higher antibiotic and corticosteroid use despite lower PICU rates and similar LOS. These findings highlight the need for better characterization of this age group to optimize future immunoprophylaxis strategies.

title: <b>Clinical effectiveness and safety of metadoxine in the management of acute alcohol intoxication: A single-center retrospective cohort study</b>.
Massive envenomations by bees in French Guiana: A ten-year retrospective study (2014-2023).
abstract: Background Massive bee stings can cause systemic manifestations and life-threatening complications. In French Guiana, data on such envenomations are scarce. This study aimed to describe the epidemiology, clinical characteristics, and management of patients presenting to the emergency department. Methods We retrospectively reviewed medical records of all patients admitted for bee stings over the period 2014-2023 at Cayenne Hospital. A composite variable of systemic involvement was created (neurological, respiratory, hemodynamic and digestive). All analyses were descriptive. An exploratory two-graph receiver operating characteristic (TG-ROC) analysis was used to describe the sensitivity and specificity of sting-count cut-offs for four binary indicators of systemic involvement. Results Among 143 patients included, 40% (n = 57) presented at least one systemic manifestation. The median number of stings was 50 [20-150]. In the exploratory TG-ROC analysis, the cut-offs maximizing the Youden index were approximately 72 stings for digestive and hemodynamic manifestations and 99 stings for neurological and respiratory manifestations, with modest sensitivity (0.50-0.76) and specificity (0.68-0.76). Overall mortality was low (0.7%, n = 1/143). Conclusions This study provides the first detailed epidemiological and clinical description of massive bee envenomations in French Guiana. Exploratory analyses suggested that systemic manifestations may occur at sting counts below the conventional 200-sting threshold. These findings should not be interpreted as a validated clinical cutoff and require confirmation in prospective multicenter studies.

title: Preserved anabolic skeletal muscle capacity in response to exercise and protein intake after critical illness.
abstract: Background Low muscle mass and persistent weakness are common after critical illness, but the mechanisms behind impaired recovery are incompletely understood. The aim of this study was to investigate the skeletal muscle anabolic response to combined resistance exercise and protein intake in intensive care unit (ICU) survivors, compared to matched controls without a history of critical illness. We hypothesised that residual anabolic resistance limits muscle regeneration after ICU stay. Methods Former patients were enrolled within 3 to 6 months of intensive care unit discharge. Muscle biopsies were obtained before and after resistance exercise using a flywheel leg extension ergometer, combined with ingestion of 24 g hydrolysed protein. Muscle protein fractional synthetic rate was determined from the incorporation of [ring-²H₅]phenylalanine into mixed-muscle protein during a primed continuous intravenous infusion. Anabolic and proteolytic pathways were measured using standard assays. Group-by-time differences were analysed using linear mixed models. The primary comparison was the between-group difference in pre-to-post change in muscle protein synthesis. Results Twenty ICU survivors (60 ± 12 years, 30% female, BMI 26.9 (IQR 22.9-28.7), SAPS 3 62.3 ± 15.8) and 20 age- and sex-matched controls were included. ICU survivors had significantly lower quadriceps muscle thickness (p = 0.02) and handgrip strength (p = 0.04) than controls. In ICU survivors, muscle protein synthesis from plasma precursor amino acids was higher at baseline than in controls (0.041%/hour vs. 0.030%/hour, p = 0.009), but increased less (Δ 0.031 vs. Δ 0.040%/hour, p = 0.04). Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis was similar between groups (0.071%/hour vs. 0.070%/hour, p = 0.70). At baseline, ICU survivors showed lower activation of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway. In both groups, the intervention increased anabolic signalling, decreased initiation of autophagy and increased parts of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. Conclusions In ICU survivors with persistent muscle loss and weakness, the increase in muscle protein synthesis after combined resistance exercise and protein intake was smaller than in controls, in the context of a higher baseline fractional synthetic rate. Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis rates were similar between groups. These findings provide the first mechanistic support for structured exercise-nutrition rehabilitation to promote muscle recovery after critical illness. Trial registration This study was prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05261984), 2022-02-20.

title: The First 48 Hours: Incidence, Timing and Predictors of Adverse Events After ICU-To-Ward Transfer: A Prospective Cohort Study.
Syndromic Testing in Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases: An Updated Review of Diagnostic Performance, Clinical and Healthcare Impact, and Emerging Developments.
abstract: Syndromic testing, defined as the simultaneous nucleic acid amplification-based detection of multiple potential pathogens and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants directly from clinical specimens, has transformed laboratory diagnosis of infectious diseases in the United States over the past two decades. In contrast to traditional microbiology workflows that rely on culture, phenotypic susceptibility testing, and sequential single-target assays with turnaround times of 24-72 h or longer, syndromic multiplex panels provide comprehensive pathogen identification within 1-5 h, enabling timely clinical decision-making, targeted antimicrobial therapy, and improved patient outcomes. In this review, the current landscape of FDA-cleared syndromic testing panels across seven major clinical syndromes is examined, including respiratory tract infections, pneumonia, bloodstream infections, gastrointestinal infections, meningitis/encephalitis, joint and bone infections, and global febrile/travel-related illnesses. For each syndrome, commercially available panels in the United States are summarized, with emphasis on diagnostic performance, clinical applications, and limitations. Available evidence demonstrates that syndromic testing, when integrated with institutional diagnostic and antimicrobial stewardship programs, can reduce time to optimal therapy and unnecessary antimicrobial use and, in selected settings, shorten hospital length of stay. A mortality benefit has been reported in some patient populations, particularly those with bloodstream infections. Nevertheless, rapid turnaround time and earlier pathogen identification do not necessarily translate into timely clinical action and improved patient outcomes. Challenges related to implementation and optimization of appropriate panel utilization, including evolving AMR epidemiology, dynamic and geographically variable pathogen distributions, the critical role of diagnostic and antimicrobial stewardship, and emerging developments for diagnosis and management of infectious disease, are also discussed.

title: Current Incisional Negative Pressure Wound Therapy Systems: Technical Characteristics and a Decision Framework for Device Selection.
abstract: Incisional negative pressure wound therapy has expanded from a niche adjunct to a widely adopted strategy for the prevention and management of wound complications in selected surgical settings. However, available systems differ in pressure profile, fluid handling, dressing interface, and suitability for fragile skin or anatomically challenging incisions, while practical guidance for device selection remains limited. Whether iNPWT should be used selectively is an established question; which system characteristics are relevant once its use has been judged appropriate is not. We conducted a structured narrative review of the literature on incisional negative pressure wound therapy published between January 2013 and September 2026, based on a targeted PubMed/MEDLINE search. Clinical studies addressing primarily closed surgical incisions were reviewed across elective, emergency, and reconstructive settings; conventional negative pressure wound therapy for open wounds was considered only in order to define the boundary between the two indications. Device technical characteristics were extracted separately from manufacturers' instructions for use and clinician guidelines. Evidence was synthesised in relation to clinical indication, incision and patient characteristics, device features, reported outcomes, and treatment-related adverse events. On this basis, a clinical-requirement-first decision framework for bedside device selection was developed, with each component labelled as direct clinical evidence, indirect clinical evidence, documented technical characteristic, or expert clinical consideration. The available evidence supports a selective rather than routine use of incisional negative pressure wound therapy. The greatest clinical value appears in high-risk incisions and in settings where oedema, superficial fluid accumulation, or limited soft-tissue protection are likely to contribute to wound morbidity. Reported benefits vary according to procedure type, baseline risk, endpoint definition, and device configuration. Published studies evaluate complete proprietary systems rather than isolated technical variables. The only randomised comparison between two commercial systems identified was small and found no difference between them. Adverse events remain relevant and may limit treatment in fragile skin or when drainage exceeds the fluid-handling capacity declared for the selected dressing. Incisional negative pressure wound therapy should be considered an adjunct to standard preventive measures, not a universal solution. A structured approach integrating anticipated fluid-handling requirements, perilesional skin tolerance, seal feasibility over the relevant anatomy, and intended therapy duration may support more rational and transparent device selection once iNPWT has been judged appropriate. Current evidence does not establish a hierarchy among commercially available incisional systems, and the framework should be regarded as structured decision support rather than as a validated algorithm.

title: Implementation of the HUGO™ RAS system for robot-assisted radical prostatectomy: a single-center comparison with the da Vinci Xi<sup>®</sup> system.
abstract: Purpose To compare early perioperative and pathological outcomes between the HUGO™ RAS and da Vinci Xi ® robotic platforms for robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) at a single center. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 107 consecutive patients who underwent RARP (50 HUGO™, 57 da Vinci™) between April 2024 and December 2025, performed by two surgeons who both used both systems. Outcome-specific propensity score models with overlap weighting were used to estimate adjusted associations between platform and operative duration, length of hospital stay, anastomotic integrity, positive surgical margins, lymph node yield, complications, and achieved nerve sparing. Results Baseline characteristics were broadly comparable, although the HUGO™ cohort included a higher proportion of high-risk D'Amico tumors. Operative duration was longer with HUGO™ in the unadjusted analysis (211 vs. 193 min, p = 0.036); after overlap weighting and covariate adjustment, the difference was 14.6 min (95% CI -3.0 to 32.2) and not statistically significant. No statistically significant adjusted differences were observed between platforms for length of hospital stay, anastomotic integrity, positive surgical margins, lymph node yield, complications, or achieved nerve sparing. Conclusion In this early single-center experience, RARP performed with the HUGO™ RAS system showed no statistically significant differences in early perioperative and pathological outcomes compared with the established da Vinci Xi ® platform after adjustment for measured confounders. Larger prospective multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these findings and to evaluate long-term oncological and functional outcomes.

title: CT-Referenced Diagnostic Performance and Complementary Error Patterns of Artificial Intelligence Versus a Single Emergency Physician in Chest Radiograph Interpretation: A Retrospective Paired Diagnostic Accuracy Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support chest radiograph interpretation, but its clinical value depends not only on stand-alone accuracy but also on whether its errors differ from those of clinicians. We evaluated CT-referenced, target-specific diagnostic performance and complementary error patterns of a commercial chest radiograph AI system and a single emergency physician. Methods: In this retrospective, single-center, paired diagnostic accuracy study, 920 consecutive adults who underwent posteroanterior chest radiography and thoracic computed tomography (CT) within 4 h during the same emergency department encounter were included. A commercial AI system (hChestXR version 1) and a single blinded emergency physician independently assessed eight prespecified thoracic findings using CT as the reference standard. Paired differences were estimated with 10,000 patient-level bootstrap resamples and tested with exact McNemar tests with Holm adjustment. Exact-target complementarity and simulated same-target OR/AND rules were secondary exploratory analyses. Results: Across 7360 patient-target assessments, including 1232 CT-positive findings, AI had significantly greater Holm-adjusted sensitivity for pneumothorax (90.8% vs. 50.8%), nodule/mass (63.3% vs. 32.7%), and rib fracture (77.2% vs. 46.5%). AI-only detections were most frequent for pneumothorax (47.7%), nodule/mass (44.9%), and rib fracture (43.6%), whereas physician-only detections were most frequent for atelectasis (24.8%), pulmonary edema (21.0%), and lung opacity (19.7%). In exploratory pooled analyses, sensitivity was 73.0% for AI and 62.0% for the physician. Exploratory simulated same-target OR/AND analyses demonstrated a sensitivity-specificity trade-off across pooled patient-target assessments but did not represent observed AI-assisted clinical performance. Conclusions: The AI system and the single emergency-physician reader in the study showed target-dependent, partly non-overlapping error patterns in this CT-selected emergency cohort. The findings support prospective multireader evaluation of AI as a second-reader tool but do not establish benefit from real-time AI-assisted interpretation.

title: A Mixed Methods Evaluation of a Model of Care for Domestic Violence Within the Emergency Department.
abstract: Objective To describe the scope and extent of the Domestic Violence (DV) Model of Care at Campbelltown Emergency Department (ED). We detail patient population characteristics, means of identifying victim-survivors, care provided, and factors associated with social work review. Methods This mixed-methods evaluation utilised (1) retrospective audits of medical records of patients admitted to Campbelltown ED in 2024, who (a) responded affirmatively on the DV Routine Screening (DVRS) tool, and/or (b) were reviewed by social work relating to DV; and (2) semi-structured interviews with 19 clinicians and support workers about their understanding of and role within the model of care. Descriptive analyses quantified the scope and characteristics of the DV patient population and care provision; logistic regression identified factors associated with DVRS-identified patients seeing social work. Thematic analysis of interview data supplemented audit findings. Results In 2024, 249 ED patients responded affirmatively to the DVRS tool (DV identified prior for 52.2%), and 231 patients were reviewed by social work relating to DV. Victim-survivors were identified through DVRS tool use, explicit disclosure, referral from community partners, and clinician judgement. Transfer to the ED short stay unit facilitated safety and trauma/violence-informed care, including social work consultation for 49.8% of identified victim-survivors. Explicit disclosure or help-seeking, presenting concerns, and child safety risks were associated with seeing social work; however, presentation day/time was not. Conclusions This evaluation demonstrates that a comprehensive ED model of care, employing multiple means of identifying victim-survivors, is able to facilitate trauma/violence-informed psychosocial care alongside medical management for patients experiencing DV.

title: Comparison of Peripherally Inserted Central Catheters versus Central Venous Catheters in a Medical Intensive Care Unit: A Single-Center Retrospective Study.
abstract: Background Patients in medical intensive care units (MICUs) often require prolonged intravenous therapy, making optimal catheter selection critical. While central venous catheters (CVCs) remain common, peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs) are increasingly used. This single-centre retrospective study compared indwelling time, clinical utility, and complication profiles between PICCs and CVCs in MICU patients. Methods We analyzed 276 MICU patients with either a PICC or CVC, comparing catheter selection, length of stay, dwell time, and complication rates. Complication rates were also standardized per 1000 catheter-days. Results PICCs were used more frequently in patients with malignancy ( P P P = 0.012), diabetes ( P = 0.012), COVID-19 ( P = 0.020), or vasopressor infusion ( P = 0.001). PICCs were associated with longer indwelling times (≥12 days, P P P = 0.005), but lower rates of puncture-site complications (bleeding, hypersensitivity, fluid leakage; all P P = 0.038). After standardization per 1,000 catheter-days, dislodgement remained significantly more frequent with PICCs, whereas the difference in occlusion was no longer statistically significant. No bloodstream infections occurred with PICCs, versus 5.4% with CVCs ( P = 0.169). Because groups differed substantially in patient selection, clinical indication, dwell time, insertion site, and securement method, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than evidence of superiority. Conclusion PICCs were associated with longer indwelling times and a higher rate of dislodgement, but lower rates of puncture-site complications and deep vein thrombosis; the difference in occlusion was no longer significant after standardization. Vascular access selection should be individualized according to patient characteristics, therapy requirements, anticipated duration, and device-related risks.

title: Effects of Extended ICU Length of Stay on Braden Scale Validity: A Retrospective Analysis.
journal: The journal of nursing research : JNR
abstract: Background Pressure injuries prolong hospitalization, increase costs, and increase mortality risk. Intensive care unit (ICU) patients experience a high prevalence of these injuries due to multiple risk factors. Although the Braden Scale is widely used to predict pressure injury risk, its accuracy in ICU settings is limited, underscoring the need for improvement. Purpose This study was designed to evaluate the variance in predictive validity of the Braden Scale for pressure injury development based on ICU length of stay. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted in the medical and surgical ICUs of a university-affiliated hospital in Korea on data from 2,190 patients (419 with and 1,693 without pressure injuries) admitted between January 2017 and February 2020. Predictive validity was assessed using a Braden Scale cutoff of 14 points, and logistic regression was used to analyze the association between risk classification and pressure injury development. Results For predicting pressure injuries in patients with ICU stays ≤7 days and ≥8 days, the final Braden Scale score yielded respective Youden Index values of .39 and .18 and respective area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of .76 and .64. Those with ICU stays ≤7 days and classified as high-risk were more likely to develop pressure injuries than their peers classified as lower risk (odds ratio [ OR ] 7.33, 95% confidence interval [CI; 4.75, 11.31]). Those with ICU stays ≥8 days had an OR of 3.04 (95% CI [1.85, 4.98]). Conclusions/implications for practice The findings of this study support that the accuracy of the Braden scale in terms of predicting pressure injury risk declines as ICU stay length increases. This lower scale performance may be attributable to multiple confounding clinical factors present in ICU settings. To minimize pressure injury risk during extended ICU stays, the Braden Scale should be supplemented with comprehensive assessments of nutritional status, skin perfusion, mobility, and hemodynamic stability, as these indicators more effectively capture patient-specific risks during prolonged hospitalization.

title: Estimated plasma volume status (ePVS) as a prognostic marker in polytrauma: predicting 30-day mortality and coagulation support needs.
Physician Sex and Outcomes Among Hospitalized Patients.
abstract: Importance Prior studies have shown that patients treated by female physicians experience better outcomes than those treated by male physicians, but evidence has often focused on surgical populations. The association between physician sex and outcomes among hospitalized medical patients across different health care systems remains less well understood. Objective To examine associations between physician sex and care outcomes among hospitalized medical patients admitted with common medical diagnoses in Ontario, Canada. Design, setting, and participants This population-based, retrospective cohort study was conducted between January 1, 2008, and December 31, 2022, among inpatients aged 18 years or older admitted with 1 of 7 common acute medical conditions in Ontario, Canada. Data were analyzed from August 16, 2024, to July 13, 2026. Exposure Physician sex, defined in 2 ways: binary sex of the most responsible physician during hospital admission and proportion of in-hospital days managed by a female physician. Main outcomes and measures Primary outcomes were 30-day mortality and hospital readmission. Secondary outcomes included 90-day and 1-year mortality and readmission and index hospital length of stay. Multivariable generalized estimating equations were used to calculate adjusted odds ratios (AORs) accounting for patient-, physician-, and hospital-level covariates. Results The cohort included 958 150 patients (54.3% male; median age, 74 years [IQR, 62-83 years]). After adjustment, care by female compared with male physicians was associated with lower 30-day mortality (12.3% [95% CI, 7.2%-21.1%] vs 13.7% [95% CI, 7.9%-23.8%]; AOR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.85-0.91]) and hospital readmission (18.6% [95% CI, 17.0%-20.2%] vs 18.9% [95% CI, 17.3%-20.5%]; AOR, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.97-1.00]). When physician sex was operationalized as proportion of in-hospital days managed by a female physician (per 10% increment), greater exposure to care by a female physician was associated with lower 30-day mortality (AOR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.90-0.97) and readmission (AOR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.98-0.99). Conclusions and relevance In this cohort study of hospitalized medical patients, those cared for by female physicians experienced lower 30-day mortality compared with those treated by male physicians. These findings warrant further investigation to elucidate underlying mechanisms and potential differences in physician practice patterns.

title: Dexmedetomidine Versus Dexamethasone in Pediatric Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass: An Exploratory Randomized Controlled Trial of Inflammatory Biomarkers and Opioid Consumption.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) triggers a systemic inflammatory response in children undergoing congenital heart surgery. Although dexmedetomidine has been proposed as an alternative to corticosteroids, the two agents have not previously been directly compared in a pediatric randomized trial. This study aimed to compare the effects of dexmedetomidine and dexamethasone on inflammatory biomarkers and analgesic outcomes in children undergoing congenital heart surgery with CPB. Methods: In this prospective, randomized, controlled exploratory trial, 50 children aged 6 months to 18 years undergoing elective congenital heart surgery with CPB were randomized 1:1 to dexamethasone ( n = 25) or dexmedetomidine ( n = 25), using institutional regimens that were not equipotent anti-inflammatory doses. Serum interleukin-6 (IL-6) and interleukin-8 (IL-8) were measured at baseline, immediately after separation from CPB (post-CPB), and 12 h postoperatively. The primary endpoint was IL-6 at the two postoperative time points; IL-8 was a secondary biomarker outcome. Secondary outcomes also included Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability (FLACC) pain scores, fentanyl consumption, and time to first rescue analgesia. Effect estimates included Hodges-Lehmann (HL) median differences with 95% confidence intervals (CIs); a post hoc baseline-adjusted mixed-effects model of log-transformed concentrations served as a sensitivity analysis. Secondary and exploratory analyses were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Results: All 50 randomized children were analyzed. Median IL-6 was lower in the dexmedetomidine group at 12 h (50 vs. 178 pg/mL; HL difference 86 pg/mL, 95% CI 59 to 144; p p = 0.045) was imprecise and not significant after post hoc Bonferroni correction for the two primary comparisons. In the post hoc baseline-adjusted sensitivity model, the ratio of geometric mean IL-6 concentrations (dexmedetomidine/dexamethasone) was 0.35 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.58; p p -values are nominal, IL-8 was also lower post-CPB (159 vs. 381 pg/mL; p = 0.001) and at 12 h (120 vs. 311 pg/mL; p = 0.002). Dexmedetomidine was associated with lower intraoperative (83.0 ± 30.7 vs. 142.6 ± 51.7 µg; p p p p = 0.204). Intensive care unit length of stay, an exploratory outcome recorded in days, was distributed toward shorter stays with dexmedetomidine (median 2 [interquartile range 1-2] vs. 2 [2-3] days; p = 0.007). No pre-specified adverse events occurred in either group, although the trial was too small to exclude clinically important safety differences. Conclusions: In this exploratory trial of two non-equipotent institutional regimens, dexmedetomidine was associated with lower early postoperative IL-6 and IL-8 concentrations and lower opioid consumption than dexamethasone. These hypothesis-generating biomarker and analgesic signals do not demonstrate therapeutic superiority or patient-centered clinical benefit and require confirmation in larger, adequately powered multicenter trials.

title: Anesthetic technique is associated with complication risk and healthcare utilization following total shoulder arthroplasty.
journal: European journal of orthopaedic surgery & traumatology : orthopedie traumatologie
abstract: Purpose Compare perioperative complications and healthcare utilization among total shoulder arthroplasty (TSA) patients receiving general (GA), regional (RA), or combined anesthesia (RA + GA). Methods Using the TriNetX database, patients undergoing primary TSA were identified and stratified into three groups based on anesthetic technique: GA, RA, and combined RA + GA. 1:1 Propensity score matching was performed to using the GA cohort as reference to control for baseline demographic and clinical covariates. Outcomes of interest included 90-day complication rates including UTI, venous thromboembolism (VTE), acute kidney injury (AKI), prosthetic joint infection (PJI), pneumonia, constipation, and revision TSA, emergency department (ED) visits and hospital readmission, Foley catheter insertion, postoperative opioid prescriptions and mean opioid number of prescriptions. Statistical significance was set at p Results Comparing GA with RA, each cohort consisted of 28,564 patients. RA was associated with lower rates of UTI, AKI, constipation, pneumonia, fewer patients prescribed opioids and fewer opioid prescriptions per patient while being associated with increased healthcare utilization compared to GA alone. Comparing RA + GA with GA alone, 17,926 matched patients were included in each cohort. RA + GA was associated with lower rates of UTI and opioid prescriptions, and higher rates of healthcare utilization compared to GA alone. Conclusion These findings suggest that while RA provides early analgesic and opioid-sparing benefits after TSA, it is associated with increased post-operative healthcare utilization. These findings help guide surgical decision making and highlight the need for standardized perioperative protocols to optimize postoperative pain control and manage rebound pain-related care utilization with RA techniques. Level of evidence III.

title: Impact of individualized opioid protocols on post-cesarean discharge prescriptions.
abstract: Introduction Consensus on optimal prescribing of opioids at discharge following cesarean delivery remains limited. Since inpatient opioid use is a strong predictor of outpatient need, individualized approaches may improve prescribing accuracy. The optimal individualized prescribing protocol for post-cesarean pain management at discharge is unknown. While multiple studies have demonstrated benefit with individualized protocols, direct comparison of different protocols has not yet been demonstrated. This study evaluated the modeled application of four individualized prescribing protocols (based on inpatient opioid consumption) on post-cesarean discharge prescriptions compared to actual prescribing patterns. Methods This retrospective cohort study included all patients ≥18 who underwent cesarean delivery from September 1 to December 31, 2023 at a single tertiary academic center. Inpatient opioid use was abstracted from electronic medical records and used to calculate discharge prescriptions based on the following previously published protocols: Bleicher et al. (2024), Osmundson et al. (2018, 2022), and the Prescription After Cesarean Trial (PACT). These modeled prescriptions were compared to the actual prescriptions received at discharge. The primary outcome was total dose prescribed in morphine milligram equivalents (MME); secondary outcomes included number of tablets prescribed and number of patients receiving a prescription at discharge. Results A total of 197 patients were included. There were 124 primary cesarean deliveries (63%) and 73 repeat cesarean deliveries (37%). Of these, 186 (94%) received an opioid prescription at discharge and had a median total dose of 75 MME. Total MME prescribed at discharge decreased among >60% of patients using the Bleicher, Osmundson 2022, and PACT protocols, but increased among 64% of patients using the Osmundson 2018 protocol. Compared to actual prescribing, both Bleicher and PACT models reduced the proportion of patients receiving an opioid prescription by 38%, while both Osmundson models resulted in a 6% increase in patients receiving prescriptions. Conclusion Within the same population, the impact of individualized post-cesarean opioid prescribing protocols varied widely. These findings demonstrate that the choice of individualized prescribing model may meaningfully influence discharge prescribing and highlight the need for prospective comparative studies incorporating patient-reported pain and satisfaction outcomes to identify the optimal approach.

title: Primary non-adherence to newly prescribed discharge medications and 30-day adverse outcomes by mental health status: a retrospective cohort study in two tertiary care hospitals in Montréal, Québec, Canada.
Enhanced recovery after colorectal surgery in patients with inflammatory bowel disease to reduce hospital length of stay: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
journal: Colorectal disease : the official journal of the Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland
abstract: Aim Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) improves outcomes in colorectal cancer surgery; however, patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) have been relatively excluded from these analyses. The purpose of this systematic review was to evaluate the effects of ERAS protocols in adult patients with IBD. Methods Relevant databases were searched for randomised-controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled observational studies that assessed ERAS protocols versus conventional care in adult patients with IBD, in any language until July 21, 2025. Two authors independently identified trials, extracted data, assessed risk of bias (ROB 2.0 and ROBINS-I) and evidence certainty (GRADE). Primary outcomes were length of stay (LOS), 30-day readmissions, re-operations and complications. Results Eighteen studies (one RCT, 17 observational) were included. LOS was significantly lower in the ERAS group (mean difference: -1.62 days; 95% CI: -2.03, -1.21, 15 studies, 4225 patients, moderate certainty). There was no difference in 30-day readmissions (odds ratio, OR: 0.83; 95% CI: 0.62, 1.12, 15 studies, 4157 patients, low certainty), 30-day reoperations (OR: 0.68; 95% CI: 0.46, 1.02, 8 studies, 2161 patients, very low certainty), or 30-day complications (OR 0.69; 95% CI: 0.45, 1.08, 14 studies, 4074 patients, low certainty). Evidence certainty was limited by non-blinding, and observational data at serious risk of bias. Conclusions ERAS for patients with IBD reduces LOS with no difference in 30-day readmissions, reoperations and complications. Subgroup analyses generated the hypothesis that procedure-specific ERAS pathways incorporating greater preoperative optimisation may provide additional benefit, but this requires confirmation in adequately powered randomised trials.

title: National Clinician Survey of Outcomes for Trials in Surgical Wounds Healing by Secondary Intention (SWHSI).
abstract: Surgical wounds healing by secondary intention are often complex, costly and slow to heal. Consistent outcome reporting ensures that interventional trials are directly comparable and less vulnerable to reporting bias, thereby enhancing the efficiency of evidence generation. Currently, no framework for outcome reporting from interventional studies of SWHSI exists. We present a national survey of clinicians as the first step to producing a core outcome set for studies involving interventions for this wound type. A pre-piloted online survey was administered in September 2024 via the Qualtrics system, comprising three sections: perceptions, decision-making and key outcomes in SWHSI management. Recruitment was via professional organisations, membership mailing lists and social media. One hundred and two clinician responses were received. The most common reasons reported for choosing secondary intention healing were concerns about infection (46%, 35/76), primary wound closure (48.7%, 37/76) and potential reintervention (89.5%, 68/76). All-cause mortality at 30 days (73%, 49/67) and 1 year (70%, 47/67), wound healing at 30 days (100%, 67/67), surgical site infection (98%, 66/67), pain score (94%, 63/67), wound size (94%, 63/67), quality of life (99%, 66/67), length of hospital stay (85%, 57/67) and reintervention requirement (90%, 60/67) were reported to be important clinical trial outcomes in this population. This survey explored the main decision-driving factors in choosing secondary intention healing and identified important trial outcomes for clinicians in this research area.

title: A clinical-deep learning model for prolonged length of stay following endovascular aortic repair.
abstract: Background Prolonged length of stay (PLOS) after endovascular aortic repair (EVAR) for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is associated with increased complications, resource burden, and patient distress. Early identification of high-risk patients remains challenging. This study aimed to develop and externally validate a predictive model integrating clinical variables and three-dimensional deep learning (3D-DL) features from preoperative computed tomography angiography (CTA) to predict PLOS after EVAR. Methods A total of 788 patients with AAA who underwent elective EVAR were enrolled from two hospitals. The internal training cohort consisted of 556 patients, and the external validation cohort included 232 patients. PLOS was defined as a LOS above the 75th percentile of the distribution. A clinical nomogram was developed using LASSO regression followed by multivariate logistic regression. Deep learning (DL) features were extracted from manually segmented computed tomography angiography (CTA) images using a 3D ResNet200 network, and LASSO regression was applied to select the most informative features. An ensemble model integrating the clinical predictors and the selected DL features was constructed. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic curves, calibration plots, and decision curve analysis. Results LASSO combined with multivariate logistic regression identified five independent clinical predictors: age, hemoglobin, albumin, maximum aneurysm diameter, and diabetes. The clinical model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.917 in the internal cohort and 0.944 in the external cohort. From the 3D ResNet200 network, 32 DL features were extracted. LASSO regression further selected two of these features. The ensemble predictive model, which integrated the clinical predictors and DL features, demonstrated improved discrimination, with an AUC of 0.971 in the internal cohort and 0.958 in the external cohort. Internal validation with 1,000 bootstrap resamples yielded optimism-corrected AUCs of 0.911 for the clinical model and 0.966 for the ensemble model. Subgroup analyses demonstrated consistent model performance across age and diabetes strata, while performance in the female subgroup warrants further evaluation in larger cohorts. Conclusion This study developed an ensemble predictive model to predict PLOS following EVAR. The model demonstrated excellent discrimination and provided significant prognostic value beyond clinical variables alone. This nomogram may serve as a preoperative tool for risk stratification and resource planning in this population. Future studies should focus on prospective validation and clinical integration.

title: Ultrasound Archiving in the Emergency Department: Implementation, Governance and 4-Year Outcomes at an Australian Tertiary Emergency Department.
abstract: Objective Image archiving is one of the least developed aspects of emergency department ultrasound (ED-US) in Australasia, despite its recognised role in governance, education, quality assurance (QA) and medicolegal protection. A middleware-based ED-US image workflow solution was installed at Nepean Hospital ED in October 2021. We describe our implementation and 4-year experience with a dedicated ED-US archiving solution at a tertiary Australian ED. Methods Single-centre retrospective analysis of service implementation, technical requirements, governance, QA and operational outcomes over a 4-year period. Results Archived 7281 ED-US studies across 15 modalities between October 2021 and April 2026, with annual volume growing from 1083 (2022) to 2224 (2025). Bidirectional EMR connectivity, worklist generation, seamless DICOM image transfer, segregation of clinical from educational studies, structured reporting, interdepartmental image access, automated trainee logbooks and structured QA review are implemented. No failures occurred, and no data were lost. Costs of implementation and maintenance depend on vendor negotiation and local IT costings; the dominant recurring cost is clinician time, not software. The most challenging aspects were IT resource allocation, multivendor integration and governance workload. The automated logbook alone saves each trainee approximately 2 h/week. No medicolegal incidents were reported. Conclusions A structured ED-US archive and workflow are achievable and sustainable in an Australian tertiary ED. In our case, it strengthened accountability, quality of scans, education, research, interdepartmental collaboration and institutional risk management. Our experience provides Australasian EDs with a practical starting point for planning their own implementation.

title: Postoperative hemorrhage and perioperative outcomes in single-port versus multi-port transoral robotic surgery for upper airway disease.
abstract: The integration of transoral robotic surgery (TORS) has catalyzed a paradigm shift in the management of upper airway pathologies; however, the multifaceted operational distinctions between next-generation single-port (SP) platforms and conventional multi-port systems warrant comprehensive investigation. This retrospective analysis delves into the perioperative metrics and postoperative hemorrhage profiles of 126 patients undergoing TORS via the Si, Xi, and SP platforms. Procedures were categorized by complexity as single- or multilevel. To mitigate baseline confounders, we engineered a propensity-matched cohort of multilevel cases (n = 21 per platform). Overall, major postoperative hemorrhage manifested in 9.5% of the cohort. As anticipated, multilevel interventions underscored significant increases in operative duration, postoperative pain, and hospitalization length. In our unmatched analysis, the SP platform demonstrated a robust safety profile, yielding an overall hemorrhage rate of merely 3.1% (0% in single-level; 4.8% in multilevel), contrasting with higher incidences in the Si and Xi cohorts. Within the intricately matched multilevel subset, the SP system showcased significantly fewer major hemorrhage events compared to the Xi platform (4.8% vs. 28.6%). Crucially, this synergy cannot be solely attributed to robotic mechanics, as topical hemostatic agents were universally leveraged in matched SP cases. Exploratory hierarchical Firth penalized logistic regression illuminated that incorporating the robotic platform significantly augmented the predictive model (Firth p = 0.048), indicating the SP platform is associated with reduced hemorrhage odds (adjusted odds ratio = 0.22). Ultimately, this compelling evidence sheds light on the SP system's potential to optimize safety in complex airway reconstruction, necessitating future standardized prospective trials.

title: Point-of-care ultrasound in obstetrics and gynecology: latest advancements and evolution.
abstract: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) in obstetrics and gynecology has evolved from a pragmatic bedside adjunct into a rapidly expanding clinical, educational and technological field. Since the publication of earlier narrative reviews, the discipline has been reshaped by handheld ultrasound systems, wireless probes, cloud-based image management, tele-ultrasound, artificial intelligence (AI) for image acquisition and interpretation, and the first specific practice guidance for POCUS in obstetrics and gynecology. This narrative review summarizes recent advances and proposes a clinically useful framework for the European ultrasound community. POCUS should be understood as a focused, problem-oriented and immediately actionable ultrasound examination performed and interpreted by the treating clinician. It is not a replacement for guideline-based screening, detailed fetal anatomy assessment, comprehensive transvaginal gynecologic imaging, Doppler surveillance or expert ultrasound. The strongest evidence supports POCUS for early pregnancy triage, confirmation of fetal viability and presentation, basic assessment of placental location and amniotic fluid, intrapartum evaluation of fetal head position and selected postpartum or gynecologic emergencies. In gynecology, POCUS can accelerate triage of acute pelvic pain, suspected ectopic pregnancy, intrauterine device position and adnexal pathology, but definitive risk stratification of complex masses remains a task for standardized specialist sonography. Technological progress has been substantial: handheld devices now provide diagnostically useful images for several focused tasks, AI-enabled blind-sweep protocols can estimate gestational age and fetal malpresentation in low-resource settings, and tele-ultrasound can extend expert support beyond tertiary centers. The next phase of OB/GYN POCUS will depend less on device availability than on implementation: indication-specific protocols, formal training, competency assessment, documentation, image archiving, infection control, data protection, quality assurance and clear escalation rules. POCUS in obstetrics and gynecology should therefore be framed as a governed clinical pathway rather than a device-driven shortcut.

title: Use of hospital care among centenarians in France: implications for health-system planning in extreme old age-insights from a nationwide study of temporal patterns, regional variation and care settings (2014-2023).
An Audit on the Management of Adult Patients With Renal Colic Presenting to the Emergency Department.
abstract: Introduction Renal colic is a common emergency department presentation requiring timely assessment, appropriate analgesia, and investigation. This clinical audit evaluated adherence to predefined standards for pain assessment, timely analgesia, investigations, imaging, and medication selection, and assessed changes in practice following a structured implementation phase. Methods A retrospective, single-center, two-cycle clinical audit was conducted in an adult emergency department. The primary audit included 100 patients presenting between December 2020 and December 2024, and the re-audit included 100 patients presenting between March and September 2025, giving a total sample of 200 patients. Nine audit criteria were derived from the Royal College of Emergency Medicine (RCEM) and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance. Following the primary audit, departmental education, audit feedback, an educational infographic, and a standardized renal colic analgesia pathway were implemented. Categorical outcomes were reported as frequencies and percentages and compared between audit cycles using two-sided Chi-square or Fisher exact tests, as appropriate. Results First-line nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) administration increased from 39/100 patients (39.0%) in the primary audit to 60/100 patients (60.0%) in the re-audit, representing an absolute increase of 21.0 percentage points (95% CI: 7.5-34.5). This difference was statistically significant (χ²(1, N = 200) = 8.00; p = 0.005). Avoidance of first-line opioid administration increased from 89/100 patients (89.0%) to 94/100 patients (94.0%); however, this difference was not statistically significant (χ²(1, N = 200) = 1.03; p = 0.310). Pain-score documentation, timely analgesia, urine dipstick testing, laboratory investigations, computed tomography (CT) imaging, and avoidance of antispasmodic medication remained broadly consistent between the two audit cycles. Conclusion Following implementation of a standardized renal colic pathway, departmental education, an educational infographic, and audit feedback, first-line NSAID use increased significantly and first-line opioid use decreased. Other key measures of assessment, investigation, and analgesic care remained generally stable between audit cycles. These findings support the value of a structured departmental approach to promoting guideline-concordant analgesic prescribing and provide a basis for continued quality-improvement activity and future re-audit.

title: Minimally Invasive Aortic Valve Replacement and Perioperative Stroke Risk: A Propensity-Matched Analysis.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Stroke is a devastating complication after aortic valve replacement (AVR). Whether minimally invasive AVR (miniAVR) reduces perioperative stroke risk versus conventional sternotomy remains uncertain. Methods: This single-center retrospective cohort study used propensity score matching (PSM) in 1741 consecutive patients undergoing isolated AVR (2014-2025). After exclusions, 1:1 PSM using 10 covariates created 155 matched pairs with excellent balance (all standardized mean differences Results: Stroke/TIA occurred in 0/155 (0.0%) miniAVR versus 7/155 (4.5%) conventional patients ( p = 0.015); the rule-of-three upper 95% limit for miniAVR was ~1.9%. Thirty-day mortality was similar (0.6% vs. 2.6%; p = 0.371). Five-year survival favored miniAVR (94.6% vs. 87.2%; log-rank p = 0.047). miniAVR was independently associated with lower stroke/TIA odds (odds ratio [OR] 0.052; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.003-0.832; p = 0.037); longer cardiopulmonary bypass time was associated with higher odds (OR 1.014/minute; 95% CI 1.001-1.028; p = 0.032). Conclusions: miniAVR was associated with zero observed perioperative strokes and higher 5-year survival; however, this survival comparison is limited by short median follow-up in the miniAVR group (1.9 years). Given the small number of events and the single-center design, these findings should not be interpreted as proof of a causal neuroprotective effect. Multicenter validation with longer, balanced follow-up is required.

title: Awake craniotomy as a routine pathway for supratentorial tumor surgery: A 500-case awake-craniotomy experience with institutional resource and charge benchmarking.
abstract: Background Integrated safety, tolerability, and resource data on awake craniotomy in resource-constrained settings are lacking. Improving accessibility has remained central to our program. We report an experience exceeding 500 awake craniotomies with structured comparator synthesis. Methods Three nested cohorts from one Central American institution were analyzed: 218 awake craniotomies (2007-2018, audited safety), 500 procedures spanning neoplastic and non-neoplastic lesions (2007-2026, program tolerability), and 30 awake versus 30 contemporaneous general-anesthesia craniotomies (2024-2026, descriptive benchmarking). The two contemporary groups were restricted to elective supratentorial intraparenchymal tumor resections. The contemporary cohort was derived from billing and administrative records; baseline clinical, radiological, and histopathological data were unavailable; groups were managed by different teams. Results Across the 500-case program, completion without conversion was 99.0%; 30-day mortality, ascertainable only for the 282 registry-era procedures, was 3.2%. In the 218-case cohort, seizures occurred in 5.1%, perioperative mortality was 0.5%, and none required ventilation; extent of resection was 73%, 94%, and 100% in eloquent, adjacent to eloquence, and non-eloquent cortex. In the contemporaneous institutional benchmark, the awake pathway showed shorter stay (1.0 vs. 2.0 days), no intensive-care use (0/30 vs. 9/30), shorter incision-to-closure time, and $5,205 lower median billed charges than the general-anesthesia pathway. Outcomes were consistent with 14 comparator studies. Conclusion In this high-volume, resource-constrained program, to the best of our knowledge, the only protocolized awake-craniotomy program in the region, awake craniotomy served as a routine pathway for eligible supratentorial intraparenchymal lesions, with high completion, favorable safety, short hospitalization, no intensive-care admission, and lower observed billed charges than conventional practice.

title: Cognitive heuristics in the operating room: the role of 'left-digit bias' in ophthalmic surgical selection.
abstract: Introduction Left-digit bias is a cognitive heuristic in which the leftmost digit of a number disproportionately influences judgment. This study evaluates the impact of perceived patient age on ophthalmic surgical decision-making. Methods Using a multicentre federated electronic health record network, patients aged 40-85 years with a routine health visit, followed by at least 1 documented ophthalmic examination and a diagnosis code specific to the surgical outcome under study, were followed for 1 year. Patients were grouped into consecutive 2-year age cohorts and matched 1:1 on demographic characteristics, healthcare utilisation, systemic comorbidities, and ocular diagnoses and procedures. Prespecified decade-boundary comparisons were 48/49 versus 50/51, 58/59 versus 60/61, and 68/69 versus 70/71. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for each surgical outcome. Results Among 8,156,608 eligible patients, 218,816 (2.68%) underwent an included ophthalmic procedure, including 201,591 phacoemulsification procedures. The younger cohort had lower odds of phacoemulsification at each decade boundary: 48/49 vs. 50/51 (OR, 0.956; 95% CI, 0.926-0.986), 58/59 vs. 60/61 (OR, 0.935; 95% CI, 0.909-0.961), and 68/69 vs. 70/71 (OR, 0.903; 95% CI, 0.879-0.927; all P Conclusions Consistent with left-digit bias, surgical frequency for phacoemulsification increased at decade transitions. Clinicians should consider the potential influence of age perception in surgical decision-making.

title: Trends in the Use of Neuraxial vs. General Anaesthesia for Transurethral Resection of the Prostate.
journal: Turkish journal of anaesthesiology and reanimation
abstract: Objective Historically, neuraxial anaesthesia (NA) was preferred for transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) to allow monitoring for TURP syndrome, but modern surgical techniques have largely eliminated this risk. We aimed to characterise trends in anaesthesia utilisation for TURP over a 15-year period and to identify patient factors associated with anaesthetic technique selection. Methods We performed a retrospective cohort study of patients undergoing primary TURP using the ACS-NSQIP database (2009-2023). Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of the use of general anaesthesia (GA) versus NA. Subgroup analyses examined trends by patient health status and age. Results Of 73,214 patients identified, GA utilisation increased significantly from 69.9% in 2009 to 88.8% in 2023 ( P P =0.005). Conclusion The anaesthetic management of TURP has evolved over the last 15 years, and GA has further solidified its status as the dominant modality. This evolution likely reflects the diminished risk of TURP syndrome, allowing practice to be driven by airway control and efficiency rather than by historical safety constraints.

title: Nursing radiation-protection compliance and 30-day wound and pin-site adverse events after supracondylar humerus fracture fixation in children.
abstract: Background Fluoroscopy is integral to operative fixation of supracondylar humerus fractures in children, but case-level nursing radiation-protection compliance (NRPC) has not been well characterised as a potential marker of broader perioperative process quality. We examined the association between NRPC and early wound- and pin-site-related outcomes. Methods We conducted a single-centre retrospective cohort study of children aged Results Of 360 children identified, 256 children met the eligibility criteria and had ascertainable NRPC and primary-outcome data; 164 (64%) were classified as High NRPC and 92 (36%) as Low NRPC. Overall, 37/256 children (14.5%) experienced the primary outcome. The observed event rate was 11.0% (18/164) in the High NRPC group and 20.7% (19/92) in the Low NRPC group, corresponding to a crude OR of 2.11 (95% CI 1.04-4.27; p = 0.037) for Low versus High NRPC. In the primary adjusted model, the association was attenuated and imprecise (adjusted OR 1.70, 95% CI 0.80-3.57; p = 0.165). Firth penalized regression yielded OR 1.67 (95% CI 0.80-3.49; p = 0.168), while separate mixed-effects models yielded OR 1.65 (95% CI 0.76-3.58; p = 0.205) for nurse clustering and OR 1.68 (95% CI 0.77-3.66; p = 0.190) for surgeon clustering. Per 1-point increase in the NRPC score, the adjusted OR was 0.70 (95% CI 0.48-1.02; p = 0.061). Conclusion Higher NRPC was associated with lower unadjusted rates of 30-day wound- and pin-site-related adverse events, but the association was attenuated and statistically imprecise after temporal and clinical adjustment. Similar directional estimates across sensitivity analyses support NRPC as an exploratory marker of broader perioperative process quality rather than as an independently established predictor or causal determinant of wound outcomes.

title: The Effect of Medication Self-Management During Hospitalisation (SelfMED) on Medication Adherence Post-Discharge in Oncology Patients with Polypharmacy: A Prospective, Exploratory, Single-Centre, Non-Randomised Pre-Post Intervention Study with Sequential Control and Intervention Cohorts.
abstract: Objectives : To evaluate the effect of in-hospital medication self-management (SelfMED) on medication adherence two months post-discharge in polymedicated oncology patients. Methods : A prospective, exploratory, single-centre non-randomised pre-post intervention study with sequential control and intervention cohorts was conducted. During a five-month control phase, patients received usual care, in which medication was managed by healthcare providers. In the subsequent five-month intervention phase, patients self-managed their medication during hospitalisation using the SelfMED procedure. SelfMED consists of: (1) an eligibility assessment for self-management, (2) a monitoring tool to follow up medication intake and detect problems and (3) a support tool for healthcare providers to assist patients with problems. Medication adherence was assessed two months post-discharge using pill counts and self-report. Secondary outcomes included self-management problems, medication knowledge, patient and healthcare provider satisfaction, workload and healthcare service utilisation. Results : Sixty-four patients completed the study (control: n = 34; intervention: n = 30). Two months post-discharge, patients in the intervention group were, on average, adherent to 74.5% of their prescribed medications, versus 59.1% in the control group (difference 15.4 percentage points; 95% CI -0.8 to 31.7). This difference was not statistically significant ( p = 0.062). Patients in the intervention group reported fewer medication self-management problems in their diaries (3.3% vs. 26.5%, p = 0.015) and more often felt adequately prepared for medication self-management at home (93.1% vs. 71.4%, p = 0.041). No differences were observed in medication knowledge, healthcare service utilisation, or workload. Conclusions : SelfMED did not significantly improve medication adherence after discharge but may support patients' preparedness for medication self-management at home. Given the small achieved sample size, these findings should be regarded as exploratory. Studies with larger samples and more diverse populations are needed to confirm these findings.

title: Cost-Utility and Clinical Impact of a Multicomponent Maternal Safety and High-Dependency Care Model in Three Colombian Caribbean Hospitals: A Before-and-After Study.
abstract: Background: Obstetric high-dependency units may improve rescue care when embedded within broader maternal safety strategies. Objective: To evaluate a multi-component maternal safety and technological strengthening model, including obstetric high-dependency capacity, across three Colombian Caribbean institutions with different governance models. Methods: We conducted a multisite before-and-after implementation evaluation within a Ministry-funded maternal safety project. The model was implemented in one private clinic and two public hospitals in La Guajira and Bolívar, Colombia, with staggered implementation and varying data maturity. Data sources included billing records, administrative databases, and monthly quality indicators. Costs, severe maternal morbidity indicators, and longitudinal quality metrics were analysed by institutional implementation window. Pandemic-period variation from 2018 to 2023 was treated descriptively. Interrupted time series analyses were performed where post-implementation data allowed. Findings: Implementation was associated with heterogeneous but generally favourable patterns. At Clínica CEDES, costs increased after implementation, while intensive care utilisation and several severe maternal morbidity indicators declined. At ESE Hospital San José de Maicao, mature post-implementation economic and conventional pre/post-clinical comparisons were unavailable; however, interrupted time series analyses showed favourable changes in longitudinal quality indicators, including reductions in weighted adverse outcome score (WAOS) level ( β = -8.30, P = 0.0016) and slope ( β = -1.20, P = 0.0064), adverse outcome index (AOI) level ( β = -1.13, P = 0.0032), and severity index (SI) slope ( β = -0.27, P = 0.030). ESE Hospital La Divina Misericordia showed mixed early clinical signals and descriptive quality improvement, but follow-up was limited. Conclusions: A multi-component maternal safety model including obstetric high-dependency capacity may improve maternal care in high-risk settings, although effects vary by institutional context. High-dependency units appear most effective as part of an integrated rescue system rather than isolated infrastructure.

title: Patient safety and health equity of AI-enabled triage tools in primary care: a systematic review.
abstract: Objectives This review synthesised real-world patient safety evidence for artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled triage tools in primary care and mapped whether safety has been examined across sociodemographic groups.Methods PubMed, Embase, Web of Science and Scopus were searched (January 2015–November 2025) with citation searching. Prospective studies evaluating AI triage tools in real-world primary care settings were eligible. Quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool; equity dimensions were mapped using PROGRESS-Plus. Random-effects meta-analysis pooled comparable proportion-based outcomes.Results Four studies were included; all evaluated rule-based or decision-tree tools as no machine learning or generative AI system met the eligibility criteria. Safe triage rates ranged from 81% to 97.6%, under-triage rates ranged from 2% to 17.2% and over-triage rates ranged from 8% to 29%. An exploratory random-effects meta-analysis of three studies (n=1303) gave a pooled safe triage proportion of 0.908 (95% CI 0.319 to 0.995) with substantial heterogeneity (I²=97.0%); given incompatible outcome definitions across studies, these estimates are hypothesis-generating rather than summary measures. No study analysed differential triage accuracy by any sociodemographic factor despite available demographic data.Discussion Safety outcomes were confined to technical performance proxies rather than direct measures of harm, and the absence of equity-stratified analysis may reflect a systemic evidence gap.Conclusion To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review to examine both real-world patient safety and equity of AI-enabled triage in primary care; findings may not extend to machine learning or generative AI systems. A Safety-Equity Evidence Mapping (SEEM) matrix and an evidence maturity framing are proposed to characterise this evidence and inform emerging consensus on evidence thresholds.PROSPERO registration number CRD420251179046.

title: Describing the patient trajectory for unplanned care in a region of Flanders, Belgium: A prospective observational study.
journal: The European journal of general practice
abstract: Background Demand for unplanned care in Belgium is high, placing pressure on both out-of-hours primary care facilities (OOHPCF) and emergency departments (ED). Understanding patient trajectories may help optimise care pathways and resource planning for planned and unplanned care. Objective To describe patient presentations and trajectories at OOHPCF and EDs in a region of Flanders, Belgium. Methods Data were collected in six EDs and three OOHPCF in the greater {redacted} region. All consultations were recorded during three randomly selected days in EDs and one full week in OOHPCF in 2024. Results A total of 1,469 ED and 857 OOHPCF consultations were analysed. In EDs, trauma was the most common presentation (32%), followed by ear, nose and throat (ENT) and dermatology conditions (22%). In OOHPCF, trauma and orthopaedic problems accounted for 20% of consultations, followed by ENT (17%) and dermatology (14%). Most ED patients (71%) were discharged home. Self-referral accounted for 65% of ED visits; these patients were generally younger and presented with lower-acuity conditions. One in five patients had consulted another healthcare provider within the previous week. Pain and worry were the main drivers for attendance. Attending clinicians in both settings considered up to one-third of consultations manageable in planned care. Conclusion Rather than restricting access or apportioning blame to patients, our findings indicate the need to reassess measures throughout planned and unplanned care pathways for timely access to the most appropriate care setting while maintaining patient safety and equitable access to services.

title: A semi-rapid deployment workflow to reduce device time in Evolut FX self-expanding transcatheter aortic valve implantation.
Integration of IoT-based healthcare devices within the smart grid architecture model: a conceptual framework with economic and energy assessment for elderly care in Europe.
abstract: Introduction This study investigates the integration of IoT-enabled medical devices within the Smart Grid Architecture Model (SGAM) to support elderly home-based care in Europe. The study develops a conceptual SGAM-IoT framework that maps healthcare devices, actors, communication pathways, and functions across the SGAM interoperability layers, domains, and zones, with particular attention to interoperability, data exchange and integration between the home environment, healthcare services, and energy-aware infrastructure. Methods The conceptual framework is complemented by a quantitative analytical assessment of the economic and energy implications of five commonly used home-monitoring devices: a pulse oximeter, blood pressure monitor, digital thermometer, smart ECG monitor, and blood glucose monitor. The assessment relies on secondary European healthcare data, literature, manufacturer information, and market-based estimates rather than primary empirical measurements or experimental deployment. Economic feasibility is examined through Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR), Net Present Value (NPV), and a three-scenario sensitivity analysis, while electricity consumption is estimated from rated device power and assumed operating time. Results Under the reference-scenario assumptions, the analysis produces a BCR of 2.75 and a positive NPV, while the sensitivity analysis indicates that the economic result remains positive under conservative assumptions. The revised energy assessment estimates a combined electricity consumption of approximately 0.12 kWh per month, confirming that the direct energy demand of the selected devices is marginal. Discussion These findings suggest that the main value of SGAM in this context lies not in device-level energy savings, but in providing a structured framework for interoperability, communication, data exchange, and integration with wider home-healthcare infrastructure. Potential benefits for continuity of care, autonomy and elderly well-being are discussed as expected implications requiring future empirical validation.

title: Stakeholder perspectives on adolescent sexual and reproductive health service utilization in Uganda's Busoga region: A qualitative study.
abstract: Background Adolescents in low- and middle-income countries face high rates of unintended pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and unmet sexual and reproductive health (SRH) needs. In Uganda, 24% of girls aged 15-19 years have begun childbearing, yet modern contraceptive prevalence among adolescents remains low (15%). These challenges are particularly severe in the Busoga region, where sociocultural norms, poverty, and limited health system capacity hinder access to adolescent-friendly SRH services. Despite national guidelines, utilization remains low. Few studies have triangulated perspectives from adolescents, health providers, and community/religious leaders. We explored stakeholder views to provide an integrated understanding of factors influencing adolescent SRH service utilization in Busoga, Uganda. Methods An exploratory qualitative study was conducted in Iganga and Bugweri districts. Four focus group discussions with 38 adolescents (13-19 years), stratified by sex, age group, and residence, and 12 key informant interviews with health providers and community leaders were conducted. Adolescents were recruited through peer networks, while key informants were purposively selected. Data were collected (November-December 2024), transcribed verbatim, and analyzed inductively using thematic analysis with NVivo 14. Ethical approval and informed consent/assent were obtained. Results Adolescents, health providers, and community stakeholders described SRH service utilization as shaped by adolescent motivation alongside persistent barriers. Adolescents showed strong preventive intent, but uptake was limited by misconceptions about contraception, fears of infertility, long distances, lack of privacy, negative provider attitudes, and commodity stock-outs. Providers and community leaders echoed concerns around misinformation, limited parental guidance, moral norms, and structural constraints. All stakeholders converged on the need for confidential, accessible, and peer- and community-based adolescent SRH services. Conclusion Adolescents in Busoga are motivated to use SRH services, but intersecting sociostructural and system barriers limit utilization. Strengthening adolescent-friendly services, improving provider responsiveness, addressing misinformation, and expanding community-based delivery are essential to enhance equitable access.

title: Health Economic & Implementation Determinants of Prehospital Stroke Triage Tools: A Systematic Review.
journal: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
abstract: Rationale Effective prehospital stroke triage enables faster treatment and better patient outcomes. Although prehospital triage innovations are rapidly emerging, evidence regarding the balance between costs and benefits as well as implementation issues remains limited. Aims and objectives This review aims to synthesise published evidence on health economics and implementation determinants of prehospital triage tools for acute suspected ischaemic stroke patients. Method A systematic search was conducted across five databases (CINAHL, Cochrane, EMBASE, PubMed, and Web of Science) between 1995 and 2025. Results were reported narratively, and reporting quality was assessed using CHEERS, STROBE-simulation, COREQ, CONSORT, SQUIRE, and GRAMMS. Included were empirical studies of EMS-operated prehospital triage innovations for acute suspected stroke patients. The main outcome measures were health economic outcomes (e.g., ICER) and system-level implementation determinants (CFIR constructs). Results From 6491 screened studies, thirty-one were included: thirteen studies included health economic outcomes and eighteen reported implementation determinants. Prehospital triage tools assessed were: MSU (n = 14), telemedicine (n = 13), clinimetrics (n = 1), prehospital MRI (n = 1), biomarkers (n = 1), and an AI-based microwave tool (n = 1). Most studies (68%) were of high reporting quality.
