The Congress was preceded by a dedicated pre-congress session focused on education, research, and clinical practice, with particular attention to the involvement of nursing students and early-career professionals in scientific activities. Across plenary sessions, round tables, workshops, oral communications, and digital poster presentations, the scientific programme addressed major areas of contemporary nephrology nursing, including professional development, patient-centred care, vascular access management, dialysis technologies, kidney transplantation, symptom management, home and community care, digital health, artificial intelligence, sustainability, and nutritional care. Particular attention was given to the integration of evidence-based practice, clinical expertise, technological innovation, interprofessional collaboration, and patient education. This Conference Proceedings provides an overview of the scientific and educational activities of the meeting and brings together the accepted contributions presented during both the pre-congress session and the main Congress. Collectively, these contributions illustrate the diversity and continued development of nephrology nursing practice and research in Italy and highlight the importance of scientific societies in promoting professional competence, knowledge exchange, and innovation in kidney care.

title: Challenges in the Transition of Patients with Rare Diseases from Pediatric to Adult Care: Toward an Individualized, Person-Centered Model.
abstract: Rare diseases (RDs) collectively affect millions of people in the European Union, and advances in early diagnosis, neonatal screening, and treatment mean that increasing numbers of patients with childhood-onset RDs now reach adulthood, often with chronic sequelae and complex, long-term care needs. Transition from pediatric to adult care is therefore a critical juncture, yet it remains, in most healthcare systems, an insufficiently structured in many healthcare systems. We performed a targeted narrative review that examines the concept of biomedical literature and relevant institutional sources, prioritizing rare-disease-specific evidence while identifying evidence extrapolated from other chronic childhood-onset conditions. We examine the distinction between transition and administrative transfer; the barriers involving healthcare systems, professionals, patients, and families; and the heterogeneous evidence regarding transition outcomes. We propose a literature-informed conceptual framework centered on early identification, assessment of readiness and clinical and psychosocial complexity, named coordination, structured handover, supported decision-making, and active post-transfer follow-up. These elements support a personalized approach in which timing, intensity, professional involvement, and patient and caregiver support are adapted to individual needs rather than chronological age or diagnosis alone. European Reference Networks, patient organizations, and national support frameworks may facilitate implementation. Structured, individualized transition pathways may preserve continuity of care, treatment adherence, and patient experience, although effects on healthcare utilization and clinical outcomes require prospective evaluation.

title: Improving paediatric quality of care through a Sweden-Uganda twinning partnership - reflections on implementation and early experiences from the child thrive project.
abstract: Despite major global progress in child health, significant inequalities remain between low- and high-income countries. In Uganda's Busoga region, child mortality is still high, largely due to preventable conditions and limited healthcare resources. In response, a paediatric health partnership was established in 2021 between the Busoga region and Stockholm, Sweden. Following a quality-of-care assessment in two Ugandan hospitals, the collaboration identified four priority areas: paediatric emergency care, neonatology, child neurology with a focus on epilepsy, and child rights. Over 3 years, 63 staff exchanges have taken place, enabling joint reviews of clinical practices and identification of improvement needs. A key achievement is the implementation of the WHO Emergency Triage, Assessment and Treatment Plus (ETAT+), supported by training 14 national facilitators who now serve as focal persons in their facilities. Initiatives in neonatology have strengthened early interventions for premature and low birth weight infants such as improved nursing care, infection prevention, and nutrition practices. In neurology, the introduction of an epilepsy registry and education programmes has reduced stigma and improved management. The child rights initiative has trained more than 80 ambassadors and fostered child-friendly hospital environments that promote participation. The in-hospital mortality dropped over the project period (2020-2025) from 26.4% to 21.7% for neonates ( p = 0.021) and from 3.8% to 2.8% ( p = <0.01) for children less than five outside the neonatal period. Despite resource constraints, the partnership has benefited both regions. This twinning model highlights how equitable international collaborations can sustainably advance child health and reinforce healthcare systems in diverse settings.

title: Development and validation of a questionnaire assessing nurses' negative emotional responses to single-checking medications: a cross-sectional survey in Japanese university hospitals.
abstract: Objectives Medication errors are a major patient safety concern, and double-checking is a commonly used method to mitigate risks during administration. Despite its questionable efficacy, Japanese hospitals are reluctant to transition to single-checking, particularly due to nurses’ resistance. This study developed and psychometrically evaluated a questionnaire assessing nurses’ negative emotional responses to single-checking medications to enable targeted interventions aimed at easing their resistance. Design Cross-sectional survey, with multisource questionnaire development and psychometric validation. Setting Three Japanese university hospitals. Surveys were distributed in September–October 2023. Participants Full-time registered nurses working in inpatient wards, not in management positions, with more than 1 year of experience. Of 1861 questionnaires distributed, 1224 (66%) were analysed. Outcome measures Psychometric evaluation included exploratory factor analysis (EFA), internal consistency reliability (Cronbach’s α), convergent validity against the Japanese version of the State–Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) and known-groups validity across levels of nursing experience and duration of single-checking practice. Results EFA (maximum-likelihood extraction, Promax rotation) supported a final four-factor, 18-item solution (Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin=0.947, 64.6% variance explained). Factors were as follows: lack of self-confidence (α=0.92), fear of error due to situational factors (α=0.84), fear of being held responsible (α=0.91) and fear of being perceived as inadequate (α=0.80). Items were scored 1–5, with higher scores indicating stronger negative emotional responses; factor means ranged from 2.23 to 3.23. Correlations with the STAI were low-to-moderate (r=0.23–0.45), supporting convergent validity while indicating the questionnaire is not simply a proxy for state and trait anxiety. Known-groups validity was supported: early-career nurses scored 11.1 points higher than experienced nurses (d=0.85, p<0.001), with similar patterns for recent versus veteran single-checkers (d=0.67, p<0.001)—all exceeding the prespecified minimal important difference. Conclusions The questionnaire demonstrates promising preliminary reliability and validity for assessing nurses’ negative emotional responses towards single-checking medications. Its factor structure could allow targeted interventions to address resistance during the transition to single-checking.

title: From 'Little Things' to 'Seagulls': A Mixed Methods Exploration of Patients' Experiences of Person-Centred Compassionate Care in General Medical and Surgical Wards.
journal: Health expectations : an international journal of public participation in health care and health policy
abstract: Background Person-centred compassionate care (PCCC) shapes the quality of relationships between health care professionals (HCPs) and patients, influences how healthcare is experienced, and ultimately can impact patient outcomes and HCP satisfaction. There is limited evidence about patient perspectives of multidisciplinary PCCC in acute general medical and surgical wards. Objective This study aimed to explore patients' perceptions of PCCC to inform co-design of an intervention to enhance PCCC in general medical and surgical wards. Methods Sixty (60) inpatients on a general medical or general surgical ward completed the Sinclair Compassion Questionnaire (SCQ) three times-considering their interactions with doctors, nurses, and allied health separately. They also completed five qualitative questions about PCCC. An additional 20 patients or their carers were interviewed exploring the same five topic areas. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to analyse qualitative data. Results The median SCQ score was high (4.5; SEM = 0.05) indicating that participants perceived high levels of compassion from HCPs during their hospital admission. Fewer than 20 per cent (17.9%) of the SCQ scores were less than 4 out of 5 and more than half (51.2%) were 4.5 or higher. Analysis revealed no significant differences (p = 0.066) between professional groups (Doctors: median = 4.2, SEM = 0.10; Nurses: median = 4.75, SEM = 0.07; Allied Health: median = 4.25, SEM = 0.09). There were no significant differences in scores (p > 0.01) by ward type, length of stay, cultural diversity, or disability. Females rated allied health staff as significantly higher on SCQ (median = 4.9, SEM = 0.1) than males (median = 4, SEM = 0.15) (p = 0.003). Qualitative responses indicated many recommendations to enhance care. From 'little things' to 'seagulls' was a phrase co-created by the research team to encapsulate the range of participant perspectives across the themes. Co-produced themes and key messages to staff focussed on being in the moment, finding out about the whole patient and their journey, partnering with the patient to the level they choose, knowing that patients make allowances for the pressures on staff, and that small acts of kindness are critical to the patient experience. Conclusion This co-produced research privileged the voice of a diverse group of patients and provided new and actionable insights regarding PCCC across HCPs in acute hospital general medical and general surgical wards. Findings emphasised that SCQ scoring was a useful 'temperature check' regarding PCCC indicating that some improvements were needed. However, there may be a ceiling effect for the tool which requires further research. Qualitative data indicated where improvements were needed.

title: Training and Experiential Factors Associated With Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Referral Readiness Among Psychiatric Providers.
abstract: Objective Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is an established treatment for patients with treatment-resistant depression (TRD); however, barriers remain in clinical practice. This study examined how psychiatric clinicians view TMS and evaluated whether training exposure and prior experience were associated with their readiness to refer patients for treatment. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey of psychiatric providers in Florida, including attending psychiatrists, psychiatry residents, and psychiatric nurse practitioners. The survey assessed beliefs about TMS effectiveness, comfort discussing and referring the treatment, familiarity with referral processes, and perceived barriers. Responses were dichotomized to reflect endorsement, and group differences were analyzed using chi-square or Fisher exact tests. Results Ninety-four clinicians completed the survey. Conceptual endorsement of TMS was high, with more than 90% agreeing that it is an effective treatment for depression. Operational readiness was more variable, particularly for referral comfort, counseling confidence, and knowledge of referral pathways. Prior TMS training and prior TMS recommendation experience were associated with greater comfort referring patients, greater confidence counseling patients, and higher awareness of referral steps. Psychiatry residents reported lower referral-pathway awareness than attending psychiatrists. Insurance coverage and treatment costs were frequently reported barriers, and lack of training was a commonly endorsed modifiable barrier. Conclusions While psychiatric providers widely accepted TMS conceptually, operational readiness to counsel and refer was more variable. Training exposure and prior TMS recommendation experience were associated with greater confidence, comfort, and familiarity with referral pathways, although causality cannot be inferred from this cross-sectional design. These findings suggest that efforts to improve utilization should emphasize building operational competence and confidence, along with clearer referral workflows and accessible system-level processes.

title: Nurse-Led Longitudinal Screening and Care Transitions for Post-Traumatic Stress Symptoms After Acute Type A Aortic Dissection: A 12-Month Retrospective Longitudinal Cohort Study.
abstract: Objective To identify longitudinal trajectories of post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) after acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD) and to examine baseline and time-varying psychological factors associated with subsequent symptom burden in a nurse-led follow-up cohort. Methods This single-center retrospective longitudinal cohort study included 278 ATAAD survivors discharged from Henan Provincial Chest Hospital between 1 August 2023 and 30 July 2024. Clinical and nurse-led follow-up records through 1 August 2025 were reviewed for assessments at discharge and at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months. The primary trajectory analysis used PCL-5 scores from 1 to 12 months among participants with at least two valid assessments. One- through four-class latent class mixed models were compared according to convergence, Bayesian information criterion, classification quality, and minimum class size. Baseline correlates were examined with multinomial regression. Lagged models separated between-person means from within-person changes in illness threat, insomnia, and repetitive negative thinking; social support was examined across the 3-to-6-month interval. Results A three-class solution was selected: low-decreasing (n=153, 55.0%), recovering (n=77, 27.7%), and persistent-high (n=48, 17.3%). Within-person increases in illness threat, insomnia, and repetitive negative thinking were associated with higher subsequent PCL-5 scores, whereas higher social support was associated with a lower subsequent score. Baseline associations were attenuated after multiplicity correction. Conclusion The model identified three PTSS trajectories during the first year after ATAAD discharge. Repeated nurse-led assessment may help identify survivors with a persistent symptom burden, and changes in illness threat, insomnia, repetitive negative thinking, and social support may inform the timing and focus of transitional care. The effectiveness of screening or targeted care was not tested.

title: Implementation of a universal psychosocial screening program across the pediatric cancer treatment trajectory: a standard of care.
journal: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer
abstract: Purpose Guided by Rapid Evaluation and Assessment Methods (REAM) and using rigorous quality improvement processes, we describe implementation of an evidence-based psychosocial screening program at key transitions in childhood cancer treatment to guide care matched to need. Methods Pediatric cancer patients (≥ 11 years) and caregivers (patients 0-17 years) were offered screening questionnaires electronically at 4-6 months, 18-24 months, and 4-6 years post-diagnosis through a phased implementation across three cancer center sites and in their preferred language (English, Spanish, Arabic). Screening questionnaires assessed cancer-related symptoms, health-related quality of life, cognitive function and school needs, caregiver adjustment and family risk, and resource needs. To assess adoption, feasibility, penetration, and sustainability, data related to screening processes, documentation completion rates, and adaptations were tracked and summarized. Qualitative interviews with patients, caregivers, and clinicians, based on the Consolidated Framework for Intervention Research (CFIR), were coded for acceptability and screening program optimization. Results Across sites and timepoints, from June 2023 through November 2025, there was a 56% screening completion rate (470/846). Patient physical functioning, emotional functioning, and neurocognitive functioning, caregiver adjustment, and resource needs were consistently flagged for follow-up. Documentation of follow-up varied with rates of 74% for social workers and 34% for medical clinicians. Patients, caregivers, and clinicians endorsed moderate acceptability. Barriers to electronic health record integration complicated clinician workflows. From initiation, over 2 years, 55 adaptations were made to improve workflow, implementation strategies, screening processes, and measures. Conclusion We achieved development, implementation, and optimization of a psychosocial screening program across our cancer center.

title: Evaluation of a Clinical Protocol-Guided Chatbot to Support Telecarers in Diabetes Management: Embedded Mixed Methods Study.
abstract: Background Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a chronic condition that requires ongoing self-management. While chatbots offer scalable monitoring and management, evidence on their integration into structured hospital tele-support workflows, where patient engagement and digital readiness may differ from those in standalone digital interventions, remains limited. Objective This study aimed to describe the design of a clinical protocol-guided chatbot, Sharing Information with Users on Diabetes Actions and Interventions ( Siu Dai ), and evaluate its feasibility, usability, and acceptability among patients and telecarers within a hospital tele-support program. Methods We used an embedded mixed methods design (QUAL [quan]) guided by the World Health Organization (WHO) monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions and the theoretical framework of acceptability. Through a co-design process involving clinicians, researchers, telecarers, and developers, the chatbot was aligned with established clinical protocols. It featured 7 precall sessions designed to collect patient data, generate summary reports for staff, and deliver targeted educational content. Patients (≥21-year-old individuals with T2DM) and telecarer nurses (with experience ≥6 mo) were recruited from an existing tele-support program. Data sources included interviews, online surveys (5-point Likert scale), and chatbot usage logs. Qualitative data were analyzed thematically; quantitative data were summarized descriptively to supplement and contextualize the qualitative findings. Results Fourteen participants (7 patients and 7 telecarers) completed both interviews and surveys and were included in the analysis. Patients (mean age 45.3, SD 15.4 y) had a median diabetes duration of 10 (IQR 3-25; range 1-30) years, and all were digitally literate. Telecarers had a median of 5 (IQR 4-9) years of telehealth experience. Quantitatively, patients showed high engagement, completing 79% of started sessions with a median completion time of 2 minutes and 58 seconds. Patient satisfaction was high, with 86% (6/7) willing to recommend the tool; however, telecarer endorsement for universal rollout to patients in other clinical programs or outpatient clinics was more cautious (3/7, 43%). Qualitative findings revealed 5 themes: (1) perceptions of chatbot usability, (2) alignment and integration into telecarers' processes, (3) factors influencing acceptability of the chatbot, (4) perceived efficacy of the chatbot for T2DM self-management and care delivery, and (5) suggested improvements and enhancements. Integrated findings revealed that the chatbot was usable and functioned as a precall support tool that optimized the personalization of tele-support sessions. However, its perceived efficacy in self-management behavior was limited by this cohort's extensive experience with T2DM management. Key barriers to adoption included administrative burden for telecarers due to a lack of electronic medical record integration and content redundancy for patients. Suggested enhancements included multilingual support and adaptive content catering to different levels of disease-specific literacy. Conclusions A clinical protocol-guided chatbot is feasible for hospital tele-support, complementing rather than replacing human care. It automates routine assessments and reinforces education, but future iterations must prioritize workflow integration and adaptive content to sustain engagement.

title: Three Ambient Listening Systems in Simulated Dutch-Language Multispeaker and Multidialect Clinical Encounters: Comparative Study.
abstract: Background Clinicians spend a lot of time on electronic health record (EHR) documentation, often at the expense of direct patient interaction. Ambient listening technology uses AI to passively record and summarize clinical encounters. Although early studies are promising, there is limited evidence on system performance in complex, non-English settings. Objective This study aimed to compare the documentation performance of 3 commercially available ambient listening systems in simulated Dutch-language outpatient consultations by assessing note completeness, correctness, and conciseness under predefined linguistic and interactional challenges. Methods Standardized audio recordings of 10 scripted physician-patient interactions across 2 specialties were used. Scenarios included multispeaker dynamics (patient companion), conversational disruptions (nurse interruption), evasive patient communication, and a regional dialect (Gronings). Three ambient listening providers (provider 1, provider 2, and provider 3) processed the audio files. Generated notes were divided into 4 note sections: patient history, physical examination, diagnostic impression, and treatment plan. For each system output, each note section was scored for completeness, conciseness, and correctness using a 5-point ordinal scale against physician-developed reference summaries. In total, 8 clinicians participated in scoring: 4 junior clinicians evaluated all outputs, and 4 senior clinicians each reviewed a subset of scenarios. Analyses were based on 351 rater-averaged section-domain scores. Interrater agreement was assessed using Gwet agreement coefficient 2 (Gwet AC-2). System-level technical characteristics were assessed alongside clinical performance to aid interpretation of between-provider differences. Results Across 351 rater-averaged section-domain scores on a 5-point scale, overall interrater agreement was high (Gwet AC-2=0.827). Provider-level mean scores ranged from 3.82 to 4.26 (4.26, SD 0.73 for provider 3, 4.00, SD 0.90 for provider 2, and 3.82, SD 1.07 for provider 1). Mean scores were higher in otolaryngology than in surgical oncology (4.36, SD 0.56 vs 3.68, SD 1.10). Across scoring domains, correctness received the highest mean score (4.21, SD 0.98), while completeness received the lowest (3.81, SD 0.90). Variation in mean scores was observed across script scenarios. Dialect-containing scenarios had the lowest mean score overall (3.77, SD 1.21), although this pattern was not uniform across specialties and systems. Median summary generation times ranged from 13.5 seconds (IQR 12-15; provider 3) to 22.0 seconds (IQR 18-24; provider 2). Conclusions Ambient listening systems demonstrated generally strong performance in this simulated Dutch-language evaluation, including under several common conversational challenges. However, mean scores varied across scripted scenarios, with lower scores observed in some dialect-containing and otherwise challenging interactions. Future deployment studies must prioritize linguistic equity, real-world validation of efficiency gains, and evaluation of both clinician and patient perceptions to understand how these systems influence consultation dynamics and care delivery across diverse patient populations.

Accessing Care and Treatment in the Emergency Department for Self-Harm and Suicidal Ideation: A Qualitative Study of Service Users' Experiences.
journal: International journal of mental health nursing
abstract: Despite the availability of guidelines and protocols, service users' experiences of accessing care and treatment for self-harm and suicidal ideation at the Emergency Department (ED) are variable. There is a need to better understand what impacts service user experiences given the important role of the ED for accessing care and influencing future interactions with mental health services for people who experience self-harm and suicidal distress. This study aimed to identify the experiences of service users when presenting to the ED with self-harm and suicidal ideation. A descriptive qualitative approach was utilised encompassing in depth semi-structured interviews with 50 adult service users who attended EDs across the Republic of Ireland for self-harm and suicidal ideation. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings are reported in accordance with COREQ guidelines and focus on three themes that were developed from the data: (1) Experiences of assessment, (2) Interpersonal interactions, (3) Discharge, onward referral and next steps to care. Participant experiences of care and treatment in the ED were largely negative with reports of an over-reliance on mechanistic assessments, poor interpersonal interactions and lack of support following discharge from the ED. The use of evidence-based protocols is important to ensure standardised and effective care and treatment of people attending the ED with self-harm and suicidal ideation. However, a relational approach needs to underpin their use to ensure that service users feel respected and listened to by all staff in the ED, and more positively inclined towards future help-seeking.

title: Extent of Digital Health Fragmentation and Potential Implications for Antimicrobial Prescribing: Rapid Evidence Review.
abstract: Background Prior microbiology results, resistance patterns, and antimicrobial exposure are central to safe and effective antimicrobial prescribing. Digital health fragmentation refers to the dispersal of patient data across multiple electronic systems and the associated challenge of accessing complete information at the point of care. Antimicrobial prescribing for infections represents a critical use case to investigate the impact of digital health fragmentation on patient care. While interoperability has been studied in the context of patient safety, no review has described digital health fragmentation within the United Kingdom and examined its impact on antimicrobial prescribing and antimicrobial stewardship (AMS). Objective This study aimed to (1) characterize the extent of digital health fragmentation in the United Kingdom, (2) summarize the available evidence on its impact on AMS and prescribing practices in high-income countries, and (3) identify potential solutions. Methods A rapid review of the peer-reviewed literature was conducted following published guidance for rapid reviews and the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) statement. MEDLINE ALL and PsycInfo were searched on August 19, 2025, using search terms relating to digital health fragmentation or interoperability, patient safety, and antimicrobial use. Searches were limited to English-language publications from 2015 (for characterizing the recent trends or current state of digital health fragmentation in the United Kingdom) or 2010 onward (for AMS-related impacts and solutions). Screening was conducted by 4 researchers following predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Extracted data were synthesized narratively through framework analysis. Study quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Results Fourteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Ten studies described the extent and nature of digital health fragmentation in the United Kingdom. Digital health fragmentation affects a large number of patients and is linked to clinical care efficiency, quality, and safety risks, including limited access to external clinical records, missing or incomplete information, duplicate investigations, delays in decision‑making, and substantial time spent searching for data. Evidence specific to antimicrobial prescribing was limited (4 studies) but indicated that AMS relies on information spread across multiple systems, with poor interoperability disrupting workflows, hindering communication, and undermining stewardship activities. Only 1 study reported the development of a digital tool designed to address digital health fragmentation and support AMS. Conclusions Digital health fragmentation negatively affects patient care across the United Kingdom, yet evidence on how it impacts AMS remains scarce. Given the urgency of the global antimicrobial resistance crisis, future research should therefore quantify the scale and impact of digital health fragmentation for AMS to inform investment and innovation in digital infrastructure and clinical-supportive solutions. Trial registration PROSPERO CRD420251126067; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251126067.

title: Real-World Implementation and Evaluation of a Digital Health Platform for Children Living With Type 1 Diabetes: Protocol for a Real-World Implementation Study.
abstract: Background Digital platforms that integrate continuous glucose monitoring, patient-generated data, and clinical decision support could enable more proactive pediatric type 1 diabetes (T1D) care. Sustained uptake of digital platforms in routine practice is limited, and the evidence of effectiveness is mixed. Implementation science approaches are needed to clarify how context, workflows, and strategies shape adoption and outcomes. Haibu Diabetes is a new platform that brings together wearable, patient-reported, and clinical diabetes data to generate personalized, data-driven insights for patients and clinicians. Objective This study evaluates the clinical effectiveness and implementation processes of Haibu Diabetes in routine pediatric T1D care using a hybrid design guided by an Implementation Research Logic Model. Methods We will conduct a nonrandomized, quasi-experimental, type 2 hybrid implementation-effectiveness trial at a hospital that provides multidisciplinary pediatric diabetes care. Youth aged 3 to less than 18 years with T1D and caregivers will be onboarded to Haibu Diabetes as part of routine workflows; health care providers will use a clinician dashboard to review data, assign tasks/forms, and communicate asynchronously. Effectiveness analyses will compare Haibu Diabetes users to a matched control group drawn from the BC Pediatric Diabetes Registry. Effectiveness outcomes are hemoglobin A 1c , continuous glucose monitoring device-derived time in range over 12 months, and diabetes self-care behaviors. Implementation outcomes will be assessed using mixed methods guided by an Implementation Research Logic Model that links determinants, implementation strategies, mechanisms, and outcomes. These outcomes will include reach, adoption, feasibility, acceptability, and maintenance. Health care improvement outcomes will include patient and caregiver experience, clinician experience, and operational workflow indicators. Results Study funding commenced in January 2023. Patient recruitment began in September 2026, and 7 participants had consented as of October 2026. Data collection is anticipated to conclude by December 2027, with analysis to follow. Study findings are expected to be published in summer 2028. Conclusions This trial will generate real-world evidence on both effectiveness and the conditions required to implement and sustain a data-integrating digital platform in pediatric T1D care, informing scale-up and optimization.

title: Bridging the Awareness-Action Gap in Disaster Preparedness: A Qualitative Study of Immersive Virtual Reality Learning Among Nursing Students.
abstract: Background Disasters increasingly challenge healthcare systems, highlighting the need to strengthen preparedness among future healthcare professionals. Although disaster risk awareness is important, it does not consistently translate into preparedness behaviours, reflecting the awareness-action gap. Immersive virtual reality (VR) may enhance experiential disaster learning, but how it influences preparedness processes remains insufficiently understood, particularly in healthcare and critical care education. Aims To explore how immersive VR-based disaster simulations influence disaster risk perception and preparedness among nursing students, with particular attention to the awareness-action gap and implications for future healthcare and critical care practice. Study design A qualitative descriptive study using immersive VR-based disaster simulations followed by semi-structured interviews. Twelve undergraduate and graduate nursing students in Japan experienced immersive VR simulations depicting floods and landslides. Individual semi-structured interviews explored emotional responses, disaster risk perception, preparedness awareness and anticipated behavioural responses. Data were analysed using Krippendorff's content analysis with researcher triangulation. Results Five categories were identified: (1) heightened vulnerability and psychological burden through immersion; (2) persistence of the awareness-action gap despite increased risk perception; (3) enhanced risk recognition and preparedness intentions; (4) recognition of the need for social and structural support systems; and (5) emerging responsibility accompanied by perceived limitations. VR transformed abstract disaster risk into emotionally salient experiences, strengthening threat appraisal and preparedness awareness; however, awareness did not consistently translate into preparedness behaviours, reflecting insufficient coping appraisal and self-efficacy. Conclusions Immersive VR may strengthen disaster risk perception and preparedness awareness, but immersive experiences alone may be insufficient to bridge the awareness-action gap. Combining VR with reflective learning, skills-based training and collaborative simulation may strengthen coping appraisal and preparedness action. Relevance to clinical practice Immersive VR combined with reflective and skills-based learning may support psychological readiness, situational awareness and disaster preparedness competencies among future nurses, including those preparing for critical care practice.

title: Implementing Routine Mental Health Screening and Structured Follow-up for Youth With Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis: A Single-center Quality Improvement Project.
abstract: Introduction Youth with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) have higher rates of anxiety and depression, yet pediatric rheumatology clinics rarely embed systematic mental health care into routine care. Unrecognized symptoms can impair physical functioning and disease management. The objectives of this quality improvement initiative were to increase (1) anxiety/depression screening from 0% to ≥75% and (2) algorithm-concordant follow-up for youth screening positive from 0% to ≥75%. Methods Our team implemented iterative plan-do-study-act cycles in a pediatric rheumatology clinic at McMaster Children's Hospital. A key driver diagram and fishbone analysis informed interventions, including workflow redesign, staff training, electronic medical record supports, and a standardized follow-up algorithm. We screened youth with JIA 12-18 years of age using the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4), an ultra-brief self-report tool used to detect anxiety and depression. Process measures included the percentage of eligible visits with PHQ-4 screening completed and the percentage of screened visits with documented algorithm-concordant follow-up. Outcome measures captured screening results while balancing measures assessed patient and healthcare provider acceptability. Results PHQ-4 screening increased from 0% to sustained percentages of ≥75% across 266 audited visits (May 2024-August 2025). Overall, 17% of youth screened positive (PHQ-4 ≥ 3). After implementing the follow-up algorithm, ≥75% of screened visits documented education, referral, and/or safety planning. Screening was acceptable to patients and health care providers, with no reported workflow disruption. Conclusions Embedding PHQ-4 screening with a structured follow-up pathway is feasible and sustainable in a pediatric rheumatology clinic, supporting timely and equitable identification of mental health needs and advancing integrated biopsychosocial care for youth with JIA.

title: Development and validation of the Environment-Technology-Task Model-based self-assessment scale for intraoperative rescue readiness among operating room nurses.
abstract: This study aimed to develop and validate a self-assessment scale based on the Environment-Technology-Task Model to evaluate operating room nurses' readiness for intraoperative rescue and to evaluate its psychometric properties. A methodological study focusing on the development and psychometric validation of the scale was conducted. The initial item pool was generated through an integrative literature review (11 core articles) and field observations of 7 real intraoperative rescue videos. A 2-round Delphi consultation with 20 experts, followed by pilot testing, was carried out to refine the items. Subsequently, a survey of 280 operating room nurses was performed to evaluate construct validity using exploratory factor analysis and to assess reliability. The final 21-item scale comprised 3 dimensions: task (11 items), environment (5 items), and technology (5 items). Exploratory factor analysis confirmed the 3-factor structure, explaining 73.83% of the total variance. Content validity was satisfactory (item-level content validity index: 0.875-1.000; scale-level content validity index, averaging method: 0.932). Internal consistency was high (Cronbach α = 0.970 for the total scale; 0.962, 0.912, and 0.865 for the 3 subscales). Split-half reliability was 0.931, and test-retest reliability was 0.847 for the total scale (0.725-0.872 across the subscales). The Environment-Technology-Task Model-based scale showed high internal consistency, a theoretically coherent 3-factor structure, and acceptable-to-good temporal stability. It is the first instrument specifically designed to assess operating room nurses' intraoperative rescue readiness, and it holds practical utility for self-assessment, targeted training, and quality improvement initiatives to enhance perioperative patient safety.

title: Coenzyme Q10 for Acute Stanford Type A Aortic Dissection: Protocol for a Prospective, Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Single-Center Feasibility Trial.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Acute Stanford type A aortic dissection (TAAD) is a catastrophic cardiovascular emergency. Emergency surgery is the standard life-saving treatment, but some patients decline operative repair, and no established pharmacological therapy has been shown to stabilize acute TAAD. Preclinical work by our team implicates mitochondrial dysfunction and smooth muscle cell phenotypic switching in aortic dissection and suggests that coenzyme Q10 may reduce dissection-related injury. This study aims to determine the feasibility of a future definitive randomized trial and to obtain preliminary safety and exploratory efficacy information. Methods: This prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-center feasibility trial will enroll 60 adults with CTA-confirmed Stanford type A aortic dissection within 24 h of symptom onset who decline emergency surgical repair after standard surgical counseling. Participants will be randomized 1:1 to oral coenzyme Q10 100 mg three times daily or matched placebo for 14 days, in addition to the same guideline-directed supportive medical care. The primary feasibility outcome is recruitment feasibility, defined as randomization of 60 participants within 12 months after recruitment initiation. Secondary feasibility outcomes include treatment adherence, follow-up completion, dropout, missingness, outcome-assessment feasibility, and candidate endpoint event rates. The primary exploratory clinical outcome is 14-day all-cause mortality; additional exploratory outcomes include aortic rupture death, false-lumen thrombosis, cardiac tamponade, worsening pericardial effusion, and organ malperfusion syndromes. Safety outcomes include adverse events, serious adverse events, adverse drug reactions, suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions, and prespecified laboratory indices. Results: The trial is designed to establish whether recruitment, blinded treatment delivery, follow-up, outcome collection, and safety monitoring are operationally feasible and to provide estimates for planning a larger confirmatory trial. Conclusions: This feasibility trial will inform the design and conduct of future definitive evaluation of coenzyme Q10 in acute TAAD. Trial registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2600123230.

title: Information needs and engagement profiles of adults undergoing ambulatory surgery: a qualitative study.
journal: International journal of nursing studies advances
abstract: Background Ambulatory surgery compresses preparation, treatment and discharge into a short period, followed by recovery at home. Information support must address emotional concerns, information preferences and ways of engaging with care. Although unmet information needs have been described, less is known about how these needs form recognisable engagement profiles. Objective To explore adult patients' information needs across the ambulatory surgery pathway and develop empirically informed engagement profiles to guide future personalised information support, this qualitative descriptive study recruited thirty-three adult patients through purposive maximum-variation sampling at an ambulatory surgery centre at a tertiary hospital in Eastern China from October to December 2025; nine caregivers of children interviewed in the original study were excluded from this analysis. Methods Individual semi-structured interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Thematic analysis identified information domains, followed by cross-case synthesis to construct exploratory engagement profiles from adult patient accounts. Results Six domains concerned disease and diagnosis, surgical procedures, anaesthesia, post-discharge care and follow-up, psychosocial and practical support, and information delivery preferences. Four non-exclusive profiles were constructed: Anxious Proceduralist, Guidance-Seeking User, Collaborative Learner and Pragmatic Self-Manager. These profiles describe differing preferences for procedural detail, clear guidance, dialogue and practical recovery support. Conclusions Similar information needs may be organised through different ways of engaging with care. The profiles offer preliminary, hypothesis-generating design tools for personalised information support. Refinement, item development, co-design and feasibility testing are required before clinical use. The findings concern adult patients and cannot be transferred directly to caregivers of children. Registration Not registered.

title: Mishel theory-based perioperative nursing after trabeculectomy for primary glaucoma: effects on illness uncertainty, self-management, and quality of life.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the effects of a perioperative nursing intervention based on Mishel's Uncertainty in Illness Theory in patients with primary glaucoma undergoing trabeculectomy. Methods This single-center, two-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled study enrolled 198 patients undergoing first trabeculectomy at The First Affiliated Hospital of Suzhou University between February 2024 and December 2025. Participants were randomly allocated 1:1 to routine perioperative ophthalmic nursing or routine care plus a structured Mishel theory-based nursing intervention. Assessments were conducted 1 day before surgery (T0), at discharge (T1), and at 1 month (T2) and 3 months (T3) after surgery. The primary outcome was illness uncertainty measured using the Mishel Uncertainty in Illness Scale. Secondary outcomes included psychological status, discharge readiness, self-management, medication adherence, sleep quality, vision-related quality of life, satisfaction with nursing care, postoperative ophthalmic outcomes, and complications. All randomized participants completed follow-up and were analyzed according to their assigned groups. Results After Holm adjustment, the intervention group had lower illness-uncertainty scores at T1, T2, and T3; lower anxiety scores at T1 and T3 and lower depression scores at T2 and T3; higher discharge-readiness and satisfaction-with-nursing-care at T1; higher self-management and medication-adherence scores and lower sleep-quality scores at T2 and T3; and lower GQL-15 scores at T3. At T3, the model-estimated between-group differences were -8.13 points for illness uncertainty (95% CI, -10.74 to -5.53), 5.64 points for self-management (95% CI, 4.08-7.19), 6.05 points for medication adherence (95% CI, 2.98-9.12), and -3.71 points for GQL-15 (95% CI, -5.41 to -2.00). At discharge, the between-group difference in discharge readiness was 1.23 points (95% CI, 0.99-1.47). No statistically significant between-group differences were detected in postoperative intraocular-pressure trajectories, visual-acuity recovery, medication-free status, postoperative procedures, or complications within 3 months. Conclusion In this single-center randomized study, Mishel theory-based perioperative nursing was associated with greater improvements in illness uncertainty and several psychological, behavioral, and recovery-related patient-reported outcomes after trabeculectomy. No statistically significant differences were detected in short-term objective ophthalmic outcomes or postoperative complications.

title: Psychological impact and resilience among healthcare workers following the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes: systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background Healthcare workers are uniquely vulnerable to psychological distress following large-scale disasters, through simultaneous exposure as survivors and responders. The 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes placed extraordinary demands on frontline health professionals in Türkiye. This mixed-methods systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesise quantitative and qualitative evidence on post-traumatic psychological outcomes and resilience strategies among healthcare workers following the earthquakes. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 and Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, we conducted a mixed-methods systematic review with convergent segregated synthesis. Nine sources (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, DergiPark, TR Dizin and Google Scholar) were searched for studies published between February 2023 and September 2025, supplemented by forward and backward citation chasing. Twenty studies met inclusion criteria (fifteen quantitative, five qualitative). Random-effects meta-analysis estimated pooled probable-PTSD prevalence and pooled resilience-distress correlations, with leave-one-out, risk-of-bias, instrument and population sensitivity analyses. Qualitative findings were synthesised thematically and integrated with quantitative results. Results Pooled prevalence of probable PTSD was 36.3% (95% CI 28.2-45.4), with high heterogeneity (I 2 = 86.2%). Prevalence was 43.8% (95% CI 36.1-51.9) among direct survivors and 19.5% (95% CI 3.5-61.8) among deployed responders, but the latter was imprecise and is not interpreted as an exposure effect. Measurement was one apparent contributor: two studies applying PCL-5 ≥ 47 agreed closely (39.0%, I 2 = 0.0%), but two applying IES-R ≥ 33 diverged widely (8.1 and 47.7%); measurement could not be separated from exposure, timing or sampling. Higher resilience, hardiness and adaptive coping were consistently associated with lower traumatic stress (pooled r = -0.42, 95% CI - 0.52 to -0.31, k = 4). Structural models indicated direct and coping-mediated associations, while fatigue and unmet basic needs predicted worse outcomes. Qualitative synthesis identified acute distress, secondary traumatisation, spirituality-based meaning-making, peer support and psychological distancing. Conclusion Healthcare workers following the Kahramanmaraş earthquakes experienced high levels of trauma-related distress, particularly those with direct exposure. Resilience and adaptive coping were consistently inversely associated with distress, although cross-sectional designs cannot establish direction of effect, and organizational conditions were strongly implicated. Disaster preparedness and recovery efforts must integrate individual, social, and structural interventions to safeguard healthcare workers' mental health. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251247026, identifier CRD420251247026.

title: Increasing Awareness and Identification of Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young in a Pediatric Diabetes Program.
abstract: Introduction Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) is frequently misdiagnosed, but an accurate diagnosis can inform tailored diabetes management. A quality improvement project was launched in 2022 at a pediatric tertiary care center to (1) increase MODY testing among individuals with islet autoantibody-negative (IAb-) new-onset diabetes mellitus (NODM) and (2) increase provider awareness of MODY. Methods Interventions targeted the primary drivers, including provider recognition of MODY and barriers to testing. Each month, an electronic medical record report identified patients with IAb- NODM diagnosed within the prior 3 months. A standardized previsit email was sent to the treating provider that (1) flagged IAb- status, (2) outlined MODY testing criteria, and (3) provided instructions for ordering genetic testing when indicated. The primary outcome, MODY tests ordered among eligible patients, was analyzed longitudinally using a control chart. Provider awareness of MODY and perceptions of the intervention were assessed in May 2023 and March 2024. Results The proportion of patients with IAb- NODM tested for MODY at a clinic visit within 365 days of diagnosis increased from 2.87% at baseline (January/February 2021-May/June 2022) to 9.94% after the quality improvement project launch in July/August 2022. Among completed tests through October 2025, 9 of 28 (32.1%) identified a pathogenic or likely pathogenic MODY variant. Providers' familiarity with MODY testing criteria also improved, with those reporting being "extremely familiar" increasing from 0% (0/20) to 17% (3/18). Conclusions The project, including the targeted previsit provider email, was associated with increased MODY testing and improved provider awareness in a pediatric diabetes clinic.

title: Comparison of three emergency department triage systems among Thai medical students: A randomized three-period crossover simulation study.
abstract: Introduction In Thailand, the Emergency Severity Index (ESI) and Ministry of Public Health Emergency Department triage system (MOPH) are commonly used, whereas the Thai Rapid Initial Assessment and Grading for Emergency (TRIAGE) system has been newly proposed. Comparative evidence is limited. We compared correct triage as the primary outcome, with under-triage, over-triage, and completion time as secondary outcomes. Methods We conducted a randomized three-period crossover simulation study at the Lampang Medical Education Center from October 2025 to January 2026. Fifth- and sixth-year medical students without recent standardized triage reinforcement classified 50 standardized patient cards per system in one of six sequences, with a one-week washout between periods. Multilevel mixed-effects models were used to estimate between-system differences, with adjustment for period, sequence, and academic year. Results Sixty students completed all periods. No significant overall differences were detected in correct triage across TRIAGE, ESI, and MOPH (63.2%, 64.5%, and 61.8%, respectively), or in under-triage (19.6%, 20.0%, and 18.8%). Among sixth-year students, correct triage differed significantly across systems (global P = 0.004), with higher adjusted probabilities for ESI and TRIAGE than MOPH. Over-triage differed across systems and was highest with MOPH (7.0%), followed by TRIAGE (5.7%) and ESI (4.9%). Completion time was longest with TRIAGE (32.8 minutes), compared with ESI (24.3 minutes) and MOPH (23.2 minutes). Conclusion No significant overall differences in correct or under-triage were detected, but the study was not powered to establish equivalence. MOPH showed higher over-triage, Completion time was longest with TRIAGE. Generalizability to experienced clinicians requires further study. Trial registration Thai Clinical Trials Registry (TCTR) TCTR20260316003.

title: Information gaps across care interfaces in home care and patient safety incidents: a cross-sectional survey of home care professionals in Finland.
abstract: ABSTRACT: OBJECTIVES: To examine the occurrence and severity of information gaps across care interfaces in home care networks and to identify priority interfaces for improving information continuity and patient safety. DESIGN: Cross-sectional survey study. SETTING: Four publicly funded home care organisations in Finland, covering approximately 22% of Finland’s long-term home care clients nationally. PARTICIPANTS: 555 home care professionals engaged in direct client care, including practical nurses, registered nurses, physicians and physiotherapists. PRIMARY OUTCOME MEASURES: Frequency of information gaps across 11 predefined care interfaces (reported as always, often, sometimes, seldom or never) and severity of associated patient safety incidents (near miss, minor/moderate or severe) in the past 3 months, reported by the participants based on their experience. RESULTS: The number of professionals working across the analysed interfaces ranged from 326 to 441. Information gaps were reported across all 11 interfaces, with those occurring always or often most frequently associated with emergency departments (21.5%), hospital discharge (19.1%) and private health centre (16.9%). Patient safety incidents were identified across all interfaces, particularly in relation to hospital discharge (44.1%) and emergency department (40.4%). Severe adverse events were most frequently reported in emergency care (4.3%), informal care (3.7%) and hospital discharge (3.4%), indicating variation in both occurrence and severity across interfaces. CONCLUSIONS: Information gaps and related patient safety incidents may concentrate at time-critical transitions but extend across the wider care network including informal care. These findings highlight system-level vulnerabilities and the need to prioritise safety-critical interfaces and strengthen information continuity in home care.

title: Retrospective Patient Perspectives on Symptom Burden, Emotional Experiences, and Unmet Needs in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma: A Qualitative Study.
abstract: Objective To explore how adults with nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) retrospectively described physical symptoms, emotional experiences, and unmet supportive care needs across diagnosis, active treatment, and home recovery in a Chinese tertiary-care setting. Methods This retrospective, cross-sectional qualitative descriptive study followed the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research. A purposive sample of 13 patients with pathologically confirmed NPC (7 men and 6 women; aged 28-64 years) was recruited from a tertiary hospital in central China between April and May 2026. Each participant completed one semi-structured, face-to-face interview lasting 30-45 minutes and recalled experiences across diagnosis, active treatment, and home recovery. Recruitment continued until three consecutive interviews yielded no new codes, subthemes, or contextual information. Data were analyzed using Colaizzi's seven-step procedure with NVivo 15.0. The themes were organized in a Patient Journey Map informed by Corbin and Strauss's Chronic Illness Trajectory Framework. Results Three themes and nine subthemes described distinct phase-specific experiences. At diagnosis, participants reported misattribution of early symptoms, diagnostic shock, role disruption, and unmet information needs. During active treatment, co-occurring oral mucositis, xerostomia, dysphagia, fatigue, body-image concerns, and reduced access to support at night contributed to substantial distress. During home recovery, persistent symptoms, uncertainty about rehabilitation, difficulty resuming daily roles, and fear of cancer recurrence remained prominent, although some participants also described renewed engagement in valued activities. Conclusion Participants' retrospective accounts identified phase-specific supportive-care gaps at diagnosis, during active treatment, and after discharge. The findings support structured diagnostic communication, coordinated management of co-occurring symptoms with accessible out-of-hours support, and transitional follow-up that includes rehabilitation guidance and psychological screening. Because the study used one retrospective interview per participant at a single center, the findings should be interpreted as a qualitative synthesis rather than evidence of a longitudinal or quantitative pattern.

title: Patient Experiences of Access, Stigma, and Trust and Preferences for Non-Opioid Drug Delivery Systems in Chronic Pain Management.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Chronic pain is common in Saudi Arabia, where opioid analgesics are prescribed and dispensed within a tightly regulated, electronically monitored controlled-substance framework. Qualitative evidence on how patients experience restrictive access comes almost entirely from high-consumption countries; to our knowledge, no study has examined these experiences among Saudi adults with chronic non-cancer pain or linked them to how patients appraise non-opioid alternatives. This study explored opioid access, stigma and therapeutic trust among adults with chronic non-cancer pain in Al-Ahsa and examined the anticipated acceptability of non-opioid drug-delivery systems. Methods: A qualitative interview study was conducted across seven public and private health settings in Al-Ahsa (May-June 2026). Thirty adults with chronic non-cancer pain were purposively sampled for maximum variation; 12 clinicians were also interviewed to contextualise the service conditions patients described, with patient accounts remaining the analytic focus. Sample adequacy was judged using information power, i.e., the capacity of a specific sample and focused dialogue to address a narrow aim. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis and reported according to COREQ. Results: Four themes were constructed: navigating a restricted access pathway ("A door with many locks"); enacted and anticipated stigma ("As if I came to steal"); institutional distrust alongside trust in individual clinicians ("The person, not the system"); and conditional, anticipated acceptability of topical and transdermal non-opioid formats ("Something I can put on my skin"). Conclusions: Participants described restrictive opioid pathways in terms of access burden, stigma and disrupted trust. Their stated openness to non-opioid formats was hypothetical and conditional on affordability, reliable supply, credible efficacy, devotional compatibility and endorsement by a trusted clinician. Less stigmatising dispensing, explained dose reduction and a nurse-led continuity role are proposed as strategies requiring prospective evaluation.

title: Development and Validation of a Dynamic Nomogram for Predicting Postdischarge Nausea and Vomiting in Adults Undergoing Ambulatory Surgery: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
Mind the Gap: A Qualitative Study of Patients' Experiences of Acute Elective Care Across the NHS and the Private Sector in England.
journal: Health expectations : an international journal of public participation in health care and health policy
abstract: Introduction Whilst the use of the private sector to deliver acute elective care in the United Kingdom is increasing, there is limited understanding of the patient experience when moving between NHS and private organisations to receive treatment. This study aims to explore how patients make choices and navigate care pathways across NHS and private sector organisations. Methods A qualitative semi-structured interview study was conducted with 27 patients and 73 clinical and non-clinical senior leaders across NHS and private organisations between September 2023 and April 2025. Analysis was conducted using a reflexive thematic approach and abductive analysis to position themes against wider knowledge. Results Three key themes structured around the patient journey were identified through analysis. First, the ability of patients to make informed decisions on receiving treatment in private sector organisations was constrained by long waiting times and challenges accessing NHS care. Second, there was a lack of consistency in the timely and thorough transfer of patient information between NHS and private sector organisations, which undermined patient trust in the safe provision of care when delivered across the interface. Third, the provision of aftercare across the interface was fragmented, and its effects compounded by ambiguity for patients, and at times, providers, for who was responsible for the ongoing management of patient care once they had received treatment in a private hospital. Conclusion Patients receiving elective care across the NHS and the private sector faced some barriers in decision-making, transfer of information and aftercare. In order to address these challenges, there is a need for stronger collaboration between the sectors to improve information sharing, continuity of care and patient safety across the interface. Patient or public contribution Patients and carers were involved in our study from inception to dissemination. Our Patient and Public Involvement (PPI) forum was involved throughout project design and planning and gave us feedback and guidance on research materials and outputs (e.g., interview schedules, participant recruitment material, theme development). Our PPI group co-produced our patient interview schedule and were involved in analysis of patient interviews. Our PPI co-applicant was involved in the preparation of this manuscript.

title: Co-Design of a Theory-Informed, Multicomponent, Intervention for Diagnostic Stewardship in a Major-Referral Emergency Department: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.
abstract: Objective Low-value diagnostic tests harm patients. Stewardship of tests can improve patient safety. Co-design and behavioural change theories can enhance the effectiveness of diagnostic stewardship interventions. This study aimed to co-design a theory-informed diagnostic stewardship intervention at a major-referral emergency department in Queensland, Australia. Methods A qualitative study was conducted at Townsville University Hospital Emergency Department. The Theoretical Domains Framework underpinned intervention design. Emergency clinicians ordering pathology tests were eligible for inclusion. A purposive sample of consenting participants was recruited. Data were collected via workshops facilitated by the lead author. Conversations were audio recorded and digitally transcribed. Data were managed with NVivo. Data were analysed by inductive and deductive approaches to generate codes, categories and themes. Thematic saturation and optimal stakeholder engagement influenced the final sample size. Trustworthiness was ensured via reflexivity, audit trail, thick description and participant validation. Results Seven workshops were conducted with 35 emergency physicians (18 male, 17 female) with a range of specialist experience (1-31 years). Urine culture was the diagnostic test of choice. Culture, complexity, and efficiency were identified as the major drivers of low-value urine cultures. Education, nudge, clinical champions, and audit/feedback were selected as intervention components. Credibility of change and workflow inefficiency were perceived as intervention challenges. Conclusion Stakeholder engagement has enhanced perceived acceptability of this co-designed intervention for urine culture diagnostic stewardship. Behavioural change theories strengthen co-designed interventions by addressing context-specific drivers of low-value tests. Co-design and behavioural change theories can inform bespoke interventions to nurture a culture of diagnostic stewardship in emergency medicine practice.

title: Validation of a nursing consultation protocol for preterm infants after hospital discharge.
abstract: Objective To analyze the evidence of content and semantic validity of a nursing consultation protocol aimed at the care of preterm infants after hospital discharge. Methods Methodological study. In the content validation stage, nurse experts with experience in neonatology were selected. After the modifications to the protocol suggested by the experts, semantic validation was carried out with the target audience, composed of nurses working in primary health care. Results Eleven experts participated in the content validation, in which the protocol received 70.0% full recommendation and 30.0% recommendation with modifications. In the semantic validation, 30 nurses participated, and the global evaluation showed a full recommendation rate of 93.3% and 6.7% recommendation with modifications. Conclusions The protocol demonstrated satisfactory validity evidence, indicating that it can be considered an appropriate tool for outpatient follow up services for preterm infants and for primary health care.

title: Early applications of apple vision pro in clinical medicine and medical education: a scoping review.
abstract: The Apple Vision Pro (AVP), a next-generation spatial computing device, has demonstrated potential applications in multidisciplinary clinical diagnosis, treatment, and medical education, by leveraging its unique technical architecture and performance advantages. In clinical practice, its fundamental advantages of three-dimensional (3D) visualization, real-time image integration, and immersive interaction have been preliminarily employed in disease diagnosis and treatment, surgical planning, precise operations, and postoperative rehabilitation across multiple disciplines. In medical education, AVP surpasses the limitations of conventional models, offering a novel methodology for anatomy education, clinical skills development, specialized practical training, and collaboration of distance learning, thereby alleviating persistent challenges such as unequal distribution of teaching resources, low efficiency in skills and specialized training, and the high cost of distance education. However, AVP faces some limitations, including limited hardware portability, insufficient system compatibility, a lack of specialized medical applications, high costs, and incomplete medical certification. Currently, most evidence derives from feasibility studies, case reports, and opinion pieces. Only two Stage 2b confirmatory studies were identified. Thus, high-level evidence for clinical benefit remains scarce. Readers should interpret all reported benefits as preliminary technical demonstrations rather than established clinical outcomes. Future advancements necessitate iterative development of lightweight hardware design, development of specialized medical software, cross-system optimization, and establishment of standardization protocols. Moreover, more randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and multicenter studies are urgently needed to fully explore and validate its intrinsic value in precision medicine and the equitable allocation of medical resources.

title: inproTeamED - clinical reasoning in the emergency department as an individual and interprofessional process: a qualitative analysis.
abstract: Background and objective Patients in the emergency department (ED) are assessed and treated by the ED-Team consisting of nurses and physicians. The clinical assessment (CA) of emergency patients and the clinical reasoning (CR) of both professions play a decisive role in determining the quality of emergency care. This pilot study explores CR in daily routine practice of the ED on a cognitive-individual level, relying on the Dual-process Theory and on a social-interprofessional level, arguing interprofessional collaboration (IPC) as a part of CR. At least, organizational-structural factors influencing CR are analyzed as a third level. Methods This is a qualitative study of 13 semi-structured individual interviews with nurses and physicians from three EDs in Germany, analysed using content analysis and methodological fundation. Results In the individual-cognitive CR, both physicians and nurses groups identified similar key factors for CA and used Systems 1 and 2 of the Dual-process Theory in their CR. On the social-interprofessional level, IPC was generally described positively, naming characteristics of good IPC and communication barriers were reported as rare. As possible organizational-structural factors influencing CR working experience as a prerequisite, size and region of the ED, age structure of the team and digitization were found. Conclusion This pilot study provides insights into the CR of nurses and physicians in the ED and analyzes CR on an individual-cognitive, a social-interprofessional and an organizational-structural level, allowing to conclusions regarding the prerequisites for successful ED-teams.

title: Detecting spiritual pain in electronic medical records using large language models.
journal: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer
abstract: Purpose Spiritual pain is one dimension of total pain in terminally ill patients with cancer. Reducing the burden of assessing spiritual pain in electronic medical records is essential for improving the quality of spiritual care. Large language models may offer a solution. This study explored whether large language models can be used to develop an automatic system for accurately identifying spiritual pain in patients with terminal cancer. Methods We used unstructured nursing records from patients with cancer who died in an inpatient palliative care unit at a university hospital in Japan between July and December 2024. A total of 500 records generated within 3 weeks before patients' death were randomly selected for analysis. Records were labeled for the presence of spiritual pain. Gemini-2.5-flash and Microsoft Copilot, accessible within the Tohoku University network environment, were utilized. Prompts included definitions of spiritual pain and example sentences. Results The analyzed records were derived from 109 patients with cancer (57 (52.3%) male; mean age, 70.9 years). Manual review identified spiritual pain in 56 records (11.2%). Sensitivity for Gemini and Copilot was 1.00; specificity was 0.75 and 0.61; positive predictive value was 0.34 and 0.25; and negative predictive value was 1.00 and 1.00, respectively. Error analysis of false positives indicated that the models frequently misclassified decreased physical functions and delirium as spiritual pain. Conclusion This study demonstrates that large language models can identify spiritual pain with performance comparable to, or exceeding, that of previous studies utilizing classical natural language processing methods.

title: Preparing HSCT and CAR‑T therapy programmes for JACIE inspection: a structured methodological approach to implementing a quality management system.
journal: International journal for quality in health care : journal of the International Society for Quality in Health Care
abstract: Background Certification by the Joint Assurance Committee of the International Society for Cell & Gene Therapy and the European Society for Blood and Marrow Transplantation (JACIE) is a key mechanism for strengthening quality, safety, and organizational performance in haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) and chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR‑T) therapy programmes. However, practical guidance on implementing a JACIE‑aligned quality management system (QMS) and preparing programmes for inspection remains limited. We present a structured methodology, developed and implemented within our programme, to support HSCT and CAR‑T therapy programmes in achieving inspection readiness while establishing a sustainable QMS that promotes continuous quality improvement. Methods We developed and implemented a stepwise approach based on the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle. It encompasses programme mapping and regulatory alignment, implementation of core QMS components across the collection, processing, and clinical areas, and QMS maintenance and inspection readiness, culminating in JACIE inspection with subsequent corrective actions. Key elements include process mapping, standard operating procedures, personnel competency, quality indicators, incident and deviation management, audits, validations and qualifications, product traceability, data submission, change control and risk assessment, feedback mechanisms, document management, and structured QMS review. Results The framework was successfully implemented within our HSCT and CAR‑T therapy programme, establishing a unified JACIE-aligned QMS across the collection, processing, and clinical areas. It strengthened governance, multidisciplinary coordination, and standardization of quality management activities, providing an approach applicable to both initial JACIE accreditation and subsequent reaccreditation. Conclusion This structured methodology provides a practical and scalable framework for implementing and maintaining a JACIE-aligned QMS in HSCT and CAR-T therapy programmes, supporting inspection readiness, multidisciplinary coordination, and the safety of patients, donors, and haematopoietic cellular therapy products. JACIE certification and its associated QMS should be viewed not as the endpoint of quality management but as part of an ongoing process of organizational learning and continuous quality improvement.

title: Ersodetug for refractory hypoglycemia due to malignant insulin-secreting tumors.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism
abstract: Background Refractory hypoglycemia is common in malignant insulin-secreting tumors and is associated with substantial morbidity. Ersodetug is a fully human monoclonal antibody that allosterically attenuates insulin receptor signaling with the potential to treat various forms of hyperinsulinism (HI). We retrospectively report outcomes from compassionate use of ersodetug in 8 individuals with refractory hypoglycemia due to tumor HI. Methods Ersodetug was administered intravenously at 6 or 9 mg/kg every 1-2 weeks initially, followed by a frequency of every 2-5 weeks, as appropriate. Glycemic, functional, and safety outcomes were analyzed. Results Eight adults (4M/4F; 24-74 years; Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group [ECOG] 1-3) received ersodetug for insulin-secreting tumors (metastatic insulinoma, n = 7; cervical neuroendocrine carcinoma, n = 1). No drug-related serious adverse events were observed. Most patients experienced improved glycemic control, including discontinuation of parenteral glucose in 6 of the 7 applicable patients (median, 4.5 days) and a 35.6% relative reduction from baseline in time in hypoglycemia ( Conclusion Ersodetug therapy resulted in reduced hypoglycemia burden, ability to discontinue parenteral glucose infusion, allowing discharge from hospital, use of fewer antihypoglycemic therapies, and improved ECOG performance status in individuals with severe, refractory tumor HI.

title: Reimagining Healthcare Management and Leadership in Somalia: A Commentary Proposing an Eight-Pillar Conceptual Framework for a Mixed Public-Private Health System.
abstract: Somalia's health system is a fragmented mixed market. Private for-profit and not-for-profit providers deliver most curative care, external donors finance most health spending, and the instruments needed to regulate this market remain largely in draft or unenforced. National plans set out what the system should deliver, but they say less about how leaders and managers should run organizations and purchasing arrangements within such a market. This evidence-informed policy commentary addresses that gap. It is not a systematic review: sources were selected purposively by the author from peer-reviewed literature and from official Somali, World Health Organization, and World Bank Group-supported reports, without a protocol-driven search or formal quality appraisal. From these sources the author proposes an eight-pillar conceptual framework: public stewardship of the healthcare market; accountable public-private partnerships; value-based management; sustainable healthcare financing; a national quality and accreditation system; digital and managerial innovation; procurement and supply-chain reform; and leadership and the healthcare workforce. The central argument is that leadership and stewardship capacity, more than the number of providers, is the binding constraint, and that management instruments borrowed from business strategy help only when they are sequenced behind that capacity and kept subordinate to equity, quality, and patient safety. The pillars largely reorganize established health-system strengthening principles; the contribution lies in linking each to a documented Somali problem, a leadership requirement, and a feasibility condition. The framework is author-generated and has not been validated through stakeholder consultation, costing, or empirical testing, and the evidence for several of its instruments, including contracting, performance-based payment, and community-based insurance, is mixed. It should therefore be read as a set of policy considerations for consultation, piloting, and evaluation, not as a demonstrated solution.

title: Optimising hospital pharmacy inventory for high-value, intermittent-demand drugs using a machine-learning approach with LightGBM-Tweedie regression: a single-centre, retrospective study.
abstract: ABSTRACT: OBJECTIVE: Hospital pharmacies operate under a persistent dilemma: ensuring uninterrupted access to essential medicines while minimising capital tied up in inventory. This challenge is most acute for drugs with lumpy or erratic demand, where traditional manual ordering often fails because of limited forecasting capability. Therefore, this study aimed to develop and evaluate a LightGBM-Tweedie regression model for forecasting weekly demand of high-value intermittent-demand drugs.
