title: Increasing Early Inpatient Hospitalization Discharges.
Partitioning All-Cause Pre-Analytical Laboratory Rejections: A 25-Month Retrospective Audit of Specimen Quality Failures with Six Sigma, IFCC, and Pareto Analysis.
abstract: Objectives: Aggregate pre-analytical rejection rates conflate specimen-quality failures and administrative events, which require distinct mitigation protocols. We disaggregated rejection events to isolate specimen-quality failures and benchmarked them against global frameworks. Methods: We conducted a 25-month retrospective audit (July 2023 to August 2025) of test orders received by the Al Rass General Hospital laboratory. Using an AI-assisted classification protocol, we isolated pre-analytical Specimen Quality Failures from operational and administrative events. We mapped Specimen Quality Failure causes into IFCC WG-LEPS Quality Indicators (QIs) and evaluated via Six Sigma metrics, IFCC benchmarks, and Pareto analysis-stratified by laboratory section, sample type, priority, and work shift. Results: Of 905,018 test orders received, 35,476 were rejected (overall rejection rate 3.92%). However, the specimen-quality failures were 2.21% (σ = 3.51), with 15,495 entries excluded as operational events. Clotted samples (26.2%), hemolysis (23.0%), wrong sample type (20.2%), sample not received (7.8%), and insufficient volume (7.1%) together accounted for 84.3% of specimen quality failures (the Vital Few). Most individual categories scored Good (≥4.0) on Sigma, despite a pooled Sigma of 3.51 (Acceptable). Benchmarking against IFCC WG-LEPS targets showed that 6 of 13 quality indicators, including clotted sample, wrong sample type, and insufficient volume, fell Below Minimum, demonstrating divergent absolute internal process capability metrics and population-relative external benchmark performance signals. STAT samples had a lower specimen quality failure rate than Routine samples (1.25% vs. 2.51%). Although the morning shift accounted for 80.98% of total rejections, only 53.4% represented true specimen quality failures. Conclusions: Headline laboratory rejection rates are inflated by operational and administrative events, necessitating partitioned reporting models. While individual Westgard Sigma scores demonstrate satisfactory absolute process capability across most specimen quality failure categories, cross-referencing against population-relative IFCC targets contextualizes these results and identifies areas performing in the lower international quartiles. Quality improvement strategies require structural changes and workforce training.

title: Case Report: Allogeneic adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells for severe chronic kidney disease in a dog.
abstract: This case report explored the clinical improvement and short-term tolerability of allogeneic adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (AD-MSCs) in the treatment of severe chronic kidney disease (CKD) in dogs. A 9-year-old female Pomeranian was diagnosed with chronic kidney disease (CKD) caused by acute kidney injury and, after conventional treatment failed, received intravenous infusion of AD-MSCs from healthy donor dogs. The AD-MSCs were aseptically collected, isolated, cultured, characterized, and subjected to microbiological safety testing, and were then administered intravenously at a dose of 3 × 10 6 cells/kg every 2 weeks for a total of four infusions, with dexamethasone premedication to reduce the risk of adverse reactions. Following AD-MSC administration and continued conventional care, reductions in serum creatinine and phosphorus and a downward trend in blood urea nitrogen were observed, along with improvements in body weight, body condition score, appetite, and mental status; no adverse events were observed. The results of this case suggest the feasibility and short-term tolerability of allogeneic AD-MSCs for severe CKD in dogs and provide a reference for clinical research on cell-based therapy for canine CKD.

title: Estimating the effect of familiarity in surgical teams on procedure time under a causal graphical model.
abstract: This study estimates the causal impact of surgical team familiarity on surgery duration across various procedures in a hospital, under an assumed Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) structure. While existing literature indicates that greater familiarity among surgical team members, measured by their shared work experience, is linked to reduced surgery times, these studies typically focus on a specific type of surgical procedure and only suggest a correlational relationship. Our study is the first to examine the hospital-wide relationship between surgical team familiarity and procedure duration using a formal causal inference framework. To explore this relationship, team familiarity is measured based on interaction frequency, and data across procedures are standardized to facilitate analysis via structural causal modeling and regression analysis. An analysis of 33,374 procedures performed in a high-volume academic medical center in the US from January 2017 to November 2023 reveals a negative causal relationship between surgeon-scrub familiarity and surgery duration under our DAG assumptions. Specifically, increasing familiarity by one standard deviation leads to a reduction of 1.9 to 3.7 minutes in surgery duration. Similar, albeit smaller, effects are observed for surgeon-circulator familiarity, whereas no significant impact is found for scrub-circulator familiarity. To our knowledge, this is the first study to estimate the causal effect of surgical team familiarity across an entire hospital's surgical portfolio under the assumptions of a DAG, moving beyond prior correlational analyses limited to specific specialties or methods. Ultimately, the study reveals that improving team familiarity, particularly between surgeons and scrub nurses, could hold significant implications for improving surgical team efficiency. This is especially relevant in high-volume hospitals, where even minor time savings can accumulate significantly, underscoring the value of leveraging team familiarity to optimize performance in hospital operating rooms.

title: Mid-term clinical outcomes and isokinetic performance after primary total knee arthroplasty within a modified ERAS protocol: a single-blinded randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Background Persistent muscular deficits are a major contributor to functional limitations following total knee arthroplasty (TKA). While Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols are increasingly adopted to improve postoperative outcomes, their influence on mid-term objective muscle strength recovery remains insufficiently defined. This study aimed first, to determine whether a modified ERAS protocol enhances mid-term recovery of knee muscle strength after primary TKA and second, compare associated clinical outcomes using validated functional and patient-reported measures. Methods The study received ethical approval from the Ethics Committee of the University of Regensburg, Germany (Reference No. 19-1470-101 on 31 July 2019) and was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. In this prospective, single-blinded randomized controlled trial, 58 patients undergoing primary TKA were assigned to either a modified ERAS protocol (n = 31) or conventional perioperative care (n = 27). Assessments were conducted at 5 days, 4 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, and 12 months postoperatively. Isokinetic muscle strength - including peak torque (Nm), total work (J), and power (W) - was measured using the Biodex ® System 3 Dynamometer. Clinical outcomes were evaluated using the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) for pain, Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs), and the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS). Results At 5 days postoperatively, the ERAS group demonstrated significantly higher isokinetic muscle strength and improved active knee flexion compared to the conventional group (p Conclusion The modified ERAS protocol led to significantly improved early postoperative recovery of knee muscle strength without adversely affecting short- or mid-term outcomes. Although isokinetic and clinical measures aligned across groups over time, the ERAS approach appears to be a safe and effective strategy for enhancing early functional recovery and overall patient experience following primary TKA.

title: Peripheral Nerve Stimulation Reduces Opioid Use and Facilitates Early Ambulation Following Fibular Flap Harvest: A Retrospective Study.
journal: Plastic and reconstructive surgery. Global open
abstract: Background Fibular free flap (FFF) reconstruction is the gold standard for mandibular and maxillary defects, but donor-site pain remains challenging. Multimodal analgesia (MMA) relies on opioids, which risk dependence, systemic side effects, and delayed recovery. Regional nerve blocks reduce pain but have inconsistent efficacy owing to variable drug metabolism, potential effects on flap perfusion, and motor blockade. Temporary percutaneous peripheral nerve stimulation (TPNS) is a promising alternative that selectively modulates sensory pathways while preserving motor function. Methods This retrospective, single-center study evaluated 26 patients who underwent FFF reconstruction between July 2021 and November 2025, divided into 2 cohorts: MMA alone and MMA with peroneal nerve TPNS. The primary outcome was opioid consumption, expressed as oral morphine equivalents. Secondary outcomes were postoperative pain scores, time to independent ambulation, and length of stay. Results The TPNS group had significantly lower pain scores on postoperative days 2-5 ( P P = 0.1), as was median time to independent ambulation (3.71 versus 4.76 d; P = 0.24). Conclusions TPNS may be a safe, opioid-sparing adjunct that promotes earlier mobilization after FFF harvest. Further study is needed to justify prospective, multicenter trials validating efficacy, cost-effectiveness, and broader applicability in head and neck reconstructive surgery.

abstract: Unlabelled This research letter describes the development and initial validation of SAFE-Nurse, an artificial intelligence-assisted patient safety incident reporting system for nurses, which demonstrated excellent content and face validity (average scale-level content validity index [S-CVI/Ave] 0.99; average scale-level face validity index [S-FVI/Ave] 1.00) and is ready to progress to usability testing.

title: Patient and family engagement in patient safety in resource-limited intensive care units: A qualitative exploratory study.
journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
abstract: Background Patient and family engagement (PFE) in the intensive care unit (ICU) enhances patient safety through detection and reporting of safety incidents that may be missed by healthcare professionals, providing an important and additional safeguard against harm. However, empirical evidence to inform policy and practice in resource-limited critical care settings remains scarce. Objectives The aim of this study was to explore the perspectives and experiences of patients, families, and healthcare professionals on PFE in patient safety in Ethiopian ICUs. Methods A pragmatic, exploratory qualitative descriptive study was conducted using in-depth interviews guided by a semistructured interview protocol. Participants were purposively selected and included patients, families, and healthcare professionals. Participants were recruited from four ICUs, including both adult and paediatric/neonatal ICUs in a major university hospital in Eastern Ethiopia. Reflexive thematic analysis with inductive orientation guided by Braun and Clarke's six-phase approach was employed. Convergence and divergence of perspectives across participant groups were identified and reported. Criteria for rigour and trustworthiness including credibility, dependability, transferability, confirmability, and integrity guided the research process. The consolidated criteria for reporting qualitative research were followed to ensure the transparency and consistency of reporting. Results Fifty-nine in-depth interviews were conducted, including patients (5; 9%), families (15; 25%), and healthcare professionals (39; 66%). Three overarching themes were identified: First, contested safety roles reflected the competing views on engagement, which were endorsed rhetorically but constrained in practice due to structural and hierarchical power dynamics. Second, sociocultural logics of engagement underscored inequities between rural and urban patients/families shaped by sociocultural attributes and faith-based sense-making. Third, tensions inpatient safetyincident disclosure highlighted the discordance between the expectation of transparency and hesitancy to involve patients and families in incident disclosure due to fear of reprisals. Conclusion PFE in patient safety in Ethiopian ICUs was endorsed in principle yet remained constrained by sociocultural contexts, hierarchical power dynamics, and limited institutional support mechanisms. Clearly defining patient safety roles, implementing family-activated escalation pathways, and strengthening formal patient safety incident reporting and disclosure systems are essential to promote inclusive, equitable, and sustainable PFE in patient safety across Ethiopian ICUs and beyond.

title: Incident and Adverse-Event Reporting in Undergraduate Dental Education: A Scoping Review of Educational Evidence, Curricular Integration, Perceptions, and Barriers.
abstract: Incident and adverse-event reporting is an important component of patient safety and provides opportunities for risk reduction and organizational learning. In undergraduate dental education programmes, students deliver patient care as they develop clinical competence; however, the extent to which incident reporting is taught, practiced, and integrated into clinical education or the dental curriculum remains unclear. This scoping review mapped the available evidence on the reporting of incidents and adverse events in undergraduate dental education. The review was undertaken in accordance with the framework of Arksey and O'Malley, JBI guidance, and PRISMA-ScR. Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched for English-language studies published from 2015 to 2026 that addressed incident or adverse-event reporting in undergraduate dental education programmes, and data were collated and synthesized descriptively and thematically. Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Students' knowledge, confidence, and preparedness for incident reporting varied widely, and reporting was more often taught within general patient-safety education than as a distinct subject. Underreporting was common, particularly for incidents perceived as minor. Recurring barriers included fear of adverse consequences, limited support within the clinical hierarchy, and uncertainty about how to report. Few studies described any formal assessment of reporting competence, whereas studies in which adverse events were reviewed and fed back to students pointed to clear educational value. Undergraduate dental education addresses incident and adverse-event reporting inconsistently; clear reporting pathways, supportive supervision, constructive feedback, and a non-punitive clinical environment may strengthen reporting competence and patient-safety learning.

title: Incidence and Characteristics of Adverse Events: The 2024 Patient Safety Incidents Inquiry in Korea.
authors: Central Patient Safety Center of the Korea Institute for Healthcare Accreditation
abstract: Background In accordance with Article 7-2 of the Patient Safety Act, the Ministry of Health and Welfare conducts a Patient Safety Incident Inquiry every 5 years to support patient safety policy. This study aimed to describe the methodology and main findings of the 2024 Patient Safety Incident Inquiry. Methods Ten Accountable Care Hospitals (five tertiary and five general hospitals) participated. From each hospital, 500 patients discharged in 2021 were randomly selected. A standardized three-stage retrospective medical record review was conducted: first-stage screening by nurses or health information managers, second-stage review and reporting of suspected adverse events by physicians or nurses, and final adjudication by a central expert committee. Results Of 5,000 patients, 2,208 (44.2%) met one or more the screening criteria. Following adjudication in the third review stage, confirmed adverse events were identified in 565 patients (11.3%), resulting in 612 confirmed adverse events. The most common type was patient care-related events (37.3%), followed by medication-/fluid-/blood-related (36.1%) and surgery-/procedure-related (26.8%) events. Temporary harm requiring intervention accounted for 62.4% of adverse events, and 3.6% of patients died. Prolonged hospitalization was associated with 36.3% confirmed adverse events, and 28.3% were classified as preventable. Variation in the incidence of confirmed adverse events across institutions was observed. Conclusion Using a standardized three-stage medical record review, the 2024 Patient Safety Incident Inquiry provides updated descriptive baseline data on confirmed adverse events across tertiary and general hospitals in Korea. These findings may support institutional patient safety improvement efforts and inform national patient safety planning.

title: Adverse event reporting in healthcare-Regulatory frameworks, institutional governance, and economic implications with evidence from Poland.
abstract: Adverse events constitute a major challenge not only for patient safety but also for the effectiveness, sustainability and equity of healthcare systems. The present analysis demonstrates that patient safety cannot be reduced to a purely clinical or legal issue, as adverse events generate substantial social and economic consequences that frequently extend beyond healthcare institutions and are borne by patients and their households. The findings indicate that the current Polish model of adverse event monitoring, based predominantly on internal reporting mechanisms within individual healthcare entities, provides limited opportunities for national learning, regulatory evaluation and evidence-based policy-making. The absence of a centralized adverse event register restricts the ability to assess the effectiveness of patient safety interventions, estimate the full social and economic burden of adverse events and identify systemic risk factors that require regulatory action. Effective reporting systems require an organizational culture based on trust, transparency and learning, supported by the principles of no-blame and just culture, which encourage incident reporting while maintaining accountability for reckless or intentional misconduct. Therefore, future reforms should focus on strengthening information infrastructure, improving data quality and comparability, and developing integrated national reporting systems that facilitate organizational learning and regulatory evaluation. The establishment of a central adverse event register, combined with transparent reporting mechanisms and systematic assessment of patient safety policies, could significantly improve both patient outcomes and the allocative efficiency of healthcare systems. Integrating legal and economic perspectives into patient safety governance is essential for designing regulations that adequately reflect the full social costs of adverse events and promote more resilient, equitable and patient-centered healthcare systems.

title: Transitioning from anonymous to real-name genetic testing in Japan: Implementation and implications for medical safety.
abstract: Background Traditionally, genetic testing in Japan has been conducted using coded or pseudonymized identifiers to protect patient privacy. However, the 2022 revision of the Japanese Association of Medical Sciences guidelines emphasized integrating genetic information into routine clinical information-management systems for patient safety. This study aimed to clarify the status and medical safety challenges associated with transitioning to real-name genetic testing in Japan. Methods A nationwide survey of 149 medical institutions was conducted, receiving 69 responses (46.3%). [Results] University hospitals reported a higher implementation rate of real-name testing (71.1%) than other institutions (41.9%, p = 0.027). Among 62 institutions with evaluable responses regarding coded/pseudonymized workflows, 8 (12.9%) reported an incident and 8 (12.9%) a near-miss. Among 66 evaluable responses regarding real-name workflows, 45 reported no safety issue, 15 no real-name outsourcing, and 6 were uncertain. Excluding the latter two categories left 45 outcome-eligible institutions; none reported an incident. The workflows were not statistically compared because eligibility, exposure opportunity, and outcome ascertainment differed. Qualitative analysis of 14 descriptions revealed vulnerabilities involving manual relinking, transcription errors, and erroneous integration of results into electronic health records. The most frequently cited barrier was the lack of readiness in testing companies' ordering systems (68.3%). Conclusion These findings identify practical vulnerabilities in workflows requiring manual relinking but do not establish that using patient names independently reduces safety risks. Healthcare providers and testing laboratories should coordinate to standardize patient-identification and information-management procedures while maintaining confidentiality to ensure patient safety as genomic medicine enters routine clinical practice in Japan.

title: Analysis of incident reports in information systems for patient safety management.
abstract: Objectives to analyze the characteristics of reports of serious incidents and deaths, as well as the improvement actions implemented, considering organizational learning in patient safety management. Methods documentary, descriptive, and quantitative research, conducted in a private electronic system for adverse event reports of an accredited organization. Descriptive and inferential statistics were used for association analysis. Results reports were mostly from hospital services (98.8%), from the Southeast region (76.7%), from level 1 accredited institutions (36.7%), made after 30 days of the event (49.4%), and occurred with older patients (48.2%). As an organizational consequence of the incidents, there was additional use of resources, treatment, and examinations (54.3%). Among the improvement actions related to professionals, informal guidance stood out (43.9%), and to organizational factors, actions to improve safety culture (31.9%). Conclusions the reported events did not present objective information about institutional learning and implementation of actions for care quality and safety.

title: The Hidden Wounds of Care: Organizational Responses to the Second Victim Phenomenon Among Nurses
abstract: Abstract Background Patient safety incidents can have psychological and professional consequences for nurses experiencing the second victim phenomenon. Although organizational support is increasingly recognized as important, evidence concerning nurses’ experiences and organizational support needs in Indonesian hospitals remains limited. This study explored nurses’ second-victim experiences and perceived organizational responses following patient safety incidents. Methods A qualitative single-case study was conducted at PHC Hospital in Indonesia, a Type B teaching hospital with established quality and patient safety reporting systems. The hospital was purposively selected as an information-rich case for examining nurses’ post-incident experiences and organizational responses within a formal patient-safety setting. Nine informants, comprising eight nursing participants and one physician, were purposively selected. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and analyzed using deductive and inductive approaches, with the Gioia methodology informing the development of first-order concepts, second-order themes, and aggregate dimensions. Results Six dimensions characterized nurses’ second-victim experiences: psychological distress, physiological distress, socio-cultural factors, professional identity crisis, support systems, and individual coping resources. Three organizational support dimensions were identified: Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs), work flexibility, and team support. Participants emphasized the need for confidential psychological counseling, supportive work arrangements, peer support, and non-punitive managerial responses. Nurse managers were perceived as important in providing initial support and facilitating access to additional organizational resources. Conclusions Nurses’ second-victim experiences extend beyond psychological distress to encompass threats to social and professional resources. Viewed through the lens of the Conservation of Resources Theory, the findings highlight the perceived importance of complementary organizational support in addressing post-incident needs. These findings have implications for Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3, particularly Target 3.4 on mental health and well-being, and SDG 8, particularly Target 8.8 on safe and secure working environments. Further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of these organizational interventions.

title: Nurses' knowledge and practice on patient safety in tertiary medical college hospitals in Bangladesh: a cross-sectional study.
abstract: Background Patient safety is critical to healthcare and depends on a safety culture to ensure high-quality care. A strong patient safety culture (PSC) reduces preventable patient harm, with nurses' knowledge and practices central to delivering safe care in hospitals. Yet, evidence remains limited in tertiary medical college hospitals in Bangladesh. Therefore, this study aimed to assess nurses' knowledge, practices, and associated factors regarding PSC in tertiary medical college hospitals in Bangladesh. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted from April to September 2025 in eight medical college hospitals across all eight administrative divisions in Bangladesh. Of 7,170 eligible nurses, 4,982 (valid response rate 69.5%) were analyzed using a self-administered questionnaire. Descriptive, inferential statistics and correlation were performed. Results Participants' mean scores were 5.44 (SD 1.82) (range: 0-10) for patient safety knowledge and 28.92 (SD 7.76) (range: 10-50) for practice. At the item level, 49.3% correctly identified adverse events, and only 9.8% knew the appropriate reporting methods. In terms of practice, 48.6% reported never using incident-reporting forms, and 26.4% reported never using structured communication tools. In bivariate analysis, participants' education, working ward, and having in-service training were significantly associated with knowledge and younger age, hospital experience, working ward, and in-service training were significantly associated with practice. After adjusting in a mixed-effects model, professional experience ( p p p p p p p p p Conclusion Nurses' knowledge of patient safety increased with professional experience and in-service training; however, gender and education had negative associations. Nurses' practices also increased with professional experience, while age and in-service training showed negative associations. Targeted, context-specific in-service training with post-training monitoring by Quality Improvement Teams is essential to improve nurses' knowledge and practice. Strengthening patient safety reporting systems with leadership engagement, logistical support, and oversight by the government regulatory bodies may improve patient-safety practice and quality of care.

Workplace bullying, speak-up climate and perceived patient safety compromise among radiographers practising in the United Kingdom.
abstract: Introduction Workplace bullying and harassment (WBH) may undermine speak-up climate, suppress organisational voice, and negatively affect patient safety. However, quantitative evidence examining these relationships within radiography practice remains limited. This study aimed to examine associations among WBH exposure, speak-up climate, and perceived compromise of patient safety among UK radiographers. Methods A UK-wide cross-sectional survey of 385 HCPC-registered radiographers, recruited via non-probability sampling, was conducted using an online questionnaire that incorporated the Negative Acts Questionnaire-Revised (NAQ-R), patient safety impact items, and speak-up climate indicators. Composite Safety Impact and Speak-Up Climate scores were constructed. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's alpha. Associations were evaluated using Spearman correlations with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Multivariable linear regression models with HC3-robust standard errors were used to assess adjusted associations. Exploratory mediation analyses using 5,000 bootstrap samples examined the indirect association involving Speak-Up Climate. Optional free-text responses were analysed using inductive qualitative content analysis. Results Greater WBH exposure was associated with poorer Speak-Up Climate (rho = 0.51, q N = 369; B = 0.688, 95% CI 0.550-0.825, p 2 = 0.250, adjusted R 2 = 0.231) and greater perceived Safety Impact ( N = 358; B = 0.316, 95% CI 0.179-0.453, p 2 = 0.118, adjusted R 2 = 0.096). When Speak-Up Climate was added to the Safety Impact model, the adjusted NAQ-R association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant ( N = 357; B = 0.052, 95% CI -0.095-0.199, p = 0.488). By contrast, poorer Speak-Up Climate remained associated with greater perceived Safety Impact (B = 0.378, 95% CI 0.255-0.501, p 2 = 0.230, adjusted R 2 = 0.208). An exploratory 5,000-resample bootstrap analysis identified an indirect association via Speak-Up Climate (B = 0.264, 95% bootstrap CI 0.169-0.373). Complete-case sensitivity analyses produced materially unchanged estimates. Qualitative findings included the following categories: organisational silence and psychological unsafety, leadership and organisational accountability and building psychologically safe workplace cultures. Conclusion Speak-Up Climate statistically accounted for part of the observed cross-sectional association between WBH exposure and perceived compromise of patient safety. Longitudinal research is required to evaluate temporal or causal relationships. Implications for practice Psychologically safe reporting environments and anti-retaliation cultures are plausible organisational priorities that warrant prospective evaluation.

title: Smartphone applications in domestic abuse referral pathways: implications for dental practice.
abstract: Domestic abuse is a persistent public health, safeguarding and human rights challenge. In England and Wales, the Crime Survey for England and Wales estimated that approximately 3.8 million people aged 16 years and over experienced domestic abuse in the year ending March 2025. Dentistry has an important role because interpersonal violence frequently affects the face, mouth and teeth, and a dental appointment may provide an opportunity to access healthcare. However, general dental practitioners may be uncertain how to progress from recognising possible abuse to an appropriate safeguarding response, particularly when disclosure is hesitant or incomplete. Smartphone applications can provide information, safety planning, incident recording and routes to specialist support, but their evidence base and safety implications vary. The strongest peer-reviewed evidence among the resources considered relates to myPlan and related safety decision aids, with benefits for selected outcomes that vary by intervention and population. Digital tools should therefore support, rather than replace, professional judgement. This narrative review critically appraises selected digital resources and sets out a conceptual dental safeguarding pathway centred on privacy, sensitive enquiry, objective documentation, risk assessment and proportionate referral or escalation.

title: Hospital Preparedness for CBRNE Threats in Iran: A Qualitative Policy Analysis of Risk Assessment Using the Walt and Gilson Framework.
abstract: Background and objective Chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and explosive (CBRNE) threats are among the complex and multidimensional crises that pose serious challenges to health systems. Hospitals, as the frontline in dealing with these threats, require structured preparedness based on documented policy frameworks. This article aims to conduct a policy analysis of risk assessment in the management of CBRNE incidents in hospitals of Iran based on the Walt and Gilson policy triangle framework. Methodology This policy analysis examined the four dimensions of content, context, actors, and process in hospital CBRNE preparedness policies using the Walt and Gilson framework. Data were collected through 14 semi-structured, in-depth interviews with purposively sampled experts, managers, and specialists (emergency medicine, hospital administration, and health policy) in Iran; sampling continued until data saturation was achieved. Data were analyzed using framework content analysis, and trustworthiness was ensured through the Lincoln and Guba criteria (credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability). Findings The findings showed that in terms of content, the main gaps were the absence of an integrated governance and crisis command structure, unclear accountability, and a lack of standardized policies and procedures. Regarding context, security, economic, and technological factors - including hybrid and cyber threats and resource constraints - strongly shaped preparedness. With respect to actors, CBRNE management emerged as inherently multi-sectoral, dependent on coordination among internal hospital actors and external organizations. Finally, in terms of process, risk assessment was seen as a continuous cycle weakened by the absence of structured feedback and the failure to use lessons learned, reflecting a persistent gap between policy formulation and implementation. Conclusion Applying the Walt and Gilson framework to CBRNE risk management in Iranian hospitals offered analytical insight into the gaps in hospital preparedness rather than generalizable findings, given the qualitative design and purposive sampling. The study suggests that strengthening inter-organizational cooperation, developing standard protocols, allocating resources, and ensuring continuous staff training are important strategies for improving hospital resilience. On this basis, the authors propose that establishing a national CBRNE risk-management framework, reinforcing intersectoral coordination, developing technological infrastructure, and institutionalizing monitoring and policy learning warrant consideration as policy priorities.

title: Failure Mode and Effects Analysis of the In-Hospital Medication Process: Identification of Systemic Risks and development of Improvement strategies.
journal: International journal for quality in health care : journal of the International Society for Quality in Health Care
abstract: Background Flaws in the in-hospital medication process compromise patient safety. A structured evaluation of the process using Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) can identify and prioritize potential risks and help to develop targeted measures to improve medication safety. Methods A prospective risk analysis using FMEA was conducted between February 2025 and February 2026 in a large tertiary care hospital by an interprofessional team including physicians, nurses, pharmacists, and a chief risk manager. In six structured workshops, the medication process was analyzed including admission, prescribing, order/delivery, dispensing, and discharge. Potential failure modes, their causes, and effects were identified based on expert experience and known errors from the hospitals critical incident reporting system. Each failure mode was independently rated for severity, occurrence, and detectability on a 5-point scale. Risk Priority Numbers (RPN) were calculated to prioritize risks. Based on these results, targeted mitigation strategies were developed. Results A total of 101 potential failure modes were identified, with the highest proportion in admission (n = 37; 36.6%). RPN values were moderate (median 22; IQR 14-29; range 8-53). The highest ranked risks were missing drug interaction checks (RPN = 53) and lack of dose adjustment in renal impairment (RPN = 46). Additional high-risk areas included incomplete medication histories and communication deficits at process interfaces. Contributing factors were predominantly related to human and communication domains. Mitigation strategies included standardized medication reconciliation procedures, training programs for medical staff, pharmacist consultation service, and system level interventions such as software improvements and improved communication processes. Conclusion The FMEA identified specific risks within the in-hospital medication process. Furthermore, it revealed interdependencies between process stages and system level vulnerabilities. The derived measures may contribute to improved medication safety across multiple stages of care in similar hospital settings. Future studies should evaluate their implementation and impact on medication errors.

title: Transformational Leadership and the Reporting of Patient Safety Events Among Emergency Nurses: The Mediating Role of Psychological Safety.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Underreporting of patient safety events is a persistent problem in high-risk clinical settings such as emergency departments, yet the managerial and psychological conditions associated with reporting remain underexamined. This study aimed to examine the relationship between transformational leadership and patient safety event reporting behavior among emergency department nurses, and to test the mediating role of psychological safety in this relationship. Methods: This descriptive, cross-sectional study was conducted with 295 nurses working in the emergency departments of two city hospitals in Ankara, Turkey. Data were collected using a personal information form, the Transformational Leadership Scale, the Psychological Safety Scale, and the "Reporting Patient Safety Events" composite of the Hospital Survey on Patient Safety Culture 2.0 (HSOPSC 2.0). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, confirmatory factor analysis, Pearson correlation analysis, and path analysis with bootstrap-based mediation testing (SPSS 29 and AMOS 24). Results: Transformational leadership was positively associated with psychological safety (β = 0.505). Psychological safety was positively associated with reporting behavior (β = 0.427). Transformational leadership was associated with reporting both directly (β = 0.167) and indirectly through psychological safety (β = 0.215, 95% CI [0.134, 0.305]), consistent with partial mediation. The model explained 28% of the variance in reporting behavior. Conclusions: The findings are consistent with psychological safety functioning as a partial mediator in the association between transformational leadership and patient safety event reporting. Strengthening nurse managers' transformational leadership skills and fostering nurses' perceived psychological safety may support reporting in emergency departments, although longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to confirm these relationships.

title: Implementation of a Structured Hot Debrief Tool in a Metropolitan ED: A Quality Improvement Study.
Refined Exclusion in Medical AI: Data Justice and Patient Safety Governance.
abstract: Medical AI is often evaluated using aggregate measures of discrimination, calibration, and accuracy. However, these measures can obscure clinically important variation across patient groups, institutions, devices, and workflows. This viewpoint defines refined exclusion as a governance condition in which an AI system appears successful in aggregate, while uncertainty, error, or reduced clinical reliability is concentrated in populations that are insufficiently represented, measured, validated, or monitored. The concept does not replace algorithmic fairness, hidden stratification, dataset shift, or subgroup performance analysis. It connects these mechanisms to a distinct consequence: an unequal distribution of safety that remains inadequately detected or corrected. Drawing on purposively selected, illustrative evidence from population health management, chest radiography, dermatology, computational pathology, medical foundation models, and clinical measurement, we distinguish model-level disparity, patient safety signals, and documented patient harm. We then frame data justice as a complementary governance approach with distributional, procedural, and substantive dimensions. The proposed lifecycle decision gates address intended use, subgroup learnability, data provenance, validation, procurement, local deployment, monitoring, updates, and patient feedback. Each gate links minimum evidence to decision authority and 1 of 4 actions: proceed, enrich or validate, restrict use, or pause or retire. Governance intensity should be proportionate to clinical risk and evidentiary uncertainty. By linking subgroup evidence gaps to institutional decisions and corrective action, the framework shifts attention from whether a model performs well on average to whether its safety is demonstrable for the populations and settings in which it will be used.

title: Underreporting of blood and body fluid exposures among nurses: prevalence, reporting cascade, and modifiable organizational correlates.
abstract: Background Occupational exposure to blood and body fluids is common among nurses, and incomplete reporting limits occupational surveillance and access to post-exposure assessment. This study estimated underreporting at the nurse level and the proportion of aggregate exposure counts that were unreported, and examined associated individual and workplace characteristics. Methods A census-based analytical cross-sectional survey was conducted between November 2025 and March 2026 among registered nurses at a tertiary infectious disease referral hospital in China, using a structured questionnaire with a 12-month recall period. Underreporting was defined among exposed nurses as failure to formally report at least one exposure. Modified Poisson regression with robust variance was used to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs). Negative-binomial and hurdle models with an exposure offset served as sensitivity analyses for exposure opportunity. Results Of 1,110 eligible nurses, 872 responded (78.6%); 392 (45.0%) reported at least one exposure, contributing 747 aggregate exposure counts. Underreporting affected 232 exposed nurses (59.2, 95% CI 54.3-63.9), and 373 of 747 exposure counts (49.9%) were unreported. Among under-reporters, 48.3% reported receiving none of the five assessed services after any exposure during the recall period, compared with 0.6% of complete reporters; clinical indications and exposure-specific service receipt were unavailable. Underreporting was associated with individual perceptions of safety climate (aPR per SD 0.77, 95% CI 0.70-0.84), vague or absent procedural knowledge (aPR 1.56, 95% CI 1.31-1.86), non-permanent employment (aPR 1.30, 95% CI 1.07-1.57), and night-shift frequency (aPR per level 1.14, 95% CI 1.04-1.25). Conclusion Underreporting was common at both the nurse level and across aggregate exposure counts. Perceived safety climate, procedural knowledge, employment security, and night-shift work were associated with underreporting and are potential targets for intervention research; the cross-sectional design does not establish causation or event-specific clinical consequences.

title: Perceived reporting-system function, reporting barriers, and formal near-miss reporting among operating room nurses in China: a cross-sectional study.
abstract: Background Near-miss reporting provides an early signal of perioperative system failure, yet formal reporting remains limited in operating rooms. This study examined correlates of formal near-miss reporting among operating room (OR) nurses at a two-campus tertiary hospital in China. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 2,281 OR nurses returned a structured questionnaire and 2,200 were analyzed, covering self-reported 12-month near-miss observation and reporting, four safety-culture indices, workload, and professional characteristics. Exposures were purpose-built indices rather than validated scales. Multivariable logistic regression, with a prespecified parsimonious model as the principal specification, examined factors associated with formal reporting among observers (Model A) and, as an exploratory aim, near-miss observation in the full sample (Model B). Results Of 2,200 OR nurses, 1,551 (70.5%) observed at least one perioperative near-miss during the preceding 12 months, yet only 478 (30.8%) formally reported an event; the remaining 1,073 (69.2%) made no report, a nurse-level rather than event-level measure. Count discrepancies predominated (47.3%). In the principal model, perceived reporting-system function was the strongest correlate of formal reporting (aOR: 2.19 per 1-SD increase, 95% CI: 1.84-2.60), whereas greater barrier burden was inversely associated (0.67, 0.57-0.79); speaking-up and safety climate, which overlapped substantially, were not independently associated. The reporting-system association persisted after removal of the feedback item, which may reflect earlier reporting, and ordinal modeling of reported event volume reproduced both associations. Model A discrimination was acceptable (AUC 0.741). In the full sample, higher time pressure was associated with near-miss observation (1.14, 1.03-1.25), but this exploratory model discriminated poorly (AUC 0.600). Conclusion Perioperative near misses were commonly observed but seldom documented. These cross-sectional, self-reported associations cannot establish direction, but they are consistent with formal reporting depending on accessible, easy-to-use reporting systems and on reduced hierarchy-related and relational barriers, rather than on willingness to speak up alone.

title: Hepatitis B and Sharps Safety Before Nursing Clinical Placement: A Narrative Review and Proposed Framework for Resource-Constrained Hospitals.
journal: Advances in medical education and practice
abstract: Clinical placements expose nursing students to blood, body fluids, and sharps while procedural routines and reporting behaviors are still developing. In resource-constrained hospitals, incomplete hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination, limited infection prevention and control (IPC) capacity, variable supervision, and unclear post-exposure pathways may compound this risk. This structured narrative review critically synthesized evidence relevant to prelicensure nursing students and interns and used the synthesis to derive a provisional clinical-readiness framework. PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar were searched through September 29, 2026, with a targeted update on October 11, 2026; backward/forward citation searching and World Health Organization (WHO) and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidance were also used. Empirical studies from 2014 onward were prioritized, while earlier authoritative guidance and seminal education literature were retained when directly relevant. A 32-study meta-analysis estimated needlestick injury prevalence at 35% (95% CI, 28%-43%) and non-reporting at 63% (95% CI, 51%-74%), with substantial heterogeneity. Recent studies from multiple regions show marked variation in vaccination documentation and persistent gaps between knowledge and safe practice; a 2026 Egyptian study found practice and attitude, but not knowledge score alone, independently associated with injury. A single-group 2026 simulation study reported improved knowledge, practice, and observed behavior, but causal inference is limited by the absence of a control group and unequal injury recall periods. Direct evidence linking student HBV-readiness programs to patient-level outcomes remains limited; patient safety is therefore treated as a candidate downstream domain. We propose six linked domains - vaccinate, train, verify, supervise, report, and improve - supported by an evidence-to-domain matrix and a practical pilot package. The framework is evidence-informed rather than validated and requires local co-design, psychometric testing, feasibility assessment, and prospective evaluation before wider adoption.

title: Verbal de-escalation techniques for the prevention and management of workplace violence in healthcare: a systematic review.
abstract: Background Workplace violence (WPV) remains a significant and escalating challenge across healthcare settings, threatening the safety, well-being, and retention of frontline healthcare professionals (HCPs). Verbal de-escalation is widely promoted as a first-line strategy to prevent or manage aggressive patient behavior. However, the scope, implementation, and effectiveness of these techniques have not been consistently synthesized. Methods This systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Studies were eligible if they examined verbal de-escalation as a primary strategy for preventing or managing WPV in healthcare settings, including hospitals, emergency departments, psychiatric units, long-term care, and outpatient clinics. All study designs were considered, including empirical research and structured descriptive guidance relevant to clinical practice. Searches were conducted in Ovid MEDLINE ALL, Embase, Emcare, PsycINFO, and CINAHL from database inception, with results downloaded on August 29, 2024, and updated on January 30, 2026. Of 15,987 records identified, 9,096 were screened following duplicate removal, 446 underwent full-text review, and 36 studies met inclusion criteria. Methodological quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Results Substantial heterogeneity was observed in how verbal de-escalation was defined, delivered, and evaluated. Intervention studies commonly assessed structured training programs delivered through didactic sessions, interactive workshops, simulation-based education, technology-enhanced learning, or clinical unit-based training. These studies frequently reported improvements in staff knowledge, confidence, and preparedness to manage aggression. Observational and descriptive studies emphasized communication behaviors used during escalated encounters and highlighted recurring strategies, such as empathetic listening, calm verbal tone, validation, and collaborative problem-solving. Outcome measures varied considerably across studies, limiting direct comparison. Conclusions Verbal de-escalation represents a central component of WPV prevention in healthcare, yet implementation approaches and evaluation methods remain inconsistent. The evidence suggests associations with improved clinician confidence, reduced patient agitation, and enhanced perceptions of safety. Healthcare organizations can use these findings to strengthen training curricula, integrate de-escalation within broader safety frameworks, and support sustainable workforce protection strategies. Systematic review registration OSF, identifier https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/S7QD9.

title: Mapping Technologies, Support Functions, Evaluation Outcomes, and Safety Governance Related to Conversational AI Agents for Psychological Support of Patients With Cancer: Scoping Review.
abstract: Background Psychological distress and unmet psychosocial needs are common across the cancer continuum. Conversational AI agents may offer scalable support, but their technologies, support functions, evaluation approaches, and safety governance remain fragmented. Objective This review aimed to map the technologies, psychological support functions, evaluation outcomes, and safety governance of conversational AI used by patients with cancer and cancer survivors. Methods We conducted a scoping review following Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews). Thirteen databases and additional registers were searched through May 5, 2026. Eligible reports examined conversational agents in real or simulated patient-facing oncology contexts with explicit psychological or psychosocial relevance. We summarized system forms and support functions by project and other characteristics by report. No formal critical appraisal was undertaken. Results We included 24 reports representing 25 study units and 23 underlying projects. Large language model (LLM) or generative AI systems accounted for 39.1% (9/23) of projects. Information or education (23/23, 100%) and symptom or self-management support (n=20, 87%) were the most frequently mapped functions, although these counts included delivered, planned, simulated, co-designed, and participant-reported functions. Structured psychological or behavioral components were delivered in 21.7% (5/23) of projects. An explicit theoretical or conceptual framework was reported in 25% (6/24) of reports. Reports or plans to assess acceptability or user experience (17/24, 70.8%) and engagement (13/24, 54.2%) were more common than reports or plans to assess psychosocial clinical outcomes (8/24, 33.3%) or safety and adverse events (4/24, 16.7%). Human or expert oversight was reported in 62.5% (15/24) of reports, crisis escalation or referral in 33.3% (8/24) of reports, and user-facing AI identity disclosure in 12.5% (3/24) of reports. Conclusions Conversational AI research in psycho-oncology spans heterogeneous technologies and stages of development. Clinical and safety evaluation, theoretical foundations, population representation, and oversight responsibilities remain incompletely reported. These findings represent a map of reporting patterns and do not establish effectiveness or safety. Future studies should evaluate psychosocial benefit and safety prospectively and define professional oversight and referral responsibilities. Trial registration OSF Registries UM65W; https://osf.io/um65w.

title: Patient and Family Perspectives on Statutory Duty of Candour Following Serious Adverse Patient Safety Events.
journal: Health expectations : an international journal of public participation in health care and health policy
abstract: Background The Statutory Duty of Candour (SDC) legally requires healthcare organisations to notify patients, families, and carers who experience a serious adverse patient safety event (SAPSE), provide an apology, and explain steps taken to prevent recurrence. However, despite growing international adoption of SDC, evidence on its implementation and impact on patients and families ('consumers') remains limited. This study examined consumer awareness, understanding, and lived experiences of SDC in Victoria, Australia, two years after its introduction. Methods A mixed-methods study integrated data from an online survey and semi-structured interviews with healthcare consumers in Victoria, Australia. Descriptive analysis was undertaken for quantitative items, while reflexive thematic analysis was applied to qualitative data from survey free-text responses and interview transcripts. Results In total, 80 consumers participated: 72 completed the survey and 13 completed interviews, with five participating in both. Although nearly two-thirds (61%) had no prior knowledge of SDC, over three-quarters (78%) perceived it as useful. Among those who had experienced an adverse event, half reported that staff were not open following the incident, over half reported that no post-incident meeting occurred, and satisfaction with meetings was low (26%). Six themes were identified: (1) Candour as Moral Reassurance; (2) Persistent Scepticism and Conditional Trust; (3) Limited Awareness and Accessibility of SDC; (4) Genuine Apology for Trust Repair; (5) Emotional Labour, Power, and the Risk of Re-traumatisation; and (6) Demonstrating Accountability with Organisational Learning and Improvement. An overarching theme, Candour as a Relational Process for Trust, described how trust was tested, repaired, or further eroded through SDC processes following an adverse event. Conclusion SDC holds significant potential to repair trust following adverse events, but its impact depends on how it is enacted. When delivered with empathy and meaningful follow-up, SDC supports repair of trust. However, when experienced as procedural or defensive, SDC may compound distress and further erode trust. Therefore, SDC must be embedded not just as a regulatory requirement, but as a relational and person-centred practice for patients and families. Patient or public contribution Healthcare consumer representatives were part of the research team, assisting with the study design, data analysis, and article writing.

title: Severe Infection Outcomes With SGLT2 Versus DPP-4 Inhibitors in Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Active-Comparator Meta-Analysis of Real-World Cohorts.
abstract: Introduction To update and methodologically refine the synthesis of real-world evidence on severe infection outcomes with sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) versus dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP-4i), emphasising limits of causal interpretation. Methods PubMed, Embase, Scopus and CENTRAL were searched from inception through 29 June 2026. Quantitative synthesis was restricted to DPP-4i active-comparator estimates. Incident pneumonia and sepsis were prespecified co-primary outcomes. Hazard ratios and incidence rate ratios were pooled as related but non-identical estimands using restricted maximum likelihood with modified Hartung-Knapp inference, with leave-one-out, prediction-interval and effect-measure-stratified analyses. ROBINS-I and GRADE were applied. Results Eighteen cohorts were included; the 11 contributing quantitatively were all at moderate risk of bias. For incident pneumonia (five studies), the pooled ratio was 0.65 (95% CI: 0.55-0.75; prediction interval 0.45-0.93; I 2 = 89.8%; very low certainty); omitting one multinational cohort whose follow-up began 2 years after drug initiation yielded 0.61 (0.56-0.67; I 2 = 0%). For incident sepsis (five studies), the prediction interval crossed the null (0.38-1.13); the exploratory pooled ratio was 0.65 (0.53-0.80; I 2 = 90.6%, and 88.1%-92.4% after every omission; very low certainty). Hazard-ratio-only point estimates were similar, although the sepsis estimate was imprecise (95% CI including 1.0). Two cohorts reported identical, unpooled estimates for infection-related hospitalisation (0.74 each; low certainty). Comparisons with GLP-1 receptor agonists did not show a consistent lower-risk pattern across four cohorts, two in selected populations, and randomised-trial syntheses have not shown a consistent class-wide preventive effect. Conclusions The available evidence did not suggest an increased average risk of severe infection with SGLT2i compared with DPP-4i. Given low to very low certainty and substantial heterogeneity, the lower pooled estimates should not be interpreted as a preventive effect. Review registration PROSPERO: CRD420261390509.

title: The Unseen Side of Nursing Leadership: Conceptualizing Leadership Blind Spots in Healthcare Settings.
abstract: Background Nursing leadership effectiveness depends not only on clinical expertise and formal authority but on the capacity to perceive how one's own conduct is experienced by staff. Leadership blind spots-unrecognized gaps between a nurse leader's self-perception and the actual impact of their behaviour on staff voice, trust, and psychological safety-represent a consequential and theoretically underdeveloped phenomenon in nursing management. Left unrecognized, these gaps may silently undermine staff well-being, patient safety, and organizational culture. Aim To clarify and conceptually define leadership blind spots in nursing using Walker and Avant's concept analysis framework, identify their defining attributes, antecedents, consequences, and empirical referents, and propose a Leadership Blind Spot Pathway Model and recommendations for measurement, practice, and policy. Methods Walker and Avant's eight-step concept analysis framework was applied. A structured literature search was conducted across six electronic sources-PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and Google Scholar-covering publications from 2020 to 2025 and supplemented by foundational theoretical works. From an initial pool of 58 records, 30 sources were retained for analysis following duplicate removal and two-stage screening. Results A nursing leadership blind spot is proposed as a recurring and insufficiently recognized discrepancy between a nurse leader's self-perceived behaviour and how that behaviour is experienced by staff. Four core defining attributes were identified: self-other perceptual discrepancy, limited recognition and integration of corrective feedback, miscalibrated confidence in leadership judgement, and relational-contextual unawareness of leadership impact. These attributes are clinically expressed through six manifestations-communication, fairness, emotional, power, performance, and change-related blind spots. Antecedents operate at individual, contextual, and organizational levels; consequences extend to nurse leaders, nursing staff, patients, and healthcare organizations. A Leadership Blind Spot Pathway Model incorporating a self-reinforcing feedback loop is proposed, in which staff silence both reflects and perpetuates leader unawareness. The concept is distinguished from destructive leadership, incompetence, burnout, and related constructs by the combination of a self-other perceptual discrepancy and limited recognition of that discrepancy. Conclusion Leadership blind spots represent a potentially distinct and operationalizable construct in nursing that warrants empirical validation. Embedding multisource feedback, reflective practice, and psychological safety into leadership development represents a promising, though not yet empirically tested, pathway to their detection and reduction. Development and psychometric validation of a Nursing Leadership Blind Spot Scale is recommended as a research priority.

title: Effectiveness of a structured educational program on knowledge about medication errors and stress of conscience among psychiatric nurses.
abstract: Background Medication errors are a persistent threat to patient safety in psychiatric settings, where complex pharmacotherapy and ethical conscience heighten nurses' stress of conscience. Aim This study evaluated the effectiveness of a structured educational program on knowledge about medication errors and stress of conscience among psychiatric nurses. Methods A one-group pre-post quasi-experimental design was implemented with 89 nurses from Assiut University Psychiatric Hospital and at Assiut Mental Health Hospital (Ministry of Health hospital), Egypt. The four-week program integrated educational sessions, reflective discussion, and scenario-based learning. Data were collected using validated medication-error and stress-of-conscience questionnaires. Results Knowledge about medication errors improved significantly following the structured educational program, with mean scores increasing from 63.20 ± 22.27 pre-intervention to 72.19 ± 18.92 post-intervention (t = 3.01, p Conclusion The structured educational program was associated with improved knowledge about medication errors and reduced reported medication errors among psychiatric nurses. Although stress-of-conscience scores decreased slightly following the educational program, the difference was not statistically significant.

title: Associations of Interprofessional Adaptive Coordination and Intercultural Communication Competence with Missed Nursing Care in Remote Hospitals in South Papua, Indonesia.
abstract: Background: Missed nursing care remains an important patient safety concern in geographically isolated and culturally diverse healthcare settings. Evidence remains limited on how cognitive safety capabilities, interprofessional coordination, and intercultural communication are associated with missed nursing care in remote multicultural settings. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 312 nurses from four hospitals in Merauke Regency, South Papua, Indonesia. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Results: Risk pattern recognition, safety sensemaking, and learning from events orientation were positively associated with nurse moral resilience. Risk pattern recognition, safety sensemaking, and nurse moral resilience were also positively associated with interprofessional adaptive coordination, whereas learning from events orientation was not statistically associated with it. Interprofessional adaptive coordination was negatively associated with perceived missed nursing care, while nurse moral resilience showed no significant direct association. Nurse moral resilience also showed a significant indirect association with missed nursing care through interprofessional adaptive coordination. Intercultural communication competence moderated the association between interprofessional adaptive coordination and perceived missed nursing care, with a more negative association at higher levels of intercultural communication competence. Conclusions: The findings position interprofessional adaptive coordination as a distinctive relational component of the pattern surrounding perceived missed nursing care, with intercultural communication competence representing a pathway-specific contextual condition. The study provides an explanatory perspective on missed nursing care in a remote, culturally diverse healthcare setting.

title: When are large language models medical devices? Navigating the MDR and AI Act for healthcare applications.
abstract: The flexibility of generative artificial intelligence (AI), and specifically large language models (LLMs), holds promise to transform healthcare by offering new tools to improve patient care and enhance clinician efficiency. However, this flexibility introduces new challenges, as LLM applications might inadvertently be used in ways that do not align with the intended purpose of the manufacturer, raising patient safety concerns and liability issues. We have identified a regulatory gap whereby LLM applications that could be repurposed, malfunction or be inadvertently misused for medical purposes fall outside the scope of the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) because they lack a medical intended purpose, and outside meaningful AI Act safety obligations because they do not qualify as high-risk systems, yet still present patient safety risks without adequate regulatory guidance. In this manuscript, we aim to address this regulatory gap for LLM applications in healthcare by identifying these ambiguous grey-area applications and providing four recommendations-validation, mitigation, compliance and alignment-focused on prevention and risk mitigation rather than reclassification as medical devices. These recommendations are intended to advance the responsible implementation of LLM applications in healthcare while ensuring patient safety.

title: Use of SGLT2 Inhibitors, GLP-1 Receptor Agonists, and DPP-4 Inhibitors in Incident Hyponatremia in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes: Multicenter Target Trial Emulations.
Self-Medication: A Critical Review of Clinical, Economic, and Health-System Trade-Offs.
abstract: Background Self-medication is an established component of self-care, but its implications for patients and health systems are not uniformly beneficial or harmful. This critical review examines the clinical, economic and health-system trade-offs. Methods PubMed, Scopus and Google Scholar informed a focused critical synthesis of 52 sources. The original literature check was conducted in August 2026; revision-stage source verification continued through 13 October 2026. Selection and descriptive critical appraisal were undertaken by one author. Results Pharmacist-supported minor-ailment care improved selected clinical and referral outcomes. An Australian trial reported symptom resolution or relief in 94% versus 88% with usual pharmacy care, with no statistically significant difference in reconsultation; its economic evaluation estimated an additional AUD7.14 per patient and AUD2277 per quality-adjusted life-year. In a Ugandan hospital-based study, self-medication was associated with admission attributed to adverse drug reactions (adjusted odds ratio 2.27; 95% confidence interval 1.14-4.55). Pharmacy interventions reduced non-prescription antibiotic dispensing in some settings, but persistent supply and limited clinical-outcome evidence constrained interpretation. Overall, benefits and risks varied by medicine, patient characteristics, professional support and healthcare access; evidence did not establish a single net clinical or economic benefit across these different practices. Conclusion Policy should support suitable non-prescription care through medicine-safety checks and defined referral criteria. In low- and middle-income countries, higher-risk-medicine restrictions should accompany affordable diagnosis and treatment. Local evaluation should measure adverse outcomes, completed referrals and household and health-system costs. Focused single-author selection limits coverage and causal interpretation.

title: Decision-Supported Collaborative Care for Gestational Diabetes: A Narrative Review of Development Pathways and Evaluation in Routine Clinical Practice.
journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy
abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) requires frequent glucose monitoring, rapid behavior adjustment, and timely escalation within a short pregnancy window, yet routine care is often episodic and fragmented across teams. Digital tools have improved data capture, but many systems still stop at logging and messaging and do not consistently translate patient-generated data into clinical action. This review frames decision-supported collaborative care for GDM as a workflow-centered care model that links glucose and clinical context to interpretable decision logic and role-based team processes for triage, escalation, and closed-loop feedback. We conducted a structured narrative review of English-language studies indexed in PubMed/MEDLINE and Web of Science from database inception to 2026, supplemented by manual screening of relevant reference lists. Owing to substantial heterogeneity in intervention design, clinical settings, and reported outcomes, the evidence was synthesized narratively. We summarize key system components, outline a practical development pathway from defining actionable use cases to embedding safety guardrails and workflow integration, and propose a multidimensional evaluation approach that combines clinical outcomes with process, implementation, and system-level measures. We also discuss major barriers to scale, including alert burden, role accountability, data governance and privacy, and digital equity. This framework may support clinicians, healthcare organizations, and policymakers in designing, implementing, and evaluating safe, equitable, and workflow-compatible GDM services.

title: Blockchain and Internet of Medical Things for Resilient Healthcare.
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed persistent weaknesses in health-data interoperability, cybersecurity, provenance, cross-organizational governance, and continuity of digital care. This short communication presents an updated focused narrative synthesis and a five-layer governance framework for integrating blockchain and the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) in patient-centered digital health. The literature was updated through 10 August 2026, with recent peer-reviewed evidence complemented by authoritative standards and European regulatory sources. The synthesis positions blockchain primarily as a distributed governance, provenance, and audit layer rather than a clinical database or stand-alone security solution, while IoMT provides heterogeneous sensing infrastructure for continuous and distributed care. The framework separates: (1) device and data acquisition; (2) network and edge orchestration, including 5G/SDN where clinically justified; (3) blockchain-based governance; (4) privacy-enhancing data, analytics, and AI; and (5) application and service delivery. Homomorphic encryption, zero-knowledge proofs, secure aggregation, differential privacy, and federated learning are treated as complementary controls with distinct threat models and computational trade-offs. The revised framework also incorporates the European Health Data Space, the EU AI Act and its medical-device interplay, and NIS2 as a regulatory overlay. Across six use-case domains, evidence is strongest for technical feasibility, provenance, and programmable access control; evidence for clinical effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, equity, sustainability, and large-scale deployment remains limited. The proposed model therefore emphasizes standards-based interoperability, minimization of on-chain personal data, endpoint trust, auditable human oversight, and prospective real-world validation.

title: Comparative analysis of quality indicators in two ISO 9001:2015-certified community pharmacies (2020-2025).
abstract: Objective To comparatively analyse the results of selected quality indicators from the quality management system certified in accordance with ISO 9001:2015 in two community pharmacies during the period 2020-2025. Methods A retrospective comparative study was conducted in two community pharmacies certified according to ISO 9001:2015. The following indicators were analysed: dispensing errors, complaints, recorded pharmaceutical interventions, follow-up of new medical prescriptions, adverse drug reactions (ADRs) reported to the Andalusian Pharmacovigilance Centre, negative outcomes associated with medication (NOMs) detected, ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), and documented referrals to physicians. Dispensing errors and complaints were assessed quarterly and compared using paired-sample tests. The remaining indicators were analysed annually using count regression models adjusted for year and number of operations. Results Statistically significant differences were observed in five of the eight indicators analysed. Pharmacy B showed higher values for complaints and reported ADRs, whereas Pharmacy A showed higher values for detected NOMs, ABPM, and recorded pharmaceutical interventions. No significant differences were observed between the two pharmacies in dispensing errors, documented referrals to physicians, or follow-up of new medical prescriptions. Conclusions Quality indicators made it possible to identify variability between two ISO 9001:2015-certified community pharmacies and proved useful in supporting continuous improvement processes. The interpretation of the observed differences should take into account the contextual, organisational and healthcare-related characteristics of each pharmacy. Comparison between pharmacies remains limited by the absence of a common framework of validated indicators and reference standards in community pharmacy.

title: Bone Anabolic Treatment in Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Background Chronic kidney disease (CKD) associated osteoporosis leads to an increased risk of bone fracture in patients with CKD. Evidence on the efficacy and safety of anti-osteoporotic medications is limited for this group. This systematic review aimed to examine the efficacy and safety of anabolic parathyroid hormone (PTH) treatment in patients with CKD Stages 4-5D. Methods MEDLINE, EMBASE and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched systematically for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating teriparatide, natpara, or abaloparatide in adult patients with CKD Stages 4-5D, including kidney transplant recipients. The primary outcome was the change in bone mineral density (BMD) during follow-up measured at the lumbar spine (LS), femoral neck (FN) and total hip (TH). The secondary outcomes included bone turnover markers, fractures, histomorphometric results from bone biopsies and adverse events (AEs). Results Two RCTs were included. A subgroup analysis of patients with CKD Stage 4 (n = 5) showed that teriparatide improved BMD at the LS and FN. Another trial (n = 61) in CKD Stage 5D showed significant BMD improvement at the TH compared to the control group. AEs were observed with higher frequency in the teriparatide-treated group. Conclusion Treatment with teriparatide seems to improve BMD in patients with CKD Stages 4-5D, but evidence on efficacy and safety is limited. Trial registration PROSPERO: CRD42024527086.

title: Nursing Competencies in Helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) in Spain: A Qualitative Study of Professional Profiles and Advanced Training.
abstract: Aim(s) To explore how HEMS professionals perceive the role, competencies, training and professional development of nursing within aeromedical transport services in Spain, incorporating the perspectives of different professional profiles involved in HEMS operations. Design An interpretative qualitative study using phenomenologically informed thematic analysis. Methods Semi-structured, in-depth interviews were conducted and analysed using phenomenologically informed thematic analysis. Data were systematically coded through open coding and organised into themes and subthemes using ATLAS.ti. Data sources Primary qualitative data were obtained from 17 purposively selected HEMS professionals through individual interviews. Interviews lasted 45-60 min, were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Results Four main categories emerged from the analysis: (1) access to the HEMS environment; (2) technical skills and competencies; (3) professional perspective and role development; and (4) structured professionalisation of the HEMS profile. Participants perceived that extensive prior experience in critical care settings, specialised academic training, supervised practice and advanced clinical simulation were necessary. Fully online training was widely perceived as insufficient. Participants identified core competencies, including advanced technical skills, knowledge of aerophysiology, aviation safety training, Crew Resource Management and Helicopter Underwater Escape Training. In addition, participants identified emotional resilience and physical fitness as personal attributes relevant to HEMS practice. Conclusion According to participants, HEMS nursing in Spain was described as a complex and highly specialised professional profile, characterised by extensive critical-care experience, advanced technical competencies and structured, practice-oriented training. The absence of a formalised training pathway contrasts with international standards and points to a perceived need for greater professional recognition and standardisation of competencies to support safe and high-quality care. Implications for the profession and/or patient care The findings provide qualitative evidence that may inform the future development of structured training pathways, competency frameworks and professional recognition for HEMS nurses in Spain.
