This study describes the systematic, evidence-based process used to develop an MSc Digital Health program at Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences (MUHAS), Tanzania. Methods A mixed-methods curriculum development approach was undertaken, comprising document review and benchmarking, a quantitative stakeholder survey, qualitative interviews with alumni of the MSc Health Information Management program, and a stakeholder consultative workshop. Nine higher-education and competency-framework sources were reviewed to identify gaps and emerging competency domains. A structured survey was administered to 48 stakeholders purposively selected from government, non-governmental, private-sector, and start-up organizations. Qualitative data from alumni interviews and open-ended survey responses were analyzed thematically using manual coding by two independent coders. A two-day consultative workshop involving 22 stakeholders from academia, professional associations, non-governmental organizations, government, and clinical practice reviewed and validated the proposed curriculum. Results Benchmarking demonstrated substantial variability in digital health curriculum content, with no single program comprehensively covering all priority competency domains. Stakeholders identified AI and machine learning (48.0%) and big data and analytics (41.7%) as prominent emerging technology competencies, while data science and predictive analytics, health information systems and interoperability, cybersecurity and data privacy, and epidemiology and biostatistics were also emphasized. Overall, 81.3% of survey respondents considered digital health competencies highly important to their organizations, while 89.6% indicated willingness to employ MUHAS MSc Digital Health graduates. Qualitative findings emphasized five priority areas: advanced computing and emerging technologies; applied health data science and analytics; health systems architecture and interoperability; experiential learning and program delivery; and governance, cybersecurity, leadership, and professional ethics. Workshop participants endorsed the proposed curriculum and recommended stronger practical learning, field attachment, innovation-oriented projects, and alignment of course content with emerging workforce needs. The resulting program was structured as a two-year, full-time MSc Digital Health program with three specialization tracks: Digital Health Leadership, Digital Health Systems Development, and Health Data Science and AI. Conclusion The MUHAS MSc Digital Health curriculum was developed through an iterative, evidence-informed, and stakeholder-driven process that integrates multidisciplinary digital health competencies with practical, implementation-oriented learning. The approach provides a potentially adaptable model for curriculum development in LMIC settings. Future evaluation should assess program implementation, graduate competencies, employment outcomes, employer satisfaction, and contribution to national digital health transformation.

title: Health policy and facility factors influencing the effectiveness of medical assessments for people with disabilities in Hanoi, Vietnam: A qualitative study.
abstract: Disability assessment determines access to social and healthcare support, yet the operation of assessment pathways may be shaped by policy implementation and facility capacity. We conducted a qualitative descriptive study at the Hanoi Medical Assessment Center, Vietnam, using purposive sampling and semi-structured, in-depth interviews with 13 stakeholders, including people with disabilities, guardians, administrative and reception staff, district social-protection officials, medical examiners, and center leaders. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using thematic analysis. Four interconnected themes were identified: administrative fragmentation and procedural burden, communication gaps and reliance on informal information channels, infrastructure constraints and system-level inefficiencies, and financial ambiguity and trust-related concerns. Participants described multilevel administrative handoffs and episodic dossier submission as sources of delay; official information was often difficult to interpret, leading users to rely on healthcare professionals; limited on-site diagnostic capacity required external referrals; and uncertainty about fees, insurance coverage, and the distinction between paying for assessment and qualifying for benefits undermined trust. These findings reflected experiences at 1 urban center and were not intended to estimate prevalence or represent disability assessment nationally. They identify context-specific service priorities for Hanoi, including clearer inter-level responsibilities, accessible and standardized guidance, better coordination of diagnostic services, and transparent communication of costs. Multicenter research, including rural and under-resourced settings, is needed before broader policy implications can be drawn.

title: Epidemiology, determinants, and microbiological profile of implant-associated infections following intramedullary nailing in a tertiary hospital in Ethiopia.
journal: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery
abstract: Background Implant-associated infections after intramedullary nailing (IMN) are a major cause of morbidity in patients with long bone fractures. This study aimed to determine the magnitude, determinants, and microbiological profile of such infections in a tertiary hospital in Ethiopia. Methods A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 260 patients who underwent IMN for lower extremity long bone fractures between January 2021 and December 2023. Clinical data, operative details, and microbiological results were collected, and logistic regression was applied to identify determinants of infection. Results The overall infection rate was 8.46% (95% CI: 5.38-12.53; 22/260), comprising 4.62% deep and 3.85% superficial infections. We found that emergency surgery and hospital stay longer than 14 days were independently associated with an increased risk of infection. Among the limited number of culture-positive infections, Gram-negative bacteria predominated, with Escherichia coli as the most frequently identified pathogen. Conclusion The infection rate was higher than in many other settings, underscoring the need for improved perioperative infection prevention and reduced hospital stays. Findings highlight the importance of perioperative optimization and hospital infection control in LMICs.

title: Aligning Antimicrobial Stewardship and Infection Prevention Through Repeated Assessment and Feedback: A Multisite Quality Improvement Initiative in Viet Nam
Efficacy, Effectiveness, and Immunogenicity of the Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prefusion F Vaccine Administered During Pregnancy: Protocol for a Living Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of lower respiratory tract disease in infants, with the highest burden in the first 6 months of life. Maternal immunization with the bivalent (RSV-A and RSV-B) prefusion F (RSVPreF) protein subunit vaccine (ABRYSVO) is a recently recommended strategy for preventing RSV-related outcomes in infants. First licensed for use in pregnancy in 2023, the RSVPreF vaccine demonstrated efficacy in a single pivotal randomized trial (Maternal Immunization Study for Safety and Efficacy; MATISSE); postlicensure real-world evidence on vaccine effectiveness across settings, seasons, and subgroups and on antibody durability and transplacental transfer remains limited and has not been synthesized in a continuously updated framework, motivating this review. Objective This living systematic review and meta-analysis will synthesize emerging postlicensure data on the efficacy, effectiveness, and immunogenicity of the RSVPreF vaccine in real-world settings. Methods We will conduct, in real time, a living systematic review and meta-analysis following Cochrane methods and PRISMA-P (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols) guidance, including randomized clinical trials and postlicensure real-world studies (eg, cohort, case-control, test-negative, and quasi-experimental studies). Primary objectives are evaluation of vaccine efficacy and effectiveness in preventing RSV-specific and all-cause respiratory disease and immunogenicity in infants and pregnant individuals. Vaccine effectiveness outcomes include RSV laboratory-confirmed infection, RSV acute respiratory illness, RSV lower respiratory tract disease, RSV hospitalization, RSV complications, all-cause lower respiratory tract disease and hospitalization, and antibiotic use in infants with RSV infection. Immunogenicity outcomes include maternal neutralizing antibody titers, maternal-infant transfer ratios, infant titers over time, and RSV viral load. We will search MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Library, LILACS, Science Citation Index Expanded, Chinese biomedical and citation databases, clinical trial registries from January 2023 onward with no language restrictions, updating at least monthly. Two investigators will independently select studies, extract data, and assess risk of bias. Adjusted estimates will be standardized to vaccine efficacy and effectiveness. Certainty will be graded using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) system. Results This living systematic review was funded in June 2025. Searches began in January 2023 and will continue with surveillance updates at least monthly until April 2028. As of January 2026, 837 records were screened, 105 (12.5%) were assessed in full text, and 12 (1.4%) met the inclusion criteria, of which 10 (1.2%) contributed extractable data. Data collection and analysis are ongoing and displayed on an interactive dashboard. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, conferences, and a real-time dashboard, with the first effectiveness estimates available in July 2026. Conclusions This living systematic review and meta-analysis will provide a continuously updated synthesis of real-world evidence on maternal RSVPreF vaccination to inform clinical and policy decisions.

title: UNIFIED HEALTHCARE DATA INFRASTRUCTURE FOR PATIENT FLOW, BED UTILIZATION, CLINICAL OPERATIONS AND HOSPITAL PERFORMANCE ANALYTICS - (HOSPITAL PULSE)
journal: International Journal of Engineering Research and Science & Technology
authors: Mrs. Y. Ramya,  Ponnaboina Akhila,  Gottemukkala Bhavya, Peniganbla Yesaswini Chandr,  Rathod Chandu Naik
abstract: Hospitals generate a large volume of operational data every day through registrations, admissions, transfers, discharges, laboratory orders, operation theatre schedules, and billing. This data is usually spread across separate systems for the outpatient desk, wards, laboratory, pharmacy, and finance, and each department sees only its own part of the picture. As a result, questions such as how many beds will be free this evening, why emergency patients wait for admission, or which ward has the longest length of stay are answered slowly and often from memory. This paper presents Hospital Pulse, a unified healthcare data infrastructure that integrates these sources and provides analytics for patient flow, bed utilisation, clinical operations, and hospital performance. The infrastructure is built around an extract, transform, and load pipeline together with change data capture from the hospital information system. Admission, discharge, and transfer events, bed status updates, laboratory and radiology orders, theatre bookings, and billing records are ingested into a raw layer, standardised into a common patient encounter model, and loaded into a clinical operations data warehouse. Patient identifiers are pseudonymised before data enters the analytical layer, and role-based access controls limit what each user can see. On the integrated data, the system computes key performance indicators such as bed occupancy rate, average length of stay, bed turnover, emergency department waiting time, theatre utilisation, and laboratory turnaround time. Predictive models add a forward-looking view. A gradient boosting model estimates each inpatient's remaining length of stay and the probability of discharge within 24 hours, and a timeseries model forecasts daily admissions by department. Together they give a projection of bed availability for the next day, which bed managers can use to plan admissions and transfers. The same data also shows where time is lost during the day, for example between a discharge decision and the release of the bed after billing clearance and cleaning.

title: #320 Big data for predictive patient flow: linking operational, population and environmental data at hospital level
Stage-wise analysis of outpatient department patient flow and waiting time at a government tertiary teaching hospital in North India: a mixed-method study
journal: International Journal of Community Medicine and Public Health
abstract: Background: Outpatient department (OPD) waiting time is a recognised indicator of hospital service quality. There are few studies from large Indian government tertiary hospitals combine direct time-motion observation with patient reported timing within a single design. This study measured stage-wise OPD patient flow at a large tertiary teaching hospital in North India to identify the primary contributor(s) to patient delay. Methods: A descriptive, cross-sectional, mixed-method study was conducted from May 2026 to June 2026 among 255 OPD patients selected by convenience sampling. Patient reported timing was used for the arrival to consultation stages, and direct time-motion observation for the pharmacy stage. Data were analysed descriptively, and examined using Pareto analysis and fishbone (Ishikawa) root cause analysis. Results: Mean total patient journey time was 260.4 minutes (arrival to consultation) and 318.6 minutes (arrival to pharmacy completion), of which consultation itself accounted for only 12.8 minutes (under 5% of total time). Waiting time from arrival to being called by the doctor was the primary bottleneck (242.8 minutes; 76.2% relative contribution), followed by pharmacy dispensing time (119.4 minutes; 37.5%). Root cause analysis identified registration-counter misallocation, absence of patient-guidance infrastructure and centralised, multi-stop pharmacy layout as the primary structural causes, rather than clinical staffing or patient volume. Conclusions: OPD delay at this tertiary hospital is driven predominantly by process and layout design rather than from insufficient service points, although staffing and patient volume were not measured here. Target interventions are registration reallocation, patient-guidance infrastructure, digital queue systems, and decentralised dispensing of generic medicines offer a practical, low-resource pathway to measurable improvement.

title: Optimizing Patient Flow in the Outpatient Departments of Bangladeshi Public Hospitals Using Arena Simulation and the Elimination of NonValue-Added Tasks
609 Applying Lean Strategy and Hoshin Kanri in a County Hospital: A Framework for Organization-Wide Improvement in Patient Flow and Access
Reducing Wait Times for Unscheduled Outpatient CT and Ultrasound Services in Indian Tertiary-Care Hospitals: A Narrative Review of Patient Flow Interventions
journal: International Journal of Integrative Health and Mind-Body Medicine
abstract: Background: Long waiting times in outpatient diagnostic imaging remain a persistent source of patient dissatisfaction in Indian tertiary-care hospitals, particularly for computed tomography (CT) and ultrasound (USG) services. Unlike magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which is typically scheduled in advance, outpatient CT and ultrasound studies in India are frequently ordered reactively - a physician examines a patient in the outpatient department (OPD) and determines, at that moment, that imaging is required. Because most Indian tertiary-care hospitals, both private and government-run, continue to process such requests on a first-come, first-served walk-in basis, patients commonly experience wait times far exceeding the actual scan duration. Objective: To synthesise Indian and international literature on outpatient waiting-time patterns and workflow interventions relevant to unscheduled CT and ultrasound demand, and to propose an operational framework adapted specifically to Indian hospital imaging departments. Methods: A narrative review was conducted using web-based academic search tools between July and August 2026, combining Indian hospital-based waiting-time literature with international radiology-specific workflow-improvement studies. Results: Indian outpatient department (OPD) waiting-time studies consistently document waits of 90–120 minutes or more against consultation or procedure times of only a few minutes, with delay attributable primarily to departmental process factors rather than patient behaviour. Radiology-specific Indian evidence remains comparatively limited, while a well-developed body of international literature - largely from insurance-billed, appointment-capable health systems - demonstrates that Lean/Value-Stream-Mapping interventions, decoupled emergency pathways, and predictive scheduling can substantially reduce imaging wait times. Conclusion: A seven-point operational framework adapted to the Indian walk-in, physician-initiated imaging model - spanning real-time order transmission, decoupled billing, predictive staffing, priority-weighted queuing, parallel preparation, transparent queue communication, and turnaround-time monitoring - is proposed as a starting point for prospective quality-improvement work in Indian radiology departments.

title: Integrating Model-Based Systems Engineering With Lean Management to Optimize Patient Flow in a Hospital Endoscopy Center: A Simulation-Based Retrospective Case Study in China
abstract: Background: Endoscopy centers worldwide are experiencing increasing demand for cancer screening, leading to prolonged patient wait times, staff burnout, and overcrowded environments. Traditional quality improvement methods, such as Lean management, often struggle to maintain consistency across documents, visualize complex workflows, and predict outcomes before implementation. Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE), a graphical, model-driven approach widely used in aerospace, may offer advantages for optimizing healthcare processes; however, the application of MBSE in this setting remains unexplored. This simulation-based retrospective study uses data from the post-pandemic recovery period (2022), when many healthcare systems were operating under maximum strain, to evaluate an optimization framework that integrates MBSE with the value-based healthcare paradigm. The findings represent simulated projections rather than results from an implemented intervention; thus, prospective validation through pilot implementation is recommended before widespread adoption. Objective: To apply MBSE integrated with Lean management to optimize patient flow in a hospital endoscopy center and to evaluate the potential impact on total patient visit time, waiting time, staff overtime, and patient density using discrete-event simulation. Methods: We conducted a simulation-based, single-center retrospective case study at the endoscopy center of a tertiary hospital in Jinan, China. All pre-optimization data were collected from May to December 2022. Following the MagicGrid MBSE methodology, we modeled the current (“as-is”) patient journey using SysML diagrams. Lean tools including value stream mapping, root cause analysis (RCA), and a 531-scoring system were applied to identify waste and generate system requirements. An optimized (“to-be”) model was developed across six subsystems and simulated in AnyLogic using discrete-event simulation with 20 Monte Carlo iterations. The model was validated using historical data fitting (2019–2022) and sensitivity analysis. A second scenario with additional equipment investment was also evaluated. A third conservative scenario (50% implementation effectiveness) was added to reflect realistic implementation conditions. The primary outcomes were total patient visit time, waiting time, staff overtime, and patient density, reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: The first optimization scenario projected mean total patient visit time from 69.1 minutes (historical baseline) to 53.7 minutes (95% CI: 52.9–54.5), a simulated reduction of 22.3%; waiting time from 19.5 minutes to 10.8 minutes (95% CI: 10.3–11.3), a simulated reduction of 44.7%; patient density from 20.2 to 15.1 per 1000 m2 (95% CI: 14.6–15.6), a simulated reduction of 25.2%; and projected elimination of staff overtime (from 88.2 to 0 minutes/day). The second scenario further projected reducing visit time to 48.5 minutes (95% CI: 47.8–49.2) and enabling 6 additional patients per day, with a projected five-year net profit of CNY 5.49 million (USD 0.823 million) under the specified assumptions. Scenario 3 (conservative, 50% realization) projected a total visit time of 61.4 minutes (95% CI: 60.5–62.3), an 11.0% reduction; waiting time of 15.6 minutes (95% CI: 14.8–16.4), a 20.0% reduction; and staff overtime of 22.1 minutes (95% CI: 18.5–25.7), a 75% reduction. Model validation showed that simulation output fell within ±5% of historical data for baseline conditions, and additional validation metrics, including queue behavior, peak crowding, daily throughput, and overtime distribution, confirmed model credibility. Conclusion: This simulation-based study shows that integrating MBSE with Lean management can substantially improve endoscopy center efficiency within the value-based healthcare framework. The MBSE + Lean approach offers a consistent, visual, and simulation-supported methodology that addresses key limitations of document-based management. However, the findings are simulated projections rather than implementation outcomes; therefore, prospective validation through a pilot implementation is recommended before widespread adoption. The conservative scenario suggests that meaningful improvements are achievable even with partial implementation.

title: Modeling Patient Flow With Queueing Theory and Poisson Processes
Application of behavioral simulation models to patient flows in Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs)
journal: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
abstract: ABSTRACT The effectiveness of care provided by Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs), which often operates in resource-scarce environments with limited personnel and infrastructure, is closely linked to coordinated patient flow management. Although widely used in conventional hospital settings, structured patient flow optimization seems to be rarely promoted in these contexts. To support this quantitative analysis, this paper explores the use of a behavioural computer simulation to model patient flow through an EMT facility and evaluate main leading strategies which can potentially improve operational rapidity while solving critical interactions among patients. An agent-based behavioural simulation model, capable of representing individual movements and interactions between patients, staff members, and physical layout of the health care facility, is provided, characterizing each agent with specific attributes and constraints related to the emergency scenario. Then, behavioural key performance indicators (KPIs) are defined to analyse simulation outputs and assess the effectiveness of EMTs organization under several patient-related and operational scenarios, in terms of operational rapidity and (over-)crowding. An application to a typological field hospital under relevant working conditions demonstrates the methodology capabilities, quantitatively tracing the effective impact of consolidated strategy, dedicate facility accesses, optimization in supporting staff number and implementation of internal wayfinding systems). Behavioural simulations can be incorporated in WHO EMT decision-support frameworks in field hospitals, supporting informed re-design and adaptation of EMT management and layouts in different deployment contexts, and training and preparedness thanks to better understanding of patient flow dynamics.

title: Clinical profile of patients with hypertension and gout in a cardiology hospital
abstract: Objective : To study the clinical features of patients with arterial hypertension (AH) and gout with an assessment of the ongoing antihypertensive therapy (AHT) hospitalized in a cardiology hospital. Materials and methods : The study included 40 patients over 18 years old who were hospitalized at the Chazov EI National Medical Research Center for Cardiology with diagnoses of AH and gout. The average age of the patients was 59.6±12.8 years, and 80% were men. The assessment of sex, age, body mass index (BMI), medical records, comorbidities and harmful habits was conducted. Laboratory tests measured uric acid (UA), glucose, and lipid profile parameters. Instrumental methods included echocardiography (EchoCG) and 24-hour blood pressure monitoring (ABPM). Depending on whether the target blood pressure (BP) of less than 140/90 mmHg, patients were divided into groups with controlled and uncontrolled hypertension. Result : Uncontrolled AH was found in 18 (45%) patients, while controlled AH was seen in 22 (55%). The average office systolic blood pressure (SBP) in the uncontrolled group was 154,0±16,4 mmHg, and in the controlled group — 121,0±7,2 mmHg (p<0.001*). Elevated pulse pressure was predominant in over 70% of patients not reaching target BP levels, compared to 17% in the BP control group (p<0.001*). When evaluating the 24-hour BP profile, non-dippers (61.1%) and night-pickers (16.7%) were significantly more common in the first group, compared to the group that reached target BP levels (13.6% and 4.5%, p<0.001*). Correlations were found between office SBP and uric acid (UA) (rxy=0.386, p=0.029), low-density lipoprotein (LDL) levels (rxy=0.382, p=0.024), triglycerides (rxy=0.454, p=0.006), and total cholesterol (rxy=0.505, p=0.002). Regression analysis showed a dependence of office SBP on the level of UA: with an increase in UA by 50 μmol/L, an increase in office SBP by 4 mm Hg an should be expected. Conclusions : In patients with hypertension and gout, an increased level of office SBP correlates with hyperuricemia and high blood lipids, while there is a linear relationship between UA and office SBP. In patients with hypertension and gout, in addition to off-target levels of UA and lipid metabolism indicators, there is an insufficient decrease in BP at night, especially in the group with uncontrolled flow of hypertension, which requires routine ABPM to assess the daily BP profile.

title: Clinical characteristics and in-hospital prognostic factors in young patients with myocardial infarction
abstract: Objectives This study aims to analyze the clinical characteristics and short-term prognostic factors of young patients with acute myocardial infarction. Methods This retrospective observational study included young patients (aged 18 to 45 years) who visited our center for AMI from January 1, 2014, to October 31, 2023. Baseline and outcome data were collected through the medical records system, with the primary endpoint being in-hospital major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Patients were divided into MACE and non-MACE groups based on the occurrence of in-hospital MACE. Coronary angiography was performed in 154/158 patients, all achieving post-procedural TIMI 3 flow. Multivariable logistic regression using Firth penalized likelihood with a priori -selected variables (LVEF, serum uric acid, age) was used to identify independent predictors of MACE. Results Of 166 young patients initially screened, 158 were included in the final analysis after excluding 8 due to incomplete data. Among these, 27 (17.1%) experienced in-hospital MACE. Patients in the MACE group had a lower prevalence of diabetes (0.00% vs. 19.08%, P = 0.008), lower admission blood pressure and worse left ventricular dysfunction [lower left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), larger left ventricular end diastolic diameter (LVEDD)]. Single-vessel disease was the most common (38.96%), with 83.77% of patients having involvement of the left anterior descending artery. The proportion of left main disease was higher in the MACE group (15.38% vs. 3.91%, P = 0.045). In the Firth model, lower LVEF was the sole independent predictor of MACE (OR 0.859, 95% CI 0.794–0.917, P < 0.001), while serum uric acid and age were not significant. Conclusion The clinical characteristics and coronary artery lesion features of young AMI patients are unique. Reduced LVEF is the sole independent predictor of in-hospital MACE in our cohort, underscoring the value of ventricular function assessment for short-term risk stratification.

title: Predictors of suboptimal peak inspiratory flow in patients with COPD exacerbation
abstract: Incorrect inhalation technique is one of the main causes of ineffective inhaled therapy in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), leading to increased frequency of exacerbations and hospitalizations. Measuring peak inspiratory flow (PIF) and determining its optimal values for a specific dry powder inhaler (DPI) can significantly assist in selecting COPD maintenance therapy. The aim of this study was to determine the frequency and predictors of suboptimal PIF among patients hospitalized due to COPD exacerbation. Methods. The study included 100 patients with COPD exacerbation requiring hospitalization. The analysis comprised basic demographic, clinical, and functional patient characteristics at admission and discharge. PIF was assessed using an IngalOk device at resistance levels corresponding to the DPIs used by patients as maintenance therapy. Measurements were taken before and after training on proper inhalation technique upon hospital admission, as well as before discharge. Results. At admission, suboptimal PIF values were initially recorded in 46% of patients. However, this rate decreased to 20% (p < 0.0001) after training in proper inhalation technique. ROC analysis identified independent predictors of suboptimal PIF such as age > 70 years, FVC < 70% pred., FEV 1 < 30%pred., RV/TLC > 70%pred.. The most significant predictors were age (OR – 0.79; 95% CI – 0.68 – 0.91; p = 0.001) and FEV1pred. (OR – 1.15; 95% CI – 1.09 – 1.25; p = 0.002). Conclusion. The likelihood of suboptimal PIF values should be considered when selecting an optimal inhalation device for maintenance therapy in patients with COPD exacerbation, especially in the elderly, among patients with very severe bronchial obstruction and patients with pulmonary hyperinflation.

title: Exploring the integrative effect of care pathway practices and their impact on patient flow in Norway: a multiple case study
abstract: Abstract Background This study investigates care pathway practices and their impact on patient flow in Norwegian hospitals. Care pathways, which aim to enhance the efficiency and quality of patient care, are increasingly implemented to address the growing demand and resource constraints in healthcare systems. Despite their increasing adoption, the mechanisms through which care pathways influence patient flow remain underexplored. Methods This research employs a multiple case study approach, examining colorectal and prostate cancer care pathways across three hospitals. Through 35 semi-structured interviews, the study explores how fifteen care pathway practices recognised in literature foster integration and their effects on patient flow. Results Findings reveal that care pathway coordinators play a crucial role in reducing non-value-added activities and bottlenecks; however, challenges remain in leveraging real-time data and extending the planning horizon beyond operational level. While care pathway practices have the potential to foster integration and improve patient flow, their effectiveness depends on how they are operationalized and the specific contextual factors of each hospital. Conclusions The study contributes to the theoretical understanding of patient flow in healthcare by exploring how specific care pathway practices stimulate cross-department integration within the aspects of organizational, planning and control, and information flow. Future research should study a larger set of cases and potentially explore additional practices that are applied in care pathways.

title: Evaluation of Hospital Information System Integration to Support Interunit Information Flow at Grand Med Hospital in 2026
abstract: Integration of the Hospital Management Information System (SIMRS) determines whether registration, examination, diagnostic service, pharmacy, and administrative data are available to the next unit in a timely manner. This article aims to develop a framework for evaluating SIMRS integration at Grand Med Hospital in 2026. The method consists of a narrative review of regulations, interoperability standards, and research on health data exchange, followed by the design of a mixed methods case study. The units of analysis are information transfers among registration, outpatient clinics or the emergency department, laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, inpatient wards, and the cashier. Key indicators include data completeness, latency, transaction failures, duplicate data entry, consistency of patient identity, and traceability of request status. The proposed assessment matches patient and visit identifiers across systems, measures the time from data transmission until the receiving unit can use the data, and records failed transactions or those requiring manual correction. Indonesia’s Minister of Health Regulation No. 24 of 2022 on Medical Records provides the regulatory reference, while HL7 FHIR, the standard used by SATUSEHAT, provides a reference for tracing relationships among patient, encounter, examination request, and result data. The review produces an audit matrix, operational definitions of indicators, and improvement priorities that can be tested using system logs, observations, documents, and interviews. Applying this framework can yield a measurable evaluation once the hospital validates the scope of integration and provides operational data for 2026

title: Analysis Of The Impact Of Hospital Management Information System (HMIS) Use On The Efficiency Of Outpatient Service Flow At Maranatha Hospital
abstract: Outpatient services require a reliable information system to accelerate work processes, improve information accessibility, and support coordination among service units. This study aimed to analyze the impact of the Hospital Management Information System (HMIS) on the efficiency of outpatient service processes at Maranatha Hospital and to identify supporting and inhibiting factors in its implementation. A descriptive qualitative approach with a case study design was employed. HMIS implementation was analyzed using the Human–Organization–Technology Fit (HOT-Fit) framework proposed by Yusof et al. (2008), operationalized through technology, human, and organizational dimensions according to the scope and available data. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, observations, documentation, and questionnaires as supporting data. The study involved 19 purposively selected informants, consisting of 10 outpatient registration officers and 9 medical record officers. The findings indicate that HMIS supported efficiency through faster registration, easier access to patient information, reduced movement of physical records, and improved coordination among units. However, these benefits were not yet optimal because of unstable networks and servers, limited system features, inconsistent data integration, and users’ competency needs. Optimization should focus on strengthening technological infrastructure, improving data integration and validation, developing user-oriented features, strengthening downtime procedures, and providing regular training and user assistance.

title: Nonlinear association between provincial implementation intensity of county-level medical communities and patient flow patterns
abstract: Introduction As a key initiative of China’s healthcare system reform, tightly integrated county-level medical communities (CCMCs) are designed to optimize the allocation of high-quality medical resources and advance the tiered healthcare delivery system. However, evidence on their policy effects remains mixed, and most studies treat CCMC construction as a binary intervention while overlooking continuous variations in implementation intensity. Meanwhile, the international literature on integrated care and referral governance focuses largely on established universal health systems, with limited attention to how progressive reforms unfold nonlinearly in developing countries facing resource constraints and patient outflows. This study addresses two unresolved questions: does intensifying CCMC construction continuously promote local patient retention, or does it initially generate patient diversion toward county-level hospitals at the expense of grassroots resources?. Methods Departing from prior work that relies on dummy variables, we construct a multidimensional CCMC Construction Intensity Index (CII) covering policy coverage, organizational integration, and institutional safeguards. Using provincial panel data from 2014 to 2024 and a two-way fixed-effects model, we identify the causal relationship between CII and patient flow patterns. Results We observe a U-shaped association between CII and the relative scale of in-county visits, though this association is attenuated under more demanding trend controls and the estimated inflection point shows some sensitivity to sample composition. At lower levels of construction intensity, patient diversion toward county hospitals accompanies the resource integration process; once intensity crosses the threshold, substantive integration and long-term mechanisms are gradually unleashed, and patient retention within counties begins to dominate. This pattern is mirrored by an inverted U-shaped trend in out-of-county care-seeking. Heterogeneity analysis shows that these patterns are more pronounced in western regions and in areas with a higher density of private hospitals; within grassroots facilities, benefits accrue primarily to township health centers, while community stations and village clinics lag behind. Discussion Theoretically, this study reveals that CCMC development in China follows a threshold-dependent trajectory, contributing Chinese evidence on the nonlinear evolution of referral dynamics to the global integrated care literature and helping reconcile mixed prior findings. From a policy perspective, the findings offer empirical support for calibrating implementation intensity to local contexts and for prioritizing township health centers as the main recipients of resource devolution, so as to mitigate early-stage patient diversion and support the gradual advancement of the tiered healthcare system.

title: The Impact of Digitization of Hospital Health Promotion (PKRS) on Patient Health Literacy in Indonesian Hospitals: Literature Review
abstract: Hospital health promotion (Promosi Kesehatan Rumah Sakit, PKRS) in Indonesia has increasingly incorporated digital platforms, including social media, hospital websites, educational videos, and mobile applications. However, the contribution of digital hospital health promotion to patient health literacy has not been systematically examined. This review aimed to examine how the digitalization of hospital health promotion influenced patients' abilities to access, understand, appraise, and apply health information. A structured narrative literature review was conducted using 30 relevant national and international articles published between 2018 and 2026, retrieved through Google Scholar, PubMed, Scopus, the Science and Technology Index (SINTA), and the Garuda portal. Data were extracted into a synthesis matrix and analyzed thematically, considering the methodological designs and strength of evidence of the included studies. The findings indicated that digital hospital health promotion improved patients' access to health information and facilitated their understanding of health-related content. Several studies also reported benefits in patients' abilities to navigate and utilize digital health information and services, although the evidence supporting these outcomes was less consistent than that concerning information access and comprehension. Meanwhile, evidence regarding patients' abilities to critically appraise health information, make informed health decisions, and adopt healthier behaviors remained limited. The effectiveness of digital hospital health promotion was influenced by digital literacy, access to technology, healthcare professionals' readiness, health information system integration, and data privacy considerations. These findings suggested that digital hospital health promotion initiatives should incorporate patient-centered educational content, appropriate guidance and support, and evaluation frameworks that prioritize patient-level outcomes rather than relying solely on digital content reach and engagement metrics.

title: Capturing the configuration of hospital-based services: a comparison of national surveys and individual patient data for liver disease in England
abstract: National surveys of health care providers are increasingly being used to assess if complex disease service configurations meet the needs of specific populations. We evaluated one-off national surveys of hospitals in the English National Health Service and compared their results against routinely collected individual patient data, using liver disease services as an example. We identified one-off national surveys describing liver disease services provided by NHS hospitals through stakeholder communication and developed a content framework, and compared information about patient flow, capacity, workforce, and specialist service provision against a number of routinely collected datasets. Nine national datasets were identified that provide information about liver disease services with notable levels of duplication. Four datasets were derived from one-off hospital surveys. Five were routinely collected, and two of these included individual patient data. Whilst providing some unique detail, the one-off surveys had inconsistent service definitions, inferior response and completeness rates, and marked discrepancies, compared to routinely collected data. Response and completeness rates were highest for the one-off survey with the lowest number of items and quantitative metrics. Response and completeness rates of the routinely collected datasets were always near-100%. When assessing the national configuration of complex disease services, one should first consider if routinely collected datasets already provide the required information. If used, one-off hospital surveys should avoid unnecessary collection of data, ensure consistent service definitions used in other relevant datasets, and optimise response and completion rates.

title: Designing eye outpatient clinics using patient flow data: a graph-theoretic framework for facility layout planning
abstract: Abstract Background Facility layout planning plays a critical role in healthcare delivery, as spatial design directly influences patient flow, operational efficiency, safety, and patient experience. In outpatient settings—particularly eye clinics where patients often undergo multiple sequential diagnostic tests—inefficient layouts can increase patient fatigue, staff workload, and safety risks. Despite its importance, data-driven methodologies for outpatient clinic layout planning remain limited. Methods This study developed a graph-theoretic framework for facility layout planning in an eye specialist outpatient clinic within a public hospital. Patient visit data were analyzed to quantify movement patterns and interaction frequencies between service stations. These interactions were represented as a weighted adjacency matrix, from which a maximal planar graph was constructed using a modified greedy heuristic algorithm to approximate optimal spatial connectivity. Clinical and operational input from the hospital team was incorporated to ensure functional relevance. The resulting planar graph was converted into block layout designs that accounted for both workflow requirements and practical design constraints. Results Analysis of patient flows revealed strong connectivity among key service stations involved in visual assessment, diagnostic testing, consultation, and discharge. Two alternative block layouts were developed. The first featured a linear, sequential configuration suitable for clinics with existing structural constraints. The second employed a centralized consultation-core design intended for new facilities, emphasizing connectivity, flexibility, and efficient patient circulation. Both designs were informed by real patient journeys and refined through stakeholder engagement. Conclusions By integrating patient flow data with graph-theoretic modeling and clinical input, this study demonstrates a practical approach to informing outpatient clinic layout planning. The framework identifies high-priority adjacency relationships from observed patient journeys and translates these into candidate block-layout configurations through stakeholder-informed design. The resulting layouts are planning concepts rather than validated geometric floor plans. Although applied to an eye outpatient clinic, the framework can be adaptable to other outpatient settings where patients require multiple sequential investigations.

title: Socioeconomic analysis of the in-hospital neurosurgical continuum of care for patients in Nigeria
abstract: Background In Nigeria, neurosurgical care is primarily financed by out-of-pocket (OOP) payments due to minimal health insurance coverage, leading to high rates of financial distress, limited access, and delayed care. This study aimed to quantify patient-level OOP costs, evaluate the risk of catastrophic and impoverishing expenditures, and assess the socioeconomic impacts of neurosurgical hospitalization. Methods We conducted a prospective cohort study of neurosurgical patients at the University College Hospital, Ibadan, from January to August 2024. Structured questionnaires were administered at admission, discharge, and 2–4 weeks post-discharge to capture direct medical, direct non-medical, and indirect costs of care. Catastrophic health expenditure (CHE) was assessed using two established thresholds: out-of-pocket health expenditure exceeding 10% of total household income, consistent with the SDG 3.8.2 framework, and expenditure ≥40% of household capacity to pay, using the WHO approach. Impoverishment was assessed against the World Bank poverty line for Nigeria. Ethical approvals were obtained from the University of Ibadan/University College Hospital Ibadan and Duke Health Institutional Review Boards. Results We enrolled 99 neurosurgical patients (median age 33, 75% male). Traumatic brain injury was the most common diagnosis (48%). The median length of stay was 14 days. Most patients (92%) relied on household savings, and 52% borrowed money to cover their cost of care. Only 12% had any health insurance, which covered a median of 30% of expenses. The median direct medical cost per patient was ₦969,000 ($633), non-medical cost ₦202,000 ($132), and indirect cost ₦141,639 ($93). The median total OOP expenditure was ₦1,410,787 ($922; IQR: ₦815,951–₦2,442,176). Among households with sufficient baseline economic data, 97.0% were already below the specified poverty threshold before healthcare payments. Both households initially above the threshold crossed below it, following OOP expenditure, while the mean daily per-capita poverty gap increased from ₦3,296 to ₦30,350. Conclusion These findings underscore the inadequacy of current financial protection mechanisms. To improve access and equity, urgent policy action is needed to expand pooled health financing, increase public investment in neurosurgical services, and provide targeted subsidies for high-cost surgical care. Strengthening public neurosurgical services and decentralizing care (to reduce travel and indirect costs) will also help shield vulnerable households. These measures are critical as Nigeria advances toward universal health coverage.

title: Patient Satisfaction and Associated Factors in a Tertiary Hospital in Ibadan, Nigeria
abstract: Abstract Background Patient satisfaction is an important indicator of perceived healthcare quality and patient-centred care. However, evidence integrating interpersonal, technical, organisational and access-related dimensions of satisfaction in Nigerian tertiary hospitals remains limited. This study assessed factors associated with patient satisfaction across selected service domains in a tertiary hospital in Ibadan, Nigeria. Methods A hospital-based analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 350 adult patients receiving care across seven departments. Patients were selected using systematic sampling, while 70 healthcare workers were purposively recruited for contextual assessment. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire. Overall satisfaction was classified as satisfied or dissatisfied, with neutral responses classified with dissatisfied responses. Associations were examined using chi-square tests and binary logistic regression. Adjusted odds ratios (AORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated from a comprehensive multivariable model. Results Among 350 patients, 267 (76.3%) were satisfied and 83 (23.7%) dissatisfied. Bivariate analyses demonstrated significant associations between satisfaction and multiple service-quality, infrastructure, staff-related, communication and financial-accessibility factors. In the final comprehensive model, satisfaction was independently associated with dignity and respect (AOR = 10.29, 95% CI: 4.32–24.50), access to medical specialists (AOR = 4.97, 95% CI: 2.26–10.96), and functional equipment (AOR = 4.09, 95% CI: 1.70–9.84). Patients aged 31–35 years had higher odds of satisfaction than those aged 18–24 years (AOR = 5.50, 95% CI: 1.35–22.34), while post-tertiary education was associated with lower odds (AOR = 0.12, 95% CI: 0.02–0.90). Gender, marital status and department were not independently associated with satisfaction. The final model was statistically significant (likelihood-ratio χ²(18) = 151.10, p < 0.001). Department and waiting time were significantly associated with satisfaction at bivariate level. Patients strongly endorsed transparent billing (97.4%), modern equipment (96.9%) and shorter waiting times (96.3%). Conclusion Patient satisfaction reflected multiple dimensions of tertiary healthcare delivery, with dignity and respect, specialist access and functional equipment emerging as independent correlates. Quality-improvement efforts should prioritise respectful patient-centred care, functional resources and access to specialist services while addressing broader service, communication and financial-accessibility concerns. (Fig. 1)

title: Scenario-driven simulation and multi-objective optimization strategies for enhancing patient satisfaction in sustainable hospital resource management
Left Ventricular End‐Diastolic Diameter Predicts Clinical Outcomes in Patients Supported With Surgically Implanted Microaxial Flow Pump
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
abstract: Background This study sought to determine the impact of left ventricular size on clinical outcomes after a microaxial flow pump was surgically implanted. Methods In this retrospective cohort study, we included patients who received a surgical microaxial left ventricular assist device from May 2020 to February 2024 at 2 high‐volume centers in the United States. Patients were categorized into 2 groups based on their preimplant left ventricular end‐diastolic diameter (LVEDD): “small LVEDD,” defined as LVEDD ≤5.5 cm, and “large LVEDD,” defined as LVEDD >5.5 cm, respectively. End points were all‐cause death at 30 days after device implantation, in‐hospital death, death 30‐days after discharge, and survival at 30‐month follow‐up. Results Two‐hundred sixty‐two patients received an Impella 5.5. Preimplant LVEDD was documented in 194 (74%) patients, where 50 patients had LVEDD ≤5.5 cm and 144 patients had LVEDD >5.5 cm. Patients with a small LVEDD had a higher rate of all‐cause death at 30 days after device implantation (32% versus 11.8%, P =0.002), in‐hospital death (42% versus 20.1%, P =0.004), and death 30 days after discharge (44% versus 20.8%, P =0.003). In adjusted analyses, patients with a greater LVEDD had 62% decreased risk of long‐term death (hazard ratio, 0.39 [95% CI, 0.19–0.76]; P =0.001), compared with patients with a smaller LVEDD. Conclusions In this real‐world, all‐comer study, we found that patients with reduced left ventricular dimension who required an Impella 5.5 had worse outcomes. Further research is warranted to recapitulate our observations across more centers.

title: Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome in emergency cardiovascular patients with COVID-19: from clinico-laboratory markers to hospital outcomes
abstract: Background. Clinical manifestations of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) range from asymptomatic course to severe pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome. At the same time, patients with concomitant cardiovascular disease have a significantly higher risk of adverse events and death. The aim of this study was to evaluate the incidence, risk factors, potential for prevention of multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS), and its effect on in-hospital complications in patients with emergency cardiovascular conditions and concurrent COVID-19. Materials and methods. This prospective cohort single-center study included 139 participants with acute cardiovascular conditions who were also diagnosed with COVID-19. Their mean age was 67.9 ± 12.7 years, 70 (50.4 %) of them were men. Emergency cardiovascular conditions leading to hospitalization included acute coronary syndrome (49.6 %), hypertensive emergency (23.7 %), acute heart failure (17.3 %), or arrhythmias. MODS was diagnosed in 38 (27.3 %) patients based on the presence of at least two out of three criteria: respiratory failure (decreased SpO2 < 92 %), renal dysfunction (increase in creatinine level ≥ 26.5 μmol/L), or liver dysfunction (ALT and AST levels elevated ≥ 3 times the upper limit of normal). The primary endpoint was in-hospital mortality depending on absence or presence of MODS. Also, MODS-associated clinical and laboratory risk factors, other in-hospital complications and length of stay were evaluated. Results. MODS development significantly increased mortality, to 28.9 % (11/38) versus 9.9 % (10/101) in the control group (p < 0.01). The highest MODS-associated mortality occurred in patients with acute heart failure (44.4 %; 4/9) and acute myocardial infarction (26.7 %; 4/15). MODS was more prevalent in men and was related to comorbidities (chronic kidney disease, coronary artery disease, chronic heart failure), baseline hypoxia, systemic inflammation, and hypercoagulation. Patients with MODS had significantly more hospital complications, including acute psychosis/delirium (31.6 vs. 8.9 %, p < 0.01) and required more intensive support: high-flow oxygen (68.4 vs. 30.7 %, p < 0.001), non-invasive ventilation (36.8 vs. 10.9 %, p < 0.001), and inotropic therapy (34.2 vs. 6.9 %, p < 0.001). Conclusions. MODS complicates emergency cardiovascular diseases in over 25 % of COVID-19 cases. Its development is associated with a more severe hospital course, a higher need for intensive care, and increased in-hospital mortality.

title: Queuing Theory as the Interpretable Core of Adaptive Hospital Operations: A Theory-Building Synthesis and the LASI Framework
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Hospital patient flow and resource allocation are problems of decision-making under stochastic, non-stationary demand in a complex adaptive system, yet analytical queuing models, simulation, and artificial intelligence (AI) are treated as competing techniques, and no theory specifies how an interpretable core could safely constrain an adaptive one. This paper makes a theory-building contribution. It formalizes hospital operations as a single controlled-stochastic-process problem — defending that abstraction against network-optimization, partially-observable, cyber-physical, and decentralized alternatives — of which the analytical, simulation, and learning paradigms are three approximation strategies. From four functional requirements it derives the LASI framework (Layered Analytical–Simulation–Intelligence), argues each layer’s indispensability and the necessity of their dependency ordering, and specifies the core mechanism as a constrained-Markov-decision-process safety filter. Its most developed contribution is the validity-region mechanism: the analytical core may bound learning only where the core is validated, with the boundary estimated continuously by simulation through an analytical–reality divergence measure, and authority transferring between the analytical and simulation layers by a hysteresis rule. Governance is elevated from a passive gate to an active supervisory controller that resolves inter-layer conflicts and sets a responsible decision weight — the delegable authority to learning that keeps violation risk below a governance tolerance. Seven falsifiable propositions with boundary conditions state the theory. The synthesis repositions queuing theory not as a stage superseded by AI but as the interpretable, auditable core of accountable adaptive hospital operations.

title: The Synchronized Patient Turnaround Protocol (SPTP): An Operational Architecture for Resolving Hospital Discharge Delays via Cross-Industry Milestone Synchronization
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A strategic working paper and operational architecture adapting Airport Collaborative Decision Making (A-CDM) to eliminate acute hospital discharge bottlenecks[cite: 3, 5]. By backward-scheduling clinical and logistical dependencies against a locked Estimated Discharge Target (EDT) at T-48h, SPTP synchronizes pharmacy batching, patient transport dispatch, and social care placement[cite: 3, 5, 7]. The model runs natively on existing EPR systems or ward whiteboards[cite: 4, 7], recaptures up to 135 minutes of administrative time per nursing shift[cite: 8], unlocks 18–24 beds of continuous acute capacity without capital expenditure[cite: 4, 10], and reduces aborted patient transport journeys[cite: 10]. title: Examining Hospital Experiences in Online User Reviews of Children’s Hospitals: A Qualitative Study
abstract: Aim: This study aimed to examine hospital experiences expressed in online user reviews of children’s hospitals using inductive content analysis, to identify the thematic areas in which these experiences were concentrated, and to assess the concordance between star ratings and textual evaluation direction.Method: This descriptive qualitative study analyzed publicly accessible Google Maps user reviews of three public children’s hospitals in Türkiye that exclusively provide healthcare services to children. Reviews published in 2022 or later were eligible. Of 499 accessible records, 136 records without textual content and 13 off-topic records were excluded, leaving 350 reviews for analysis. The data were analyzed using an inductive content analysis approach. The coding process resulted in a final codebook comprising 88 codes, which were organized into 22 subthemes and 7 main themes.Results: The most frequently represented theme was “Communication, Staff Attitudes, and Interpersonal Interaction” (n=184, 52.6%), followed by “Overall Judgment and Preference Behavior” (n=171, 48.9%), “Access, Appointments, and Process Flow” (n=104, 29.7%), “Clinical Competence, Treatment, and PatientSafety” (n=93, 26.6%), “Physical Environment, Hygiene, and Support Services” (n=79, 22.6%), “Child-and Family-Specific Care Experience” (n=78, 22.3%), and “Institutional and System-Level Responsibility” (n=61, 17.4%). In terms of textual evaluation direction, 174 reviews (49.7%) were classified as negative, 110(31.4%) as positive, 64(18.3%) as mixed, and 2 (0.6%) as neutral. Star ratings were generally consistent with textual evaluation direction; however, the mixed reviews and the nine reviews (2.6%) showing a clear discrepancy between the star rating and the direction of the textual evaluation indicated that numerical ratings did not fully capture the complexity of the experiences expressed in online reviews.Conclusions: Hospital experiences expressed in online reviews of children’s hospitals were multidimensional and were shaped particularly by communication and staff attitudes, as well as by clinical care, access, the physical environment, child- and family-specific needs, and institutional processes. The textual content of online user reviews may provide a complementary source of information for evaluating patient and family experience and for identifying areas for quality improvement in children’s hospitals.

title: Clinical and patient-reported predictors of days alive and out of hospital in decompensated cirrhosis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Days alive and out of hospital (DAOH) is a patient-centered outcome, but has not been studied in decompensated cirrhosis (DCC). We aimed to quantify DAOH and to identify clinical and patient-reported factors associated with DAOH. METHODS: Using an ongoing prospective cohort study of adults hospitalized with DCC, DAOH was calculated by subtracting days hospitalized, transplanted, or deceased from 90 days post-discharge from index hospitalization. Univariable and multivariable negative binomial hurdle models were used to identify clinical and patient-reported variables associated with DAOH, where DAOH was treated both as a categorical (any readmission, transplant, death vs. all 90-DAOH) and continuous (proportion of event days) outcome. RESULTS: Among 363 adults (median age 54 y; MELD 3.0 score 23), 40% experienced all 90-DAOH while 90-day readmission, death, and transplant occurred in 49%, 21%, 11%, respectively. Mean DAOH was 68.3 (SD: 29.0). In multivariable models, transplant evaluation status (listed vs. not listed/evaluated: OR 7.55, p=0.004) was associated with experiencing an event within 90 days. In comparison, when considering the number of event days, higher PROMIS Ability to Participate in Social Roles and Activities scores were independently associated with a lower proportion of event days (rate ratio, RR 0.91 per 3-point increase, p=0.030) in addition to MELD 3.0 >25 (vs. <15, RR 2.75, p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: DAOH is a holistic, patient-centered outcome for decompensated cirrhosis that integrates readmission, transplantation, and mortality into a single measure of post-discharge burden. By using DAOH and moving beyond readmissions, we show that lower MELD 3.0 and higher patient-reported social well-being were independently associated with more days at home after hospitalization.

title: Rigid bronchoscopy using high-flow oxygenation and deep sedation: A feasibility, safety, and patient-reported tolerability survey
abstract: BackgroundRigid bronchoscopy (RB) is conventionally performed under general anesthesia with jet or mechanical ventilation in an operating room and requires anesthesiologist support. Deep sedation with high-flow oxygenation (HFO), without anesthesiologist or mechanical ventilation, has recently been used for RB at our hospital.ObjectivesWe evaluated the feasibility, safety, and patient-reported tolerability of RB performed under deep sedation with HFO, without general anesthesia or neuromuscular blockade.DesignRetrospective, single-center cohort study.MethodsWe reviewed our institutional registry to identify all consecutive patients who underwent therapeutic RB under deep sedation with HFO. Sedation depth was targeted to a Modified Observer's Assessment of Alertness/Sedation score of 2 or less. Vital signs, end-tidal carbon dioxide, and oxygen saturation were continuously monitored. A patient-reported tolerability survey was administered on the procedure day and 1 week later. The primary endpoint was procedural success; secondary endpoints included intra- and post-procedural complications and patient-reported tolerability.ResultsSixty-eight cases (66 patients) were analyzed between August 2023 and June 2025, including patients with ASA class III or higher (38.2%), a baseline oxygen requirement (80.9%), and urgent or emergent indications (41.2%), reflecting an unselected, all-comers cohort. Procedural success was achieved in 67 cases (98.5%), with a mean procedure time of 45.1 minutes. Complications included hypoxia (13.2%), arrhythmia (7.4%), bleeding (5.9%), and hypotension (1.5%), with no 72-hour procedure-related complications or in-hospital mortality. Sore throat and voice change occurred in 25 (36.8%) and seven (10.3%) cases, respectively, all resolving within a week. Three cases (4.4%) experienced distress during the procedure, and 94.1% were willing to undergo re-examination.ConclusionsRB using HFO and deep sedation, without mechanical ventilation or anesthesiologist support, was feasible across a heterogeneous, unselected cohort, with an acceptable complication profile and favorable patient-reported tolerability. These findings support further prospective, comparative evaluation of this approach, particularly in settings with limited anesthesiology support.

title: Predicting 30-Day Hospital Readmission in Diabetic Patients Using Machine Learning
abstract: Hospital readmissions are a significant problem in healthcare, particularly in diabetic patients. The research question guiding this study was: Can 30-day hospital readmission for diabetic patients be predicted using common machine learning models applied to hospital record data? This study aims to predict this using three machine learning models: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost. The analysis was conducted on the Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, which contains over 100,000 patient records. After data cleaning, 98,053 complete records with 20 features were used for model training and evaluation. Random Forest achieved the highest accuracy at 88.73%, Logistic Regression at 88.67%, and XGBoost at 88.59%. Moreover, the XGBoost model’s Area Under the Curve (AUC) was only 0.653, indicating performance slightly better than random guessing. The number of lab procedures were found to be the strongest predictor of readmission, followed by different diagnoses and number of medications. The models struggled to identify readmitted patients due to dataset imbalance, with only 11.3% of patients readmitted. These findings suggest that while machine learning can predict readmission status with reasonable overall accuracy, current models are not reliable enough for clinical use without additional features and improved data quality.

title: Association of one-stop administrative and logistics services with patient satisfaction in smart hospitals
abstract: This study aims to examine whether the quality of one-stop administrative and logistics services is associated with patient satisfaction in smart hospitals and identify indicators that may merit attention in service redesign. This multicenter cross-sectional study included 837 service users at 4 sites in 3 public hospitals in Dongguan, China (January 2023-December 2025). A 27-item questionnaire covered 9 service-experience domains. Overall satisfaction (0-10) was the primary outcome; high satisfaction (score ≥ 8) was a secondary outcome. Eight operational indicators were extracted from work-order systems. Analyses included confirmatory factor analysis, hierarchical linear and logistic regression with site fixed effects, structural equation modeling, and an exploratory gradient-boosting analysis. Mean age was 47.2 years; 57.1% were women. Cronbach α ranged from 0.72 to 0.79. The prespecified 9-domain structure showed satisfactory fit in this sample; independent psychometric validation is needed. In the fully adjusted linear model (n = 774), first-contact resolution (β = 0.31; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.23-0.38) and problem closure (β = 0.29; 95% CI, 0.25-0.33) were positively associated with satisfaction. Convenience, reliability, responsiveness, transparency, and digital access were also positively associated (β, 0.12-0.19). Longer response time (β = -0.26), complaint or second feedback (β = -0.20), and repeated visits (β = -0.16) were negatively associated. Problem closure showed the strongest association with high satisfaction (odds ratio, 2.87; 95% CI, 2.18-3.82). In structural equation modeling, the standardized direct association between digital access and satisfaction was 0.08 (P = .052), and the summed standardized indirect associations through convenience, responsiveness, and problem closure were 0.35. The exploratory, unvalidated ranking placed problem closure, convenience, responsiveness, reliability, and digital access highest. Service-process quality was associated with patient satisfaction. First-contact resolution, problem closure, and related indicators are candidate targets for prospective evaluation. The cross-sectional design precludes causal interpretation, and the instrument requires independent validation.

title: Patient Experience with Phlebotomy and Laboratory Testing at a University Hospital: A Mixed-Methods Exploratory Study
journal: The Journal of Applied Laboratory Medicine
authors: Maurits C F J de Rotte
abstract: BACKGROUND: Patient satisfaction with the phlebotomy center or the laboratory in general is often only infrequently measured in single touchpoint surveys. In addition, patient complaints are scarce and patients rarely proactively provide feedback by themselves. The aim of this single-center study was to explore patient satisfaction and perceived improvement opportunities regarding phlebotomy and laboratory testing at a university hospital phlebotomy center. METHODS: We conducted a mixed-methods study combining survey data (including Net Promoter Score [NPS] and Customer Effort Score [CES], n = 109) and semi-structured interviews with 8 patients frequently visiting the phlebotomy center. RESULTS: In the survey, 34.9% of the respondents were promoters, 53.2% were passives, and 7.3% were detractors, resulting in an NPS of 27.6%. The median CES was 1 (interquartile range 1-2), indicating low perceived effort. Interview findings suggested that while the service was considered well-organized, "waiting"-rather than the phlebotomy procedure itself-emerged as the most important theme. Key recommendations included reducing waiting times, improving the waiting area, providing more instructions on the phlebotomy process, offering reliable online information on laboratory tests and results, and facilitating phlebotomy close to home. While most recommendations addressed functional needs, some also targeted emotional needs (e.g., free coffee, private seating). CONCLUSIONS: This mixed method study illustrates how involving patients in examining the laboratory-related patient journey can yield concrete, patient-reported insights and suggestions for improvement. Implementing recommendations derived by open-ended survey responses and interviews is likely to improve the patient journey, on both functional and emotional levels.

title: ROYAL PRESTON HOSPITAL VIRTUAL SPINE ADVISORY SERVICE
The Effect of Bed Occupancy Rate (BOR) On Patient Satisfaction and Its Implications for Patients’ Revisit Intention at Sumber Sentosa Hospital Malang
journal: Indonesian Interdisciplinary Journal of Sharia Economics (IIJSE)
abstract: Bed Occupancy Rate (BOR) is an important indicator for assessing the efficiency of bed utilization and the operational workload of inpatient hospital services. At Sumber Sentosa Hospital Malang, BOR values have fluctuated and have not yet reached the ideal range, which in several periods was accompanied by a decline in patient satisfaction and repeat visit intention. This condition indicates weaknesses in inpatient capacity management that may affect service quality and patient loyalty. Therefore, this study aims to analyze the effect of BOR on patient satisfaction and its implications for inpatient repeat visit intention at Sumber Sentosa Hospital Malang. This study employed a quantitative method using descriptive and verificative approaches. The population consisted of inpatients at Sumber Sentosa Hospital Malang, with respondents selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using questionnaires that had been tested for validity and reliability. The data were then analyzed using path analysis to examine direct and indirect effects among the research variables. The results indicate that BOR has a positive and significant effect on patient satisfaction. Patient satisfaction also has a positive and significant effect on repeat visit intention. In addition, BOR directly influences repeat visit intention and indirectly affects it through patient satisfaction as a mediating variable. These findings confirm BOR management is essential for sustained inpatient service quality.

abstract: Managing hospital resources is a key strategic challenge in high-volume tertiary care, where turn-around time (TAT)—the time interval from the physician discharge order to physical. In this mixed-methods study of 320 inpatient cases in an Indian tertiary hospital, we utilize quantitative HIS time-stamp data and qualitative stakeholder perspectives to identify systemic bottlenecks. The results show that most discharges are timely, but a substantial proportion fail to meet benchmarks because of the administrative complexities brought by insurance-linked cases (TPA and PSU approvals), delayed billing processing, and logistical challenges. There was a significant temporal mismatch in late exit patients that resulted in them leaving at times when admissions are starting again in the early morning, which creates ED congestion and does not allow the most appropriate use of the beds (e.g., for patients being observed post-discharge). To tackle these challenges, the work suggests a formal structure that includes real-time digital dashboards, dedicated discharges coordination, along with the creation of lounges for discharge to liberate clinical recovery from bed occupancy. These evidence-based solutions are presenting a scale model roadmap for the healthcare executives to advance the hospital through put, financially sustainability and the patient care experience in healthcare facilities. Keywords: Hospital Resource Management; Discharge Turnaround Time (TAT); Patient Flow; TPA Approvals; Bed Utilization; Indian Healthcare; Discharge Lounge.

title: Evaluation Of Electronic Medical Record Downtime Management On Patient Service Efficiency At Hospital X
abstract: Electronic medical record (EMR) implementation in hospitals is vulnerable to downtime, during which the system becomes inaccessible because of infrastructure disruption, network failure, software malfunction, or cyberattack, potentially delaying care and increasing patient-safety risks. Evidence concerning how downtime management affects service efficiency in Indonesian hospitals remains limited. This study evaluated EMR downtime management and its implications for patient service efficiency at Hospital X. A descriptive qualitative design was applied using semi-structured interviews with four informants directly involved in downtime management. Data were analyzed using the Miles and Huberman interactive model and validated through source triangulation with internal standard operating procedures and official downtime reports. Hospital X had a basic response mechanism consisting of conversion to manual documentation followed by data re-entry after system recovery, with responsibilities divided between electrical-facility maintenance and the hospital information-system unit. Official documentation for March-April 2026 recorded five downtime events totaling approximately 4 hours 28 minutes, caused by a firewall anomaly, Transmedik server anomalies, and a total power outage. Server anomalies occurred most frequently, while the firewall anomaly produced the longest single disruption. Downtime resulted in patient backlogs, slower clinical services, longer waiting for supporting examinations, and additional staff workload from retrospective data entry. Major constraints were delayed or unclear notifications, uncertain recovery estimates, and dependence on hierarchical approval, whereas existing standard operating procedures did not explicitly define escalation criteria or decision-making authority. Current management is operationally usable but remains predominantly manual. Hospital X therefore requires more structured communication triggers, explicit escalation authority, and consideration of digital backup mechanisms to strengthen service continuity, efficiency, and patient safety during EMR disruption.
