title: Comparison of Hospital Stay of Burn Patients Undergoing Early Tangential Excision and Delayed Tangential Excision in The Burn Unit of Cipto Mangunkusumo Hospital in 2023 - 2024
abstract: Background: Burns remain a major challenge in plastic surgery due to their high mortality and morbidity. Tangential excision, a surgical procedure to remove necrotic tissue while preserving viable tissue, should be performed as soon as possible, as it has been shown to decrease hospital stay in burns ≤30% TBSA. While early excision has shown benefits in smaller burns, evidence is lacking for larger burns and in resource-limited settings such as Indonesia. This study compared hospital stays among burn patients who underwent early versus delayed tangential excision.Methods: This retrospective cohort study included burn patients who were discharged alive and underwent early or delayed tangential excision between January 2023 and December 2024. We divided subjects into two groups: early excision and delayed excision. We analysed data using the Mann-Whitney test to assess differences in hospital stay between the two groups.Results: This study included 100 patients: 63 who underwent early tangential excision and 37 who underwent delayed tangential excision. The median TBSA was 29.5% (range 10–71%). The median length of hospitalisation was lower in the early excision group than in the delayed excision group, although not statistically significant (20 [5–49] vs 20 [7–66]; p=0.274).Conclusion: Although no statistically significant difference was observed, the trend toward shorter hospital stay in the early excision group provides important preliminary evidence to guide national burn protocols.

title: Determinants of Delivery Hospital Choice in Georgia, 2016–2021
abstract: BACKGROUND: US maternal mortality and severe maternal morbidity (SMM) are marked by substantial disparities by race, payer, and geography. To the extent that such disparities are driven by differences across hospitals rather than within hospitals, understanding what shapes delivery hospital choice can inform policy responses. OBJECTIVES: To examine how distance, hospital attributes, and maternal characteristics jointly shape delivery hospital choice, and whether patterns differ between urban Atlanta and smaller Georgia markets. RESEARCH DESIGN: Retrospective observational study using a conditional logit model to estimate delivery hospital choice. Hospital markets were defined through community detection on patient-flow data. We report marginal effects on selection probability. SUBJECTS: Seven hundred ten thousand eight hundred seventy deliveries across 84 Georgia hospitals, 2016-2021. MEASURES: Deterministically linked hospital discharge, birth, and fetal death records, supplemented with American Hospital Association, CMS, and Area Resource Files data. RESULTS: Distance (in miles) strongly deterred hospital selection in both markets, with greater sensitivity in Atlanta (-2.7 percentage points [pp] per additional mile) than outside Atlanta (-1.9 pp/mile). Individuals preferred hospitals with higher perinatal levels of care and teaching status. A hospital's elective C-section rate was negatively associated with its selection outside Atlanta (-1.3 pp) but positively in Atlanta (+2.5 pp). Higher comorbidity was associated with higher-quality hospital selection, though the highest-risk Atlanta individuals showed lower preference for high-elective-C-section hospitals. CONCLUSIONS: Delivery hospital choice in Georgia reflects distance, practice environment, insurance, and clinical complexity, with urban/nonurban differences. Medicaid-insured individuals show delivery patterns consistent with provider supply-side constraints, which may raise concerns to the extent that they face an elevated risk of adverse maternal outcomes. Findings inform payment and referral policies improving access to risk-appropriate delivery settings and reducing maternal health disparities.

title: CYMEDSEC Cybersecurity Performance in Remote Patient Monitoring Systems in a Live Hospital Setting: Protocol for an Observational Study
abstract: Background: Remote patient monitoring (RPM) systems based on the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) technologies are increasingly integrated into chronic disease management and telemedicine pathways. Despite their widespread adoption, cybersecurity performance, system resilience, and user behavior in real-world clinical environments remain underexplored. Existing evidence is fragmented, often limited to laboratory simulations or vendor-driven assessments, leaving a critical gap in understanding how cybersecurity risks across the full life cycle of RPM systems deployed in health care settings. Objective: This study aims to systematically analyze the cybersecurity posture, system resilience, and user behavior across the full life cycle of IoMT-enabled RPM systems in a real-world hospital and home-care environment. The study aims to generate empirical evidence on how technical safeguards, operational workflows, and human factors influence cybersecurity risks during procurement, integration, deployment, routine use, and decommissioning of these platforms. Methods: This observational study will analyze 2 independent RPM systems used for chronic disease monitoring in a real-world hospital setting. The assessment framework includes (1) system-log analytics to evaluate authentication events, device connectivity, update and patch management, and anomalous behaviors; (2) a controlled phishing simulation targeting health care professionals to assess susceptibility and response patterns; (3) an evaluation of update management processes and vendor-hospital interactions; (4) measurement of cybersecurity awareness and practices among patients and health care professionals using validated instruments; and (5) mapping of vulnerabilities across all life cycle phases, from procurement to decommissioning. Although the study includes cybersecurity training, preassessments/postassessments, and controlled phishing and update-management scenarios, these activities are part of the observational framework and are not designed as experimental interventions that have an impact on the clinical aspects of patient care. Quantitative data will be analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while qualitative insights from operational workflows will be integrated to contextualize system performance. Ethical approval has been obtained from the institutional ethics committee. Results: The CYMEDSEC (enhanced cybersecurity for networked medical devices through optimization of guidelines, standards, risk management, and security by design) project received funding from the European Union's Horizon Europe program (grant 101094218) and started on November 1, 2024. Ethical approval was obtained on December 18, 2025, and institutional authorization on January 29, 2026. Patient enrollment is scheduled to begin on April 1, 2026. At the time of paper submission, no patients were recruited. Data analysis will begin after completion of patient involvement, with results expected before the project end date in October 2027. Conclusions: This study will provide real-world evidence on the cybersecurity performance of IoMT-enabled RPM systems, capturing the interplay among technical safeguards, operational processes, and human factors. Findings are expected to support the development of security-by-design approaches, inform procurement and regulatory frameworks, and guide the safe integration of connected medical devices into routine care within the framework of the CYMEDSEC research project.

title: Protocol for: Diagnostic trajectories of patients receiving unspecified psychosis-spectrum diagnoses – A retrospective, longitudinal, register-based study in a large UK secondary mental healthcare service from 2007–2024
abstract: Abstract Background Unspecified psychosis-spectrum diagnoses (ICD code F29) are commonly used when the underlying disorder remains uncertain, particularly at first presentation. These diagnoses may persist or later be revised as the clinical picture evolves, yet little is known about their long-term trajectories or implications for treatment and service use in routine mental healthcare. Objectives To describe the usage and persistence of unspecified non-organic psychosis (F29) and other non-specific diagnoses, and the time to transition to a specific diagnosis. Secondary objectives are to describe temporal trends in their use, identify demographic and clinical characteristics associated with diagnostic persistence, and characterise treatment patterns, service utilisation, mortality, and discharge across diagnostic groups. Methods We will conduct a retrospective longitudinal cohort study using de-identified electronic health-record data from the South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust (SLaM), accessed through the Clinical Record Interactive Search (CRIS) system, between 1 January 2007 and 31 December 2024. The study population will include patients with an ICD-10 psychosis-spectrum diagnosis (F2x.x), substance induced psychotic disorder (or F1x.5), bipolar disorder or affective disorder with documented psychotic symptoms(F32/3.3). Diagnoses will be classified as specific or non-specific according to their ICD-10 category. Primary analysis will examine time from first F29 diagnosis to first subsequent specific psychosis-spectrum or bipolar diagnosis using Cox proportional hazards regression, with discharge from SLaM, death and administrative end of follow-up treated as censoring events. Associations with diagnostic transition will be examined adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, area-level deprivation, route of service entry, and calendar period. Secondary competing-risk analysis will estimate the cumulative incidence of diagnostic transition using the Aalen– Johansen estimator, treating discharge and death as competing events. Ethics and Dissemination CRIS operates under ethical approval from the South Central–Oxford C Research Ethics Committee (23/SC/0257). Project-specific approval was received from the CRIS Oversight Committee as Project 23-095. The study will be reported in accordance with the RECORD extension of the STROBE guidelines. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication and will provide evidence on the longitudinal use and refinement of non-specific psychosis-spectrum diagnoses in routine secondary mental healthcare.

title: 55 Same-day discharge after pulmonary vein isolation; a safe and efficient protocol to tackle hospital bed shortages
Burst Analysis of the Slurry Discharge Pipeline Header in a Slurry-Bed Residue Hydrogenation Unit
abstract: The header of the slurry discharge pipeline in a slurry-bed residue hydrogenation unit burst after six months of operation. To identify the causes of the header burst, a series of tests were carried out, including macro-morphology observation, SEM-EDS analysis, chemical composition analysis, and mechanical property testing. The results show that the burst fracture of the header is ductile. Low welding quality led to multiple defects, such as incomplete penetration and gas pores in the slurry discharge pipeline; additionally, Widmanstätten structure was formed in the heat-affected zone (HAZ), which significantly impaired the performance of the welded joint. During operation, the internal pressure of the pipeline exceeded the bearing capacity of the welded joint, resulting in the burst. Corresponding improvement suggestions are put forward in this paper based on the identified causes of the burst.

title: Improving emergency department efficiency through integrated bed management and radiology workflow optimization: An organizational intervention study
abstract: Background and aim: Emergency Department (ED) overcrowding is a major challenge for healthcare systems worldwide and is associated with delayed diagnosis, prolonged waiting times, and increased risk of adverse clinical outcomes. Organizational factors such as inefficient bed management and delays in diagnostic imaging contribute significantly to ED congestion. This study describes the implementation of an organizational model aimed at improving patient flow, optimizing hospital bed turnover, and enhancing radiology workflow in the Emergency Department of “M. Dimiccoli” Hospital in Barletta (Italy). Methods: A quasi-experimental organizational improvement study was conducted over six months in 2024. The intervention included the implementation of a real-time digital dashboard based on the National Emergency Department Overcrowding Score (NEDOCS), the introduction of a structured hospital bed reserve system for emergency admissions, the appointment of a dedicated nursing coordinator for bed management, and optimization of radiology workflow through prioritization of urgent imaging requests and improved ED–radiology coordination. Operational indicators, including waiting times, ED overcrowding levels, bed availability, and diagnostic imaging turnaround times, were monitored during the study period. Results: Implementation of the organizational model enabled continuous monitoring of ED congestion and improved coordination between the emergency department and inpatient units. The structured bed reserve system facilitated hospital admissions and reduced delays in bed allocation. Improved integration between emergency physicians and radiology services supported a stable and efficient radiology workflow within the emergency care pathway, facilitating timely diagnostic evaluation and clinical decision-making. Conclusions: Integrated hospital management strategies combining digital monitoring tools, structured bed management, and optimized radiology workflow can significantly improve emergency department operational efficiency. The organizational model described may represent a replicable framework for hospitals seeking to address ED overcrowding and improve patient care processes.

title: Data-driven bed capacity planning using Mt/Gt/∞ queueing models with an application to neonatal intensive care units
journal: Operations Research Data Analytics and Logistics
abstract: Hospitals face challenges in long-term intensive care unit (ICU) capacity planning under uncertain demand. Admission rates fluctuate over time, and LOS distributions vary with patient heterogeneity, hospital location, case mix, and clinical practice. Common approaches rely on steady-state queueing models or heuristic rules with fixed parameters, which often fail to capture real occupancy dynamics. The widely used 85% occupancy rule, for example, recommends keeping average utilization below this level to preserve responsiveness, yet it is grounded in stationary assumptions and may lack resilience in time-varying systems. Our analysis shows that even when long-run utilization targets are satisfied, daily occupancy often exceeds 100% capacity. We propose a data-driven framework to estimate ICU bed occupancy using an $M_t/G_t/\infty$ queueing model with time-varying arrival rates and empirically fitted LOS distributions. The approach combines statistical decomposition and parametric fitting to capture temporal patterns in admissions and LOS, and is applied to multi-year data from neonatal ICUs (NICUs) in Calgary. We evaluate capacity scenarios including average-based thresholds and Poisson-based surge estimates. Results show that static heuristics are inadequate under fluctuating demand and underscore the importance of modeling LOS variability when estimating bed needs. Although the case study focuses on NICUs, the framework has potential applicability to other ICU settings and provides interpretable, data-informed support for systems facing rising demand and constrained capacity.

abstract: Acute NHS hospital trusts face severe capacity constraints driven by step-down exit gridlock. This operational white paper presents the Predictive Intake Clearing Protocol. Grounded in Lean waste reduction and Six Sigma defect-prevention mechanisms, the framework replaces reactive discharge searches with upstream pre-clearance logic inspired by maritime logistics at the Port of Rotterdam. title: ANALYSIS OF INPATIENT ACTIVITY AND HEALTHCARE STAFFING UNDER CONTEMPORARY REFORMS: EXPERIENCE OF THE VOLODYMYR TERRITORIAL MEDICAL ASSOCIATION
abstract: Introduction. Transformation of healthcare financing and hospital networks in Ukraine requires assessment of how changes in inpatient capacity are associated with bed utilization and workforce availability. Aim. To evaluate trends in inpatient care volume, hospital bed utilization, and staffing at the Municipal Enterprise “Volodymyr Territorial Medical Association” of the Volodymyr City Council from 2021 to 2025. Materials and methods. A single-center retrospective longitudinal observational study used aggregated annual data from official statistical reporting Form No. 20. The calendar year was the unit of analysis. Staffing rates, bed occupancy, average length of stay, bed turnover, and in-hospital mortality were calculated. Temporal dynamics were assessed using Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients; the linear mortality trend was tested with the Cochran–Armitage test, and heterogeneity of annual proportions with the Pearson χ² test. Statistical significance was set at 0.05. Results. From 2021 to 2025, the average annual number of beds increased from 280 to 520, admissions from 9,150 to 16,971, discharges from 8,833 to 16,634, and bed-days from 75,075 to 135,257. The corresponding increases were 85.7%, 85.5%, 88.3%, and 80.2%. Average length of stay ranged from 7.2 to 8.2 days, bed turnover from 27.5 to 32.9 patients per bed annually, and bed occupancy from 55.6% to 73.5%; no statistically significant monotonic trend was identified. In-hospital mortality was 3.35% in 2021, 1.27% in 2024, and 1.81% in 2025. The Cochran–Armitage test identified a negative linear component (z=−8.004; p<0.001), and the Pearson χ² test showed between-year heterogeneity (p<0.001), whereas the rank trend across the five annual proportions was not statistically significant. The physician staffing rate increased from 81.73% to 91.38%, while the staffing rate for nursing personnel did not change materially. Conclusions. Expansion of inpatient capacity was accompanied by a proportionate increase in patient flow without sustained deterioration in bed utilization indicators. Positive workforce dynamics primarily concerned physician positions. Analyses by department, diagnosis, case severity, and episode of care are required to support more specific managerial decisions.

Interventions to Reduce Post-Anaesthetic Care Unit Discharge Delays: A Systematic Review
journal: Perioperative Care and Operating Room Management
abstract: Background Post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU) congestion contributes to perioperative delays, reduced operating room efficiency, and suboptimal patient and staff experiences. Effective management of PACU flow is therefore essential to maintain safe, efficient, and patient-centred care. Purpose This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions designed to improve PACU flow and discharge efficiency. Design A systematic review with narrative synthesis was conducted. Methods This review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome (PICO) framework guided study selection, and the Donabedian structure–process–outcome framework informed data extraction and synthesis. Given the heterogeneity of interventions, study designs, and outcome measures, a narrative synthesis was undertaken. Findings Twenty-three studies were included. Most evaluated process-related interventions (n = 19, 82.6%), including workflow redesign and quality improvement (n = 8, 34.8%), discharge decision-making criteria (n = 7, 30.4%), technology-enabled interventions (n = 3, 13.0%), and multidisciplinary downstream flow and discharge processes (n = 1, 4.3%). Four studies (17.4%) evaluated structure-related interventions involving PACU pathway redesign and capacity optimisation. Workflow redesign and quality improvement interventions offered the most comprehensive operational benefits, while the remaining interventions targeted specific aspects of discharge efficiency and operational performance. Evidence quality was limited by the predominance of non-randomised study designs. Conclusion Both process- and structure-related interventions were associated with improvements in PACU flow and discharge efficiency, highlighting the importance of implementing context-specific, systems-based strategies that address workflow, capacity, communication, and discharge processes across the perioperative pathway.

Transportability of ICU discharge tools for 72-hour unplanned ICU readmission across two health systems: a preregistered comparative external validation of SWIFT, NEWS2, MEWS and discharge SOFA.
abstract: This project is a preregistered comparative external validation of four tools used at intensive care unit (ICU) discharge. The tools are the Stability and Workload Index for Transfer (SWIFT), the National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2), the Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS) and the discharge Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score. The outcome is unplanned ICU readmission within 72 hours. We use two existing datasets from contrasting health systems. The primary cohort comes from a 22-bed adult ICU at Trakya University Hospital, Edirne, Türkiye (2023–2025; 1,199 discharge events). This hospital has no step-down or intermediate care beds and no outreach or rapid response team. The comparison cohort is MIMIC-IV (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, USA, 2008–2019), where intermediate care units and a ward rapid response system exist. In each cohort we will estimate: discrimination (AUC); calibration after recalibration; clinical utility, using decision curve analysis and performance at published thresholds. We will then test transportability: whether the score–risk relationship estimated in MIMIC-IV holds in the Trakya cohort. In the Trakya cohort we will also explore whether discharge lactate and albumin add information to each tool. We expect all tools to show modest discrimination. We also expect the absolute risk at a given score to differ between the two systems. The results should show whether these tools can be used as published in ICUs without step-down care, or whether they need local recalibration. No new prediction score is developed. This plan was registered before any outcome analysis.

title: A COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW OF PATHOLOGICAL CHANGES IN DUSHTAVRANA WITH SURGICAL AND NON-SURGICAL MANAGEMENT, WSR TO CHRONIC NON-HEALING ULCERS
journal: European Journal Pharmaceutical and Medical Research
abstract: Vrana is one of the clinical pathology which is described in Ayurvedic science by almost all classical texts which can be considered as wound in contemporary science. Acharya Sushruta mentioned Vrana gatra vichoornanae vranayati iti vrana which means break in the continuity of the surface epithelium. When this fails to heal by its own or early treatment later this Vrana changes to Dushta Vrana following with many Avasthas and because of Krichra Sadhyata and Dheergha Kalanubandhi will proceed with many surgical and non-surgical choices. Dushtavrana is an important clinical condition described in Ayurveda, characterized by delayed healing and unhealthy local features such as abnormal discharge, foul odour, discoloration, pain, induration and altered wound-bed characteristics. In contemporary science, chronic non-healing ulcers are a significant clinical challenge and may arise due to diabetes mellitus, venous or arterial insufficiency, pressure, infection, neuropathy, trauma and other systemic or local factors. The clinical understanding of microenvironmental changes from Vrana to Dushta Vrana will guide us for proper treatment assessment. The clinical approach of Dushta Vrana will be diagnosed by Vrana Pariksha, Vrana Srava Lakshanas, Vrana Vasthu, Vrana Varna and Vrana Avastha, analyzed and treated by the principles of Shodhana, Ropana and Shashti Upakrama Chikithsa. Depending upon the stage and condition of the wound, both local and systemic measures, along with appropriate surgical and non-surgical treatments are explained elaborately. Contemporary management emphasizes identification and correction of the underlying cause, wound-bed preparation, debridement, infection control, maintenance of an appropriate wound environment, vascular assessment, pressure relief and nutritional optimization. This review explores the surgical and non-surgical approaches to Dushta Vrana with special reference to chronic non-healing ulcers and examines the possible relationship between classical Ayurvedic principles and contemporary wound-care practices with management of associated systemic factors and prevention of recurrence.

title: European Hospital Discharges by EUROSTAT
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This dataset consists of a collection of separate files retrieved from Eurostat, the statistical office of the European Union, as part of the GeoAI4EI project. The files contain statistical data on hospital discharges across European countries, providing information on healthcare service utilization and hospital activity. Hospital discharge data are relevant for monitoring, analyzing, and assessing healthcare service provision, as well as for epidemiological purposes. The dataset covers different aspects of hospital activity, including: Hospital discharges: number of patients discharged following inpatient and day-case hospital stays. Bed-days: total number of days spent in hospital by patients. Average length of hospital stay: average duration of inpatient hospital episodes. Primary diagnosis: hospital discharges classified according to the main condition diagnosed at the end of the hospital stay, using the International Shortlist for Hospital Morbidity Tabulation (ISHMT). Where available, data are further disaggregated by age group, sex, geographical area, and patients' country of residence, as well as by type of hospital admission (inpatient or day-case). The databases may also distinguish between residents and non-residents. Temporal and geographic coverage The dataset covers European countries, with geographical coverage varying according to data availability in the individual Eurostat databases. Data are primarily provided at the national level, while regional breakdowns are also available in some datasets according to the NUTS classification. Temporal coverage varies across the individual files, with some time series extending up to 2025. The availability of geographical and demographic breakdowns also differs between datasets, reflecting national reporting practices and data availability. All files are provided separately and have been preserved in their original downloaded format, without modifications, processing, or harmonization. The original data and associated metadata are available through the Eurostat database (https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat). This collection is intended to support comparative analyses of hospital activity, healthcare utilization, and disease-related hospitalization patterns across European countries and regions, contributing to the assessment of healthcare system capacity and preparedness for public health emergencies, including pandemics.

title: Improving Hospital Discharge Efficiency through Lean Six Sigma, Discrete-Event Simulation, and Optimized EWMA Monitoring
abstract: Hospital discharge delays affect patient flow, bed availability, patient satisfaction, and overall hospital efficiency. Despite the wide use of Lean Six Sigma in healthcare, few studies test discharge improvements virtually before implementation or provide an optimized monitoring tool to sustain them. This study proposes an integrated Lean Six Sigma (LSS), discrete-event simulation, and optimized exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) control chart approach to improve the inpatient discharge process in a public hospital. Historical data of discharge cases were collected from the hospital information system. Using the DMAIC methodology, the current discharge process was mapped and analyzed to identify major sources of delay. Root-cause analysis, Pareto analysis, and XY matrix prioritization showed that discharge-related examinations/tests and medication preparation were the most critical bottlenecks. Two improvement scenarios were then evaluated using Arena discrete-event simulation. The simulated baseline model (20.39 h) was consistent with the observed baseline discharge time (20.5 h). The simulation results indicate that prioritizing discharge-related examinations combined with a dedicated discharge-medication pharmacy line could reduce the average discharge time to a projected 8.99 h, and the estimated sigma level could increase from an observed 2.88 to a projected 4.14. Finally, an EWMA control chart was optimized using simulated discharge-time data and is proposed for monitoring the process after implementation. The findings suggest that integrating LSS with simulation and optimized statistical monitoring can support evidence-based decisions before committing hospital resources to implementation.

title: 13 National outcomes of patients admitted following an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest - an analysis of Irish acute hospital discharge data
Influence of dual-laser in-situ remelting on laser powder bed fused 316L steel: defect evolution, residual stress relaxation and mechanical properties
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology
abstract: Laser in-situ remelting (LISR) provides an effective route for regulating melt-pool thermal-fluid behavior in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), yet whether a larger remelting spot necessarily benefits microstructure and mechanical reliability remains unresolved. In this study, LPBF-fabricated 316L stainless steel was processed by LISR with different remelting spot sizes of 70 μm, 140 μm, and 210 μm. The results show that, under fixed secondary laser power and scanning speed, the combined effect of remelting spot-size variation and the associated redistribution of laser energy leads to distinct remelting conditions, resulting in different melt-pool morphologies, thermal behaviors, solidification characteristics, and defect evolution. The 70 μm spot size provides sufficient remelting intensity and stable melt-track continuity, effectively suppressing defects, improving surface integrity, and producing the best tensile and fatigue properties. The 140 μm spot size promotes a more uniform thermal field and achieves the most effective residual-stress relaxation, but its mechanical improvement is limited by less efficient defect elimination. When the spot size increases to 210 μm, the remelting energy is dispersed over a larger area, reducing local remelting efficiency, leading to persistent defects and degraded mechanical performance. Despite the distinct initial microstructures, all specimens evolve toward a deformation-controlled steady state characterized by self-organized dislocation structures during large plastic deformation. Fatigue failure is primarily governed by surface/near-surface defect-induced crack initiation, while optimized LISR delays crack nucleation and stabilizes crack propagation. These findings provide guidance for balancing defect control, residual-stress relaxation, and mechanical performance in LISR-fabricated 316L stainless steel.

title: Perioperative Nursing Care of a Patient With 70% TBSA Second‐ To Third‐Degree Flame Burns Complicated by Pseudomonas aeruginosa Infection: A Case Report
Effectiveness of combined bed pedaling and accelerated rehabilitation versus accelerated rehabilitation alone after total knee replacement: a randomised controlled trial
abstract: Abstract Background Total knee replacement (TKR) is the gold standard treatment for end-stage osteoarthritis. Postoperative conventional rehabilitation has shown limited benefits. Accelerated rehabilitation focuses on early mobilization and improving postoperative outcomes. Pedaling based interventions in acute setup have also shown potential benefits in improving functional outcomes. Thus, this study aimed to compare the combined effect of bed pedaling and accelerated rehabilitation with accelerated rehabilitation alone on knee pain, range of motion, muscle strength, swelling and functional outcome following TKR. Methods A single-center, parallel-group randomized controlled trial enrolled 72 patients (age 45–70 years) undergoing primary unilateral TKR from March 2025 to March 2026. Participants were randomly assigned to experimental group ( n = 36) or control group ( n = 36) using block randomization with allocation concealment. The experimental group received bed pedaling (forward and backward rotations) and accelerated rehabilitation. The control group received only accelerated rehabilitation. Both groups received treatment from day 0. The assessor was blinded to the intervention provided. Primary outcomes were pain, knee range of motion, knee flexor and extensor muscle strength, and knee swelling. Secondary outcome was functional outcome measured using Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC). Outcome measures were assessed at postoperative day 3, day of discharge (postoperative day 5), and 1-month follow-up. Analysis was done using two factor repeated measure ANOVA. Results 34 participants completed the follow-up in control group and 33 in the experimental group. Significant group differences were observed for pain ( p < 0.001), knee flexion ROM ( p < 0.001), extension lag ( p = 0.032), extensor strength ( p = 0.046), knee swelling ( p = 0.004), and WOMAC scores ( p < 0.001). Flexor muscle strength improved similarly in both the groups ( p = 0.286). Conclusions Combined bed pedaling and accelerated rehabilitation provides additional benefits compared to accelerated rehabilitation alone in improving pain, ROM, extensor strength, and functional outcomes after TKR. Although swelling improved over time, its long-term reduction may not be solely attributable to bed pedaling. These findings support incorporating bed pedaling with accelerated rehabilitation in early postoperative period. Trial registration Clinical Trials Registry of India (CTRI/2025/03/082973). Registered on 20/03/2025.

title: S104 Exploring costs associated with suspected non-ventilator-associated hospital-acquired pneumonia (nv-HAP) within the HAP-FAST trial
Analisis Kebutuhan Tempat Tidur Tersedia untuk Implementasi Kelas Rawat Inap Standar (KRIS-JKN) di Rumah Sakit Bhayangkara Tk. I Pusdokkes Polri
abstract: The implementation of Kelas Rawat Inap Standar (KRIS) within the Jaminan Kesehatan Nasional (JKN) program requires hospital readiness, particularly in meeting efficient and standardized inpatient bed capacity. This study aims to analyze trends in bed utilization and forecast inpatient bed requirements as a basis for planning KRIS-JKN implementation. This research employs a quantitative method to calculate bed requirements and a qualitative approach to assess readiness for KRIS-JKN implementation at Rumah Sakit Bhayangkara Tk.I Pusdokkes Polri. The data used are secondary data obtained from inpatient recapitulation reports from the Medical Record Unit during the period 2022–2025, including the number of available beds, number of discharged patients, and total inpatient days. The research utilized Tableau Public with a data mining approach following the CRISP-DM (Cross Industry Standard Process for Data Mining) framework. The results present forecasting of bed requirements using BOR scenarios of 60%, 70%, and 80%. The forecasts show that for January–March 2026, bed requirements range from 233–347 units for Class I, 78–146 units for Class II, and 250–487 units for Class III. These findings provide a basis for hospital planning to support efficient and standardized KRIS-JKN implementation.

title: EE40 BUDGET IMPACT AND CAPACITY-GENERATION ANALYSIS OF A POST-PROCEDURAL CLINICAL DECISION SUPPORT SYSTEM FOR LENGTH-OF-STAY OPTIMIZATION IN ELECTIVE PERCUTANEOUS CORONARY INTERVENTION ACROSS TWO ASIA-PACIFIC PUBLIC HEALTH SYSTEMS
abstract: Conservative discharge protocols prolong hospitalization after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), consuming bed-days that constrain throughput and lengthen elective waiting queues, despite consensus that same-day and 2-3 day discharge is safe for uncomplicated elective PCI. This study estimated the budget impact, bed-day capacity generation, incremental throughput, and gross procedural revenue of a post-procedural clinical decision support system (CDSS) providing algorithmic discharge-readiness scoring versus standard of care for elective PCI and diagnostic angiography across two Asia-Pacific public health systems (Singapore and Thailand), from payer and societal perspectives over a one-year horizon.

title: Post-Earthquake Field Hospital Bed Capacity Allocation Problem Solving Two-Stage Stochastic Programming: A Case Study in Istanbul Avcılar
abstract: Field hospitals are temporary healthcare facilities deployed to provide medical services in scenarios where conventional healthcare infrastructure is disrupted due to natural or human-induced disasters, migration, armed conflicts, or similar crises. Depending on the anticipated needs, these facilities may be categorized into specialized types, such as orthopedic and traumatology field hospitals, surgical field hospitals, or general medical aid field hospitals. Bed capacity is a critical determinant of the scale of a field hospital, which in turn influences the spatial requirements for setup, personnel allocation, and associated costs. Typically established for short-term use, ranging from six months to two years, the operational duration, bed capacity, and structural configuration of field hospitals collectively define their functional capabilities. This study proposes a two-stage stochastic mathematical programming model to address the problem of calculating the optimal bed capacity for field hospitals delivering post-disaster healthcare services, with a focus on earthquake scenarios. Compared with two-stage stochastic models, the mathematical model proposed in this study exhibits distinct differences from existing models in the disaster and hospital bed capacity modeling literature. The model integrates uncertainties inherent in disaster contexts, such as fluctuating patient influx and resource availability, to optimize decision-making for bed allocation. The proposed framework is applied to Avcılar, a district within Istanbul, Türkiye, identified as a high-risk zone for seismic activity due to its proximity to the North Anatolian Fault. By leveraging geospatial and demographic data, the model aims to enhance preparedness and operational efficiency of field hospitals in mitigating healthcare service disruptions following a major earthquake. The results underscore the utility of stochastic optimization in resource planning under uncertainty, offering actionable insights for policymakers and disaster response coordinators.

title: 166 Optimising Timing of Day 1 Post-Operative MRI for Brain Tumour Patients
Fluid mud impacts on estuarine sediment import
abstract: Abstract. In hyperturbid estuaries, fine sediment accumulation frequently generates fluid mud layers that pose major challenges to ecology and navigation. Few studies have addressed the relation between fluid mud and residual sediment transport mechanisms to date. Here, we present Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP) and water-sampling observations from the hyperturbid Emden Fairway (Ems Estuary), collected under three river discharge conditions (45–200 m3 s-1), including two 13 h tidal-cycle surveys with full-depth suspended sediment concentration (SSC) profiles. The thickness of the fluid mud layers differed among surveys with contrasting discharge in the research area, exceeding 2 m at high discharge (200 m3 s-1), whereas no fluid mud was present at low discharge. When a thin fluid mud layer was present (∼1 m), the net landward sediment flux per unit width over around 12 h observation windows reached 200 t m-1, which is one order of magnitude larger than that measured when the fluid mud was absent. The presence of a fluid mud layer coincided with a two-layer estuarine circulation, and enhanced tidal pumping through elevated near-bed SSC, which both promote landward sediment transport. In contrast, when the fluid mud layer has retreated, the residual flow is seaward over the full water depth, likely due to a sediment-induced density gradient opposing that of salinity, weakening estuarine circulation. The net landward transport relies mainly on tidal pumping. During the highest-discharge survey, near-bed sediment-induced density gradients were larger than the salinity gradient, indicating that fluid mud is not merely passively advected but may exert a control on the near-bed residual flow. Our results show that resolving the full near-bed layer is essential for quantifying sediment transport and understanding the discharge-driven redistribution of sediment in hyperturbid estuaries.

title: Delayed biliary drainage and inpatient outcomes in pancreatobiliary malignancy: A National Inpatient Sample analysis, 2020-2023.
Finding capacity in the NSW statewide PICU System—collaborative MVP simulation development in a complex stakeholder environment
journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society
abstract: Managing bed capacity and patient flow in paediatric intensive care units poses ongoing challenges, particularly in large and geographically dispersed health systems. In New South Wales, Australia, three Paediatric Intensive Care Units serve as key nodes within a statewide network of more than 400 hospitals, collectively receiving critically ill children with diverse clinical needs. To address growing concerns about capacity constraints and uneven demand across these units, a collaborative study was undertaken to explore strategies for system-wide improvement. Simulation is well-suited to this kind of problem. However, modelling such a complex system while capturing the perspectives of many stakeholders remains challenging. Ultimately, a hybrid discrete-event and agent-based method was developed. This model captured both detailed bed-occupancy dynamics within each unit and the inter-hospital transfer rules that match patient diagnoses to clinical capabilities. Ensuring ongoing engagement with clinicians and hospital managers proved integral to defining structure, validating outputs and iteratively identifying feasible policy interventions such that a useful decision-making tool emerged. In addition to informing capacity-management decisions, the project also strengthened local simulation expertise. The article discusses the value of an incremental (Minimum Viable Product) development approach for managing and delivering highly complex healthcare-simulation studies. The approach deliberately revisited CM assumptions as the model became more detailed and disciplined the team to deliver the most valuable model achievable within the available time, data, and resourcing constraints.

title: 146 Day Case Biopsy Pathway: Assessment of Safety and Efficacy – Single-Centre Experience
Healthcare Infrastructural and healthcare performance in the University of Uyo Teaching Hospital, Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria.
abstract: This study explored how infrastructural development impacts public healthcare performance at the University of Uyo Teaching Hospital (UUTH) in Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria, over the period from 2015 to 2023, with a particular emphasis on hospital bed capacity. Guided by Systems Theory, the research utilized a survey design. A total of 399 questionnaires were distributed among healthcare staff and patients, yielding 339 valid responses for analysis, which translates to an impressive 85.0% response rate. Data collection involved structured questionnaires based on a five-point Likert scale, and the analysis was conducted using descriptive statistics (like frequencies, means, and standard deviations) and inferential statistics (specifically Pearson correlation) via SPSS version 25. The findings indicated that hospital bed capacity has a significant impact on healthcare performance at UUTH. Respondents expressed low satisfaction regarding bed adequacy (mean = 2.43) and reported high levels of ward congestion (mean = 2.29), highlighting ongoing infrastructural challenges. The efficiency of emergency admissions and bed allocation systems showed moderate performance, with mean scores of 2.53 and 2.85, respectively. Hypothesis testing revealed a statistically significant positive correlation between the number of hospital beds and healthcare performance (r = 0.698, p = 0.015), leading to the rejection of the null hypothesis. The study concluded that insufficient hospital bed capacity adversely affects admission efficiency, patient flow, and overall service delivery at UUTH. It is recommended that the federal government and the hospital management board prioritize expanding hospital bed capacity through ward enlargement and better space utilization strategies to boost efficiency, alleviate overcrowding, and enhance timely access to healthcare services.

title: Assessing Emergency Department Crowding: A Structured Literature Review of the National Emergency Department Overcrowding Score
abstract: Background: Emergency department crowding requires reliable measurement to distinguish operational pressure from patient severity and clinical outcomes. Objectives: This review evaluated evidence regarding the National Emergency Department Overcrowding Score (NEDOCS) and its potential application in emergency service evaluation. Methods: A structured narrative review examined eight previously selected studies within the reported 2021–2026 eligibility period. Searches reportedly covered PubMed, ScienceDirect, Taylor & Francis, and ProQuest, identifying 126 records. Search dates and several selection procedures remained unverified. Findings were synthesized across crowding perceptions, workload, waiting and boarding, and leaving without being seen. Results: NEDOCS demonstrated agreement with staff perceptions in some settings, while associations with alternative crowding indices and waiting times varied. Workload findings relied on repeated questionnaires, and pediatric leaving without being seen was associated with crowding in adjusted observational analysis. Simulated boarding removal reduced calculated scores without demonstrating clinical benefits. Methodological heterogeneity and incomplete review documentation limited interpretation. Conclusions: NEDOCS may complement existing emergency department performance indicators, but evidence does not establish its effectiveness at Dr. Soeradji Tirtonegoro General Hospital. Local validation, standardized outcome measurement, and transparent review documentation are necessary before implementation.

title: A Constrained-Flow Lens for Emergency Department Crowding and Ambulance Ramping: Analogy, queues and evidence
journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Health Management
abstract: Objective: To present a conceptual research note that integrates a constrained-flow analogy, queueing relationships and emergency-care evidence to support investigation of emergency department (ED) crowding and ambulance ramping. Design: Evidence-informed conceptual research note. Setting: Australian public hospitals, with Queensland examples where definitions are jurisdiction-specific. Main outcome measures: Candidate measures of demand, census, time, utilisation, variability, boarding, patient off-stretcher time and safety. Results: Bernoulli’s principle is retained only as an intuitive analogy for restrictions and upstream accumulation. Little’s law provides the principal descriptive relationship between average number, effective flow and time; Kingman’s approximation explains how high utilisation magnifies variability. Established input-throughput-output models and Australian evidence locate ambulance ramping within whole-of-hospital access block. Intervention evidence is mixed and does not support universal prescriptions. Conclusions: The framework may translate visible congestion into measurable hypotheses, but it is not a predictive hydraulic model. Construct validation, retrospective analysis, queueing analysis, simulation and prospective testing are required before operational use.

title: 287 Prolonged Boarding Exposure in Older Adults at Freestanding and Hospital-Based Emergency Departments
Waiting Time and Patient Satisfaction in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review of Time Intervals, Perceived Waiting, and Queue Management Interventions
abstract: This systematic review will synthesise evidence on the association between waiting time and patient satisfaction in hospital emergency departments (EDs). It addresses three questions: (1) the direction and consistency of the association between waiting time (actual or perceived) and ED patient satisfaction; (2) which time intervals, such as door-to-doctor, doctor-to-disposition, boarding, and total length of stay, are most strongly associated with satisfaction, and whether this depends on patient characteristics or disposition; and (3) whether interventions that change waiting time or the waiting experience, such as queue management systems, text-message recall, or waiting-time estimates, improve satisfaction. PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect will be searched for observational studies and randomised trials published from 2015 to October 2026 in English or Indonesian. One reviewer will screen studies, using an inclusive approach in which uncertain records proceed to full-text assessment, and will assess risk of bias using the JBI checklist for analytical cross-sectional studies and RoB 2. Because exposures and outcomes are expected to be heterogeneous, findings will be synthesised narratively following the SWiM guideline, and certainty of evidence will be rated with GRADE. We expect an inverse association between waiting time and satisfaction, strongest for the interval before physician assessment.

title: Emergency Department Operational Measures Associated with EMS Redirection Activation and Duration
abstract: Introduction: Emergency medical services (EMS) redirection is used to manage emergency department (ED) strain, but whether it reflects operational conditions is unclear. We compared associations of prespecified ED operational measures, including visit volume, patient flow times, admissions, boarding, and left-early measures, with redirection activation and total daily redirection minutes. Methods: We performed a retrospective study at a single urban tertiary care center over 392 consecutive days from April 7, 2021 through May 3, 2022. Redirection temporarily routed ambulances away from the study hospital and was activated centrally by EMS. New York City’s 9-1-1 system included about 500 ambulance units and over 60 hospitals. The primary outcome was activation, defined as any redirection during a calendar day. The secondary outcome was total redirection minutes among days with redirection. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated activation, and negative binomial regression evaluated duration. Results: Redirection occurred on 250 of 392 days (63.8%). Median daily duration was 47 minutes (interquartile range 23-78). Higher ED visit volume was associated with activation (odds ratio [OR] 1.14 per 10 patients; 95% CI, 1.02-1.27). Longer door-to-room time was associated with activation (OR 1.42 per 5 min; 95% CI, 1.04-1.92) and duration (incidence rate ratio 1.022 per min; 95% CI, 1.002-1.042). Boarding time and admission count were not associated with either outcome. Conclusion: Emergency department visit volume was associated with activation but not duration, while door-to-room time was associated with both. Evaluating redirection as a single outcome may obscure differences between activation and cumulative duration.

title: Emergency department crowding and boarding in the Middle East: a systematic review
581 Impact of Onsite Psychiatric Response Team on Emergency Department Length of Stay
From emergency department length of stay to delay until hospital admission
#431 A scoping review of emergency department crowding in Ireland
Scoping review of models predicting emergency department length of stay
journal: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
abstract: Emergency Department (ED) length of stay (LOS) is a critical performance indicator in healthcare systems, influencing patient outcomes, overcrowding, and resource utilization. Predicting LOS can enhance patient flow and resource management. While traditional statistical methods have been used, the advent of machine learning (ML) has introduced more sophisticated analytical approaches, though their comparative advantage over traditional methods remains context-dependent. A systematic search was conducted across PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus using terms related to ED LOS and predictive modeling. Eligible studies were English-language studies published from January 2014 through September 2024 that developed or validated an ED LOS prediction model using a traditional statistical, machine-learning, or deep-learning approach. Studies were excluded if they did not develop or validate an eligible ED LOS prediction model or if ED LOS was not the prediction target. Two reviewers independently screened all titles and abstracts, and three reviewers independently assessed the full texts of potentially eligible reports. Two reviewers independently extracted data from all included studies, with disagreements adjudicated by an emergency physician who served as the study supervisor. Of 4,773 records identified, 18 met the inclusion criteria. The studies spanned multiple continents, with the majority conducted post-2020. Decision-tree models were evaluated most frequently, followed by random forests, logistic regression, and support vector machines or support vector regression. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and accuracy were the most common performance metrics; however, direct cross-study statistical comparisons were precluded by substantial methodological heterogeneity (e.g., varied LOS cut-offs, patient populations, and validation methods). Extracted predictors commonly represented laboratory testing and ED operational factors, although inconsistent feature-importance reporting precluded comparison of their predictive importance. Calibration was rarely reported, with only two studies providing calibration assessments. Reported performance varied across modeling approaches, predictor sets, LOS outcome definitions, validation procedures, and ED settings. Because substantial methodological heterogeneity limits direct performance comparisons, future research should adopt standardized reporting frameworks (e.g., TRIPOD) and explore the impact of different LOS cut-off values to facilitate meaningful evidence synthesis and improve resource allocation. Not applicable.

title: Diagnostic Turnaround Time as a Determinant of Emergency Department Length of Stay and Admission Delay: A Systematic Literature Review (2019–2025)
abstract: Emergency Department (ED) crowding remains a persistent challenge for healthcare systems worldwide, with prolonged length of stay (LOS) contributing to compromised care quality, heightened clinical risks, and operational inefficiencies. Diagnostic turnaround time (TAT) has emerged as an important determinant of patient flow, potentially delaying clinical decisions and hospital admissions. This systematic review aimed to examine contemporary evidence published between 2022 and 2026 regarding the influence of diagnostic delays on ED LOS and subsequent hospital outcomes. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, covering observational studies, predictive modeling research, and interventional studies addressing ED LOS, diagnostic processes, and admission delays. The findings indicated that diagnostic delays, particularly in laboratory testing and radiological examinations, were consistently associated with longer ED LOS and increased boarding time. Furthermore, interventions designed to streamline diagnostic pathways demonstrated measurable reductions in LOS and, in certain cases, mortality. These findings suggest that diagnostic TAT constitutes a modifiable operational factor with substantial implications for clinical outcomes and healthcare efficiency. Therefore, integrated, system-level strategies to optimize diagnostic workflows, improve coordination between clinical services, and accelerate decision-making are essential to enhancing patient flow, reducing unnecessary delays, and strengthening patient safety in emergency care settings. Keywords: Emergency Department, Diagnostic Turnaround Time, Length of Stay, Diagnostic Delay, Patient Flow.

title: Hospital and emergency department length of stay before and after virtual nursing implementation
483 Comprehensive Emergency Department Redesign Improves Length of Stay and Patient Experience in a High-Volume Occupational Emergency Department in Chile
Emergency Department Boarding and Mortality: A Systematic Review and Proportional Meta‐Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Background and Aims Emergency department (ED) crowding, worsened by ED boarding (EDB), is defined as the stay of admitted patients in the emergency department due to the unavailability of inpatient beds. This occurrence poses a significant public health challenge, leading to adverse patient outcomes. Despite efforts to improve patient care pathways, the relationship between EDB and mortality is still contentious. This study aims to synthesize and compare reported in‐hospital mortality (IHM) among ED patients across studies stratified by ED boarding duration thresholds, with particular attention to shorter boarding durations. Methods A systematic review and proportional meta‐analysis were conducted following PRISMA guidelines. MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched up to April 2024. Pooled mortality proportions were estimated using random‐effects models with DerSimonian–Laird estimation and Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation. Heterogeneity was assessed using I 2 . Leave‐one‐out analyses were performed to assess the robustness of subgroup estimates, with particular attention to longer boarding thresholds. Results Twenty studies published between 2007 and 2024 were included. The overall pooled in‐hospital mortality proportion was 8.3% (95% CI: 7.6%–9.0%; I 2 = 99.9%). Subgroup analyses showed pooled mortality estimates of 10.2% for early admission/no boarding, 4.4% for 1‐h boarding, 5.9% for 2‐h boarding, 4.8% for 4‐h boarding, 13.5% for 6‐h boarding, 20.5% for 8‐h boarding, 21.8% for 12‐h boarding, and 11.8% for 24‐h boarding. Shorter boarding thresholds were not associated with higher pooled mortality estimates compared with early admission/no boarding. Although longer boarding thresholds showed higher pooled mortality estimates, the 8‐, 12‐, and 24‐h subgroup estimates were based on few studies and were materially influenced by Verma et al. 2021. After excluding this study, the pooled mortality estimates decreased to 7.9%, 3.9%, and 4.0% for the 8‐, 12‐, and 24‐h subgroups, respectively. Given the extreme heterogeneity, these pooled estimates require cautious interpretation. Because different studies contributed to different threshold‐specific pools, the estimates are descriptive and should not be interpreted as evidence of a threshold or dose‐response relationship. Conclusion This study highlights the possible association between prompt admissions, targeted interventions, and outcomes in the context of ED boarding. Improving ED operations and reducing boarding times within these durations remain important organizational objectives. Further research with standardized methodologies is essential to fully understand and address this complex issue. However, the present pooled proportions do not establish a boarding‐duration threshold, dose‐response relationship, or causal association, and their interpretation is limited by extreme heterogeneity (I 2 = 99.9%).

title: 16 Impact of Emergency Department-Performed Trauma Tertiary Exams on Patient Length of Stay
Impact of an Overnight Stay in the Emergency Department Hallway on Admitted Geriatric Patients
abstract: Introduction: Patients frequently board overnight in the emergency department (ED) while awaiting medical admission, sometimes in hallway care spaces. Prior literature suggests that timing of boarding may matter; a single overnight stay in the ED may be associated with increased mortality and adverse events, especially for older adults. Given the deliriogenic ED environment, these effects may be magnified in the hallway. However, little is known about the effects of prolonged hallway stays. We evaluated whether an overnight stay in the ED hallway, compared to an ED room, was associated with increased delirium and adverse outcomes for geriatric patients. Methods: We conducted a retrospective multisite cohort database study of patients aged 65 years and older admitted to a general medicine service January 1, 2022, to December 31, 2023, who spent an entire night (midnight to 8 am) in the ED prior to admission. We compared those who spent the entire night in the ED hallway with those who were in ED rooms. Our primary outcome was a composite outcome for incident delirium and severe agitation (defined by the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Rev, code for delirium, positive nursing screen, use of parenteral antipsychotics, and/or physical restraints, since delirium was not routinely screened for at these sites). Secondary outcomes included hospital length of stay (LOS), inpatient and 30-day mortality, and 30-day ED revisit and readmission. We implemented mixed-effect regression models and adjusted for confounders. Results: A total of 8,576 patients met inclusion criteria, including 1,231 patients (14%) in the hallway group. Overall, 847 patients (9.9%) developed incident delirium and severe agitation: 160 (13%) of the hallway group and 687 (9%) of the non-hallway group. An overnight stay in the ED hallway was not associated with delirium and severe agitation (OR, 1.06, 95% CI, 0.58–1.94; P = .84), but increased ED LOS was independently associated with delirium and severe agitation (OR, 1.01; 95% CI, 1.0–1.01 per hour; P = .01). There was no association between an overnight stay in the hallway and secondary outcomes except increased hospital LOS (OR 1.01, 95% CI, 1.00–1.01 per hour; P = .01). Conclusion: An overnight in the ED hallway care space was not associated with increased delirium and severe agitation for geriatric patients, but prolonged ED LOS was associated with this outcome. Hospital systems should consider prioritizing geriatric patients for expedited transfer from the ED to inpatient units, and prospective research with consistent delirium screening is needed to rigorously evaluate the safety of hallway care for older adults.

title: 626 A Provider-in-Triage and Continuous Flow Tract Model Improves Left Without Being Seen Rate in a Veterans Affairs Emergency Department
Increased Safety and Improved Length of Stay for Patients With Suspected Mild Traumatic Brain Injury in the Emergency Department
authors: María Cecilia Martín Fernández De Basoa
abstract: Abstract The Hospital Universitario Nuestra Señora de Candelaria enhanced the evaluation of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) in emergency departments by introducing a novel blood test based on the biomarkers glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and ubiquitin carboxy-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCHL-1), aimed at reducing unnecessary computed tomography (CT) scans. This innovation enabled 36.8% of mTBI patients to avoid CT imaging, thereby decreasing radiation exposure. It also shortened the average emergency department (ED) stay by 4.2 hours, improving patient flow. The approach alleviated 4,490 hours of radiologists’ time and generated annual healthcare savings of approximately €274,000. Physicians reported increased confidence and satisfaction in managing mTBI cases.

title: A Pediatric Emergency Medicine and Psychiatry Collaboration: An Intervention Time Series Analysis of the Length of Stay for Pediatric Mental Health Emergency Department Visits
journal: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting

title: 156 Individualized Plans For Emergency Department High Utilizers Shows Reduced Length of Stay, Testing and Narcotic Use
15 Boarded and Leaving: How Hospital Crowding Drives Patient Walkouts
161 Implementation of an Evidence-Based Seizure Clinical Pathway Reduces Emergency Department Length of Stay and Neurology Consultation Utilization
Emergency department crowding and cardiac arrest: A retrospective time-series study
abstract: Abstract Background Emergency department (ED) crowding has been associated with adverse patient outcomes, but emergency department cardiac arrest (EDCA) remains understudied. We examined the association between daily ED crowding and EDCA rates and described temporal changes in EDCA before and after implementation of a fast-track model designed to reduce crowding. Methods We conducted a retrospective time-series study at a single emergency department from October 1, 2021, to December 31, 2024. Daily crowding was quantified using the maximum emergency department occupancy rate (EDOR), and daily EDCA counts were analysed using Poisson regression with the number of ED contacts as an offset. Models included calendar time, weekday, and season. EDOR was analysed both continuously and categorically (< 100%, 100–129%, and ≥ 130%). A segmented time-series analysis was used to describe changes in EDCA rates around implementation of the fast-track model. Negative-binomial models were used as sensitivity analyses. Results During 1,188 observation days, there were 158,886 ED contacts and 72 EDCA events. The crude EDCA rate was 6.61 per 10,000 ED contacts before and 2.78 per 10,000 contacts after implementation of the fast-track model. Maximum EDOR ≥ 130% occurred on 292 (53.4%) pre-intervention days and 126 (19.7%) post-intervention days. In the adjusted analysis, each 10-percentage-point increase in maximum daily EDOR was associated with a 22% higher EDCA rate (IRR 1.22, 95% CI 1.09–1.36; p < 0.001). Compared with days with EDOR < 100%, days with EDOR ≥ 130% had a higher EDCA rate (IRR 5.90, 95% CI 1.83–19.04; p = 0.003). Negative-binomial sensitivity analysis yielded similar estimates. The segmented time-series analysis did not demonstrate a statistically significant immediate change in EDCA rates at the start of the post-intervention period (IRR 0.90, 95% CI 0.37–2.16; p = 0.810). Conclusion Higher maximum daily ED occupancy was associated with higher EDCA rates in this single-centre retrospective study. EDCA rates and exposure to extreme crowding were both lower during the post-intervention period, but the temporal analysis did not demonstrate a statistically significant immediate change in EDCA rates following implementation of the fast-track model. These findings describe an association between ED crowding and EDCA but do not establish a causal relationship.

title: Association Between Targeted Early EKG Ordering and Emergency Department Length of Stay Among Psychiatric Patients in Southern New Jersey: A Retrospective Study
abstract: IntroductionMental health-related visits make up a significant and growing share of emergency department (ED) utilization in the United States.At the Inspira Mullica Hill Emergency Department, a Six Sigma DMAIC analysis of the behavioral health intake process identified EKG ordering as a rate-limiting step in medical clearance, which is required before behavioral health evaluation.This study evaluates whether implementing a targeted early EKG order for psychiatric patients affects length of stay (LOS). Materials and methodsTargeted early EKG ordering was implemented for patients presenting with suspected behavioral health conditions, and outcomes were evaluated over a three-month post-intervention period.A retrospective chart review was conducted to compare the pre-intervention and post-intervention groups.Encounters were compared between a pre-intervention period, January 1, 2025, to March 9, 2025, and a post-intervention period, April 16, 2025, to July 31, 2025.Encounters during the implementation/washout period were excluded.The primary outcome was ED LOS in minutes.Secondary outcomes included LOS >6 hours and LOS >12 hours.Because LOS was non-normally distributed, outcomes were summarized using median (IQR), 90th and 95th percentiles, Mann-Whitney U testing, and chi-square testing.Multivariable log-linear regression was performed using natural log-transformed LOS.Statistical process control and interrupted time-series analyses were performed to evaluate process stability and secular trends. ResultsA total of 412 encounters were included, with 133 pre-intervention and 279 post-intervention encounters.Median LOS decreased from 854 minutes (IQR 389-1301) pre-intervention to 785 minutes (IQR 304-1404) post-intervention, though this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.245).The proportion of encounters with LOS >6 hours decreased from 78.2% to 71.3% (p = 0.174), and LOS >12 hours decreased from 60.9% to 52.7% (p = 0.144).In the adjusted analysis, the pre-intervention period was associated with longer LOS than the post-intervention period (LOS ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.02-1.49,p = 0.032), equivalent to approximately 19% lower adjusted LOS in the post-intervention period.Statistical process control analyses demonstrated common-cause variation without special-cause variation, and interrupted time-series analyses did not demonstrate statistically significant level or slope changes. ConclusionsEarly targeted EKG ordering was associated with lower adjusted ED LOS among psychiatric encounters.However, unadjusted comparisons and time-series analyses did not demonstrate statistically significant process-level changes.These findings suggest a potential association between standardized early EKG acquisition and improved psychiatric ED throughput but should be interpreted cautiously given the singlecenter retrospective design and limited operational covariate data.

title: 512 Emergency Department Boarding and Outcomes Among Intensive Care Admissions: Pre and Post-Pandemic
259 The Architecture of Urgency: Linking Emergency Department Design to Timeliness of Care
Association between prolonged emergency department boarding of mental health patients and aggression or violent incidents: a systematic review
journal: Frontiers in Disaster and Emergency Medicine
abstract: Background Emergency department (ED) boarding of psychiatric patients has reached unprecedented levels, with mean boarding times exceeding 60 h in some jurisdictions. Prolonged boarding exposes vulnerable patients to adverse events, including aggression and violence, yet the relationship between boarding duration and these outcomes remains poorly characterized. Understanding this association is critical for improving patient safety and informing ED policy. Methods We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines. We searched SciSpace, Google Scholar, PubMed and Embase for studies published between 2016 and 2026. Eligible studies included psychiatric ED populations with measured boarding duration and reported aggression or violence outcomes. Two reviewers screened paper's titles and abstracts, and when shortlisted, they reviewed the full texts independently. Data on study design, sample characteristics, boarding duration, and aggression outcomes were extracted. Results We identified 665 records, removed 114 duplicates, and screened 551 unique records. Fourteen full-text papers were assessed for eligibility, and 12 studies met inclusion criteria. Evidence consistently demonstrated a positive association between prolonged ED boarding and increased aggression or violent incidents. Youth with aggressive behaviours experienced 193% longer boarding times than those without aggression. Patients experiencing adverse events including physical assault had boarding times of 35 h compared to 6.5 h for those without such events. Specialized interventions reducing boarding time were associated with decreased violent incidents and reduced use of restrictive interventions. Conclusions Prolonged ED boarding of psychiatric patients is associated with increased aggression and violence. These findings underscore the urgent need for system-level interventions to reduce boarding times, expand acute psychiatric resources, and implement evidence-based care models that prioritize early therapeutic intervention over prolonged observation in ED settings.

title: EVALUATING THE IMPACT OF EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT NURSING WORKLOAD DYNAMICS ON CLINICAL QUALITY INDICATORS AND ADVERSE PATIENT SAFETY OUTCOMES
abstract: Background: Emergency departments (EDs) operate under unpredictable demand, time pressure, high clinical turnover, and frequent interruptions. Nurses are central to surveillance, triage, treatment coordination, deterioration recognition, and communication, but the relationship between staffing conditions and outcomes in emergency care remains less developed than in inpatient settings. Aim: To examine how emergency nursing workload and staffing conditions relate to patient safety and timeliness, and to demonstrate a practical secondary analysis using national ED data. Methods: A narrative review of recent evidence was combined with a descriptive secondary analysis of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) 2022 NHAMCS Emergency Department Summary Tables. Published estimates were extracted for total visits, waiting time, nursing contact, length of ED stay, arrival by ambulance, and disposition. Derived indicators were calculated from the reported aggregate estimates. No patient-level causal or inferential analysis was performed. Results: The 2022 NHAMCS estimated 155.4 million U.S. ED visits. A registered nurse or licensed practical nurse was reported as seen in 91.1% of visits. Only 40.6% of visits involved less than 15 minutes waiting to see a physician, advanced practice registered nurse, or physician assistant; 11.5% resulted in hospital admission, including approximately 2.0% to critical care. The evidence review indicates that poorer ED nurse staffing is associated with longer waits, more patients leaving without being seen, longer length of stay, delayed medication or therapeutic intervention, and increased risk of cardiac arrest, although the empirical evidence remains heterogeneous. Conclusion: ED nursing capacity should be planned around acuity, patient turnover, arrival surges, boarding, skill mix, and support resources rather than a fixed ratio alone. Routine monitoring should combine staffing and workload measures with nursing-sensitive and flow-related safety outcomes.

title: Triage, Early Warning and Comorbidity Scores for Predicting Hospital Admission, Revisit and Length of Stay Among In-mates Presenting to the Emergency Department: A Prospective Single-Center Study
