title: Considering the Present and Future of Advanced Practice Nursing in the Emergency Department
Emergency Department Experience in Four Tertiary Hospitals in Oman: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: This study assessed patient- and family-reported emergency department experience in four tertiary public hospitals in Oman, examined the internal structure of the adapted Brief Emergency Department Patient Satisfaction Scale (BEPSS), and identified associated factors. In this cross-sectional study, 822 respondents completed the adapted 20-item, five-category BEPSS between February and August 2025. Reliability analysis, polychoric exploratory factor analysis with parallel analysis, Welch tests with Holm adjustment, Games–Howell comparisons, and HC3-robust multiple linear regression were performed. Overall experience was favorable (mean item score, 4.05; SD, 0.86). Internal consistency was high (Cronbach α = .971; ordinal ω = .981), and parallel analysis supported one dominant factor. Unadjusted differences by hospital, visit shift, and self-reported length of stay were small. After adjustment, hospital and shift were not independently associated with experience, whereas length of stay, first-visit status, and disposition remained significant. Stays longer than three hours were associated with a 0.31-point lower score than stays of one to two hours. Monitoring experience and improving communication during delays may strengthen patient- and family-centered emergency care in Oman.

title: Comment Regarding “Reducing Blood Culture Contamination in the Emergency Department Using PIVO”
227 An Expedited Outpatient Radiology Pathway for Advanced Imaging From the Emergency Department
481 Clinical Characteristics and Risk of Admission in Emergency Department Patients Awaiting Placement
Dedicated Vertical Physician Pilot in a Rotational Patient Assignment Emergency Department
abstract: Introduction: Emergency department (ED) vertical patient pathways (VPP) assign patients to a dedicated care area with chairs, avoiding the use of traditional ED beds. The effect of reassigning a dedicated vertical emergency physician (EP) onto an established rotational patient assignment (RPA) system, which prospectively assigns arriving patients to EP queues, is unknown. We sought to describe operational outcomes and staff satisfaction with trialing this role. Methods: We conducted a single-center, hypothesis-generating exploratory pilot at a 56-bed tertiary-care ED in which one 8.75-hour EP shift on five Mondays was repurposed into an 8.75-hour dedicated VPP role within a chair-based vertical patient care area while the rotational patient assignment system remained in place; three prior comparable Mondays served as comparison. Primary outcome was discharged-patient ED length of stay (LOS); secondary outcomes included VPP upgrades to a bed, patient numbers seen by the dedicated shift, and staff satisfaction. We report descriptive analyses. Results: We analyzed 529 discharged-patient encounters: 199 (37.6%) during the preintervention period and 330 (62.4%) during the postintervention period. Median ED LOS for discharged patients did not demonstrate a consistent directional change, decreasing by seven minutes (3.1%) in the overall ED (226 vs 219 minutes) and increasing by 18.5 minutes (13.0%) among patients initially evaluated via the VPP (142.5 vs 161 minutes). The dedicated VPP EP saw three more patients per shift (21.4%; median 17 vs 14), and VPP upgrades fell from 15/68 (22.1%) to 5/130 (3.8%). Timeliness and communication were rated favorably by 4/4 VPP physician respondents and 10/12 and 16/17 registered nurse/allied health respondents, respectively; 3/4 VPP physician respondents vs 1/29 non-VPP physician respondents supported continuing the model. Conclusion: Reassigning an existing EP to a dedicated vertical EP role within an ongoing rotational patient assignment system was not accompanied by shortened discharged-patient length of stay. Fewer VPP upgrades and a modest increase in patients seen by the dedicated shift were observed, but patient selection and acuity limit interpretation. Staff reported favorable teamwork within the vertical space, whereas non-VPP physicians reported less manageable workloads and little support for continuing the model.

title: Stochastic analysis of an emergency department with two levels sharing the servers
47 Initiation of Venovenous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in the Emergency Department: A Pilot Investigation
Association Between Physician Handoffs and Major Adverse Outcomes in the Emergency Department: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: IntroductionHandoffs between emergency physicians are common and suspected to contribute to communication errors, yet their association with clinical outcomes remains poorly documented.This study aimed to evaluate the association between physician handoffs and in-hospital mortality, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, and hospital length of stay among patients hospitalized following an emergency department (ED) visit. MethodsA multicenter retrospective cohort study was conducted among all adult patients hospitalized following a visit to any of the five EDs of the CHU de Québec-Université Laval in Québec City, Canada, between April 2016 and March 2017.Data were extracted from the hospital administrative databases (MED-ECHO and SIURGE).Analyses were performed using generalized estimating equation (GEE) models with overlap weighting based on propensity scores, allowing adjustment for confounding and accounting for repeated visits.Subgroup analyses and multiple sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of the findings. ResultsAmong the 21,136 ED visits resulting in hospitalization, 50.6% involved at least one handoff.No significant association was observed between handoffs and in-hospital mortality (adjusted risk ratio [aRR] = 1.11; 95% CI: 0.94-1.30),ICU admission (aRR = 1.06; 95% CI: 0.91-1.23),or hospital length of stay (adjusted geometric mean ratio [aGMR] = 1.01; 95% CI: 0.96-1.08).Results were consistent across all subgroup and sensitivity analyses. ConclusionHandoffs between emergency physicians were not associated with an increased risk of death, ICU admission, or prolonged length of stay.Improvement efforts should focus on other components of ED operations.

title: Delay in Recognition and Treatment of Sepsis in Emergency Departments: A Prospective Observational Study
abstract: Background: Sepsis remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality globally, with outcomes heavily dependent on the promptness of recognition and antimicrobial administration in the emergency department (ED). Objectives: To evaluate the frequency, causes, and clinical consequences of delays in the recognition and treatment of sepsis among adult emergency department patients. Methods: A prospective observational study was conducted over a 12-month period across three tertiary care EDs, enrolling 1,248 adult patients presenting with sepsis or septic shock according to Sepsis-3 criteria. Data regarding triage vital signs, time to physician evaluation, time to lactate measurement, time to broad-spectrum antibiotic initiation, and in-hospital mortality were collected and analyzed using multivariable regression. Results: The median time from ED arrival to physician evaluation was 42 minutes (IQR, 24–68), while the median time to intravenous antibiotic administration was 168 minutes (IQR, 112–235). Only 34.2% of patients received antibiotics within the benchmark 60-minute window. Each 60-minute delay in antibiotic administration was independently associated with a 1.18-fold increase in in-hospital mortality (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.18; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.09–1.28; p < 0.001) and prolonged intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay. Multivariable analysis identified triage by non-accredited nursing staff, atypical presentation (afebrile or normotensive), and ED overcrowding as primary independent predictors of treatment delay. Conclusions: Significant delays in sepsis recognition and treatment persist in emergency departments, substantially worsening patient survival. Interventions must target early automated clinical decision support, rapid biomarker turnaround, and streamlined triage protocols.

title: Cardioversion of stable atrial fibrillation in the emergency department: electrical versus pharmacological in the era of overcrowding
Age-Related Differences in Emergency Surgery, Diagnostic Testing, and Disposition Among Adults Presenting to the Emergency Department With Abdominal Pain: A Retrospective Cohort Study
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This repository contains the data and analysis code supporting the study entitled “Age-Related Differences in Emergency Surgery, Diagnostic Testing, and Disposition Among Adults Presenting to the Emergency Department With Abdominal Pain: A Retrospective Cohort Study.” The study is a retrospective cohort analysis of adult emergency department visits for abdominal pain at Geneva University Hospitals, Switzerland, in 2023. It investigates age-related differences in emergency surgery within 72 hours, diagnostic testing, emergency department length of stay, and patient disposition. The repository provides the materials necessary to reproduce the statistical analyses and results reported in the manuscript, including descriptive analyses, multivariable regression models, and sensitivity analyses. These resources are made available to promote transparency, reproducibility, and further research in emergency medicine and geriatric emergency care.

title: Patient flow and Efficiency Measurements DescribingEmergency Departments’ Performance in Bogotá
abstract: Introduction: Patients flow and efficiency measurements are used to optimize resources, improve care times and reduce overcrowding in Emergency Departments (ED). Aim: Describe the performance of the ED at different levels of complexity of the healthcare institutions (HI) in Bogotá. Methods: Cross-sectional study with data of the year 2022 corresponding to clinical, management, staffing, and infrastructure factors to characterize the performance of ED in Bogotá related to HI with different levels of complexity. The statistical analysis described the variables according to their nature in summary measures according to their dispersion. 38 HI agreed to participate. Results: We present the results of patient flow characteristics and efficiency measurements such as readmission rate, overcrowding, leaving without being seen indicator, leaving before treatment is complete indicator, length of stay, admission rate indicator and boarding phenomenon that correspond to clinical and management factors. We found a high variability between the performance of the ED influenced by the level of complexity, the health service provider system, and the educational link of the HI in Bogotá. Conclusions: There is high variability between ED regarding the characteristics of patients flow and the use of efficiency measurements in Bogotá. Describing these results establish a starting point to improve the performance of the ED, enhance processes that have already been successful and intervene those processes that still lack efficiency in the heterogenous HI in Bogotá.

title: AI-based hourly prediction of emergency department demand integrating social determinants of health
abstract: Emergency department (ED) crowding is associated with delayed treatment and increased mortality, and proactive staffing requires reliable short-term demand forecasts. Most operational models rely on temporal or weather patterns but may insufficiently capture underlying population vulnerability. We evaluated whether community-level social determinants of health (SDoH) improve the prediction of near-term ED demand compared with weather factors using XGBOOST, and developed an interpretable model to inform resource allocation. The study included 213,138 encounters aggregated into 22,883 hourly observations at a tertiary teaching hospital in Wuhan, China. Neighbourhoods differed markedly in age structure and diagnostic profiles, indicating heterogeneous healthcare needs across the catchment area. Models incorporating dynamic SDoH features consistently outperformed those using weather variables alone. Overall, the composite model achieved the best performance with an RMSE of 3.48 visits per hour, an MAE of 2.62 visits per hour, and an R ² of 0.68. Mean absolute prediction errors were approximately 2 to 3 patients per hour across scenarios, suggesting practical utility for short-term staffing and capacity planning. The study indicates that community-level social vulnerability may provide more informative signals than weather conditions for anticipating short-term ED demand. Integrating SDoH-informed forecasts into hospital operations may enable earlier staffing adjustments and help mitigate crowding-related risks.

title: Ethnoracial disparities in emergency department triage are more pronounced in lower-risk visits: a multicenter study
abstract: Ethnoracial disparities in emergency department triage decisions persist, despite efforts to standardize protocols. Here, we analyze 1.35 million encounters at four U.S. emergency departments that all use the Emergency Severity Index triage protocol. We independently score visits as emergent (level 2) or urgent (level 3) by applying the criteria computationally and compare to nurse assignments. We show that, matched on clinical presentation and hospital context, Hispanic patients are less often triaged emergent than Non-Hispanic White (NHW) patients at every site (odds ratios (ORs): 0.75 [95% CI 0.72–0.78] to 0.90 [0.86–0.94]), and Non-Hispanic Black patients at two (0.73 [0.71–0.74], 0.89 [0.86–0.92]). Disparities increase where the algorithm scores patients lower-risk (Hispanic-NHW ORs: 0.73 [0.69–0.77] to 0.88 [0.83–0.94]), and attenuate where it scores them higher-risk (0.83 [0.79–0.89] to 0.95 [0.90–1.00]), suggesting a disparate “benefit-of-the-doubt” pattern of clinical discretion. Standardized decision support may reduce these disparities, and we estimate a worst-case increase on ED lengths of stay to be 1.0 -3.8% across sites. Analysis of 1.35 million emergency department visits found that racial and ethnic disparities in triage scores were concentrated in lower-risk visits, where assessment relies more on clinical judgment.

title: Paediatric escalation area and corridor care in the emergency department: a secondary analysis of the UNCORKED study
abstract: Abstract Objective To describe the use of, and outcomes following, Emergency Department (ED) escalation area care among children. Design Two-stage prospective multicentre observational study. Stage one was a cross-sectional snapshot study reporting the point prevalence of escalation area care; stage two was an observational cohort study of eligible participants present in the EDs during snapshots. Setting 5 snapshots of 96 type 1 UK EDs. 83/96 (86.5%) of sites were mixed EDs and 13 sites were paediatric-only EDs. Patients Patient level data was collected on those who experienced escalation area care and/or were admitted. Outcomes The primary outcome was the proportion of patients cared for in escalation areas in paediatric-only EDs. Secondary outcomes were demographics, length of stay (LOS), 28-day mortality, type of escalation area experienced and time in escalation areas in all ED types; stratified by escalation area experience. Results 6.6% (n=75/1132) of patients in paediatric-only EDs were receiving escalation area care during the study snapshots, the majority of this occurred in a minority of departments. Across all ED types, 15.4% (n=104/675) of admitted children experienced escalation area care during their ED stay. 124/244 (50.8%) of those cared for in escalation areas were cared for in a non-clinical area such as a corridor. 9.6% (n=8/83) of mixed EDs reported caring for adults in paediatric areas. Three children died within 28 days; all admitted to hospital without experiencing escalation area care. Hospital LOS was 2.00 days (1.00, 3.00) for those in escalation areas and 2.00 days (2.00, 4.00) for those not cared for in escalation areas. Conclusions Escalation area care is a common and systemic feature of paediatric emergency care in the UK which requires urgent action to ensure children are cared for in appropriate environments.

title: Impact of MRSA nasal PCR in the emergency department on duration of vancomycin and linezolid for pneumonia
journal: The American Journal of Emergency Medicine

title: Simulation-based evaluation of alternative care pathways and capacity configurations in pediatric mental health emergency care
Simulation-based evaluation of alternative care pathways and capacity configurations in pediatric mental health emergency care
abstract: Pediatric mental and behavioral health visits place growing pressure on emergency departments, where long evaluation times, disposition delays, and extended stays while waiting for placement or discharge increase crowding and resource strain. This study evaluated how alternative care pathways and capacity configurations are likely to affect pediatric emergency department performance for mental and behavioral health care. We developed a discrete-event simulation model of a pediatric emergency department using electronic medical record data, clinician input, and observed workflow. The model tested five scenario groups: psychiatric emergency unit routing, patient volume growth, disposition-to-departure delay, mental and behavioral health case-mix, and psychiatrist coverage. In the simulated emergency department, psychiatric emergency unit routing reduced time to psychiatric evaluation and space utilization. Reducing disposition-to-departure delays produced the largest improvements in throughput and space utilization, whereas expanded psychiatrist coverage primarily improved outcomes for mental and behavioral health patients, especially length of stay and time to disposition. Varying the patients case-mix had smaller effects within the tested range. Interventions should be matched to the bottlenecks. Psychiatric emergency unit routing may ease space constraints, psychiatrist coverage may reduce delays for mental and behavioral health patients, and shorter disposition delays may improve throughput.

title: Emergency department nurse-led systematic nursing model for septic shock: impact on 1-hour bundle adherence and mortality
abstract: Objective To evaluate the impact of a systematic septic shock nursing model led by emergency department (ED) nurses on adherence with resuscitation protocols and clinical outcomes in patients with septic shock. Methods Our team employed the Delphi method to develop a systematic nursing model, and it was implemented in August 2023. To verify its application effect, a retrospective controlled study was conducted in the emergency resuscitation room of the First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University. Patients who met the Sepsis-3 criteria for septic shock were consecutively enrolled from January 2022 to February 2025. According to the nursing model received during different periods, they were divided into two groups: the control group (enrolled from January 2022 to July 2023, n = 331) received conventional nursing, and the observation group (enrolled from August 2023 to February 2025, n = 343) received the systematic nursing model led by emergency nurses. Propensity score matching (1:1, caliper value 0.2) was used to balance differences. Primary outcomes included the 1-hour bundle adherence rate, 28-day and 90-day mortality, and 24-hour resuscitation success rate. Secondary outcomes included SOFA score, duration of vasoactive agent use, mechanical ventilation duration, ICU length of stay, and incidence of adverse events. Results After propensity score matching, 524 patients were successfully matched, with 262 patients in each group. The 1-hour bundle adherence rate was significantly higher in the observation group than in the control group (23.66% vs. 14.12%, p = 0.005), although the absolute adherence rate remained low in both groups. Compared with the control group, the observation group showed a significant decreases in 28-day and 90-day mortality, and a significant increase in the 24-hour resuscitation success rate ( p < 0.05). Moreover, SOFA scores were significantly reduced, and both the duration of vasoactive agent use and ICU length of stay were shortened ( p < 0.05). The incidence of adverse events was also significantly lower in the observation group ( p < 0.05). Conclusion The systematic nursing model led by ED nurses significantly improves adherence in patients with septic shock, reduces short and medium-term mortality, enhances organ function recovery, and shortens ICU length of stay, demonstrating good potential for clinical implementation.

title: Admission-time prediction of hospital length of stay in diverticular disease using explainable machine learning models
abstract: Acute diverticulitis (AD) is a leading cause of emergency department admissions and hospitalizations worldwide. Accurately predicting hospital length of stay (LOS) at the time of admission is essential for optimizing the utilization of resources, planning discharges and managing patients. The aim of this study was to develop and validate an explainable machine learning framework for predicting LOS at the time of admission in patients with diverticulitis and diverticulosis. A retrospective dataset comprising 148 hospitalized patients was analyzed. Advanced feature engineering techniques were applied, including interaction terms, nonlinear transformations, logarithmic scaling and clinically derived inflammatory indices. Multiple regression-based and machine learning model such as Linear Regression, Ridge Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost and a Voting Regressor ensemble were trained using log-transformed LOS values. Model performance was evaluated using five-fold cross-validation, bootstrap-based stability analysis, calibration assessment, SHAP-based explainability and Kaplan-Meier-based risk stratification. The mean LOS was 2.08 ± 2.5 days. Tree-based ensemble models demonstrated better predictive performance compared to linear models. XGBoost performed best in the full cohort (mean absolute error (MAE) = 0.03; R² = 0.99), while Random Forest and ensemble approaches showed comparable or improved performance in the diverticulitis subgroup with MAE of 0.74 and R² of 0.77. XGBoost showed exceptionally high apparent performance in the full cohort. However, stricter internal validation produced more conservative estimates. Patient-level nested out-of-fold (OOF) evaluation resulted in an R² of approximately 0.57, while bootstrap optimism correction yielded an optimism-corrected R² of 0.8314 and MAE of 0.3512 days. SHAP analysis indicated that Hinchey class and inflammatory characteristics contributed substantially to model predictions. Calibration and residual analyses indicated acceptable agreement between predicted and observed LOS, while prediction intervals provided clinically relevant uncertainty estimates. Subgroup analysis revealed decreased predictive performance and increased variability, reflecting the challenges associated with reduced sample size and heterogeneity. Combining explainable machine learning with clinically informed feature engineering provides a promising framework for estimating LOS at the time of admission for diverticular disease. However, the more conservative nested cross-validation results highlight the need for larger, independent cohorts in order to establish the generalizability and potential utility of the proposed approach.

title: Epidemiologic Trends and Practice Patterns in the Management of Sepsis in Emergency Departments: A Five-Year Singapore Cohort Study (2017-2021)
abstract: Objective: Southeast Asia is undergoing rapid population ageing, yet longitudinal ED-based sepsis data from the region are absent.We characterised sepsis epidemiology and management trends across three adult emergency departments (EDs) in Singapore over five years, establishing regional benchmarking data and examining evidence-to-practice translation during a period of active guideline change.Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult ED encounters with explicit sepsis ICD-10 codes across three EDs (January 2017-December 2021) using the EM-RADAR database.Outcomes included incidence, demographics, admission rates, length of stay, mortality, fluid resuscitation, antibiotic timing, and vasopressor use.Temporal trends were assessed by regression with calendar year as a predictor.Results: Among 1,636,828 ED encounters, 17,117 (1.05%) had explicit sepsis codes.Admissions (98.4%), hospital length of stay (median 6.03 days), in-hospital mortality (8.9%), and vasopressor requirement (4.9%) remained stable.The proportion of patients ≥65 years increased from 68.5% to 72.2% (OR 1.05 per year, 95% CI 1.02-1.07).Balanced crystalloid adoption increased six-fold (11.3% to 61.9%; OR 1.81 per year, 95% CI 1.76-1.86).Median time to antibiotics decreased to 80.8 minutes (IQR 45.5-124.2) by 2021; 64.2% of patients who required vasopressors received antibiotics within one hour.First-line vasopressor use shifted from dopamine (57.8%) to norepinephrine (67.1%).Conclusions: Sepsis incidence (1.05%) was comparable to international reports, predominantly affecting elderly patients.Rapid balanced crystalloid adoption and risk-stratified antibiotic timing reflect successful evidence-to-practice translation.Opportunities remain in reducing antibiotic delays for patients requiring vasopressors and optimizing vasopressor selection.Findings provide benchmarking framework for ED sepsis quality improvement.

title: Association of the ISAR Score with Clinical and Operational Outcomes in Older Emergency Department Patients
abstract: Background/Objectives: The Identification of Seniors at Risk (ISAR) score is widely used to identify older emergency department (ED) patients at increased risk of adverse outcomes. However, its association with immediate disposition and operational outcomes remains incompletely characterized. This study evaluated the association of ISAR scores with hospital admission and emergency department length of stay (EDLOS). Methods: This retrospective observational cohort study included ED presentations of patients aged ≥65 years at a tertiary university emergency department in 2024. Of 12,105 eligible presentations, 10,090 (83.4%) had a documented ISAR score and constituted the descriptive cohort; 9401 presentations with classifiable admission status were included in the primary admission analysis. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, presenting complaint, triage category, treating specialty, and referral source. The incremental contribution of ISAR beyond routinely available clinical variables was assessed by nested model comparison and receiver operating characteristic analysis. Prolonged EDLOS was defined as ≥6 h. Results: Higher ISAR scores were independently associated with hospital admission and prolonged EDLOS. In the continuous-score admission model, each one-point increase in ISAR was associated with higher odds of admission (OR 1.155, 95% CI 1.121–1.191; p < 0.001), although categorical sensitivity analysis demonstrated a nonlinear association with a plateau at higher scores. ISAR alone showed modest discrimination for admission (AUC 0.589, 95% CI 0.577–0.600). Addition of ISAR to the clinical model increased the AUC from 0.696 to 0.705 (ΔAUC = 0.009, 95% CI 0.005–0.012; p < 0.001). Median EDLOS increased from 326 min (IQR 215–494) at ISAR 0 to 596 min (IQR 324–1312) at ISAR 6. After adjustment including hospital admission status, each one-point increase in ISAR was associated with higher odds of prolonged EDLOS (OR 1.178, 95% CI 1.143–1.214; p < 0.001). Conclusions: Higher ISAR scores were associated with both hospital admission and prolonged EDLOS. ISAR provided statistically significant but modest incremental prognostic information beyond routinely available clinical variables and should be regarded as a geriatric risk-screening tool rather than a stand-alone disposition instrument. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether ISAR-guided clinical pathways improve patient or operational outcomes.

title: Handover from the emergency department to the intensive care unit and patient outcomes: a systematic review
abstract: Transitions of care between the emergency department (ED) and the intensive care unit (ICU) are high-risk moments in which critical information can be lost, and patients admitted to the ICU from the ED represent a large and growing proportion of critical care admissions. Handover practices at this interface vary widely, ranging from unstructured verbal reports to structured tools such as SBAR/ISBAR, purpose-built checklists, and electronic handover modules. Handover has been extensively studied in ward and operating theatre settings, but no systematic review has specifically synthesised the evidence on ED-to-ICU handover and its association with patient and nursing outcomes. This systematic review aims to (1) describe how ED-to-ICU handover is structured, measured and reported; (2) synthesise the association between handover structure and completeness and patient outcomes, including ICU length of stay, duration of mechanical ventilation, mortality, unplanned ICU readmission, and handover-related adverse events; and (3) summarise reported facilitators, barriers and implementation strategies for structured handover in this setting. We will search six English-language databases (MEDLINE via PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane CENTRAL and Scopus) from inception to the search date, with no date restriction and restricted to records published in English, supplemented by grey literature, trial registries, and backward/forward citation chasing. Two reviewers will independently screen and extract data. Risk of bias will be assessed with RoB 2, ROBINS-I, the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, AXIS and CASP, and certainty of evidence will be rated with GRADE. Random-effects meta-analyses will be performed where at least three comparable studies report the same outcome; otherwise a SWiM-guided narrative synthesis with harvest plots will be used. This registration is completed before any database search is executed.

title: International Delphi on a medical screening tool for emergency department patients with psychiatric complaints
abstract: Abstract Background: Medical screening in the emergency department (ED) is performed to identify underlying medical conditions that may contribute to a patient’s psychiatric presentation and/or require treatment. This process frequently causes disagreement between emergency physicians and psychiatrists regarding objectives and scope of medical screening, leading to potentially unnecessary testing, prolonged ED length-of-stay, and increased costs. This study aims to develop an evidence-informed and consensus-based medical screening tool through a transdisciplinary, international Delphi process. Methods: This modified international Delphi study was conducted between May and November 2025 using a 4-round modified Delphi process with online surveys and online steering committee discussions. Participants included 25 society representatives from 7 emergency medicine and psychiatry societies across 4 continents and 6 patient representatives with prior ED medical screening experience as patients or patient relatives. Participants generated, rated, refined, and reached consensus on proposed screening elements. Consensus was predefined as ≥80% agreement in Round 3. In Round 4, the resulting tool was applied to 37 standardized clinical vignettes. Interrater agreement was assessed using Gwet agreement coefficient (AC). Results: Of 28 invited society representatives and steering committee members, 25 (89.3%) participated in Round 1, 23 (82.1%) in Round 2, 22 (78.6%) in Round 3, and 23 (82.1%) in Round 4. The 6 patient representatives completed all 4 rounds. In Round 1, participants generated 91 statements from society representatives and 27 from patient representatives. Following refinement in Round 2, consensus in Round 3 was achieved for 48 of 91 society representatives’ statements (52.8%) and 21 of 27 patient statements (77.8%), which were synthesized into the Delphi-Informed Medical Evaluation (DIME) tool. In Round 4, application of the draft DIME tool to 37 clinical vignettes demonstrated almost perfect agreement among society representatives (Gwet AC, 0.86; 95%-CI 0.78–0.93; p < .001) and substantial agreement among patient representatives (Gwet AC, 0.76; 95%-CI 0.66–0.86; p < .001). Conclusions This international modified Delphi study developed the DIME tool, a consensus-based medical screening tool to identify adult ED patients with psychiatric complaints who are at low risk for acute medical illness. Prospective multicenter validation studies are required before clinical implementation. Trial registration clinicaltrials.gov, NCT06936826

title: Impact of geographic localization on hospital length of stay: Evidence of a dose–response relationship
abstract: BACKGROUND: Geographic localization of patients and clinicians is a common approach to improve teamwork and efficiency, reduce hospital length of stay (LOS), and improve patient experience. We implemented a multidisciplinary initiative, called Patient-Centered Teams (PaCT), which reengineered bed management procedures and localized several hospital medicine teams to specific nursing units. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the impact of PaCT on LOS and whether hospital units with a greater increase in localization experienced more LOS reduction. METHODS: Observational study of patients hospitalized at a large academic medical center between July 1, 2023 and February 26, 2025. Patients discharged from five hospital units that implemented geographic localization in September 2024 were included (N = 5868). Log-linear models quantified the impact of localization on hospital LOS overall and for each hospital unit separately, pre- versus postintervention, while adjusting for case mix index. Degree of localization was quantified as the percentage of patients discharged from the unit who were under the care of the main hospitalist team(s) assigned to that unit. RESULTS: Overall, a 10% reduction in LOS was observed following the localization initiative. In the two units which experienced the greatest increase in localization, LOS decreased by 13%-19%. In contrast, in two units which saw less of an increase in localization with this initiative, LOS did not significantly change in the postimplementation period. CONCLUSIONS: Implementing the PaCT geographic localization intervention was associated with shorter LOS, particularly among hospital units with the greatest increase in localization from baseline.

title: Pharmacogenetic testing to improve care in the emergency department
abstract: Nearly 20% of emergency department (ED) encounters involve medications with actionable pharmacogenomic (PGx) guidance available, and population-based studies suggest over 90% of patients carry at least one PGx variant potentially affecting drug response. Despite this, PGx testing in emergency medicine remains rare. This perspective summarizes current evidence supporting PGx implementation in the ED, key barriers to integration, and future directions for PGx testing in acute care. Feasibility studies demonstrate that PGx testing can be incorporated into ED workflows. Observational data suggest clinically important associations between CYP2C19 variability and clopidogrel-related bleeding, CYP2D6 metabolism and opioid-related ED visits, and a high prevalence of actionable gene–drug interactions in older adults presenting with falls. In pediatric psychiatric populations, combinatorial PGx testing has been associated with differences in drug exposure and clinical outcomes. However, no randomized controlled trials testing the clinical utility of PGx testing have been conducted in ED populations. Key barriers to implementation include prolonged PGx testing turnaround times, lack of standardized ordering workflows, limited clinician familiarity with PGx interpretation, inconsistent reimbursement, and challenges integrating results into clinical decision support systems. Future priorities should include prospective interventional trials assessing clinical outcomes, targeted implementation focused on high-risk gene-drug pairs, and incorporation of PGx education into emergency medicine training. Although current evidence is largely feasibility-based, the ED represents a potentially high-yield setting for PGx integration given frequent exposure to actionable medications and the high burden of potentially preventable adverse drug events.

title: Cumulative Weighted-Average Acuity Level: A Novel Clinician-Level Metric to Detect Emergency Department Surge Conditions in Real Time
abstract: Introduction: Emergency department (ED) surge events, defined as the episodic clustering of high-acuity patients that transiently overwhelms available clinician capacity, are associated with delays in care and potential patient harm. Existing crowding metrics do not quantify real-time clinician-level workload. This paper describes the development and preliminary feasibility evaluation of a novel acuity-weighted metric—the cumulative weighted-average acuity level (CWAAL)—to detect physician-level surge conditions in real time. Methods: This multiphase observational feasibility study was conducted at two rural community EDs. The CWAAL is defined as the sum of weighted acuity scores for all active patients under a single clinician’s management: it incorporates a feasibility threshold derived by combinatorial enumeration. The primary outcome was door-to-doctor time (DDT); secondary outcomes included length of stay (LOS) and CWAAL distribution. The DDT comparisons at Hospital B (n = 4 surge events per condition) used the Mann-Whitney U test. All data were obtained from the practice of a single physician. Results: We evaluated a single emergency physician across 354 patients on 10 study dates at two rural community EDs, tracking 11 surge events and one proof of concept. A CWAAL feasibility threshold of ≤ 12 (±1)—equivalent to four simultaneous Level 3 patients (~120 minute demand within a 60-minute window)—emerged consistently across both sites. At Hospital B, surge-period DDTs were substantially lower with advanced practice clinician (APC) coverage than without (median, 31.5 minutes [interquartile range {IQR}, 24.7–38.0] vs 107.7 minutes [IQR, 85.7–133.5]); Mann-Whitney U = 0, P = .03, 2-tailed exact; rank-biserial r = 1.0), with complete distributional separation across eight surge events. All APC-supported events occurred at CWAAL ≤ 12; all unsupported events at CWAAL > 12. A proof-of-concept application on May 28, 2024, demonstrated operational feasibility; supplemental staffing reduced the physician’s weighted acuity burden by 31 points and normalized DDT and LOS. Conclusion: In this development cohort, the physician reached functional care capacity at cumulative weighted average acuity level = 12 (four simultaneous Level 3 patients; ~120 minutes demand within a 60-minute physician-hour). Complete separation of APC-supported and unsupported outcomes across eight events supports this novel acuity-weighted metric as a meaningful operational signal. Formal prospective validation across independent datasets is required before generalizing.

title: Body Temperature in the Emergency Department—Predictive Value for the Diagnosis of Appendicitis. A retrospective single-center cohort data set
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A total of 510 children between the ages of 3 and 15 were included in the data collection. The main inclusion criteria were a clinically suspected diagnosis of appendicitis and inpatient admission. Patients were divided into four groups: Observation (no surgery); Minimal changes (appendectomy, histologically only mild, often focal changes); phlegmonous appendicitis, and complicated appendicitis. The following variables were recorded: age (years) and sex; body temperature upon hospital admission (°C); length of hospital stay (LOS); C-reactive protein in the blood (mg/dL); hemoglobin (g/dL); hematocrit (%); white blood cell count (10^3/µL); neutrophils—absolute number and percentage, lymphocytes and monocytes (absolute number), platelets (10³/µL), and blood sodium. Data on the differential blood count were available for only a limited number of children (n = 287). The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, the lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio, and the platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio were also calculated. When using the data, please note that some columns are sorted, while others contain unsorted numbers. Therefore, only columns can be compared with one another. There is no horizontal connection between the individual rows.

title: CLINICAL AND EPIDEMIOLOGICAL PROFILE OF SNAKEBITE PATIENTS PRESENTING TO A TERTIARY REFERRAL EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT IN EAST JAVA, INDONESIA
abstract: Background. . Indonesia carries one of the highest snakebite burdens in Southeast Asia, yet national epidemiological data are scarce and derive almost entirely from isolated hospital reports. This study aims to describes the clinical and epidemiological profile of snakebite patients presenting to the emergency department (ED). Research Method. A descriptive observational study was conducted on all 82 snakebite patients who presented between January and December 2025, identified by total sampling from the ED register and medical records of Dr. Saiful Anwar General Hospital, Malang. The variables evaluated included demographic characteristics, reported snake type, clinical manifestations classified using standard envenoming criteria, emergency department disposition, and short-term outcomes. Findings. Bites attributed by patients to green snakes, consistent with Trimeresurus species, accounted for 46 cases (56.1%). Majority patients presented without symptoms or with mild local manifestations only (29 asymptomatic, 35.4%; 33 mild local, 40.2%), whereas severe local and systemic envenoming occurred in 11 (13.4%) and 7 (8.5%) patients respectively. Sixty-one patients (74.4%) were discharged after ED observation, for a median of 5.10 hours (interquartile range 3.55–6.60), and 21 (25.6%) were admitted, of whom 12 (57.1%) received antivenom. The median length of stay was 3 days (interquartile range 3–4). Readmission within 48 hours occurred in 4 discharged patients (6.6%) and one death was recorded (1.2%). Conclusion. The profile is dominated by green pit viper bites of low initial severity, a pattern for which the nationally available polyvalent antivenom offers no coverage.

title: The Nursing Diagnoses and Length of Stay Among Hospitalized Pediatric Patients: A Retrospective Study
abstract: Background: Nursing diagnoses reflect patients’ clinical needs and may indicate the complexity of pediatric care during hospitalization. However, evidence regarding patterns of nursing diagnoses, terminology consistency, and their association with length of stay (LOS) remains limited. Objectives: To describe nursing diagnoses documented among hospitalized pediatric patients and examine differences in LOS according to patient and nursing diagnosis characteristics. Methods: This descriptive retrospective study analyzed medical records of 186 pediatric patients. The Indonesian Nursing Diagnosis Standards (SDKI) was used to classify clinically equivalent diagnostic terminology. Categorical data were summarized using frequencies and percentages, while LOS was presented as the median and interquartile range (IQR) because of its non-normal distribution. Bivariate analyses used Mann–Whitney U and Kruskal–Wallis tests. Results: Acute pain (14.0%), ineffective airway clearance (10.8%), and ineffective breathing pattern (9.1%) were the most frequently documented nursing diagnoses. Standardized terminology was consistently documented in 31.7% of records. LOS differed significantly by age group (p=0.018), sex (p=0.046), care unit (p<0.001), and number of nursing diagnoses (p=0.025), but not by terminology consistency (p=0.259). Conclusion: LOS varied according to patient characteristics, care unit, and the number of documented nursing diagnoses, whereas terminology consistency was not associated with LOS. The substantial terminology inconsistency highlights the need to strengthen standardized terminology and pediatric nursing documentation.

title: Prospective evaluation of the clinical presentation and outcomes of complicated groin hernias in an emergency surgical department at a resource-limited setting of North India
abstract: Abstract Background Groin hernias carry a lifetime risk of approximately 27% in men and 3% in women, making it one of the common surgical conditions worldwide. A significant proportion of these hernias presents as surgical emergencies due to incarceration or strangulation, with complication rates ranging from 10% to 37%. High-quality prospective data from northern India on this condition remain limited. So, this study was undertaken to prospectively evaluate the clinical presentation, management and outcomes of incarcerated groin hernia. Material and Methods A prospective, single-centre observational study was conducted involving 70 consecutive patients who underwent emergency surgical repair for incarcerated groin hernias. Demographic data, clinical features, white blood cell (WBC) counts and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), surgical techniques and postoperative complications were recorded and analysed. Results Among 70 patients (85.7% male), 17.1% required bowel resection and anastomosis (R&A). The mean duration of acute symptoms was 22.5 ± 16.7 hours. Delayed presentation was significantly associated with surgical morbidity; patients needing R&A presented much later than those who did not (44.7 vs. 17.9 hours, p = 0.0002). Notably, every one-hour delay increased the odds of requiring an R&A by 11.6% (OR = 1.116, p = 0.00017). Elevated WBC counts and NLR served as powerful independent predictors for ischemia and the necessity of bowel resection. The overall complication rate was 34.3%. Non-mesh repairs had significantly higher complication rates compared to mesh repairs (52.9% vs. 16.7%, p = 0.003). Postoperative complications significantly prolonged the hospital stay (6.92 vs. 3.78 days, p < 0.0001). Conclusion Incarcerated groin hernia in northern India predominantly affects middle-aged males presenting late after prolonged symptom duration. Open mesh hernioplasty is safe and associated with shorter hospital stay in the absence of gross contamination. Bowel resection significantly increases morbidity and length of stay. Early diagnosis and prompt surgery are the important factors in improving outcome. Clinical trial registration Not applicable.

title: Comparative efficacy and safety of antiemetics for pediatric gastroenteritis-related vomiting in emergency departments: a network meta-analysis
abstract: Vomiting is a leading cause of emergency department (ED) visits among children with acute gastroenteritis (AGE). Although antiemetics are commonly used, uncertainty persists regarding the comparative efficacy and safety of individual agents across clinically relevant timeframes. To compare the efficacy and safety of commonly used antiemetics for pediatric AGE-related vomiting in ED settings using a network meta-analysis (NMA) of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). A systematic search of major databases was conducted through 2025. Eligible studies were RCTs enrolling children ≤21 years presenting to the ED with AGE. Interventions included ondansetron (all routes), dimenhydrinate, domperidone, metoclopramide, bromopride, and placebo. Outcomes included vomiting frequency (short-, intermediate-, and long-term), cessation of vomiting, need for intravenous (IV) rehydration, ED length of stay, hospitalization, and adverse events. A random-effects frequentist NMA was performed. Risk of bias was assessed using ROB-2, and certainty of evidence was evaluated with GRADE. Thirty-three RCTs were included. In the short term, all ondansetron formulations reduced vomiting compared with placebo, with the strongest effect seen with IV administration (MD −1.86, 95% CI −3.25 to −0.47). For intermediate-term outcomes, IV ondansetron was the only agent consistently superior to placebo and active comparators. For long-term vomiting, dimenhydrinate (oral and rectal) demonstrated significant benefit (rectal: MD −0.72, 95% CI −1.14 to −0.30). Vomiting cessation within 24 h favored IV ondansetron (RR 1.56, 95% CI 1.29–1.89), with additional benefit from rectal dimenhydrinate (RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.08–2.04). Ondansetron reduced the need for IV rehydration (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.44–0.88) and modestly shortened ED stay. Safety comparisons were imprecise, though ondansetron showed fewer adverse events than metoclopramide. Ondansetron provides the most consistent benefit for acute vomiting control and reducing IV fluid use in pediatric AGE, while dimenhydrinate may support longer-term symptom control. Acute gastroenteritis (AGE) is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in children worldwide, with severe vomiting and diarrhea causing rapid fluid loss. Antiemetics are commonly used to reduce vomiting and prevent complications, yet their relative efficacy and safety remain uncertain. Ondansetron was the most effective antiemetic for pediatric AGE-related vomiting, significantly reducing vomiting episodes and intravenous fluid requirements, although its effect on hospital admission was not statistically significant. Dimenhydrinate was highly effective for intermediate- and long-term outcomes, particularly in reducing emetic episodes and supporting vomiting cessation. Domperidone and metoclopramide showed variable efficacy, with limited effectiveness compared with ondansetron and dimenhydrinate. These findings support ondansetron as the first-line antiemetic in pediatric AGE, with dimenhydrinate as a useful option for prolonged vomiting.

title: Decarbonising the Indian operating room: Beyond banning desflurane
abstract: Climate change is no longer a distant threat.It is already affecting public health through heatwaves and changing the distribution of vector-borne diseases.At the same time, the healthcare system itself contributes to greenhouse gas emissions.Therefore, it becomes a responsibility of clinicians to reduce the avoidable environmental harm while caring for the patients.Operating rooms (ORs) are among the most resource-intensive areas of a hospital.Studies evaluating the lifecycle emissions of surgical theatres show that when volatile inhalation anaesthetics (particularly desflurane) are used, anaesthetic gases can account for up to 63% of the total carbon footprint of surgical care.1,2 The growing focus on "green anaesthesia" has appropriately drawn attention to desflurane.However, eliminating one high-impact agent is only a part of the solution.In Indian hospitals, where costs, infrastructure and availability vary widely, meaningful decarbonisation must extend beyond banning desflurane to low fresh-gas flows, appropriate anaesthesia techniques, handling of consumables and waste, and judicious energy use.

title: Job preferences of operating room nurses: A discrete choice experiment
abstract: BACKGROUND: The global nursing shortage is particularly acute in operating rooms, where staffing deficits can compromise surgical efficiency and patient safety. Although previous studies have identified factors associated with nurse retention, quantitative evidence on how operating room nurses value and trade off different job attributes remains limited. OBJECTIVE: To quantify the job preferences of operating room nurses and examine the relative importance of different job attributes. DESIGN: A cross-sectional study utilising a discrete choice experiment. SETTING(S): Four public tertiary hospitals in Sichuan Province, China. PARTICIPANTS: 385 operating room nurses. METHODS: Data were collected through an anonymous online survey in which participants completed a series of discrete choice tasks comparing hypothetical jobs defined by six attributes: income, work climate, career development, leadership, working hours, and National Nosocomial Infections Surveillance (the proportion of assigned surgeries with a risk index score of 2 or 3). Preferences were estimated using a mixed logit model. Relative importance scores were calculated to quantify the contribution of each job attribute to overall utility, and subgroup analyses were conducted to examine preference heterogeneity. RESULTS: A total of 385 operating room nurses were included in the analysis. Among the attribute levels evaluated in this discrete choice experiment, work climate had the highest relative importance (38.16%), followed by working hours (21.63%), monthly income (14.25%), career development (12.89%), leadership (9.20%), and National Nosocomial Infections Surveillance (3.87%). Improving the work climate from a negative to a positive level was associated with the largest relative utility gain within the discrete choice experiment design. Subgroup analyses showed no statistically significant preference differences according to sex, age, marital status, professional title, years of nursing experience, and weekly working hours (all interaction P-values >0.05). CONCLUSIONS: In this discrete choice experiment, work climate had the highest relative importance across the evaluated attribute levels among the participating operating room nurses, followed by working hours and income. Improving work climate, supporting work-life balance, and providing appropriate financial incentives may be considered when developing strategies to recruit and retain these nurses, although caution is warranted given the limited recruitment setting. REGISTRATION: Not registered. SOCIAL MEDIA ABSTRACT: For operating room nurses, a positive work climate is the top job priority, followed by working hours and income.

title: ENHANCING OPERATION THEATRE MANAGEMENT THROUGH MOBILE APP INTEGRATION
abstract: Background: Effective operation theatre management requires coordination of patients, surgical teams, anaesthesia services, operating-room availability, instruments, resources and postoperative processes. Conventional OT planning may involve fragmented communication and manual scheduling, increasing the possibility of scheduling conflicts, delays and inefficient resource utilization. Mobile application-based integration may provide a structured approach for coordinating these activities. Aim: To develop and validate a mobile application for integrated operation theatre management. Objectives: The study aimed to analyse existing OT planning practices and identify operational gaps, develop a comprehensive mobile application incorporating major OT management functions, and validate the performance of the developed application. Methods: A methodological application-development and validation study was undertaken. Existing OT planning processes were assessed through document analysis and multidisciplinary stakeholder inputs. Focus-group discussions included anaesthetists, surgeons, a final-year postgraduate student, nurses and OT technicians to identify operational requirements. Major domains included pre-anaesthetic optimization, patient readiness, OT availability, booking and scheduling, procurement, resource management, CSSD requirements and postoperative documentation. The application was developed as a progressive web application incorporating case creation, anaesthesia planning, scheduling, conflict detection, instrument-tray mapping, case dashboards, OT timetable visualization, PDF export, cross-device synchronization and role-based access. The scheduling module covered 18 OT rooms with defined operating hours and a 30-minute turnover buffer. Validation of conflict detection was performed using a diagnostic test dataset. Results: The application successfully integrated multiple components of OT management within a single digital platform. For scheduling conflict detection, the application demonstrated 89.47% sensitivity, 95.24% specificity, 94.44% positive predictive value, 90.91% negative predictive value and 92.50% overall accuracy. It correctly identified 17 of 19 true scheduling conflicts and 20 of 21 non-conflicting schedules. The findings demonstrated good technical performance of the developed system in identifying scheduling conflicts. Conclusion: The developed mobile application provided an integrated digital framework for operation theatre management and demonstrated good accuracy in detecting scheduling conflicts. Its integration of scheduling, case preparation, anaesthesia planning, instrument-tray mapping and resource-related functions may support more standardized OT coordination. Further prospective and multicentre studies are required to determine its impact on actual OT utilization, cancellation rates, turnover time, waiting time, resource utilization and user satisfaction.

title: Interventions to Reduce Day-of-Surgery Cancellation of Elective Surgery: A Systematic Review Protocol
abstract: Day-of-surgery cancellation of elective operations wastes operating-room capacity and harms patients. Existing reviews address single intervention types (such as pre-anaesthesia clinics, virtual preoperative assessment or nurse-led assessment), are mostly narrative, or describe the incidence and causes of cancellation rather than the effect of interventions. This systematic review will identify and synthesise comparative studies of any deliberate pre-operative or organisational intervention versus usual care in patients scheduled for elective surgery. Eligible interventions include telephone, SMS or app contact and reminders; preparation checklists or protocols (fasting, medication instructions); pre-anaesthetic assessment (in-person, virtual or nurse-led); clinical optimisation pathways; and algorithm- or AI-guided tools. The primary outcome is day-of-surgery cancellation, expressed as a risk ratio. Secondary outcomes are no-show, cause-specific cancellation, operating-room utilisation, and perioperative complications and length of stay as balancing measures. Randomised and controlled studies, controlled cohorts and before-after studies, and interrupted time series will be analysed in separate strata. Meta-analysis will be done only where studies are clinically and methodologically compatible; otherwise synthesis will be narrative (SWiM). Pre-specified subgroups are intervention class, country income level, cause of cancellation, and adults versus children. Risk of bias will be assessed with RoB 2 and ROBINS-I, certainty with GRADE, and reporting will follow PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S. Status at registration: only an exploratory PubMed search has been done. Screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment and analysis have not started. No direction of effect is assumed for subgroup differences. This protocol is registered on OSF only; it is not registered in PROSPERO.

title: Precision in practice: Developing and validating a protocol and a checklist for standardization of ‘surgical counts’
abstract: Background: The prevention of unintentional retention of surgical items (RSIs) inside a patient’s body is one of the primary responsibilities of operating room nurses. Surgical counting is a simple and efficient method that helps prevent this human error. Aim: To develop and validate a standard operating protocol (SOP) and a checklist for surgical counts conducted during abdominal surgeries. Methods and materials: A methodological study, divided into six phases (2021-2023), was conducted in the paediatric surgery operating theatre of a tertiary care centre in northern India. Initial observations (N = 30), focus group discussions (N = 20) and nurses' knowledge assessment (N = 24) were carried out to explore baseline knowledge and practices related to surgical counts. The first draft of the SOP and checklist was prepared. A three-round Delphi process involving nine experts was employed to ensure content validity. The reliability of the protocol was evaluated across 75 surgical procedures using Cronbach’s alpha coefficient and nurses' acceptance of the protocol was gauged through a structured questionnaire. Results: Content validity was high, with a scale-level content validity index based on the average method (S-CVI/Ave) of 0.98 and a scale-level content validity index based on the universal-agreement method (S-CVI/UA) of 0.80. The mean item-level content validity index (I-CVI) was 0.90. The checklist comprised 37 items covering the key phases of surgery. Internal consistency was strong (Cronbach’s α = 0.82). Following implementation, surgical counting practices improved considerably, and nurses reported greater clarity and confidence. Conclusion: The SOP and checklist were found to be valid, reliable and well accepted in this single-centre study; further multicentre validation is recommended.

title: Research on multi-objective scheduling optimization of emergency resources based on simulated annealing algorithm
abstract: Abstract Emergency departments face persistent challenges including prolonged patient wait times, unbalanced resource utilization, and high staff overtime. To address these issues, this study proposes a multi‑objective resource scheduling model based on real hospital data and optimizes it using a simulated annealing (SA) algorithm. The model discretizes time slots and integrates multiple resources (doctors, consultation rooms, beds), with objectives of minimizing weighted waiting time and labor cost under triage‑priority and maximum‑wait constraints. A neighborhood operation set (patient exchange, cross‑doctor reallocation, shift fine‑tuning) was designed to fit clinical workflows. Simulation on annual 2023 data from a tertiary hospital showed that, compared to the current system, the SA‑optimized schedules reduced average waiting time by 20–35%, lowered the overall threshold-violation rate by 46.8% (26.7 to 14.2%), and balanced resource utilization across weekday, peak‑day, and night‑shift scenarios. These gains were not cost-neutral: total daily labour cost rose by 11.4% (CNY 31,680 to 35,280) and cost per patient visit by 10.6% (CNY 102.3 to 113.1), while overtime hours fell by 29.7% and overtime cost by 30.2%. The SA-based framework converged reliably and retained its ordering across scenarios, and is best described as a candidate decision-support component that buys substantial improvements in timeliness, resource equity and staff workload at a quantified increase in labour expenditure. Although the framework was validated only in a simulation environment calibrated with one year of real ED data and has not yet undergone prospective real-world deployment, the results suggest that it constitutes a potentially deployable decision-support component for intelligent ED scheduling. All results derive from a single-centre in-silico evaluation calibrated on one tertiary emergency department; prospective and multi-centre validation is required before any claim of generalisability or operational readiness can be supported.

title: Multi-Agent Scheduling of Instrument-Time for High-Throughput Palladium-Catalysed Cross-Coupling
abstract: NMR time and a shared liquid-handling robot are scarce, noisy and only partially observable, so the practical question is which experiment to run next on which instrument. Existing reaction-optimisation benchmarks measure budgets in experiments rather than instrumenthours, and they learn chemical feasibility only by paying for infeasible runs. We present CHASE, a centralised-training decentralised-execution scheduler with three coupled modules: a belief encoder (PEB) infers per-instrument throughput and channel health from local event histories and exchanges only low-bandwidth summaries; a chemistry feasibility gate (CFG) masks chemically impossible actions with a four-layer compatibility graph; and a counterfactual attribution module (CFA) converts delayed campaign reward into per-step credit through leave-one-experiment-out surrogate scoring. On the Buchwald–Hartwig (3,955 reactions) and Suzuki–Miyaura (5,760 nanomole-scale conditions) HTE datasets, the ten Olympus benchmarks and a plant-wide Tennessee Eastman process, CHASE reaches 94.1% best-found yield under a shared 60 instrument-hour budget, +3.3 points over the strongest same-setting baseline, attains 90% of the attainable optimum with 25.6% fewer experiments, and cuts infeasible actions to 0.7–1.6% across plate, flow and fault-injection settings.
