The Efficacy of External Aortic Compression in the Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage in a High-Resource Setting: A Case Series
abstract: This case series presents four cases of postpartum haemorrhage arising from a range of clinical scenarios other than the classical indication of atony. All cases were treated with external aortic compression as a temporising measure. External aortic compression is a technique that may provide a safe and effective means of limiting bleeding in postpartum haemorrhage; however, the technique has not been extensively studied in clinical trials. These four cases contribute to the growing body of knowledge on the use and safety of external aortic compression. The four clinical cases presented illustrate the use of external aortic compression in different clinical settings. Case one had a bicornuate uterus and suffered PPH due to retained placenta after a vaginal delivery and was transferred to the operating theatre, Case two was a caesarean section with an undiagnosed placenta accreta, Case three had a vaginal delivery with retained placenta treated at the maternity ward, and Case four had a vaginal delivery with placenta accreta, that ultimately proceeded to a hysterectomy in theatre due to the inability to deliver the placenta safely. This case series shows that external aortic compression can be used as a temporising measure across different clinical scenarios and causes for PPH in a high-resource setting. There is a definite need for further research into this important field within obstetric care, as increased use of external aortic compression, being a simple, teachable, and potentially life-saving procedure, can make a significant impact on maternal morbidity and mortality in both high- and low-resource settings.

title: Energy-aware and AI-enabled offloading framework in edge-to-cloud continuum
journal: Edinburgh Napier Research Repository (Edinburgh Napier University)
abstract: The rapid expansion of the Edge-to-Cloud (EOC) computing continuum has enabled a new generation of distributed, low-latency applications by pushing computation closer to data sources through edge and fog nodes. However, the heterogeneity of these environments, device-level energy constraints, and the absence of sustainability-aware optimisation models make accurate device-health and performance prediction, task scheduling, and computation offloading extremely challenging. Existing offloading approaches are typically designed around single-objective optimisation and only limited work considers device degradation or sustainability factors. This thesis addresses these limitations through three integrated contributions. Firstly, it introduces LiRUL, a lightweight edge-deployable model for Remaining Useful Life (RUL) prediction of Lithium-ion batteries. Battery degradation directly affects device reliability, energy availability, and offloading feasibility; therefore, accurate RUL estimation is essential for sustainable and health-aware decision-making. By combining degradation-sensitive features with efficient temporal learning, LiRUL provides accurate health estimation with minimal overhead. Although LiRUL is developed as an independent contribution, its predictions provide the foundational device-health information that future offloading frameworks can exploit to avoid unreliable nodes and improve long-term system sustainability. The model is validated using industrial datasets from the University of Warwick (UK) and the Korea Electronics Technology Institute (KETI). Secondly, the thesis proposes a dynamic multi-objective optimisation framework for energy-centric offloading (ECO-PSO/ECO-CSA) in heterogeneous fog/cloud environments. Most Existing schedulers ignore memory and transfer energy or rely on fixed static weighting schemes, leading to suboptimal and unstable performance under varying workloads. Leveraging hybrid metaheuristics (PSO–CSA) with adaptive coefficient adjustment, the proposed framework jointly minimises computation, transmission, and memory energy consumption alongside makespan and load imbalance. Simulation results demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline schedulers in terms of energy efficiency and end-to-end latency. The proposed framework enables more stable and adaptive offloading decisions under dynamic workload conditions, effectively balancing performance and resource utilisation. This contribution establishes a robust optimisation foundation for sustainable and performance-aware offloading across the EOC continuum. Finally, the work extends optimisation towards carbon-aware offloading (CAGWO, CACSA, CASSA) by incorporating both renewable and non-renewable energy availability alongside dynamic grid carbon intensity into the decision-making process. Unlike conventional approaches that prioritise latency or energy consumption in isolation, the proposed framework explicitly models carbon emissions as an optimisation objective, enabling environmentally informed task allocation across heterogeneous nodes. By jointly considering performance, energy consumption, and carbon impact, the framework enables adaptive scheduling decisions that respond to temporal and spatial variations in energy sources. This demonstrates that sustainability can be treated as a first-class design objective in computation offloading without undermining system responsiveness. Together, these contributions establish a unified research direction for sustainable computation offloading across the EOC continuum. By combining battery health prediction, multi-objective optimisation, and carbon-aware scheduling as complementary components, the thesis advances both the reliability and environmental efficiency of distributed systems. The results bridge the gap between theoretical optimisation and practical deployment, providing a solid foundation for next-generation energy- and carbon-efficient offloading strategies.

title: Beyond donor shortage: tissue utilization and resilience in modern corneal transplantation
abstract: For decades, the global shortage of corneal tissue has been framed as a donor supply problem: increase donor numbers, increase transplants. While inadequate donation and local procurement remain major constraints in many settings, including countries that rely heavily on imported corneal tissue, procurement alone does not fully explain access to transplantation. Once donor tissue enters the transplantation pathway, preservation, allocation, logistics, surgical capacity, and recipient readiness also determine whether it ultimately reaches a patient. Corneal surgery has evolved far beyond the traditional model of penetrating keratoplasty. Lamellar keratoplasty, selective endothelial replacement, stromal augmentation, tectonic applications, and regenerative strategies have changed how tissue is used and how shortage should be understood. Donor tissue may be recovered yet not ultimately be used for clinical transplantation. Some non-utilization is unavoidable and appropriate, reflecting donor eligibility, tissue quality, microbiological or serological findings, or allocation to research and training. In other circumstances, potentially transplantable tissue may not reach a recipient because of logistical constraints, limited preservation time, case cancellation, or difficulties in timely reallocation.Globally, an estimated 12.7 million individuals are waiting for a corneal transplant, with only one donor cornea available for every 70 patients in need. [1] Importantly, the number of corneas recovered should not be equated with the number available for transplantation. Recovered tissue may subsequently be excluded because it does not meet clinical or safety criteria, including inadequate endothelial quality or findings identified during donor screening and microbiological or serological evaluation; tissue may also be allocated to research or training. [2,3] Therefore, recovery-to-transplantation ratios alone cannot quantify avoidable tissue non-utilization. A more informative assessment requires distinguishing appropriate exclusion from failure to transplant tissue that had already been deemed suitable for clinical use. The challenge is not only whether tissue exists, but whether it reaches the right patient, in the right form, at the right time. What ultimately matters is how effectively recovered tissue is preserved, allocated, repurposed when appropriate, and translated into clinical use.Centers that depend heavily on imported tissue are exposed to these pressures. King Khaled Eye Specialist Hospital (KKESH) in Riyadh is a tertiary referral center serving patients from across Saudi Arabia. The role of the KKESH Eye Bank has evolved over time. Historically, KKESH served a broader national distribution role, receiving predominantly imported corneal tissue and supplying tissue to other centers in Saudi Arabia. More recently, several centers have established their own eye-bank services and obtain imported tissue directly according to their clinical needs. The KKESH Eye Bank now primarily supports transplantation within the institution through tissue receipt, storage, allocation, and coordination with surgical services, while maintaining a smaller local procurement pathway. Its role is also evolving toward more systematic and advanced local tissue processing. Although Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK) tissue has been prepared at KKESH for more than two decades, preparation was historically performed largely in the operating room according to individual surgeon preference. In 2025, a transition toward systematic DSAEK tissue processing within the Eye Bank using multiple technologies was initiated. This expansion also includes the development of an accurate, cost-effective laser-based method for local preparation of corneal allogenic intrastromal ring segments (CAIRS), with potential application to patch graft preparation. Femtosecond-laser technology is currently being implemented to further expand local processing capabilities, including CAIRS preparation, Bowman membrane transplantation, and DSAEK tissue preparation.The vulnerability of import-dependent systems has been demonstrated during periods of major disruption. During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, corneal procurement and transplantation rates dropped sharply worldwide. [4] More recently, the regional Middle East conflict beginning in mid-February 2026 disrupted supply chains at KKESH. Closure of major regional airport hubs required alternative shipping routes and adjustments to surgical scheduling. The surgical impact was measurable: in the second and third weeks of March, 100% of available surgical sessions were cancelled. Recovery was gradual, with only 25% of sessions proceeding in the first week of April and capacity fluctuating between 48% and 67% of normal levels in the following weeks. Pre-processed DSAEK and Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) grafts were particularly vulnerable because their procedure-specific preparation limited opportunities for reallocation. In response, pre-cut tissue orders were reduced, processing and surgical timing were adjusted to anticipated delivery, and priority was given to patients who could reach the hospital at short notice. This experience illustrates how quickly disruption in international transport can translate into reduced access to transplantation, even when donor tissue remains available elsewhere.The evolution of corneal surgery has also changed how we think about the donor cornea itself. Historically, penetrating keratoplasty meant one donor for one recipient. Modern lamellar techniques have transformed that model: only the posterior layers are needed for endothelial keratoplasty, while anterior techniques leave posterior tissue untouched. A donor cornea can therefore be viewed as a collection of functional components rather than as a single graft.Studies have shown that multiple stromal lenticules can be prepared from a single donor cornea, meaning one donation can help several patients. [5] Lenticules obtained during small-incision lenticule extraction (SMILE) procedures, once routinely discarded, are being explored for therapeutic applications, including inlay and overlay additive keratoplasty and other ocular surface applications. [6] The uses of corneal tissue extend beyond optical keratoplasty. In glaucoma surgery, gammairradiated corneal tissue can be used for patch grafting over drainage devices. [7,8] Corneal tissue also has tectonic and reconstructive applications in other settings. In some cases, a single donor cornea can serve two patients: the endothelial component for keratoplasty and the remaining tissue as a glaucoma patch graft. [9] The versatility of donor corneal tissue continues to expand. Descemet membrane, harvested from corneas unsuitable for keratoplasty due to low endothelial cell counts or anterior stromal pathology, has been used as an epiretinal graft in patients with refractory full-thickness macular holes, with encouraging rates of anatomical closure and visual recovery. [10] Procedure-specific tissue preparation may reduce flexibility when the intended transplantation cannot proceed as scheduled because of patient-related, clinical, or logistical factors. In such circumstances, successful reallocation depends on identifying another suitable recipient within the remaining preservation window. At KKESH, patient scheduling and confirmation are primarily managed by the clinical services, whereas the Eye Bank coordinates tissue availability, allocation, and preparation with the surgical schedule. When transplantation cannot proceed as planned, the Eye Bank works with the clinical team to identify and contact suitable alternative recipients who can attend within the remaining preservation period. When feasible, surgery may be arranged outside the surgeon's originally allocated operating schedule, provided that both the patient and surgeon are available and agree to proceed. Preservation strategy influences not only tissue viability but also the flexibility with which donor tissue can be allocated and transplanted. Hypothermic storage, commonly used in the United States and for imported tissue received at KKESH, provides a relatively simple preservation pathway but a limited storage window, generally approximately 7-14 days. [3,11,12] This shorter interval requires closer coordination among tissue delivery, recipient readiness, surgeon availability, and operating-room access. Delays or cancellations occurring late in the preservation period may therefore leave less time for successful reallocation.Organ culture, widely used by European eye banks, permits storage for approximately 4 weeks or more and allows microbiological surveillance before tissue release. [3,11,12] This longer preservation window can facilitate tissue allocation, recipient selection, surgical scheduling, and reallocation when an intended procedure cannot proceed. Its principal advantage from a utilization perspective is therefore greater logistical flexibility rather than an increase in the underlying donor supply. However, organ culture requires dedicated infrastructure, controlled incubation and monitoring, microbiological testing, and additional tissue-handling procedures before transplantation. [3,11,12] Thus, the relative advantages of hypothermic storage and organ culture extend beyond endothelial preservation to their effects on eye-bank workflow and the ability of transplantation systems to use available human tissue efficiently.Glycerol-preserved and similarly processed tissues further expand the potential use of tissue that might otherwise expire, particularly in emergency and tectonic settings where optical clarity is not the primary concern. [13] These approaches do not fully replace fresh tissue for optical keratoplasty but can provide additional flexibility during periods of system stress. Tissue stewardship also extends to reducing the need for transplantation when effective alternatives are available. In keratoconus, earlier diagnosis and interventions that preserve or rehabilitate the native cornea may delay or avoid keratoplasty in appropriately selected patients. This represents another dimension of tissue conservation: reserving donor tissue for eyes in which transplantation remains necessary.Looking ahead, biosynthetic implants, xenograft platforms, and gene-edited bioengineered corneas have shown promise and may eventually reduce reliance on human donors for selected indications. [14][15][16] These technologies remain investigational, but they reinforce a broader shift: the future of corneal transplantation will depend as much on innovation in utilization and preservation as on donor recruitment itself.More efficient use of available tissue does not diminish the importance of expanding the donor pool. In import-dependent centers such as KKESH, strengthening local corneal procurement remains a strategic priority. Expanding domestic procurement would improve resilience during supply-chain disruptions while complementing efforts to maximize the value of available tissue.If corneal shortage is partly a problem of access and tissue utilization, the metrics used to evaluate eye-banking and transplantation-system performance should also evolve. Procurement and distribution volumes alone do not fully reflect how effectively available tissue is translated into patient care. Measures such as transplantation rates, appropriate versus potentially avoidable non-utilization, successful tissue reallocation, and use of different components of a donor cornea may provide a more complete picture. Integration of procurement, processing, allocation, surgical scheduling, and clinical outcome data could help identify barriers along this pathway. Practical measures, including coordinated patient readiness, backup-recipient pathways, flexible operating-room access for time-sensitive grafts, and redistribution between eye banks, may further improve utilization of transplant-suitable tissue.The global corneal shortage will not be solved by increasing donation alone. The challenge is to ensure that eye-banking and transplantation systems evolve alongside surgical innovation: preserving tissue longer, using each donor cornea more effectively, anticipating disruptions to planned transplantation, and improving allocation and redistribution. Reducing potentially avoidable tissue non-utilization offers an opportunity to expand access without relying solely on donor recruitment.Contributions: HBH conceived the idea. IA, HD, HBH, MA and RF contributed to the development of the concepts, drafting, and critical revision of the manuscript. All authors approved the final manuscript.

title: Lean Management of Surgical Instruments in Multidisciplinary Collaboration: Practice Research With Multidimensional Evaluation of Cost and Quality
Solarisation of rural primary health centres for reducing healthcare delays in Karnataka India using grounded theory
abstract: The Primary Health Centres (PHCs) are vital for achieving universal health coverage; however, energy poverty remains a critical yet overlooked barrier to the efficiency of primary healthcare services in rural and remote settings. This study explored the community’s perspective on healthcare services before and after solarisation and how it has impacted service availability, healthcare utilisation, and improved health outcomes. We conducted a qualitative study employing the grounded theory methodology in Karnataka, India. Six focus group discussions (FGDs) were conducted among 36 rural community members – 21 women and 15 men. The FGDs were digitally recorded, transcribed and translated into English and analysed using MAXQDA software. A conceptual model was developed using all categories. The findings revealed that solarisation of PHCs acts as a catalyst for reducing healthcare delays. A cascade of better decision-making and improved resource use resulted in actual improvements in service utilisation and care delivery. Key results include faster admission and treatment initiation, a lower risk of complications, and improved patient safety and satisfaction. The use of solar energy in healthcare facilities has increased service quality, accessibility, and community trust, especially in maternal and child health. Solar electrification enhances healthcare quality and community trust, improving service utilisation and health outcomes. Future research should integrate digital health and evaluate cost-effectiveness for scalable, sustainable solar electrification models in rural areas.

title: Failure Analysis, Maintenance Strategies and Models for Enhancing Reliability Performance of Hospital HVAC Systems: A Review
abstract: Heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems are among the most safety-critical infrastructure in hospitals. Beyond thermal comfort, they govern airborne infection control, surgical-suite sterility, isolation-room pressurisation, and the environmental stability of pharmacies, laboratories, and intensive-care units. Because these systems must operate continuously and to tight tolerances, their reliability is inseparable from patient safety and regulatory compliance. Yet the majority of healthcare facilities still rely on reactive or fixed-interval preventive maintenance, which leaves them exposed to unplanned failures, emergency repairs, and compliance drift. Predictive maintenance (PdM)-condition-based intervention driven by real-time sensor data, reliability analytics, and machine learning-offers a route to intervene before functional failure occurs. This review synthesises the literature on hospital HVAC reliability, the evolution of maintenance strategies, reliability-engineering foundations such as reliability-centred maintenance, failure mode and effects analysis, and remaining-useful-life modelling, and enabling technologies including the Internet of Things, digital twins, and data-driven prognostics. Building on this synthesis, the paper proposes a conceptual predictive-maintenance management model that integrates asset criticality analysis, condition monitoring, prognostic decision-making, and computerised-maintenance-management-system and building-management-system workflows into a governance-aware framework tailored to the healthcare context. Reported outcomes from adjacent domains, including substantial reductions in maintenance cost and emergency calls, extended mean time between failures, and improved uptime, suggest that a well-governed predictive-maintenance model can materially enhance reliability performance. The review closes by identifying persistent research gaps, including the scarcity of validated hospital-specific datasets, weak coupling between prognostic outputs and maintenance governance, interpretability limits of opaque models, and cybersecurity and change-management barriers, and outlines a research agenda for their resolution.

title: Leveraging integrated speciality nursing councils to explore new frontiers in nursing practice: A mult council governance model in a hospital network
journal: International Journal of Advance Research in Nursing

title: An Analysis of Adolescents’ Utilization of Reproductive Health Counseling Services in the Adolescent-Friendly Health Services (PKPR) Program
abstract: Adolescent-Friendly Health Services (Pelayanan Kesehatan Peduli Remaja, PKPR) provide counseling to address adolescents’ reproductive health needs. However, program implementation does not necessarily translate into optimal service utilization. This study aimed to examine adolescents’ understanding of reproductive health and their utilization of reproductive health counseling within the PKPR program in the service area of Tanjung Marulak Community Health Center, Tebing Tinggi City, Indonesia. A mixed methods approach involved 92 adolescent respondents and 10 informants. Data were collected through questionnaires, in-depth interviews, observations, and document review. The findings showed that only eight respondents (8.7%) reported having participated in PKPR, while 84 (91.3%) had never participated. Fifty respondents had limited understanding of reproductive health, and 70 had limited understanding of ways to improve reproductive health. Qualitative findings indicated that the program was supported by health personnel who had received PKPR orientation and by collaboration across sectors and health programs. However, the counseling room was shared with nutrition services, educational resources and funding were limited, peer counselors’ roles were underdeveloped, and PKPR-specific standard operating procedures were unavailable. Barriers to service utilization included conflicts between service hours and school activities, confidentiality concerns, and fear of stigma. PKPR participation remained low, alongside limited reproductive health understanding and shortcomings in counseling delivery. The health center should ensure privacy, adapt service hours to adolescents’ needs, strengthen peer counseling and education, and establish program-specific procedures and adequate funding.

title: Healthcare providers’ perceptions of barriers and facilitators to implementation of an acute traumatic brain injury clinical practice guideline: a CFIR-informed qualitative study at a regional referral hospital in Northern Tanzania
abstract: Background: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs), where the burden of injury is disproportionately high, and healthcare resources are often limited. Clinical Practice Guidelines (CPGs) improve the consistency and quality of TBI care by shifting medical decision-making from individual judgement to evidence-based recommendations. The strong link between improved TBI outcomes and CPG adoption has largely been established in high-income country (HIC) hospital settings; evidence on implementing TBI CPGs in LMIC hospital settings is limited. Objective: This study explored healthcare providers' experiences to identify barriers and facilitators to implementing a TBI CPG in the Emergency Department (EMD) at Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Center in Northern Tanzania, guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research 2.0 (CFIR). Methods: We conducted semi-structured in-depth interviews (IDIs) with doctors and nurses who regularly managed TBI patients at the EMD. We purposively sampled participants between June and August 2023. The research team analysed data using thematic content analysis guided by CFIR domains, developing codes and memos iteratively. Results: 7 nurses and 8 doctors with an average of 5 years of experience caring for patients in the EMD completed in-person, in-depth interviews. Most providers reported frequent exposure to TBI cases and regular use of the CPG in routine clinical practice. However, not all participants reported consistent CPG use, highlighting variation in implementation among providers. Key facilitators included strong interprofessional teamwork, readily accessible guideline materials in clinical areas, availability of diagnostic imaging, and perceived improvements in patient outcomes. Barriers to consistent adherence included ICU bed shortages, limited operating theatre capacity, equipment and medication stock-outs, high patient volumes, staffing pressures, and a lack of structured refresher training or formal audit and feedback mechanisms. Variability in procedural confidence, particularly among less experienced providers, also affected implementation consistency. Conclusion: Our findings show that a TBI CPG is well accepted and largely integrated into routine care among experienced providers. However, sustainability depends on strengthening training, mentorship, audit, and feedback systems for CPG use and on addressing system-level resource constraints. Institutional investment in capacity building is essential to ensure consistent and sustained CPG uptake in our setting.

title: Information Technology Helps Achieve Efficient Management of Day Surgery Wards
abstract: Changes in the management of day surgery wards have been driven by information technology. With the help of electronic medical record systems, surgical scheduling software, remote monitoring equipment, etc., the surgical process can be improved, the working efficiency of medical staff will be enhanced, and the waiting time for patients will be reduced. Information technology can organise the medical resources properly and distribute them fairly. An Information Platform can be introduced to improve communication among doctors and patients and enhance the medical services available to the public. Information technology can be used to improve the management efficiency of day surgery wards and enhance the quality of medical services.

title: CARE-Mid: Context-Aware IoT Middleware for Real-Time Resource Management in Smart Environments
journal: EAI Endorsed Transactions on Internet of Things
abstract: Smart settings, such intelligent buildings, campuses, and hospitals, rely on a lot of different IoT devices that are always sending and receiving data and control tasks. Most middleware solutions today only focus on either connection or static service orchestration. They don't know much about the surrounding context, future workload, or Quality-of-Service (QoS) limits. This often results in poor task placement, wasteful cloud offloading, and frequent Service Level Agreement (SLA) violations when traffic is high. This article puts forth CARE-Mid, a context-aware IoT middleware designed for real-time resource management across both edge and cloud levels. CARE-Mid combines four important features: (i) getting semantic context and evaluating Quality-of-Context (QoC), (ii) predicting workload and resource demand based on context, (iii) scheduling multiple objectives that optimise latency, energy, and SLA compliance at the same time, and (iv) adaptive priority control based on current utility and recent violations. The framework is set up as a microservice-based platform on an edge-cloud testbed and tested with a genuine smart-building dataset. Experimental results indicate that, in comparison to a standard baseline middleware, CARE-Mid decreases average end-to-end latency by 20–30%, enhances the deadline-hit rate to around 97%, and minimises SLA violations by over 50% during heavy load conditions. A context-aware hybrid placement technique, on the other hand, uses 20–25% less energy and costs 20–25% less to run than cloud-only execution. Ablation experiments show that context modelling, prediction, and adaptive scheduling all play a big role in these improvements.

title: An Audit of Postanaesthesia Care Units in Selected Hospitals in Southwest Region of Cameroon: A Neglected Threat to Patient Safety
abstract: Background: In perioperative medicine, postanaesthesia recovery is the period immediately following the end of anaesthesia until the patient’s physiological derangements are sufficiently normalised for discharge. Achieving favorable outcomes requires substantial human resources and hospital infrastructure. In this study, we audit selected hospitals in the South-West Region of Cameroon on anaesthesia equipment, staff strength, quality, and the use of standard operating procedures. Materials and methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted in purposively selected hospitals, with data collected using a structured tool. Data were collected on the availability and functionality of equipment, the use of standard operating procedures, and staff strength and quality. The data were summarized and presented using counts and percentages and charts. Results: Thirteen hospitals were selected, out of which five (38.5%) had postanaesthesia care units (PACUs) staffed with nurse anaesthetists, and trained nurse practitioners. Protocols for patient discharge (Aldrete's Score) were used in all the hospitals with recovery rooms. There was no implementation of a formal incident-reporting procedure in 40% of PACUs, and anaesthesia equipment were defective, archaic, or unavailable in all of the selected hospitals. Conclusion: Most hospitals in the South-West Region of Cameroon lack PACUs. They have defective or archaic equipment, non-anesthetist staff, and lack the recommended protocols. All these factors threaten patient safety.

title: Improving Access to Specialty Care: Analysis of Factors Affecting Follow-up Patterns in an Outpatient Academic Pulmonary Clinic
abstract: Prolonged wait times for appointments in pulmonary specialty clinics contribute to worse patient outcomes. We determined the follow-up patterns and factors associated with appointment no-show to identify opportunities to increase appointment availability while improving follow-up. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of patients scheduled from 2017-2019 in the outpatient pulmonary fellows’ clinic of an academic tertiary care hospital. A successful visit was an appointment documented as completed. Appointment-level associations with no-show were evaluated using multivariable logistic generalized estimating equations. Among 1,612 patients, 4,689 appointments were scheduled. After excluding 1,247 cancellations and 6 appointments with indeterminate disposition, 3,436 appointments among 1,479 patients were included in the no-show analysis; 1,461 (42.5%) were no-shows. Average intended and actual follow-up intervals were 11.2 weeks and 24.8 weeks, respectively. In the complete-case adjusted analysis (3,427 appointments among 1,470 patients), substance use disorders (adjusted odds ratios [aORs], 1.86-3.43; P≤.011), inpatient referral (aOR, 2.41; P<.001), and pneumonia (aOR, 2.63; P=.046) were associated with greater odds of no-show. Spanish language (aOR, 0.59; P<.001), charity care (aOR, 0.63; P=.002), and external outpatient referral (aOR, 0.49; P<.001) were associated with lower odds. Emergency department referral and driving distance were not independently associated with no-show. Our clinic had short intended follow-up intervals and a high no-show rate. These appointment-level associations may inform continuity-focused scheduling and targeted attendance support. Standardizing follow-up intervals and using prediction-based overbooking should be prospectively evaluated for effects on access, workflow, and patient experience.

title: On the possibilities and limitations of LLM-based multi-agent systems for multi-criteria decision-making in healthcare operations management
Design and Development of a Medical Appointment and Evaluation Management Model
journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTER SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY E-ISSN

title: Prediction of Radiology Appointment Cancellations Using Machine Learning Models: A Comparison of City and State Hospitals
abstract: Online appointment systems are widely used in healthcare to improve scheduling coordination and facilitate patient access to services.Compared with traditional appointment methods, these systems may reduce administrative workload, support more efficient resource utilization, and improve operational workflow through centralized scheduling and automated processes (4-7).Recent studies have demonstrated that machine learning models can effectively predict radiology appointment no-shows with moderate to high accuracy, typically achieving area under the curve (AUC) values ranging from approximately 0.75 to 0.93 depending on the dataset and clinical context (8-13).However, evidence also suggests that model performance may vary across healthcare settings and often declines when transitioning from retrospective analyses to real-world deployment, highlighting the need for context-specific evaluation and continuous recalibration (8).

title: E-referrals to a general paediatric outpatient service – lessons learned
abstract: Background. Use of electronic patient referral platforms may improve access to specialist paediatric care, but research on its implementation in resource-constrained settings is lacking. Objectives. To characterise the utilisation, participant demographics, clinical conditions and outcome of e-referrals to a South African specialist general paediatric service. Methods. A retrospective review of e-referrals at Tygerberg Hospital’s general paediatric department was performed assessing referral patterns and indications, clinical advice provided and response time (1 April 2020 - 31 March 2022). Results. A total of 579 e-referrals were analysed; referral volumes increased by 50% in the second year. Most e-referrals originated from primary healthcare facilities (355/579, 61.3%) and registered professional nurses (197/355, 55.3%). Children under 5 years of age predominated (375/579, 64.7%), and a quarter of cases were referred after hours. Three-quarters were referred for medical conditions (435/579, 75.5%), most commonly neurological disorders (89/435, 20.4%) and infectious diseases (62/435, 14.3%). E-referral outcomes included: urgent emergency department transfer (92/579, 15.9%); advice for local case management (104/579, 18.0%); outpatient department bookings (132/579, 22.8%); and referral to lower levels of care (63/579, 10.9%). Most e-referrals received a response within <1 hour (444/579, 76.7%). Conclusion. An electronic referral platform supported a large and increasing volume of paediatric referrals, predominantly from nurses in primary care settings. The e-referral platform successfully delivered prompt access to clinical care advice and directed central hospital transfer of urgent cases. E-referral applications present a viable alternative to telephonic referrals in this setting.

title: An iterative column generation-based heuristic approach for brachytherapy patient scheduling with multi-scheduling horizons
abstract: Efficient scheduling of brachytherapy treatment sessions is challenging, particularly because radioactive-source decay can affect treatment duration, while patients with different priorities must be accommodated across multiple scheduling horizons. This paper investigates the brachytherapy patient scheduling problem by determining the precise treatment dose for each patient in each session while accounting for radioactive-source decay and treatment dose limitations. To address this problem, we propose an Iterative Column Generation-based Heuristic (Iterative CGH) that integrates a pre-scheduling strategy and an adaptive dose-bound strategy. The pre-scheduling strategy prevents infeasibility in subsequent horizons by controlling patient allocation in earlier stages, while the adaptive dose-bound strategy provides tighter, horizon-specific dose ranges to ensure treatment continuity and therapeutic effectiveness throughout the treatment process. A mixed-integer programming model is formulated for the single-horizon case, forming the basis of both the restricted master problem and the subproblem within the column generation framework. The restricted master problem selects a set of treatment plans for patients, while the subproblem generates a detailed treatment plan for each patient, including treatment days and doses. A dynamic programming algorithm is developed to solve the subproblem. Extensive computational experiments are conducted under both single- and multiple-horizon scheduling scenarios. Comparisons with a predetermined-dose model and alternative approaches demonstrate that the proposed Iterative CGH substantially improves solution quality, resource utilization, and patient throughput. Furthermore, the iterative multi-horizon framework reduces patient waiting times and increases the total number of treated patients, highlighting its effectiveness in addressing the complex dynamics of brachytherapy scheduling.

title: Adoption of Outpatient Management of Acute Low-Risk Pulmonary Embolism
abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVE: To assess longitudinal outcomes of a multicomponent intervention designed to address key barriers to the outpatient management of low-risk pulmonary embolism (PE), and to define the most appropriate target population and metric for evaluating adoption. METHODS: We implemented a multicomponent intervention in the emergency department (ED) of a quaternary academic medical center. Outcomes were evaluated using the RE-AIM framework, comparing a 3-year preimplementation period (2016-2019) with active implementation (year I), postimplementation (year II), and maintenance (year III) periods. The primary outcome (adoption) was the proportion of low-PESI (≤85) patients discharged from the ED. Following implementation, the charts of all hospitalized low-PESI patients were reviewed to determine reasons for admission. RESULTS: Among 1,810 patients with acute PE, 705 (39.0%) had low-PESI scores. Adoption rose from 5.1% preimplementation to 16.1% (odds ratio [OR] 3.43, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.77 to 6.63), 24.0% (OR 5.98, 95% CI 3.04 to 11.78), and 33.3% (OR 9.24, 95% CI 5.04 to 16.92) in years I to III. There were no recurrent venous thromboembolism or deaths within 30 days of any ED discharge. Bleeding complications were rare (0%-4.3%) and none required hospitalization. Hospitalization decreased primarily among low-PESI patients without Hestia criteria, whereas admission of low-PESI Hestia-positive patients remained relatively constant. Excluding Hestia-positive cases, adoption increased from 9.0% preimplementation to 75% in the maintenance phase. CONCLUSION: In this single-center implementation study, a multicomponent intervention guided by RE-AIM resulted in a sustained increase in outpatient management of low-risk PE. Both the PESI score and Hestia criteria could be incorporated into the definition of the target population and future quality metrics.

title: UNIHAA: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Autonomous Healthcare Appointment Management – From Behavioral Theory to Agentic Action
abstract: Background: No shows are a loss of clinical time, add to waiting lists and break continuity of care. The literature review indicates that the prediction of no-shows is still a significant challenge and reminder and targeted-intervention strategies have been shown to decrease no-shows, but with varying effects depending on the context [25-27]. The new healthcare literature also recognizes agentic and multi-agent AI as the new strategies of coordinated and goal-oriented workflows [1,5]. The aim of UNIHAA was to transcend the passive risk prediction, and to work towards coordinated, transparent and safety-governed action.Methods: We analysed 3,275,731 eligible non-cancelled outpatient visits of Saudi military healthcare facilities in 2021-2025; three records with missing covariate data were not included in the multivariable regression analysis, resulting in N=3,275,728. The empirical analysis looked at the trends of time, the impact of lead time, the variation of facilities and specialties, and history-conscious forecasting. UNIHAA combines the Individual, Clinical, System and Environmental levels of the Integrated Behavioral Access Network (IBAN) with a 10-agent architecture. It consists of history-sensitive risk stratification, LinUCB contextual-bandit intervention selection, dynamic slot recovery, federated multi-site learning, Page-Hinkley concept-drift detection, PPO-based coordination with Centralized Training Decentralized Execution (CTDE), FHIR interoperability, explainable AI, and human oversight.Results: The overall no-show rate in the retrospective study was 22.6% and the historical rate of no-show has decreased from 30.2% in 2021 to 18.7% in 2025. There was a strong association between extended lead times ( >60 days) and non-attendance (adjusted OR 2.47, 95% CI 2.44-2.51). The administrative-only model had an AUC of 0.605, on the complete data set. The development AUC=0.790 (95% CI 0.789-0.791), temporal holdout AUC=0.782, Brier score=0.171, PR-AUC=0.523 and ECE=0.018 were obtained in the companion AALAM analysis of a separate history-eligible cohort (N=672,441). Due to the different cohorts used for evaluation, the AUCs of the two models are descriptive benchmarks and not a same-cohort effect estimate. An assumption-based LinUCB policy simulation projected a 4.2 percentage-point attendance uplift (28,243 additional attended appointments over two years in the modeled cohort), while dynamic overbooking simulation recovered 12.3% of otherwise lost capacity. Federated prediction achieved AUC=0.785 versus 0.790 under centralized pooled training.Conclusions: UNIHAA extends the previously published AALAM empirical study through an original, theory-informed architecture for AI-driven healthcare appointment decisions. Its proposed contributions include hierarchical multi-agent coordination, contextual-bandit intervention selection, reinforcement-learning-based operational optimization, fairness-constrained decision governance, and human oversight. Retrospective predictive findings and simulation-derived operational projections provide a foundation for system design but do not establish the effectiveness of integrated PPO/CTDE coordination or live autonomous deployment. The proposed fairness target of DPR ≤ 1.05 also requires operational validation. UNIHAA therefore contributes a computational decision-support architecture whose effectiveness, safety, and scalability require prospective evaluation.

title: B-162: Quality Improvement: Involvement of Neuropsychology in a Multidisciplinary Pediatric Spinal Differences Clinic
Telehealth as a strategy to build outpatient care resilience during extreme weather
abstract: Abstract Extreme weather events are becoming more frequent and severe, disrupting outpatient care and endangering the health of patients with chronic illness and social vulnerability. Telehealth has the potential to help health systems build resilience during extreme weather, but evidence linking telehealth strategies to specific vulnerabilities and impacts remains fragmented. We conducted a scoping review of 14 studies describing telehealth use during extreme weather events. We mapped telehealth strategies to the system- and patient-level vulnerabilities and impacts they addressed, including chronic disease management, medication access, acute needs triage, and reaching displaced or homebound patients. In every study, telehealth was repurposed from existing infrastructure rather than built for disaster response, functioning as adaptive infrastructure. This mapping identifies actionable pathways for health systems to build resilience in outpatient care to mitigate health risks posed by extreme weather and highlights purpose-built disaster telehealth, integrated into formal preparedness planning, as a significant unmet need.

title: Cost Benefits of an Outpatient Diagnostic Pathway for Low-Risk Transient Ischemic Attack: A Narrative Review
Citizen Satisfaction in e-Health Services: A Social Media Analysis of T¨urkiye’s Centralized Doctor Appointment System
journal: Sakarya University Journal of Computer and Information Sciences
abstract: National e-appointment systems play a critical role in access to healthcare, while users’ experiences with these systems are increasingly reflected in public online discourse. This study examines social media content related to T¨urkiye’s Centralized Doctor Appointment System (CDAS) to characterize sentiment patterns, temporal changes, and prominent themes in online user discourse. Publicly available comments posted on X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube between 1 January 2023 and 21 September 2025 were collected (N = 47,699), of which 34,827 were retained after preprocessing. A Turkish BERT-based sentiment analysis model was used to identify overall sentiment orientations. To evaluate the model’s classification performance on the current CDAS dataset, a random sample of 400 comments was manually labeled and compared with model predictions. This domain-specific validation yielded 85.5% accuracy and Cohen’s κ = 0.776. To examine changes in sentiment over time, change-point analysis was performed on monthly mean sentiment scores, and the pre- and post-break periods were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test and effect-size measures. Overall, 50.2% of comments were classified as positive, 29.4% as negative, and 20.4% as neutral, with a mean sentiment score of 0.19. A structural break was identified around November 2023; the mean sentiment score increased from 0.131 before the break to 0.215 after the break (U = 35, p = .00184), accompanied by a large effect. Finally, BERTopic was applied separately to positive and negative comments to identify the topics shaping favorable and unfavorable discourse. Negative discourse was dominated by appointment unavailability and cancellation problems (86.29%), whereas positive discourse mainly concerned smooth appointment booking and system usability (64.95%) and institutional guidance and standard feedback messages (24.40%). The findings show that social media analytics can serve as a complementary data source for monitoring temporal and thematic patterns in public discourse surrounding national digital appointment services and can provide meaningful indicators for service improvement processes.

title: Analysis Of Outpatient Data Entry Processes On The Quality Of Medical Record Services At Hermina Arcamanik General Hospital
Postoperative anaesthesia follow-up via telemedicine after outpatient surgery: a proof-of-concept study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative anaesthesia visits after inpatient procedures guarantee a comprehensive assessment of the patient's status. As the number of outpatient surgical cases in hospitals increases, more patients are recovering at home. Telemedicine may provide an efficient and effective link between anaesthesiologists and patients at home without restricting their freedom and self-determination. METHODS: After an initial acceptance survey, a single-arm, observational pilot study piloted an optional postoperative anaesthesia visit for patients undergoing outpatient surgery under general anaesthesia. It was implemented using videochats and patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) questionnaires. RESULTS: Of the 300 people initially surveyed in the initial acceptance survey, nearly two-thirds (62.0%) expressed interest in using videochats to contact an anaesthesiologist after discharge. One hundred patients (n = 100) were included in the subsequent observational pilot study. The offer of an optional postoperative visit was used by 65 participants (n = 65, 65%). Videochats were considered a reliable tool for communicating medical issues and perceived as superior to telephone calls. The use of PROM questionnaires was considered meaningful by more than 80% of participants. Sixty-two of the sixty-five participants considered the postoperative anaesthesia visit a useful and beneficial part of the treatment and recovery process. CONCLUSIONS: Postoperative anaesthesia visits via videochat combined with PROM questionnaires after outpatient surgery were successfully piloted and consistently perceived positively by participants. Telemedicine-assisted postoperative anaesthesia visits may be a feasible component of patient-centred care in settings with limited resources. TRIAL REGISTRATION: German Clinical Trials Register; https://drks.de/search/en; registration number: DRKS00028755, registration date: 26th January 2023.

title: Time to Discontinuation and Risk Factors for Outpatient Medical Nutrition Therapy in Primary Care: A Retrospective Cohort Study Using Survival Analysis
journal: Journal of General and Family Medicine
abstract: Background: Medical nutrition therapy (MNT) provided by registered dietitians is effective for managing non-communicable diseases, but patient discontinuation remains common in clinical practice. Studies examining the timing and predictors of MNT discontinuation are limited. This study aimed to identify the timing and patient factors associated with MNT discontinuation in primary care settings. Methods: This single-center retrospective cohort study included patients who initiated outpatient MNT at a primary care clinic between April 2018 and March 2023. Patients aged < 18 years and those with cancer- or malnutrition-related conditions were excluded. Discontinuation was defined as no MNT visit or scheduled appointment within 3 months after the last visit. Patients were followed for up to 24 months through March 2025. Kaplan-Meier analysis estimated continuation rates, and multivariable cause-specific Cox proportional hazards models identified factors associated with discontinuation. Multiple sensitivity analyses were performed. Results: Among 470 patients (median age, 63 years; 59.4% women), 241 (51.3%) discontinued MNT during follow-up. Median time to discontinuation was 15 months (95% confidence interval [CI], 12-21). Continuation rates were 88.3% at 3 months, 70.4% at 6 months, and 43.5% at 24 months. Obesity, dyslipidemia, and medication use were associated with lower discontinuation risk, whereas complications, living with family, and preparation stage of behavior change were associated with higher risk. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the results. Conclusions: MNT continuation declined rapidly within 6 months. Multiple patient factors were associated with discontinuation risk, suggesting the need for early risk identification and individualized support strategies.

title: Equity in access through a digital hospital appointment system: a reflexive thematic analysis of frontline registration staff perspectives in Türkiye
abstract: Introduction: Digital appointment systems increasingly mediate access to healthcare. However, not all individuals benefit equally from these systems, and the experiences of the frontline staff responsible for operating them remain underexplored. This qualitative study examined how hospital registration staff perceive access inequities, exercise discretion when formal procedures fail to meet patients' needs, and understand equality and equity. Methods: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 frontline registration staff working in two public hospitals in Central Anatolia, Türkiye. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, combining semantic and latent interpretation. Coding was conducted primarily in a data-driven manner, while the multidimensional model of access, street-level bureaucracy theory, and a social justice perspective informed the analytical interpretation. Results: The analysis generated five interconnected themes. The findings indicate that formally equal access to the appointment system does not translate into substantively equal opportunities to obtain care. Differences in digital proficiency, social support, transportation access, and temporal flexibility shape patients' ability to navigate the system, while social connections may provide additional informal access advantages. Staff exercise discretion to assist patients when formal procedures prove insufficient. However, such assistance may make access dependent on staff members' willingness and capacity to intervene, as well as on organisational approval and available resources. Support for disadvantaged patients is commonly understood not as an institutional right but as an act of conscience and humanity. Discussion: Overall, the findings reveal a process of conscience-based repair of structurally unequal access: staff attempt to reduce inequities through individual efforts, while the underlying structural conditions remain unchanged. When equitable access is not institutionally guaranteed, responsibility for compensating for these inequalities is partly transferred to frontline staff. Transparent, consistent, and rights-based institutional arrangements are therefore needed to ensure equitable access.

title: Timing of initial post-discharge walk-in bridge clinic visit and outpatient linkage to care in opioid use disorder
abstract: Introduction: Opioid use disorder (OUD) bridge clinics are used as temporary post-discharge “bridges” for OUD treatment after a hospital or emergency department (ED) discharge while patients wait to obtain a regular outpatient provider. The objective of this study was to assess whether earlier initial follow up after discharge in a walk-in based OUD bridge clinic is associated with increased outpatient OUD treatment linkage. Methods: This was a retrospective cohort study of patients (N=165, 66% male) referred to a single walk-in, urgent care center-based OUD bridge clinic within a county safety-net hospital system after hospital or ED discharge. A modified Poisson regression model with a log link and robust standard errors was used to estimate adjusted risk ratios and 95% confidence intervals. Results: There was no significant association between the amount of time until a patient’s first OUD bridge clinic visit after being referred at discharge from the hospital or ED and eventual outpatient treatment linkage (unadjusted RR 1.00; 95% CI: 0.99, 1.01; p=0.84). Discussion: Our study contrasts with previous studies showing that earlier appointments after discharge improve linkage to care in patients with OUD. This may suggest that the walk-in structure of our bridge clinic may attenuate the negative impact of delays to follow-up care by allowing patients to present according to readiness and availability.

title: Reducing diagnostic delays in uninsured patients: Quality improvement evaluation of an expedited cancer workup clinic in a metropolitan safety-net hospital.
Solving operating room scheduling problems using large language model based multi-agent architecture
abstract: Efficient operating room scheduling is a complex task due to the diversity of surgical types, high patient demand, and limited hospital resources. Since OR operations account for a substantial share of hospital costs, effective scheduling solutions are critical. Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems offer new opportunities to support optimization for this problem. This study evaluates an LLM-based multi-agent framework for generating and refining optimization code for OR scheduling. Leveraging iterative collaboration among specialized agents, the proposed iterative multi-agent (IMA) framework consistently outperformed both single-agent and traditional multi-agent baselines. Across 10 LLMs and 35 scenarios, IMA achieved an average feasible schedule rate of 82.91%, compared with 65.59% and 52.53% for the baselines. Experiments on 1050 synthetic cases and three real OR datasets further showed that IMA-generated code produced solutions close to those of expert-written mixed-integer programming models, while a case study of hospital as-is schedules demonstrated improvements in OR utilization and overtime reduction. These results suggest that LLM-based multi-agent systems can provide a practical and effective approach for OR scheduling optimization.

title: EnvSched: Environment-Aware Scheduling for Rollout-Efficient Agent Reinforcement Learning
Collaborative Solutions to Identify Scheduling Barriers for Timely Post-Hospital Discharge Primary Care Follow-Up: A Quality Improvement Initiative
abstract: Background: Post-hospital discharge primary care follow-up visits are associated with lower readmissions but may be underutilized. Limited structured data exist on clinic-, PCP-, and patient-level barriers encountered during scheduling. Methods: We implemented a quality improvement (QI) initiative with hospital operations and scheduling teams. Schedulers used a new in-house Epic SmartForm to document real-time barriers when scheduling post-discharge PCP follow-up. The SmartForm was refined through Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycles to improve usability, barrier classification, and data reliability. SmartForm data were reviewed with interdisciplinary teams to guide scheduling interventions. Results: From August 2022 through October 2024, schedulers documented 13,823 SmartForm notes for 13,420 patients. Barriers were documented in 4,024 notes (29%), with 2,896 barrier notations after excluding "reason not listed." The most common barriers were PCP availability constraints (46%), namely accommodation requests (30%); and patient-related reasons (42%), namely patients feeling the appointment was not needed (12%). These findings informed education on protected post-hospital follow-up slots and targeted outreach to clinic directors and staff. Discussion: Barrier identification gave leadership clearer visibility into why timely post-discharge PCP follow-up was not being scheduled. PCP availability barriers directly informed education on protected follow-up slots and clinic outreach when accommodations were needed. Patient-related barriers suggested a need for stronger communication during discharge planning. Conclusions: Embedding an in-house SmartForm within scheduler workflows and refining it through PDSA cycles enabled structured, real-time capture of scheduling barriers. Schedulers are key contributors to care transitions and systematic monitoring of barriers can support data-driven QI efforts to improve timely post-discharge PCP follow-up.

title: Evaluating administrative workflow efficiency, procedural scheduling, and patient preparation in endoscopic services: a systematic review of primary research involving endoscopy specialists and medical secretaries
Improving Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (POLST) Documentation Through an Age-Friendly Health Systems 4Ms What Matters Workflow in an Outpatient Geriatric Clinic
abstract: Background: Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (POLST) translate treatment preferences into portable medical orders for people with serious illness or advanced frailty.We evaluated POLST documentation after integrating an advance care planning prompt into an Age-Friendly Health Systems 4Ms What Matters workflow in an outpatient geriatric clinic.Methods: This single-center quality improvement project compared aggregate provider data for 2024 and 2025 in a clinic serving approximately 2,000 adults aged 65 years or older.Beginning in January 2025, a standardized electronic health record template incorporated the 4Ms and POLST prompts.Implementation included individual provider training, staff instructions, and quarterly one-to-one provider feedback on all 4Ms measures with encouragement to use the templates.Reported POLST documentation proportions used counts of encounters associated with scanned forms and total encounter denominators.Analyses were descriptive; monthly Provider C percentages were plotted without statistical process control limits.Results: Overall documentation increased from 11.7% (335/2,865) to 26.9% (1,158/4,305), an increase of 15.2 percentage points and approximately 130% relative to baseline.Provider-level proportions increased from 4.8% to 15.9% for Provider A, 7.3% to 10.1% for Provider B, and 21.7% to 61.9% for Provider C. Provider C reached at least 84.5% in each of the final four months of 2025.The investigator's account of his own workflow identified in-visit discussion and form completion as practices warranting further study.Conclusions: An Age-Friendly Health Systems 4Ms What Matters workflow was associated with increased reported encounter-level POLST documentation, with substantial variation among clinicians.The findings support further testing of conversation training and workflow support.This uncontrolled encounter-level evaluation does not establish causality, new form completion, or goal-concordant care.

title: Non-medical drivers of health and pediatric no-show prediction: identifying modifiable risk factors
abstract: BACKGROUND: No-shows to medical appointments contribute to disruptions and inefficiencies in healthcare delivery. While artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML) models are increasingly used to predict no-shows, few have incorporated non-medical drivers of health (NMDOH), particularly in pediatric populations. This study evaluated the inclusion of NMDOH in pediatric AI/ML no-show prediction and identified modifiable factors associated with no-shows. METHODS: A retrospective study was conducted of scheduled pediatric appointments across six general pediatrics clinics during April-August 2024 using electronic health record and NMDOH screening data. A transformer-based AI/ML no-show model was evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC). Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate factors associated with no-show status. RESULTS: Among 7,931 included appointments, 2761 (34.8%) were no-shows. Models with and without NMDOH variables showed similar performance (AUROC 0.708 for both; AUPRC 0.536 vs. 0.535, respectively). Inclusion of patient demographic and insurance variables produced a small improvement in performance, with similar results with and without NMDOH inclusion (AUROC 0.721 and AUPRC 0.542 for both). No-shows were associated with unconfirmed appointments, non-active patient portal status, transportation needs, and housing instability. CONCLUSIONS: NMDOH variables did not significantly change model performance but identified actionable factors associated with no-shows. Prediction models may be most useful when paired with targeted outreach and barrier-reduction strategies. IMPACT: Non-medical drivers of health (NMDOH), including transportation needs and housing instability, as well as appointment confirmation and patient portal activation, were associated with missed pediatric appointments. Inclusion of NMDOH in AI/ML no-show prediction models did not meaningfully change prediction performance. The associations highlight modifiable barriers that can be targeted through clinical and operational interventions. AI-based no-show prediction may be most effective when paired with outreach and barrier-reduction strategies.

title: AI-Driven Healthcare Management and Service Quality: Examining the Effects of Digital Transformation on Patient Satisfaction — A SimulationBased Framework Linking Clinic Operations to SERVQUAL Perceptions
abstract: Hospitals are increasingly turning to AI for appointment scheduling, patient triage and flow and are anticipating more positive outcomes for satisfaction. Will this happen will depend on the impact that changes in operation have on the perceived service quality by patients. This paper proposes and implements a two-layer model, which connects them. The operational layer is a discrete-event simulation of an outpatient clinic executed as a 2³ leveled factorial experiment consisting of 500 simulated days (per scenario) using common random numbers. It assesses 3 different AI interventions: no show prediction and targeted reminders (NS), AI enabled triage (TR), and digital check in with pre-visit intake (DC). The simulated waiting times are transformed into top-box satisfaction through a response model with Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis. The perceptual layer is a SERVLOAD based survey model with PLS estimated and consistent PLS (PLSc). All its inference properties are based on the Monte Carlo simulation of synthetic respondents; no patient data are used or claimed. NS increased mean waiting time by 5.5 min while delivering 10.0 additional patients per session, which was partially mitigated by the NS×DC interaction (−1.32 min), and by DC (−4.5 min). Consequently, the combined system's satisfaction level was located close to zero (+0.3 percentage points; 95% interval between minus 2.1 and plus 2.8), and DC alone increased the satisfaction level of 98% of the draws. TR was significant only at 115% load where it reduced wait time for urgent patients by 2.5 min. Group-wise reminder quota and assisted check-in closed the gap to patients' satisfaction at +1.2 points, but a less accurate model for patients with low digital literacy did so. Within the survey layer, PLS was 9% off the truth for the estimates of the paths, while PLSc was almost unbiased. These small hypothesized effects (β≠¼0.10) required several hundred or more than 1,000 respondents to reach 80% power, far more than are commonly believed to be necessary by the rules of thumb. The study concludes with design guidance for AI based clinics and a patient survey analysis protocol which is ready for use in future surveys.

title: Prediction without intervention: why fifteen years of no-show models have not closed the loop on patient adherence
abstract: Fifty-two published studies since 2010 have modeled which patients will miss which appointments. Ambulatory no-show rates have moved only modestly. This Perspective asks why fifteen years of prediction research has produced so little change in care, and argues that the answer is architectural, not algorithmic. In most health systems, the no-show model, the patient outreach platform, and the clinical risk tool are separate tools run by separate teams. Prediction is now routine, and prediction-guided interventions have reduced no-shows in trials. None of the systems in the studies and reviews examined here sense the full behavioral signal of their own outreach, fuse behavioral prediction into clinical risk, or learn in routine practice from the interventions they deliver. I describe three failures behind this gap: outreach platforms that discard the behavioral data they generate, behavioral and clinical risk models that never exchange a feature, and interventions that are never measured. I then propose three design principles for a closed-loop alternative, and a research agenda to test them. Maternal health, where a missed prenatal visit can mean an unmonitored pregnancy complication, is the motivating case; the principles apply wherever outcomes depend on sustained engagement with care.

title: Strategies to Manage Missed Appointments in Private Physical Therapy: A National Cross-Sectional Study of Use and Perceived Effectiveness
P064 When mind matters: a complex combination of giant cell arteritis, steroids and psychiatric history
abstract: Abstract Introduction Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is a rheumatological emergency requiring prompt recognition and treatment to minimise irreversible complications such as permanent visual loss. Patients typically present via primary care to acute medical teams or directly to ophthalmology with visual symptoms. We describe a patient presenting with evolving visual disturbance whose management was complicated by multimorbidity and a complex past medical history, limiting the use of standard high-dose corticosteroid therapy requiring deviation from the normal treatment pathway. This case highlights the need for an individualised approach with regular multidisciplinary (MDT) input and demonstrates that straightforward conditions may not follow conventional treatment algorithms. Case description A 76-year-old woman with a history of polymyalgia rheumatica, atrial fibrillation, severe major depression and psychosis, requiring sectioning under the Mental Health Act, presented to ophthalmology with sudden vision loss in her right eye. She had experienced increasing fatigue and declining mobility over several weeks. Ophthalmological examination demonstrated right optic disc swelling with a relative afferent pupillary defect. GCA was suspected; oral prednisolone 60mg daily, urgent temporal artery ultrasound (TAUSS) and rheumatology referral were arranged. Blood tests demonstrated a C-reactive protein (CRP) of 13mg/L. TAUSS showed bilateral hypoechoic halo signs with positive compression signs, together with occlusion of the frontal and parietal branches, confirming GCA. Within days, she developed new visual symptoms affecting the left eye with optic disc swelling, requiring admission for intravenous methylprednisolone. Given her psychiatric history and an incidental vertebral fracture, early advice was sought from the local tertiary rheumatology team who supported the use of tocilizumab as a steroid-sparing agent. She received two doses of intravenous tocilizumab 4-weeks apart, before switching to long-term subcutaneous (SC) treatment whilst steroids were tapered. A few weeks into steroids, she developed increasing agitation and medication refusal, requiring covert administration under the Mental Capacity Act (MCA). A cautious but more rapid steroid taper was adopted with close monitoring. Admission exceeded two months, requiring regular psychiatry input. It was complicated by worsening mobility, which prompted CT brain imaging, demonstrating bilateral cerebellar infarcts. This necessitated further therapies input, complicating both treatment and discharge planning. Despite physical and psychiatric decline, she responded well to treatment with intravenous tocilizumab, and her clinical symptoms stabilised and CRP normalised. Discharge planning required careful consideration of suitable administrative methods given her fluctuating mental state and limited social support. Social circumstances created challenges in arranging ongoing treatment. To date, she remains in-patient with uncertain discharge outcomes. Discussion This case outlines a GCA presentation where clinical decisions were shaped by evolving visual symptoms, multimorbidity, psychiatric history and frailty. Steroids were escalated promptly from oral prednisolone to intravenous methylprednisolone when contralateral visual symptoms developed to prevent further ischaemic optic nerve damage. Behavioural disturbance, worsened by admission and high-dose steroids, necessitated covert administration (under MCA) and early steroid-sparing therapy. Prompt escalation to intravenous tocilizumab aimed to reduce steroid-related psychiatric harm and mitigate bone fragility in the context of frailty. Once remission was established, a cautious but rapid steroid taper was initiated alongside tocilizumab. GCA predominantly affects older adults, making steroid-related risks an inherent challenge. BSR guidance recommends assessing glucocorticoid-relevant comorbidities at diagnosis. Although GCA is common, standard management here was constrained by multimorbidity and severe psychiatric vulnerability. The case progression was atypical; visual symptoms progressed rapidly despite high-dose oral prednisolone and initial CRP was low (13mg/dL) despite ultrasound and ophthalmological confirmation. While tocilizumab is typically used in relapsing disease, it is underutilised as an early steroid-sparing agent. Tocilizumab was favoured over methotrexate due to its more rapid onset, stronger evidence base and parenteral route, which was advantageous given covert medication needs and adherence concerns. Early MDT involvement was crucial to guide commencement of tocilizumab and the rapid steroid taper, emphasising the need for individualised management. Given the complexity, early pharmacy and social planning were essential. Several questions arise from this case. While SC delivery is the standard outpatient regimen, the patients fluctuating mental state and limited social support challenged discharge planning, prompting consideration of community support and ongoing intravenous therapy. Furthermore, monitoring on tocilizumab is challenging due to CRP suppression, requiring heavier reliance on clinical symptoms, and whilst this remained easier to assess as an inpatient, we are still yet to see the practicality of this as an outpatient. Key learning points • Two key learning points arise from this case. Firstly, individualised management is essential in elderly, multimorbid patients with GCA, aligning with BSR guidance on baseline steroid assessments. Standard pathways must remain flexible, and early MDT input is vital when evidence-based guidance is limited. Secondly, effective long-term management requires planning beyond the acute phase. IL-6 inhibition suppresses traditional inflammatory markers, necessitating a precise clinical monitoring plan. Furthermore for complex patients, clear communication of the follow up, transport and appointment scheduling, is essential. Ongoing biologic delivery and administration must be carefully coordinated with relevant teams in those who are vulnerable or socially unsupported, with a clear plan established prior to discharge. • Additional discussion relates to optimising existing GCA pathways for high-risk cohorts. Given the recommended steroid prescribing assessment, a formal psychiatric risk assessment should be incorporated into GCA care pathways, particularly for patients with relevant histories to reduce the risk of steroid-induced psychiatric issues in vulnerable patients. Crucially, explicit discussion of mental health side effects must form a routine part of clinical care and drug counselling, so patients and families are fully informed. • Secondly, prolonged hospitalisation exposes elderly patients to high risk of hospital acquired infections, deconditioning and cognitive decline, particularly alongside psychiatric comorbidities. Early, proactive discharge planning should be prioritised, alongside consideration of admission avoidance pathways where appropriate. This may include greater utilisation of outpatient models such as same-day emergency care (SDEC) and coordinated community services to support safe management and reduce prolonged hospital admissions in similar cases. • Finally, a further consideration is whether tocilizumab could be incorporated earlier within pathways, including as a first-line agent in complex patients and those deemed at high-risk of steroid-related complications. This approach would need to be balanced against current guideline recommendations, cost considerations, and the challenges of monitoring disease activity with IL-6 inhibition.
