title: Evaluation Of Recorded Data Leaks Risk Management Electronic Medical Post Implementation Of The Pdp Lawat X Regional Hospital, Kebumen
Bridging Infant Mental Health Screening and Intervention from NICU to Home: A Single-Center Quality Improvement Project
abstract: Having an infant admitted to a NICU increases parental anxiety, depression and traumatic stress, heightens infants' developmental and mental health risk, and may disrupt infant-parent relationships. Early Connections is a dyadic, trauma-informed universal infant mental health program implemented at Children's Hospital Los Angeles. Child-Parent Psychotherapy-informed dyadic psychological intervention is offered during admission in the NICU. The Parent Navigator model utilizes a parent with lived NICU experience to support linkage to early intervention as families transition home. Finally, a psychologist provides infant mental health screening and tiered intervention in the interdisciplinary outpatient Newborn Follow-up Program (NFP), a high-risk infant follow-up clinic. This manuscript describes preliminary findings from a single-center quality improvement project to explore implementation of the program from December 2025 through March 2026. Of the 63 (55.3%) families who met with the NICU psychologist, 88.9% had at least one infant mental health family session and 65.1% had more than one infant mental health session during their child's admission. Of the 66 (57.9%) supported by the parent navigator, 90.9% completed applications for early intervention for their infant; future follow-up will determine the outcome of the application for services. Based on outpatient infant mental health screening conducted with 85 patients (50.5% of those who had appointments), 23.6% of infants and 40.0% of toddlers screened in the NFP were at risk for social-emotional concerns, suggesting there may be a continued need for ongoing screening and intervention following discharge from intensive care. As the needs of families and infants change across inpatient and outpatient medical settings, it is important to offer multiple opportunities to screen needs flexibly and provide tiered intervention.

title: Understanding Cognitive Care Planning: Providers’ Insights on Paper-Based and Digital Tools
journal: Dementia and Geriatric Cognitive Disorders Extra
abstract: Introduction: This study explores healthcare providers’ perceptions and experiences with two tools designed to assist providers in implementing cognitive care planning (CCP): the Alzheimer’s Association Cognitive Impairment Care Planning Toolkit, which is a paper-based tool and BrainCheck Plan, a digital platform. Methods: Semi-structured interviews were carried out with 17 healthcare providers from three medical centers (i.e., each located in an urban, a rural, and suburban setting) and one outpatient clinic in the Pacific Northwest area of the United States. All interviews were conducted from July to December 2023 on Zoom. We analyzed interviews that explored providers’ experiences with and perceptions of anticipated use of digital and paper-based tools to assist in CCP. Inductive analysis was employed. Results: Four major themes and subthemes that characterize the key attributes contributing to the desirability and feasibility of CCP tools for routine use in clinical practice were identified. Major themes included: adaptive features, ready-to-use, patient willingness and feasibility, and infrastructure. Conclusion: The possibility of CCP tools that can be easily integrated into the existing appointment structure and used alongside systems, such as EHRs, are perceived positively. Providers also emphasized the importance of tools that would be well received by older adult patients and their caregivers who may experience distress when dealing with an excess of information and face challenges navigating digital tools.

title: Telepharmacological Consultation for Polypharmacy Management in Primary Care: A Qualitative Study of General Practitioners' Experiences With Cross‐Sectoral Coordination
abstract: The telepharmacological outpatient clinic (TPOC) is a hospital service in which clinical pharmacologists and clinical pharmacists review a patient's full medication regimen and hospital record, then discuss it with the referring general practitioner (GP) by video conference. Seven GPs in the Region of Southern Denmark who had used or been introduced to the service were interviewed to explore how it was used and what prevented wider use. Interviews were semi-structured and analysed thematically. GPs described practices organised around single diagnoses, with no separate pathway for patients who are difficult because they are complex. This was the setting the service entered. Four themes were identified. Whether the service was used depended on integration into existing clinical software. Its value reached past the referred patient, as GPs applied what they had learned to patients never referred. GPs described a coordination gap for patients attending several outpatient clinics, where no clinician held an overview of the whole treatment. They wanted the intensity of the service matched to the complexity of the case. GPs who wanted to refer more often pointed to awareness and time pressure, not to doubts about the service. Uptake appears to depend on workflow integration.

title: Post-Stroke Shoulder Pain: Prevalence and Impact on Physiotherapy Adherence - A Cross-Sectional Study
journal: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
abstract: Background: Post-stroke shoulder pain (PSSP) is a common complication that interferes with recovery and rehabilitation participation. Objectives: To determine the prevalence, onset and severity of post-stroke shoulder pain, and to assess its association with physiotherapy adherence and exercise performance. Methods: A cross-sectional study of 108 stroke patients was conducted. Data on shoulder pain, its impact on daily activities, adherence rate, and exercise performance were analyzed using chi-square tests (p < 0.05). Results: Post-stroke shoulder pain was reported by 51.9% of participants, most commonly developing within 1-3 months post-stroke. Pain was predominantly moderate to severe (89.3%), and significantly affected daily activities (69.6%) and sleep (66.1%). Only sex showed a significant association with shoulder pain (female patients were more likely to develop shoulder pain after stroke compared to males), age, stroke type, stroke onset, and hemiplegic side were not significantly associated with shoulder pain. Physiotherapy adherence was low (34%), mainly due to lack of accompaniment and financial constraints. Shoulder pain was not significantly associated with appointment adherence (p = 0.415); however, pain severity was significantly associated with difficulty performing clinic-based (p = 0.001) and home-based (p = 0.01) exercises. Conclusions: Post-stroke shoulder pain is common. While shoulder pain did not significantly influence physiotherapy appointment adherence, pain intensity was a key determinant of exercise limitations.

title: Patient satisfaction with health care services in Saudi Arabia: a cross-sectional study
journal: Interpersona An International Journal on Personal Relationships

title: Utilization Pattern of General Medicine Services in OPD Department of a Multispecialty Hospital - A Case Study
abstract: Background: Outpatient departments (OPDs) are a key component of hospital service delivery and often serve as the first point of contact for patients seeking healthcare. Understanding patterns of OPD utilization is essential for assessing service demand, planning staffing, and allocating resources effectively. This study examined the utilization pattern of General Medicine and selected subspecialty services in a multispecialty hospital in Kathmandu. Methods: A retrospective descriptive analysis was conducted using routinely available OPD data for three fiscal years: FY 2080/81, FY 2081/82, and FY 2082/83. Data from Internal Medicine, Cardiology, Pulmonology, Endocrinology, and Gastroenterology services were analyzed using frequency and percentage. Results: The total utilization was 34,066, 35,509, and 34,117 visits respectively. Internal Medicine accounted for the largest proportion of visits 37.74%, followed by Gastroenterology 22.21%, Pulmonology 16.17%, Cardiology 12.64%, and Endocrinology 11.24%. General Health Checkup attendance increased from 998 to 1,090 during the study period. Overall utilization remained relatively stable, with a 4.2% increase followed by a 3.9% decrease. The findings indicate substantial demand for medicine-related OPD services and highlight the importance of regular utilization analysis for workforce planning, resource allocation, and improving outpatient service delivery.

title: Short‐Term Outcomes of Two Interventions for Patients With Active Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy in an Urban, Safety‐Net Hospital
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Proliferative diabetic retinopathy carries significant visual morbidity and loss to follow‐up can lead to poorer visual outcomes. This study aims to evaluate the short‐term impact of two systems‐focused clinical initiatives directed toward reducing loss‐to‐follow‐up and increasing pan‐retinal photocoagulation (PRP) rates in patients with active proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) in an urban, safety‐net, teaching‐hospital setting. The introduction of an additional weekly PRP clinic was followed by the creation of an active PDR patient registry with an appointment reminder system. Methods This was a single‐center, observational, retrospective cohort study between December 2022 and May 2024. We established three cohorts of encounters based on the number of eyes with active PDR in sequential order: historical controls (115 encounters) in the 8 months preceding the first intervention, increased provider PRP volume (74 encounters) over the next 4 months, and patient registry with an appointment reminder system in addition to increased provider PRP volume (65 encounters) for the following 4 months. We used linear and generalized linear mixed‐effects models clustered at the patient level. Short‐term process measures included the number of monthly PRP clinics, time to PRP after referral, rates of PRP and full PRP, PRP clinic adherence rate, 3‐month ophthalmology clinic adherence rate, and 3‐month loss‐to‐follow‐up rate. Results The introduction of an additional weekly PRP clinic was associated with a decrease in time from referral to PRP by 37 days ( p < 0.001), increased odds of 3‐month PRP (odds ratio [OR]: 6.53; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 3.03–14.10; p < 0.001) and 3‐month full PRP (OR: 4.66; 95% CI: 2.22–9.78; p < 0.001). Subsequent introduction of a patient registry/appointment reminder system was associated with decreased odds of 3‐month loss‐to‐follow‐up (OR: 0.10; 95% CI: 0.01–0.79; p < 0.05) compared to historical cohort and improved odds of 3‐month ophthalmology clinic adherence (OR: 2.96; 95% CI: 1.18–7.47; p < 0.05) compared to the increased PRP clinic cohort. Conclusions Dedicating additional clinic time for PRP and introducing a high‐risk registry and reminder system were associated with improved access to care, reduced loss‐to‐follow‐up, and increased overall clinic adherence in an urban, safety‐net hospital system. Long‐term visual and functional outcomes of these initiatives are an essential area of future study.

title: From legal entitlement to administrative delivery: A comparative sociolegal analysis of external health care access in custody
journal: International journal of law, crime and justice
abstract: External medical access in custody depends not only on legal entitlement or clinical need, but on whether penal institutions translate those obligations into specific administrative routines. This article examines how written custody-facing policies structure the “last mile” between referral and external care. Using a convergent mixed-methods legal and policy design, the study analyzes public statutes, correctional directives, facility procedures, inspection and ombuds materials, procurement documents, and judicial decisions across four comparative cases: the United States, Canada's federal correctional framework, England and Wales, and Australia. The article develops and applies a Policy Facilitation Index (PFI) to assess five domains: escort duty explicitness, escort authorization and prioritization, scheduling and rebooking, notification and confirmation, and documentation, oversight, and contractual clarity. Scores show substantial cross-jurisdictional variation. England and Wales and Canada score highest, with composite scores of 88 and 85, reflecting more explicit duty allocation, authorization pathways, rebooking expectations, notification practices, and documentation requirements. Australia scores 65, indicating moderate specificity with state and territory variation. The United States scores 47, reflecting fragmented authority across constitutional doctrine, accreditation, local policy, contract design, and litigation. The findings show that external health care access in custody is a problem of penal administrative governance: formal rights become meaningful only when converted into visible, assignable, and reviewable routines. The PFI provides an exploratory framework for comparing how written custody-facing policies specify the administrative pathway to external medical care.

title: Waiting times for inpatient CT after the introduction of a five-level priority system: a retrospective quality-control study in a Swiss tertiary-care centre
journal: Swiss Journal of Radiology and Nuclear Medicine
abstract: Objectives: Inpatient computed tomography (CT) is frequently scheduled on a first-come, first-served basis with fixed slots and remains under-studied relative to emergency and outpatient imaging. We described waiting times for inpatient CT after the introduction of a five-level priority system (P1–P5), with the institutional historical dashboard value reported separately for context. Methods: Single-centre, retrospective quality-control study with a contextual historical comparison in the inpatient CT pathway of a Swiss tertiary-care hospital. A five-level priority system (P1, immediate, to P5, not urgent) was introduced on 1 May 2025. The post-implementation period (1 May to 31 July 2025) was compared with the same calendar window in 2024 as the historical reference. Waiting time was measured as the difference between the request date and the examination date, at calendar-day resolution. The historical dashboard value was reported separately because its measurement definition and inclusion criteria differed from those of the study cohort; placing each priority stratum against it required calibration and was retained only as an exploratory analysis. The ordering of waiting times across strata was assessed by Kruskal–Wallis and Dunn tests, with an urgent (P1–P3) versus non-urgent (P4–P5) contrast. Examinations that were manually accelerated or performed at a fixed time were excluded. Results: Of 1847 examinations screened, 1341 were analysed. Mean waiting time on the measured calendar-day scale was 0.09 days for P1 (n = 11), 0.19 days for P2 (n = 245), 0.49 days for P3 (n = 852), 1.34 days for P4 (n = 214) and 3.00 days for P5 (n = 19); the proportion examined on the same day decreased from 91% for P1 to 5% for P5. Waiting time differed significantly across strata (Kruskal–Wallis p < 0.001), and the urgent strata (P1–P3) waited less than the non-urgent strata (P4–P5) (0.42 vs 1.47 days, difference 1.05 days, p < 0.001). Mean waiting time increased monotonically from P1 to P5. The institutional dashboard reported 1.28 days for the same months in 2024 and 1.06 days in 2025, on its own metric. Conclusions: In this single-centre descriptive evaluation, observed calendar-day intervals increased across the final assigned priority categories from P1 to P5, while same-day examination proportions decreased. The findings describe the post-implementation pattern; they do not establish a causal improvement over the previous scheduling system or demonstrate clinical benefit.

title: Risk factors for inadequate bowel preparation and quality improvement strategies in colonoscopy: a narrative review
abstract: Colonoscopy is the gold-standard screening test for colorectal cancer, yet its diagnostic yield relies heavily on adequate bowel preparation. Despite standard protocols, 20%-30% of procedures still have inadequate cleansing, which lowers adenoma detection, prolongs procedures, increases repeat examinations, and wastes resources. Preparation quality is influenced by multiple interacting factors: patient characteristics (age, comorbidities, medication use, adherence), regimen features (purgative type, dose, split-dose scheduling), and healthcare delivery (education quality, appointment timing). Most previous studies have examined these factors in isolation, leaving a gap in integrated, evidence-based guidance. This narrative review synthesizes current knowledge on determinants of preparation quality, with emphasis on emerging strategies such as risk-stratified protocols, low-volume purgatives, digital health tools (mobile apps, SMS reminders), and AI-based real-time assessment. We aim to provide a practical framework for individualized preparation, thereby improving both the efficiency and quality of colonoscopy-based screening.

title: ORGANISATION OF EARLY INTERVENTION FOR PRETERM INFANTS: EXPERIENCE OF STRUCTURED COORDINATION BETWEEN A FOLLOW-UP CLINIC AND A REHABILITATION DEPARTMENT

title: Patient and healthcare provider satisfaction in the era of electronic health records and electronic medical records: a systematic review
journal: International Journal of Community Medicine and Public Health
abstract: Electronic health records (EHRs) and electronic medical records (EMRs) are now central to clinical practice worldwide, including in low-and middle-income health systems, yet their effect on patient and healthcare provider satisfaction remains uncertain. Objectives to synthesize evidence published between 2015 and 2025 on how EHR and EMR use relates to patient satisfaction, provider satisfaction, patient-provider communication, workflow and burnout, and to identify the factors that shape these outcomes across different health-system contexts. A systematic review of primary studies was conducted by searching PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, MEDLINE and Google Scholar. Studies were eligible if they reported patient or provider satisfaction, communication, quality, workflow or burnout in real-world clinical settings. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. Methodological quality was appraised using the mixed methods appraisal tool (MMAT), version 2018. Thirty-six studies were included and synthesized narratively. Patients generally reported moderate to high satisfaction, particularly in primary care and outpatient settings, citing shorter waiting times and clearer explanations. Provider experience diverged by role: nurses and allied health professionals reported benefits in legibility and coordination, whereas physicians reported documentation burden, workflow disruption and burnout. Usability, training quality and organizational support, rather than adoption itself, were the consistent determinants of satisfaction. Evidence from low-and middle-income settings showed that provider-side efficiency gains did not automatically translate into patient benefit. EHR adoption alone does not improve satisfaction. Investment in usability, role-specific training, documentation relief, and patient-centered communication is required.

title: The Acceptance of Contingency Management as a Stand-alone Treatment for Cocaine Use Disorder in Routine Addiction Care: a Naturalistic Cohort Study
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Contingency management (CM) is currently recommended for cocaine use disorder by international scientific collaborations and public health institutions. This study addresses the gap between the established efficacy of CM and its implementation in routine clinical practice, by examining the acceptance and course of CM as a stand-alone intervention in patients with cocaine use disorder. METHODS: Twenty-nine cocaine-dependent outpatients participated in a naturalistic cohort study and received a 12-week CM intervention. The primary outcome measures were treatment acceptance and treatment retention. Secondary outcomes included cocaine and other substance use, physical and mental health, quality of life, and impulsivity. RESULTS: Of the 355 patients assessed for eligibility, 57 were offered CM and 29 initiated treatment, resulting in an acceptance rate of 50.9%. Participants attended CM for an average of 6.8 weeks and submitted 42% of scheduled urine samples. Among the 17 participants who submitted at least one cocaine-negative urine sample, eight were classified as having a relatively higher level of abstinence based on the median number of cocaine-negative samples (≥15). In this exploratory subgroup, cocaine use decreased significantly from 13.8 days in the four weeks preceding treatment to 0.6 days in the final four weeks of the intervention, alongside significant reductions in depressive and anxiety symptoms. No serious adverse events occurred. CONCLUSIONS: Despite the small sample size and high dropout rate during CM treatment, this study provides a comprehensive overview of the implementation, progression, and acceptance of CM in a complex patient population. Further research is needed to identify factors influencing treatment acceptance and retention, as well as clinical outcomes and predictors of effective participation in CM.

title: Rapid Access in Neurosurgery (RAIN) Clinic: Successes and Challenges
journal: Canadian Journal of Neurological Sciences / Journal Canadien des Sciences Neurologiques
abstract: OBJECTIVES: The Canadian healthcare system faces a critical access block, with neurosurgical wait times reaching a median of 49.9 weeks from referral to treatment. This study evaluates the impact of the Rapid Access in Neurosurgery (RAIN) Clinic, a rapid access ambulatory model on reducing specialist wait times and diverting non-emergent cases from overburdened emergency departments (EDs). METHODS: A prospective analysis was conducted on 2,979 patients referred to the RAIN Clinic at the University Health Network between April 2024 and December 2025. Key metrics included the referral-to-consultation interval, diagnostic distribution, clinical disposition (surgical vs. conservative management) and patient satisfaction. RESULTS: The RAIN Clinic achieved a median referral-to-consultation wait time of 9 days (interquartile range (IQR) 6-15). The most common diagnoses were radiculopathy/myelopathy (41.3%) and brain tumors (13.4%). Clinical disposition data revealed that 79.9% of patients were managed conservatively or discharged to primary care, while 11.7% were triaged directly to elective surgery. Critically, only 0.54% of patients required immediate ED transfer, suggesting the model safely identifies and manages high-acuity patients in an outpatient setting. CONCLUSIONS: The RAIN Clinic serves as a vital pressure valve for the healthcare system, providing a scalable blueprint for reducing ED congestion and specialist bottlenecks. By compressing the assessment timeline from months to days, the model optimizes resource allocation, improves patient throughput, and ensures timely intervention for subacute neurosurgical conditions.

title: Chair Time Is Access Time: Governed Artificial Intelligence, the CLEAR-Dent Framework and the Recovery of Dental Care Capacity for Underserved Americans
journal: IOSR Journal of Business and Management

title: Predictors of readmission in adolescent anorexia nervosa: a 24- month retrospective cohort study
abstract: Abstract Background Why do some adolescents with anorexia nervosa relapse after discharge while others sustain recovery? Up to 45% are readmitted, yet the determinants of readmission remain poorly understood and have rarely been studied in paediatric Southern European cohorts. This study aimed to explore clinical, psychiatric, treatment-related and psychosocial predictors of readmission over 24 months in a Portuguese paediatric cohort, to identify markers for risk-stratified discharge and post-discharge care. Methods Retrospective cohort study of 113 adolescents aged 12–17 years hospitalised for anorexia nervosa (DSM-5-TR criteria) in a public adolescent psychiatry inpatient unit between January 2015 and December 2023. Data were extracted from clinical records. Readmission was defined as any overnight inpatient admission to the unit within 24 months of discharge. Groups were compared using chi-square, Fisher’s exact and Mann–Whitney U tests; Kaplan–Meier analysis with log-rank tests and multivariable Cox regression were used to identify independent predictors of time to readmission. Results Among the cohort (median age 15.0 years; 93.8% female), 39 (34.5%) were readmitted within 24 months, with relapse occurring at a median of four months after discharge and at a markedly low weight (median BMI 13.9 kg/m² at readmission). In multivariable Cox regression, shorter time to readmission was independently predicted by comorbid depression (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 6.45, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.50–27.79), nasogastric tube feeding during the index admission (adjusted HR 3.57, 95% CI 1.83–6.97), and the number of missed outpatient consultations (adjusted HR 1.12 per missed consultation, 95% CI 1.06–1.19), with a dysfunctional family environment showing a borderline association (adjusted HR 2.46, 95% CI 0.98–6.17). Conclusions In this cohort, readmission was associated less with nutritional severity at admission than with affective comorbidity, treatment intensity and post-discharge engagement. Systematic monitoring of outpatient attendance, active treatment of comorbid depression and closer transitional support for patients who required nasogastric feeding are potential targets for relapse prevention; the role of family intervention warrants further study.

title: Evaluating multidisciplinary integrated perinatal mental healthcare versus monodisciplinary care: a multicentre mixed-methods study protocol
abstract: Background Perinatal mental health problems are common and may negatively affect mother and (unborn) child. Given the intersection of psychiatric, obstetric, paediatric and social factors, a multidisciplinary approach is needed. In the Netherlands, multidisciplinary integrated perinatal mental healthcare (MIP) outpatient clinics provide individual treatment plans. Two MIP-models exist, differing in whether healthcare providers provide monodisciplinary or multidisciplinary consultations. To date, the added value of multidisciplinary compared to monodisciplinary approaches is unknown and the optimal model has not yet been identified. Methods This mixed-methods research uses a parallel convergent design to investigate pregnant women 1 up to 32 weeks' gestation who visit MIP-outpatient clinics of 8 hospitals across the Netherlands. Using a quantitative approach, depressive and anxiety symptoms (primary outcome) and neonatal outcomes (secondary outcomes) of current MIP will be evaluated against earlier monodisciplinary care (PROMISES-cohort: GP-care or cognitive behavioural therapy) based on a sample of 167 women. Primary outcome is decrease in psychiatric symptoms (EPDS: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale) at 6 weeks postpartum compared to baseline, analyzed using linear mixed-models. Additionally, maternal and neonatal outcomes, compliance with the agreed-upon treatment plan, and experience with care, of both MIP-models will be evaluated separately and compared exploratively. Also, using a qualitative approach, experiences with care of women, partners, and healthcare providers are explored by thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews. Discussion This research will provide novel quantitative and qualitative data on MIP-outcomes and experiences among pregnant women with mental health problems. The results will offer initial insights into MIP-practices and inform recommendations to improve perinatal mental healthcare.

title: Effect of pre-visit computer-assisted history-taking with a structured copy-ready summary on documentation completeness in screening for inflammatory rheumatic diseases: a randomized pilot study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Clinical encounters in outpatient care are constrained by high demand, limited consultation time, and documentation requirements. Computer-assisted history-taking (CAHT) may improve the structured collection of patient information before consultations and disease screening, but evidence is limited. This randomized pilot study evaluated whether pre-visit CAHT combined with a copy-ready summary increased documentation completeness and assessed patient and physician acceptance. METHODS: MAESTRI was a multicenter, parallel-group, randomized pilot study conducted across rheumatology, dermatology, and orthopedics outpatient services. Adults at increased risk of an underlying inflammatory rheumatic disease (IRD) were randomized to pre-visit CAHT or usual care. Specialty-specific questionnaires generated structured narrative summaries covering predefined screening-relevant items. The primary outcome was documentation completeness, assessed by a blinded reviewer as the percentage of these predefined items present in the final clinical documentation. Secondary and exploratory outcomes included patient and physician acceptance, usability ratings, and free-text feedback. RESULTS: Of 45 screened patients, 43 were randomized and analyzed. The mean age was 54.2 years (SD 14.3), and 29 participants (67.4%) were female. All intervention-group clinical notes contained the generated summary. Overall median documentation completeness was 100.0% (IQR 100.0-100.0) in the intervention group compared with 46.9% (IQR 10.0-68.8) in the control group (p < 0.001), with consistent differences across rheumatology, dermatology, and orthopedics. CAHT acceptance was high among both patients and physicians, with 41 of 43 patients (95.3%) willing to complete and the six responding physicians (100%) willing to offer digital pre-visit questionnaires before future appointments. Qualitative feedback was predominantly positive, with patients reporting that pre-visit questionnaires could improve consultation preparation, support recall of symptoms, and help physicians focus the visit on relevant issues. Some participants emphasized that digital questionnaires should complement, rather than replace, direct physician interaction. CONCLUSIONS: Pre-visit CAHT combined with a structured, copy-ready summary substantially increased the completeness with which predefined screening-relevant information was transferred into clinical documentation while also suggesting high acceptance among both patients and physicians. These findings support further evaluation in a larger trial assessing workflow impact and clinical impact. TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was registered at German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS; ID: DRKS00036519). Date of Registration: 2025-03-31.

title: Paediatric‐Pharmacy Shared Care Improves Access and Efficiency in Developmental Paediatrics
journal: Journal of Paediatrics and Child Health

title: National and state-level analysis of peripheral nerve stimulation reimbursement patterns
abstract: Background: Peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS) is an increasingly utilized neuromodulation therapy for refractory chronic pain. However, physician reimbursement patterns for PNS procedures under Medicare, Medicaid, and other insurers remain poorly characterized. Because Medicaid reimbursement influences provider participation and patient access - particularly among low-income populations - quantifying these differences may highlight barriers to equitable access to neuromodulation. Objective: To quantify interstate variation in Medicaid reimbursement on an absolute basis and relative to Medicare for common PNS procedures, and to analyze national Medicare utilization and payment trends for these procedures. Methods: State-level Medicaid professional fee reimbursement rates for three common PNS CPT codes (64555: percutaneous lead implantation; 64575: open lead implantation; 64590: pulse generator insertion/replacement) as well as CPT 64553 (percutaneous cranial nerve lead implantation) were compared with corresponding 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule rates. Medicaid rates were extracted from publicly available 2026 state fee schedules and analyzed before and after Medicare Wage Index adjustment. Medicaid-to-Medicare Indices (MMI) and reimbursement differentials normalized by work relative value units (wRVUs) were calculated to characterize the size and consistency of this payer gap across states and procedures. Secondary analyses examined national Medicare utilization and payment trends (2013-2024) using the CMS Physician & Other Practitioners by Geography and Service dataset to assess whether reimbursement patterns aligned with changes in procedural demand over time. Results: Median wage-adjusted Medicaid reimbursement was less than Medicare for all four codes: 32.1% for CPT 64555 (facility setting), 27.3% for CPT 64555 (non-facility setting), 14.0% for CPT 64575 (facility), 19.2% for CPT 64590 (facility), 27.3% for CPT 64590 (non-facility), 26.8% for CPT 64553 (facility), and 36.7% for CPT 64553 (non-facility). Reimbursement fell below Medicare parity in 61.7% to 86.5% of evaluated states depending on code and setting. From 2013 to 2024, Medicare utilization trends diverged by procedure: services, providers, and beneficiaries increased substantially for CPT 64555 and CPT 64590, but decreased for CPT 64575 and CPT 64553, even as average standardized payment rose for all four codes. Conclusions: Medicaid reimbursement for common PNS procedures is consistently lower than Medicare, with largest shortfall and interstate variability differing meaningfully by procedure and site of service. These procedure-specific disparities, alongside divergent utilization trends, suggest that targeted reimbursement adjustments may be needed to mitigate access barriers for Medicaid beneficiaries.

title: Integrated Healthcare Administration, Administrative Coordination, and Daily Workflow Management in Health Centers: A Multidisciplinary Review of Best Practices in Nursing, Radiological Technology, and Medical Laboratories
journal: Saudi Journal of Medicine and Public Health
abstract: The increasing complexity of modern healthcare delivery, driven by multimorbidity, specialization, and rising patient expectations, has exposed the limitations of fragmented, siloed operational models in health centers. This narrative review synthesizes contemporary evidence on integrated healthcare administration, administrative coordination, and daily workflow management, with a focused examination of best practices across three critical disciplines: nursing, radiological technology, and medical laboratories. A comprehensive literature search of PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, and Google Scholar was conducted for publications between 2017 and 2026. The review identifies that strategic integration of administrative coordination functions—including master scheduling, referral loop management, and health information management—is essential for achieving the Quintuple Aim of healthcare. Key findings indicate that automation, Lean methodologies, and interoperability-driven workflow engines significantly reduce administrative burden, turnaround times, and error rates. Nursing workflow optimization through virtual care models and command centers enhances care delivery and reduces burnout. Radiology workflow improvements, including decision support and dashboard systems, reduce scan overscan and turnaround times. Laboratory automation and auto-verification systems substantially decrease turnaround times and manual errors. The review concludes that a conscious, system-wide commitment to dissolving interdisciplinary boundaries, supported by structured communication protocols, integrated health information technology, and interprofessional education, is the definitive pathway to operational excellence and patient-centered care.

title: Socioeconomic status and loss to follow-up after orthopedic trauma surgery
abstract: BACKGROUND: Follow-up after surgery is important, to monitor patient recovery and to identify potential complications. Our primary objective was to determine the association between patient socioeconomic status and loss to follow-up after orthopedic trauma surgery. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study of patients aged 18 to 75 years who underwent orthopedic trauma surgery at a trauma centre in Ontario between January 2022 and December 2023. Patient socioeconomic status was determined by linking postal code with Material and Social Deprivation Index and presented as quintiles. We measured clinic follow-up attendance for 6 months after index surgery. We used logistic regression modelling to estimate the association between material deprivation quintiles and loss to follow-up, accounting for baseline patients and perioperative factors. RESULTS: The study cohort included 1764 patients. Approximately 1 in 4 patients missed at least 1 follow-up appointment in the 6 months after surgery. Odds of missed follow-up with no return were 83% higher in patients in the most deprived quintile, compared with patients who were least deprived (odds ratio 1.83, 95% confidence interval 1.09 to 3.08). Younger age and higher American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status score were associated with increased odds of loss to follow-up. Geographic distance to hospital was not independently associated with loss to follow-up. CONCLUSION: Loss to follow-up is common after orthopedic trauma surgery, and the risk is higher in patients who are most socioeconomically disadvantaged. Innovative solutions should address the needs of specific patient groups to optimize patient access to appropriate, timely follow-up after orthopedic trauma surgery.

title: Efficacy and acceptability of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia in adolescents with insomnia and co-morbid mental health conditions: a systematic review; and Brief behavioural treatment for insomnia as a waiting list intervention for adolescents with insomnia and co-occurring mental health difficulties: a single-case experimental design study
Linking Dispense Data to Electronic Health Orders: Tutorial for Querying Commercial Pharmacy Databases to Support Systemwide Quality Improvement
abstract: Background: Assessing medication adherence is central to quality care, yet linking electronic health record (EHR) medication orders to outpatient pharmacy dispense data remains technically complex. Objective: This study aimed to present a generalized, reproducible tutorial for linking EHR medication orders to pharmacy dispense data that can be used to assess medication dispense proportions. Methods: We developed and validated a structured query approach to link EHR medication orders to external pharmacy dispense data using patient identifiers, medication-level identifiers, pharmacy identifiers, and temporal constraints. The tutorial emphasizes key design decisions, including handling multiple triggering events, deduplication across vendors, and managing formulation changes. A retrospective cohort of pediatric acute otitis media encounters (January 1, 2021, to January 1, 2024) was used as an illustrative example. Results: Overall, 98.3% (302/307) of pharmacies in the cohort returned at least 1 dispense record during the study period and were therefore classified as reporting pharmacies. Among 3404 orders, 2616 (76.9%) had a recorded dispense. Conclusions: EHR-integrated pharmacy data provide a feasible, timely proxy for assessing medication adherence. This tutorial provides a scalable framework for linking EHR and pharmacy data for medication adherence studies, while highlighting key methodological considerations for SQL coding.

title: Real-World Sacubitril/Valsartan Adoption and Post-Initiation Dose Reassessment and Titration in Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction: An Explanatory Sequential Mixed-Methods Study from Northern Saudi Arabia
abstract: Background/Objectives: Sacubitril/valsartan is a foundational therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), but real-world implementation extends beyond initiation to laboratory monitoring, follow-up, dose reassessment, and documentation of reasons for sub-target therapy. We evaluated this prescribing pathway in a regional Saudi heart-failure service. Methods: This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study included 296 adults with HFrEF (left ventricular ejection fraction ≤40%) treated at a public referral hospital in Al-Qurayyat, Saudi Arabia, during 2020–2025. Quantitative analyses described active prescription, calendar-period variation, selected physiological caution features among non-users, initiation pathways, early monitoring, follow-up, escalation attempts, and dose status. Fifteen clinicians participated in semi-structured interviews analyzed using the Framework Method and the updated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research; reporting followed COREQ. Results: Sacubitril/valsartan was active in 239/296 patients (80.7%). Among 57 non-users, 41 (71.9%) had at least one selected physiological caution feature. In 221 treated patients with ≥6 months of follow-up, 75.1% completed renal-function/potassium reassessment within 14 days, 67.9% had follow-up within six weeks, and 60.6% had an escalation attempt within 90 days. Current target-dose use was 16.7%, and 21.7% had reached target at any point. Of 116 patients currently receiving 24/26 mg twice daily, 91 had never been documented above the lowest dose, and 25 had previously reached a higher dose. Reasons for current lowest-dose therapy were clinical/physiological in 49, health-system/access-related in 5, patient preference/adherence-related in 4, and undocumented in 58. Qualitative findings emphasized monitoring continuity, explicit role ownership, appointment access, dose availability, and communication. Conclusions: High ARNI uptake did not ensure complete post-initiation dose reassessment and titration. The clearest measurable gap was uncertainty around current lowest-dose therapy when no reason or reassessment plan was documented; this represents a documentation/reassessment gap rather than proof of inappropriate care. Clinical audit should distinguish target-dose attainment, clinically limited sub-target dosing, active titration, return to a lower dose after prior escalation, access-related barriers, patient preference/adherence, and unresolved sub-target therapy.

title: Balancing work and health: A cross-sectional study on the relationship between paid employment and treatment adherence in Dutch people with a chronic condition
abstract: BACKGROUND: People with a chronic condition struggle with treatment adherence. At the same time, a majority of the working-age population with a chronic condition actively participates in the workforce. Having a paid job might affect the ability of people to incorporate treatments into their daily schedule, but it is currently unclear how and to which extent job-related factors affect treatment adherence. METHODS: The Nivel Panel Stronger Together was used to collect self-reported data from 309 individuals with one or more chronic illnesses, who have paid work and use medication. Correlation analysis and univariate and multiple logistic regressions were performed to examine the effects of employment type, contract type, hours of work, extent of both physical and psychological demands, limitations at work, inclusion at work and work-related medication self-efficacy on treatment adherence. For this study, treatment adherence was defined as following the treatment plan as agreed with health professionals, and consisted of adherence to both medication and healthcare appointments. RESULTS: The treatment adherence rate was 56%. Inclusion at work was positively associated with adherence (AOR 1.50, 95% CI 1.00-2.25, p = .049). Also, a relationship between moderate physical job demands and adherence was found (AOR 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.92, p = .026). No significant associations were found between adherence and the other studied variables. CONCLUSIONS: These results imply that the extent to which the working population with a chronic condition is able to adhere to their prescribed treatment, is not affected by practical workplace characteristics. Also, we found no evidence for an effect of self-efficacy, though results warrant further research. Still, working at a workplace where one feels acknowledged and valued improves the likelihood of being adherent, highlighting the importance of fostering an inclusive workforce for individuals with a chronic condition to improve adherence and workability.

title: Healthcare Service Quality among Residents Enrolled in the Resident Medical Insurance Program: Evidence from Primary Healthcare Institutions in Zigong City, China
abstract: This study aimed to examine residents’ expectations and perceptions of service quality in primary healthcare institutions in Zigong City, Sichuan Province, compare expectation–perception gaps across five SERVQUAL dimensions, and explore residents’ experiences and recommendations for improvement using a mixed-methods design. A SERVQUAL-based survey included 400 residents selected through stratified sampling, while semi-structured interviews involved ten residents and one government official. Quantitative data were analyzed with descriptive statistics, paired samples t-tests, and qualitative data through content analysis. 1) The results showed that residents’ overall expectations of healthcare service quality were very high, while their overall perceptions were high. Expectations exceeded perceptions across all five dimensions. 2) Residents’ overall expectations were significantly higher than their perceptions, with statistically significant differences across all five dimensions. Responsiveness exhibited the largest expectation–perception gap, whereas Assurance exhibited the smallest. 3) The interviews helped interpret the main service-quality gaps by highlighting inefficient care-seeking processes, limited doctor–patient communication, and insufficient understanding of insurance policies. Residents proposed improvements in service efficiency, medical equipment, health education, reimbursement procedures, and referral coordination to address these gaps. The findings indicate that primary healthcare institutions performed relatively well on professional competence but require systematic improvements in service responsiveness, communication, and policy transparency.

title: Long‐Term Real‐World Utilization and Continuity Patterns in Injectable Aesthetic Dermatology: A 10‐Year Single‐Center Study
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Injectable aesthetic dermatology increasingly depends on repeated maintenance care, yet long‐term real‐world evidence on utilization and continuity is limited. Aims To characterize long‐term real‐world utilization in injectable aesthetic dermatology, with attention to maintenance cadence, patient‐origin composition, and continuity of care. Methods We retrospectively analyzed outpatient registration and billing records from one center (2015–2024). Geographic origin was an administrative address category, not measured travel burden. Annual visit‐frequency comparisons used patient‐years from 2022 to 2024; retention used index years 2015–2023, with a recent‐window analysis. Patient‐year models used standard errors clustered by patient. Time to second visit was analyzed by Kaplan–Meier and Cox methods, overall and by strictly recorded first‐visit indication proxy. Billing outcomes were exploratory. Results Among 48 798 visits in 29 437 patients, service volume increased, especially in 2023–2024. The proportion with ≥ 2 visits/year rose from 17.6% to 27.2%, with a positive trend after age and sex adjustment. Most patient‐years in each origin group comprised one visit (75.5%–77.2%); adjusted annual count differences were small. Among 25 399 patients with resolvable origin, 29.8% had a second observed visit. Distant nonlocal origin was associated with a lower second‐visit hazard (adjusted HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.78–0.88); proportional hazards were imperfect, so time‐specific estimates are also reported. The origin‐by‐indication interaction was exploratory ( p < 0.001). Recent‐window next‐year retention was 26.0%, 21.9%, and 21.2% in Beijing, nearby nonlocal, and distant nonlocal patient‐years. Conclusion Repeat attendance increased, although single‐visit patient‐years remained common. Geographic origin had modest associations with observed re‐engagement at this center. These descriptive findings may inform prospective evaluation of follow‐up and communication strategies.

title: Patient Navigation Plus mHealth Incentives for Linkage to OUD Care for Adults Who Also Use Methamphetamines
abstract: Importance: Hospitalization is common among people with opioid use disorder (OUD) and is recognized as a reachable moment to start treatment. Methamphetamine use among people with OUD is associated with decreased linkage to postdischarge OUD care. Objective: To determine the feasibility, acceptability, and exploratory clinical outcomes of a pilot randomized clinical trial (RCT) of an adherence-focused mobile health (mHealth) intervention aiming to increase linkage to and retention in outpatient buprenorphine services for patients hospitalized with OUD and methamphetamine use. Design, Setting, and Participants: This single-site, 2-arm pilot RCT was conducted from January 3, 2024, to April 14, 2025, at a single-site, large urban safety net hospital in Seattle, Washington. Patients 18 years or older were eligible if they had initiated buprenorphine for OUD while in the hospital and had used methamphetamine within the past 30 days. Participants were randomized to the mHealth Incentivized Adherence Plus Patient Navigation (MIAPP) intervention or to treatment as usual (TAU). Intervention: The MIAPP intervention combined financial incentives via mHealth-based adherence monitoring with a patient navigator (PN) during the first 30 days after discharge. Main Outcomes and Measures: Feasibility was assessed by meeting the target enrollment of 40 participants and intervention delivery. Acceptability was measured by patient satisfaction ratings on a scale from 0 to 10, with 0 indicating not at all satisfied and 10 indicating extremely satisfied. The main pilot clinical outcome was linkage to outpatient OUD care within 30 days of hospital discharge, defined as medications for OUD being prescribed or dispensed. Other outcomes included retention in buprenorphine treatment and hospital readmissions at 90 days; past 30-day methamphetamine use was measured at the 30-day follow-up visit. Results: The target enrollment of 40 participants (mean [SD] age, 43.4 [12.6] years) was met. Most participants (33 [82.5%]) were male. The intervention was allocated to 20 participants and delivered to 19 (95.0%); 20 participants received TAU. Participants reported being highly satisfied with the PN, with a mean (SD) patient satisfaction rating of 9.9 (0.3). Linkage to OUD care at 30 days occurred in 11 participants (55.0%) in the intervention arm compared with 10 (50.0%) in the TAU arm (risk ratio, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.61-1.99). Conclusions and Relevance: In this pilot RCT of the MIAPP intervention, study procedures were feasible and acceptable. While no difference in linkage rates was noted in this pilot study, larger studies are needed to determine intervention effectiveness. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06027814.

title: Using model-driven techniques for specifying and solving optimisation problems in the healthcare domain: A case study based on the Integrated Healthcare Timetabling Problem
journal: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS)
abstract: Optimisation problems are ubiquitous in healthcare, underlying decision-making in a variety of contexts like resource allocation, scheduling, and treatment planning. However, there is sufficient variation between individual healthcare contexts and their specific associated optimisation problems to make reuse of solutions, and even problem specifications, difficult. Moreover, optimisation problems are typically specified in mathematical terms or in programming code, which is often inaccessible to clinical experts. Model-driven techniques have been used in other fields of engineering to tackle similar problems by providing means to express specifications at an appropriate level of abstraction and in terms suitable for the modelled domain. Therefore, it is promising to explore how far Model-Driven Optimisation can help in the healthcare domain. We do this in the context of the Integrated Healthcare Timetabling Problem, a challenging resource-allocation problem in the healthcare domain presented at the Integrated Healthcare Timetabling Competition 2024. Our solution, based on the Graph-Based (M)ILP Problem Specification tool, uses class diagrams to model domain concepts, the Object Constraint Language to define domain constraints, and Graph Transformation rules to capture available decisions. Such a specification can be translated into a Mixed Integer Linear Programming formulation that can be solved by the off-the-shelf solver Gurobi. Our solution solves all 30 benchmark instances within the original time limit of 10 min , and two of the public instances to optimality with a relaxed time limit, but is not yet as efficient as hand-crafted problem formulations. It also provides a more accessible and flexible problem specification, which we believe can be further improved and automated in future work.

title: Integrating quantitative biometrics and automated risk stratification for ophthalmic surgical triage
abstract: Ophthalmology generates extensive quantitative data from ocular biometry and imaging, yet these device-derived measurements are often separated from medical, social, and utilization data in the electronic health record (EHR). No validated ophthalmic tool currently integrates these streams for real-time, patient-specific perioperative decision support. This mini-review examines how automated EHR-based risk stratification and quantitative ocular biometrics could support perioperative decision-making. Across surgical specialties, cancellation models using demographic, comorbidity, socioeconomic, and appointment-related variables have achieved development areas under the curve (AUC) of 0.75–0.92 with a validation range of 0.70–0.74. When the bundle is paired with targeted care pathways, reduced same-day cancellations have been observed, although bundle designs prevent quantifying the independent contribution of the model. In cataract surgery, Epic's Health Composite Score independently predicts same-day cancellation but provides only limited discrimination, and does not predict operative or postoperative outcomes, which remain more closely associated with ocular complexity and surgeon-related factors. Cataract and glaucoma literature identifies additional candidate predictors of technical complexity, surgical outcomes, and access, including pupil and lens characteristics, axial length, anterior chamber anatomy, prior ocular surgery, angle dimensions, conjunctival imaging, frailty, and social vulnerability. We propose an EHR-integrated framework with endpoint- and procedure-specific models for surgical readiness, technical complexity, and adverse outcomes. Each output should be linked to a defined response, such as patient navigation, anesthesia review, case assignment, operative setting, equipment planning, or intensified postoperative follow-up. Prospective multicenter development should assess whether model-guided interventions improve access, efficiency, and outcomes.

title: (Non)Problematizing patient non-attendance: Staff attitudes towards a predictive model for missed hospital appointments in Denmark
abstract: ABSTRACT Patient non-attendance is a persistent organizational challenge in healthcare, linked to prolonged waiting times, inefficient resource allocation, and disrupted care pathways. Recently, predictive modelling has been proposed as a promising solution to prevent missed appointments. However, little is known about how such technologies are perceived by the staff expected to engage with them. As staff attitudes may influence whether such technologies are adopted or resisted in practice, it is crucial to examine how they perceive its relevance, value, and risks. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork and interviews with physicians, nurses, and medical secretaries in three hospital clinics, this study examines how patient non-attendance is understood and how staff relate to the prospect of implementing predictive modelling to forecast missed appointments. Building on the “What’s the Problem Represented to Be?” approach, the study highlights a misalignment between system and practice level framings of patient non-attendance. Although problematized from organizational and political perspectives, staff experienced missed appointments as a minor and manageable phenomenon. Staff understood non-attendance as contingent and unpredictable, and they worried that the technology would bring new responsibilities, ethical dilemmas, and coordination tasks that may exacerbate existing workloads. However, while the value of predictive modelling appears limited when framed as a tool for operational optimization, it holds greater promise when reframed as an instrument for identifying and supporting vulnerable patients. The study contributes to debates on the sociotechnical implications of predictive analytics by highlighting how problem framing shapes the perceived relevance, legitimacy, and effects of algorithmic interventions in healthcare.

title: AI-supported first consultation preparation in oncology: a real-world clinical usability study
abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) may support clinicians by facilitating information management, but their usability in real-world oncology practice remains understudied. This study evaluated the workflow performance of Artificial Intelligence-based First Consultation Preparation (AI-FCP), generating structured summaries from unstructured clinical documentation, co-created with end users. In a prospective single‑group pre‑post design, nine clinicians completed a person-level baseline, followed by 33 consultations with AI-FCP. Case numbers varied by clinic scheduling and enrollment timing, potentially introducing survivorship bias. Usability was evaluated using validated questionnaires and study-specific instruments. Post AI-FCP, overall perceived workload (NASA-TLX) was 28.9% lower than baseline (Hodges-Lehmann estimate difference −12.3; 95% CI –21.7 to –3.3), with self-reported average time savings of 3.26 min (SD = 2.65) per case. Preparation succeeded in 84.9% of consultations; 63.6% of summaries were complete. These exploratory findings suggest clinicians perceived lower workload and reported improved workflow efficiency with AI-FCP. Further research is needed to determine generalizability.

title: Integrated and Person-Centred Inpatient Mental Health Care in Colombia: A Qualitative Study of Patient and Caregiver Experiences
abstract: Abstract Background Mental health care in Colombia continues to face challenges related to access, fragmentation, and continuity. The University Hospital Fundación Santa Fe de Bogotá developedZona Lavanda, an inpatient mental health unit designed to provide integrated and person-centred care through interdisciplinary coordination, supportive relationships, caregiver involvement, and a therapeutic environment. This study explored how patients and caregivers experienced this model. Methods We conducted a qualitative evaluation based on 13 semi-structured virtual interviews with patients and caregivers who had experienced care inZona Lavanda. Participants were 13–70 years old, and some caregivers provided continuous accompaniment during hospitalization. Interviews explored the physical environment, clinical care, communication, emotional support, caregiver experiences, administrative processes, and continuity after discharge. Interviews were transcribed and analyzed using thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke. The evaluation was conducted as part of institutional quality-improvement activities. Results Five themes were identified. Participants described integrated and relational care as a source of safety and trust, particularly when specialists communicated and a coordinating professional helped connect decisions. Communication, participation in decisions, and respectful treatment supported experiences of dignity and autonomy. Natural light, individual rooms, art, and music were perceived as part of what made the environment therapeutic, although participants also identified limitations related to space, noise, and mechanical restraint. Caregivers were recognized as active partners but reported fatigue, inadequate rest conditions, and limited support for their own needs. Participants also described a contrast between coordinated care inside the unit and greater fragmentation before admission and after discharge, including emergency delays, insurance barriers, difficulties obtaining follow-up care, and out-of-pocket costs. Some described access to this type of care as “almost a privilege” and wanted elements of the model to be adapted elsewhere. Conclusions Patients and caregivers experiencedZona Lavandaas a model in which interdisciplinary coordination, relational care, communication, caregiver involvement, and the physical environment worked together to support person-centred inpatient mental health care. However, integration inside the unit became more fragile when access and continuity depended on administrative, financing, and outpatient arrangements. Strengthening caregiver support and continuity across the care pathway are important areas for future practice and research.

title: Access, Engagement, and Depression and Anxiety Outcomes in an Employer-Sponsored Virtual Behavioral Health Program: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: BackgroundMental health (MH) conditions impose a growing burden on US employers through lost productivity, absenteeism, and downstream medical use.Timely access to MH care remains an unmet need, particularly in underserved and rural communities.Employer-sponsored models that integrate behavioral health with primary care may improve access and outcomes, but evidence is limited. ObjectiveThe primary objective was to describe access to care and engagement among members who completed at least one visit with the virtual MH program at First Stop Health, an integrated employer-sponsored health platform, during 2025.The secondary objective was to describe change in depression and anxiety symptoms among members with clinically elevated baseline symptoms and follow-up assessments. MethodsThis retrospective cohort study included 1,480 members who completed at least one MH visit between January 1 and December 31, 2025 (study cohort), used for all access and engagement analyses.Symptom outcomes were analyzed in a nested outcome cohort (N = 298) with a baseline Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) or Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) score ≥ 10 and at least two assessments on each instrument.Outcomes included time to first visit, visit completion, remission (any post-baseline score < 5), response (≥ 50% decrease and score < 10, or remission), and clinical improvement (≥ five-point decrease, or response or remission). ResultsThe median time from scheduling to first visit was seven days; 54.5% (N = 807) of members were seen within seven days and 82.8% (N = 1,226) within 14 days.Access was similar for the 27.3% (N = 404) of members living in mental health professional shortage areas.Two-thirds (66.0%,N = 977) completed two or more visits.Members using two or more service types had lower dropout after the first visit than those using one (25.7% vs. 39.5%;p < 0.001).In the outcome cohort, remission was achieved by 53.7% (N = 160) on the PHQ-9, 44.0% (N = 131) on the GAD-7, and 60.1% (N = 179) on either instrument, and clinical improvement by 62.1% (N = 185) and 59.1% (N = 176), respectively.Members seen within seven days had numerically higher remission (61.9% vs. 57.4%;p = 0.47) and clinical improvement (76.7% vs. 67.2%;p = 0.09).At the latest assessment, 28.9% (N = 86) were in remission on both instruments. ConclusionsA virtual, integrated employer-sponsored MH program delivered timely access across diverse geographies, including shortage areas, and most members with elevated symptoms improved.Earlier access to care was associated with better outcomes, and use of multiple service types was associated with greater engagement.These findings support embedding virtual behavioral health within integrated employer-sponsored health platforms.

title: The effect of work environment on work-life balance among nurses at Riyadh Hospitals in Saudi Arabia: A Systematic Review
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Reported Health Workforce Stock, Staffing Adequacy, and Reporting Completeness in Somalia: A Secondary Analysis of 2024 DHIS2 Data
abstract: Abstract Background Reliable health workforce information is essential for workforce planning and progress toward universal health coverage, yet evidence from fragile health systems remains limited. This study assessed Somalia’s reported health workforce, subnational distribution, reporting coverage, and attainment of Essential Package of Health Services (EPHS) minimum staffing requirements. Methods A cross-sectional secondary analysis of 2024 Human Resources for Health (HRH) data reported through Somalia’s District Health Information Software 2 (DHIS2) was conducted across Banadir Regional Administration and five Federal Member States. Workforce stock, occupational composition, geographic distribution, reporting coverage, and EPHS staffing adequacy were summarized using frequencies and proportions. Results A total of 10,928 health workers were reported. Nursing personnel constituted the largest occupational group (37.4%), followed by midwifery personnel (13.5%) and community/female health workers (12.7%). Of 771 facilities expected to report HRH data, 527 (68.4%) contributed data. Among reporting facilities, 210 met the applicable EPHS minimum staffing requirement, corresponding to an observed staffing adequacy of 39.8%. Reporting coverage and staffing adequacy varied substantially across administrative areas. Conclusion Somalia’s reported health workforce is characterized by limited staffing capacity, uneven subnational distribution, and incomplete HRH reporting. Strengthening workforce supply and skill mix alongside routine HRH data completeness and quality is essential for reliable workforce planning and EPHS implementation.

title: Anticipatory Attitudes and Emotional Responses of Nurses in the Central Sterile Supply Department towards Prospective Service Outsourcing: A Qualitative Descriptive Study
abstract: Abstract Background The outsourcing of Central Sterile Supply Department (CSSD) services has been increasingly adopted in public hospitals worldwide, yet little is known about how frontline nurses psychologically anticipate this organizational transformation when no outsourcing decision has been announced in their own hospital, even though outsourcing is already in place elsewhere. Understanding nurses' anticipatory attitudes and emotional responses is critical for designing supportive transition strategies and maintaining workforce stability. This study aimed to explore CSSD nurses' anticipatory attitudes and emotional experiences towards the prospect of outsourcing reform in Chinese public hospitals where no outsourcing plan had been announced. Methods This study adopted a qualitative descriptive research design. From June to July 2026, 17 CSSD nurses were recruited from seven tertiary hospitals in Anhui Province where no outsourcing plan had been announced or implemented, although outsourcing had already been adopted in comparable local hospitals and was known to participants through professional networks and peer hospitals. Data were collected through individual semi-structured​ interviews conducted online via Tencent Meeting, using a study information sheet and a semi-structured interview guide. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Reporting followed the COREQ guidelines. Results Four main themes were identified: (1) perceived uncertainty risks of outsourcing; (2) identity threat and emotional experiences; (3) coping strategies and emotional expression; (4) making sense of the prospect of outsourcing: information gaps, institutional contradictions, and a contested professional niche. Twelve subthemes further elaborated on these dynamics. Conclusions CSSD nurses hold no monolithic stance towards outsourcing. Multiple risk perceptions trigger negative emotions and differentiated coping behaviours. Even before any outsourcing decision is announced, nurses already perceive structural contradictions between the public-hospital system and market-driven outsourcing, aggravated by information deficiency. Administrators should establish an outsourcing management framework integrating rights protection and humanistic care. Measures including information transparency, participatory decision-making and phased transition are required to stabilize the nursing workforce and facilitate sustainable development of speciality nursing. Trial registration Not applicable. This study is not a clinical trial.

title: Compliance and barriers of infection prevention and control strategies among healthcare workers in Erbil public hospitals
abstract: Background and objective: Infection prevention and control (IPC) is essential for protecting patient and healthcare worker safety. IPC adherence within a resource-constrained environment, such as Erbil, Iraq, continues to be suboptimal due to multifactorial barriers. The objective of this study was to determine adherence to IPC among healthcare workers (HCWs) and the associated barriers in public hospitals in Erbil. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among healthcare workers between October 2024 and end of May 2025, in five public hospitals in Erbil city. A total of 415 HCWs were surveyed via proportionally allocated convenience sampling, using a validated, pilot-tested questionnaire adapted from a WHO tool. SPSS version 26 was used for data entry and analysis. A p-value ≤0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: Of the total study sample, 14.2% were in full compliance with IPC practices. Nurses carried the greatest burden of human and environmental barriers, including inadequate training, inadequate support from staff, and inadequate equipment availability. Occupation and qualification showed statistically significant associations with compliance (p=0.003 and p=0.013, respectively), with nurses — including infection control nurses — and Master's degree holders showing higher compliance. Lack of manpower, role conflict, lack of experience, lack of IPC training, lack of IPC staff contact, equipment shortage, quality of materials and equipment, and non-compliance of healthcare workers with IPC protocol were significantly reported as barriers. Conclusion: IPC practice among HCWs in Erbil is low, especially among disproportionately exposed nurses. There is an urgent need for routine training, institutional support, better infrastructure, and objective monitoring to strengthen IPC compliance and enhance patient safety.

title: Toxic Leadership and Nurses’ Turnover Intention in a Bangladeshi Healthcare Context: Does Job Satisfaction Play a Role?
abstract: Abstract Background Retaining nurses is a critical health workforce concern, particularly in resource-constrained health systems. Toxic leadership has been linked to adverse workforce outcomes among nurses, but the mechanisms linking toxic leadership behavior to turnover intention may vary across healthcare contexts. This study examined the relationship between toxic leadership behavior and nurses’ turnover intention and investigated whether job satisfaction mediated this relationship in a tertiary public hospital in Bangladesh. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 203 registered nurses selected through simple random sampling. Data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results Toxic leadership behavior was positively related to turnover intention ( β = 0.551, 95% CI [0.425, 0.677], p < .001) and negatively related to job satisfaction ( β = −0.270, 95% CI [−0.416, −0.158], p < .001). Job satisfaction was not significantly associated with turnover intention ( β = −0.072, 95% CI [−0.212, 0.064], p = .304). The indirect effect through job satisfaction was also not significant ( β = 0.020, 95% CI [−0.019, 0.068], p = .357). Conclusions Toxic leadership behavior positively predicted turnover intention and negatively predicted job satisfaction. Job satisfaction did not mediate the relationship between toxic leadership behavior and turnover intention. Alternative mechanisms linking toxic leadership to withdrawal intentions require further investigation.

title: Knowledge and attitudes toward palliative care and their association among nurses and physicians at a secondary referral hospital in Oman: A cross-sectional study
abstract: Background & Aim: Providing comprehensive, holistic care is a fundamental goal of healthcare systems, and palliative care constitutes an essential component of such care. Nurses' and physicians' attitudes may influence the integration of palliative care into routine clinical practice. This study aimed to characterize nurses' and physicians' knowledge of and attitudes toward palliative care, assess the relationship between these variables, and identify factors independently associated with attitudes in a secondary referral hospital in Oman. Methods & Materials: A cross-sectional descriptive correlational study was conducted among 280 nurses and physicians recruited through convenience sampling from clinical departments at Nizwa Hospital, Oman. Data were collected using a demographic questionnaire and the Health Care Providers' Knowledge and Attitude of Palliative Care Questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, nonparametric tests, Spearman's rank-order correlation, and hierarchical multiple linear regression were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 26.0. Results: The mean attitude and knowledge scores were 140.20 ± 13.47 and 18.60 ± 4.11, respectively. Knowledge and attitude scores showed a statistically significant, positive, moderate correlation (rₛ = 0.348, p < 0.001). In the final hierarchical regression model, higher knowledge scores were independently associated with higher attitude scores (β = 0.353, p < 0.001), and the model accounted for 21.0% of the variance in attitude scores. Conclusion: Knowledge was positively and moderately associated with attitudes toward palliative care, and this association persisted after adjustment for the examined variables. These findings may inform educational planning at the study hospital; however, given the cross-sectional design, they do not establish that higher knowledge leads to more favorable attitudes or improved quality of care. The effectiveness of educational programs should be evaluated in intervention studies.

title: Hubungan Motivasi Perawat Dengan Pelaksanaan Discharge Planning Di Ruang Rawat Inap Di RSUD Dr. Rasidin Padang Tahun 2025
abstract: Suboptimal implementation of discharge planning impacts patients. This impact increases the number of readmissions, ultimately resulting in patients having to bear the costs of inpatient care. The purpose of this study was to determine the relationship between nurse motivation and discharge planning implementation in the Inpatient Ward of Dr. Rasidin Padang Regional Hospital in 2025. This research used a quantitative analytical method with a crosssectional design. The study was conducted from May 26 to June 15, 2025, at Dr. Rasidin Regional General Hospital, Padang. The population of nurses in the inpatient unit of Dr. Rasidin Regional General Hospital was 70, with a sample size of 60,. The sampling technique used was total sampling. Data collection used a questionnaire. Data analysis used univariate analysis in the form of frequency distributions and bivariate analysis using statistical tests, namely the ChiSquare test. The results showed that less than half (48.3%) of respondents had incomplete discharge planning implementation. More than half (56.7%) of respondents had poor motivation. There was a significant relationship between motivation and discharge planning implementation in the inpatient unit of Dr. Rasidin Regional General Hospital, Padang, in 2025(pvalue=0,008). The conclusion of this study is that there is a relationship between motivation and discharge planning implementation. It is hoped that it will provide suggestions and information for Dr. Rasidin Padang Hospital to consider and determine policies regarding incomplete discharge planning implementation.

title: Mental Health, Burnout, and Turnover Intention Among Nurses in Conflict-Affected Yemen: A Multicenter Study Across Eight Accessible Governorates
abstract: Background: Yemen’s long-standing armed conflict has decimated the health system and subjected nurses to unprecedented levels of occupational and conflict-related stress. The role of nurses is pivotal, yet little is known about their mental health in Yemen, limiting the evidence available to inform nursing leadership and workforce protection strategies. Methods: A multicenter cross-sectional study was carried out between January and December 2025, involving 800 registered nurses from 24 health facilities across eight conflict-affected Yemeni governorates using a multistage sampling strategy with probability-based selection of facilities and nurses within accessible governorates. Validated Arabic PHQ-9 and GAD-7 questionnaires (cut-off ≥ 10) were used to assess depression and anxiety. Burnout was assessed using a single-item self-rated measure with pilot validation against the Maslach Burnout Inventory emotional exhaustion subscale (r = 0.82), selected for pragmatic feasibility in a highly stressed population. Mixed-effects logistic regression was used to account for clustering at the facility level. Exploratory supplementary analyses examined associations involving self-rated burnout and reported availability of psychological support. Results: 52.0% (95% CI: 48.5–55.5) of nurses experienced moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms, while 47.0% (95% CI: 43.5–50.5) experienced moderate-to-severe anxiety symptoms. High self-rated burnout was prevalent in 34.0% (95% CI: 30.7–37.4), and 54.8% (95% CI: 51.2–58.3) reported their intention to leave within 12 months.
