Psychological distress was independently associated with displacement (AOR = 2.31, 95% CI: 1.68–3.17), workplace violence (AOR = 2.84, 95% CI: 2.03–3.97), inadequate income (AOR = 2.53, 95% CI: 1.80–3.56), nurse-to-patient ratios ≥ 1:20 (AOR = 1.68, 95% CI: 1.07–2.63), and frequent night shifts (AOR = 1.26, 95% CI: 1.17–1.36 per additional shift). Not all expected associations were significant; nurse-to-patient ratios of 1:15, facility type, and type of employment showed no consistent associations. Sampling-weighted prevalence estimates were very similar to the unweighted estimates (absolute differences < 1 percentage point), supporting the robustness of the findings against differential selection probabilities across governorates. Conclusions: Armed conflict and structural workforce stressors were associated with a substantial mental health burden among nurses in southern, central, and eastern governorates in Yemen. Because the most heavily conflict-affected northern governorates were inaccessible for security reasons, the findings are generalizable only to accessible areas, and the direction of difference in burden in inaccessible areas cannot be determined from these data. While the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, the findings identify potential targets for intervention. Mental health support, workplace violence prevention, and safe staffing in nursing leadership and humanitarian workforce strategies may be relevant to workforce resilience strategies in fragile health systems, but these are implications consistent with observed associations rather than evidence of intervention effectiveness. Findings should be interpreted given the cross-sectional design, limited geographical access, and the use of a single-item self-rated burnout measure that does not capture the multidimensional nature of burnout. Future longitudinal studies should include multidimensional burnout instruments and trauma-related assessment.

title: THE INFLUENCE OF DISCIPLINE, NON-PHYSICAL WORK ENVIRONMENT AND CAREER DEVELOPMENT ON NURSES TURNOVER INTENTION AT WULAN WINDY HOSPITAL MEDAN
journal: Journal of Accounting Research Utility Finance and Digital Assets
abstract: The purpose of this study is to determine and analyze the effect of discipline, non-physical work environment, and career development on nurses' turnover intention at Wulan Windy Hospital Medan. This study used a quantitative approach. The population in this study consisted of all nurses at Wulan Windy Hospital Medan, totaling 147 nurses. The sample consisted of 60 respondents who were determined using the sampling technique applied in the study. Data were collected through questionnaires, while data analysis was conducted using multiple linear regression with the assistance of the SPSS program. The results showed that discipline had a significant effect on nurses' turnover intention, the non-physical work environment had a significant effect on nurses' turnover intention, and career development had a positive and significant effect on nurses' turnover intention. The Adjusted R Square value was 0.772 or 77.2%, indicating that discipline, non-physical work environment, and career development were able to explain 77.2% of the variation in turnover intention, while the remaining 22.8% was explained by other factors outside the research model.

title: Occupational heat stress in nurses working in hot environments and wearing personal protective equipment: mechanisms, health and safety implications, and prevention
abstract: Climate change is increasing the frequency, intensity, and duration of extreme heat, while infection prevention and other clinical demands require many nurses to work in personal protective equipment (PPE). Hot environments and PPE use can coexist in emergency departments, intensive care units, infectious disease wards, operating rooms, prehospital services, and other settings in which workload, restricted recovery opportunities, and limited access to hydration may compound thermal strain. This narrative review integrates current evidence on the pathways through which environmental heat, metabolic workload, and PPE-related resistance to heat loss may affect nurses and other healthcare workers. An initial set of 31 references identified by the authors was updated through a PubMed search conducted on 2 September 2026 (three queries covering January 2024 to September 2026, plus one calibration query without date limits). For each cited study, the population, design, main findings, and directness to nurses were extracted, and the evidence was synthesized narratively across four domains: pathways, health and safety implications, risk assessment and monitoring, and prevention. Available studies, mostly of mixed healthcare-worker populations, consistently describe thermal discomfort, sweating, thirst, fatigue, headache, dizziness, and impaired well-being among PPE-exposed healthcare workers; however, nurse-specific longitudinal evidence and direct evidence linking heat strain to occupational injuries or patient-safety events remain limited. Effective prevention therefore requires more than individual coping. Healthcare facilities should combine environmental surveillance, task and PPE-sensitive risk assessment, accessible hydration and cooled recovery areas, work-rest and staffing arrangements, risk-appropriate PPE, personal cooling where feasible, symptom reporting, and emergency response. Future research should prioritize nurse-specific prospective cohorts, standardized exposure and outcome measures that include nurses’ well-being and occupational safety, field-based intervention studies, and implementation outcomes across diverse climates and clinical settings. Integrating occupational heat protection into climate-resilient health-system planning may protect both the nursing workforce and continuity of care.

title: Adherence to the Revised National Malaria Case Management Guidelines Among Healthcare Workers at Mzimba District Hospital in Northern Malawi
abstract: Background: Management of severe malaria among children remains a challenge in sub-Saharan Africa, including Malawi. Therefore, this study examined the adherence to the national malaria case management guidelines among Malawian healthcare workers. Methods: This was a mixed-methods study that used purposive sampling to recruit nurses and clinicians in paediatric and nursery wards. Quantitative data were collected from 33 participants through a clinical observational checklist. Qualitative data were collected from 12 participants through in-depth interviews. Quantitative data were analysed using SPSS version 22.0, and qualitative data were analysed using thematic analysis. Results: The results indicated that 32/33 of the participants effectively treated under-five children with severe malaria, whereas 23/33 of the participants made incorrect diagnoses. Additionally, the general paediatric ward nurses did not appropriately monitor the patients. Most healthcare workers failed to provide adequate health education and follow-up appointments for the discharged children and their guardians due to a shortage of staff, lack of equipment and lack of commitment. Conclusion: The study suggests that there is poor adherence to the national malaria guidelines on the management of children with severe malaria.

title: Hospital workflow compliance and timeliness of inpatient medical record return: Evidence from a cross-sectional study in indonesia
abstract: Introduction: Timely return of inpatient medical records is essential for continuity of care, hospital reporting, coding, insurance claims, and administrative efficiency. This study aimed to examine factors associated with timely inpatient medical-record return at Andi Makkasau Regional Hospital, Parepare, Indonesia. Research Methodology: A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted among 40 nurses working afternoon and night shifts, selected using total sampling. Data were collected using questionnaires and observation checklists. Staff attitude, workload, and compliance with standard operating procedures (SOPs) were examined in relation to timely record return using Chi-square analysis. Results: Of 40 respondents, 16 (40.0%) returned inpatient medical records on time, whereas 24 (60.0%) did not. Staff attitude was not significantly associated with timeliness (*p*=0.638), nor was workload (*p*=0.681). In contrast, SOP compliance showed a significant association (*p*<0.001). Among respondents with good SOP compliance, 14 of 21 returned records on time, compared with 2 of 19 among those with poor compliance, corresponding to a calculated crude OR of 17.00 (95% CI: 3.03–95.26). Conclusion: SOP compliance was the principal factor associated with timely inpatient medical-record return. Strengthening procedural adherence, routine monitoring, and documentation accountability may improve medical-record workflow and hospital service efficiency. Keywords: health personnel; medical records; patient discharge; standard operating procedures; workload

title: What makes continuing professional development clinically useful for nurses? A qualitative study across primary and hospital care in Spain
abstract: Abstract Background Continuing professional development is essential for maintaining nursing competence, but completing accredited education does not necessarily ensure clinically relevant or transferable learning. This study explored the characteristics nurses consider necessary for continuing professional development to be clinically relevant, credible, accessible, and applicable, and examined similarities and differences between primary and hospital care, using diabetes and ostomy care as clinical reference contexts. Methods A qualitative descriptive–interpretive study was conducted with 28 nurses from nine Spanish autonomous communities: 11 worked in primary care and 17 in hospital settings. Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews between January and June 2024. Purposive maximum-variation sampling included different age groups, professional experience levels, care settings, and generalist or expert profiles. Data were examined using thematic and comparative analyses. Results Five interrelated themes were identified: continuing professional development as a negotiated professional responsibility; the disconnect between credentialing and clinically meaningful learning; contextual alignment; credibility; and adaptive educational architecture. Nurses across settings valued current evidence, nursing-relevant content, competent educators, practical learning, accessibility, and organizational support. Primary care nurses prioritized broad, concise, and immediately retrievable resources, whereas hospital nurses emphasized specialized knowledge, procedures, devices, simulation, and supervised practice. Online education increased flexibility and geographic access but could facilitate superficial completion when poorly designed. Blended education was valued for connecting theoretical preparation with experiential learning. Conclusions Clinically useful continuing professional development depends less on accreditation or modality alone than on the alignment of content with clinical needs, care context, credible evidence, educational design, and organizational conditions. Programs should be differentiated by setting and professional trajectory, include meaningful competency assessment, and be supported through protected learning time and opportunities to apply learning in practice.

title: The Relationship Between Nurses' Knowledge Level and Compliance with Patient Safety Implementation in the Outpatient Unit of Grandmed Hospital, Lubuk Pakam
abstract: Patient safety has become a critical concern in the global healthcare sector due to the relatively high incidence of medical errors in hospitals. Although patient safety programs have been implemented, challenges remain in their practical application. Despite previous socialization and training, incidents such as patient injuries, fall risks, medication errors, and inaccurate patient handover delegation continue to occur, indicating that the implementation of patient safety principles is not yet optimal. This study aimed to determine the relationship between nurses' knowledge level and compliance with patient safety implementation. This study employed a quantitative method with a cross-sectional design. The sampling technique used was total sampling, involving 25 nurses as respondents. The results showed that the majority of respondents were female nurses (72.0%), with the largest age group ranging from 31–40 years (44.0%). Most nurses had a good level of knowledge (80.0%) and demonstrated good compliance with patient safety implementation (84.0%). The Chi-square test indicated a significant relationship between nurses' knowledge level and compliance with patient safety implementation (p-value = 0.000). It can be concluded that adequate knowledge plays an important role in improving nurses' compliance with patient safety practices.

title: Effectiveness of a Video-Assisted Programme on Alcohol-Related Knowledge and Behaviour Regarding Excessive Alcohol Use among Nurses Working in a De-Addiction Centre and Hospital in Sri Ganganagar, Rajasthan: A Pilot Study
journal: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
abstract: Background: Excessive alcohol use is a public health concern associated with physical illness, psychological difficulties, injuries and social consequences. Nurses play an important role in recognizing alcohol-related problems, providing appropriate health education and facilitating referral and treatment. Structured audiovisual education may be useful for improving nurses' knowledge and professional responses to alcohol-related problems. Aim: To evaluate the effectiveness of a video-assisted educational programme on the prespecified alcohol-related outcome among nurses working in a de-addiction centre and hospital in Sri Ganganagar, Rajasthan. Methods: A quantitative, one-group pre-test-post-test pre-experimental design is proposed for this pilot study. The planned sample comprises 100 nurses working in selected healthcare settings. The intervention consists of a structured video-assisted educational programme addressing excessive alcohol use and its relevant health and professional implications. A suitable structured assessment instrument is used before and after the intervention. Descriptive statistics, a paired-samples t-test and a non-parametric sensitivity analysis are proposed. Results: In a simulated dataset of 100 paired observations, the mean knowledge score increased from 12.50 ± 3.01 to 15.82 ± 3.25 on a 20-point scale. The mean paired difference was 3.32 points (95% CI: 2.81-3.83), with t (99) = 12.98, p < .001, and Cohen's dx = 1.30. Conclusion: A video-assisted educational programme can be evaluated using paired outcome measurements and appropriate statistical methods. The findings shows the effectiveness of the programme in the participating nurses.

title: Assessment of the Impact of Training of Health Care Workers in Nigeria: The Role of Nurses Towards Effective Health Care Delivery
journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF HEALTH AND PHARMACEUTICAL RESEARCH

title: Charting the future: A multi-setting medical chart study of advance care planning in Parkinson's disease and atypical Parkinsonism
abstract: BackgroundAdvance Care Planning (ACP) enables people with progressive diseases to document and communicate future treatment preferences. For Parkinson's disease (PD) and atypical parkinsonism (AP), ACP is particularly important because of disease complexity, symptom burden, the progressive nature of the disease, and cognitive decline, yet its implementation across care settings remains unclear.MethodsWe conducted a medical chart review of 189 deceased patients with PD or AP who died in nursing homes (n = 91), hospitals (n = 58), or at home (n = 40) in the Netherlands. For patients who died at home, data were obtained from their general practice records. Data on treatment preferences, care discussions and palliative care goals were extracted at one year and six weeks before death.ResultsDocumentation of treatment preferences increased towards death but differed markedly between settings. Nursing homes recorded resuscitation and ICU limitations early and comprehensively, whereas hospitals made major updates only in the final weeks of life. In general practices, ACP documentation was limited. Nursing homes and hospitals more frequently addressed disease-specific scenarios, palliative sedation and end-of-life issues, while general practices more often reported preferred place of death and euthanasia. Palliative care goals in nursing homes covered all domains, while in hospitals and general practices they mainly related to physical aspects.ConclusionACP remains inconsistently documented and frequently delayed until the final weeks of life, when crises or cognitive decline may hinder meaningful participation. Earlier, iterative ACP-supported by clinician training, PD-specific guidance, and system-level measures such as ACP prompts in electronic medical records-could foster a more proactive and person-centered palliative approach aligned with patient values throughout the disease trajectory.

title: Analysing the Concepts of Hospital and Illness in Illustrated Children’s Books Prepared for Children Between the Ages of Three and Six
Gender and Age Diversity Management as Drivers of Organisational Effectiveness in Public Health Institutions: Evidence from Ondo State, Nigeria
journal: Journal of Economics Finance and Management Studies
abstract: This paper examines two dimensions of workforce diversity management gender diversity management and age diversity management and their relationship with organisational effectiveness in selected public health institutions in Ondo State, Nigeria. The paper is anchored on Social Identity Theory and the Resource-Based View, which jointly explain how workforce differences can either fragment or strengthen institutional performance depending on how they are managed. A descriptive cross-sectional survey design was adopted across Federal Medical Centre, Owo; Federal University of Technology Akure Teaching Hospital, Akure; and University of Medical Sciences Teaching Hospital, Ondo. Using an illustrative accessible population of 245 employees, a sample of 152 was derived through the Taro Yamane (1967) formula at a five per cent margin of error. A structured instrument measuring gender diversity management, age diversity management and organisational effectiveness was analysed, for methodological demonstration, using a reproducible, transparently disclosed synthetic dataset of 152 cases, generating frequency, percentage, mean and standard deviation statistics. Gender diversity management recorded a favourable grand mean (M = 3.604, SD = 0.639), driven by fair access to leadership, non-retaliatory complaint handling and development opportunity, while fair work assignment and scheduling remained comparatively uncertain. Age diversity management was similarly favourable (M = 3.545, SD = 0.688), anchored in intergenerational respect and competence-based career progression, though recruitment fairness and protection from age stereotyping attracted more moderate ratings. Organisational effectiveness was rated favourably overall (M = 3.570, SD = 0.559), with responsiveness to stakeholders and organisational learning outperforming consistent goal attainment. The results suggest that gender and age diversity management are perceived as relevant contributors to organisational effectiveness in Nigerian public hospitals, but that fairness must be visible in routine, day-to-day practice scheduling, assignment and recruitment and not only in formal policy statements. Because the dataset is synthetic, the paper draws no causal or field-validated conclusions; it is offered as a conceptual and methodological template requiring authentic field replication.

title: Unraveling the Antecedents of Job Satisfaction and Turnover Intention Among Private Hospital Nurses in Nepal: A PLS-SEM Mediation Analysis of Work Environment, Salary, Job Enrichment, and Job Stress
journal: Quest Journal of Management and Social Sciences
abstract: Background: Nurses play a critical role in delivering healthcare services, and their job satisfaction can influence their motivation, commitment, and intention to remain in an organization. However, challenging work environments, inadequate salaries, limited opportunities for career development, job stress, and difficulties in maintaining work-life balance may negatively affect nurses' job satisfaction and increase their intention to leave. Purpose: The purpose of this research is to study the factors influencing job satisfaction and turnover intention among nurses of private hospitals in Kathmandu valley. Design/methodology/approach: The research design utilized in this study is explanatory. A total of 400 nurses were questioned using a structured questionnaire as part of a purposive sampling study, and KOBO Toolbox was utilized to collect data. Both inferential and descriptive statistics were used to assess the data. Smart PLS software was utilized to investigate the associations between variables using SEM. Findings: Study reveals that work environment, salary, job enrichment, and job stress have significant relationship with job satisfaction. Job satisfaction mediates a role between these factors and turnover intention. Majority of respondents face the challenge of work-life balance, lack of career development opportunities, job security and low salary which can be solved by providing flexible working hours, sufficient salary, career development opportunities, paying attention to employee happiness, etc. Conclusion: The findings of this study demonstrate that employees are more content when they work in a friendly and positive environment with opportunities for growth. Moreover, employment satisfaction promotes a safe working environment.

title: Burnout among Healthcare Professionals: A Review of Prevalence, Contributing Factors, and Organizational Interventions
journal: International journal of medical and health research.
abstract: Burnout among healthcare professionals has become a major occupational health concern because of its implications for workforce well-being, patient safety, healthcare quality, and organizational sustainability. Healthcare workers frequently operate in demanding environments characterized by high workloads, emotional exhaustion, staffing shortages, administrative pressures, shift work, and sustained exposure to suffering and death. This review examines the prevalence of burnout among healthcare professionals, its principal contributing factors, its consequences for individuals and healthcare organizations, and the effectiveness of organizational interventions designed to prevent and mitigate its effects. The review synthesizes evidence from existing research on physicians, nurses, allied health professionals, and other healthcare workers, drawing attention to differences across professional groups, healthcare settings, measurement instruments, and geographical contexts. The literature indicates that burnout is widespread, although reported prevalence varies considerably according to the definition, assessment tool, population, and study period. Workload intensity, inadequate staffing, limited autonomy, poor leadership, insufficient recovery time, moral distress, and organizational injustice emerge as important contributors. Burnout is associated with reduced job satisfaction, absenteeism, turnover intentions, impaired professional functioning, and concerns regarding patient safety and quality of care. Evidence suggests that organizational interventions addressing working conditions, staffing, scheduling, leadership, teamwork, and employee participation are essential for sustainable improvement. Individual approaches, including mindfulness, resilience training, and psychological support, may provide additional benefits but cannot independently resolve structural workplace problems. The review concludes that healthcare organizations should adopt integrated, evidence-informed strategies that combine prevention, early identification, supportive leadership, and continuous evaluation. Addressing burnout requires treating professional well-being as a core organizational responsibility rather than solely an individual obligation.

title: Gestão Hospitalar: desafios e estratégias para a qualidade da assistência à saúde
authors: Ana Lúcia Pereira dos Santos Barbirato
Renata Cristina Correia da Silva Amorim
abstract: Hospital management plays a fundamental role in the organization and functioning of healthcare institutions, as it coordinates the human, financial, technological, and material resources necessary for the provision of safe, high-quality care. This article is a literature review that aimed to describe the key components of hospital management and their contributions to the quality and efficiency of healthcare institutions. Results: Hospital management should be understood as a strategic, dynamic process oriented toward the quality of care. Conclusion: Effective hospital management requires an integrated approach, in which strategic planning, participatory leadership, the valuing of nursing staff, and patient safety are considered interdependent components. In this way, hospital management can establish itself as an instrument for institutional transformation, one committed not only to the sustainability of services but also to human dignity and the effectiveness of healthcare.

title: Intensive care staff perception of medical clowns to an adult intensive care unit: a before-and-after study
Are patient safety structures associated with safety culture in healthcare facilities?
Differences in information acquisition from electronic medical records between nursing students and nurses: An eye-tracking study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Understanding how nursing students and nurses acquire information from electronic medical records (EMRs) is essential for clinical reasoning development in nursing education. However, most studies on information acquisition in nursing have focused on physiological indicators in crisis situations. Moreover, reliance on self-report approaches limits the capture of reasoning that is difficult to verbalise and information attended to in information-rich clinical environments. AIM: To identify differences in information acquisition from the EMR between nursing students and nurses, using eye-tracking and high-dimensional data analysis. METHODS: In this exploratory cross-sectional study, 20 students and 20 nurses were recruited from one hospital and two nursing universities in Japan. Eye-tracking data were collected while reviewing the EMR of a patient with heart failure. Viewer numbers and viewing time across 15 EMR sections were compared between groups. Fixation durations of 4118 areas of interest (AOIs) were analysed using a kick-one-out-based variable selection method to identify differences in records consulted and information attended to. RESULTS: Data from 18 students and 20 nurses were analysed. Fewer students than nurses viewed treatment-related EMR sections, and students spent less time on them. A total of 111 AOIs were identified. AOIs characterising students were primarily derived from nurse-documented assessments, care plans and screening scores, reflecting daily-life and psychosocial information. In contrast, AOIs characterising nurses were mainly derived from physician documentation and orders, reflecting information related to disease severity and treatment management. CONCLUSION: Nursing students and nurses differ in information acquired from the EMR. Educational interventions should support students in integrating perspectives on disease severity, treatment response and patients' daily lives. These findings also suggest that students' reliance on others' judgements and explicit criteria may reflect an imitative stage in the development of clinical reasoning, supporting education tailored to students' readiness.

title: Exploring implementation of clinical practice guidelines in burn care among nurses in emergency and critical care departments: a mixed methods study
Hopelessness among Healthcare Workers during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Experiences and Perceptions
Injection safety knowledge and practice among nurses working in medical centers in Kosovo
abstract: Assessing nurses’ knowledge and practices about injection safety is important to prevent healthcare-associated infections and the transmission of bloodborne pathogens among patients and healthcare workers. Understanding current practices in medical centres can help identify gaps in infection prevention and control. However, limited studies evaluating these variables particularly among nurses in Kosovo. This study aimed to assess knowledge and practices regarding injection safety among nurses working in medical centres in Kosovo. A cross-sectional study was conducted across medical centres in Kosovo from 5 to 31 January 2025, involving 189 healthcare professionals. Data were collected using an electronic questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests to describe the study variables and identify factors associated with injection safety knowledge and practices. The findings showed that the majority of nurses (81%) had good knowledge of injection safety, particularly regarding the risks of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and hepatitis B virus (HBV) transmission associated with unsafe practices. However, adherence to safe practices remained a concern, as only 31.1% of participants reported following safe practices regarding needle recapping after injection. Statistically significant associations were found between years of professional experience, gender, and educational level and nurses’ knowledge and practices regarding injection safety. Although most nurses demonstrated good knowledge, the findings highlight a gap between knowledge and practice. Therefore, regular training sessions, practical workshops, and the implementation of facility-level protocols aligned with national policies are recommended to strengthen adherence to injection safety standards. These measures can help improve patient and healthcare worker safety in medical centres across Kosovo. This study has international relevance by providing evidence on knowledge and injection safety practices, offering insights for infection prevention strategies, nursing education, and patient safety policies in healthcare settings worldwide. Keywords: Infection prevention and control, injection safety, knowledge, nurses, nursing practice

title: Advanced practice provider integration into the pediatric hospital medicine workforce
abstract: As Pediatric Hospital Medicine (PHM) programs confront increasing clinical demands, workforce shortages, Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education changes affecting resident coverage, and concerns about physician burnout, there is growing demand to incorporate advanced practice providers (APPs) into staffing models. Despite growing utilization, physicians lack a universal understanding of APP education, training, and scope of practice. No widely adopted frameworks exist for hiring, integrating, and sustaining APPs on PHM teams. Here, we outline a practical framework for PHM leaders seeking to incorporate APPs into inpatient staffing models while maintaining high-quality, sustainable pediatric care.

title: A FOCUS-PDCA quality improvement model involving unlicensed assistive personnel for improving clinical effectiveness and efficiency in inpatient physical examination: a quasi-experimental, historical-control study
abstract: The accuracy and efficiency of inpatient examinations depend on a well-collaborated working team that involves doctors, nurses, and unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP). This study aimed to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and efficiency of a FOCUS-PDCA quality improvement model involving UAP in improving inpatient physical examinations. A quasi-experimental, historical-control before-and-after study was conducted among 372 patients who received the FOCUS-PDCA quality improvement examination management (the observation group) and another 385 patients under normal management (the control group). Clinical effectiveness and efficiency were compared between the two groups. Compared to the control group, the FOCUS-PDCA group had significantly lower rates of defect examinations (19.6% vs. 44.7%, p < 0.01), nursing interruption events (14.5% vs. 26.4%, p < 0.01), and nurse referral events (6.1% vs. 24.7%, p < 0.01). Furthermore, the FOCUS-PDCA group had higher patient satisfaction (9.04 ± 0.82 vs. 8.45 ± 0.96, p <0.01) lower hospital cost [Median: 29,434.70 RMB (IQR: 9,705.00–52,451.40) vs. 34,537.60 RMB (IQR: 14,689.98–64,222.12), p < 0.001], and shorter length of hospital stay [Median: 4.00 days (IQR: 3.00, 5.00) vs. 5.00 days (IQR: 4.00, 6.00), p < 0.001]. The FOCUS-PDCA model involving UAP was associated with improved clinical effectiveness and efficiency of inpatient physical examination, which may be applied in hospital management to enhance the quality of care and patient outcomes. Further validation in other clinical settings is needed to test its broader application.

title: A Multidimensional Analysis of Stress and Communication Processes in the Emergency Department: The Role of Communication Barriers and Crisis Exposure
Explainable Process Intelligence for Workforce Allocation and Operational Governance in Digital Healthcare Systems
journal: Saudi Journal of Engineering and Technology
abstract: Healthcare organizations face challenges in workforce allocation because fixed staffing approaches may not adequately reflect changing demand, workflow bottlenecks, staff qualifications, workload, and operational constraints. This study develops an Explainable Process Intelligence framework for Workforce Allocation and Operational Governance in Digital Healthcare Systems to connect healthcare process analysis with transparent staff-to-task recommendations. A quantitative, simulation-based design was used with a simulated healthcare event log and workforce records. The framework integrates process discovery, conformance analysis, bottleneck identification, demand estimation, constrained workforce allocation, explainable artificial intelligence, and governance monitoring. The allocation model was compared with a historical baseline roster using identical demand periods and eligibility rules. The proposed approach increased demand coverage from 78.1% to 88.7%, reduced median waiting time from 1.70 to 1.29 hours, decreased workload coefficient of variation from 0.31 to 0.21, and reduced overtime exposure from 12.4% to 8.9%. Explanations were available for accepted and rejected recommendations, while human reviewers retained authority to modify or reject recommendations. The findings indicate that integrating process intelligence, explainable allocation, and governance can support more transparent workforce planning, workload management, and operational oversight in digital healthcare environments.

title: Determinants of Attitude Users Electronic Medical Record: A Study of the Psychological Factors, Information Accuracy, and Supervisory Techniques
journal: Jurnal Manajemen Kesehatan Yayasan RS Dr Soetomo
abstract: Electronic medical records (EMRs) are essential for easy information access, better documentation, and fewer human errors. EMR implementation success depends largely on users’ attitudes. This study examined factors influencing EMR users’ attitudes—psychological factors, information accuracy, and supervision techniques—in the inpatient unit of Adhyaksa Hospital. This quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted from June 2024 to April 2025 and included all 119 nurses and midwives in the inpatient unit using saturated sampling. Data were collected using a questionnaire covering all variables, with responses on a 4-point scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree, and analyzed with Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). Most respondents were women (66.4%), aged 31-35 years (60.5%), held a bachelor’s degree (63.9%), and had 1-5 years of work experience (59.7%). Psychological factors, information accuracy, and supervision techniques significantly influenced EMR users’ attitudes. Supervision techniques had the strongest direct effect, followed by psychological factors and information accuracy. The study highlights the need to strengthen supervision techniques to foster positive attitudes toward EMR use in the inpatient unit of Adhyaksa Hospital.

title: Correct patient identification in a Nicaraguan referral hospital: knowledge, practices and barriers of health personnel
authors: Erick Alexander de Jesús Chamorro Segovia
abstract: Describir los conocimientos declarados, las prácticas autoinformadas y las barreras percibidas relacionadas con la identificación correcta del paciente entre trabajadores de un hospital nicaragüense. Estudio observacional, descriptivo y transversal realizado entre enero y junio de 2026, con 209 trabajadores seleccionados mediante muestreo no probabilístico por bola de nieve. Se aplicó un cuestionario digital autoadministrado y se realizó un análisis descriptivo mediante frecuencias y porcentajes. El 69,9 % pertenecía a enfermería y el 22,0 % al personal médico. El 99,0 % reconoció la identificación correcta como prioridad de seguridad y el 96,7 % manifestó conocer el protocolo institucional. El 88,5 % declaró verificar al menos dos identificadores antes de procedimientos o administración de medicamentos. El 45,9 % informó haber observado situaciones de riesgo sin consecuencias y el 14,8 % situaciones con consecuencias; además, el 25,8 % manifestó dudas sobre la identidad de pacientes. Las principales barreras percibidas fueron resistencia del personal (26,3 %), falta de supervisión (20,1 %) y problemas de legibilidad de brazaletes (17,2 %). El elevado reconocimiento declarado coexistió con experiencias de riesgo y barreras percibidas. Estos hallazgos exploratorios justifican evaluaciones observacionales del proceso de identificación, sin permitir establecer el cumplimiento institucional ni la frecuencia real de errores asistenciales.

title: Adoption and Implementation of Framework Contracting for Essential Medicines in Ghana: Qualitative Insights from Stakeholders
abstract: Abstract Background Access to essential medicines is a prerequisite for universal health coverage (UHC), yet in Ghana shortages, procurement delays, financing constraints and supply chain inefficiencies continue to constrain availability. The Ministry of Health introduced framework contracting (FWC) in 2018 to consolidate demand, improve price predictability and strengthen supplier relationships. Little empirical evidence exists on how the reform operates in practice, and published accounts do not specify the design parameters that govern its behaviour. This study examined the factors influencing its adoption and stakeholders' experiences of its implementation. Methods A qualitative case study combined a review of eleven legal, policy, technical and evaluation documents with in-depth interviews with ten purposively selected senior stakeholders from institutions responsible for the design, regulation, financing, implementation, supply and use of framework contracting. Coding was inductive and conducted in NVivo 14; transaction cost, institutional and agency theory framed interpretation rather than data collection or coding. Documentary and interview evidence were compared for convergence and divergence, and design parameters charted against international guidance. Reporting follows the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ). Results The arrangement appoints multiple suppliers per product at firm cedi prices with no standard adjustment formula and indicative volumes, while call-off and payment obligations rest with regional stores and teaching hospitals rather than the Ministry that negotiates price. Participants described FWC as a response to fragmented purchasing and considered it to have improved structure, price consistency and supplier accountability, but reported that these gains had not translated into uninterrupted availability. The documentary record showed substantial reductions in contract prices and supplier lead times alongside low supplier fill rates, weak forecast accuracy, continuing facility-level stockouts and accumulated indebtedness across the financing chain. Conclusion Framework contracting is better understood as a health system intervention than as a procurement mechanism. Its effect on availability depends on financing, supplier incentives, logistics and institutional coordination, and the supplier behaviour observed is consistent with the way the contract design allocates price, volume and payment risk. Reform confined to implementation is therefore unlikely to suffice: the design parameters require revision alongside strengthening of the complementary systems on which delivery depends.

title: Optimization of Pharmacy Supply Chains Using AI and Machine Learning
journal: International Journal of Medical Research And Innovation in Applied Science (IJMRIAS)
abstract: Pharmacy supply chains are under intensifying pressure to deliver the right medicine, in the right quantity, at the right time—while minimizing costs, preventing expiries, and complying with stringent regulatory and quality standards. Conventional forecasting and replenishment methods often struggle with volatile demand, multi-echelon dynamics (manufacturer–wholesaler–pharmacy), and constraints such as cold-chain integrity and controlled-substance regulations. This manuscript presents an integrated framework for optimizing pharmacy supply chains using artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML). We synthesize current methods in demand forecasting, inventory control, routing and scheduling, and risk management, and we propose a practical methodology that combines feature-rich forecasting (gradient-boosted trees and sequence models), stochastic inventory optimization, reinforcement learning for adaptive reorder policies, and constraint-aware vehicle routing. A detailed study protocol outlines quasi-experimental deployment across community and hospital pharmacies, including data governance, evaluation metrics, and change-management steps. Illustrative results (based on a realistic implementation scenario) indicate reductions in stockouts (30–50%), expiries (25–40%), and total holding costs (10–20%), with improvements in service level (3–10 percentage points) and forecast accuracy (MAPE reductions from ~22–28% to ~9–14%). We conclude with discussion on interpretability, workforce upskilling, and governance, emphasizing a socio-technical approach that blends human oversight with algorithmic optimization to achieve resilient, ethical, and efficient pharmacy supply chains.

title: Analysis of Drug Inventory Control in Indonesian Hospitals Using the ABC Critical Index Method: A Systematic Review
abstract: Background: Drug inventory management in hospitals is very important to ensure the availability of safe and effective drugs, especially within the framework of the National Health Insurance (JKN). The ABC critical index method has been recognized as an efficient strategy for improving drug inventory control. Objective: This study aims to investigate the application of the ABC Critical Index method in drug inventory management in hospitals, as well as to improve the overall quality of health services. Methods: This systematic review followed the PRISMA guidelines and involved a literature search in four databases, namely Garuda, Scopus, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar, using relevant keywords. Of the 169 articles found, eight articles were selected to meet the criteria for further analysis. Results: This review shows that drug inventory control can be improved through the application of the Critical Index ABC analysis method, which groups drugs into categories A, B, and C based on their usage value and contribution to the budget. Category A drugs, despite their small number of items, absorb the largest portion of the budget and therefore require close monitoring. In addition, the study also emphasized the importance of integrated information systems and electronic prescription systems to improve the accuracy of stock monitoring and reduce the risk of stock outs. Several studies also highlighted the benefits of the Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) and Reorder Point (ROP) methods in determining the optimal order quantity and reorder time, which overall contribute to the efficiency of hospital pharmacy logistics. Conclusion: The implementation of the ABC Critical Index method in controlling drug inventory in hospitals can improve operational efficiency and ensure the availability of quality drugs. Cooperation between pharmacists and hospital management is very important to ensure the effectiveness of the control system, which in turn can improve the overall quality of health services.

title: Hospital logistics in Somalia: why health-specific supply chain expertise matters—an opinion
abstract: Hospital logistics determines whether care promised on paper can actually be delivered at the bedside. A hospital may have trained clinicians and functioning wards, yet treatment can still fail when oxygen interfaces, essential medicines, sterile supplies, laboratory reagents, blood-bank consumables, or device accessories are unavailable. In Somalia, this issue deserves greater policy attention because the health system operates under financial constraints, import dependence, insecurity, fragmented service delivery, and uneven institutional capacity. Somalia's Health Sector Strategic Plan 2022-2026 describes important pharmaceutical-sector challenges and a private pharmacy logistics network that, although rapid, operates largely through informal and trust-based processes without formal forecasting or contracting arrangements (1).In a WHO report on Somalia's 2020 pharmaceutical-sector assessment, stock-outs averaged 27.3 days per year in surveyed public health centres and warehouses (2). Although this finding should not be generalized to all Somali health facilities, it illustrates the operational vulnerabilities affecting pharmaceutical availability. Research examining Somalia's humanitarian health response has also documented recurrent procurement and transport-related shortages affecting medicines and other essential health commodities (3). Recent Somalia-focused health-systems commentary has additionally highlighted severe health-workforce scarcity, weak regulation, uneven deployment, and financing instability as threats to continuity and resilience of health services (4). These observations are not evidence that all Somali hospitals experience the same logistics weaknesses or that existing logistics personnel are ineffective. Rather, they expose a broader healthpolicy question: whether hospital logistics is best treated mainly as a generic administrative function or as a specialized health-system capability requiring competencies specific to medicines, medical devices, clinical demand, quality assurance, and patient safety. In this Opinion, health-specific supply-chain expertise refers to the combination of conventional supply-chain competencies with sufficient technical knowledge of medicines, medical devices, diagnostics, medical gases, storage and quality requirements, and the clinical consequences of procurement and inventory decisions.Generic supply-chain competence remains essential. Procurement planning, tendering, supplier management, inventory control, warehousing, transportation, budgeting, and contract management all matter. Health care, however, introduces technical requirements that substantially change the consequences of purchasing decisions. Ordering an unsuitable office product may create inconvenience; purchasing an incompatible ventilator circuit, an inappropriate oxygen regulator, a reagent without a compatible analyzer, a medicine with insufficient remaining shelf life, or equipment that cannot be maintained locally may interrupt treatment and waste scarce resources. Somalia's Essential Medicines List is intended to guide procurement, management, distribution, and regulation of medicines while supporting standardized medical care (5). Translating such guidance into hospital purchasing decisions requires more than comparing prices and delivery times. Supply-chain personnel must understand clinical consumption patterns, dosage forms and strengths, storage conditions, substitution risks, expiry management, cold-chain requirements, infection-prevention specifications, regulatory requirements, and the relationship between equipment and the consumables required to keep it functional.The international health-supply-chain literature increasingly recognizes the workforce itself as a core health-system resource. A recent professionalization framework emphasizes defined competencies, standardized job descriptions, education pathways, and career structures for health supply-chain personnel (6). Related work argues that reliable health supply chains depend on a competent, supported, and recognized workforce rather than ad hoc assignment of supply-chain responsibilities (7). Evidence from Ghana, Rwanda, and Uganda similarly demonstrates the importance of supply-chain competencies, dedicated roles, organizational support, and functional logistics information systems (8)(9)(10). Although these studies come from other settings, they provide a transferable framework for considering which competencies may be relevant to Somali hospitals; local adaptation and evaluation remain necessary.Health-specific supply-chain expertise does not require every logistician to become a physician, nurse, or pharmacist. Nor does it imply that already overburdened clinicians need to operate procurement departments and warehouses. A potentially appropriate model is a professional health supply-chain function that combines modern supply-chain expertise with sufficient understanding of health products and formal collaboration with clinical, pharmacy, laboratory, biomedical, finance, and infection-prevention teams.At minimum, hospital supply-chain personnel would benefit from the capability to translate service activity into quantification and forecasting; distinguish essential from discretionary products; verify technical specifications; evaluate suppliers beyond price; manage batch, expiry, temperature, and traceability requirements; calculate reorder levels and buffer stocks; identify single-source vulnerabilities; and use logistics data for management decisions. Purchases carrying substantial clinical or technical risk would warrant review by the relevant professional department.Medical equipment illustrates why this distinction matters. A systematic review of medical-device procurement in low-and middle-income countries found that equipment selection is better informed by infrastructure, end-user capability, maintenance requirements, and life-cycle costs rather than acquisition price alone (11). WHO health-technology-management guidance similarly places procurement within a continuum extending through incoming inspection, inventory, user training, maintenance, performance monitoring, and eventual decommissioning (12). For Somali hospitals, purchasing a monitor, ventilator, anesthesia machine, oxygen system, or laboratory analyzer would therefore benefit from assessment of electricity requirements, compatibility, spare parts, consumables, end-user training, preventive maintenance, technical support, and replacement planning. Hospitals can begin this transition without creating a large new bureaucracy. First, hospitals could define a health supply-chain competency profile for personnel responsible for procurement, stores, inventory, and internal distribution.Recruitment and promotion could assess these competencies, while existing staff could be offered structured professional development through short courses, postgraduate education, certification, mentorship, and continuing professional development. Although addressing disaster and emergencycare education rather than supply-chain management specifically, recent Somali commentary has similarly emphasized profession-specific competencies, explicit learning objectives, interprofessional coordination, and adaptation of training to resource-constrained environments (13). These principles may be relevant to building a competent hospital supply-chain workforce in Somalia.Second, hospitals could establish multidisciplinary procurement and supply oversight with clear thresholds for technical review. Routine low-risk commodities can remain administratively streamlined, whereas medicines, medical gases, high-risk consumables, diagnostics, and medical devices could undergo pharmacy, clinical, laboratory, biomedical, infection-prevention, or other relevant technical review as appropriate. Such an approach preserves the essential role of logistics and finance personnel while reducing the probability of technically unsuitable purchases.Third, logistics-management information can function as a management instrument rather than merely a record-keeping requirement. A minimum hospital supply-chain performance set could be grouped into four domains: availability (stock-out days, order fill rate, and emergency purchases); efficiency (forecast accuracy, supplier lead time, and inventory turnover); quality and safety (expiry and wastage, traceability, and equipment downtime); and resilience (qualified alternative suppliers and critical-item contingency plans). Persistent logistics failures can then be reviewed alongside clinical quality and patient-safety indicators because commodity shortages may directly undermine care.For emergency preparedness, structured stockpiling may also strengthen continuity. The 5P Strategic Medical Stockpile model integrates stockpile planning within the emergency-management cycle and offers a conceptual reference for emergency buffers, alternative supply arrangements, and replenishment planning, although adaptation to the Somali context would be required (14).Fourth, procurement decisions could place greater emphasis on total value rather than unit price alone. For medicines and consumables, value includes quality, shelf life, regulatory compliance, storage requirements, and delivery reliability. For medical devices, it includes installation, compatibility, consumables, spare parts, warranties, training, maintenance, and expected useful life. In resourceconstrained hospitals, the lowest-priced item may ultimately be the most expensive if it cannot be safely used or kept functional.Finally, hospitals, universities, and health authorities could increasingly recognize health supplychain management as a legitimate professional and educational pathway. Somalia needs personnel who understand both supply-chain science and the health-service consequences of logistics decisions. Specialized postgraduate education, competency-based in-service programs, and multidisciplinary training involving logisticians, pharmacists, nurses, physicians, biomedical professionals, finance teams, and hospital managers could help build this capability. The objective is professionalization, not professional displacement.Strengthening hospital logistics in Somalia is not principally about changing job titles. It is about improving the governance of decisions that determine whether essential inputs reach patients in the correct form, quality, quantity, condition, and time. Generic logistics expertise remains indispensable, but hospitals manage products for which procurement and supply errors can cause immediate clinical harm, service interruption, financial waste, or unusable technology. This additional risk justifies healthspecific competency standards and multidisciplinary technical oversight.The policy direction is therefore practical rather than prescriptive. Somali hospitals could recognize health supply-chain management as a specialized clinical-support function, define competency-based roles, integrate technical review into high-risk procurement, use logistics data in executive decisionmaking, and develop formal education and career pathways. National health authorities, universities, hospitals, professional organizations, and development partners can facilitate this transition by aligning curricula, job descriptions, procurement standards, and performance indicators. Somalia does not need to replace existing logistics systems or personnel to pursue this agenda. It can strengthen them by ensuring that supply-chain decisions incorporate the technical realities of healthcare delivery. In a health system where every scarce resource must generate maximum patient benefit, professionalizing hospital supply chains can be viewed as an investment in safer, more reliable, and more resilient health services.

title: Relationship of Logistics Management Information System Data Quality With Essential Medicine Stockouts in Malawi Using Spearman Rank Correlation Analysis
abstract: Abstract Background Strengthening health research and information systems in low- and middle-income countries requires evidence on how data quality failures in routine health systems translate into poor health outcomes. In Malawi, stock-outs of essential medicines remain persistent despite the national rollout of the Open Logistics Management Information System (Open-LMIS). However, the statistical relationship between LMIS-derived performance indicators and stock-out burden has not previously been quantified at district level using real national LMIS data. This study examined the association between LMIS availability metrics, order fill rates, and essential medicine stock-out burden across government-managed health facilities at Blantyre District Health Office (DHO). Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted at six government-managed health facilities under Blantyre DHO. Nine essential medicines were extracted from the national Open-LMIS dataset for five months (January to June 2023; April was absent from the national LMIS data pull), generating 196 facility-product-month observation units. Spearman rank correlation analysis tested associations between mean facility-level availability percentage, order fill rate, accumulated stock-out days, and stock-out frequency. Bonferroni correction was applied for four simultaneous comparisons (adjusted α = 0.0125). Descriptive Key Performance Indicator (KPI) analysis was structured around the Supply Chain Operations Reference (SCOR) model domains. The study is reported in accordance with the STROBE statement for cross-sectional studies. Results Madziabango Health Centre had the highest accumulated stock-out burden (269 days; 10 events; mean availability 69.1%), while Chilomoni Health Centre had zero stock-out days (mean availability 100.0%). Phenobarbitone 30mg had the highest accumulated stock-out days (251 days; 37.0% observation-level stock-out rate). Morphine sulphate had the highest observation-level stock-out rate (60.0%). Mean order fill rate across all facilities was 28.24%. Spearman rank correlation demonstrated strong, statistically significant negative associations between mean availability and both accumulated stock-out days (rₛ = −0.829, p = 0.042) and stock-out frequency (rₛ = −0.829, p = 0.042). Order fill rate was not significantly correlated with either stock-out outcome at facility level (rₛ = −0.257 to − 0.600, p = 0.208–0.623). Conclusions Mean medicine availability recorded in Open-LMIS is a strong, statistically significant predictor of stock-out burden across government health facilities in Blantyre DHO. These findings validate LMIS data quality metrics as proxy indicators suitable for health system monitoring, early-warning system design, and policy prioritisation in LMIC public health supply chains. Investment in LMIS data quality and adherence is a high-priority, low-cost health system strengthening intervention with direct implications for medicine access and patient safety.

title: eLMIS Pharmaceutical Forecasting, Approval and Receipt in Relation to Stock-Outs and Availability in Kigoma, Tanzania
journal: Research Journal of Business and Finance
abstract: This study examined the associations between eLMIS-recorded pharmaceuticals forecasting, approval and receipt in relation to stock-outs and availability in Kigoma, Tanzania. A retrospective quantitative case study used 1,725 medicine-level observations from three purposively selected public healthcare facilities across reporting cycles spanning from July 2025 to July 2026. Five mixed-effects regression models examined forecasting-to-approval, approval-to-receipt, and the associations of previous-period receipts with availability, stock-out occurrence and positive stock-out duration. Overall medicine availability was 92.56%; however, availability varied across pharmaceuticals and facility types, whereas some products had availability below 80%. Also, product-specific gaps occurred between forecasted, approved and received quantities. Forecast quantity was positively associated with approved quantity (β = 0.787, p < 0.001), while previous-period approved quantity was positively associated with following receipts (β = 0.391, p < 0.001). Previous-period receipt quantity was negatively and significantly associated with lower odds of stock-out occurrence (β = -0.217, p < 0.001). The study was limited to three purposively selected public healthcare facilities and retrospective records covering approximately one year. Health facilities should track differences between forecasted, approved and received quantities to identify medicine supply gaps and address stock-outs. The study distinguishes the relationships associated with successive supply chain stages and demonstrates why forecast and approval quantities alone may not adequately indicate medicine availability. Pharmaceutical availability requires alignment between information-based planning, supply decisions, and operational fulfilment by the MSD.

title: Hospitals as Anchor Institutions: Adapting a US Framework to Advance Equity in Low‐ and Middle‐Income Countries
Impact of Health Facility Essential Commodity Out of Stock on Child Care Seeking Behavior and Treatment Rates in Ethiopia: A Multilevel Mixed- Effects Analysis of the 2024/2025 EDHS
abstract: Abstract Background; Child mortality in Ethiopia remains driven by preventable infectious conditions acute respiratory infections, diarrhea and fever. While demand side factors are widely studied, the impact of supply side health facility readiness specifically the consistent availability of essential pediatric medicines on care seeking and clinical treatment is less clear. This study evaluated the impact of essential commodity stock outs on child care seeking and treatment rates in Ethiopia using the 2024/2025 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey. Methods; A secondary multilevel analysis was conducted using linked data from the 2024/2025 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey and facility readiness audits. The sample included 8452 children under five who experienced acute respiratory infections, fever or diarrhea in the preceding two weeks. Outcomes modeled included formal care seeking and receipt of recommended treatment (oral rehydration salt/zinc, dispersible amoxicillin or Artemisinin based Combination). Multilevel mixed effects logistic regression models assessed adjusted odds ratios at a 95% confidence interval. Results; Formal care seeking occurred for 48.2% of sick children and appropriate treatment was received by 36.5%. Overall, 41.3% of local primary health facilities experienced essential pediatric medicine stock outs in the preceding month. Children served by facilities with stock outs had 42% lower odds of formal care seeking (adjusted odds ratio = 0.58) and 56% lower odds of receiving appropriate clinical treatment (adjusted odds ratio = 0.44). Maternal education, household wealth and urban residence were strong positive predictors of care seeking. Community level differences accounted for 28.4% of the total variance in care seeking. Conclusion; Health facility commodity stock outs act as a major structural bottleneck in Ethiopia, suppressing treatment rates and eroding care seeking behavior. National authorities must emphasize supply chain digitization and support primary healthcare logistics to increase child survival.

title: Integration of Multicriteria Matrix and Drug Need Forecasting in Support of Budget Policy: Literature Review
A Policy for the Delivery of Essential Medicines to Vulnerable Population in Argentina: A Case Study of the REMEDIAR Program
abstract: The REMEDIAR Program, established during Argentina's 2001-2002 crisis, provides free essential medicines to the uninsured population through direct delivery to more than 8,000 primary healthcare centers. Over two decades, the program has alternated between two financing models: international concessional loans from the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and national treasury funding. Using the Nexus Working Group framework linking public financial management to supply chain performance, this longitudinal single-case study (2002-2024) examines how each financing model shaped the program's funding, procurement, and distribution. This study analyzes the two financing models of the REMEDIAR Program from 2002 to 2024, focusing on budgetary planning, procurement efficiency, and supply chain performance. We combined descriptive time-series analysis of budgetary and operational indicators with a review of normative and administrative documents; no causal effects are estimated. IDB-financed operations showed more stable budget execution, procurement timelines 48% shorter than nationally financed processes, and lower awarded prices, while treasury financing exhibited greater volatility tied to fiscal cycles and currency depreciation. Centralized procurement averaged 25% of market prices versus 46% under a decentralized subnational benchmark, though at the cost of slower formulary adaptation. Per-capita distribution was highest in poorer provinces, and declining household out-of-pocket spending on medicines was associated with periods of higher program intensity. The efficiencies observed under international financing reflect its associated management rules-multi-year budgeting, ring-fenced funds, predictable payments-rather than the source of funds itself. Internalizing these rules under domestic financing emerges as a key priority for the program's sustainability.

title: Health Facility Factors Associated with Access to Essential Medicines for Non-Communicable Diseases Among Insured Patients in Level 4 Public Health Facilities in Nairobi City County, Kenya
journal: East African Journal of Health and Science
abstract: Access to essential medicines is critical for effective management of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), particularly among patients requiring continuous pharmacological treatment. However, health facility constraints may limit medicine access even among insured patients. This study examined health facility factors associated with access to essential medicines for NCDs among insured patients attending selected Level 4 public health facilities in Nairobi City County, Kenya. A mixed-methods cross-sectional design was employed among insured adult patients diagnosed with NCDs. Of the 422 questionnaires administered, 351 were completed, yielding a response rate of 83.2%. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson's chi-square test, and binary logistic regression, with statistical significance set at p < .05. Qualitative data were analysed thematically to complement the quantitative findings. The findings showed that 62.1% of respondents reported frequent medicine stock-outs, 53.0% indicated that they did not receive all prescribed medicines, and 73.8% reported referral to private pharmacies because of stock-outs. In the bivariate analysis, frequent medicine stock-outs were significantly associated with access to essential medicines (χ² = 11.233, p = .047), as were receipt of all prescribed medicines (χ² = 16.577, p = .001), waiting time (χ² = 10.583, p = .032), and efficiency of the medicine supply system (χ² = 12.539, p = .014). The logistic regression model was statistically significant, χ²(38) = 70.420, p = .001, with a Nagelkerke R² of .246. After adjustment, an efficient medicine supply system remained a significant independent predictor of access; patients reporting an efficient system had approximately 3.9 times higher odds of accessing essential medicines (AOR = 3.939, 95% CI [1.284–12.086], p = .017). The study concludes that facility-level pharmaceutical system performance remains critical to medicine access despite insurance coverage. Strengthening forecasting, procurement, inventory management, timely replenishment, and supply-system efficiency is necessary to improve access and continuity of NCD treatment in public health facilities.

title: Responsible Supply Chain Management
Supply Chain and Workforce Capacity Development for Diagnostic Services in Low‑and Lower Middle‑Income Sub‑Saharan Countries
abstract: The diagnosis of communicable and noncommunicable diseases cannot be made without radiology/imaging and pathology and laboratory medicine (PALM) services. These diagnostic services are often an under‑recognized vital component of health care systems. Supply chain challenges and limited human resource capacity and capability are major impediments to delivering accurate, timely, and comprehensive diagnostic services in low‑income and lower‑middle‑income countries (LMICs) in sub‑Saharan Africa (SSA) and other low‑resource regions. This viewpoint provides a current assessment of these supply chain and human resource challenges and addresses possible solutions. Chronic underfunding, lack of transparency, and an over‑dependence on inadequate or obsolete methods of supply chain management at all levels are common in many low‑resource regions. Furthermore, overdependence on high‑income countries for basic diagnostic supplies jeopardizes diagnostic and health care services. Resource limitations impede attaining laboratory accreditation and certification. The scarcity of training programs at all levels of laboratory medicine and pathology as well as imaging and the serious problem of brain drain to high‑income countries are major problems in many, if not all LMICs. Training in supply chain management is generally vastly underdeveloped in many low‑resource countries. Diagnostic services in rural and remote low‑resource settings are often very limited. Stakeholder engagement and the adoption of needs‑based solutions to gaps in supply chain management and human resource capacity are essential, as well as political will, public–private partnerships, and adequate funding. Development of effective, sustainable local and regional policies and governance is essential to strengthen diagnostic supply chains and workforce training in SSA and other LMIC areas. Diagnostic services in rural and remote areas in many LMICs need to be vastly improved.

title: AI-DRIVEN PREDICTIVE INTELLIGENCE FOR REAL-TIME PHARMACY INVENTORY OPTIMIZATION AND MEDICATION SUPPLY CHAIN RESILIENCE
abstract: In healthcare, pharmacy inventory levels of essential medications can fluctuate unpredictably and rapidly, compromising patient safety. Real-time predictive intelligence based on enterprise-grade data can optimize inventory levels and order quantities by capturing and distilling the key influencing dynamics. An intelligent pharmacy inventory optimization framework can utilize time-series data on medications (types, quantities in stock, consumption patterns) and major activity events (cancellations of elective surgeries, patient surges, weather forecasts) from internal and external sources to feed supervised learning models and predict expected pharmacy inventory levels and order quantities for the next days/weeks. The approach facilitates precision pharmacy, enhances resilience in the medication supply chain, and tools and methods readily available for implementation by interested pharmacies. The overarching goal of predictive intelligence is the real-time optimization of pharmacy inventory levels of essential medications in tandem with reshaped order quantities. A formalized case study in a large public urban hospital system showed that predictive intelligence captured and distilled the key influencing dynamics surrounding medication consumption and made them available for decision-making. Streamlined analytics pipelines ingested time-series and event-driven data feeds, fed an ensemble of supervised learning models, and produced highly relevant outputs for multiple executive and operational decision-makers aligned around month-long planning horizons. Inventory intelligence further extended the application of these assets to other pharmacy processes, addressing the specific problem of anxiety-inducing medication supply distortions.

title: Evaluating the Synergistic Impact of Digital Logistics Systems (eLMIS) and Financial Auditing (APTS) on Essential Commodity Availability in Ethiopian Public Healthcare Facilities: A Multilevel Analysis of the 2024/2025 National Survey
abstract: Abstract Background Chronic pharmaceutical stock outs hinder Universal Health Coverage in Ethiopia. To address this, the Ministry of Health introduced the electronic Logistics Management Information System for inventory visibility and Auditable Pharmaceutical Transactions and Services for financial management. However, no national study has tested their combined impact. This study evaluated the individual and synergistic effects of electronic Logistics Management Information System and Auditable Pharmaceutical Transactions and Services on essential commodity availability across Ethiopian public healthcare facilities. Methods We conducted a secondary analysis of the 2024/2025 Ethiopian Service Provision Assessment dataset utilizing 1245 public facilities nested within 125 clusters. The primary outcome was optimal essential commodity availability (zero stock outs and 100% tracer commodity presence). A two-level mixed-effects logistic regression model with an interaction term evaluated synergy, reporting Adjusted Odds Ratios with 95% Confidence Intervals. Results Overall optimal availability was 54.2% (95% CI; 51.4%–57.0%). Implementation rates were 41.2% for eLMIS, 38.2% for APTS and 26.5% for dual implementation. Facilities using eLMIS alone (AOR = 2.15; 95% CI: 1.52–3.04) and APTS alone (AOR = 1.82; 95% CI; 1.28–2.58) showed higher security. Dual implementation showed a profound synergistic effect (AOR = 4.32; 95% CI; 3.25–5.74, p < 0.001). Positive predictors included functional cold chains (AOR = 2.08), qualified staffing (AOR = 1.68), hub proximity (AOR = 1.58) and urban settings (AOR = 1.95). The model explained 66.2% of regional variance. Conclusion Dual implementation of electronic Logistics Management Information System and Auditable Pharmaceutical Transactions and Services creates a powerful synergistic impact on pharmaceutical availability. Synchronized national scale-up and cold chain investments are urgently needed to achieve supply chain resilience and Universal Health Coverage in Ethiopia.

title: Integration of Strategic CSR and Digital Leadership to Supply Chain Sustainability in Jordanian Public Hospitals: Moderating Role of Green Technology and E-Knowledge Sharing
journal: Journal of Logistics Informatics and Service Science

title: A hybrid data-driven and qualitative approach for critical factor identification in pharmaceutical supplier selection: safeguarding the continuity of pharmaceutical in disruption-prone settings
journal: Journal of Humanitarian Logistics and Supply Chain Management
abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop a comprehensive and integrated approach for identifying and prioritizing critical factors influencing pharmaceutical supplier selection and supply chain performance, with direct implications for health system resilience and access to essential medicines. By positioning supplier selection as an upstream determinant of preparedness, the study addresses the concerns of humanitarian and health supply chain actors that depend on commercial pharmaceutical suppliers for the uninterrupted availability of essential medicines during disruptions and emergencies. Design/methodology/approach A hybrid methodology is adopted, combining Principal Component Analysis (PCA), a machine learning-based dimensionality reduction technique and qualitative analysis using NVivo. Initially, 67 factors were identified through literature and expert input, reduced to 20 using PCA and subsequently validated through qualitative thematic analysis. Findings The analysis identified seven key themes encompassing operational, risk, supplier capability, financial, governance, technological and ethical dimensions of pharmaceutical supply chains. Operational factors such as delivery accuracy, availability of supplies and cold chain capabilities are fundamental to supply continuity and patient safety. Risk-related factors, including political instability and labour disruptions, significantly impact supply chain resilience. Supplier capabilities, governance factors, technological innovation and ethical considerations jointly drive resilience, sustainability and competitiveness. Research limitations/implications The current study contributes to supplier selection theory by combining PCA with qualitative thematic analysis, with a focus on operational, technological, governance and ethical aspects. The hybrid method of dimensionality reduction using machine learning and qualitative depth increases the reliability and interpretability of the data and understanding of the assessment processes for the healthcare supply chain. The framework also extends the humanitarian logistics literature by connecting commercial upstream supplier decisions to the preparedness and resilience of downstream health supply chains serving populations affected by disruptions and crises. Practical implications Healthcare organizations should adopt a multi-criteria approach to supplier evaluation, considering delivery accuracy, cold chain, financial sustainability and regulatory compliance, all of which affect patient safety and the continuity of essential medicines. Building resilient, health-system-aligned supply chains requires investment in digital technologies like AI, along with proactive measures such as multi-sourcing and geographic diversification. For humanitarian organizations, national procurement agencies and global health programmes, the prioritized factors provide a screening template for evaluating pharmaceutical suppliers whose reliability ultimately determines whether essential medicines reach crisis-affected and underserved populations. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by providing a holistic, multi-dimensional framework that integrates PCA-based machine learning and NVivo-based qualitative insights for supplier selection – an approach not previously applied in the pharmaceutical supply chain context.
