It further contributes to the humanitarian logistics and health supply chain literature by demonstrating how upstream supplier selection functions as a preparedness mechanism for maintaining access to essential medicines under conditions of political instability, labour disruption and demand shocks.

title: Improvements to pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity; Ethiopia
journal: Bulletin of the World Health Organization
abstract: Problem: Ethiopia's heavy dependence on imported pharmaceuticals created public health vulnerabilities, foreign exchange pressures and recurrent medicine stock-outs. Approach: In 2015, Ethiopia launched a 10-year National Strategy and Plan of Action for Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Development to improve access to quality-assured medicines. The strategy, overseen by a Joint Steering Committee co-chaired by the Ministries of Health and Industry with technical assistance from the World Health Organization (WHO), combined industrial incentives, preferential centralized procurement and regulatory strengthening. Local setting: Before strategy implementation, Ethiopia had limited manufacturing capacity. Local manufacturers supplied approximately 20% of national generic medicine demand, while supply chain fragmentation and foreign exchange constraints compromised access to imported medicines. Relevant changes: By 2025, six facilities had achieved national good manufacturing practice compliance, 11 manufacturers were operational and the Ethiopian Food and Drug Authority reached WHO Maturity Level 3. Locally produced coverage of the National Essential Medicines List increased from 90 to 140 chemical entities, across 167 dosage forms, and a vaccine manufacturing initiative was launched. However, domestic supply only increased to 23% against a 60% public procurement target; active pharmaceutical ingredient production and WHO prequalification remained unachieved, and export and workforce targets were missed. Lessons learnt: Combined, the strategy's cross-sectoral governance, regulatory strengthening, preferential centralized procurement and industrial incentives advanced local production. However, foreign exchange constraints, dependence on imported raw materials and financing and capacity gaps limited progress. Future efforts should prioritize WHO prequalification, upstream manufacturing, skilled workforce development, export competitiveness and sustainable financing while maintaining patient-centred objectives.

title: Improving rational prescribing at a public district hospital in southwestern Uganda, January-November 2021: A quality improvement initiative
journal: Journal of Interventional Epidemiology and Public Health
abstract: Abstract Irrational prescribing can compromise patient safety, medicine availability, and antimicrobial stewardship. At a public district hospital in southwestern Uganda, a 2019 internal audit prompted by recurrent stock-outs found approximately three medicines per outpatient prescription, four per inpatient prescription, and antibiotics in about 60% of outpatient prescriptions. We implemented a six-month quality improvement initiative to increase prescribing concordant with the Uganda Clinical Guidelines (UCG) and improve key indicators of rational medicine use among outpatients. From January to November 2021, we conducted an uncontrolled before-and-after quality improvement evaluation. Prescription records were selected by systematic random sampling at baseline and six-month endline. We reviewed 350 baseline and 101 endline outpatient prescriptions. The primary outcome was prescription concordance with UCG. Secondary outcomes included antibiotic prescribing, number of medicines per encounter, generic prescribing, and injection use. Adjusted analyses accounted for age, sex, and diagnostic group. Following root-cause analysis, the hospital quality improvement (QI) team implemented prescriber education, provided clinicians with soft-copy PDF versions of the UCG and essential medicines lists, restricted prescribing to recognized clinicians with signature verification, and instituted periodic prescription audit and feedback. Guideline-concordant prescribing increased from 43.7% to 76.2% (adjusted change, +32.8 percentage points; 95% CI, 21.9–43.8; aPR=1.82; 95% CI, 1.51–2.20). Antibiotic prescribing decreased from 83.4% to 65.3% (adjusted change, −17.9 points; 95% CI, −27.8 to −8.0; aPR=0.80; 95% CI, 0.70–0.91). Mean medicines per encounter decreased from 3.35 to 2.66 (adjusted mean difference, −0.61; 95% CI, −0.79 to −0.43), while prescriptions containing only generic medicines increased from 78.6% to 94.1% (adjusted change, +13.6 points; 95% CI, 5.8–21.4). Guideline-concordant prescribing increased, while antibiotic use and medicine burden declined and generic prescribing improved. Antibiotic use nevertheless remained high, underscoring the need for continued stewardship, audit, and iterative QI.

title: Drone technology in medical supply chain management: A survey on enabling technologies, frameworks, and applications
journal: Journal of Decision Analytics and Intelligent Computing
abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), or drones, have become known as a disruptive technology that can potentially enhance efficiency and accessibility in the medical supply chain by allowing the timely delivery of medical supplies such as vaccines, blood, organs and emergency drugs in remote and disaster-prone regions. This study provides a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of existing international research on the use of drones in medical supply chains, with a sample of 1,209 articles retrieved from the Dimensions.ai database for 2015-2026. VOSviewer was used to process the bibliographic information to determine publication growth and trends, leading authors and journals, country contributions and collaboration patterns, while a thematic analysis was conducted to identify the major and emerging research themes. The findings indicate that the past few years have witnessed a significant increase in the number of publications, which signifies increased interest in UAVs in healthcare supply chains, and that the most important research themes are emergency medical transportation, vaccine delivery, last-mile delivery of health care and drone system efficiency. In addition, a country-by-country examination reveals that the United States is at the forefront. Overall, the study provides information about recent trends and future perspectives on capitalizing on drone technology in medical supply chains.

title: Reconstructing Indonesia’s Pharmaceutical Patent Governance: TRIPS Flexibilities, Essential Medicines Access, and Social Justice
journal: International Journal of Law and Society (IJLS)
abstract: Patent protection in the pharmaceutical sector may constrain equitable access to essential medicines. Indonesia reflects this tension: although its regime incorporates TRIPS flexibilities, implementation remains institutionally fragmented. This study examines how patent governance, institutional capacity, and health-system integration affect compulsory licensing (CL) and government use (GU) in Indonesia, using Thailand and India as comparative cases. The study employs doctrinal legal research using statutory, conceptual, case, and comparative approaches, supported by policy-document analysis. Primary legal materials include the TRIPS Agreement, Doha Declaration, Indonesia’s Patent Law No. 13 of 2016 as amended by Law No. 65 of 2024, Presidential Regulations No. 76 of 2012 and No. 77 of 2020, Section 51 of the Thai Patent Act, Sections 83–84 of the Indian Patents Act, and Bayer Corporation v. Natco Pharma Ltd. Secondary materials include peer-reviewed literature and authoritative WTO, WHO, WIPO, and UN documents. The findings show that Indonesia’s main gap is not the absence of CL or GU authority, but the lack of an integrated pathway connecting access-problem identification, intervention selection, decision-making, implementation, and medicine procurement. Comparative evidence from Thailand and India identifies institutional conditions that remain unavailable or insufficiently integrated in Indonesia, particularly coordinated authority, evidentiary procedures, pharmaceutical capacity, procurement linkages, and accountability. The study is limited by its doctrinal and documentary basis and absence of patient-level or primary institutional evidence. Its scientific contribution is a governance-oriented reconstruction framework linking TRIPS flexibilities, institutional coordination, and the right to health in Indonesia. Strengthening procedural guidelines, interinstitutional coordination, and pharmaceutical capacity is necessary.

title: Governing healthcare supply-chain resilience across preparedness, response, and recovery: A systematic review and integrated performance and risk indicator architecture
abstract: Healthcare supply chains sustain essential care during severe disruptions, but routine efficiency measures do not necessarily reveal exposure, adaptive capacity, or recovery readiness. Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement, this review synthesizes 44 Scopus-indexed journal studies published from 2019 to 2025, retained from 97 identified records, of which 69 advanced to eligibility assessment. The review combines thematic analysis and diagnostic evidence profiling. Digital technologies and performance measurement each account for 13 studies, risk exposure for 11, and resilience capabilities for 7. Although these streams provide relevant signals, capabilities, technologies, and measures, they rarely form a complete governance chain linking warning to decision and follow-through. Named owners, trigger thresholds, escalation routes, corrective-action closure, recovery review, and post-event learning remain inconsistent. We define this failure as resilience-measurement decoupling and distinguish it from broader organizational decoupling and capability-performance gaps. The review develops an integrated performance and risk indicator architecture linking risk understanding, preparedness, exposure sensing, adaptive response, recovery measurement, accountability, escalation, and learning. It advances disaster-risk governance by showing how healthcare supply-chain evidence can move from hazard awareness to measurable preparedness, accountable response, and reviewable recovery.

title: Digital Twins as Socio-Technical Decision Systems: A Comparative Systematic Review of Supply Chain Management and Healthcare
abstract: Digital Twin (DT) technology is rapidly evolving from a digital representation of physical assets into a decision-support infrastructure that integrates real-time data, analytics, and simulation. However, existing research remains fragmented across application domains, limiting understanding of how DTs enable decision-making under different socio-technical conditions. This study presents a systematic literature review and decision-centric comparative analysis of DT applications in two contrasting decision environments: Supply Chain Management (SCM) and healthcare. Following a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) protocol, 193 peer-reviewed studies (95 SCM and 98 healthcare) were identified, screened, and synthesized across six analytical dimensions: application domains, technological integration, decision-making levels, business value, stakeholder involvement, and implementation challenges. The findings reveal fundamentally different decision logics despite a shared technological foundation based on Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and cloud computing. SCM-DTs primarily support coordination, optimization, resilience, and organizational scalability, whereas healthcare-DTs emphasize personalization, patient safety, and ethical governance under stringent regulatory constraints. Building on these findings, the study proposes a decision-centric comparative framework and a value–complexity perspective suggesting that value realization is increasingly associated with technological, organizational, and governance complexity as DT ecosystems mature. The paper advances the conceptualization of DTs as socio-technical decision systems and provides practical guidance for researchers, managers, and policymakers seeking responsible and effective digital transformation.

title: Antimicrobial Stewardship in Multispecialty Hospital Care: Evidence From Medicine, Surgery, Intensive Care, and Oncology- A Systematic Review
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Assessing Compliance: An Audit of the Medical Supplies Division's Storage Practices Against NMRA Good Storage Guidelines in Sri Lanka
journal: Sri Lankan Journal of Medical Administration
authors: O. K. D. S. M. Abeysekera
W. G. A. N. J. Senanayake
abstract: This article presents an audit of the storage practices at the Medical Supplies Division (MSD) in Sri Lanka, evaluating their compliance with the Good Storage Practices (GSP) guidelines set by the National Medicines Regulatory Authority (NMRA). The MSD plays a critical role in the national healthcare supply chain, responsible for the procurement, storage, and distribution of essential medical supplies to public health institutions across the country. Ensuring proper storage conditions is paramount to maintaining the quality, efﬁcacy, and safety of these vital products. This audit assesses various aspects of MSD's storage facilities and procedures against the NMRA's comprehensive GSP guidelines, identifying areas of compliance and non-compliance. It also highlights the imperative for digital transformation and the role of international collaboration in addressing systemic challenges. The article proposes recommendations for continuous improvement to enhance the integrity of the medical supply chain in Sri Lanka.

title: Supplier Contracting and Perceived Healthcare Service Delivery in Selected Referral Hospitals in Kenya
A Case Study of Systemic Challenges in Maternal Healthcare Delivery in South Africa,
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Maternal mortality remains a critical public health issue in South Africa, with systemic challenges persistently hindering the provision of quality obstetric care. Understanding the specific barriers within the healthcare system is essential for developing effective interventions. This study aimed to identify and analyse the systemic challenges affecting maternal healthcare delivery within the South African public health sector, focusing on structural, resource, and operational barriers. A qualitative, instrumental case study design was employed. Data were collected via in-depth, semi-structured interviews with 24 healthcare professionals and through analysis of key policy documents and facility reports from a purposively selected tertiary hospital and its referral network. The analysis revealed three primary, interlinked systemic challenges: critical staff shortages, inconsistent supply chain management for essential medicines, and fragmented referral pathways. A prominent theme was the strain on human resources, with a reported midwife-to-patient ratio frequently exceeding 1:15 on the labour ward, directly impacting care quality. Systemic failures in human resources, logistics, and coordination continue to undermine maternal healthcare delivery in the studied context. These challenges are entrenched and require multifaceted, systemic solutions. Prioritise the development of a national human resources for health plan with specific retention strategies for midwives. Strengthen pharmaceutical supply chains through improved forecasting and distribution. Formalise and monitor integrated referral protocols between primary and tertiary care facilities. Maternal health, healthcare systems, case study, South Africa, midwifery, health services accessibility This research provides an in-depth analysis of the interconnected systemic barriers in a South African maternal healthcare context, offering evidence for policymakers to design integrated improvements.

title: MediCycle AI: A Smart Framework for Safe and Sustainable Redistribution of Surplus Medicines
How Sierra Leone Developed its First National Hospital Strategy 2025–2030: A Policy Analysis Case Study of Process, Actors, and Procedural Legitimacy
journal: Journal of Epidemiology and Global Health
abstract: Sierra Leone’s hospital system faces persistent challenges, including high maternal and under-five mortality, infrastructure and supply deficits, workforce shortages, fragmented governance, and high out-of-pocket health expenditure. These constraints limit the contribution of hospitals to Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and service delivery. In response, the Ministry of Health (MoH) developed the first National Hospital Strategy for Service Delivery Transformation 2025–2030. We conducted a mixed-methods policy analysis case study of the development of the hospital strategy. The analysis was guided by the Walt and Gilson Health Policy Analysis Triangle, focusing on context, content, process, and actors. Data sources included a desk review of policy documents, assessments of nine purposively selected hospitals, fifteen key informant interviews with health sector stakeholders, and three validation workshops using a modified nominal group technique, a structured consensus method in which participants generate priorities individually, present them in turn, discuss them as a group, and then rank them. The accountability for reasonableness framework was applied to assess the procedural legitimacy of the strategy development process. The strategy was shaped by Sierra Leone’s epidemiological, economic, institutional, and health system context, including high mortality rates, limited fiscal space, weak infrastructure, severe shortages of skilled health workers, irregular supply of essential medicines, and fragmented hospital governance. These contextual factors informed a strategic vision for an equitable, accessible, affordable, resilient, and transformative hospital system. The strategy includes ten interlinked strategic objectives covering legal and regulatory reform, governance, financing, infrastructure, human resources, service delivery, supply chain management, health information systems and research, human rights and community engagement, and emergency preparedness. The development process was iterative and participatory, involving MoH leadership, hospital managers, clinicians, district health teams, development partners, professional associations, civil society, and community representatives. Assessed against the accountability for reasonableness framework by the author team, the process showed features consistent with procedural legitimacy, including evidence-informed priority-setting, stakeholder deliberation, iterative revision, and political endorsement, although formal public appeals mechanisms were limited. The development of Sierra Leone’s first hospital strategy illustrates how structured policy analysis, evidence synthesis, and participatory deliberation can support the formulation of a context-sensitive hospital reform agenda in a low-income setting. The analysis covers strategy formulation only. It makes no claim about implementation or health outcomes, which remain to be evaluated. The experience offers transferable lessons for countries seeking to strengthen hospitals as part of progress toward UHC, while highlighting the importance of sustained financing, implementation capacity, accountability and monitoring.

Drug costs and antibiotic stewardship in a tertiary care hospital in Kazakhstan: ABC/VEN, 2022–2025
journal: Journal of Clinical Medicine of Kazakhstan
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Multi-year hospital-level data on drug expenditure in Kazakhstan are scarce, although antimicrobial resistance and the growing use of high-cost biologics require expenditure monitoring tools. This study aimed to quantify four-year trends in drug expenditure, formulary structure and antibiotic spending in a multidisciplinary tertiary care hospital. Methods: Annual pharmacy dispensing ledgers for 2022–2025 were analyzed retrospectively. Each item was assigned an International Nonproprietary Name and an Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical code. ABC analysis and vital, essential and non-essential classification were performed by nonproprietary name, and antibacterials were mapped to the World Health Organization Access, Watch and Reserve groups. Expenditure was normalized per bed-day. Results: The number of nonproprietary names dispensed decreased from 194 to 172, whereas expenditure increased by 40.6% to 523.8 million Kazakhstani tenge and expenditure per bed-day by 35.1%. The share of immunosuppressants rose from 2.9% to 22.8%; ustekinumab and vedolizumab accounted for 20.3% of expenditure in 2025. Group A comprised 15.1–19.1% of names and 80.0–80.8% of expenditure; no non-essential medicine entered group A, but non-essential expenditure increased to 1.9% in 2025. Antibacterial expenditure rose by 66.6% in 2025; Watch agents accounted for 75.5–78.1% and Reserve agents for 10.3–14.4% of antibacterial spending. Conclusions: Formulary contraction coincided with a shift of the budget toward biologics and Watch and Reserve antibiotics. The findings are limited by the single-center design, nominal prices and the absence of consumption metrics based on defined daily doses; expenditure-based Access, Watch and Reserve signals should be combined with such metrics in multicenter studies. Keywords: Drug costs; Drug utilization; Anti-bacterial agents; Antimicrobial Stewardship; Tertiary Care Centers; Formulary management;

title: A Temporally Validated Machine Learning Framework for Predicting Anti-Tuberculosis Drug Stockouts: A Synthetic-Data Evaluation
journal: Journal of Applied Informatics and Computing
abstract: Continuous availability of anti-tuberculosis drugs is essential for maintaining tuberculosis treatment services, yet future stockouts arise from interacting demand, inventory, procurement, and supply conditions that are not fully represented by static stock thresholds. This study evaluates a temporally validated machine-learning framework for future anti-tuberculosis drug stockout prediction using synthetic longitudinal data as a methodological test bed prior to evaluation with operational hospital data. Drug-day predictors were derived from four domains: demand and consumption, inventory, procurement and supply, and historical stockouts. A 14-day horizon was used as the primary prediction target, with 7- and 30-day horizons considered for sensitivity analysis. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM were evaluated using temporally separated training, validation, and locked out-of-time test periods and compared with reorder-point and coverage-based inventory rules. Model assessment included recall, precision, specificity, F1-score, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Brier score, calibration, alert burden, temporal robustness, feature ablation, and predictive explanation. Logistic Regression was selected during validation but its recall decreased to 0.556 in the locked test period, whereas LightGBM descriptively achieved a recall of 0.889 and XGBoost a PR-AUC of 0.960. The results demonstrate the importance of locked temporal evaluation, multidomain predictors, threshold selection, and operationally oriented assessment. These findings validate the analytical pipeline rather than establish real-world effectiveness; external evaluation using SIMRS data remains required.

title: Large language medicine needs a foundation, not only a frontier
abstract: At the Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly this year, more than 150 official statements on data, digital health, and artificial intelligence (AI) were delivered by 74 countries and 10 regional blocs, alongside 42 side events, and over 30 Ministers of Health affirming digital transformation as a core feature of resilient health systems. The through line was consistent across every region: countries are calling for concerted global leadership towards shared standards and clear governance to validate, benchmark, and regulate AI in health.Sustainable, effective AI requires an ecosystem to function, and often carries real risks to data sovereignty, privacy, and equity. AI trained on incomplete data, tested in narrow settings, or deployed without attention to bias and local context can reproduce, and even amplify, the very inequities it aims to close. It is against this backdrop that we read the lead article by Guni et al. on "large language medicine (1)." We share the authors' optimism but sharpen their central question: not whether generative and multimodal AI will reshape medicine, but how we build the scaffolding that ensures the reshaping happens safely, equitably, and sustainably.Deep learning, generative AI, large language models (LLMs), and connected agentic systems promise both incremental and transformative change across diagnostics, disease management, surveillance, prevention, and drug discovery. Yet, as Guni et al. candidly note, today's clinically mature, regulator-approved tools remain predominantly diagnostic and built on older machine learning architectures. LLMs have not yet crossed into routine practice; interconnected agentic systems are being introduced only in a fraction of cutting-edge facilities. Health systems and clinical medicine, although a rich proving ground for technical experimentation and innovation, are also understandably cautious and risk averse. The principles of evidence-based medicine further solidify the need for requisite, repeated, and rigorous demonstration of efficacy before well-established practices are altered. Some Author 1 et al. Short title/running header 4 critique this caution as innovation recalcitrance; given the duty of care in health, it is better understood as the scientific scrutiny that any clinical tool, however heavily promoted, should be expected to survive.An AI solution does not scale on its own; it scales when an ecosystem for scale exists or is built around it. This includes clear regulatory capacity and governance, strong health information systems, and trained health personnel. We posit that a key element of that enabling foundation is digital public infrastructure for health. Some of the most durable gains come not from what makes headlines but from the unglamorous parts of the system no one photographs: the unique identifiers and information exchanges, the semantic standards which allow systems to interoperate, powering supply chains that keep essential medicines on the shelf, and persistent records that follow a patient across facilities within a health system to maintain continuity of care. Countries that adopted monolithic, donor-funded digital health tools have already seen those systems collapse when funding shifted; language models deployed as parallel silos, disconnected from a shared reference architecture, risk repeating that failure at greater speed and scale. Technology-neutral reference architectures, developed collaboratively across health and telecommunications agencies and built on open standards, offer a map for where these foundations should sit (2). AI cannot pervade "every aspect of medicine," as Guni et al. envision, without an underlying layer of high-quality data structured for interoperability, disciplined evaluation protocols, and the systems analysis required to introduce AI into existing clinical workflows. Experimental systems may be introduced into clinical practice, but without clear proof points and performance benchmarks, their transition from pilot to clinical standard will likely be slow and inequitable. Ministries and hospital systems are already experiencing a glut of vendors promising impressive solutions to long-standing challenges, often without the accompanying (3,4), or countries with the least regulatory capacity will simply import externally reviewed systems without local ownership. Regulatory sandboxes, such as the United Kingdom's AI Airlock, which allows supervised testing of AI tools that fit no existing device category (5), remain an underused bridge between principle and practice. Harmonization does not mean uniformity; it means enough common evidentiary ground that a safety finding in one country still holds in another, since the models themselves will cross borders faster than any single regulator's jurisdiction can follow. Language, disease burden, health system maturity, and data availability vary enormously; a model validated in one setting cannot be assumed safe in another. Multi-institutional, privacy-preserving evaluation designed into deployment from the start, not bolted on afterward, should be the norm, particularly for populations already under-represented in training data. This brings us to what authentic inclusion in AI design actually looks like. It is not access to a shared global model. It is each country's ability to shape a model on the data of its own population, keep it under its own governance, regulate it according to its own values and context, and operate it through a health workforce with the capacity to evaluate its outputs. A ministry that cannot inspect a model, audit its performance against its own population's outcomes, or withdraw it from clinical use does not exercise meaningful oversight.Sovereignty in this context is not isolation; it is knowing where data sit, who processes them, under whose law, and on what terms access can be revoked. Without populationrepresentative data, locally grounded regulation, and a trained workforce able to question and override the system where necessary, the populations furthest behind will bear the greatest exposure to model failure, precisely because they are least represented in training data and least resourced to identify when a system is underperforming. This is a critical moment to set a shared direction for how AI in health is governed. The including an AI "commons" for shared health data assets, a verifiable AI framework grounded in clinical evidence, and the newly launched Open Health Stack Software Foundation (7), so that they remain public goods rather than proprietary platforms. The UN's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, in its first preliminary report this year, named health among the domains where AI's benefits remain unevenly distributed and warned that safeguards cannot keep pace with its growth (8). Hopf bifurcation, bistability and transient grazing in apiecewise-smooth hospital-overload model
abstract: Abstract Hospital overload can occur during an epidemic wave even when the endemic state is compatible with routine admission. We analyse a continuous piecewise-smooth epidemic model in which severe cases enter a waiting class and hospital admission is the minimum of a demand-driven flux and a capacity-driven bed-filling flux. Three thresholds are separated: the basic reproduction number $R_0$, the endemic capacity threshold $b_{\mathrm{crit}}$, and the trajectory-dependent transient threshold $b_{\mathrm{trans}}$. The two one-sided Jacobians share an exact eigenpair, reducing each sixth-degree characteristic polynomial to a quintic. At the baseline parameters, the capacity-limited equilibrium undergoes a subcritical Hopf bifurcation at $b_H=0.2263\,b_{\mathrm{crit}}$. Single-shooting continuation with Floquet multipliers connects the unstable Hopf branch to a stable piecewise-smooth periodic branch through a lower fold of cycles and identifies an upper fold beyond $b_{\mathrm{crit}}$, producing two bistable capacity intervals. At $b=b_{\mathrm{trans}}$, the normal-care outbreak has a non-degenerate quadratic tangency with the switching surface. The overload duration scales as $(b_{\mathrm{trans}}-b)^{1/2}$, while the cumulative admission deficit and the trajectory perturbation are of order $(b_{\mathrm{trans}}-b)^{3/2}$. A Metzler comparison system gives a rigorous global lower bound on the first switching time. Independent symbolic and fixed-step computations reproduce the Hopf coefficient and a representative attracting cycle. An NHS England stock-flow check tracks held-out COVID-19 bed occupancy but does not identify the latent waiting class or capacity thresholds. The results show that equilibrium hospital adequacy does not guarantee transient or dynamical safety. MSC (2020): 92D30; 34A36; 37G15.

title: Ensuring a reliable blood supply during a pandemic in a Caribbean setting: The Curaçao experience
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: National blood systems require a resilient mechanism for ensuring safe blood supply during pandemics. For small island developing states (SIDS) additional specific challenges exist not normally addressed in guidelines and the literature. Here we describe the model used by the Caribbean island of Curaçao for pandemic preparedness during the COVID-19 pandemic. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Key measures taken by the Red Cross Blood bank Foundation Curaçao during the COVID-19 pandemic were examined. National blood program data were analyzed retrospectively. RESULTS: For pandemic preparedness, critical main processes were adapted during the COVID-19 pandemic. These included individual donor time-scheduled phlebotomy sessions and government-authorized lockdown travel permits. Work procedures focusing on the prevention of simultaneous presence of personnel during shifts were introduced. Donor information was provided during governmental public health briefings. Patient blood management programs were adopted according to international recommendations in consultation with the blood bank. During the COVID-19 pandemic, characterized by four severe outbreaks over 2 years, donor availability and donations were maintained with sufficient labile blood product supply to all hospitals served. CONCLUSION: For SIDS, effective small-scale implementation of international recommendations on pandemics remains challenging. The national blood program preparedness model of Curaçao proved to be successful during the COVID-19 pandemic, ensuring uninterrupted donor participation and sufficient labile blood product availability. Key success factors of the model were a voluntary, non-remunerated, repetitive donor program, a central blood collection facility, acknowledgement of the blood bank as important in the public health pandemic response, and effective communication with donors, hospitals, and health authorities.

title: Emergency Medicine Reimagined: Development of the Patient Rights Index for Emergency Medicine
abstract: Introduction: Emergency medicine has evolved beyond episodic acute care to encompass a growing range of clinical, social, and system-level responsibilities. This scholarly perspective proposes the Patient Rights Index in Emergency Medicine (PRI-ED), a conceptual framework designed to organize recurring domains through which emergency departments promote access to care, patient safety, relief of suffering, autonomy, and dignity. Methods: The PRI-ED was developed through iterative domain generation informed by clinical observation, professional experience, and targeted review of peer-reviewed literature, policy analyses, and professional organizational reports. No primary data collection, systematic review, formal consensus process, or empirical validation was performed. Results: We identified 12 domains that represent recurring clinical, operational, and system-level challenges encountered in emergency medicine. These domains were organized within a standardized framework linking domain-specific objectives, intervention strategies, measurable indicators, and relevant policy or funding mechanisms. Conclusion: The PRI-ED is a proposed conceptual framework for organizing and evaluating domains in which emergency medicine intersects with access, safety, autonomy, relief of suffering, and dignity. The framework is intended to inform future implementation, evaluation, and policy discussion and requires feasibility testing and outcome validation before effectiveness can be determined.

title: Governance‑Driven Integration of Multi‑Source Renewable Energy Systems in South African Private Hospitals
journal: International Journal of Business Ecosystem and Strategy (2687-2293)
abstract: This study investigates how a major South African private hospital group adopts and scales multiple renewable energy sources (MRES) within a mission-critical healthcare environment characterised by chronic grid instability. Using a qualitative single‑case study design, the research draws on semi-structured interviews with senior executives and technical managers, complemented by documentary analysis, to explore the barriers, enablers and governance mechanisms underpinning MRES adoption. The results reveal that financial and economic constraints, regulatory fragmentation, legacy infrastructure, and supply chain limitations constitute multidimensional barriers. In contrast, economic viability, executive leadership, risk-managed implementation, and energy-security imperatives serve as decisive enablers. The study demonstrates that effective adoption arises not from technology choices alone, but from an integrated organisational approach that combines diversified energy portfolios, phased implementation strategies, contractual procurement, and structured sustainability governance. The proposed Integrated MRES Adoption Framework synthesises these dimensions, offering a holistic model for energy transition in high-risk medical settings. The study concludes that hospitals can meaningfully advance renewable energy penetration when technical diversification is embedded within robust governance, financial feasibility assessments, and patient-safety-aligned risk management. Limitations include a single-case scope and senior-level perspectives; future research should compare public and private systems, evaluate long-term performance, and deepen inquiry into staff-level change processes.

title: Optimal Resources for Children's Surgery 2: Tiered Recommendations for Minimum Essential Children's Surgical Procedures Across Health System Levels
abstract: BACKGROUND: In 2015 the World Health Assembly (WHO), based on recommendations by the Lancet Commission on Global Surgery, passed resolution (68:15) on strengthening emergency and essential surgical care and anesthesia as a component of universal health coverage. However, children's surgery was not adequately represented and in response, the Global Initiative for Children's Surgery (GICS) published the Optimal Resources for Children's Surgical Care (OReCS) in 2019 providing insight into procedures which should be performed at different facility types. OReCS 2 addresses a gap in both policy and published literature to further define surgical conditions and procedural capabilities by hospital level. METHODS: We performed a review of the literature to identify procedures routinely performed in a variety of settings. We then used an iterative Delphi like approach to identify specialty-specific procedures and nursing skills by hospital level. Participation was open to all members of GICS with representation from 21 working groups and more than 50 low-middle income countries (LMICs) and high-income countries (HICs). Data on essential procedures were collected for twelve specialty groups. Modifications of the recommendations provided by the working groups were made by the executive board based on firsthand knowledge of capabilities at lower-level facilities where subspecialists have less experience. Final recommendations were made based on greater than 75% agreement by respondents and review of the executive board of GICS. RESULTS: Procedures performed at health centers were limited to those not requiring anesthesia or sedation and were largely identified to help triage and stabilize patients for transfer to higher level care. Similarly, first level hospital procedures focused on stabilization and transfer to referral level hospitals for most specialties. Alternatively, specialties such as ophthalmology and dental surgery have identified definitive procedures for lower-level facilities. Procedures performed at the National Children's Hospital level include those requiring specialty providers and equipment such as transplantation, repair of congenital heart disease, and reconstructive surgery for complex trauma, congenital anomalies, and burns. CONCLUSIONS: This updated version of OReCS provides specific examples of procedural capabilities for twelve subspecialties at the health center, first, second, third, and referral level hospitals in LMICs. Whereas the list is not meant to be all inclusive, it provides a framework within which to define the minimum essential material resources, equipment, and personnel by hospital level.

title: Medetomidine in the Illicit Drug Supply: Emergency Management of Intoxication and Withdrawal
abstract: Background Medetomidine, a highly potent α₂-adrenergic agonist veterinary sedative, has emerged as an adulterant in the unregulated opioid supply, producing a distinct spectrum of intoxication and withdrawal that poses new challenges for emergency clinicians. Objective To summarize the epidemiology, pharmacology, diagnosis, clinical features, and emergency department management of medetomidine intoxication and withdrawal. Methods We conducted a narrative review of PubMed/MEDLINE from database inception through October 10, 2026, supplemented by reference-list review. Peer-reviewed human studies, toxicologic surveillance reports, relevant pharmacologic and veterinary studies, governmental and public health reports, prescribing information, and clinical guidance were included when pertinent to emergency care. Discussion Acute medetomidine intoxication is characterized by profound central nervous system depression, marked bradycardia, and variable blood pressure abnormalities, often in the setting of fentanyl co-exposure. Routine hospital toxicology screens do not detect medetomidine, making diagnosis primarily clinical and dependent on local epidemiology. Management is supportive, with naloxone directed toward concomitant opioid-induced respiratory depression. Withdrawal can produce severe autonomic hyperactivity with hypertension, tachycardia, agitation, nausea, and vomiting and may require oral α₂-agonists or intravenous dexmedetomidine, along with treatment of concurrent opioid withdrawal. No reversal agent is approved for medetomidine intoxication in humans; atipamezole remains investigational. Conclusions Emergency clinicians should recognize both intoxication and withdrawal, provide syndrome-directed supportive and α₂-agonist therapy, and incorporate harm reduction and addiction treatment while evidence continues to evolve.

title: Research Progress and Development Trends in Smart Hospital Operations Management under Digital Transformation
abstract: Digital transformation is changing hospital management from fragmented information processing toward integrated, data-driven, and increasingly intelligent operations. Smart hospitals combine electronic health records (EHRs), interoperable data platforms, artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), cloud computing, automation, real-time dashboards, and emerging digital twin technologies to support clinical services and organizational management. This narrative review synthesizes recent research on the progress, management value, implementation barriers, and development trends of smart hospital operations. Current applications are concentrated in patient flow and bed management, operating-room scheduling, workforce and equipment allocation, medication and supply-chain management, quality and safety monitoring, and administrative automation. Evidence suggests that digital technologies can improve information visibility, forecasting, coordination, and process standardization; however, technology deployment alone does not guarantee better outcomes. Benefits depend heavily on interoperability, data quality, workflow redesign, organizational leadership, user acceptance, cybersecurity, governance, and continuous performance evaluation. In particular, poorly designed EHR workflows may increase documentation burden, while AI systems introduce risks related to bias, transparency, accountability, and lifecycle monitoring. Future smart hospitals are likely to evolve toward integrated command platforms, multimodal AI, ambient intelligence, predictive and prescriptive analytics, and digital twins capable of simulating operational scenarios before real-world implementation. From a medical management perspective, the central task is therefore to shift from technology-centered construction to value-oriented digital governance. Hospitals should align digital investment with measurable operational objectives, establish multidisciplinary governance mechanisms, and evaluate efficiency, quality, safety, workforce experience, equity, and return on investment simultaneously.

title: BIG DATA ANALYTICS IN HEALTHCARE AND PHARMACY
Complex Adaptive Systems in Healthcare: Evidence and Challenges in a Large Public University Hospital: a single case study
abstract: Abstract Background This study investigates the organizational and operational dynamics of a large public university hospital and emergency room, addressing the reductionist paradigm that conceptualizes hospitals as mechanical factories resulting in operational silos and fragmentation. The aim of this research is to analyze these dynamics utilizing the framework of Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS) theory. Methods The research employs a single case study design with a mixed-methods approach. Between April and December 2025, 57 institutional areas and processes were mapped using the SIPOC tool, while intersectoral interactions were modeled through graph analysis. Data triangulation was achieved through semi-structured interviews, direct observation, and document analysis. Results The constructed network included 585 interaction pairs, illustrating an integrated ecosystem characterized by critical mutual dependencies. It highlighted that administrative and logistical information flows are as essential to care delivery as clinical actions. Analysis of 510 outputs indicated a predominance of administrative and logistical support (65.9%). Of 322 cataloged operational problems, the most frequent categories were "Processes and Systems" and "Infrastructure and Logistics." The diversity of surgical procedures and the skewed distribution of intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay underscore the necessity for adaptable organizational structures to address the complexity and uncertainty inherent in hospital care. Conclusions Hospital efficiency is primarily driven by local interactions rather than centralized directives. Conceptualizing the hospital as a value network, rather than a linear chain, addresses the limitations of siloed management and supports a more resilient, integrated care model consistent with Healthcare 4.0. Managers are encouraged to facilitate "adaptive spaces" that enhance horizontal communication and information flow. Trial registration : Not applicable.

title: Strategies for sustaining sexual and reproductive health services during recurrent flooding in Adamawa State, Nigeria: a qualitative study
abstract: Abstract Seasonal flooding in Adamawa State, Nigeria damages health facilities, breaks supply chains, and displaces health workers and communities, while increasing health needs. Sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services are often deprioritized, yet evidence on how they are sustained remains limited. We examined how SRH services were sustained during recurrent flooding. We conducted a qualitative descriptive study in the flood-prone Local Government Areas of Numan and Fufore. We held eight focus group discussions with women and girls and 20 key informant interviews with health providers, supply chain actors, and program implementers. Flooding closed or damaged health facilities, broke supply and cold chains, and displaced health workers. Participants linked these disruptions to unattended births and to rising hemorrhage, stillbirth, miscarriage, and genital infections. Service continuity depended less on the formal health system than on anticipatory, community-led adaptation across three phases. Before floods, stakeholders mapped risk, pre-positioned commodities, trained women in contraceptive self-injection, and dispensed medicines in advance. During floods, care shifted to mobile outreach, task-sharing, transport by canoe and boat, and community-led referral. Community health workers, traditional birth attendants, Ward Development Committees, and women’s groups reached cut-off communities. Across seasons, adaptations evolved toward cash transfers, savings groups, local reusable-pad production, and decentralized commodity hubs. Continuity relied heavily on unpaid community labor and women’s own resources. Sustaining SRH services in flood-prone settings requires institutionalized preparedness, decentralized supply, empowered communities, and protected health financing. Community-led models offer a transferable approach to health security in a changing climate.

title: Selected Abstracts from PSGH AGM 2026 Scientific Session
abstract: This supplement presents the abstracts selected for the scientific session of the 90th Anniversary Annual General Meeting and Scientific Conference of the Pharmaceutical Society of Ghana (PSGH), held in Accra in September 2026 under the theme "Science. Impact. Legacy. 90 Years of Pharmaceutical Excellence." The Scientific Review Committee selected 38 abstracts for oral and poster presentation. They report original work from teaching hospitals, district health services, community pharmacies, regulatory and public health programmes, and universities across Ghana. The largest group addresses antimicrobial stewardship, including: antibiotic prescribing audits using the WHO AWaRe and WHO/INRUD indicators local antibiogram development stewardship programmes and training for clinicians and pharmacists A second group assesses the quality of medicines on the Ghanaian market, chiefly by validated reverse-phase HPLC and pharmacopeial testing of cardiovascular, antidiabetic and antibiotic products. Other contributions cover: medication safety and pharmacist-led interventions malaria commodity security and supply chain integrity expanded community pharmacy services, including STI testing, hypertension screening, vaccination and adherence support oncology outcomes and pharmacogenomics mental health regulatory confidentiality law the effects of illegal mining on the pharmaceutical sector Together, the abstracts document the growing contribution of pharmacists to patient safety, medicine quality and health system strengthening in Ghana. They also identify priorities for policy, practice and further research. Abstracts are published as accepted by the Scientific Review Committee and have not undergone full peer review.

title: A Systematic Review of the Adequacy of Hypertension Treatment in Women Attending Azadi Teaching Hospital During Crises in Kirkuk, Iraq
journal: International Journal of Scientific Research Updates
abstract: Background: Elevated intraocular pressure is a major, dangerous and modifiable risk factor, as the resulting deaths are primarily due to cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases worldwide. Control of this condition is particularly important in the context of the disruptions caused by humanitarian crises; it has been found that in the city of Kirkuk in Iraq, there have been prolonged periods of instability, and among the causes of this during the period from 2014 to 2017, during the time of ISIS’s control and the widespread displacement that occurred repeatedly. This has been a major cause of sustained pressure on Azadi Teaching Hospital, which is considered a key referral centre in that governorate. Women attending outpatient clinics for this condition have faced overlapping problems that have prevented them from receiving treatment. Ultimately, the evidence regarding the appropriateness of treatment for these women remains extremely limited, fragmented and incomplete. Objective: To systematically review the available evidence on the adequacy of hypertension treatment among women attending Azadi Teaching Hospital, Kirkuk, during periods of crisis, and to synthesize contextual, regional, and global data to inform recommendations. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Google Scholar, regional journals (Kirkuk Journal of Medical Sciences, Eastern Mediterranean Health Journal), and grey literature was conducted (search period: inception to September 2026). Studies were eligible if they reported on hypertension prevalence, treatment, adherence, or control among adults attending Azadi Teaching Hospital, or among Iraqi/crisis-affected populations where data were relevant to that setting. The exposure of interest was treatment adequacy, defined by four domains: (1) proportion receiving antihypertensive treatment, (2) guideline-concordance of prescribed regimens, (3) medication adherence, and (4) achieved blood pressure control (<140/90 mmHg). Risk of bias was assessed narratively given the predominance of cross-sectional designs. Results: Seven studies met inclusion criteria. Only two studies were conducted directly at Azadi Teaching Hospital; the remainder provided Iraqi, Kurdistan-region, or crisis-setting contextual evidence. The prevalence and incidence of high blood pressure amongst patients attending Azadi Teaching Hospital reached a very high rate of 41 per cent, whilst treatment coverage was very low and control of the condition, where possible, was very poor. A 2018 Azadi study found 93% of hypertensive patients uncontrolled. Evidence from Baghdad and Erbil showed control rates of 38.7% and 22% (rising to 47% with intensive follow-up), respectively. Female sex appeared protective for control in Erbil but not in Baghdad. Crisis-related barriers medication supply disruption, cost, out-of-pocket purchase, and interrupted follow-up were consistent across settings. Evidence specific to women at Azadi during crises remains sparse, and no study disaggregated treatment adequacy fully by sex and crisis phase. Conclusions: Hypertension treatment adequacy among women attending Azadi Teaching Hospital during crises is likely inadequate across all measured domains, consistent with national Iraqi and crisis-affected regional data. Priority actions include sex-disaggregated prospective monitoring, medication supply-chain strengthening, adherence support, task-sharing with clinical pharmacists, and integration of hypertension into crisis-preparedness planning.

title: What Do Patients with Long-Term Conditions Disclose About Medication Adherence During and After Hospital Discharge? A Qualitative Study at an Internal Medicines Ward in Norway
abstract: Purpose: To explore how patients' life circumstances, perceptions, lived experiences and behaviors may influence medication adherence in the social context surrounding hospital discharge. Patients and Methods: Ten patients aged 48-89 years were included at a hospital ward close to the presumed day of discharge, observed during healthcare personnel (HCP) encounters and interviewed 1-2 weeks after discharge. Medication adherence was reconstructed through medication reconciliation and by comparing observations of hospital encounters and discharge information with patients' post-discharge accounts of medication use. Data were analyzed using content analysis to identify themes across participants and narratives to explore individual experiences. Results: The analysis revealed the themes 1) "beliefs about medicines" and 2) "self-efficacy". We found that patient beliefs about medicines were often not fully explored during clinical encounters, however according to the patients, these factors play a key role in explaining adherence challenges. Although all patients stated that they intended to take their medications as instructed by the HCPs at the hospital, more than half of them had consciously or unconsciously changed the medication treatment compared to the discharge summary. The patient narratives illustrate multiple factors contributing to non-adherence after hospital discharge. Conclusion: This study suggests that important influences on medication adherence may remain insufficiently explored during routine discharge encounters. Our findings indicate that discharge processes could be strengthened by incorporating more structured and patient-centred conversations that invite patients to discuss their beliefs, concerns, and anticipated challenges with medication management. This could include asking open-ended questions about how patients understand their treatment, how they expect to manage it in daily life, and what uncertainties or barriers they foresee. Such conversations might help identify barriers to adherence and better support patients' self-management after discharge.

title: Assessing the importance of trained technicians in hospital management: A study of hospitals in Gujarat
journal: International Journal of Research in Management

title: Global insulin supply insecurity and the role of manufacturing innovation
abstract: Insulin availability and affordability have long limited access in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), and recent shortages and product withdrawals in higher-income settings underscore the need for reliable supply worldwide. While documented disruptions do not establish an aggregate global manufacturing deficit, commercial decisions, regulatory barriers, procurement, financing, and distribution can restrict access even where production capacity exists. Nevertheless, product prioritization and investment decisions can constrain the capacity allocated to insulin and reduce the ability to respond to changing demand. This narrative review examines global insulin demand, supply insecurity, market structure, affordability, and health-system barriers, distinguishing the circumstances of the United States, other high-income countries, and LMICs. We consider the potential effects of incretin therapies on insulin requirements and industrial investment and assess manufacturing modernization, including continuous production, as one component of a broader response. Proposed technological benefits require insulin-specific validation of quality, productivity, cost, and commercial feasibility. Priorities include stronger shortage surveillance, diversified qualified suppliers, regulatory cooperation, sustainable procurement, reduced waste, and dependable distribution. Supply security must extend through safe storage, administration, education, and glucose monitoring. Coordinated action across manufacturing and health systems is needed to maintain uninterrupted, affordable access to appropriate insulin treatment.

title: Quality control of blood components: A Six-Year Multicentre Retrospective Study in Tertiary Care Hospitals in Bangladesh
abstract: Background Before prescribing blood components physicians must know the quality of blood that actually fulfil the requirements of patients. In the field of transfusion medicine, blood components therapy is also a standard care therapy globally. In this study we evaluated three hospital data related to quality control of blood components that we prepare and issue. Objectives To evaluate compliance of blood components with AABB quality standards. Materials and Methods A multicentre retrospective study with 95% confidence interval, the study were done in three tertiary care hospitals in Dhaka, Bangladesh. In which total number of Whole Blood (WB) were 55650, RCC were 45420, SDP were 20124, RDP were 25264 and FFP were 48530. Sampling method was simple random sampling technique. Four of each blood components were analyzed every monthly throughout the study period. All blood units (RBCs, RCCs, RDPs, SDPs and FFP) from donors in Ibn Sina Medical College, Delta hospital and Green Life Hospital blood bank were included in the study with the exclusion of blood units which were not processed in these hospital (Outside Blood), leucocyte depleted blood products and washed blood products. Automated cell counter Sysmex XN-1000, and XN -2000, Stago auto analyser were used to obtain desired parameters. Results In our study, 91% of WB, 91% of RCC, 92% of RDP, 95% of SDP and 80% of FFP met the quality compliance with international standard. Conclusion The quality control (QC) data generated in this study provides essential insights into the performance of modern blood collection and processing systems. More than 90% studied blood components like WB, RCC, RDP, SDP strictly complied with international standards. However, FFP analysis could not be done according to AABB and international guideline due to financial constrain rather it was surrogate study. Ultimately, establishing a comprehensive QC program, alongside strict adherence to departmental protocols and manufacturer instructions is vital for blood centers to ensure effective and reliable operational outcomes. Bangladesh Journal of Medical Science Vol. 25 No. 04 October’26 Page: 1338-1345

title: Sustainable energy and water management in green hospitals: a narrative review
journal: International Journal of Research in Medical Sciences
abstract: Hospitals consume substantial amounts of energy and water, while intensive care units (ICUs) have high resource demands because life-support equipment, monitoring systems and heating, ventilation and air conditioning operate continuously. This narrative review examines hospital and critical-care environmental impacts, sustainable energy and water management, healthcare workers’ knowledge and practices, and the use of Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycles. Literature and guidance were identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, PubMed Central, Google Scholar, publisher databases and relevant health-agency and professional-society websites, and findings were synthesised thematically. The reviewed evidence identifies building energy, especially HVAC, and clinical consumables as major environmental hotspots. Water conservation must be planned alongside infection prevention and essential hygiene. Healthcare workers often express environmental concern but lack practical training, infrastructure and organisational support. Education combined with prompts, checklists, audit and feedback, local champions and leadership support is more likely to translate awareness into routine practice. The review also describes a 45-day quality-improvement project involving 80 staff members in ICUs at a hospital in Gurugram, India. Following two PDSA cycles, knowledge scores and observed practice adherence improved. In a descriptive comparison of one pre-intervention month with one post-intervention month, electricity use per occupied bed decreased by 17.7%, diesel use by 54.9% and water use per occupied bed-day by 11.25%. Because the project had no concurrent control group and compared only one month before and after the intervention, these changes cannot be attributed conclusively to the intervention. Longer time series, patient-safety balancing measures and transparent carbon accounting are needed to assess whether improvements are sustained.

title: Oral Health and High‐Complexity Networks: A Functional Interdependence Analysis via Health Information Systems
DIGITAL TWIN MODELS FOR PREDICTIVE MAINTENANCE OF MEDICAL EQUIPMENT
abstract: Digital twin models have become an important enabler in predictive maintenance of medical equipment to meet the increased need of reliability, safety, and cost efficiency in the contemporary healthcare setting.The traditional maintenance approaches are still more reactive or time based that results in unplanned downtime, delayed clinical process, and higher operational cost.The proposed research intends to design and test a data driven digital twinbased framework that can keep a constant check, predict, and optimize the health of critical medical equipment, including MRI scanners, ventilators, infusion pumps, and the system of patient monitoring.The proposed methodology will combine multi sensor telemetry, equipment use history with fault history records to create a high fidelity virtual replica of physical assets.The degradation modeling, fault prediction and remaining useful life estimation utilizes advanced algorithms such as physics informed models, long short term memory networks, auto encoder based anomaly detection and gradient boosting classifiers.The proposed digital twin model achieved a fault-prediction accuracy of 96.4% and a false alarm rate of 3.2%.The LSTM-based model achieved a remaining useful life prediction accuracy of 96.3% at 150 training epochs.Moreover, the framework allows reducing the unplanned equipment downtimes by 31 percent and maintenance expenses by 27 percent on the whole.The paper identifies scalability, interoperability, and regulatory preparedness in the hospital deployment situation in other clinical settings.

title: Evaluating medical device safety, equipment lifecycle management, and clinical technology optimization in health systems: a systematic review of primary research involving healthcare technology engineers, biomedical engineering specialists, and healthcare service engineers
journal: Journal of Hunan University Natural Sciences
abstract: Abstract Background and objective: Safe medical technology depends on equipment selection, maintenance, repair, replacement, and professional oversight throughout its operational life. Evidence concerning engineering contributions is dispersed across workforce research, hospital improvement projects, and decision models. This review examines primary research addressing medical device safety, equipment lifecycle management, and clinical technology optimization involving healthcare engineering personnel. Methods: Ten primary reports published before the eligibility cutoff of 31 May 2026 were examined through narrative synthesis. Studies addressed technician training, failure analysis, maintenance processes, replacement prioritization, computerized management, and predictive analytics. Findings were organized by intervention, operational outcome, and relevance to clinical safety. Results: A Rwandan comparison reported equipment out of service at 10.2% in hospitals with trained technicians versus 17.8% in comparator hospitals, alongside higher technician productivity. A Jordanian improvement project reported a 35% reduction in downtime. Predictive maintenance research reported potential diagnostic and repair savings reaching 25% in one analyzer application. A Malaysian study classified maintenance and replacement priorities using records for 13,352 devices. Other reports demonstrated structured failure assessment, replacement ranking, inventory digitization, and lifecycle-specific maintenance planning. Outcomes primarily concerned equipment performance and management processes, limiting conclusions about patient harm. Conclusion: Engineering involvement supports organized maintenance, technical workforce development, and transparent lifecycle decisions. Evidence of operational benefit exceeds evidence of clinical benefit. Comparative evaluations linking engineering interventions with patient outcomes remain necessary. Keywords: Clinical engineering; biomedical engineering; medical device safety; equipment lifecycle; maintenance management; healthcare technology management.

title: MANAGEMENT OF MEDICAL AND HOSPITAL EQUIPMENT IN THE SURGICAL CENTER: CHALLENGES AND LESSONS LEARNED BY THE NURSING COORDINATION TEAM
Analysis and Exploration of a Diversified Collaborative Maintenance Scheme for Medical Equipment in Tertiary Grade A Hospitals Based on the SPO Model
abstract: With the continuous expansion of medical equipment assets in large tertiary grade A hospitals, the contradiction between cost, efficiency, and technical depth in the traditional single maintenance mode has become increasingly prominent, necessitating a systematic governance framework to guide the optimal allocation of maintenance resources. Based on Donabedian’s “Structure-Process-Outcome” (SPO) three-dimensional quality evaluation model, this study explores the construction of a diversified collaborative maintenance framework for medical equipment applicable to large medical institutions, promoting the transformation of maintenance governance from “single-mode dependence” to “hierarchical and classified collaboration.” Through a systematic literature review and international comparative analysis, a multidimensional comparative framework for three mainstream maintenance modes was established; based on longitudinal data from a tertiary grade A hospital from 2023 to 2025, the SPO model was applied for structural diagnosis. The hospital’s three-year data showed that the total value of equipment assets increased by 21.3% (2.82 billion yuan→3.42 billion yuan), while the number of engineers increased by only 3 (14→17), with the ratio as low as 1:1123 (international benchmark: 1:250–300); annual maintenance expenditure increased by 8.8% (57.03 million yuan→62.04 million yuan), among which OEM maintenance accounted for continuously >60%, and the book COSR remained at 1.8%–2.0%, but indirect costs such as labor costs were not included. SPO diagnosis revealed progressive deficiencies in the current governance, characterized by “insufficient structural resources—incomplete process development—concentration of outcome modes.” This paper proposes a four-level hierarchical governance structure: Level A core assets adopt “OEM primary service + daily in-hospital inspection”; Level B critical equipment adopts “in-hospital preventive maintenance as the main approach + OEM technical support for major failures”; Level C general equipment adopts “in-hospital independent maintenance + audited third-party repair”; Level D low-value equipment adopts “replacement instead of repair.” This framework provides a theoretical basis and practical pathway for large medical institutions to overcome dependence on OEMs and build a sustainable maintenance ecosystem.

title: Internet of things-enabled biomedical engineering: current applications, challenges, and emerging directions
journal: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
abstract: The internet of medical things (IoMT) is a structured integrative review of the internet of things (IoT) that focuses on the medical field, specifically on the integration of physiological sensors, medical devices, communication networks, and the clinical information systems to monitor and track patients' health and conditions continuously, and use data to support medical treatment. Through July 2026, a reproducible search and evidence audit of PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, publisher/digital object identifier (DOI) records, and authoritative regulatory and standards repositories was conducted. The final evidence base consisted of 65 distinct sources that were assessed using a set of explicit eligibility criteria and evidence weighting. Wearable atrial-fibrillation screening, remote monitoring, digital inhalers and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM), and connected hospital infrastructure were shown to be clinically significant in large-scale studies, but such benefits were only seen if there was confirmatory pathway, workflow integration, data quality and persistent engagement. Cybersecurity, privacy, interoperability, validation, workforce capacity, equity, and lifecycle sustainability were all key challenges. The review also brought a synthesis and readiness framework that connects edge artificial intelligence (AI), federated learning, digital twins, advanced connectivity, and circular lifecycle management with measurable validation and governance requirements across the domains.

title: Machine learning and failure mode and effects analysis for sustainable medical equipment spare parts management
journal: IAES International Journal of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Spare parts for essential medical equipment are vital to ensure uninterrupted healthcare provision, especially in areas where resources are limited. This paper presents an integrative approach that integrates failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) with supervised machine learning (ML) models in order to allow better predictive maintenance and optimize management of spare parts. In order to increase the accuracy of the forecast, FMEA was first used to compute risk priority numbers (RPNs) of the components, quantifying the risk of each component, and then using it as an important input feature to the ML algorithms. Data from six hospitals and ten critical medical devices, such as ventilators, defibrillators, dialysis machines, and computed tomography (CT) scanners, were analyzed to identify high-risk failure modes and prioritize maintenance tasks. Three different supervised learning models (random forest (RF), artificial neural network (ANN), and support vector machine (SVM)) was built and tested based on four metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The precision of RF and ANN was 1.00 and SVM showed an excellent recall value of 0.94, indicating promising results for practical applications. The solution proposed consists of a hierarchical decision system, connecting risk assessment carried out by experts with data-driven forecasts, to create proactive and sustainable management of spare parts. This approach helps healthcare entities lessen the risk of equipment breakdowns, adhere to international healthcare standards, and increase system reliability and efficiency.

title: Remote Diagnostics to Field-Service Dispatch: An AI-Enabled Salesforce Framework for Medical Equipment
THE ROLE OF MEDICAL DEVICE SPECIALISTS IN CLINICAL ENGINEERING DECISION-MAKING FOR DEVICE REPLACEMENT AND END-OF-LIFE MANAGEMENT: A NARRATIVE REVIEW OF SAFETY, COST, AND OBSOLESCENCE PROTOCOLS
abstract: Medical device replacement and end-of-life management are important components of clinical engineering and healthcare technology management, influencing patient safety, operational reliability, financial sustainability, and environmental performance. This narrative review examines the role of medical device specialists in clinical engineering decision-making, with particular attention to equipment reliability, maintenance requirements, replacement prioritization, technological obsolescence, and sustainable resource utilization. The review synthesizes literature addressing medical equipment selection, lifecycle assessment, maintenance management, healthcare technology evaluation, and circular economy approaches. The reviewed literature highlights the importance of evaluating multiple criteria rather than relying exclusively on equipment age or acquisition costs. Technical condition, failure history, clinical criticality, repair feasibility, manufacturer support, and total lifecycle expenditure can collectively inform replacement decisions. Medical device specialists contribute by interpreting equipment performance data, assessing risks, coordinating with clinical and administrative stakeholders, and developing evidence-based recommendations. Digital monitoring and predictive maintenance offer additional opportunities to improve equipment oversight, provided that data quality, cybersecurity, and institutional capabilities are adequately addressed. The review also emphasizes the relevance of refurbishment, reuse, recycling, and environmentally responsible disposal when these options satisfy safety and regulatory requirements. An integrated decision-making framework combining safety, technical performance, economic considerations, and technological sustainability is proposed to support transparent and consistent equipment lifecycle management. Strengthening clinical engineering capacity and institutional governance may improve resource allocation and equipment availability, including within Saudi healthcare institutions. Further empirical research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of integrated replacement strategies across diverse healthcare settings.

title: INFECTION PREVENTION AND CONTROL IN MILITARY AND CORRECTIONAL HEALTHCARE FACILITIES IN SAUDI ARABIA AN INTERPROFESSIONAL NARRATIVE REVIEW OF NURSING, PHARMACY, MEDICAL LABORATORY, AND BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING ROLES
abstract: Infection prevention and control (IPC) in military and correctional healthcare depends on coordinated clinical, diagnostic, pharmaceutical, and technical work. This narrative review examines the development of IPC from hygiene and surveillance to contemporary implementation programmes and analyzes its relevance to Saudi Arabia. Targeted searches of biomedical publications and WHO, CDC, and Saudi Ministry of Health resources were updated in October 2026. The synthesis includes Saudi MERS investigations, central-line surveillance and improvement studies, antimicrobial stewardship in tertiary and military care, correctional latent-tuberculosis screening, Candida auris genomic investigation, and Hajj prevention experience. These sources show how patient movement, diagnostic communication, environmental conditions, and professional responsibilities influence prevention. International trials provide complementary evidence on rapid diagnostics and terminal disinfection. The review proposes evaluating delays between risk recognition, information transfer, and completed action, supported by practical patient- and equipment-transfer records. These proposals require local validation. Evidence is heterogeneous and much of it observational; results from individual institutions cannot establish national effectiveness or the performance of the authors’ facilities. A context-sensitive IPC programme should connect nursing practice, pharmacy stewardship, laboratory information, and biomedical engineering through clear responsibilities, reliable resources, and measurable follow-up.

title: Innovation Capability of Biomedical Engineering Enterprises Through Collaboration with Universities and R&D Institutions
MEDICAL OIL FREE SCREW & SCROLL AIR COMPRESSOR FOR HOSPITAL USE
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The air compressor in hospital will contact with the patient's body directly. The medical air compressor for hospital use is even related to the patient's life safety. Currently, the main problem is that there aren't professional directions and specifications for hospital air system construction, and the demand side often ignores this, too.
