title: From Education to Entrepreneurship: A Survey of Career Pathways for Biomedical Engineering Graduates
abstract: Biomedical engineering (BME) is an interdisciplinary field that prepares graduates for diverse professional pathways across research, industry, clinical engineering, regulatory affairs, AI-enabled digital health, pharma-biotech, public-sector organizations, and entrepreneurship. This survey synthesizes literature on BME graduate career trajectories and examines how educational experiences, professional skills, institutional support and innovation ecosystems shape post-graduation outcomes. The paper proposes a practical taxonomy of career pathways, compares pathway-specific skills and preparation needs, and develops advising sheets that connect academic preparation with software tools, certifications, internships, portfolio evidence, and entry-level roles. The review highlights that BME functions as a flexible platform degree, but its breadth can also create career uncertainty unless programs provide explicit career mapping, experiential learning, regulatory exposure, industry engagement, and entrepreneurship training. The paper concludes by identifying research gaps in longitudinal graduate tracking, entrepreneurship outcomes, and curriculum-to-career alignment, and recommends structured advising models to improve employability and career clarity for BME students.

title: Crash Cart Readiness and its Impact on Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Efficiency and Patient Safety in Hospital Emergency Settings.
Neuroengineering for Healthcare: Insights, Obstacles, and Potential Funding Sources for Biomedical Engineering Projects
abstract: Neuroengineering is an emerging field that holds the promise of revolutionising healthcare with new diagnostic and therapeutic technology. The convergence of neuroscience and biomedical engineering is leading the way for some of the most exciting advances in medicine today. The use of engineering practices within the complex structure of the human nervous system is helping to advance the treatment of formerly untreatable neurological illnesses. Many common barriers to innovation, including lack of understanding, increasing regulatory burdens, and lack of funding, prevent progress. The rapid emergence of new technology helps us understand how to innovate and learn from our colleagues in other fields. This review discusses recent advances in neuroengineering technologies and potential funding for biomedical projects. Overcoming translational barriers with integration of disciplines and technological innovation will be key to future success.

title: Microlectures teach, problem-based learning integrates: designing short clinical practicums in biomedical engineering education
abstract: Short hospital-based clinical practicums in biomedical engineering education place interdisciplinary learners in a bind: the placement is too brief for immersion, the supervising workforce is trained clinically rather than technically, and the intended competencies—which sit at the device–patient care interface—are poorly served by observation-based apprenticeship. This Perspective argues that combining problem-based learning (PBL) with microlectures—a work-integrated learning design distinct from a conventional flipped classroom and grounded in cognitive load theory—offers a tractable response, but only when the design fits the practicum's structure rather than a lecture course template. The division of labor is straightforward: Microlectures teach and PBL integrates. The former front-load the declarative knowledge and procedural routines that learners would otherwise assemble inside a compressed placement, reducing extraneous cognitive load and returning scarce on-site hours to supervised practice; PBL then supplies authentic, escalating problems that force learners to integrate engineering and clinical reasoning before they act. We propose SPICE (sequence, problem-anchoring, integration escalation, consistent facilitation, evidence-aligned assessment), grounded in cognitive load theory, situated cognition, and self-determination theory: a design framework of five coupled commitments—Sequence, Problem-anchoring, Integration escalation, Consistent facilitation, and Evidence-aligned assessment—each of which we specify as operationalizable and evaluable. Evaluators may expect procedural skill, reasoning performance, and learning experience to move more readily than declarative knowledge, and should not read a flat theory result as failure. We close by identifying what remains unresolved, including transfer, measurement, and equitable access.

title: Review Of Readiness For The Use Of The Hospital Management Information System In The Medical Record Unit Using The 7M Approach At Mulyasari Hospital
abstract: The Hospital Management Information System (HMIS/SIMRS) plays a crucial role in improving the efficiency and quality of healthcare services and therefore requires adequate organizational readiness for implementation. This study aimed to determine readiness for the use of SIMRS at Mulyasari Hospital based on the 7M approach: Man, Money, Materials, Methods, Machine, Management, and Market. A descriptive qualitative method with a cross-sectional approach was employed. Data were collected through interviews, observation, documentation review, and literature review involving nine informants selected by purposive sampling. The findings showed that the Management and Market aspects were categorized as good, whereas Man, Money, Materials, Methods, and Machine were categorized as fairly good. Identified constraints included training that had not yet been sufficiently comprehensive, limited human resources, facilities that did not fully meet service needs, delays in completing medical resumes, unstable networks, slow computers, and system disruptions during maintenance. Overall, Mulyasari Hospital was considered ready to use SIMRS, although several components still require improvement. Regular and more comprehensive training, additional personnel in understaffed units, optimization of budget utilization, development of system features according to service needs, stronger discipline in completing medical documentation, and improvement of information technology infrastructure are recommended to support more optimal and sustainable SIMRS utilization.

title: A comprehensive survey of communication technologies, security frameworks, and intelligent architectures for medical internet of things and quantum-enabled healthcare
abstract: The convergence of the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), advanced communication technologies, and biomedical engineering has advanced intelligent, connected healthcare. This comprehensive survey investigates the evolution of IoMT architectures and communication protocols, along with their application across a range of healthcare scenarios. It provides a comparative analysis of short-range and long-range communication technologies, with emphasis on secure, privacy-preserving, and energy-efficient designs tailored for IoMT devices. The review also highlights recent advances in enabling technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, and quantum computing, and their growing role in enhancing system intelligence, data security, and diagnostic precision. In addition, the study examines the integration of edge and cloud computing for real-time health monitoring, diagnostics, and decision support. Emerging trends, including AI-enabled IoMT systems, blockchain-based privacy frameworks, and next-generation biomedical sensors, are analyzed in depth. Drawing on over 200 peer-reviewed publications, this work identifies persistent challenges in current IoMT ecosystems, including interoperability, scalability, reliability, and data governance. It also reviews key use cases such as remote patient monitoring, smart hospitals, and emergency response systems, exploring their deployment strategies, success factors, and technical barriers. Despite notable advancements, critical gaps remain in areas such as standardization, energy optimization, and secure data management. The survey concludes by outlining future research directions focused on quantum-secured communication protocols, AI-driven adaptive healthcare architectures, and innovative sensing technologies. This work aims to serve as a foundational reference for researchers, engineers, and healthcare professionals dedicated to developing the next generation of secure, intelligent, and resilient biomedical IoT solutions.

title: D2.1 Healthcare Technology Competences and Barrier Analysis in Tunisia Report
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Purpose and scope. This report is deliverable D2.1 of the MeDCare project (Erasmus+ Capacity Building in the field of Vocational Education and Training, grant agreement no. 101242512). It answers the question on which work package 3 builds the new qualification: what competences an EQF level 5 medical technology and digital health care technician needs in Tunisia, how far the existing training provides them, and what stands in the way of teaching them. It integrates the three strands of evidence produced by work package 2: the desk study on policy, labour market and training provision (ATFP, 2026), two focus groups with thirteen system and market actors (Elemtiez, 2026a, 2026b) and twenty-six interviews with healthcare organisations, the vocational training provider and the authorities (ATAS, 2026). The analysis followed a reflexive thematic approach, with a competence perimeter of twenty-seven cards derived from the ESCO occupation profiles 2149.5 (bioengineer) and 2149.5.1 (biomedical engineer) and narrowed to EQF level 5, and a typology of institutional, pedagogical, technological and socio-economic barriers. Context. The Brevet de technicien supérieur in biomedical equipment maintenance is anchored in a structured body of legislation and sits at level 4 of the Tunisian national classification of qualifications; its learning outcomes are argued to align with EQF level 5 in autonomy, problem solving and responsibility, but no formal referencing links the two frameworks and no domestic route carries its graduates into higher education. The specialty is delivered by a single public centre in Tunis. The programme in use dates from 2008; the 2019 revision, with thirty-six modules and 2,454 hours, awaits accreditation, and neither covers medical informatics or digital health. The biomedical teaching body is small and close to a retirement horizon of 2027 to 2028, the training equipment dates largely from the centre's foundation around 2000, and demand for the qualification exceeds the places available. The public-sector workforce of 234 biomedical technicians is about 65% female, against a predominantly male applicant pool, and depends on suppliers for the most specialised tasks. Digital adoption in the facilities is uneven: maintenance management systems, remote radiology reading and, in a few hospitals, electronic patient records are in place, while telemedicine, interoperability and structured cybersecurity practice remain at an early stage. Competence mapping. The twenty-seven cards held in the field: both focus groups and the employers recognised them, and the exercise added competences at the margins rather than overturning the framework. The technical core of the profession (biomedical engineering principles, maintenance and repair, calibration and testing) is essential for both groups, present in the current training and carries the strongest employer signals; its priority for reinforcement is nonetheless high, because coverage is rated only partial and the equipment is ageing. The digital health domain is the decisive finding: health information systems, telemedicine, connected devices, remote diagnostics, data protection, electronic health records and medical software are rated essential or important and covered by no module of either programme, and all but data protection and electronic health records are named by employers at recruitment; five of its eight cards are high priority to reinforce. The managerial and transversal domain is present but under-reinforced, with documentation and communication with clinical staff among the competences employers name most often. Four cards remain contested (problem solving, good manufacturing practices, cybersecurity, evidence-based practice) and ten emergent competences were recorded, among them applied artificial intelligence, predictive maintenance, device regulation and conformity, and the reading of manufacturer documentation. Barriers and enablers. Four barriers form the structural core of the analysis: insufficient continuing professional development for trainers and outdated or insufficient equipment, attested by all three stakeholder categories and by both focus groups; weak digital and connected-device competences in training, attested by the provider, by healthcare organisations and by both focus groups; and the length of administrative and qualification-approval procedures, attested by all three categories and by focus group 1. Together with the lag of the curriculum behind healthcare technology, they describe one mechanism: technology moves faster than the programme, the equipment and the trainers can follow, and the procedures lengthen every correction. The other barriers concern the single-provider structure, the recognition and progression gap, the quality of work-based learning, the staffing and workload of maintenance units, the costs of mobility, accommodation and certification borne by learners from other governorates, and the motivation of younger technicians. No formal gender-based barrier was reported in access to the training or to employment; the indirect, practical and socio-cultural obstacles concern travel, shift hours, the handling of heavy equipment and workplace attitudes. The enablers are substantial: a sound technical foundation of graduates and technicians, their ready employability, established placements and partnerships, supplier training on newly acquired equipment, serviceable workshops and premises, participatory governance between the training and health authorities, and a stated institutional appetite for digital health. Recommendations and draft profile. The findings converge with the ETF recommendations for Tunisia and with the European entrepreneurship competence framework on the need for partnerships in the skills ecosystem, trainer development, work-based learning and transversal competences. The report organises the stakeholder-tested competences into seven clusters, from which it derives the draft profile of the Medical Technology and Digital Health Care Technician at EQF level 5: biomedical maintenance and diagnosis; connected devices, health information systems and remote support; data protection and basic cybersecurity; quality, safety, regulation and documentation; clinical context, communication and teamwork; professional autonomy, project and resource management and continuous development; and an orientation to emerging technologies. Each unit is described with learning outcomes in knowledge, skills and responsibility and autonomy. Ten recommendations address the curriculum developers of work package 3: a modular architecture built on the seven units, a practice-first pedagogy, structured work-based learning, simulation where equipment cannot be owned, trainer development before the digital units are delivered, technical English as an enabling competence, learning outcomes defined with healthcare organisations, assessment in authentic situations, a recognition of prior learning route aligned with the European counterparts of the double degree, and ESCO occupation 3114.1.5 as the reference occupation. Eight address the authorities: the referencing of the national framework to the EQF, a bilateral recognition framework with Italy, a shorter cycle of qualification revision, a progression route to higher education, the renewal and development of the teaching body, the renewal of training equipment, mobility support for learners from other governorates and a graduate tracer system. Six address the provider and the healthcare organisations: placement partnership agreements, supplier training that reaches the whole team and the trainers, maintenance organised by equipment family, protected time for continuing development and self-assessment against the Tunisian framework for entrepreneurial VET centres. Use of the report. Work package 3 receives a stakeholder-tested competence perimeter, a barrier and enabler analysis, seven clusters and a draft profile of seven units, and three sets of recommendations. The profile is a draft, to be completed by work package 3 before the modules, the assessment framework and the certification process are built from it. Work package 3 is also expected to take into account the cross-cutting themes to which the MeDCare project is committed, namely sustainability and energy efficiency, the One Health approach and the DigComp, LifeComp and GreenComp frameworks, which the fieldwork did not raise. The evidence has the limits stated in chapter 1: one training provider, which is also the only provider of the specialty; healthcare organisations located in Greater Tunis; the vocational training side of governance more fully represented than the health side; the absence of learners and recent graduates among the participants; and the small number of women among the focus group participants, which limits what the evidence can support on gender. Within those limits, the three strands of evidence agree on what the qualification should contain and on what stands in the way of teaching it.

title: USE OF 3D PRINTING IN THE PRODUCTION OF CUSTOM PROSTHESES, ORTHOSES, AND ANATOMICAL MODELS FOR MEDICAL APPLICATIONS
INTEGRATING AUDIT PROCESSES WITH OPERATIONAL EFFICIENCY INDICATORS IN HOSPITAL RESOURCE MANAGEMENT
journal: Journal of International Health Sciences and Management
abstract: Objective: The objective of this study is to propose an auditor-driven framework for measuring the efficiency in the management of medical devices and materials in hospitals, with auditors as contributors to compliance and operational performance analysis. Method: This study uses a conceptual and process approach. A review of the hospital resource management literature, audit systems, equipment lifecycle management and operational efficiency was undertaken to provide a structured assessment framework. The study maps the medical device and materials management process and provides audit checkpoints with efficiency indicators. A framework linking audit findings with efficiency performance domains is proposed. Results: It indicates that audit operations can reveal hidden capacity losses, redundant procurement, underutilized devices and process bottlenecks, when they are organized around efficiency indicators and not only around compliance criteria. The study shows that efficiency-oriented audits contribute to operational continuity, risk mitigation and cost control. The results suggest that the integration of audited outputs with performance monitoring systems enhances managerial decision-making in the governance of hospital resources. Conclusion: Audit methods can provide active support to operational performance evaluation in hospital resource management rather than only compliance. The methodology links audit checkpoints to performance indicators to uncover inefficiencies and provide proof for managerial actions. The proposed approach is practically relevant for hospital audits, improving performance monitoring and resource management.

title: Deployment of a Biomedical Research Laboratory for Suborbital Spaceflight: the Experience from the Virtute-1 Mission
abstract: Suborbital spaceflight platforms are increasingly being considered as accessible environments for conducting life-science research under spaceflight conditions. Biological investigations during space missions play an important role in improving our understanding of the physiological, cellular, and molecular responses elicited by spaceflight-related stressors, thereby contributing to the scientific knowledge required to support astronaut health and the development of future space exploration programs. As access to suborbital platforms expands, appropriate laboratory facilities are needed to collect, preserve, and process biological samples within the constraints imposed by flight operations. This note describes the planning, deployment, and operations of a temporary biomedical laboratory established at Spaceport America in support of the Virtute-1 mission, conducted during Virgin Galactic’s Galactic-01 research flight. The laboratory was designed to support biomedical activities involving both human participants and cellular payloads, including pre- and post-flight biological sample collection, cell-culture management, cold-chain preservation, and logistics associated with the transport of biological materials and scientific equipment. The laboratory was integrated within the flight environment of the Gateway to Space facility and required coordination of aerospace, biomedical, clinical, regulatory, and logistical stakeholders from public and private institutions. Particular attention was dedicated to biosafety procedures, infrastructure adaptation, equipment deployment, transportation planning, and mission-driven workflow integration. This paper describes how these activities were organized and implemented during a commercial suborbital mission. The experience gained during Virtute-1 provides practical considerations for the deployment of biomedical laboratories at commercial spaceports and for future life-science investigations using suborbital platforms.

title: DEA-Based Comparison of Hospital Efficiency in Tegal Regency Before and After Medical Record Digitalization
abstract: Electronic Medical Records (EMR) play a crucial role in transforming hospital services toward greater operational efficiency and improved service quality. However, during the early stages of implementation, challenges such as inadequate infrastructure, limited digital readiness, and organizational resistance often hinder optimal efficiency outcomes. This study aimed to compare hospital service efficiency before and after EMR implementation and to identify challenges and adaptation strategies during the digital transition at Mitra Siaga Hospital, Tegal Regency. A mixed-methods approach was employed, integrating quantitative and qualitative analyses. Quantitatively, Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) using Constant Return to Scale (CRS) and Variable Return to Scale (VRS) models measured technical efficiency across four key service units: the Emergency Room (ER), Delivery room (VK), Intensive Care Unit (ICU), and Inpatient Ward. Qualitatively, in-depth interviews with healthcare professionals explored barriers and supporting factors in EMR implementation. Results indicated that post-EMR implementation, the ER, VK, and Inpatient wards achieved full efficiency (CRS = 1.000; VRS = 1.000), while the ICU reached pure technical efficiency (VRS = 1.000) but remained scale-inefficient (CRS = 0.4395). The Wilcoxon test (p = 0.655) showed no significant difference between pre- and post-digitalization periods. Identified barriers included limited hardware, network disruptions, and user resistance, while managerial support and continuous training enhanced adaptation. In conclusion, EMR implementation has a positive impact on hospital operational efficiency, particularly when supported by adequate infrastructure, skilled human resources, and adaptive change management.

title: Features of Epidemiological Surveillance, Organization of Laboratory Research and Medical Care for Cholera Patients in the Republic of Zimbabwe in 2025
abstract: The aim of the study was to comprehensively assess the cholera epidemiological situation in the Republic of Zimbabwe during the 2023–2025 epidemic surge, the organization of medical care, and sanitary-technical infrastructure, as well as the prospects for implementing modern diagnostic methods, including the use of mobile laboratory units. Materials and methods. The epidemiological situation was analyzed based on patient medical records, laboratory test protocols for patient samples, official reports on cholera and other acute intestinal infections published by the Ministry of Health and Child Protection of the Republic of Zimbabwe, and WHO data. Visits to hospitals designated for cholera treatment included assessments of the quality of medical care, laboratory testing capacities, and the condition of engineering systems. Results and discussion. The data confirm that the adverse cholera situation was driven by a complex interplay of sanitary-technical, environmental, social, and organizational factors. Similar patterns have been observed during cholera outbreaks in other African countries, where the spread of infection is closely linked to inadequate water supply and sanitation systems, high population density, seasonal climatic fluctuations, and limited healthcare system capacity. Most cases during the outbreak in question were characterized by a mild course, the absence of severe dehydration, and rapid improvement following the restoration of water-electrolyte balance. The assessment of laboratory capacities revealed several issues: a shortage of diagnostic reagents and a lack of experience in determining the toxigenicity and biovars of isolated Vibrio cholerae cultures in laboratory practices, as well as a lack of monitoring studies aimed at detecting the cholera pathogen in epidemiologically significant environmental samples. It should be noted that medical institutions in the Republic of Zimbabwe have accumulated extensive experience in organizing diagnostic and therapeutic care for cholera patients and implementing preventive measures, which helps contain the spread of the infection and save patients’ lives. To foster cooperation between the Russian Federation and the Republic of Zimbabwe in combating particularly dangerous infectious diseases, it is essential to conduct training courses on the epidemiology, diagnosis, and prevention of cholera and other acute intestinal infections; supply mobile laboratories, equipment, and diagnostic reagents; and organize joint, systematic monitoring of environmental objects.

title: Access to medical oxygen: a critical health-system requirement for reducing mortality from HIV, tuberculosis and malaria in sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Hypoxaemia is a frequently under-recognised complication of severe illness, including several HIV-related, tuberculosis (TB)-related and malaria-related conditions and is strongly associated with increased mortality. Despite this, critical health-system gaps across sub-Saharan Africa—including absent or non-functional oxygen equipment, unreliable electricity supply, weak procurement and supply chains and limited access to routine pulse oximetry—continue to prevent the timely identification and treatment of hypoxaemia in patients with these conditions. Evidence from paediatric pneumonia and broader hypoxaemic illness demonstrates that strengthening pulse-oximetry capacity and oxygen-delivery systems can improve clinical care and may reduce mortality; however, direct interventional evidence specific to HIV, TB and malaria remains limited. Moreover, selection of the appropriate oxygen source—whether concentrator, cylinder, liquid oxygen or pressure-swing adsorption system—should be guided by facility-level demand, electricity reliability, supply logistics, maintenance capacity and total cost of ownership. Therefore, integrating medical oxygen into national HIV, TB and malaria programmes and existing health financing mechanisms, alongside sustained investment in clinical training and health-system strengthening, represents a practical and cost-relevant policy priority for reducing preventable mortality from these conditions in sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Design Change Factors in Hospital Design-Build Projects: Variable Validation and RII Analysis
abstract: Hospital construction projects in island regions face compounded challenges that differ fundamentally from urban settings. This study investigates design change factors in hospital construction under the Design and Build (D&B) contract scheme, with empirical reference to the Tafaeri Hospital project in Nias and the Tarempa Hospital project in Anambas. A two-phase research design was employed. Phase one involved a preliminary survey using expert judgment, where five construction professionals evaluated 20 candidate variables derived from a systematic literature review, using a five-point Likert scale. Seventeen variables met the relevance threshold (mean ≥ 3.0) and were retained. Phase two involved a main survey distributed to 157 practitioners to measure the relative significance of each validated variable. Data were analysed through Pearson validity testing, Cronbach Alpha reliability assessment, and Relative Importance Index (RII) scoring. All 17 variables demonstrated valid correlation coefficients (r > 0.156, p = 0.000) and the instrument achieved high reliability (Cronbach Alpha = 0.897). The three highest-ranked variables were site condition changes (RII = 0.775), natural disaster impacts (RII = 0.767), and MEP system and medical equipment integration issues (RII = 0.708). These findings confirm that geographic vulnerability and technical complexity are the dominant design change drivers in island-based hospital D&B projects, and provide a validated empirical foundation for risk mitigation strategies in similar settings.

title: Functionality status and drivers of non-functionality of the standardised laboratory analysers in Tanzania mainland: Findings from a National Equipment Harmonisation and Standardisation Mapping Exercise
abstract: Abstract Introduction Reliable, well-maintained laboratory equipment is essential for timely, accurate and reliable laboratory results for patient care, surveillance, and health system resilience. Tanzania implemented the Standard Medical Laboratory Equipment Guideline (SMLEG-2018) to harmonise procurement and improve efficiency across a tiered laboratory system and network. However, equipment functionality gaps remain a critical challenge for healthcare delivery. This study determined the functionality status of standardised laboratory analysers in Tanzania mainland and identified the drivers of non-functionality. Methods We conducted a facility-based cross-sectional study to identify the causes of non-functionality of standardised chemistry, haematology, and urine analysers across mainland Tanzania. We assessed 3,044 analysers and used Pareto analysis to identify the primary drivers of non-functionality. Results Of the 3,044 standardised analysers assessed, 987 (32.4%) chemistry 1,308 (43.0%) haematology, and 749 (24.6%) urine) assessed; 397 (13.0%) were non-functional. Proportionally, urine analysers were the most non-functional (n=176/749, 23.5%), followed by chemistry (n=135/987, 13.7%), and haematology (n=86/1308, 6.6%) analysers, p<0.001. Urine analysers had significantly higher non-functional equipment (23.5%), followed by Chemistry analysers (13.7%), than Haematology analysers (6.6%), p<0.001. Equipment breakdown was the leading cause of non-functionality, accounting for 70.9% (61/86), 70.5% (124/176) and 60.0% (81/135) of the non-functional haematology, urine and chemistry analysers, respectively, among all causes identified for each analyser type. Conclusion Although the SMLEG 2018 implementation identified broad coverage of functional standardised laboratory equipment, persistent equipment breakdowns of more than 10% highlight a systemic, concerning gap that requires immediate corrective action to sustain high performance. Strengthening preventive maintenance, timely repair services and sustainable equipment lifecycle planning is critical to sustaining quality laboratory services for robust preventive and curative care.

title: A systematic review of the measurement of falls in hospitals
abstract: Abstract Background In-patient falls are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in the United Kingdom (UK) National Health Service (NHS). Although falls prevention guidelines exist, there is little evidence supporting the efficacy of interventions in hospital settings. Current national benchmarking based on occupied bed days (OBD) does not acknowledge varying ward layouts, differences in patient visibility, and staffing levels, which affect the ability to monitor at-risk patients. This leads to benchmarking and performance reporting that is not an accurate reflection of the challenges faced which suggests the measurement may not be a useful comparator. This systematic review seeks to evaluate the use and limitations of the measurement of accidental falls in hospital, when considered in the context of the setting in which reported. Methods This review was conducted to PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews. Interventional studies that used falls/1000 OBD as a metric were included. Thematic analysis within NVivo15® was utilised to analyse extracted narrative data, author reported limitations and contextual variables. The Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety (SEIPS) model was used to theme, interpret and present the results. Results From 3,541 articles searching 9 databases, 103 studies from 19 countries were included. The study has four key findings. The definition of a fall varies between study sites and is not stated in 42 (50%) of the full text studies. There is a lack of consistency in how the measure is expressed, resulting in comparison between hospitals that is not equivalent. The type of fall or how it is classified may mean that not all falls are reported due to subjectivity at ward level. There are multiple different interpretations of what constitutes a fall. There are multiple contextual challenges that cause substantial variability; such as ward design and patient visibility, that are not measured. Staff available on each shift has also not been measured as a variable. Conclusion The findings from this study emphasise the importance of understanding how hospital falls are shaped by interactions between technology, people, and the environment. This reinforces the need for a systems perspective and Human Factors methodologies to tackle this pervasive patient safety challenge.

title: Advances in medical plastic waste treatment methods towards sustainable development
abstract: The rapid expansion of healthcare services has led to a substantial increase in medical plastic waste (MPW), posing significant environmental and public health challenges and highlighting the need for sustainable waste management strategies. The present review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in MPW treatment and valorization strategies for sustainable development. Previous reviews have primarily focused on general biomedical waste management or individual treatment technologies. This review critically examines MPW, its classification, major medical polymers, environmental impacts, conventional and advanced treatment technologies, their comparative assessment, emerging recycling approaches, derived value-added products and their characterization, challenges and their potential solutions, and future prospects for sustainable MPW management. Conventional and advanced treatment methods are evaluated with respect to their treatment efficiency, environmental impacts, resource-recovery potential, and limitations. The analysis demonstrates that no single treatment technology is universally suitable for heterogeneous MPW rather, the appropriate pathway depends on polymer composition, contamination level, treatment objective, resource-recovery potential, environmental and economic considerations. Emerging approaches such as catalytic recycling, enzymatic depolymerization and artificial intelligence assisted waste management further expand opportunities for selective recovery. This review also highlights the conversion of MPW into fuels, syngas, carbon-based materials, construction materials, acoustic panels, and composite fillers. Overall, integrated polymer-specific treatment and valorization pathways supported by life cycle and techno-economic assessment are essential for transitioning MPW from conventional disposal toward resource recovery and a circular healthcare system. The Relationship Between the Implementation of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), Compliance with Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) Use, and Workplace Accidents Among Inpatient Nurses at Panti Waluyo YAKKUM Hospital, Surakarta
abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction: Nurses represent the largest healthcare workforce and play a crucial role in providing healthcare services. Nurses are at risk of accidents and occupational illnesses while performing procedures, so they need to understand hospital procedures, the work environment, and several other aspects. Objectives: The aim of this study was to identify the correlation between the implementation of SOPs and compliance with the use of PPE among inpatient nurses at Panti Waluyo YAKKUM Surakarta Hospital. Methods: This study employed a quantitative paradigm with an associative method and a cross-sectional approach. The population consisted of 74 inpatient nurses in 2025, and a sample size of 74 respondents was used utilizing a total sampling technique. Results: Based on the univariate analysis of the implementation of SOP, the results obtained were implemented by 73 respondents (98.65%), and the category not implemented by 1 respondent (1.35%). Compliance with the use of PPE obtained compliance results of 74 respondents (100%). Work accidents obtained high results in 2 respondents (2.71%) and low in 72 respondents (97.29%). Bivariate analysis using the Kendall's Tau test obtained a Sig. value of 0.000 < 0.05 on the variable of SOP implementation with work accidents and a correlation value of -0.576. While on the variable of the presence of PPE use and work accidents obtained a Sig. value of 0.330 > 0.05 and a correlation value of -0.097, the relationship is very weak and in the opposite direction.. Conclusions: The conclusion is that there is a significant relationship with a strong correlation value and an opposite direction of relationship between the implementation of SOPs and work accidents in inpatient nurses at Panti Waluyo Hospital, Surakarta, and there is no significant relationship with a very weak correlation value and an opposite direction of relationship between compliance with the use of PPE and work accidents in inpatient nurses at Panti Waluyo Hospital. Keyword: Implementation of SOP, Compliance with Use of PPE, Inpatient Nurses . Pendahuluan: Perawat ialah profesi kesehatan dengan jumlah terbesar dan memiliki peran krusial dalam layanan kesehatan. Perawat memiliki risiko kecelakan kerja dan terkena penyakit pada saat melakukan tindakan, sehingga perlu mengenal dan mengetahui tata cara kerja di RS, lingkungan kerja serta sejumlah elemen lain. Tujuan: Penelitian ini ditujukan guna mengetahui hubungan penerapan SOP dan kepatuhan penggunaan APD pada perawat rawat inap di Rumah Sakit Panti Waluyo YAKKUM Surakarta. Metode: Penelitian ini mempergunakan paradigm kuatitatif dengan metode assosiatif menggunaakan pendekatan cross sectional. Populasi yang diteliti ialah perawat rawat inap tahum 2025 sebanyak 74 perawat dan total sampelnya ialah 74 responden melalui tekniknya berupa total sampling. Hasil: Berdasarkan analisis univariat penerapan SOP diperoleh hasil diterapkan 73 responden (98,65%), dan kategori tidak diterapkan 1 responden (1,35%). Kepatuhan penggunaan APD diperoleh hasil patuh 74 responden (100%). Kecelakaan kerja diperoleh hasil tinggi 2 responden (2,71%) dan rendah 72 responden (97,29%). Analisis bivariat menggunakan uji Kendall’s Tau diperoleh hasil nilai Sig. 0,000 < 0,05 pada variabel penerapan SOP dengan kecelakaan kerja dan nilai korelasi sebesar – 0,576. Sedangkan pada variabel kepatuhan penggunaan APD dan kecelakaan kerja diperoleh hasil nilai Sig. 0,330 > 0,05 dan nilai korelasi sebesar – 0,097 hubungan sangat lemah dan berlawanan arah.. Kesimpulan: Kesimpulan adalah terdapat hubungan yang signifikan dengan nilai korelasi kuat dan arah hubungan berlawanan antara penerapan SOP dengan kecelakaan kerja pada perawat rawat inap di RS Panti Waluyo Surakarta, dan tak terdapatnya hubungan yang signifikan dengan nilai korelasi sangat lemah dan arah hubungan berlawanan antara kepatuhan penggunaan APD dengan kecelakaan kerja pada perawat rawat inap di RS Panti Waluyo Kata Kunci: Penerapan SOP, Kepatuhan Penggunaan APD, Perawat Rawat Inap. title: How to Reduce the Latency of Remote Medical Device Operations
journal: Science and Technology of Engineering Chemistry and Environmental Protection
abstract: As a key application of digital precision medicine, telesurgery is highly sensitive to end-to-end latency, which affects surgical manipulation synchronization, robotic control accuracy and patient safety. High-precision minimally invasive surgery requires latency below 50 ms, yet most existing methods only optimize isolated components, resulting in excessive latency that fails clinical requirements. This study proposes a full-chain latency optimization framework integrating deterministic communication, adjacent edge computing, AI motion prediction compensation and dual-link redundant transmission. Based on a cloud-edge-device architecture, the system optimizes latency across network, computation, encoding, device control and security layers via 5G URLLC, network slicing, H.265 intelligent encoding, LSTM delay compensation, lightweight encryption and zero-trust security design.Experimental results show the system stabilizes end-to-end latency at 23–50 ms, reduces network latency from 120 ms to 3–30 ms, and drops the video freezing rate from 12.7% to 0.3%. Clinical evaluations verify its surgical performance is consistent with conventional in-hospital robotic surgery, satisfying high-precision telesurgery requirements. This solution cuts the deployment cost of dedicated communication links. Despite limitations including insufficient remote 5G coverage, high device costs and unstable cross-operator networks, future research will integrate advanced communication and digital twin technologies to further reduce latency and promote standardized large-scale clinical deployment.

title: HOSPITAL INNOVATION AND ITS IMPACT ON QUALITY OF CARE AND PATIENT SATISFACTION
journal: International Journal of Versatile Research and Analysis
abstract: Hospital innovation is described as including administrative and medical innovation. Also, the evaluation process consists of three main components namely process, structure, and outcome of observation. Hence, the research tries to identify the hospital innovation and its impact on quality of care and patient satisfaction. The study results revealed that positive influence of hospital innovation on quality of care among patients. There is positive influence of hospital innovation on patient satisfaction. There is positive influence of quality of care among patients on patient satisfaction. Hence, it is concluded that retaining an existing patient is less expensive than identifying a new one. Hospital management should consider sample opportunities, referrals and ideas as a valuable resource for satisfied patients to use the clinic again and again. Limitations of our findings must be acknowledged. Quality of care and hospital innovation was assessed using perceptual measures, which have limitations in findings as they are subject to rater distortions. Future research could test the relationship between patient satisfaction and hospital innovation with a larger sample size.

title: Fire Emergency Preparedness among Healthcare Workers in Selected Hospitals in Botswana
journal: Journal of Health Medicine and Nursing
abstract: Purpose: Insufficient safety protocols during the planning and operation of hospitals can lead to hazardous incidents. With multiple incidents occurring annually that frequently go undetected and result in fatalities and service disruptions, fire emergencies remain a significant risk in healthcare settings. This study assessed the level of fire emergency preparedness among healthcare workers in selected hospitals in Botswana. Methodology: An analytical cross-sectional design was employed. Quantitative data were collected using semi-structured questionnaires and observation checklists, while qualitative data were collected through key informant interviews. The study sampled 359 healthcare workers and included seven Safety, Health, and Environment (SHE) officers from seven hospitals. Quantitative data were analyzed using SPSS version 26, with descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and binary logistic regression; qualitative data were analyzed thematically. Findings: Educational background and years of experience were significantly associated with fire preparedness. Healthcare workers with bachelor's degrees had 34.5% preparedness, while those with more than 15 years of experience had the highest preparedness at 52.9%. Only 18.5% had participated in fire drills and 34.3% had received fire safety training in the previous years. Only 40.5% knew how to properly use fire extinguishers, although 79.5% knew their location. Participation in fire safety training was the most significant indicator of individual preparedness (χ² = 121.104, p < 0.001). Overall, 87.7% were unfamiliar with specific emergency roles, and only 27% demonstrated adequate fire emergency preparedness. Hospital preparedness varied from 47.2% to 100%. Unique Contribution to Theory, Practice and Policy: The Emergency Management Preparedness Cycle guided the study, highlighting planning, training, equipping, drills, evaluation, and continuous improvement. The findings support competency-based fire safety training, clear emergency roles, regular drills, functional safety equipment, and stronger institutional communication. The Ministry of Health and relevant authorities should strengthen fire safety regulations, develop national hospital fire preparedness guidelines, provide adequate resources, and establish regular training, drills, and monitoring systems.

title: Microbial contamination and decontamination of reusable digital intraoral imaging equipment: a narrative review
abstract: Digital intraoral radiography relies on reusable solid-state sensors and photostimulable phosphor (PSP) plates that cannot be heat-sterilized, so infection control depends largely on single-use barriers and on disinfectants the equipment can tolerate. This narrative review synthesizes laboratory and clinical evidence on microbial contamination of reusable digital intraoral imaging equipment, the mechanisms by which barriers fail, and the balance between antimicrobial efficacy and device compatibility. Across the available clinical studies of barrier-protected PSP plates, contamination was reported in roughly 17% to 73% of plates and was frequently associated with handling-related factors, including perforation, incomplete sealing and non-aseptic removal, rather than with the barrier material alone. The exterior of intact envelopes becomes heavily contaminated during brief intraoral use, identifying removal technique as a distinct contamination route; these findings are integrated into a proposed six-stage contamination pathway. Evidence for solid-state sensors is largely limited to barrier-perforation testing, and data on cables, scanner internals and computer peripherals remain sparse. Studies of lead aprons and thyroid shields, mostly from non-dental settings and therefore contextual, report frequent contamination, now alongside 2023–2024 guidance recommending against routine shielding. Laboratory studies indicate that antimicrobial efficacy and plate compatibility vary independently across agents and plate brands, so the two must be evaluated together. Contamination indicates a plausible transmission pathway but does not demonstrate patient infection, and no study identified in this review has linked imaging equipment to a documented infection. The review concludes with an evidence-gap matrix and outlines emerging approaches to objective contamination surveillance.

title: Knowledge gaps in biosafety biosecurity and good laboratory practices among medical laboratory scientists in a Nigeria tertiary healthcare facility
abstract: Abstract Background: Biosafety, biosecurity, and good laboratory practices (GLP) prevent laboratory-acquired infections and misuse of biological agents. Medical Laboratory Scientists (MLS) implement these standards, yet data on their knowledge in Nigerian tertiary hospitals remain scarce. This study assessed knowledge of biosafety, biosecurity, and GLP among MLS in a tertiary hospital in South-South Nigeria. Methods: A cross-sectional study of 100 MLSCN-registered MLS at the University of Calabar Teaching hospital, Calabar. A structured, self-administered questionnaire assessed knowledge across three domains. Responses were Yes/No/Unsure or 5-point likert scale. Chi-square test determined the associations. Data were analyzed using SPSS v25.0 with p≤0.05 considered significant. Results: 54.0% understood biosafety and biosecurity (p<0.001), only 4.0% reported training on emergency plans for biological toxins. 54.0% indicated proper storage of contaminated waste (p=0.004), and 28.0% were aware of staff vaccination. 64.0% reported no biosafety discussion forum (p<0.001). PPE availability was suboptimal: 32.0% agreed PPE was always available (p=0.002), and 48.0% reported no incident reporting system (p=0.034). For GLP, 34.0% agreed access to biological agents was restricted, 36.0% were unsure about transport of agents. 92.0% reported no SOP for biological spills or biosafety drills (p<0.001). Only 30.0% used biosafety cabinets for aerosol, while 92.0% denied use (p<0.001). 30.0% lacked Formal handwashing policies (p=0.024). Conclusion: There were gaps in practical implementation of biosafety, biosecurity, and GLP despite knowledge of definitions. Deficiencies in training, emergency preparedness, waste management, PPE, incident reporting, and SOPs highlight an urgent need for targeted training, policy enforcement, and resources to improve safety and compliance.

title: State regulation of therapeutic nutrition systems in Ukrainian military medical facilities: scientific foundations of institutional modernization and implementation of international standards and practices
The cognition of dynamic evaluation of operating room environmental quality among medical staff: a qualitative study
abstract: Objective: This qualitative study, guided by the Donabedian three-dimensional quality model, aimed to explore the real perceptions of multidisciplinary healthcare professionals regarding the dynamic evaluation of the operating room environment quality. The ultimate goal was to identify current management deficiencies and propose evidence-based strategies for optimization. Method: Using a descriptive qualitative design with a hybrid analytic orientation, purposive sampling recruited 7 operating-room nurses, 6 surgeons, 5 anesthesiologists, and 2 infection-control specialists from 4 tertiary Grade A hospitals. After ethics approval, formal semi-structured interviews were conducted in March 2026. Interview data were transcribed, manually coded, and analyzed in NVivo 15.0 using Colaizzi's method. The Donabedian model informed the interview guide and later organization of evaluation-related categories. Results: Three core themes were extracted: (1) the four-dimensional connotation of operating-room environmental quality, comprising physical, chemical, biological, and humanistic dimensions; (2) nine preliminary candidate indicators for dynamic evaluation, grouped across structure, process, and outcome domains; and (3) healthcare professionals' perceptions of potential safety and health implications for staff and patients. These findings highlight a gap between current static monitoring practices and the dynamic nature of intraoperative environmental risks. Conclusion: Participants' accounts suggest that a preliminary candidate framework for dynamic evaluation could incorporate structural conditions, process monitoring, and outcome-related feedback. Integrated management that considers both occupational health and patient safety represents a practice implication to be empirically evaluated. This study provides a qualitative foundation for subsequent Delphi consultation and psychometric or empirical validation of a dynamic OR environmental assessment framework.

Assessing Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Response in Samarinda Hospitals
abstract: Hospitals represent critical urban infrastructure constitutionally mandated to maintain uninterrupted healthcare operations during catastrophic events. Due to its unique geographical and urban characteristics, Samarinda City faces severe dual threats from hydrometeorological hazards (floods) and anthropogenic hazards (fires). This study evaluates disaster preparedness and mitigation levels across six major referral hospitals in Samarinda and develops an integrated hospital resilience model. Utilizing a mixed-methods survey design, data were collected from 119 strategic personnel representing disaster mitigation teams, facilities support, and executive management. Quantitative questionnaire data were transformed via the Method of Successive Intervals (MSI) and subjected to multiple linear regression analysis to empirically validate the framework. The omnibus test demonstrated an excellent model fit, with the non-structural predictors collectively accounting for 68.4% of the variance in hospital disaster resilience ( =0.684, (4, 114) = 61.725, < 0.001). Individually, Emergency Response Planning exerted the most robust linear influence ( = 0.315, < 0.001), followed closely by Knowledge and Attitude ( = 0.280, = 0.001) and Resource Mobilization ( = 0.245, < 0.001). Observational checklists further revealed that while structural safety generally achieved an "Adequate" baseline (61%–80%), acute latent risks persist in active software parameters and technological warning networks ( = 0.081). Managerially, this study demonstrates that physical building reliability alone induces a false sense of security if not synchronized with formalized, institutionalized non-structural operational engines. It is recommended that local governments mandate the Hospital Safety Index (HSI) parameters as a legally binding prerequisite for annual hospital licensing to systematically anchor public health infrastructure within regional urban risk-reduction policies.

title: Investment or extraction? Reframing private equity in healthcare
abstract: Moral hazard is built into the structure of private equity investments, which incentivises debt-based extraction rather than value-adding investment. To craft effective regulation of private equity's participation in healthcare, and to cut through the industry's talking points, we must reframe and acknowledge private equity 'investment' as 'extraction'. In the U.S. healthcare system, this debt-based extraction has produced higher risks of bankruptcy and financial distress and associated facility closures, cost-cutting that affects patient safety and care, rising healthcare costs, inefficient use of taxpayer dollars, erosion of clinician autonomy, and increased consolidation. Policies that address extractive behaviours are the most targeted and efficient means of safeguarding patient care and may discourage the worst actors from acquiring healthcare providers. As private equity invests in health systems beyond the U.S. where regulatory regimes differ, the fundamentals of its extractive business model remain the same. Regulations must be calibrated to country specifics, but they should address the debt-based extraction built into the very structure of private equity investments. As policy debates continue, it is worth asking why we need private equity's extractive business model in healthcare in the first place.

title: Compliance-Ready Healthcare Energy Data Integration
Transforming Waste Management from Incineration to Resource Recovery in the UK
abstract: Sustainable waste management is central to the UK’s transition to the circular economy and to decarbonising healthcare supply chains. Within the NHS, high-temperature incineration remains a carbon- and cost-intensive route, often driven by over-classification of non-hazardous materials and limited segregation capacity. Furthermore, autoclaving of hospital waste adds a layer of carbon intensity to Scope 3 emissions of hospitals. This study evaluates a practical circular pathway that diverts selected non-hazardous consumables from incineration to segregation, validated sterilisation, and repurposing as a possible sustainable secondary input for engineering applications. Using an integrated sustainability framework, the paper combines policy analysis, process mapping, and scenario-based treatment-stage carbon and cost comparison of the baseline incineration pathway and the segregate–sterilise–repurpose pathway. The assessment is aligned with national targets to achieve a 20:20:60 split (HTI clinical waste: infectious waste: offensive waste) and tests how improved segregation and reclassification of suitable non-hazardous streams from healthcare codes (e.g., EWC 18 01 04 to 20 03 01) can reduce treatment-related carbon emissions and enable higher-value recovery. This proposed solution could support reductions in treatment-stage e emissions and disposal costs, while allowing higher-value recovery through better management and segregation of healthcare waste. Keywords: waste materials, UK zero waste, circular economy, resource recovery, waste management, healthcare waste

title: Valuing green infrastructure improvements at Musgrave Park Hospital in Belfast, Northern Ireland
Prevalence of Tuberculosis Among HIV Patients Treated at Public Health Facilities
abstract: This study aimed to analyze the prevalence of tuberculosis among HIV patients treated in public health units through a systematic literature review. The research was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, involving searches in PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar databases for the 2021–2026 period. This process identified 446 initial records, and—following screening by title, abstract, and full text—25 studies meeting the established criteria were included. Results showed a coinfection prevalence ranging from 4.6% to 57.3%, depending on the context; a CD4 lymphocyte count below 200 cells/mm³ emerged as the most consistent clinical predictor and the most frequently used laboratory marker for monitoring. Meanwhile, treatment discontinuation, poverty, overcrowding, and social stigma were identified as the most significant cross-cutting risk factors, alongside infectious comorbidities and associated mental disorders; evidence from Ecuador proved to be scarcer and more fragmented than that from other regions. It is concluded that TB-HIV coinfection remains a persistent public health issue with a magnitude that varies according to geographic and socioeconomic contexts; therefore, strengthening immunological screening, treatment adherence, the integration of diagnostic services, and the generation of local evidence in Ecuador is essential to narrowing the gap relative to international standards.

title: AIDriven Federated EdgeCloud Framework with Intelligent Task Offloading for Smart Healthcare
journal: JOURNAL OF ADVANCE AND FUTURE RESEARCH
abstract: Cloud computing makes shared computer resources scalable, adaptable and affordable it has become a game-changer in the healthcare industry. Traditional healthcare infrastructures are facing issues with storage, processing, latency and security due to the explosive expansion of data-intensive medical applications. This study suggests an AI-driven federated edge-cloud paradigm that combines edge computing, federated learning and intelligent job offloading for smart healthcare systems in order to overcome these constraints. Real-time data processing, privacy protection and effective resource use are made possible by the suggested architecture's three-tier approach, which consists of edge devices, a federated learning layer and a cloud server. While an intelligent offloading system dynamically divides jobs between edge and cloud based on urgency and computing requirements, lightweight AI models at the edge layer handle local data analysis and enable latency-sensitive healthcare applications. Federated learning improves privacy and compliance by ensuring safe and cooperative model training without exchanging raw patient data. For predictive and individualized healthcare services, the cloud layer offers global model aggregation, large-scale analytics and digital twin-based patient monitoring. Significant gains in system performance including up to 50% latency reduction, 55% energy savings and high accuracy levels reaching 95% in real-time healthcare monitoring are shown by experimental investigation. Comparative findings show that by striking the ideal balance between latency, scalability, energy efficiency and data security, the suggested hybrid framework performs better than conventional cloud-centric methods. The paper identifies issues with model complexity, communication overhead and heterogeneous data environments while highlighting the possibility of combining AI, federated learning and edge-cloud computing to improve next-generation healthcare systems.

title: A Complete Guide to Exploring Danube Properties in Dubai
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Introduction Dubai continues to attract homebuyers and investors with its modern infrastructure, diverse communities, and international business environment. The city offers residential options for different lifestyles, including contemporary apartments for professionals and spacious homes for families. Access to shopping destinations, healthcare facilities, schools, and public transportation adds to the appeal of many neighborhoods. However, choosing a property involves more than finding an attractive building or a convenient address. Buyers should first consider their financial position, lifestyle preferences, and long-term plans. Understanding the differences between residential communities can help them identify locations that suit their everyday needs. Taking time to research the market also encourages realistic expectations and helps buyers avoid making decisions based entirely on promotional offers or short-term excitement. Preparing for a Successful Property Purchase Good preparation can make the property buying process more straightforward. Before viewing developments, buyers should establish a practical budget that accounts for the purchase price and additional expenses, including registration fees, maintenance charges, and service costs. Researching the developer’s reputation and previous projects can offer useful insight into construction quality and delivery standards. Buyers interested in off-plan properties should carefully review payment schedules, completion dates, and contractual obligations. Location is equally important because convenient access to workplaces, schools, hospitals, and leisure facilities can influence both quality of life and rental demand. Comparing different developments helps buyers understand variations in pricing, amenities, and overall value. Asking clear questions and verifying important details before signing an agreement can prevent misunderstandings and support more confident decisions. Comparing Developments and Available Opportunities When researching residential projects in Dubai, buyers may consider Danube Properties alongside other developments to understand the available choices. Each option deserves careful evaluation based on its location, floor plans, amenities, payment arrangements, and total ownership costs. Investors may examine comparable rental prices and consider the needs of potential tenants in the surrounding area. People buying a home for personal use may place greater importance on comfortable interiors, community facilities, privacy, and convenient commuting options. It is also sensible to review official documentation and confirm details about project completion, maintenance responsibilities, and additional charges. No single development will suit every buyer, so individual priorities should guide the final decision. By comparing several alternatives instead of relying solely on advertisements, prospective owners can develop a clearer picture of the benefits, limitations, and responsibilities associated with each property. Conclusion: Making Decisions with Confidence Purchasing property is a significant commitment, and a thoughtful approach can help buyers manage the process more effectively. Setting a realistic budget, researching neighborhoods, checking documentation, and seeking independent professional advice can all contribute to better decisions. Buyers should also consider their future needs and avoid making commitments simply because a development appears popular. Those exploring Dubai’s property market may research SY Capital Estates as part of their broader search for information about real estate opportunities. Ultimately, the right purchase depends on financial readiness, reliable information, and a clear understanding of ownership responsibilities. Whether considering Danube properties for personal use or investment, buyers should focus on practical suitability, transparent terms, and lasting value. Careful planning can make the experience more rewarding while helping buyers choose a property that supports their long-term goals.

title: Healthcare ventilation and infection prevention: what infection trainees need to know, with a focus on operating theatres
abstract: Operating theatre ventilation remains a critical yet persistently under-appreciated component of infection prevention and control (IPC). Patterns of airflow, dilution and exhaust directly influence the concentration and distribution of airborne pathogens within clinical environments. This has implications for the risk of acquisition and subsequent infection among patients or staff. Despite this, ventilation may be considered under a technical or engineering domain, rather than a key component of IPC. For Medical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases trainees, a disconnect between IPC theory and practical realities, may contribute to reduced confidence for trainees preparing for exit examinations and senior clinical roles. This educational review is intended to bridge that gap by providing a practical curriculum-aligned overview of ventilation in healthcare, specifically the operating theatre for IPC practice, incorporating the principles of airborne transmission and ventilation system design. Using UK Health Technical Memorandum (HTM) 03-01 as the primary framework, the review explains airflow direction, pressure differentials, air changes per hour, filtration, along with the governance role of the Ventilation Safety Group. Conventional and ultra-clean ventilation in operating theatres, validation and verification processes, and microbiological air sampling are also discussed. Selected international literature is included situating UK practice within a broader evidence base. By linking engineering principles with everyday IPC practice, the aim is to provide a coherent framework to interpret ventilation performance, contribute to multi-disciplinary governance, participate in refurbishment projects and outbreak investigations to inform clinical practice, in addition to supporting examination preparation.

title: Transitioning from traditional hospital design to activity-based care: A longitudinal case study of differential occupational health and safety consequences across clinical settings and professional roles
abstract: The activity-based care (ABC) model, adapted from activity-based offices, has emerged as a new approach to healthcare facility design. Evidence on its consequences for occupational health and safety-relevant outcomes remains limited. The study examines how transitioning from a traditional hospital design to the ABC model is associated with changes in employee experiences of task–environment alignment and psychosocial work environment, self-reported health, sick leave and turnover over time, and differences in changes across professional roles and clinic types. A repeated-measures survey was conducted in an outpatient hospital unit across 10 specialised clinics. Data were collected 3 months before relocation and at 6 and 18 months post-relocation. Generalised least-squares models examined change over time and tested interactions with professional role and clinic type. Sick leave and turnover were analysed over approximately 1 year before and after relocation using segmented interrupted time-series regression. Ratings of task–environment alignment varied across clinic types and professional roles. Consultation-based clinics and physicians and administrative employees showed persistent declines over time, while surgical/radiology clinics and nursing roles remained stable or improved. Stress and recovery indicators worsened similarly across all groups. Psychosocial conditions were stable, though job satisfaction, perceived quality of work and referral intentions declined. Turnover remained unchanged, while sick leave varied across contexts and roles. The consequences of ABC implementation are not uniform but depend on the alignment of the redesigned workspace and the task demands of different clinical settings and professional groups, a contingency that cannot be easily detected with single time-point post-occupancy evaluation.

title: Análisis de la gestión de las contrataciones públicas para la salud y trabajo con transparencia: Revisión literaria
journal: Revista Cubana de Salud y Trabajo
abstract: Introduction: Public procurement management in health and labor is a strategic component for ensuring timely access to healthcare services, the protection of occupational health, and the promotion of decent working conditions for the benefit of citizens. In contexts where population health is a priority, service pressure and the distribution of work activities require efficient state responses; therefore, public procurement should be oriented toward priority needs Objective: To analyze public procurement management in the health and labor sector through transparency, using the PRISMA methodology. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA methodology. Thirty scientific studies published between 2023 and 2025, indexed in Scopus, Scielo, Google Scholar, Redalyc, and Dialnet, were selected. Results: The results show that when procurement aligns with public health, occupational health, and labor stability needs, process traceability improves, corruption risk decreases, and institutional capacity is strengthened to ensure labor equity, with effects reflected in the sanitary well-being of the population. Conclusion: Transparency in public procurement in the health and labor sector must become a guiding criterion to ensure equitable, efficient, and socially oriented processes, with a direct impact on quality of life, sanitation, and occupational safety, while strengthening institutional legitimacy among working citizens in complex and public scenarios.

title: Integrating System-Level Impacts into Seismic Risk Assessment Reshapes Investment Priorities for More Resilient and Sustainable Cities
abstract: Abstract Sustainable and resilient urban planning requires infrastructure investments that increase the capacity to maintain and recover essential services following disasters, yet regional seismic-risk assessments typically prioritise physical damage or direct economic loss, providing limited guidance on allocating scarce mitigation resources. Here we develop an integrated framework that quantifies a wide array of societal impact metrics across interdependent housing, transport, education and healthcare systems and identifies the least-effort mitigation strategies for attaining prescribed levels of impact reduction. Each metric is evaluated through two complementary aggregation lenses: total impacts, capturing system-wide disruption, and mean impacts, capturing the average burden borne by individual assets or users. Applying the framework to nearly 200,000 candidate mitigation strategies spanning residential buildings, bridges, schools and hospitals in Avellino, Southern Italy, under representative moment magnitude 5.0 and 6.9 earthquake scenarios, we find that residential retrofitting dominates the preferred strategy up to moderate mitigation targets, after which bridge retrofitting becomes the principal source of further impact reduction. Crucially, the value of bridge retrofitting arises less from avoided bridge damage than from preserving the road connectivity on which hospital access depends—a societal benefit invisible to damage-oriented assessments. This prioritisation remains stable across both aggregation lenses, with only the transition thresholds shifting. By linking infrastructure vulnerability, system-level societal impacts and risk-informed policy design, the framework provides a practical decision-support tool for directing resource-efficient infrastructure investment towards safer, more resilient and sustainable cities.
