title: Design of an Electronic Site-Marking Form to Improve Completeness of Surgical-Site Documentation
From tests to treatments: How is increased diagnostic testing related to inpatient and outpatient cancer care?
abstract: Timely and effective diagnostic testing, such as CT and MRI scans, supports early diagnosis, improves survival, and can reduce costs. However, it remains unclear whether rising diagnostic test volumes lead to changes in consultations, surgeries and other hospital outcomes. This study examines the relationship between diagnostic tests and outpatient consultations, surgeries, waiting times, length of stay and mortality. Using Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), we examine patients with breast cancer, lung cancer, bowel cancer and prostate cancer from January 2018 to December 2024. Monthly diagnostic tests are obtained from NHS England and linked to HES at the provider level. We apply fixed effects panel data models and an instrumental variable (IV) method, using the openings of Community Diagnostic Centres (CDCs) as an instrument for diagnostic tests. We find that higher diagnostic activity is associated with more pre-surgical outpatient consultations among patients who subsequently undergo breast, lung and bowel cancer surgery, and higher surgery volume for bowel cancer. IV elasticities at the mean suggest that diagnostic activity translates into less than proportionate increases in surgery volumes for breast (elasticity = 0.64) and bowel cancer (0.99). Consultation elasticities are larger - 1.01 for breast, 0.91 for lung and 1.26 for bowel, indicating that increases in testing may generate slightly more downstream outpatient activity than inpatient surgery, particularly for bowel cancer. We find no clear effects on waiting times, length of stay or one-year mortality among surgical patients.

title: Smart Building Energy Optimization and Green Corporate Strategy: A Structural Equation Modeling Approach
abstract: Buildings occupy a strategically important position in corporate sustainability because their energy demand affects operating expenditure, greenhouse-gas emissions, employee experience, asset value, and stakeholder perceptions. Yet smart-building investments are frequently evaluated as technical projects rather than as organizational capabilities embedded in corporate strategy. This article develops a strategy-oriented structural equation modeling (SEM) framework to explain how smart building energy optimization can contribute to green corporate strategy and competitive advantage. Drawing on the resource-based view, dynamic capabilities theory, stakeholder theory, and the natural-resource-based view, the framework connects top-management commitment, digital and energy-management capability, stakeholder pressure, and organizational readiness to smart building energy optimization. It then models energy optimization as a pathway to environmental performance, operational efficiency, green reputation, and sustainable competitive advantage. The framework also considers green strategic integration as a mediator and organizational digital maturity and building-use intensity as potential boundary conditions. An explanatory, cross-sectional survey design is proposed, with building and sustainability managers in commercial, institutional, hospitality, and industrial organizations as the target respondents. The article specifies constructs, measurement principles, hypotheses, and a rigorous SEM analysis protocol without presenting uncollected data as empirical findings. The central argument is that smart-building technologies create strategic value only when data, operational routines, employee practices, and investment decisions are integrated into a coherent sustainability strategy. The contribution is a testable model that bridges building-energy research and strategic-management scholarship while identifying governance, rebound, interoperability, and measurement challenges that can weaken the expected benefits.

title: Rehabilitation Potential as a Social Judgement
abstract: Abstract 'Rehabilitation potential' is among the quieter categories of contemporary clinical practice. It appears in referral criteria, admission decisions and discharge planning as a technical estimate of how much function a patient might regain. This article argues that, applied to older people, it operates instead as a social judgement, and that the judgement long predates the vocabulary in which it is now expressed. Reading rehabilitation through the critical medical humanities, we trace practices directed at restoring function in later life from Greco-Roman antiquity, Ayurvedic Jara Chikitsa, Chinese tonification regimens and the Islamic bimaristan, through the medieval European almshouse and the Enlightenment hospital, to the geriatric units of the post-war welfare state. Across these settings the material provision of care varied enormously; the mechanism governing access did not. Societies restored older bodies to the extent that they judged those bodies worth restoring, and expressed that judgement in whichever idiom was locally authoritative, humoral, theological, actuarial and now diagnostic. We identify three properties that allow the judgement to pass as a measurement: it is comparative, it is prospective, and it is self-confirming, since withholding rehabilitation produces the deterioration that retrospectively justifies the refusal. Naming these properties has consequences for practice. It shows why better prognostic instruments cannot correct the category from within, and why access to later-life rehabilitation requires the rights-based footing now taking shape in international law.

title: A review of machine learning and the internet of things for remote patient monitoring covering advances challenges and opportunities
abstract: As Machine Learning (ML) and the Internet of Things (IoT) have matured, their convergence has placed Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM) at the centre of personalized, cost-effective care. The present work reviews progress in ML and IoT based RPM, covering how ML is applied within RPM, the principal ML models employed, the IoT infrastructures that underpin it, the use of RPM across different patient populations, the challenges that arise, and the directions the field may take. After a PRISMA-guided screening of work indexed in Springer, IEEE, MDPI, ACM, and Elsevier, 101 peer-reviewed studies published from 2020 onward were retained for a qualitative (narrative) synthesis structured around five research questions. The review is narrative in form yet is carried out under a structured and transparent protocol. Within the studies examined, RPM was reported to enable real-time monitoring, cut the number of in-person hospital visits, and reduce the cost of patient-centred care, while IoT- and ML-based designs that built in privacy-preserving techniques strengthened data security; across these studies, deep learning and hybrid ML models often reported higher predictive accuracy than conventional approaches, though typically on particular datasets and at greater computational cost. Across the ten systems compared here, the eight that reported a single determinate figure gave accuracies with a median of 94.5% (range 92% to 98%) and latencies with a median of 265 ms (range 120 ms to 350 ms), and not one of them was evaluated at a site other than the one where it was developed, so these numbers describe individual study conditions rather than performance at population level. Among the obstacles that surface repeatedly are patient adherence, interoperability, scalability, and the protection of data. On balance, the body of evidence gathered here suggests that RPM built on ML and IoT can make monitoring safer, more flexible, and more anticipatory; reaching that level across whole populations, however, will call for sturdier systems, broader patient participation, and thorough clinical validation.

title: Resource Productivity in the context of Financial Performance in the Textile Industry: Evidence from the Visegrad
abstract: The paper investigates the impact of resource, labour and capital productivity on financial performance of textile industry companies in the V4 countries in the period 2015-2024. The study is based on data from 267 companies from the Orbis database. It combines traditional indicators of factor efficiency with modern concepts of the circular economy. The analysis shows that resource productivity has been the fastest growing factor in recent years, reflecting companies’ investments in technologies with lower material and energy intensity. It was shown with the use of correlation analysis, two sample t-tests and MANOVA that the companies with an increasing return on assets have significantly different values of the monitored indicators from the companies with a decreasing return on assets. The pyramid decomposition also shows that changes in resource productivity and return on sales have the largest impact on changes in ROA. The results confirm that technological innovation, digitalization and the transition to circular production models are key mechanisms linking more efficient use of production factors with financial stability of firms. The study also finds that labour productivity growth in the textile industry does not automatically translate into better profitability due to low value added and intense price competition. These findings contribute to the understanding of the role of industry structural characteristics and firms’ investment strategies on their long-term performance in the context of the transition toward sustainability in Europe. Keywords: Resource Productivity, Financial Performance, Enterprise, Labour Productivity, Capital Productivity

Blood culture turnaround time and antimicrobial resistance following an operational research interventions at 37 Military Hospital, Ghana
abstract: We conducted a retrospective before and after comparative observational study using routinely collected hospital data from neonates with suspected sepsis admitted between January 2022 and July 2024. Outcomes were compared with a previous study (2017–2020) following implementation of operational research interventions. The median turnaround time for culture positive results was 2 days (48 h), whereas culture negative reports took five days. A total of 78 cultures demonstrated bacterial growth, including nine contaminants. After exclusion of contaminants, 69 neonates (13.6%) had clinically significant culture positive sepsis. Gram-positive organisms accounted for most isolates (56.5%), primarily coagulase-negative Staphylococci (40.6%) and Staphylococcus aureus (13.0%), whereas gram-negative organisms constituted 43%, dominated by Klebsiella pneumoniae (23.2%) and Escherichia coli (14.5%). Approximately half of the isolates were multidrug resistant, with high levels of penicillin resistance found in several organisms. Late-onset sepsis was responsible for 26.5% ( n = 134) of cases. Notably, 28.9% ( n = 146) of neonates were discharged before culture results were available, with 27 (5.3%) being confirmed as culture positive. Post-culture antibiotic therapy changed in 25.4% ( n = 128) of neonates, including 30.8% of culture-positive cases. Differences in turnaround time were observed compared with the 2017–2020 cohort, although lower culture positivity was observed during the current study period. Mortality remained relatively unchanged at approximately 7% across both study periods. Although culture positivity declined over time, multidrug-resistant organisms remained common, highlighting the continued need for strengthened antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention measures, and ongoing antimicrobial resistance surveillance.

title: Operational Determinants of Communication Delay for Critical Complete-Blood-Count Values: A Single-Center Cross-Sectional Analysis Decomposing Turnaround Time into Analytical and Post-Analytical Phases
abstract: Background: Timely communication of critical complete blood count (CBC) results is an important quality indicator in laboratory medicine. However, factors associated with prolonged turnaround time (TAT) remain insufficiently characterised in tertiary-care settings. Objective: To quantify total, analytical, and post-analytical TAT for critical CBC results communicated through a hospital alert system and to identify predictors of communication delay. Methods: This retrospective cross-sectional study evaluated 544 CBCs with critical results recorded between January and June 2025 at a tertiary hospital in Brazil. Institutional critical-value thresholds included haemoglobin <6.0 or >18.0 g/dL, leukocyte counts <2.0 or >30.0 × 10⁹/L, platelet counts <50 or >1,000 × 10⁹/L, and the presence of circulating blasts. TAT was divided into analytical and post-analytical phases using timestamps for sample collection, technical release, and notification. Communication-time analyses included 487 records with available timestamps. Outcomes included TAT ≥2 h and ≥4 h and continuous log-transformed TAT. Results: Median total TAT was 5.45 h (IQR 3.12–13.18), predominantly reflecting the analytical phase (median 3.86 h), while post-analytical notification time was shorter (median 0.62 h). Overall, 8.0% of cases had a total TAT ≤2 h and 37.0% had a total TAT ≤4 h. Inpatient ward origin was independently associated with TAT ≥4 h (OR 4.22, 95% CI 2.65–6.71). Leukocytosis and weekend collection were also associated with prolonged TAT. Conclusions: Prolonged TAT for critical CBC results was associated primarily with operational and workflow-related factors. The analytical phase accounted for the largest proportion of total TAT, suggesting that inpatient sample logistics and weekend laboratory workflows may represent important targets for quality improvement.

title: Optimizing colorectal cancer NGS pathways: Quality gaps, workflow barriers, and digital/AI readiness.
Delayed verification and communication of critical laboratory results in a Nigerian tertiary hospital: a case based quality improvement report
abstract: Abstract Background: Timely communication of critical laboratory results is a core patient- safety function of the total testing process. Its effectiveness depends on analytical quality and also on result authorisation, communication channels, acknowledgement and clinical action. In Nigeria, critical value notification practices are reported to be variable and often unsupported by written policy Case presentation: A blood specimen from a 57 year old man admitted to the ICU was received at 4:35 p.m. and processed using a Selectra Pro XL analyser, with processing completed at approximately 4:50 p.m. Markedly abnormal biochemical results were identified, and the sample was rerun for verification, with quality-control procedures performed. Results (sodium 120 mmol/L, potassium 6.4 mmol/L, chloride 92 mmol/L, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, urea 40.5 mmol/L, creatinine 1005 µmol/L; calculated anion gap 20 mmol/L) were confirmed by rerun with acceptable quality control and prepared at about 5:10 p.m. Supervisory verification occurred at 8:05 a.m. the next day (15 h 30 min after receipt), and the results were obtained by a resident at about 10:00 a.m., when the author was informed the patient was in shock. No formal critical result policy, critical value list, after hours verification arrangement or clinician contact process existed. The patient’s outcome is unknown, and causation cannot be inferred. Discussion: The reported timeline suggests a substantial interval between result preparation, supervisory verification and the clinical team obtaining the results. Although analytical processing was completed promptly, the absence of a formal critical result communication pathway raises concerns about after hours verification, timely notification, escalation and documentation. Conclusions : Rapid analysis does not guarantee timely clinical awareness. Laboratories and clinical teams should establish clear responsibilities, accessible contact details, documented notification procedures and confirmation of receipt to strengthen patient safety.

title: Impact of combined molecular identification and rapid phenotypic drug antimicrobial susceptibility testing on the time to results for positive blood cultures – preliminary report
A-266 Improving Laboratory Efficiency and Patient Safety Through Data-Driven Autoverification in Hematology and Coagulation
Automation and artificial intelligence in the clinical microbiology laboratory
journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
abstract: Background: Clinical microbiology laboratories face persistent pressure to shorten turnaround times, reduce manual workloads, and standardize diagnostic workflows. Total laboratory automation (TLA) and artificial intelligence (AI) are complementary responses to these demands. In this review, we examine how the evidence base for automation and AI in clinical microbiology is distributed along a maturity gradient and what this distribution implies for the next phase of implementation. Content: Available evidence indicates that automated platforms shorten culture turnaround times and reduce manual workload in observational and multi-center studies, although the scale of benefit depends on specimen type and workflow configuration. Automated reading, identification, and susceptibility testing systems showed high concordance with manual standards for common specimen types, with error rates below commonly cited acceptability thresholds. Evidence for AI performance in plate reading and resistance prediction is abundant; however, most models remain in an assistive phase without prospective validation. Randomized trials of rapid testing and automation rarely demonstrate overall clinical superiority, and patient-oriented benefits remain limited and inconsistent. Guidelines provide directional support, whereas interoperability, quality control, and regulatory frameworks are still under development. Summary: The priority of the field is not additional single-center performance validation. The next phase requires multi-center prospective verification, interpretability, standardization, and comparative evidence with clinical outcomes as endpoints. AI-assisted evidence tools may accelerate evidence generation, although their utility remains preliminary.

title: Transitioning to in-house methotrexate level testing for patients receiving high-dose methotrexate.

IMPLEMENTATION OF QUALITY MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS TO IMPROVE ANALYTICAL ACCURACY AND OPERATIONAL EFFICIENCY IN MEDICAL LABORATORIES
abstract: Quality management systems (QMS) are essential for maintaining reliable analytical processes, improving laboratory workflows, and supporting effective clinical decision-making. Systematic quality monitoring helps identify weaknesses, address nonconformities, and promote continuous improvement in medical laboratories. This study aimed to assess baseline quality management performance, examine accreditation-related nonconformities, and evaluate selected operational indicators to understand laboratory quality and operational efficiency. A retrospective descriptive approach was used to analyse existing laboratory records from a supplementary dataset associated with the implementation of a QMS based on ISO 15189. The analysis examined baseline quality management assessment scores, nonconformities recorded across accreditation assessments, turnaround-time performance, external quality assessment (EQA) results, and specimen rejection rates. Descriptive summaries were used to identify patterns across the available observation periods. The baseline assessment showed variation across quality management requirements, with comparatively stronger scores in safety and information management and weaker scores in management reviews, corrective actions, and internal audits. Accreditation records showed an increase in recorded nonconformities across later assessments. Operational indicators fluctuated over time, demonstrating variation in turnaround-time performance, EQA results, and specimen rejection rates. These findings highlighted areas requiring continued monitoring and targeted quality improvement. The findings emphasize the importance of strengthening internal audits, management reviews, corrective-action follow-up, and routine performance monitoring. Consistent data collection and standardized assessment practices are recommended to support sustained laboratory quality and operational efficiency. The descriptive design does not establish causal relationships between QMS implementation and observed performance changes.

title: An independent third-party autoverification platform iXLAB Verify and its application in a core clinical biochemistry laboratory
abstract: Abstract To develop and validate a third-party autoverification system independent of the laboratory information system (LIS) and instrument middleware, and to evaluate its feasibility in clinical chemistry testing. The autoverification system iXLAB Verify was configured following Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) AUTO15 guidelines and the Autoverification of Clinical Laboratory Quantitative Test Results (WS/T 616–2018). A retrospective validation using 53,120 samples was conducted prior to formal deployment, after which autoverification pass rates and turnaround time (TAT) were evaluated over seven months of clinical operation (n = 135,257). Pre-deployment validation demonstrated 100% sensitivity and 97.28% specificity, with a false negative rate of 0%. Following deployment, the overall autoverification pass rate was 86.19%, and the 90th percentile TAT was reduced from 223 to 120 min (outpatient), 215 to 168 min (inpatient), and 204 to 124 min (health check). The autoverification system reduced turnaround time in a core clinical chemistry laboratory. Independent of laboratory instruments and information systems, the iXLAB Verify platform has the potential to be deployed across different laboratory environments without rule reconfiguration.

From species identification to AI-enabled outbreak triage: MALDI-TOF MS for early warning in hospitals
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Purpose: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) remain a major clinical and economic burden, and early detection of transmission clusters is essential for timely intervention. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is the reference standard for outbreak confirmation, but its cost, turnaround time, and operational requirements limit its use as an always-on first-line surveillance tool. Because matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) spectra are already generated during routine species identification, they may provide a rapid triage layer before confirmatory sequencing. Methods: We synthesize current evidence for artificial intelligence (AI)-based MALDI-TOF MS analysis in within-species typing, strain relatedness inference, and outbreak-oriented surveillance. We organize the literature into three methodological pathways: peak-centric biomarker typing, supervised subtype classification, and representation learning. Results: The available evidence indicates that AI-based models can extract within-species signals from MALDI-TOF MS spectra that are relevant to typing and outbreak surveillance, but performance remains context-dependent. Peak-based approaches offer interpretability but are vulnerable to spectral instability and limited portability. Supervised classifiers can perform well for narrow predefined targets, but depend on fixed label spaces and may degrade when local epidemiology changes. Representation-learning approaches are less clinically validated for typing, but may offer the most scalable route toward adaptable, similarity-based early-warning systems. Conclusions: MALDI-TOF MS should not be viewed as a replacement for WGS, but as a locally calibrated decision-support tool that prioritizes suspicious isolates for sequencing and infection prevention and control (IPC) review, similar to a screening tool. Future studies should move beyond retrospective accuracy estimates and evaluate prospective clinical utility, including time gained, sequencing saved, false-alert burden, portability to new laboratories, and performance after minimal local calibration.

Clinical characteristics and outcomes among patients admitted with Viral Hemorrhagic Fever at Mbarara Regional Referral Hospital, Uganda
abstract: Background Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) such as Rift Valley Fever (RVF) and Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever (CCHF) pose serious public health concerns in endemic regions like Uganda, where outbreaks occur sporadically. Despite this, there is limited data on the clinical characteristics and outcomes of affected patients in rural settings. Methods This is a retrospective descriptive study of 36 patients with laboratory-confirmed VHF who were treated at the isolation unit of Mbarara Regional Referral Hospital in Southwestern Uganda during the outbreaks that occurred between 2018 and 2024. We extracted data on demographics, clinical presentation including laboratory parameters, complications and outcomes from patients’ files and analyzed using descriptive statistics. We used Welch’s t test- to describe the difference in length of hospital stay between the survivors and patients who succumbed to VHF. Results Of the 36 patients included, 88.9% (n=32) were male, with a median age of 35 (IQR: 28 – 42.5) years. 69.4% (n=25) of the patients interacted directly with animals or animal products in their occupations. The most common presenting symptoms included bleeding tendencies (28 [77.8%]), fever (23 [63.9%]) and vomiting (19 [52.8%]). The median duration of symptoms was 5 days (IQR: 4 – 7). Laboratory results revealed severe kidney impairment with a median creatinine of 10.3 mg/dl (IQR: 7.46 – 13), elevated AST of 1014 (IQR 173-2570) IU/L and ALT of 795.9 (IQR 233-1634) IU/L, prolonged INR (median 1.65 [IQR: 1.5 – 1.7]), hyperbilirubinemia (mean serum bilirubin 5.7 [SD 1.2]) and thrombocytopenia (median platelet count 43000 (IQR 16000 – 65000)). The overall case fatality rate was 41.7% (n=15) with mean time from admission to death of 2.40 [SD 2.75] days. There was a statistically significant difference in the mean length of hospital stay between the survivors and those who died in hospital (mean difference 15.07 days, 95% CI 11.57–18.57; p < 0.001). Conclusion In Southwestern Uganda, patients with VHFs present with severe illness, characterized by hemorrhagic, hepatic, and renal complications. The high case fatality rate indicates the need for early detection and comprehensive supportive care interventions, such as hemodialysis.

title: A-065 Development of AIIMS Routine Microscopy-Assisted UTI Stratification Score (MUSS) for Reflex Testing and Diagnostic Stewardship
Development and evaluation of an intelligent centralized transportation dispatching information system in a large tertiary hospital: a single-center retrospective observational study
abstract: Background Traditional hospital central transportation adopts manual telephone dispatch, bringing high communication costs, poor traceability, mismatched resources and weak quality control, which impede clinical efficiency and patient safety. This study designs an intelligent dispatching system integrating RFID, IoT and mobile terminals, and assesses its performance in a large tertiary hospital. Methods A single-center retrospective observational study was carried out at West China Hospital. The system combines RFID-IoT real-time positioning and multi-objective scheduling algorithms, with two-way connections to HIS, examination platforms and PDAs. We analyzed system data of transport tasks, time metrics, tool utilization and patient satisfaction from Jan 1 to Jun 30, 2026 (post-implementation). Pre-2025 non-digital records were only used for qualitative reference; incomplete raw data excluded formal statistical comparison and inter-period hypothesis testing. Continuous variables were median (interquartile range); categorical variables n (%). Results Over 6 months, the system handled four core transport scenarios. Post-implementation median single-task dispatch time reached 0.57 (0.31–0.82) min, and emergency examination transport time 24.3 (13.41–32.87) min. Among 24,545 tool records, independent ambulation (54.5%) and wheelchairs (32.0%) made up 86.5% of transports, stretchers (6.5%) and hospital beds (7.0%) for critical and postoperative patients accounted for the rest 13.5%. In 5,508 surveyed inpatients, overall transport satisfaction hit 97.78%, with item-level satisfaction rates ranging from 95.51% (staff attentiveness) to 98.14% (staff appearance/professional grooming). Conclusion This single-center retrospective evaluation shows the RFID/IoT intelligent dispatching system achieves brief dispatch & transport durations and high patient satisfaction. Without matched complete pre-implementation baseline data, results only describe post-launch performance instead of causal improvement evidence. Prospective multi-center or interrupted-time-series studies with standardized baselines are required to verify its incremental value.

title: Laboratories as Innovation-Platforms Within Healthcare Systems: Learning From the UNIVANTS Excellences
abstract: Abstract Over the past decade, value-based healthcare (VBH) has gained prominence as a strategic response to increasing clinical complexity, resource constraints, and rising expectations regarding quality and patient-centeredness. While VBH has strongly emphasized the outcomes and costs’ measurement, its implementation has often remained confined to technical and structural dimensions, with limited integration into everyday professional practices and organizational learning processes. Drawing on insights from the UNIVANTS of Healthcare Excellence award, this chapter examines how VBH principles can be translated into actionable service models by synthesizing crosscutting lessons from 2018–2025 award winners, adopting a transversal analytical perspective rather than a descriptive case-by-case approach. The analysis highlights recurring patterns and enabling conditions that support value creation across clinical, organizational, and economic dimensions. Findings show that laboratories increasingly serve as innovation platforms, leveraging their transversal position to drive pathway re-engineering, multidisciplinary collaboration, data-driven decision-making, and workforce redesign. Successful initiatives move beyond measurement alone, embedding outcome indicators into governance mechanisms, diagnostic algorithms, and redesigned care pathways. Digital solutions and data infrastructures emerge as critical enablers when aligned with clinical and organizational needs, supporting coordination, risk stratification, and continuous improvement. Economic sustainability is achieved indirectly through appropriateness, waste reduction, and efficiency gains, rather than through cost containment alone. Overall, the UNIVANTS experience demonstrates that laboratories can evolve from technical service providers to strategic assets in system-level transformation. For healthcare leaders and policymakers, this chapter underscores that sustainable VBH implementation requires integrated governance, cultural readiness, and leadership commitment, enabling innovations to be scalable, transferable, and capable of generating lasting value.

title: The Unusual Outbreak of Sepsis in a Cancer Hospital Caused by Intrinsically Contaminated Heparin Injection Vials
journal: Asian Pacific Journal of Cancer Prevention
abstract: BACKGROUND: The outbreaks in oncology settings result in dreaded complications, especially in cancer patients who are already immunocompromised. Here, we describe the identification and response to an unusual hospital-acquired outbreak of bloodstream infections (BSIs) in cancer patients due to intrinsic contamination of a heparin injection vial with New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase (blaNDM)-positive Klebsiella pneumoniae. METHODS: An increased cluster of sepsis cases in cancer patients with chemoports was noted in the medical oncology department of a cancer center in North India in July 2024. These case clusters were identified by reviewing microbiological reports, and blood cultures were tested by automated identification and susceptibility testing, the Carba-R test, and molecular testing. Outbreak investigations were performed; causality assessment was also done. The clinical and demographic details of the case patients, along with other relevant histories, were collected from electronic medical records. Environmental samples were collected from high-touch surfaces, intravenous medications, saline, and heparin. RESULTS: A cluster of 10 sepsis cases with culture-confirmed bloodstream infections (BSIs) was identified in the medical oncology department. Out of the 10 patients, 5 (50%) were admitted to the ward after visiting the central venous access device (CVAD) clinic, and 5 (50%) presented to the emergency department after recent chemotherapy. All cases had Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from blood cultures, which alerted the oncology team to a possible outbreak. All isolates were multidrug-resistant strains sensitive to ceftazidime-avibactam and tigecycline. The multidrug resistance gene detected in all isolates was blaNDM. The heparin injection vial was found to be the primary cause and single source of the outbreak. All isolates from heparin and patients' clinical samples were confirmed by molecular typing using Enterobacterial Repetitive Intergenic Consensus Polymerase Chain Reaction (ERIC-PCR). Interestingly, the contamination was found to be intrinsic to a new batch of heparin manufactured by the company. CONCLUSION: This study highlights the importance of an infection surveillance system as part of pharmacovigilance, which helped detect the source of infection within a few days of the outbreak alert. Implementing standardized healthcare-associated infection (HAI) surveillance in a low-resource setting detected an ongoing heparin-associated outbreak. The outbreak investigation and the use of a multimodal approach reduced incident cases and informed changes in infection prevention and control (IPC) practices. The regulatory authorities (CDSCO and the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission) were also notified, which helped them enforce strict quality control and regulatory oversight in drug manufacturing.

title: Hidden Cost of Poor Quality in Laboratory Medicine: From Errors and Waste to Value-Based Care
abstract: To examine where poor laboratory quality generates economic and clinical consequences across the total testing process and to propose a practical framework for identifying preventable waste.This narrative review draws on the focused PubMed/MEDLINE search described in the original submission, reference-list checking, and a separately documented PubMed update performed on September 29, 2026.Eight topic-specific strategies used title/abstract terms and Medical Subject Headings; publications were selected for direct relevance to laboratory quality failure, resource use, test utilization, and value-based care.No pooled analysis or formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed.Preanalytical defects, repeated work, and inappropriate testing consume resources across laboratory and clinical workflows.Published monetary estimates depend on study setting and costing perspective, while evidence on downstream patient outcomes remains less complete.Our conceptual Cost of Poor Laboratory Quality (COPLQ) framework links recurrent, measurable failures to local resource use and clinical consequences.Prospective evaluation is required before it can be used as a validated economic model.

title: Rapid Offload to Avoid Delays to Mitigate Ambulance Patient Offload Time
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Ambulance patient offload time, the interval from emergency medical service arrival to completion of transfer of care to emergency department personnel, is associated with delayed treatment, prolonged emergency medical service turnaround, and operational and financial strain. In California, ambulance patient offload time has received legislative attention through Assembly Bill 40, enacted to reduce ambulance offload delays, expedite care, and improve emergency medical service community response. This quality improvement project evaluated whether a dedicated ambulance receiving area, named Ambi ROAD (Rapid Offload to Avoid Delays) supported by a dedicated nurse and standardized staff workflow training, was associated with reduced ambulance patient offload time at a high-volume emergency department. METHODS: Using a retrospective pre-post observational design, monthly data from the 12 months before implementation were compared with those from the 12 months after implementation. The intervention was refined through multiple Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles. Monthly 90th percentile ambulance patient offload time values and ambulance arrival volumes were obtained from the 2 local emergency medical service agencies that served the site. Monthly ED census was also evaluated to assess utilization trends. RESULTS: Mean monthly 90th percentile ambulance patient offload time decreased from 80.00 to 30.58 minutes for Sacramento County ambulance arrivals (t = 8.64, P < .001, d = 3.53) and from 81.58 to 33.67 minutes for Sierra-Sacramento Valley ambulance arrivals (t = 9.38, P < .001, d = 3.83). Ambulance traffic increased from 654.50 to 764.58 per month for Sacramento County (P < .001) and from 759.83 to 801.92 per month for Sierra-Sacramento Valley (P = .022). The emergency department census did not change significantly (P = .442). DISCUSSION: A dedicated ambulance receiving area, a dedicated offload nurse, and standardized workflow training were associated with substantial reductions in ambulance patient offload time despite an increased ambulance volume. This approach may help emergency departments move toward regulatory targets, or similar aims, and support more timely initiation of patient care and faster emergency medical service turnaround.

title: Surgical Outcomes and Operative Time in Parathyroidectomy With and Without the Miami Protocol: A Comparative Analysis
abstract: Introduction: Parathyroidectomy is the definitive treatment for primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT).While intraoperative parathyroid hormone (IOPTH) monitoring (the Miami Protocol) is widely used to guide surgical success and enable minimally invasive approaches, its impact on operative metrics remains debated.This study compares surgical outcomes and operative times in parathyroidectomy with and without the Miami Protocol at two tertiary care hospitals within a private academic healthcare system.Materials and methods: This retrospective, comparative study analyzed electronic medical records of 51 adult patients who underwent parathyroidectomy for PHPT at TecSalud hospitals between January 2021 and June 2025.Patients were stratified into two groups: Group 1 (Miami Protocol with IOPTH measurement, n = 11) and Group 2 (No Miami Protocol, n = 40).Evaluated variables included demographic characteristics, baseline comorbidities, presurgical localization studies, histopathological findings, early biochemical normalization rates, postoperative complications, hospital stay, and total operative time.Results: Baseline characteristics and comorbidity distributions were similar between groups.Early biochemical normalization was observed in 49/50 (98.0%) of evaluable patients: 11/11 (100%) in Group 1 and 38/39 (97.4%) in Group 2 (p = 1.000).In-hospital complications and reinterventions occurred in 1/51 (2.0%) and 2/51 (3.9%) of patients, respectively, with no statistically significant differences between groups.Mean length of hospital stay was 1.2 ± 0.77 days.Operative time was longer in the Miami Protocol group than in the group without IOPTH monitoring (127.8 ± 58.5 minutes vs. 76.2 ± 45.6 minutes; p = 0.004).Exploratory analyses also found longer operative times in patients with hyperplastic pathology and bilateral cervical exploration.Conclusions: IOPTH use was associated with a longer observed operative time.Early biochemical normalization was frequent, and in-hospital complications and reinterventions were uncommon.However, the retrospective design, small and unequal groups, surgeon-level confounding, and limited follow-up preclude conclusions regarding causality or equivalence.Further prospective studies are needed to evaluate criteria for selective IOPTH use.

title: Electronic medical records for health system strengthening in Nepal: a community case study of phased implementation across public hospitals
abstract: Robust health information systems are foundational to universal health coverage, quality of care and health-system resilience, yet many public hospitals in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) still rely on paper-based records that fragment patient histories, duplicate diagnostics and limit routine data for management and policy. This community case study describes the phased implementation and observed system-level changes of open-source electronic medical records (EMRs) across public hospitals in Nepal and reflects on transferable lessons for comparable settings. From the early 2010s, Nepal adopted open-source EMR platforms principally Bahmni, built on OpenMRS as a license-free, locally adaptable alternative to proprietary systems. Adoption accelerated after the COVID-19 pandemic and was reinforced by Nepal's 2022 Joint External Evaluation and COVID-19 Intra-Action Review, both of which called for a transition from fragmented paper-based reporting towards integrated digital systems. With technical assistance from the World Health Organization (WHO) and financing from the Pandemic Fund, EMRs were deployed through a standardized six-phase model emphasizing readiness assessment, clinician engagement, local customization and sustained capacity-building; from 2024, legacy installations were upgraded to the FHIR-aligned OpenMRS 3 interface. By May 2026, 19 government hospitals across six of Nepal's seven provinces had transitioned to functional open-source EMRs, with longitudinal records accessible across departments, integrated laboratory and radiology results, standardized electronic reporting and expanded routine data for oversight. Optimizing the whole technical environment, particularly storage and network quality rather than processing power alone proved critical. Improvements in clinical continuity and efficiency were reported by users rather than formally measured. Nepal's experience suggests EMRs are best understood as organizational transformation rather than a purely technological upgrade.

title: Achieving Project Performance through Stakeholder Participation Practices: Empirical Evidence from Catheterisation Laboratory Projects at Selected Healthcare Facilities in Nairobi City County, Kenya
journal: East African Journal of Business and Economics
abstract: Catheterisation laboratory (cath lab) projects are central to the diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular disease, yet their performance in achieving intended goals remains a concern in Kenya. This study examined how stakeholder participation in project identification, funding, monitoring and evaluation, and capacity building influences the performance of cath lab projects at three healthcare facilities in Nairobi City County: Kenyatta National Hospital, Kenyatta University Teaching, Referral and Research Hospital, and Avenue Hospital. General Systems Theory and Stakeholder Theory guided this descriptive survey, which had a qualitative component. The target population was 340 top and middle-level managers, departmental employees, patients, and representatives of government agencies and employee unions. Using Taro Yamane's formula and proportionate stratified random sampling, 184 respondents were selected and 157 returned usable questionnaires (85.3%). Data were collected through a semi-structured questionnaire and interviews with 12 cath lab beneficiaries, and were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple linear regression, and thematic analysis. All four forms of participation correlated positively and significantly with project performance (r = 0.611 to 0.706, p < 0.001). The regression model was significant and explained 70.3% of the variance in performance (adjusted R2 = 0.696; F(4, 152) = 89.9, p < 0.001). Funding (β = 0.644, p < 0.001) and monitoring and evaluation (β = 0.185, p = 0.001) were significant individual predictors, whereas project identification and capacity building were not once the other variables were controlled for, despite their strong bivariate correlations with performance. Interviewees highlighted communication on costs and timing, waiting-area privacy, and digital booking. The study concludes that stakeholder participation, particularly in funding and monitoring and evaluation, enhances cath lab project performance. Hospital managers and policymakers should institutionalise stakeholder participation across the project lifecycle, and future studies should extend to other countries and longitudinal designs.

title: A-127 An AI-Driven Mobile Tool for Rapid Morphological Identification of Filamentous Fungi
Retrospective registration of the analysis plan for an audit of in-hospital follow-up of abnormal thyroid function tests
abstract: Background: Abnormal but non-critical laboratory results — such as a mildly elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) — do not trigger critical-value alerts, and whether they are ever confirmed after being returned is not routinely measured. Closed-loop management of critical values is well established; the corresponding step for non-critical abnormalities has not been quantified. Objective: To quantify, among inpatients carrying a diagnosis of hypothyroidism, the proportion whose abnormal TSH result was followed by a repeat measurement during the same admission; to localise where the gap falls; and to determine whether the gap is distinctive relative to other routinely measured analytes. Design: Retrospective observational cohort study of a de-identified critical care database, with no intervention. The primary outcome is a process indicator (completion of follow-up testing), not a health outcome. Reporting follows STROBE and SQUIRE 2.0. Data: MIMIC-IV v3.1 (2008-2019, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center), PhysioNet; de-identified, read-only extraction. Cohort defined by four pre-specified criteria: a thyroid-related diagnosis (ICD-10 E03, E04-E07, E21, E89, C73); at least one TSH measured during admission with a first abnormal value (<0.04 or >4.0 uIU/mL); at least 3 further days of admission remaining after that result, so that a follow-up window physically existed; and the first qualifying admission per patient. Outcomes: The primary outcome is repeat TSH measurement after the index abnormal result within the same admission. Two secondary outcomes are defined in advance: free thyroxine (FT4) measured after the index result, requiring sampling strictly later than the TSH draw; and initiation of thyroid hormone therapy, requiring the first prescription to post-date the index result. Post-discharge outpatient follow-up was examined and rejected as unmeasurable, and the attribution analysis supporting that decision is documented. Analysis: Clopper-Pearson exact confidence intervals for proportions; chi-square or Fisher exact tests between groups; Cochran-Armitage trend test across ordered TSH strata; multivariable logistic regression with six covariate degrees of freedom. Five sensitivity analyses were specified in advance of the final analysis: 42 definitional variants (7 TSH thresholds x 6 follow-up windows); cross-epoch replication of the identical definition in MIMIC-III (2001-2012); four alternative FT4 reference intervals; benchmarking of re-test rates against 14 additional laboratory analytes, each judged against its own recorded clinical reference interval; and verification that the TSH threshold choice did not drive the findings. Ethics: Source data were approved by the Institutional Review Board of Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center with waiver of individual informed consent and are released under the PhysioNet Credentialed Health Data Use Agreement. This secondary analysis of de-identified data meets the criteria for exemption. Status: This registration was created after completion of data extraction and analysis and is therefore a retrospective registration, not a prospective preregistration. It is submitted to document the study objectives, variable definitions, outcome definitions, and the analytical decisions that were fixed before the final analysis was run. Numerical study results are not reported in this record.

title: A prospective study of DMAIC-based six sigma implementation for analytical quality improvement in a clinical biochemistry laboratory
abstract: Analytical errors in clinical biochemistry can compromise patient safety and clinical decision-making. Therefore, it is of interest to evaluate a DMAIC-based quality improvement programme for 20 serum chemistry analytes over 11 months. Baseline and endpoint data were compared using CLIA 2025 allowable total error, IQC-derived coefficient of variation, EQA-derived bias and Quality Goal Index analysis. Unacceptable analytes decreased from 11 to 2, while world-class and excellent performers increased from 0 to 4 and 0 to 3, respectively. Thus, data shows the DMAIC-based Six Sigma programme improved analytical performance and supported risk-based quality control planning for sustainable laboratory quality improvement.

title: Quantifying the diagnostic time gap in precision oncology: A retrospective analysis of potential time savings from same-day cartridge-based molecular testing versus next-generation sequencing in cytology specimens
abstract: BACKGROUND: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) turnaround times (TAT) exceed two weeks and can delay the initiation of targeted therapy. Rapid cartridge-based platforms such as Idylla deliver single-gene or fusion results from minimal cytology material within hours, but time savings have not been systematically quantified. METHODS: Forty-two cases of non-small cell lung carcinoma, thyroid carcinoma, melanoma, and mammary analogue secretory carcinoma of the salivary gland that underwent both Idylla testing (KRAS, EGFR, BRAF, and GeneFusion assays) and orthogonal NGS at a single academic center were reviewed. NGS TAT was calculated from specimen collection to report release, and Idylla results were modeled as available one day after collection. The primary outcome was per-case time savings (NGS TAT minus one day); treatment timelines were reconstructed from the medical record. Analyses were descriptive; no inferential testing was performed. A sensitivity analysis varied the modeled Idylla TAT from 1 to 3 days, and an adjusted estimate assigned no time saving to the two cartridge results that were not actionable on the day of collection. RESULTS: The median NGS TAT across all 42 cases was 20.0 days (IQR, 17.0-23.8; range, 8-51). Against the modeled 1-day Idylla TAT, the median time savings was 19.0 days per case (IQR, 16.0-22.8; range, 7-50), totaling 858 patient-days. Assigning no time saving to those two cases gave a median of 18.0 days and 817 patient-days. No patient received therapy that was subsequently contradicted by the sequencing result. In thirteen patients, the sequencing interval alone exceeded three weeks, and in seven, no systemic therapy was underway while the result was awaited. CONCLUSIONS: Same-day cartridge-based testing from cytology and small biopsy specimens could provide actionable results a median of 19 days earlier than standard NGS. Whether this translates into earlier treatment initiation was not assessed and requires prospective evaluation.

title: THE AUTONOMOUS CLINICAL LABORATORY: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, ROBOTICS, DIGITAL PATHOLOGY, AND THE FUTURE OF PRECISION DIAGNOSTICS AND EMERGENCY CARE CRITICAL NARRATIVE REVIEW
abstract: The autonomous clinical laboratory is often described as the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, and digital diagnostics, yet technical integration does not by itself establish clinical safety or benefit. This critical narrative review examines how these technologies can be combined into a clinically accountable laboratory service. Initial targeted searches of publicly accessible scholarly records and official guidance were completed on September 5, 2026, with a focused emergency-care update on October 20, 2026, prioritizing recent original investigations, implementation studies, and authoritative standards. Evidence was interpreted according to study design, population, reference standard, external validation, workflow effects, and the distinction between predictive performance and patient benefit. Selected investigations demonstrate faster microbiological reporting, reduced immunohistochemistry use in a small prospective pathology study, and promising classification of acute leukemia and influenza from routine laboratory parameters. However, historical controls, selected populations, simulated errors, limited prospective evaluation, and heterogeneous endpoints constrain claims of generalizable autonomy. Foundation models expand opportunities for whole-slide analysis and multimodal integration, but benchmark scale should not be mistaken for validation of unattended clinical reporting. A practical framework is proposed in which specimen identity, analytical quality, model eligibility, authorized actions, human escalation, and post-deployment surveillance form a controlled diagnostic pathway. Particular attention is given to calibration, abstention, interoperability, cybersecurity, economic evaluation, and implementation in Saudi Arabia. The most defensible near-term objective is bounded, auditable automation with accountable specialist oversight. Progress should be judged by reliable clinical decisions and equitable service delivery, rather than the proportion of tasks performed without human involvement.

title: Prevalence of Reactive Screening Markers for HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and Syphilis Among Blood Donors at the Provincial Hospital of Sarh, Chad: A Retrospective Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Introduction: Blood transfusion safety remains a challenge in resource-limited settings. This study estimated the prevalence of reactive screening markers for HIV, hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and syphilis among blood donors at Sarh Provincial Hospital, Chad. Methods: This retrospective cross-sectional study used blood bank register data from 18 September to 18 November 2023. Of 2,868 records identified, 27 were excluded and 2,841 donors were analyzed. Screening used rapid diagnostic tests; confirmatory testing was unavailable. Prevalence estimates and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Results: Participants included 2,173 men (76.49%) and 668 women (23.51%); 97.75% were family/replacement donors. Reactive markers were HBV 275/2,841 (9.68%; 95% CI 8.64– 10.83), syphilis 177/2,841 (6.23%; 95% CI 5.39– 7.18), HCV 104/2,841 (3.66%; 95% CI 3.03– 4.42), and HIV 95/2,841 (3.34%; 95% CI 2.74– 4.07). Overall, 584 donors (20.56%) had at least one reactive marker, and 64 (2.25%) had multiple-marker reactivity. No significant sex differences were observed; age trends were not significant for HBV or HCV. Conclusion: HBV and syphilis were the most frequent reactive screening markers. Because confirmatory testing was not available, results represent screening-marker reactivity rather than laboratory-confirmed infection. Findings are limited to this hospital and the two-month study period. Strengthening voluntary non-remunerated donation, quality assurance, confirmatory testing, and surveillance may improve blood safety. Keywords: reactive screening marker, HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis, blood donors, Sarh Provincial Hospital, Chad

title: A-057 Analytical and Clinical Utility of LIAISON® MeMed BV as Part of a Complementary Biomarker Strategy for Suspected Sepsis
Optimization of Leukocytic Flags in the Sysmex‐ XN Series With the Help of Flow Cytometric Differential ( FlowDiff ) Can Significantly Optimize Laboratory Efficiency
abstract: OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to adjust the default white blood cell (WBC) differential count flag settings on the Sysmex XN-9100 haematology analyser to reduce unnecessary additional leukocyte differential counts without compromising diagnostic sensitivity. METHODS: Data from 4554 routine blood samples flagged on Sysmex XN-9100 and corresponding additional leukocyte differential counts performed on the Sysmex XF-1600 flow cytometer were used to optimise the WBC flagging rules. RESULTS: A total of 1148 samples had scattergram-related flags, which are non-adjustable. Optimal cut points for Q-flags were established based on Youden's Index for the remaining 3406 samples, while the diagnostic sensitivity of the new flagging rules for acute leukaemia was assessed in a validation cohort. The optimal cut points for Q-flags were 120 for 'Atypical Lymphocytes', 170 for 'Abnormal Lymphocytes' and 160 for 'Blasts', while the Q-flag 'Left shift' offered no diagnostic value in our cohort. The count flags 'eosinophilia', 'basophilia' and 'monocytopenia' were deactivated, as the results from Sysmex XN were comparable to the flow cytometric reference method. By implementing the new flagging rules, 1709 (37.5%) of the samples would have been processed without need for additional leukocyte differential count. When evaluated in a separate validation cohort of 90 samples from patients with newly diagnosed acute leukaemia, the new rules showed similar diagnostic sensitivity to the default flagging system. CONCLUSION: Optimisation of Sysmex flagging rules for leukocyte differential counts was feasible and significantly reduced unnecessary reflex testing, while maintaining analytical accuracy and diagnostic safety.

title: ANALISIS FAKTOR-FAKTOR YANG MEMPENGARUHI PENGGUNAAN LAHAN PARKIR DI RSUD PASAR REBO JAKARTA TIMUR
abstract: Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) is a continuous quality improvement method commonly applied to clinical processes, yet rarely used explicitly for non-clinical facility management such as hospital parking. This study aimed to formulate a PDSA cycle design for optimizing parking land utilization at Pasar Rebo Regional General Hospital, East Jakarta, during a period of capacity constraints caused by Emergency Department (ED) renovation. A mixed methods sequential explanatory design was used: a quantitative baseline was obtained from a survey of 200 visitors, then deepened through in-depth interviews with management, vendor, and specialist physicians and a gap analysis of the baseline, whose results informed the Plan stage design. The PDSA design addressed a primary problem of prolonged parking search time (49.5% of visitors required more than 15 minutes) and low parking turnover (69.5% of vehicles parked longer than 2 hours). The Plan stage set a trial location in one high-density zone for 4–8 weeks; the Do stage involved providing occupancy information boards, organizing drop-off areas, and strengthening ED-route supervision; the Study stage compared pre- and post-intervention indicators; and the Act stage determined adoption, adaptation, or re-evaluation decisions based on target achievement. This PDSA design produced a staged strategy map for the short term (0–6 months), medium term (6 months–2 years), and long term (2–5 years). PDSA is a feasible mechanism for measurably and sustainably restructuring hospital parking management without relying on physical land expansion.

title: The whole is greater than the sum of the parts: insights into resilient, well performing, quality improvement teams for maternal and neonatal health care in South Africa before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: Aim This evaluation identifies the factors that shaped the performance of quality improvement teams for maternal and neonatal health, before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Method A longitudinal, qualitative evaluation of a National Department of Health quality improvement (QI) programme called Mphatlalatsane was undertaken. The programme adopts a plan-do-study-act cycle to identify and implement change ideas that support QI, through QI teams comprising existing facility staff. Mphatlalatsane was implemented in 21 facilities across three provinces, between 2018–2022. Fifteen teams were purposively selected for this evaluation, ranging from primary health care clinics to regional hospitals. The evaluation comprised of interviews with QI team leaders and members undertaken at three time points, monthly debriefings with the technical advisors, review of programme documentation, and observing Mphatlalatsane management meetings. Data were thematically analysed. Findings The COVID-19 pandemic resulted in teams introducing major, yet effective, adaptations to the QI methodology. Six teams were assessed as performing well in conducting activities to improve service delivery. Those teams had advisors who were technically skilled, leaders and members with an aptitude for QI methods, and support from facility management. Team performance was shaped by the interplay between advisor, leader, members, and prevailing work culture in the existing facility service teams. Conclusion Healthcare workers in well performing teams successfully implemented and sustained QI, despite the COVID-19 pandemic challenges. Supporting a QI team to enthusiastically and sustainably use the methodology, requires acknowledging that the advisor, leader, and members create a microsystem that becomes more than the sum of its parts. QI success lies in the interplay among elements in this microsystem, and not in the absence or presence of individual elements.

title: Integrated TQM–LM–DES framework to enhance patient satisfaction in public healthcare A Delhi NCR case study
journal: International Journal of Research in Management

title: The Effect of Six Sigma Quality Management Strategy in the Clinical Biochemistry Laboratory
abstract: This study was conducted at a tertiary teaching hospital to evaluate the performance of its clinical biochemistry laboratory using Six Sigma metrics.By assessing internal quality control (IQC) data for key liver and kidney function tests, this study aimed to identify performance gaps, optimize QC strategies, and recommend targeted interventions to enhance laboratory accuracy and reliability. Materials a n d MethodsThis descriptive, retrospective study was conducted to evaluate the quality management practices of the clinical biochemistry introduction Clinical laboratories serve as a cornerstone of modern healthcare, providing essential diagnostic information that informs patient management and treatment decisions.The reliability and accuracy of laboratory results are crucial, as errors can compromise clinical outcomes, misguide therapeutic interventions, and endanger patient safety. 1 To address these challenges, robust quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC) methodologies have been developed to minimize variability and ensure precision across all phases of laboratory operations. 2 Among these methodologies, Six Sigma has emerged as a powerful, data-driven strategy for enhancing operational efficiency and minimizing errors.Originally conceptualized by Motorola in 1986 to optimize manufacturing processes, Six Sigma has since been adapted for diverse fields, including clinical laboratory management.3 It employs statistical tools and the define, measure, analyze, improve, control (DMAIC) framework to systematically identify, quantify, and rectify process deficiencies.By aiming for a near-perfect defect rate of 3.4 per million opportunities, Six Sigma helps laboratories achieve world-class performance in analytical testing.4 The application of Six Sigma in clinical biochemistry laboratories has been extensively documented.Studies by Zhou et al. and Panda et al. have demonstrated its utility in tailoring QC protocols to specific analytes based on sigma metrics.5,6 This approach has led to improved analytical accuracy, optimized resource utilization, and enhanced patient safety.However, many laboratories continue to face challenges in achieving Six Sigma standards, particularly for analytes prone to biological variability or methodological inconsistencies.[7][8][9]

title: SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW: FREKUENSI PENGGUNAAN TOOLS PADA SETIAP FASE DMAIC DALAM LEAN SIX SIGMA
abstract: The implementation of Lean Six Sigma through the DMAIC (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control) framework has been widely recognized as effective in improving product quality and process efficiency, yet mapping the frequency of tool usage across each phase remains scarcely addressed. This study aims to identify and analyze the frequency of tool usage in each DMAIC phase within Lean Six Sigma implementation. A systematic literature review method was employed, with searches conducted via Publish or Perish based on Google Scholar data over the past five years, yielding 90 relevant papers for analysis. Findings show the Improve phase recorded the highest frequency (232), followed by Measure (229), Define (221), and Analyze (220), while Control recorded the lowest (198); the high frequency in Improve reflects the complexity of designing solutions and assessing baseline conditions, whereas Control, being more oriented toward sustaining outcomes, relies on more targeted tools. Each phase had its own predominant tools: SIPOC and Project Charter (Define), Control Chart and Pareto Chart (Measure), Fishbone Diagram (Analyze), Standard Work/SOP (Improve), and Control Chart and Standardization (Control). Bibliometric analysis using VOSviewer confirmed Lean and Six Sigma as a unified conceptual framework, with case studies as the dominant research design and Indonesia as the leading contributor.

title: Improving Pharmacy Workflow Efficiency Using The Lean Six Sigma DMAIC Methodology: A Process Optimization Study

title: Development, implementation and evaluation of a sustainable medication-use process in the intensive care unit: a lean-based quality improvement study
authors: Bart J. F. van den Bemt
abstract: BACKGROUND: In the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), substantial quantities of medication are wasted, negatively affecting ecological and economic sustainability. AIM: This study aimed to develop, implement, and evaluate an ecologically and economically sustainable medication-use process to reduce medication waste in the ICU of a Dutch academic hospital. METHOD: This lean-based quality improvement study comprised three phases: (I) Three-week baseline medication waste assessment in terms of quantity (i.e., disposed medication units) and economic value per 100 ICU beds per day. (II) Development and implementation of a sustainable medication-use process using lean principles. Causes of medication waste were identified among hospital staff using qualitative methods, and targeted interventions were identified and implemented accordingly. (III) Post-implementation effect evaluation of the sustainable medication-use process on medication waste. RESULTS: At baseline, a mean total of 113 units, worth €1037, were wasted daily per 100 ICU beds. Causes for medication waste were: insufficient knowledge among hospital staff about quantities and impacts of medication waste; suboptimal medication ordering, supplying and preparing, resulting in unnecessary medication waste; and patient's therapy changes/discontinuation. Interventions implemented were: awareness campaigns on medication waste; adjustment of protocols and work processes to prevent excess order, supply and preparation of medication; and dispensing individually labelled medication to the patient following transfer or discharge. Implementing these interventions reduced medication waste by 31.8% to 77 units per 100 ICU beds per day, and economic losses decreased by 18.4% to €846. CONCLUSION: Implementation of a sustainable medication-use process targeting staff's knowledge and work processes, reduced the extent of wasted medications in the ICU and associated costs.

title: Reducing genomic testing turnaround time through a multidisciplinary quality improvement initiative at a safety-net hospital.
Transformational leadership and quality management in health reforms in Kosovo
abstract: Introduction Healthcare reform in transitional systems requires effective leadership and robust quality-management frameworks to improve service quality and patient outcomes. Kosovo’s healthcare sector still faces organisational challenges requiring evidence-based strategies to strengthen institutional performance and patient-centred care. Aim of the research This study examines the influence of transformational leadership on quality management processes within the healthcare reforms in Kosovo. The research evaluates whether leadership behaviours facilitate improvements in patient satisfaction, service quality, and institutional efficiency through SERVQUAL and Six Sigma models/methods. Methods A mixed-method research design was applied. Quantitative data were collected through structured SERVQUAL and Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire (MLQ) instruments from 300 healthcare professionals across 10 hospitals (6 public, 4 private). Qualitative insights were gathered through semi-structured interviews with senior managers. Statistical analysis included descriptive indicators, correlation analysis, and multiple regression using SPSS. Qualitative data were subjected to thematic analysis. Based on national law the Ethical approval was not needed as the study did not include biochemical analyses, whereas all participants gave informed consent. Results Transformational leadership significantly predicted improved service quality (R² = 0.64, p < 0.001). Inspirational motivation ( = 0.34), idealised influence ( = 0.28) and intellectual stimulation ( = 0.21) were the strongest predictors of perceived service quality. SERVQUAL analysis revealed the largest gaps in responsiveness (–0.6) and empathy (–0.6). Implementation of Six Sigma DMAIC in one pilot hospital reduced waiting times by 23% and increased patient satisfaction scores by 17%. Conclusions Transformational leadership fosters a culture of excellence and accountability, enabling effective implementation of quality management tools. Integrated leadership and Six Sigma/SERVQUAL frameworks are essential for advancing health reforms in Kosovo and aligning them with European quality standards.

title: Evaluation of analytical quality improvement following NABL audit as per ISO 15189:2022 using measurement uncertainty and sigma metrics in the clinical biochemistry laboratory of a tertiary care hospital
