title: Implementing systematic distress screening in veteran oncology care: a quality improvement initiative
abstract: Distress is common among patients with cancer and is associated with worse outcomes yet routine distress screening remains inconsistently implemented in outpatient oncology clinics, particularly for Veterans. We conducted a quality improvement project (QIP) in the surgical oncology clinic at a large Veterans Affairs medical centre to improve distress screening among Veterans with newly diagnosed cancer.A multidisciplinary team designed and implemented a comprehensive psychosocial distress screening programme using the validated NCCN Distress Thermometer. Key drivers of screening reliability were identified through stakeholder interviews and used to guide intervention design. The intervention incorporated standardised screening, evaluation of positive screens, predefined referral pathways, timely follow-up with embedded mental health services and structured electronic record documentation. The programme was iteratively refined through Plan–Do–Study–Act cycles.A total of 178 veterans were included over a 6-month baseline period and 12 months of intervention. During the baseline phase, only 5% of eligible veterans had documented distress screening. Following implementation, screening rates increased from 5% at baseline to 87% by the end of the intervention period. 27 of 117 veterans (23.1%) screened positive for distress during the intervention period. 18 accepted referrals to mental health services, four were already established with mental healthcare and five declined referral. Veterans requiring urgent evaluation were seen by mental health services the same day or the following day, while all remaining veterans accepting referral were scheduled within 2–3 weeks.This project demonstrates that systematic distress screening for veterans with cancer can be successfully embedded into routine outpatient oncology care. Pairing standardised workflows with integrated referral pathways, timely follow-up and electronic health record documentation provides a scalable and sustainable model for comprehensive psychosocial distress screening in veteran oncology care.

title: Impact of Lean Healthcare Transformation on Staff Performance and Well-Being
abstract: Lean management, originating from the Toyota Production System, has been widely implemented in healthcare systems to eliminate waste, improve patient flow, and enhance value-based care. However, its effects on the healthcare workforce remain inconsistent and contested. This scoping review systematically maps empirical evidence from 2003 to 2023 regarding the influence of Lean interventions on healthcare staff performance and well-being. Using the PRISMA-ScR framework, we searched four electronic databases using Boolean operators and MeSH terms. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed, English-language empirical research conducted in hospital settings that explicitly reported staff-level outcomes. Seventeen primary studies met these criteria. Thematic synthesis identified five intersecting domains: (a) morale, motivation, and job satisfaction; (b) teamwork, communication, and coordination; (c) work intensification, stress, and burnout; (d) professional autonomy and meaning of work; and (e) the moderating role of leadership maturity and implementation depth. The review finds that Lean tools can improve teamwork and engagement but may also reduce psychological safety when managerial pressure, rather than participative cultural development, drives implementation. Outcomes depend on how Lean aligns with existing professional identities, the maturity of leadership behaviors, and when measurement occurs relative to the learning curve. These findings show the need for nuanced, socio-technical implementation strategies balancing process efficiency with the human-centered demands of clinical work.

title: From Adoption to Routinization: A Theory-Informed Qualitative Case Study of Quality-Management Implementation in a Chinese County Hospital
abstract: Background: County hospitals play a central role in delivering health services in China; however, the introduction of quality-management tools does not guarantee the sustained use of these tools in these institutions. Therefore, this study examined how a county hospital in China adopted total quality management (TQM)-oriented practices and whether these practices became embedded in routine operations or remained unimplemented. Methods: A theory-informed, qualitative single-case study was conducted at a public general hospital in Zhejiang, China. The data comprised 32 semi-structured interviews, institutional documents, and supplementary observations. Participants included 10 administrators or quality-management leaders, 15 frontline staff members, and 7 patients or caregivers. Two trained research assistants independently coded the qualitative corpus; discrepancies were resolved through three consensus meetings and adjudication by the authors. Framework analysis examined adoption, routinization, and the tension between compliance and learning. Administrative indicators were critically appraised as contextual evidence. Results: External accountability and leadership supported the adoption of quality structures; however, inspection-driven activities did not consistently translate into everyday learning. Some accounts indicated that continuous quality improvement (CQI) tools supported incident analysis and process redesign, while others described an emphasis on documentation. Training and drills helped clarify emergency roles, whereas hierarchical structures and departmental silos constrained routine collaboration. Patient and caregiver interviews provided illustrative accounts of improved communication and navigation, alongside concerns regarding participation in decision-making. Administrative trends were broadly consistent with these accounts; however, incomplete measurement information precluded causal attribution. Conclusion: Substantial adoption coexisted with uneven routinization. Local ownership, data interpretation, practical rehearsal, and continued feedback emerged as conditions relevant to sustained use. County-hospital quality management should assess how tools are used and followed up, alongside whether they have been introduced. Patient participation requires further investigation beyond satisfaction measures and the small patient/caregiver subsample.

title: Design and Development of an Intelligent Automated Dispensing System with Weight-Based Inventory Control and Role-Based Access
The golden hour: the feasibility of a quality improvement project to decrease the time to antibiotic administration in children with cancer and febrile neutropenia in Jordan
abstract: Background Febrile neutropenia (FN) is a potentially life-threatening condition in pediatric oncology; early antibiotic initiation is associated with improved survival. A quality improvement (QI) project was implemented in the Pediatric Emergency Room (ER) to improve the timeliness of antibiotic administration. Methods Starting in July 2019, the project was designed using the Find, Organize, Clarify, Understand, and Select–Plan, Do, Check, and Act (FOCUS–PDCA) framework. We aimed to give antibiotics within 60 min of ER arrival for children with suspected FN. High-risk patients received antibiotics without waiting for blood count confirmation. A structured staff education campaign was conducted over 6 months, and performance metrics were continuously monitored. Outcomes were compared with retrospective data from December 2018 to June 2019. Results The pre-intervention cohort included 119 children with cancer, accounting for 158 FN episodes. From July 2019 to December 2024, during the intervention period, 697 children with cancer (median age 4.7 years; IQR 2.6–9.2 years; 54% male) presented with FN, accounting for 1,164 ER visits (median 1 visit/patient; range, 1–11). The median absolute neutrophil count (ANC) at presentation was 50 cells/ μ L (IQR, 0–180 cells/μL). Median time from ER arrival to antibiotic administration decreased from 120 min (IQR, 97–143) at pre-intervention baseline to 50 min (IQR, 40–65) across the implementation period ( p < 0.01). The time from antibiotic ordering to first dose remained stable (median 32 min; IQR, 25–40), while time from arrival to antibiotic ordering decreased from 53 to 15 min ( p < 0.01). Compliance with the 60 min target improved from 22% in the pre-intervention period to a sustained 85%–90% range across 2021–2024, with the ≥90% target met in all 12 months of 2021 and compliance declining to 85.8% in 2024. The target was increased to 90% in September 2020. Conclusion A structured Golden Hour QI initiative is feasible, effective, and associated with substantial and sustained improvement in antibiotic timeliness in the Middle East region, without additional funding, staffing, or technology. The core drivers of sustained improvement were automatic Category-A triage for children with cancer presenting with fever, pre-ANC antibiotic initiation for high-risk cases, and monthly audit-feedback cycles — all implementable within existing workflows.

title: Enhanced observation for management of agitated, confused or distressed behaviours in acute general hospitals: systematic review of quality and safety considerations
abstract: BACKGROUND: People who are agitated, confused or distressed seldom receive holistic care within acute general hospitals. Unmet needs relating to conditions such as mental illnesses, learning disabilities or dementia can contribute to patient behaviours which staff find challenging to manage (e.g. self-harm). Enhanced observation, involving one-to-one care and monitoring, is a restrictive intervention often used to manage these presentations. The characteristics and outcomes of high-quality enhanced observation in this setting remain ill-defined, compromising quality and safety. AIMS: To understand what constitutes high-quality, safe enhanced observation in an acute general hospital for patients presenting with agitated, confused or distressed behaviours. METHOD: A systematic review was performed, involving searches of five bibliographic databases, hand-searching, and forward and backward citation searching. Data describing the characteristics of high-quality, safe enhanced observation practice were eligible and included in a framework-based synthesis. Quality and safety outcomes were summarised thematically. Studies were appraised for quality, and data interpretation was shaped by lived experience experts. RESULTS: Fifty studies were included. Enhanced observation practice was influenced by individual staff members (e.g. attitudes), teams (e.g. teamwork fluency) and wider organisational factors (e.g. leadership, organisational culture). The quality and safety problems identified included self-harm, aggression and staff neglect of caring responsibilities during enhanced observation. CONCLUSIONS: Findings on the characteristics and outcomes of high-quality, safe enhanced observation provision should inform the development of evidence-based guidance to support improved, standardised practice in acute general hospitals. Evidence gaps with respect to patient experiences of enhanced observation and trauma-informed approaches to its delivery warrant urgent attention.

title: From local improvement to spatial diffusion: healthcare digital transformation and resource allocation efficiency in China
abstract: Introduction The inefficient and spatially uneven allocation of healthcare resources remains a major public health governance challenge in China. Healthcare digital transformation may improve the use of existing resources; however, its interprovincial spillovers, regional and temporal heterogeneity, and implications for efficiency convergence remain insufficiently understood. This study examines whether healthcare digital transformation is associated with higher healthcare resource allocation efficiency, whether this association extends across provincial boundaries, how it varies across regions and over time, and whether digitalization is associated with faster interprovincial efficiency convergence. Methods We constructed a balanced panel of 30 Chinese provincial-level units from 2014 to 2023. Healthcare resource allocation efficiency was measured using a super-efficiency non-radial directional distance function with undesirable outputs, and healthcare digital transformation was measured using an entropy-weighted TOPSIS index. A two-way fixed-effects spatial Durbin model with three alternative spatial weight matrices was used to estimate direct, indirect, and total associations. Regional subgroup analysis and geographically and temporally weighted regression assessed spatial and temporal heterogeneity, while spatial sigma- and beta-convergence models examined changes in interprovincial disparities. All estimates are interpreted as associational. Results Healthcare digital transformation was positively associated with resource allocation efficiency under all three spatial weight matrices. Under the primary contiguity matrix, the indirect effect (0.0521) was approximately twice the direct effect (0.0258), yielding a total effect of 0.0779; this ordering was preserved under the alternative matrices. Regional point estimates suggested stronger spillovers in Eastern China and more localized associations in Western China, although no pairwise regional contrast remained significant after Holm adjustment. The mean local digitalization coefficient increased from 0.0095 in 2014 to 0.0658 in 2023, while the national coefficient of variation declined from 0.352 to 0.218. Estimated convergence half-lives declined from 13.0 years in the absolute model to 8.3 years after structural controls, 8.2 years after adding Dig , and 7.5 years in the full spatial digitalization model. Discussion Healthcare digital transformation was associated with higher resource allocation efficiency, with a substantial cross-provincial component and clear spatiotemporal heterogeneity. Digitalization was also associated with faster conditional convergence, although structural factors explained much of the acceleration. These findings highlight the importance of interprovincial coordination, interoperability, and capacity building, while the observational design precludes causal interpretation of specific policy mechanisms.

title: Mapeamento de processos em agência transfusional de um hospital de referência em oncologia pediátrica: uso da matriz SIPOC

authors: Prisces Amélia dos Santos B. A. Matos

title: Construction of a quality evaluation index system for waterless surgical hand antisepsis in operating rooms
abstract: Objective To develop and obtain expert consensus on a quality evaluation index system for waterless surgical hand antisepsis in operating rooms and to assign hierarchical weights to the finalized indicators. Methods Guided by the Donabedian structure-process-outcome model, candidate indicators were generated through a structured literature review and semi-structured interviews. A three-round expert consultation was conducted: Rounds 1 and 2 were used to screen and refine indicators, and Round 3 was used for AHP-based pairwise weighting. Twenty-two eligible experts received the Round-1 questionnaire; 20 returned valid questionnaires and constituted the panel retained for Rounds 2 and 3, in which all 20 responded. Expert authority was assessed using Cr = (Ca + Cs)/2. In Round 3, individual expert authority coefficients were normalized to obtain expert-specific weights, and pairwise judgments were aggregated using a weighted geometric mean before AHP weight calculation and consistency testing. Results The valid response rates were 90.9% (20/22), 100% (20/20), and 100% (20/20) in Rounds 1, 2, and 3, respectively. The panel mean expert authority coefficients (Cr) were 0.883, 0.895, and 0.900. Kendall's coefficients of concordance for the two indicator-screening rounds were 0.242 and 0.334, respectively (both P < 0.001), while coefficients of variation decreased from 0.07-0.20 to 0.05-0.18. The aggregated AHP group judgment matrices satisfied the predefined consistency criterion (CR < 0.10). The final system comprised three first-level, nine second-level, and 28 third-level indicators. The global weights of the first-level domains were structure 0.1762, process 0.4123, and outcome 0.4115. Conclusion This study produced a consensus-based and hierarchically weighted quality evaluation index system for waterless surgical hand antisepsis. The framework may support standardized quality assessment and future quality-improvement work; however, the present study establishes expert consensus and relative priorities rather than clinical effectiveness, psychometric reliability, or causal effects. Multicenter clinical validation is required before broad implementation.

title: Robust Hospital Efficiency Ranking: A Bayesian and Machine Learning Integrated Dynamic Slacks-Based Measure DEA Approach
journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Health Management
abstract: Hospitals are complex organizations operating in a dynamic environment, where multiple parameters vary over time. Ranking hospitals by efficiency using traditional methods often overlooks changes in effectiveness and quality. This study proposes a simulation-based Dynamic Slack-Based Measure Data Envelopment Analysis (Dynamic SBM-DEA) framework. The study is methodological and simulation-based, generated using Monte Carlo simulation methods, calibrated from real multispecialty hospital data, healthcare literature, etc. To evaluate intertemporal hospital performance, the methodology incorporates carry-over effects and unwanted outputs and uses bootstrap validation to evaluate the reliability of efficiency estimations. The persistence and transition of performance states across time are examined using Markov chain analysis, and the stability measurements that are obtained are combined with Dynamic SBM efficiency ratings to create a composite performance indicator. Additionally, the framework can capture operational stability, ranking robustness, and predicted efficiency trends inside a single evaluation model thanks to Bayesian forecasting's probabilistic estimations of future performance. The machine learning model attained a testing R² of 0.4765 and a cross-validated R² of 0.553 ± 0.048, indicating moderate predictive capability and stable performance. Sensitivity research showed that the composite ranking framework was resilient, with Kendall's tau values ranging from 0.716 to 0.926 across different weighting schemes and Spearman's rank correlations ranging from 0.881 to 0.983. The findings revealed a set of hospitals with continuously excellent efficiency, stable rankings, and promising future performance. Staffing levels, surgical activity, and clinical results are some of the most important factors influencing efficiency, according to the SHAP study. The development of an integrated Dynamic SBM-DEA, Machine Learning, and Bayesian decision-support framework that offers a transparent, stability-adjusted, and forward-looking benchmarking tool for evidence-based hospital management, resource allocation, and healthcare policy decision-making is the study's primary contribution.

title: Health investment efficiency and institutional quality in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Abstract Background Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) faces a paradox of rising health spending alongside persistently low life expectancy, raising fundamental questions about health investment efficiency. Understanding how institutional quality and environmental degradation shape that efficiency is essential for accelerating progress toward SDG 3. Methods The Simar and Wilson (2007) Algorithm 2 two-stage bootstrap Data Envelopment Analysis procedure is applied to 45 SSA countries over 2000–2023. Life expectancy is the output; government health expenditure per capita and mean years of schooling are inputs. A bootstrap truncated regression examines institutional quality, carbon (\(\:{CO}_{2}\)) emissions, electricity access, population ageing, and out-of-pocket expenditure as efficiency determinants. An income-group interaction framework tests whether institutional quality effects vary across income levels. Results The mean bias-corrected efficiency score is 0.866, implying a 13.4% average efficiency shortfall. Institutional quality significantly reduces efficiency among low-income countries (\(\:\beta\:=-0.105,p<0.01\)) but has no significant effect at higher income levels. \(\:{CO}_{2}\) emissions reduce efficiency (\(\:\beta\:=-0.047,p<0.01\)), electricity access improves it (\(\:\beta\:=0.005,p<0.01\)), and out-of-pocket expenditure reduces it consistently across all specifications. Conclusion Meaningful life expectancy gains are attainable through improved resource allocation without additional spending, directly supporting SDG 3.8. Governance reforms in low-income SSA countries should be carefully sequenced to minimize short-run efficiency costs. The climate-health efficiency nexus positions pollution control and clean energy as complementary health system priorities aligned with SDG 3.9 and SDG 13.

title: A State Based Dispatch Controller for Hospital Delivery Robots with Shared Human and Infrastructure Resources
abstract: Robot delivery studies can overstate transport capacity when travel to pickups and human support fall outside the modeled schedule. We formulate a location aware dispatch model that couples robot admission to transporter support and shared elevators, charging, and cleaning. The model replays 33,079 observed hospital requests; missing contents, deadlines, staffing, and completion times remain explicit scenario assumptions. Two full grids compare human dispatch, a resource aware controller, and a proximity and workload benchmark in 30 paired replications per scenario. An exploratory extension tests a simpler deadline admission rule under the same operating model. Pickup travel increases demand on a pooled elevator bank. In one high staffing case, raising assumed elevator capacity from two to four reduces human only lateness from 55.11\% to 3.18\%, exceeding the dispatch differences. Direct policy comparisons and robot coverage distinguish admission selectivity from system service. The analysis explains why a robot can pass a deadline admission test yet delay service through staff handoffs and shared facilities. Its contribution is a reproducible evaluation of coupled dispatch workflows, with a clear separation between admission, completion, and return to availability. The results are conditional comparisons, not estimates of hospital benefit or released clinical capacity.

title: Effectiveness of Kaizen-Based Programmes in Improving Patient Safety Incident Reporting: A Systematic Review Protocol with Monte Carlo Validation
abstract: Incident reporting is a fundamental component of organizational learning in patient safety. However, Kaizen-based continuous improvement programs designed to strengthen incident reporting are often evaluated using report counts, which cannot distinguish improvements in reporting culture from increases in actual patient harm. This study aimed to develop and validate an analytical framework that differentiates these effects and establish a systematic review protocol for its application. The observed reporting rate was decomposed into three components: exposure, the true incident rate, and reporting propensity. A severity-stratified Reporting Propensity Index (RPI) was developed using partial identification bounds, alongside a behavioral reporting model, an assessment of bias in before-and-after study designs, and a sustainability half-life measure. Four Monte Carlo simulation studies encompassing 52 scenarios were conducted to evaluate estimator performance, and a systematic review protocol was developed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Under the specified assumptions, the RPI estimator was unbiased and achieved nominal confidence interval coverage, whereas the conventional total-count estimator exhibited bias of up to ?0.35 log units. When assumptions were violated, the partial identification bounds contained the true parameter in at least 97.4% of simulation replications. Uncontrolled before-and-after designs overestimated intervention effects, consistent with theoretical predictions, while reusing baseline-period data in moderator analyses increased the false-positive rate to 20.7%. These findings suggest that severity-stratified incident reporting, analyzed using the RPI framework, may provide hospitals with a more reliable measure of reporting propensity and support evidence-based decisions regarding the implementation and evaluation of Kaizen-based patient safety improvement programs.

title: The Impact of Implementing CBAHI Standards on the Quality of Healthcare Services: An Applied Study on Primary Healthcare Centers in Al-Qassim
journal: World Research of Business Administration Journal

title: Management of Health Services: A Critical Analysis of Recent Literature
abstract: This study aimed to analyze scientific articles published between 2020 and 2025 in the Scopus and Scielo databases, with a focus on health services management. A total of nine articles from these databases were selected and reviewed. Health services management is a complex field that faces various challenges depending on the context and the approach of each study. Although scientific literature on the topic is abundant in databases such as Scopus, its access and dissemination may be limited in other sources like Scielo, which impacts the generation of accessible knowledge. The reviewed studies highlight that efficiency in hospital administration not only depends on process optimization and the adoption of technologies but also on equity in service distribution and the integration of healthcare personnel. Additionally, training, the use of evidence in decision-making, and strategies to improve patients' quality of life are key factors, though their implementation varies according to the priorities of each health system.

title: Development of orodispersible wafer-based delayed-release omeprazole systems for pediatric compounding
abstract: Omeprazole (OMZ) is one of the most frequently compounded active pharmaceutical ingredients for pediatric use. Despite the availability of licensed pediatric formulations in some countries, extemporaneous oral suspensions remain widely used in hospital pharmacies, although their limited chemical stability, short shelf life, and need for specific storage conditions may complicate routine use. This study aimed to develop a child-appropriate solid alternative based on a hybrid lipid–wafer platform combining gastro-resistant OMZ microparticles with an orodispersible matrix. Orodispersible wafers (ODWs), composed of pectin, κ-carrageenan, and maltodextrins, were produced by lyophilization, yielding highly porous matrices with low residual moisture (2.74%) and rapid oral disintegration. To protect OMZ during gastric exposure, two encapsulation strategies were investigated: calcium alginate–zein beads and lipid microparticles (LMPs). Morphology, particle size, drug loading, encapsulation efficiency, and solid state were characterized, and drug release was evaluated in gastrointestinal buffers and pediatric biorelevant media. Trimyristin-based LMPs showed the most favorable performance, limiting OMZ exposure to the acidic environment and providing controlled intestinal release consistent with Higuchi kinetics. Their incorporation into ODWs yielded a solid unit containing approximately 2.5 mg OMZ. Importantly, OMZ content remained unchanged for up to six months, with comparable release profiles at t 0 and after storage, including at room temperature. Overall, the proposed hybrid lipid–wafer platform provides a stable, child-appropriate solid dosage form to OMZ delivery and represents a promising formulation strategy for further development in suitably equipped hospital pharmacy compounding settings.

title: Linafexor, a Pulsatile FXR Agonist, Augments Low-Dose Semaglutide for Weight Loss in Adults with Obesity, MASH, and Type 2 Diabetes
abstract: ABSTRACT Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists produce less weight loss in people with type 2 diabetes than without, and higher compensatory doses are limited by gastrointestinal adverse events and lean-mass loss—leaving patients with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) inadequately treated. We tested whether linafexor, a pulsatile farnesoid X receptor (FXR) agonist, could augment the weight-loss efficacy of low-dose semaglutide in this population while preserving tolerability. In this multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial, 62 adults with obesity (body-mass index, 30– 45 kg/m²), treatment-naive type 2 diabetes, and MASH (MRI-PDFF ≥10%) were assigned to linafexor (4 mg orally once daily) or placebo, each with semaglutide (0.5 mg once weekly), for 16 weeks. The primary outcome was the percentage change in body weight at week 16. Adding linafexor more than doubled weight loss (−6.17% vs. −2.91%; treatment difference, −3.26%; 95% CI, −5.35 to −1.18; P=0.003), and more participants achieved at least 5% weight loss (53.3% vs. 28.1%; P=0.046). Consistent with this, combination therapy further reduced visceral adipose tissue (treatment difference, −13.85 cm²; P=0.035), the liver enzymes alanine aminotransferase and γ-glutamyl transferase, and serum bile acids, whose changes correlated with weight and liver-enzyme improvements—associations absent with monotherapy. Gastrointestinal adverse events were comparable (23.3% vs. 18.8%), with no treatment-related serious adverse events or discontinuations. Thus, in a population with blunted GLP-1 responses, adding linafexor to low-dose semaglutide enhanced weight loss and improved body composition and hepatic measures while preserving tolerability—a dose-sparing, mechanism-complementary strategy (ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06492330 ).

title: Driving Innovation in Healthcare Management to Implement Value-Based Care Financial Strategies
journal: International Journal of Healthcare and Medical Sciences

title: Administering Antineoplastic Parenteral Cancer Therapy in the Patient's Home: Perspectives of Oncology Nurses—A Descriptive Qualitative Study
abstract: AIM: To explore oncology nurses' perspectives on performing cancer treatments with parenteral antineoplastic agents in patients' homes. DESIGN: A descriptive qualitative study utilizing interviews. METHODS: Semi-structured interviews were performed with oncology nurses at a hospital oncology daycare ward between October and November 2022. The interview data were inductively analysed with thematic content analysis. RESULTS: Five themes were identified: (1) Establishing rapport in the home environment, (2) The complexity of a home, (3) Adverse events-not practicalities, (4) Solitary nursing and (5) Planning enables performance. The nurses believed patients would benefit from home treatment with antineoplastic agents but were concerned about adverse events and working alone. For successful home treatments, nurses believed sufficient resources, education and support were necessary. Practicalities such as transporting, administering and waste handling were not considered complex. Neither did the antineoplastic agents handling seem problematic. CONCLUSIONS: Although positive, especially from the patient perspective, the nurses identified concerns that need to be addressed before implementing oncology hospital-at-home services. IMPLICATIONS: Working in different contexts than the hospital can lead to extended roles and further responsibilities for oncology nurses and possibly facilitate more person-centred care. IMPACT: This study explored oncology nurses' perspectives on performing parenteral cancer treatments with antineoplastic agents in patients' homes. In general, the nurses were positive, but challenges were identified. The study provides insights into how healthcare developers can incorporate the needs of nurses when designing future hospital-at-home programmes. REPORTING METHOD: COREQ guidelines were used. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: No patient or public contribution. WHAT DOES THIS PAPER CONTRIBUTE TO THE WIDER GLOBAL CLINICAL COMMUNITY?: This paper can be used to create tools addressing barriers nurses might have working with hazardous antineoplastic agents in hospital-at-home environments. It emphasizes the importance of education, resources and support to provide nurses with an adequate and safe working environment, improving patient experiences and safety.

title: Automated phase recognition in the cardiac catheterization laboratory with deep learning
abstract: BACKGROUND: An efficient workflow in the cardiac catheterization laboratory is important to guarantee quality of care and keep healthcare affordable. Automated surgical process monitoring of diagnostic coronary angiograms (CAGs) has the potential to increase workflow efficiency, reduce non-clinical workload, and optimize scheduling. The aim of this study is to automatically classify workflow phases of CAGs using deep learning models trained on a real-world dataset. METHODS: With an observational study we collected a dataset, composed of an integration of video recorded CAGs, clinical data, and system logging data. Every procedural phase was annotated by a medical doctor based on clinically relevant key points in time. A Scaled-YOLOv4 object detection algorithm was employed to extract features from the video images. We implemented Long short-term memory (LSTM) and LSTM-Fully convolutional network (LSTM-FCN) on the integrated time series data to classify the workflow phases. The accuracy in the classification was weighted on the duration of the phase. RESULTS: A dataset including video, clinical and logging data of 222 CAG procedures was obtained. A weighted accuracy for phase classification of 91.3% was reached for the LSTM model, compared to 90.8% for the LSTM-FCN model. No significant difference was found after statistical comparison between both models. However, the LSTM network was 2.2 times faster in training while requiring around 40% less parameters. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates the potential of deploying deep learning models on a real-world integrated dataset to automatically detect CAG phases with more than 90% accuracy. No statistically significant difference was found between the performance of the two models, although the LSTM model required less training time compared to the LSTM-FCN. Thus, we suggest the employment of these models for phase recognition challenges based on composite datasets. Given the promising accuracy of these deep learning techniques, automated phase recognition could become a cornerstone of dynamic schedule optimization and increase future hospital efficiency.

title: Artificial Intelligence ( AI) ‐enhanced journal club: integrating podcasts, AI , and social media in medical education
Professional and physician-rank differences in submitted patient safety incident reports: a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of a hospital reporting database
abstract: Abstract Background Voluntary patient safety incident-reporting systems support organizational learning but capture only a selected subset of patient safety events. Although previous studies have identified differences in the characteristics of reports submitted by different healthcare professions, physicians have generally been treated as a single professional group. This study examined the composition and severity-field completion of submitted reports across professional groups and physician ranks. Methods We conducted a single-center retrospective cross-sectional study of eligible patient safety incident reports submitted to a tertiary general hospital between January and December 2025. Event-type composition, recorded severity distribution, and severity-field completion were compared across nurses, physicians, and pharmacists and across junior, intermediate, and senior physicians. Pearson’s χ² tests were used for group comparisons, Cramér’s V was reported as the effect-size measure, and selected proportions were accompanied by Wilson 95% confidence intervals. Results A total of 7,218 submitted reports were analyzed. Nurses accounted for 57.23% of reports (95% CI, 56.09%-58.37%), physicians for 38.89% (37.77%-40.02%), and pharmacists for 3.88% (3.46%-4.35%). Overall, 64.95% of reports lacked a recorded severity category (95% CI, 63.84%-66.04%) and were classified as Unclassified. Profession was strongly associated with event-type composition (Cramér’s V = 0.753) and severity-field completion (V = 0.651). Among physician-submitted reports, the associations of physician rank with recorded severity distribution (V = 0.107) and event-type composition (V = 0.081) were statistically significant but small. Conclusions The composition and severity-field completion of submitted reports differed across healthcare professions, whereas differences across physician ranks were relatively small. These findings do not estimate profession- or rank-specific reporting rates, reporting propensity, or the true incidence of patient safety events. The high and profession-dependent proportion of Unclassified reports supports clearer severity-classification guidance, profession- and career-stage-sensitive training, and review of reporting workflows and responsibility for final severity assignment.

title: Determinants of Perceived Patient Safety Impact of Incident Reporting Systems in Egypt
Knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding medical incident reporting and associated factors among nurses at Hai Phong Children’s Hospital, Vietnam
journal: Tạp chí Khoa học Điều dưỡng
abstract: Objectives: To describe the knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding medical incident reporting among nurses in clinical departments at Hai Phong Children’s Hospital in 2025 and to identify factors associated with medical incident reporting practices. Materials and methods: A cross-sectional descriptive study was conducted from November 2025 to December 2025 in the clinical departments of Hai Phong Children’s Hospital among 239 nurses. A census sampling method was used. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire consisting of four sections assessing participants’ characteristics, knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding medical incident reporting. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 21.0 with descriptive statistics and logistic regression analysis, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results: Nurses’ knowledge of medical incident reporting was limited and varied across different content areas. The proportion of nurses correctly identifying specific incidents was high for wrong-site/wrong-procedure surgery (98.3%) and accidents related to the medical gas system (94.1%), but low for the definition of a medical incident (13.4%). The majority of nurses had positive attitudes toward medical incident reporting. Overall, 71.5% of nurses reported medical incidents, whereas 28.5% did not report medical incidents. Logistic regression analysis showed that knowledge (OR = 7.12; p < 0.01) and the average number of patients cared for per day (OR = 1.97; p = 0.03) were significantly associated with medical incident reporting practices. Conclusion: Nurses’ knowledge of medical incident reporting remained limited, although their attitudes were generally positive. Knowledge and patient care workload were associated with medical incident reporting practices. Training and support for nurses in medical incident reporting should be strengthened to improve the effectiveness of incident management and ensure patient safety.

title: Safety Incident Reporting in Chiropractic: A descriptive analysis of an active and passive system
abstract: Abstract Background Safety incident reporting systems support learning from harm, but the processes and information outputs of active and passive systems within chiropractic have not been analyzed. The Chiropractic Patient Incident Reporting and Learning System (CPiRLS) is a passive, provider-driven system using voluntary, anonymous reporting, while SafetyNET is an active, research-embedded system collecting reports from both patients and practitioners. Methods A framework analysis with a structured expert consensus method was used. Both systems were assessed against the six core categories of the World Health Organization (WHO) self-assessment framework for patient safety incident reporting systems, and their incident report data fields were mapped against the WHO Minimal Information Model for Patient Safety (MIM PS). One leader from each system completed the assessment, which was independently verified by a second leader. Four panelists without system-leadership roles rated each item independently, followed by a facilitated consensus meeting. Reporting followed the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research. Results Neither system aligned fully with the WHO framework or model. SafetyNET scored higher on Reporting Rules and Content, including the largest single divergence in the framework: the ability to return to a reporter for further information. CPiRLS scored higher on Governance, consistent with its anonymous design. Both systems scored comparably in the mid-range on Analysis and Investigation, and both scored at the bottom of the rating scale on nearly every item within Patient and Family Engagement. Both scored equally low on providing personalized feedback to reporters. Both met most Basic MIM PS elements, with gaps in incident location, incident type, and incident outcome, and neither used standardized coding for suspected cause or contributing factors. Where one system was strong, the other tended to be weaker. Conclusions The differences between CPiRLS and SafetyNET reflect differences in design rather than in the quality of each system, and the two together align with the WHO self-assessment framework more completely than either does in isolation. Neither system can close the shared gaps alone, and the profession would be better served by using both approaches than by choosing between them.

title: Patient Safety Reporting Gaps as Generators of Health Misinformation: Implications for the European Health Data Space, the WHO Global Patient Safety Action Plan and Europe's Infodemic Preparedness — A Scoping Review Protocol
abstract: In high-income countries, an estimated 1 in 10 hospital patients experiences an adverse event during care [1,2], and the WHO Global Patient Safety Action Plan (GPSAP) 2021–2030 makes reporting and learning systems a dedicated strategic objective, precisely because a constant, trustworthy flow of safety information is what allows harm to be recognised, understood and reduced [1,3]. Yet independent inquiries repeatedly document the opposite. Incidents miscategorised or downgraded to avoid external scrutiny, harm not disclosed to patients and families, and safety data fragmented across institutions and borders [4,5,6]. WHO's infodemic-management framework identifies exactly this kind of information void — the absence of reliable, accessible information at the moment it is needed as fertile ground for rumour, distrust and health misinformation [7]. This scoping review will map how gaps in patient-safety reporting, surveillance and disclosure function as generators of health misinformation and eroded trust, and how the European Health Data Space (EHDS), the GPSAP and Europe's infodemic-preparedness architecture address, or could address, this pathway, scoped throughout to injury prevention and patient-safety intelligence. The review will follow JBI methodological guidance and be reported using PRISMA-ScR [18,19]. MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL Complete, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, Communication and Mass Media Complete will be searched from inception to 30 September 2026, alongside targeted grey-literature sources (WHO, WHO/Europe, the European Commission, OECD, national patient-safety agencies and ombudsman bodies) and citation searching. No language restriction will be applied. Two reviewers will independently screen titles/abstracts and full texts, with inter-rater agreement quantified using both percentage agreement and Cohen's kappa; disagreements will be resolved by discussion or a third reviewer. One reviewer will chart data using a piloted, structured form and a second will verify every field. Evidence will be organised along an explicit incident-to-misinformation causal pathway, by social-ecological level, by patient-safety reporting-gap type, and against GPSAP strategic objectives, EHDS provisions and Europe's infodemic-preparedness pillars, and synthesised through descriptive mapping and framework-based qualitative thematic analysis. The review will use published or publicly available material and is not expected to require research-ethics approval. The protocol, search strategies, eligibility manual, data-charting form, analytic code, amendment log and an appropriately licensed dataset will be deposited on OSF at registration and updated through completion. Findings will be shared through a peer-reviewed open-access publication.

title: Patient Safety Incidents Experienced by Novice Nurses During Transition to Practice: A Qualitative Phenomenological Study
Causes of incidents of delayed or omitted medications – an interview study
abstract: Abstract Background Patient safety is a global health challenge. Incidents of delayed or omitted medication is one of the most common types of medication errors found in both retrospective and observational studies. This study aims to explore the underlying causes of incidents involving delayed or omitted medication administration in a hospital setting in Norway. Methods Nine semi-structured interviews with nurses working on medical, surgical, and psychiatric wards across three hospitals in Norway were conducted. Participants were selected through purposive sampling. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed using systematic text condensation (STC) for inductive thematic analysis. Furthermore, the resulting themes were deductively mapped to the International Classification for Patient Safety (ICPS) framework to identify mitigating factors. Results Four main categories of contributing factors for omission incidents emerged: staff, patient, organizational, and external factors. Staff-related issues included procedural deviations and prioritization challenges, such as unchecked drug intake or prioritization of medication administration when shifts were busy. Patient-related factors involved health conditions such as swallowing difficulties. Organizational factors included task organization and workload, collaboration, workplace culture and feedback. Examples included confusion on responsibility for administration of non-tablet dosage forms. External factors included limitations in digital tools and equipment, such as medication administration records not being fully displayed on smaller screens. The ICPS framework assisted in contextualizing the findings and highlighted areas for targeted interventions. Conclusions The findings of this study have provided insights in nurses’ perspective on contributing factors for incidents of medication omission in hospitals in Norway. Medication omission incidents are multifactorial. Organizational factors were the most prominent topic in this study. Improvement of organization and underlying systems in response to incident reporting is key to avoid medication omission incidents and enhance patient safety.

title: Occupational hazard incident reporting systems in health facilities across sub-Saharan Africa: A scoping review protocol
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Occupational hazards (OH) in healthcare facilities are common, with 1 in 10 healthcare workers experiencing a hazard each year. These hazards can be either biological, chemical, ergonomic, or radiation. Despite their occurrence, reporting of these hazards remains limited, with very little information available, especially from healthcare facilities. Also, there is limited information on incident reporting systems (IRSs), which can help capture, track, and monitor the occurrence of these hazards within health facilities. The absence of these systems results in inaccurate and incomplete reporting and fragmented data, hindering the implementation of effective occupational safety measures in hospitals. This review will explore the extent and nature of information available on occupational hazard incident reporting systems in Sub-Saharan Africa. METHODS: The review will be conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology of scoping reviews and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). A robust search strategy shall be conducted in different scientific databases, including PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, guided by the Population, Concept, and Context framework. Studies describing incident reporting systems shall be considered in this review. The search results will be collated and uploaded to Covidence, where duplicates will be removed and titles and abstracts screened. Search and screening of studies have not yet commenced. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION: Occupational health and safety are vital to the functioning of healthcare facilities because they promote well-being and protect both patients and healthcare workers. It is vital to ensure accurate and robust IRS are in place, especially given the occurrence of occupational hazards across hospital wards. These IRS will help with surveillance and the identification of epidemiological trends in OH among health workers. PROTOCOL REGISTRATION: The protocol has not been registered.

title: FirstWatch: Safety-First Decision Drills for Non-Clinical Hospital Surge Roles
abstract: FirstWatch is a suite of ten browser-based decision drills designed to prepare adults from non-healthcare professions for support roles during hospital surge and mass-casualty exercises. This online resource record introduces the drills and provides access to the externally hosted web application and an associated YouTube playlist.The drills cover registration, triage support alongside a clinician, patient tracking, supply and logistics, communications relay, incident reporting, emergency codes and calls, observations recording and escalation, bed-board management, and patient transport coordination. Each drill includes a guided walkthrough, two difficulty levels, and an item-by-item review following a scored run.The central design priority is safety rather than speed. Safety-critical errors prevent a passing result, regardless of points earned elsewhere. Scenarios also test adherence to station rules under social pressure. Feedback is aligned with the scoring criteria, and participants use program codes rather than names.Development and evaluationFirstWatch was developed through a design science research process incorporating iterative specification and software review, subject-matter expert input, and automated formative testing. Development included AI-assisted specification and coding and role-briefed AI review panels, with human oversight and decision-making.To date, evaluation has assessed software behavior and consistency with design specifications using synthetic test runs. Learner evaluation is planned; educational effectiveness, assessment validity, and transfer to operational performance remain to be established. The drills are developmental educational resources and should not be interpreted as validated evidence of operational readiness. Access to the resourcesInteractive web application:https://dev.firstwatch.polymedx.net/Associated YouTube playlist:https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLTO1EIfMjQ3AThe application and videos are hosted externally. This record provides an introduction and access links; it does not archive the application source code, a versioned software release, or copies of the videos.

title: Experience of Mass Casualty Incident Drill for Hospital Medical Response: Two drills by a tertiary academic hospital: Brief Report
The Association between Staff Training on Utilization and Reporting Patterns of the Occurrence Variance Reporting (OVR) System at Al-Noor Specialist Hospital in Makkah
journal: Saudi Journal of Nursing and Health Care
abstract: Background: Occurrence variance reporting (OVR) systems are essential tools for identifying, mitigating, and preventing risks in healthcare, yet they are widely under-used because of inadequate training, fear of blame, and unclear definitions of what constitutes a reportable event. In Saudi Arabia, Vision 2030 reforms place incident reporting at the centre of quality and patient-safety improvement. Objective: To examine whether a hospital-wide staff training program on the OVR system was associated with changes in the number of incident reports, the distribution of risk levels, and the distribution of incident categories at Al-Noor Specialist Hospital, Makkah. Methods: A quantitative, retrospective, single-group pre–post quasi-experimental design without a control group was applied to secondary data extracted from the hospital’s electronic OVR system. The intervention was a 40-minute face-to-face session (presentation, case study, and system-demonstration video) delivered from mid-May 2024 to 430 documented attendees (≈18.7% of 2,300 employees). A total census of 4,981 reports was analysed across a pre-intervention period (1 July 2023–30 June 2024; n = 2,018) and a post-intervention period (1 July 2024–30 June 2025; n = 2,963). Monthly volumes were compared with the Mann–Whitney U test after Shapiro–Wilk testing; risk-level and category distributions were compared with chi-square tests of independence. Results: Total reports increased by 46.8%, and monthly volume rose significantly (median 154 vs. 241; U = 11.00, z = −3.52, p < .001, rank-biserial r = 0.847). The reporting rate rose from 15.90 to 24.99 per 1,000 patient-days (+57.2%) despite a 6.6% fall in patient-days. Risk-level distribution changed significantly (χ²(3, N = 4,981) = 262.44, p < .001, Cramér’s V = 0.230), shifting toward low- and moderate-risk reports (82.0% to 95.9%). Incident-category distribution also changed significantly (χ²(5, N = 4,981) = 243.42, p < .001, Cramér’s V = 0.221), with notable increases in the Incident (0.8% to 10.5%) and Adverse Event (29.7% to 34.8%) categories. Conclusion: Staff training on the OVR system was associated with a sustained increase in incident reporting and with changes in the risk-level and category profile of reports. Because the design lacked a control group and classifications were not independently verified, the changes cannot be attributed to training alone or interpreted as improved classification accuracy. Training appears to be a promising, low-cost strategy against under-reporting when combined with leadership support, feedback to reporters, and evaluation in controlled studies.

title: Optimizing Medication Administration Safety Using The Seven Rights and Patient-Family Verification
abstract: Medication administration safety is a core element of patient safety. An assessment in the General Inpatient Unit of a hospital in Jakarta found that patient/family verification during medication administration was not documented systematically. This managerial residency quality-improvement project aimed to strengthen medication safety through the seven rights and patient/family verification, supported by education, checklists, supervision, monitoring, and feedback. The project ran from 19 August to 11 September 2026. Problems were prioritized using Urgency, Seriousness, Growth (USG) and Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats (SWOT) analyses. Knowledge among 20 nurses was assessed using a 15-item pre-test and post-test; workflow implementation and adherence were evaluated through supervision; and the verification form was trialed with six inpatients. Verification received the highest USG score (15). Mean knowledge scores increased from 68.7% to 95.0% (a 26.3-percentage-point increase). Mean workflow implementation was 95.0%, while adherence to the seven rights and verification was 98.5%. Indicators requiring further improvement included incident/near-miss reporting (75%), clarity of instructions (80%), and communication and confirmation (85%). The form was reportedly used with all six patients without recorded refusal or difficulty; medication-administration opportunities were not tabulated separately. These findings indicate preliminary unit-level feasibility, not a demonstrated reduction in medication errors. Further evaluation requires paired individual data, more observations, and longer follow-up.

title: Beyond the Safety Grade: A Comparative Cross-Sectional Study of Patient Safety Culture in Secondary and Tertiary Hospitals in Bayelsa State, Nigeria
journal: International Journal of Modern Science and Research Technology

title: Characterisation of Medication-Related Errors and Prioritisation of Patient-Safety Interventions in Hospital Care: A Retrospective Observational Study
2025 Pennsylvania Patient Safety Reporting: Updated Reporting Rates for Acute and Ambulatory Care
Preventing Harm in Perioperative Care: Epidemiological Surveillance, Patient Safety Culture, and Healthcare Quality Improvement
authors: Jeanina de los Angeles Montero Galban

title: Nursing Students' Opinions on Patient Safety
abstract: Improving nursing students’ knowledge and skills regarding patient safety is crucial to providing safe care. This descriptive research was conducted between October 2021 and March 2022 to determine nursing students’ opinions on patient safety and the factors influencing these opinions. The study population consisted of third- and fourth-year nursing students in Türkiye. Data were collected from 422 participants through an online questionnaire using convenience and snowball sampling methods. According to the findings, 23.5% of the students reported encountering medical errors/adverse events during clinical practice. While 89.8% of the students believed that medical errors/adverse events should be reported, only 12.1% reported that an incident report was filed in such cases. In addition, 40% of the students believed that healthcare professionals should be punished or warned for medical errors/adverse events. A statistically significant difference was found between gender and the view that healthcare professionals should be punished or warned (p = 0.036). This view also varied according to academic year (p = 0.011). The study findings emphasize the importance of fostering positive patient safety attitudes and creating a non- punitive culture in educational and clinical learning environments.

title: Medication Safety Practices at Colombo South Teaching Hospital
journal: Sri Lankan Journal of Medical Administration
abstract: Background: Medication safety is a cornerstone of patient safety and healthcare quality. Colombo South Teaching Hospital [CSTH] implemented comprehensive strategies in line with WHO’s global challenge “Medication Without Harm” to reduce preventable medication-related harm, while promoting multidisciplinary collaboration and patient engagement [1,2,5].Objectives: To describe CSTH’s medication safety initiatives, including management of high-alert and look-alike/sound-alike (LASA) medications, introduction of digital prescribing, staff and patient education programs, and the establishment of the Medication Safety Steering Committee. Additionally, to demonstrate how these practices can serve as a model for other hospitals implementing WHO-aligned patient safety strategies [1,7].Methods: A Medication Safety Committee guided multidisciplinary actions involving doctors, nurses, pharmacists, and IT staff. Key interventions included auditing prescriptions, introducing electronic prescribing through the Hospital Information Management System (HIMS), separate storage and labelling of high-alert medications, and continuous staff and patient education. Audit ﬁndings and competition outcomes were used to assess compliance and identify areas for improvement [3,5].Results: Enhanced awareness and adherence to safe medication practices, improved interdepartmental collaboration, reduction in medication-related errors, establishment of standardized procedures for high-alert and LASA medications, and recognition of CSTH as the national demonstration hospital for medication safety by the Ministry of Health [1,7]. Units participated actively in competitions, leading to sustained motivation for safety practices and continuous quality improvement [5,6].Conclusion: CSTH’s model demonstrates practical implementation of WHO-aligned patient safety strategies, enhanced multidisciplinary collaboration, and serves as a benchmark for hospitals across Sri Lanka aiming to operationalize national medication safety initiatives [1,7,9].

title: Reporting under Fear, Silence under Hierarchy: Event Reporting, Blame and Speaking up in Secondary and Tertiary Hospitals in Bayelsa State, Nigeria
journal: International Journal of Modern Science and Research Technology

title: Associations of patient safety speaking-up climate and managerial support with patient safety nursing activities among military nurse officers: The mediating role of patient safety competency
abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to examine the associations of patient safety speaking-up climate and managerial support for patient safety with patient safety nursing activities among military nurse officers, and to determine whether patient safety competency mediated these associations. METHODS: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among 170 military nurse officers at 12 military hospitals in the Republic of Korea from June to August 2025. Validated instruments were used to assess speaking-up climate and managerial support for patient safety as predictors, patient safety competency as the mediator, and patient safety nursing activities as the outcome. A mediation analysis with multiple X variables was conducted using the PROCESS macro (Model 4) with 5,000 bootstrap samples, with both predictors considered simultaneously and each association estimated while controlling for the other predictor. RESULTS: Patient safety nursing activities were positively correlated with patient safety competency (r = .55, p < .001), patient safety speaking-up climate (r = .53, p < .001), and managerial support for patient safety (r = .41, p < .001). In the mutually adjusted model, patient safety speaking-up climate showed significant total (β = .45, p < .001), direct (β = .29, p = .001), and indirect effects through patient safety competency (β = .16, 95% CI [0.08, 0.27]). In contrast, managerial support for patient safety showed no significant total (β = .12, p = .188), direct (β = .08, p = .310), or indirect effects (β = .03, 95% CI [-0.04, 0.11]). CONCLUSION: Patient safety speaking-up climate was associated with patient safety nursing activities both directly and indirectly through patient safety competency, whereas managerial support for patient safety showed no unique association with patient safety nursing activities after accounting for speaking-up climate. These findings highlight the importance of considering workplace conditions alongside individual competency in promoting patient safety nursing activities.

title: Gaps Between Adoption and Appropriate Implementation of Patient Safety Measures in Japanese Hospitals: A Nationwide Cross-sectional Survey
journal: The Joint Commission Journal on Quality and Patient Safety
abstract: Background The need to bridge the gap between theory and implementation of patient safety interventions has been widely recognized. However, the extent to which implemented patient safety measures meet predefined criteria for appropriate implementation remains unclear. The aim of this study was to assess the adoption and appropriate implementation of patient safety measures aligned with the Joint Commission International (JCI) International Patient Safety Goals (IPSGs) in hospitals in Japan. Methods In this nationwide cross-sectional study including all hospitals in Japan between August and September 2025, measures for patient identification, critical test result management, handoff communication, medication safety, and surgical safety were investigated. Results In total, 1,644 hospitals (20.6%) participated in the study and provided valid responses. Among all 1,644 hospitals, patient identification, critical test result management, handover communication, and medication safety measures were implemented in 73.4%, 83.6%, 76.9%, and 77.1% of hospitals, respectively, whereas 36.5%, 21.4%, 31.6%, and 38.7%, respectively, met the predefined criteria for appropriate implementation. Among the 1,029 hospitals that performed surgery, 50.7% had an institution-wide surgical site marking policy, 62.1% had procedures for sign-in, time-out, and sign-out, and 25.0% met the criteria for comprehensive surgical safety implementation. There was little association between the appropriate implementation of one safety measure and that of the others. Conclusions Across Japanese hospitals, the adoption of patient safety measures was limited, and the proportion meeting the predefined criteria for appropriate implementation was even lower. Nationwide efforts are needed to support both the adoption and appropriate implementation of patient safety measures.

title: Patterns of medication errors across therapeutic drug classes: a retrospective analysis of incident reports in a Saudi tertiary hospital (2023–2025)
abstract: Background Medication errors vary in type, cause, and severity across different therapeutic drug classes, yet drug-class–specific error profiles remain poorly characterized. Understanding these patterns is essential for developing targeted prevention strategies. This study aimed to evaluate how medication error types, stages, and causes vary across therapeutic categories among voluntarily reported errors in a tertiary hospital. Methods A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted at Al-Noor Specialist Hospital in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, analyzing medication error reports from January 2023 to August 2025. Errors were classified by therapeutic drug class, error type (dosing, selection, information, duplication, other), stage of the medication process, and cause (system-related, environmental, staff experience). Error types and causes were compared across drug classes using chi-square tests with false-discovery-rate correction. Multivariable logistic regression models examined associations between drug classes and error characteristics, adjusting for patient demographics, year, and error stage, with Holm adjustment for multiple comparisons. Results Among 6,546 medication-error reports, antibiotics/antimicrobials (32.8%) and cardiovascular drugs (22.5%) accounted for the largest shares of reports. Dosing errors predominated across most drug classes, with highest proportions observed in electrolytes/supplements (78.9%) and respiratory drugs (75.3%). Cardiovascular drugs showed higher proportions of duplication errors (25.6% vs. 10.9%) and selection errors (4.1% vs. 1.3%) than other classes (both q < 0.001), whereas only three errors (0.05%) resulted in harm, precluding comparison across drug classes. Antibiotics were significantly associated with increased staff experience-related errors (OR = 1.80, 95% CI: 1.51–2.14), while electrolytes were associated with environmental causes (OR = 1.43, 95% CI: 1.20–1.71). Drug class remained a significant independent predictor of error type and cause after adjustment for confounders and multiple comparisons. Conclusion Patterns of reported medication errors vary across therapeutic drug classes, with cardiovascular drugs showing higher proportions of selection and duplication errors. These patterns describe reported errors, not error rates, but may help to prioritize targeted quality improvement.

title: Organisational silence and its impact on nurses and patient safety in nursing practice: a systematic review of global evidence
abstract: Healthcare systems improve only to the extent that they learn from what goes wrong, and learning depends on someone being willing to say so. Organisational silence is the deliberate withholding of concerns, ideas, or information that could prevent harm (Montgomery et al., 2024a; Türe et al., 2025). Silence cuts that mechanism off at the root. Morrison and Milliken's account is useful precisely because it resists the easy reading of silence as passive compliance (Morrison & Milliken, 2000). Instead, it frames silence as a collective response arising from employees' fear of negative repercussions (Seyednazari & Dorosti, 2025). Such silence blocks upward communication and organisational change (Kim et al., 2026). This reframing matters. It shifts responsibility away from individually "quiet" nurses and onto the hierarchical, power-laden structures that teach them that silence is the safer bet (Montgomery et al., 2024b; Seyednazari & Dorosti, 2025). Nursing sits at the sharpest edge of this dynamic. Nurses are the largest occupational group in healthcare and spend the most sustained time at the bedside, which makes them best placed to catch deterioration, error, and unsafe practice (Dong et al., 2026). Yet steep hierarchies, punitive management, and thin managerial support routinely discourage exactly the disclosure this position demands (Dong et al., 2026). Saudi hospital data on nurses' silence motives found concrete calculations behind the reticence: a lack of trust between staff and management, fear of social exclusion or disciplinary consequences, perceived injustice and favouritism, and reluctance to draw attention to oneself (Alhojairi et al., 2024). That is not apathy. It is a rational adaptation to environments where speaking up more often earns the label "difficult" than a genuine hearing. Over time, that adaptation hardens into something normalised rather than exceptional, a baseline culture rather than an occasional lapse. The harder question is whether silence harms patients, or whether the link is assumed because it feels intuitive. The evidence increasingly supports the former. For example, a study of Korean hospital nurses found that organisational silence had a direct negative effect on patient safety outcomes, independent of communication satisfaction (Lee & Lee, 2024). Acquiescent silence also partially mediated the relationship between leader-member exchange and patient safety culture (Lee & Lee, 2024). This is consistent with broader evidence linking silence to delayed escalation of deteriorating patients, missed nursing care and reduced incident reporting. Organisational silence is becoming more of a focus in healthcare, but the evidence is fragmented and conceptually inconsistent. Definitions, measurement and interpretation of organisational silence have varied across studies (Lainidi et al., 2023), making it difficult to compare findings or to develop a coherent understanding of the implications for nursing practice. Consequently, the lack of a clear synthesis of how organisational silence affects both nurses and patient safety presents an important gap for nursing leadership, health-service management and policy. This is relevant to SDG target 8.8, which calls for the protection of labour rights and the promotion of safe and secure working environments for all workers. A work environment in which a nurse feels unable or unwilling to raise concerns may undermine efforts to create psychologically safe workplaces and strengthen patient safety. However, the available evidence remains fragmented across different forms of silence, determinants, outcomes and intervention approaches, making it difficult to determine the pathways through which organisational silence influences nurses’ wellbeing, work experiences and safety-related practices. This lack of synthesis also limits the translation of existing evidence into practical organisational strategies. Hence, this review synthesises available evidence on the risk factors, barriers and consequences of organisational silence in nursing, and to clarify its implications for nurses and patient safety

title: Medical emergency response related to MedicAtion InciDents ( MERRMAID ): a case series and lessons to improve medication safety
abstract: BACKGROUND: Evidence suggests that some medical emergencies in hospital are associated with preventable medication errors or adverse reactions. AIM: The purpose of this case series was to investigate and describe the proportion of Medical Emergency Response Team (MERT) activations that are medication-related, the degree of preventability and underlying contributing factors. METHOD: This retrospective case series included a review of MERT activations collected from an Australian tertiary hospital by two separate multidisciplinary teams. Initial review by the research team identified those that were potentially medication-related; these cases were then reviewed by an expert panel to determine the degree of causation and preventability and to identify errors within the medication management cycle and their underlying factors. The main outcome measures were the proportion of preventable medication-related MERT activations. The secondary outcome included descriptions of medications, medication errors in the context of the medication management cycle and consideration of factors underlying the errors including pharmacy review contributing to these activations. RESULTS: Fifteen per cent (17/117) of MERT activations reviewed were medication-related, and 65% (11/17) of those were deemed preventable. The omission of medications due to errors in prescribing, administration, pharmacy review or supply stage was the main contributor to preventable medication-related MERT activations (7/11, 64%). Cardiovascular medications, predominantly metoprolol, were most implicated in preventable medication-related MERT activations. CONCLUSIONS: Medication adverse events due to potentially error-prone steps in medication management processes are a common cause of inpatient MERT activations, presenting a considerable preventable burden to patients and healthcare resources.

title: Transformational Leadership, Work Engagement, and Patient Safety Culture in Public and Private Hospitals in Mogadishu, Somalia: A Study Protocol and Statistical Mediation Analysis
abstract: Background: Effective hospital leadership can influence workforce engagement, teamwork, communication, learning from error, and patient safety, but evidence from fragile and resource-constrained health systems remains limited. Objective: To present a study protocol for examining the association between transformational leadership and patient safety culture, and for testing healthcare workers' engagement as a statistical mediating (indirect) pathway between the two, in public and private hospitals in Mogadishu, Somalia. Methods: The protocol specifies a multicentre, institution-based analytical cross-sectional design with a target sample of 300 healthcare professionals selected through multistage stratified sampling, using a questionnaire that measures transformational leadership, work engagement, and ten dimensions of patient safety culture. To demonstrate the planned analytical workflow, this document also reports an illustrative analysis based on 300 computer-generated, synthetic responses; these figures are not empirical data collected from healthcare workers and are presented solely for methodological demonstration. Illustrative Results: In the synthetic dataset, the mean transformational leadership score was 3.09 (SD 0.84), work engagement was 3.38 (SD 1.38), and patient safety culture was 3.19 (SD 0.81). Leadership was correlated with engagement (r=0.420) and patient safety culture (r=0.465), and the illustrative indirect effect of leadership on patient safety culture through engagement was 0.137 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.089 to 0.187). Conclusion: The synthetic analysis demonstrates the proposed analytical workflow for interpreting leadership, engagement, and patient safety culture together. These figures are not empirical findings from Somali hospitals; substantive conclusions require implementation of the protocol with real participants.

title: Adaptación lingüística a la lengua catalana de la encuesta «Hospital Survey on Patient Safety Culture 2.0»: CatHSOPS 2.0
abstract: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Assessing safety culture is critical to improving patient safety. There are multiple instruments. It was agreed to use the SOPS® hospital Survey 2.0 from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ). The aim of this study was to perform a linguistic adaptation into Catalan, because in our context it is a co-official language and for many professionals of primary use. MATERIAL AND METHODS: A translation was carried out by two bilingual professionals, native Catalan and Spanish speakers. Two other bilingual professionals reviewed and reached a consensus. Subsequently, an expert in linguistic adaptations, whose native language is English, performed a translation from the Catalan version into English and assessed the semantic equivalence between this translation and the original version, classifying the items in: A, when they were totally equivalent; B, when they presented minor differences caused by grammatical problems or cultural context, and C, for those with content differences. The semantic equivalence between the Catalan and Spanish versions was also assessed, rating terms/phrases on a scale of 0 to 10 (from not equivalent to fully equivalent). RESULTS: After translating the Catalan version to English language, it was necessary to adapt some terms, resulting in the final Catalan version. Furthermore, there was a high degree of consensus among the evaluators regarding the semantic equivalence of the Catalan and Spanish versions. CONCLUSIONS: A Catalan version was made publicly available and hosted in the BiblioPro repository.

title: Just culture in nursing: Implications for patient safety and nurse retention
abstract: BACKGROUND: Nurse retention is strongly shaped by organizational culture and leadership, which influence workplace behaviors, reporting practices, and staff engagement. While blame-free culture emphasizes learning over punishment, just culture balances non-punitive learning with individual accountability, promoting both transparency and fair responsibility. PURPOSE: To examine how just culture influences nurse-related and patient-related outcomes across clinical settings. METHODS: An integrative review of the literature was conducted between November 2025 and March across multiple databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and ScienceDirect, yielding 2,535 articles. Of these, 15 met the predefined inclusion criteria. Thematic analysis identified two core categories: (a) the influence of just culture on nurse retention, and (b) its impact on patient safety culture. DISCUSSION: The reviewed evidence indicates that just culture is associated with more open communication, higher incident and near-miss reporting, stronger organizational learning, and greater engagement in patient safety activities.
