Supportive and non-punitive environments appear to reduce second-victim distress, defensive practice, silence around safety concerns, burnout, and turnover intention, while strengthening trust in leadership, occupational commitment, and nurse retention. CONCLUSION: Embedding just culture within safety strategies may strengthen nurse well-being, workforce stability, resilience, and quality of care.

title: A Survey and Analysis of the Current Status of MRI Safety Management in Medical Institutions in Korea
abstract: BACKGROUND: MRI safety management is essential for patient safety and for standardizing institutional practices. However, nationwide data on MRI safety readiness in Korean tertiary hospitals remain limited. PURPOSE: To evaluate MRI safety management across all 47 Korean tertiary hospitals and identify major gaps in safety infrastructure, staffing, and education. STUDY TYPE: Cross-sectional census survey. POPULATION: MRI safety managers from all 47 Korean tertiary hospitals in 2025. ASSESSMENT: A structured 50-item questionnaire was developed based on the American College of Radiology (ACR) MRI safety guidelines. A composite safety maturity index (0-100) was calculated as the unweighted arithmetic mean of four domain scores derived from 32 binary safety-practice items, with mandatory items weighted 2 and recommended items weighted 1 in accordance with the 2024 ACR Manual on MR Safety. STATISTICAL TESTS: Descriptive statistics were used to summarize institutional characteristics and safety compliance. Comparisons of staffing patterns by time period were evaluated using inferential tests, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. RESULTS: The response rate was 100% (47/47). The mean number of MRI units per hospital was 5.32 ± 3.50, and 3.0 T systems were predominant. Compliance was universal for closed-circuit television (CCTV) monitoring and MR Conditional monitoring devices but was low for ferromagnetic detection systems (17.0%), Magnetic Resonance Safety Officer (MRSO) appointment (17.0%), and Level 1 safety education (23.4%). MRI-related safety incidents were reported by 44.7% of hospitals. Two-person staffing decreased significantly from 97.9% on weekday daytime hours to 55.3% on Saturdays, 44.7% at night, and 38.3% on holidays. The overall composite safety maturity score was 63.08 ± 15.04. DATA CONCLUSION: Considerable variability remains in MRI safety management across Korean tertiary hospitals. These findings highlight the need for national MRI safety standards in the Republic of Korea. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 4. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 4.

title: Assessment of Nurses’ Knowledge and Attitudes Toward Patient Safety Post-Cardiac Catheterization: A Descriptive Cross-Sectional Study in Hilla Hospitals, Iraq
abstract: Background: Cardiac catheterization is a cornerstone diagnostic and therapeutic procedure for cardiovascular disease, yet post-procedural complications remain a serious concern. Nurses are central to recognizing and managing these complications, making their knowledge and attitudes critical to patient safety. Objective: This study assessed cardiac nurses’ knowledge and attitudes toward patient safety following cardiac catheterization in Hilla hospitals, Iraq, and examined whether knowledge and attitudes are correlated and associated with selected socio-demographic variables. Methods: A quantitative, cross-sectional, descriptive design was used. A convenience sample of 180 registered nurses working in cardiac catheterization, coronary care, and intensive care units at two governmental cardiac centers in Hilla completed a validated, self-administered questionnaire. The instrument included socio-demographic items, a 22-item knowledge scale, and a 12-item attitude scale. Reliability was acceptable, with Cronbach’s alpha values above 0.84. Results: Nurses demonstrated intermediate knowledge (M = 3.48, SD = 0.51) and moderately positive attitudes (M = 3.62, SD = 0.49) toward patient safety after cardiac catheterization. A statistically significant positive correlation was found between knowledge and attitudes (r = 0.34, p < 0.001). Age was significantly associated with attitude scores (p = 0.04), with younger nurses demonstrating more positive attitudes. Participation in training programs was significantly associated with both knowledge and attitudes (p < 0.05). Conclusion: While nurses demonstrated adequate knowledge and positive attitudes toward patient safety post-cardiac catheterization, targeted educational interventions are needed to address specific knowledge gaps and further strengthen safety practices in Iraqi cardiac care settings.

title: Strengthening Perioperative Patient Safety Through Non-Technical Skills Training Among Surgical Teams at Hakim Gezaw Teaching Hospital, Ethiopia
abstract: Background: Non-technical skills such as communication, teamwork, situational awareness, decision-making, adaptability, task management and leadership are important for patient safety during surgery. Evidence evaluating context-adapted multidisciplinary interventions and their relationship with patient-level safety outcomes remains limited in low- and middle-income countries, including Ethiopia. Aim: To assess changes in non-technical skills following context-adapted training and examine selected perioperative patient safety outcomes at Hakim Gezaw Teaching Hospital, Ethiopia. Methods: A mixed-methods quasi-experimental pre–post study included 24 multidisciplinary operating-room professionals and 672 adult surgical patients. Staff non-technical skills were assessed before training, immediately afterwards and at one month using an eight-item, five-point Likert-scale instrument informed by NOTSS, ANTS and SPLINTS frameworks. Linear mixed-effects models assessed changes in staff scores. Patient outcomes were compared between 336 pre-intervention and 336 post-intervention patients. Focus group discussions were analysed thematically and integrated with quantitative findings. Results: Mean overall non-technical skills scores rose from 3.36 ± 0.37 at baseline to 3.82 ± 0.34 immediately after training and 4.04 ± 0.61 at one month. Adjusted mean differences versus baseline were 0.464 (95% CI 0.161–0.766) immediately after training and 0.679 (95% CI 0.373–0.985) at one month. Situational awareness, adaptability and task management showed significant improvement. The post-intervention period was associated with fewer adverse events, care delays and communication-related safety events, alongside higher patient satisfaction. Qualitative findings described improvements in teamwork, communication, shared awareness, coordination and speaking up. Conclusion: Context-adapted training was associated with improved team non-technical skills, maintained at one month. Concurrent improvements in patient outcomes cannot be attributed causally to the intervention because the study had no control group. Routine integration, refresher training and supportive leadership may help sustain improvements. Keywords: Non-technical skills; Patient safety; Teamwork; Communication; Operating room; Ethiopia.

title: Medical Errors and Patient Safety: A Narrative Review of Prevention Strategies
journal: South Asian Research Journal of Medical Sciences

title: Safety Climate and Its Association with Nursing Disaster Response Performance in Hospital Settings
abstract: Safety climate may be related to nurses’ perceived ability to respond to disaster situations in hospital settings. This study aimed to examine the relationship between safety climate and nursing disaster response performance in hospital nurses in the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Indonesia. A cross-sectional quantitative analytical observational study was conducted on 130 nurses selected by non-probability quota sampling with geographical allocation. Data were collected via questionnaires, between January and August 2026. Safety climate and nursing disaster response performance were measured by modified 16-item scales. Descriptive statistics and chi-square test were used for data analysis. Most respondents reported poor safety climate (70.0%) and 60.0% were classified as low disaster response performance. The safety climate was found to be significantly associated with disaster response performance (χ² = 9.525, df = 1, p = 0.002). Nurses who reported poor safety climate had higher likelihood of reporting low disaster response performance (OR = 3.600, 95% CI: 1.672–7.751). The findings highlight the significance of organizational safety perceptions for hospital disaster preparedness.

title: Patient safety events and outcomes in brain tumor surgery : A retrospective cohort study
journal: Journal of Neurosciences in Rural Practice
abstract: Objectives: The problem of patient safety events (PSEs) is still a significant issue in neurosurgical practice, especially when it comes to brain tumor surgery, which is associated with complex surgery and high-risk care during the postoperative period. There is, however, limited literature on the rate of PSEs and their effects on clinical outcomes and healthcare use, particularly in middle-income healthcare. The objective of the present study was to outline the incidence of PSEs among brain tumor patients who undergo the surgical procedure and to determine the factors that can predict an unfavorable outcome at hospital discharge. Also, the effect of PSEs on hospital stays and direct medical expenditure of the hospital was considered. Materials and Methods: The present study is a retrospective cohort study, which utilized medical record review of 572 brain tumor patients who had neurosurgical operations consecutively in a tertiary care university hospital. PSEs were categorized as preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative. The study period was January 2024 to December 2025. Clinical outcome on discharge was classified as either favorable or unfavorable according to the Glasgow Outcome Scale. Binary logistic regressions were done to determine factors that were related to poor outcomes. The independent t-tests compared the length of hospital stay and total direct medical costs in patients with and without PSEs. Results: PSEs were present in 29.8 percent of the patients, with most of them being postoperative. Unfavorable outcomes occurred in 76/572 (13.3%) of patients. Multivariate analysis revealed that unfavorable outcomes were independently related to diabetes mellitus, the presence of PSEs, and preoperative Karnofsky Performance Status. Patients who did not experience PSEs had significantly shorter hospital stays and lower total direct medical costs than patients who experienced PSEs ( p < 0.05). Conclusion: PSEs are incidents in brain tumor surgery and are closely related to the adverse clinical outcomes, extended hospitalization, and high healthcare expenses. Enhancement of perioperative patient safety measures can enhance the outcomes and decrease the healthcare burden in neurosurgical oncology.

title: Assessment of Safety and Hazard Management Practices and Emergency Preparedness among Employees in Hospitals of Nepal
abstract: Background: Hospitals in Nepal operate in the environment that is vulnerable to biological, chemical, physical, ergonomic, psychosocial, fire, and disaster risks. Being prone to earthquakes, floods, landslides, fires and disease outbreaks, Nepal needs hospital-based employee safety and disaster preparedness programs. Objectives: This paper will present evidence on occupational and environmental risks, practices of safety and hazard management, disaster preparedness, organizational issues and knowledge gaps of selected hospitals in Nepal. Methods: This is a narrative review based on research articles specific to Nepal, disaster preparedness literature, and selected guidelines on occupational safety, infection prevention and control, biomedical waste, and hospital disaster preparedness. Evidence is provided thematically. Results: Evidence reveals a number of risks and issues related to occupational and environmental safety, including needlesticks, infection prevention and control, personal protective equipment, biomedical waste, psychosocial issues, and preparedness for emergencies. While 84% of 25 hub hospitals have disaster plans, only 33% of hospitals with disaster plans had fire safety measures. Assessment of three public hospitals through Hospital Safety Index placed them in category B, which means that they have moderate safety and preparedness. Conclusion: Hospital safety requires implementation, not policies. Regular training, simulation exercises, hazard assessments, availability of resources, communication, incident command systems, occupational health services, and monitoring are critical for preparedness and resilience. Novelty: This paper brings together the topics of occupational safety, infection prevention, environmental health, disaster preparedness, and hospital resilience in the same Nepalese context.

title: Strengthening Conflict Management to Support Patient Safety In The Napza Rehabilitation Unit at RSKO Jakarta
abstract: Conflict among patients in substance-use rehabilitation may compromise patient safety, therapeutic relationships, and continuity of care. This article reports a nursing-management residency project designed to strengthen the conflict-management system in the NAPZA Rehabilitation Unit at RSKO Jakarta. The project used a descriptive-analytic approach and a single-group program evaluation with knowledge measured immediately before and after the intervention. Assessment included observation, interviews/discussions, review of documents and incident records from 2023–2026, 5M/7M analysis, SWOT analysis, and Urgency, Seriousness, Growth (USG) prioritization. Thirteen nurses participated in the knowledge evaluation. The intervention combined a strengthened conflict-management guide, education, de-escalation training/simulation, a response pathway, a Post-Conflict Reconciliation Form, documentation, debriefing, and a monitoring plan. Patient conflict/fighting received the highest USG score of 15 (U=5, S=5, G=5). Mean knowledge scores increased from 41.8 before the intervention to 86.8 immediately afterward, a 45.0-point difference. These findings indicate an immediate improvement in knowledge but do not demonstrate improved clinical skills or a reduction in conflict incidents. Because the project had no comparison group and documented evidence of instrument validity and reliability was unavailable, the results should be interpreted cautiously. The program’s contribution is a context-specific, system-oriented package that links education with response procedures, reconciliation, documentation, and incident learning in NAPZA rehabilitation. Program sustainability should be evaluated through regular monitoring of safety indicators, adherence to response pathways, and conflict documentation.

title: SiAman EduBot: Inovasi AI untuk Pelaporan Insiden dan Edukasi Keselamatan Pasien Dalam Satu Platform Digital.
journal: Sendimas 2021 - Seminar Nasional Pengabdian kepada Masyarakat
abstract: RSUP dr. Sitanala is committed to strengthening patient safety culture toward a smart hospital paradigm through an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven innovation named Si Aman EduBot. This interactive chatbot, integrated via WhatsApp and the hospital's proprietary application, was developed to provide real-time education on safety standards, emergency procedures, and digital incident reporting systems for both staff and patients. This study aims to evaluate the impact of Si Aman EduBot implementation on enhancing safety culture within the hospital environment. The evaluation results over a three-month period demonstrated significant achievements, including over 5,000 user interactions, a 35% increase in incident reporting volume, and a 20% improvement in patient safety culture scores from the baseline. The rapid and responsive nature of the chatbot proved effective in increasing staff awareness and fostering an open, blame-free reporting culture. Through its interactive educational features and digital system integration, Si Aman EduBot holds the potential to serve as a national model for building a sustainable patient safety culture. Future developments will focus on integrating voice assistant capabilities and electronic medical records. Keywords: Patient Safety, Educational Chatbot, Digital Incident Reporting, Blame-Free Culture.

title: A Review on the Integration of Pharmacovigilance and Materiovigilance: A Holistic Strategy for Strengthening Patient Safety
abstract: Patient safety hinges on vigilant monitoring of adverse events associated with drugs and medical devices. In India the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC) spearheads this responsibility by serving as the National Coordination Centre (NCC) for Pharmacovigilance programme of India (PvPI) and Materiovigilance programme of India (MvPI) under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The Pharmacovigilance programme addresses the adverse events caused by medicines whereas the Materiovigilance programme tracks medical devices associated adverse events. As pharmaceuticals and medical technologies evolve, integrating these vigilance programmemes is crucial. This unified approach emphasizes the advantage of an integrated framework through shared infrastructure and reporting mechanism, enhancing surveillance efficiency and facilitating timely detection of safety signals. Despite progress, hurdles such as underreporting, awareness gap, and medico-legal concerns persist. Reinforcing the integrated pharmacovigilance-materiovigilance system through capacity building unified reporting process and platform and stakeholders buy-in is crucial for improving post marketing oversight and ensuring patient safety. This review demonstrates the scope and feasibility of integrating both the programmemes, along with emerging opportunities, potential public health outcomes in a unified and cohesive national vigilance ecosystem.

title: Interprofessional Collaboration for Enhancing Patient Safety and Healthcare Quality: A Systematic Review
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Occupational violence in patient safety and quality of care: a scoping review protocol
abstract: Workplace violence (WPV) is a significant issue that negatively affects job satisfaction, compromising the physical and mental health of healthcare workers, impacting the care provided and the organizational climate, and causing harm related to the safety and quality of patient care. WPV can manifest itself both among healthcare team members and in interactions between workers, patients, visitors, and companions. This study aims to describe the planning of a scoping review that will map the evidence on the consequences of workplace violence against healthcare workers regarding patient safety and quality of care. This is a scoping review protocol that follows the methodological guidelines designated by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and the recommendations for drafting scoping reviews of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols - extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR). It will follow the subsequent steps: definition and alignment of the objective and research question, eligibility criteria, description of the planned approach for the search, selection, extraction, analysis, and presentation of evidence, and the formulation of conclusions and implications of the findings. By systematizing the existing knowledge, this protocol may support scientific advancement at the interface between occupational health and patient safety, reinforcing the need to integrate such dimensions in healthcare practice, management, and research, aiming at the qualification of care and the protection of workers and patients.

title: Engaging Parents in Healthcare Interventions to Improve Paediatric Patient Safety: A Scoping Review
abstract: BACKGROUND: Paediatric patient safety incidents remain a significant global concern, with parents often playing a crucial role in detecting and preventing harm. Despite international calls for family partnerships in healthcare, evidence on how to meaningfully engage parents as participants in improvement interventions or within their development is limited. OBJECTIVE: To summarise and describe healthcare interventions that engage parents to improve key paediatric patient safety issues (relating to medication, communication, diagnosis and assessment, documentation, and administrative processes) and to explore the nature of parental engagement within the studies, including as research participants within the interventions themselves and/or the design and conduct of the study. METHODS: In this scoping review five databases (Medline, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science and Scopus) and grey literature were searched for studies published from 2000 to August 2025. Eligible studies (published in English) described interventions aimed at mitigating key patient safety issues and engaged parents within the intervention and/or the wider study design. Data were independently charted and synthesised narratively using the Patient and Family Engagement (PFE) framework and the International Association for Public Participation (IAP2) Spectrum. RESULTS: 111 studies were included, predominantly from secondary care settings (n = 89, 80%), conducting experimental study designs (n = 43, 39%) or quality improvement projects (n = 36, 32%). Communication and medication safety were the most frequently targeted areas (n = 72, 65% and n = 55, 50%, respectively). Interventions were categorised into 17 groups, totalling 179 interventions, most commonly involving process standardisation (n = 26/111, 23%) or parent-targeted education (n = 25/111, 23%). Outcome measures largely reported parent-specific factors, such as their perception (n = 38/111, 10%) or knowledge (n = 21/111, 19%), with minimal evaluation of real-world safety outcomes. Parental engagement within healthcare interventions was focused on Direct Care (n = 108, 97.3%) and most commonly occurred through consultation-based approaches (n = 78, 70.3%). Parental engagement within research activities was primarily classified as Inform (n = 66, 59.5%), suggesting limited involvement in research design, development, or delivery. CONCLUSION: Parental engagement is essential to improving paediatric patient safety, yet it remains limited, inconsistent, and often tokenistic. Greater partnership with parents is needed, both as contributors to research and as partners in the design and delivery of healthcare services and safety interventions. Embedding engagement within research and quality improvement, alongside standardised approaches to its evaluation and reporting, will be critical to achieving a more inclusive, human-centred approach in which parental perspectives meaningfully shape safer paediatric care. PATIENT AND PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: The parent patient and public involvement and engagement (PPPIE) contributor for this study met with the principal investigator on several occasions to review the findings and shape the interpretation of the results. They contributed to reviewing and editing the manuscript to improve clarity and accessibility.

title: Developing a consensus patient safety curriculum for junior doctors in Taiwan: a modified Delphi protocol
abstract: Introduction While international frameworks guide patient safety education, their impact depends on local training structures and sociocultural context. In Taiwan, patient safety training has not yet been consolidated into a coherent curriculum, and hierarchical, blame-oriented norms may discourage incident reporting and learning. The aim of this research programme includes establishing expert consensus on the core content for a Taiwan-contextualised patient safety curriculum for junior doctors through an adapted Delphi study. Methods and analysis This protocol outlines an online modified Delphi study with three phases: (1) document analysis of international frameworks to draft curriculum statements; (2) patient and public involvement and engagement to refine statement relevance and clarity; and (3) a multiround Delphi survey. Phases I and II were completed as preparatory phases to develop the Delphi questionnaire for use in Phase III. Phase III is underway, and we are inviting 80–100 multidisciplinary experts in Taiwan, anticipating 11–30 respondents in the final round. Expert panellists are rating statements with free-text comments. Between rounds, controlled feedback will provide summary statistics and analysis of free-text comments to inform subsequent ratings. Consensus was prespecified as median ≥4 and IQR ≤1, supported by ≥70% of respondents rating 4–5. If a consensus is not reached, a further round will be conducted. Free-text data will be analysed qualitatively to support interpretation and implementation considerations. Ethics and dissemination Ethics approvals for the consensus survey were obtained in the UK and Taiwan. Outputs will include endorsed curriculum content and implementation insights to guide future curriculum development. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication and conferences.

title: THE EFFECT OF SAFETY LEADERSHIP ON COMPLIANCE WITH PATIENT SAFETY PROTOCOLS THROUGH HEALTHCARE WORKERS’ COMPETENCE IN COMMUNITY HEALTH CENTERS
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence to Improve Medication Administration Safety in Hospital Nursing Services: A Preliminary Systematic Review Synthesis
abstract: Medication administration errors can occur during preparation, verification, administration, and monitoring, threatening patient safety. Artificial intelligence (AI) may help nurses identify risks and medication mismatches, although technical performance does not always demonstrate clinical benefit. Objective: To review the use of AI to support medication administration safety and identify requirements for validation, human oversight, and integration into hospital nursing services. Methods: This systematic review with narrative synthesis followed PRISMA 2020. PubMed/PMC, Scopus, CINAHL, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar were searched for publications from 2020–2026. Of 1,425 records, 410 duplicates were removed, 1,015 records were screened, 53 full-text articles were assessed, and 13 articles were included, comprising five core empirical reports and eight supporting sources. Results: Evidence included machine-learning models for predicting error risk in neonatal care, deep-learning cameras for detecting vial swaps, and an AI–mixed-reality prototype for medication checking. One model reported an F1 score of 83.28%, while the camera system achieved 99.6% sensitivity and 98.8% specificity. Conclusion: AI may strengthen medication-safety checks, but it has not been proven to reduce errors or patient harm. Implementation requires local validation, AI literacy, human oversight, data protection, false-alert monitoring, and evaluation of workflow, nursing workload, and patient-safety outcomes through regular hospital monitoring.

title: The Multimodal Imperative: Reengineering Patient and Family Communication for Safety, Equity, and Understanding
Evaluation of the Inter-Hospital Patient Transfer Form (Health 946): A Perception Study of Medical Ofﬁcers in Base Hospital Kalmunai North, Sri Lanka
journal: Sri Lankan Journal of Medical Administration
abstract: Background: Effective communication during patient handovers is critical to ensuring continuity of care and patient safety. International evidence consistently identiﬁes communication failures as a leading contributor to preventable adverse events. In Sri Lanka, Health Form 946 (H946) has served as the nationally mandated document for inter-hospital patient transfers for several decades. However, its alignment with contemporary structured communication standards has not been systematically evaluated.Objective: This study aimed to assess the perceptions of Medical Ofﬁcers (MOs) regarding the adequacy of H946 for supporting safe and effective inter-hospital patient transfers, focusing on information content, layout, ease of use, and implications for clinical safety.Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted in September 2025 at Base Hospital Kalmunai North (BHKN). All currently employed MOs were included. Data was collected using a structured, validated, self-administered questionnaire comprising Likert-scale and open-ended questions across four domains: demographics and usage, information content, layout and usability, and key recommendations.Results: Seventy-eight percent of MOs reported using H946 two to three times per week. While 93% agreed that the form adequately captures basic patient identiﬁcation, only 13% felt it clearly prompts documentation of the precise reason for transfer, and 91% reported insufﬁcient space for a comprehensive clinical summary. Ninety-seven percent strongly disagreed that the form mandates inclusion of critical safety information such as allergies and current medications, and 92% found it ineffective in preventing documentation errors or omissions. Eighty-one percent supported integration of a structured checklist, and 77% believed a redesigned form would reduce patient risk during transfer.Conclusion: The ﬁndings demonstrate that while H946 fulﬁls its administrative role, it does not adequately support the structured clinical communication required for safe inter-hospital patient handover. A revised form incorporating internationally recommended structured handover elements would represent a meaningful, system-level patient safety improvement.

title: Feasibility, safety, and acceptability of robotic-assisted rehabilitation for patients with knee osteoarthritis
abstract: Abstract Total knee replacement (TKR) is an effective treatment for end-stage knee osteoarthritis (KOA), yet optimal preoperative rehabilitation strategies remain undefined. Robot-assisted rehabilitation offers potential advantages in delivering controlled, intensive, and reproducible exercise protocols for patients with knee osteoarthritis. This early-phase feasibility study evaluated the safety, usability, and patient acceptability of the Knee-LOCOBOT, a novel robotic rehabilitation device designed for patients with KOA. No inference regarding efficacy can be drawn given the absence of a control group, randomization, or blinding. A single-arm feasibility study was conducted at Tan Tock Seng Hospital, Singapore (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07539948; NHG DSRB Reference: 2024–3529). Ten patients with KOA were recruited, with nine completing the intervention prior to TKR. Participants underwent four sessions of robot-assisted exercises incorporating cycling, leg press, and isometric quadriceps strengthening modes. Outcome measures included the Oxford Knee Score (OKS), EQ-5D-5 L, Knee Society Score (KSS), 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT), Timed Up and Go (TUG), 30-second Chair Rise, quadriceps strength, and patient satisfaction survey. Recruitment, retention, and adherence were the primary feasibility outcomes. From 15 patients screened, 10 were enrolled (consent rate 71%, 10 of 14 eligible), of whom nine completed all four sessions, giving a retention rate of 90% (9/10) and 100% session completion and adherence among completers; the single withdrawal was for personal reasons unrelated to the device. A statistically significant within-group change in 6MWT distance was observed (median 291 m to 360 m; median within-participant change + 15 m, mean change + 31 m; p = 0.012, n = 9). In the absence of a control group this change cannot be attributed to the intervention. Right quadriceps strength showed a non-significant numerical increase ( p = 0.05, unadjusted, one of multiple comparisons). Exercised vs. non-exercised limb strength difference was small and non-significant (Cohen’s d = 0.11, p = 0.75). No adverse events were recorded. Patient acceptability was high (88.9% agreement). This small, single-arm, uncontrolled feasibility evaluation in nine selected low-pain KOA patients suggests that four supervised sessions can be completed without recorded adverse events, with high patient acceptability. No conclusions regarding clinical effectiveness or suitability for rehabilitation pathway integration can be drawn. An adequately powered randomised controlled trial is required before any efficacy claims can be made. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07539948, date of first registration 27/03/2026.

title: Leadership as a Patient Safety Intervention: Building Just, Responsive and Resilient Healthcare Organizations
abstract: Patient safety is often discussed through the language of clinical error, adverse events, protocols, and quality improvement. Yet many conditions that make harm more or less likely are created before the clinical encounter itself, through leadership decisions that shape priorities, staffing, communication, accountability, role clarity, and team capacity to respond to risk. This chapter examines leadership as an active patient safety intervention rather than as a background managerial function. It argues that just, responsive, and resilient healthcare organizations are built when leaders create conditions in which professionals can speak up, report unsafe conditions, learn from weak signals, and act before preventable harm reaches patients. Particular attention is given to administrative harm, psychological safety, leadership visibility, accountable decision-making, workforce engagement, and competency-sensitive staffing. The chapter highlights the patient safety implications of failing to use specialized nurses according to their expertise, especially when professionals are redeployed to unfamiliar clinical environments without adequate preparation, supervision, or competency alignment. It also links safe workforce deployment with just culture, speaking up, and organizational learning, showing how leadership choices can either expose patients and staff to avoidable risk or create protective barriers. A leadership-oriented patient safety framework is proposed to support healthcare leaders in translating safety intentions into everyday organizational practice and in aligning culture, competence, voice, and learning. The chapter concludes that leadership should be judged by the safety conditions it creates, not only by the intentions it declares, for healthcare organizations working under pressure and seeking safer, fairer, and more resilient models of care.

title: FROM SAMPLE TO DIAGNOSIS: PREVENTING LABORATORY ERRORS AND IMPROVING PATIENT SAFETY—AN INTEGRATIVE REVIEW
abstract: Background: Laboratory errors can occur throughout the testing pathway and may affect diagnostic accuracy, timely care, and patient safety. Prevention requires attention to the interactions between clinical workflows, staff practices, and technology. Aim: To examine laboratory testing errors, evaluate preventive interventions, and distinguish improvements in laboratory processes from demonstrated benefits to patients. Methods: A preliminary synthesis of seven selected primary reports was undertaken. Findings were compared by testing stage, intervention, implementation conditions, and outcome. The planned multi-database search, independent eligibility screening, and methodological appraisal remain incomplete; therefore, the reports do not constitute a final integrative review sample. Results: Ordering, specimen collection, identification, and result communication were recurring areas of concern. One multicomponent identification programme was associated with an approximately 97% relative reduction in the identification error rate. Another study reported a decrease in mean critical-value notification time from 11.3 to 3.03 minutes after introducing secure messaging. However, a combined education and skin-antisepsis intervention produced a reduction in blood-culture contamination that was not statistically significant. Barcode-scanning adherence was inconsistent, with equipment and training barriers reported. Direct evidence of reduced patient harm was limited. Conclusion: The selected evidence suggests opportunities to improve laboratory safety through coordinated procedures, technology, training, and communication. Process improvements should be evaluated alongside diagnostic outcomes and documented harm. Conclusions remain provisional pending completion of the planned review procedures.

title: Changes in hepatic functional reserve and renal function during hospitalization in patients with chronic liver disease
abstract: Evidence regarding inpatient rehabilitation for clinically complex patients with chronic liver disease (CLD), including those with advanced cirrhosis, remains limited. We aimed to describe real-world inpatient rehabilitation practice and unadjusted in-hospital changes in hepatic and renal laboratory measures. This single-center retrospective observational study included 200 patients hospitalized for CLD-related conditions at Wakayama Medical University Hospital between January and December 2023. Referral and treatment were determined clinically rather than by standardized criteria. We compared baseline characteristics and unadjusted between-group changes in hepatic and renal laboratory measures, with exploratory analyses stratified by Child-Pugh (CP) class. Rehabilitation-related adverse events were retrospectively assessed using complete inpatient medical records and institutional incident reports. Of 200 hospitalized patients, 57 received inpatient rehabilitation. The rehabilitation group was older, had higher Child-Pugh scores, was more often admitted emergently, and had longer hospital stays than the non-rehabilitation group. Median rehabilitation duration was 11.0 days (interquartile range [IQR], 6.0-20.0), and the median time from hospital admission to rehabilitation referral was 6.0 days (IQR, 3.0-9.0). Across Child-Pugh classes, unadjusted hepatic and renal laboratory changes did not show a consistent pattern of greater deterioration in the rehabilitation group. No serious rehabilitation-related adverse event was identified through review of the complete inpatient medical records or the institutional incident-reporting system. These real-world data characterize inpatient rehabilitation in a clinically complex CLD population, including patients with advanced cirrhosis, and may inform development of liver rehabilitation for hospitalized, medically vulnerable patients. Because referral and treatment were individualized and the comparisons were unadjusted, the observations should be interpreted as descriptive associations rather than evidence of a causal effect, overall safety, or efficacy.

title: Handovers that work: ensuring patient safety through effective team communication
Improving Medication Safety for Patients with Adrenal Insufficiency Using Electronic Health Record Optimization
abstract: Introduction: Life-threatening adrenal crisis is preventable with timely administration of a stress dose of hydrocortisone, but recognition is often delayed. Sentinel patient safety events in 2020 highlighted the need to standardize adrenal insufficiency management. The primary aim of our quality improvement project was to reduce adrenal insufficiency medication errors in the emergency department (ED) by 10% from the baseline in 2 years. Methods: We included patients younger than 21 years with adrenal insufficiency and a prescription for parenteral hydrocortisone sodium succinate or oral hydrocortisone (prescribed by endocrinology) seen at our hospital between January 1, 2019, and September 30, 2023. Electronic health record (EHR) optimization changes included usage of a best practice advisory to improve visibility of adrenal insufficiency diagnosis and standardization of orders, steroid action plans, and education documentation. ED medication errors were defined as ED encounters with an emergency service index score of 1 or 2 with suboptimal stress dose (<50 mg/m 2 of hydrocortisone sodium succinate) administration. The secondary outcome measure was safety reports related to medication errors in the ED or ambulatory setting. We analyzed outcome measures using statistical process control and tracked usage rates of EHR changes. Results: We included 776 patients and 920 ED encounters. ED medication errors reduced from a baseline of 21% to 13.9% by study end. The interval between safety reports increased from an average of 74.4 to 775 days. Process measure use was 60% or greater for the problem list, best practice advisory, and steroid action plan, and 34% for education documentation. Conclusions: We successfully leveraged EHR optimization to standardize adrenal insufficiency management, increase visibility of critical information, and significantly reduce medication errors.

title: Theorising Dementia as a Risk Classification: Sociotechnical Imaginaries of Safety and Order in Acute Hospital Care of People Living with Dementia
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
abstract: People living with dementia are one of the populations most at risk of restrictive intervention during an acute hospital admission. These restrictive interventions are typically justified by staff concerns about patient safety and as a means of mitigating against falls, itself a key metric of quality care in acute settings. Drawing on Jasanoff and Kim’s concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, this paper explores how healthcare professionals imagine risk and safety, and how these imaginaries contour the use of restrictive practice. Data collection comprised 225 days of ethnographic observation and 1168 in situ interviews with patients, families, and ward staff at (n = 6) NHS Trusts working in (n = 3) dyads for acute and mental health care across England. Data were analysed thematically using NVivo. Findings were grouped into three major themes: institutional cultures, institutional anxiety, and atrocity stories. The study reveals tensions between ways in which people living with dementia respond to admissions and the institutional imaginaries of a safe, risk-free ward, alongside expectations of “good patienthood.” It argues that these imaginaries produce dementia as a risk classification, where bed or bedside-bound patients who do not demand staff attention inform the routine use of restrictive practices. These interventions, however, often result in distress and feelings of imprisonment among people living with dementia, which in turn prompts further tightening of restraints on this vulnerable population.

title: Ghost Pharmacists in the Philippines: A Critical Analysis of Professional Accountability, Patient Safety, and Leadership
journal: POLICY LAW NOTARY AND REGULATORY ISSUES (POLRI)
abstract: Ghost pharmacist practice in the Philippines presents ethical, professional, regulatory, and leadership concerns because the use of a pharmacist’s credentials without genuine professional presence creates a gap between formal regulatory compliance and actual professional responsibility. The primary objective of this critical analysis is to examine ethical and professional issues, stakeholder responsibilities, leadership response, patient access and regulatory enforcement, potential root causes, professional accountability, and public trust. Institutional Theory, Professional Ethics Theory, and Systems Theory provide complementary lenses for examining the institutional, professional, organizational, and systemic dimensions of the practice. The analysis indicates that ghost pharmacist practice cannot be adequately examined as individual misconduct alone, as organizational practices, regulatory oversight, commercial pressures, and professional conditions may also influence its persistence. However, these factors should not be interpreted as direct causes where empirical evidence is limited. Professional accountability extends to pharmacists and to organizations responsible for pharmacy operations, while regulatory authorities have responsibilities for effective oversight and enforcement. Appropriate responses require evidence-based investigation, due process, and proportionate enforcement while protecting legitimate patient access to medicines. Genuine pharmacist presence, appropriate staffing, organizational safeguards, confidential reporting, and consistent regulatory oversight may strengthen professional accountability and reduce opportunities for nominal compliance. Addressing ghost pharmacist practice therefore requires coordinated responses across professional, organizational, institutional, and system levels, with patient welfare as the primary consideration in pharmacy practice, leadership, and regulatory decision-making.

title: Anaesthetic implications and occupational safety considerations of pressurised intraperitoneal aerosol chemotherapy procedures: An Australian 5-year single-centre experience
Health data protection and patient safety in Germany, Bulgaria, North Macedonia and China
journal: Open Access International Journal of Academic Research UNIVERSES
abstract: This review compares personal health information protection in Germany, Bulgaria, North Macedonia, and mainland China, emphasizing patient safety, biomedical research, and digital health services. Comparative legal analysis and a narrative review examined legislation, judgments, regulatory guidance, and five scholarly publications retrieved by September 24, 2026. Analytical categories included lawful processing, confidentiality, patient access, research, supervision, international transfers, and product requirements. Germany and Bulgaria share the General Data Protection Regulation but differ in sectoral implementation. North Macedonia illustrates European legal approximation, including distinctive prior-approval requirements and transfer concerns. China combines sensitive information safeguards with network data governance and additional controls on human genetic resources. Similar terminology does not imply equivalent institutions or transfer permissions. The European Health Data Space adds phased obligations, requiring separation of current compliance from future preparedness. Clinical literature supports attention to record accuracy, understandable patient access, and trustworthy research, without establishing comparative national health outcomes. Recommended practices include purpose specific governance, traceable access, appropriate impact assessments, accessible correction procedures, and separate review of research and cross border requirements. Public benefit depends on whether confidentiality, accuracy, and lawful availability jointly support safe care, equitable participation, and accountable knowledge generation.

title: Translation, Adaptation, and Validation of Survey on Patient Safety Culture for Ambulatory Care in Japan
journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Health Management
abstract: Abstract Objective There is no validated questionnaire in Japan to measure the culture of safety in ambulatory care clinics. Therefore, we developed the Japanese version of the Medical Office Survey on Patient Safety Culture (MOSPSC) of the Agency of Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) in the United States with the aim to establish a tool for evaluating and benchmarking the safety culture of outpatient clinics in Japan. Materials and methods This research uses both qualitative and quantitative approaches to translate, adapt and validate the MOSPSC questionnaire which consists of 62 questions. The process involved seven steps such as translation by two independent bilingual physicians, drafting and reviewing, backtranslation by two separate translation companies, semantic equivalence assessment by AHRQ and revision, pretest, focused discussion, and finalizing the questionnaire after expert review and proofreading. An actual safety culture survey was conducted with mainly online and paper versions at four clinics in Tokyo. The survey results were then evaluated for patient safety dimensions, reliability and construct validity. Results Efforts are made to select appropriate terminology during tool adaptation processes due to different language and medical system between Japan and the United States. The response rate in the actual survey was 66.4% (242/364). Confirmatory factor analysis showed that factor loading and goodness of fit indices were better when 3 items were removed from the original 10-composite model with 38 items. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficients of composite measures ranged from 0.62 to 0.78 in the original model and 0.62 to 0.85 in the new model, indicating good internal consistencies. Conclusions Considering the differences in medical systems, culture, and language between the United States and Japan, the instrumented was adapted with a satisfactory content validity and reliability.

title: How Clinical Governance Shapes Quality of Care: The Mediating Role of Patient Safety Culture
abstract: Purpose Clinical governance is widely implemented internationally, yet the mechanism by which it influences quality of care, and whether that mechanism operates uniformly across health systems with differing resource levels, remains untested within a single sample. This study examined whether patient safety culture mediates the relationship between clinical governance and quality of care, and whether perceptions differ between higher-resource and variable-resource health systems. Methods A cross-sectional survey collected responses from 377 healthcare professionals in seven countries (Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Egypt, Jordan, Iraq, and Lebanon) using a validated 41-item instrument measuring three constructs across eleven dimensions. Data were analysed using reliability testing, correlation, ordinary least squares regression, mediation analysis with an indirect-effect test, group comparison with false discovery rate correction, and importance-performance mapping. Findings Clinical governance predicted patient safety culture (β = 0.826, R² = 0.682) and predicted quality of care as a total effect (β = 0.580, R² = 0.337). When both were entered jointly, the direct governance-to-quality path was not significant (β = 0.093, p = 0.176) while safety culture remained a strong predictor (β = 0.590, p < 0.001). The indirect effect accounted for 84.2% of the total effect, indicating full mediation. Respondents in higher-resource systems scored higher than those in variable-resource systems on all three constructs, with large effect sizes (Cohen d = 0.78 to 1.27). Freedom from blame was the lowest-scoring dimension measured. Conclusion Clinical governance appears to influence quality of care predominantly through patient safety culture rather than directly, and perceptions diverge sharply along the resource gradient of the systems studied. Governance reform may require concurrent investment in safety culture, and aggregating health systems of differing resource levels obscures a difference exceeding one standard deviation.

title: Transformational Leadership and Patient Safety Culture: A Systematic Review of Benefits and Challenges in Healthcare Settings
journal: Jurnal Manajemen Kesehatan Yayasan RS Dr Soetomo
abstract: Patient safety remains a critical global healthcare challenge. Transformational leadership has been recognized as a strategic approach to strengthening patient safety culture; however, evidence synthesizing its benefits and implementation challenges across healthcare settings remains limited. This study aimed to systematically synthesize the benefits and challenges of transformational leadership in improving patient safety culture. A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Relevant studies were retrieved from PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, and Web of Science. Eligible articles were critically appraised using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist. A narrative descriptive synthesis was applied to analyze and integrate findings. Ten studies were included in the final synthesis. The benefits of transformational leadership included improved communication, teamwork, and interprofessional collaboration, which enhanced coordination in patient care. It also promoted staff motivation, work engagement, organizational commitment, psychological safety, and structural empowerment, leading to improved clinical performance and patient safety outcomes, including reduced medication errors and improved quality of care. Key challenges included high workload and emotional exhaustion among healthcare staff, limited organizational resources and managerial support, insufficient leadership competencies, and rigid hierarchical organizational structures that constrained collaborative practice. Transformational leadership enhances patient safety culture by strengthening communication, engagement, and collaboration among healthcare professionals. However, its effectiveness is influenced by organizational readiness, leadership capacity, and supportive work environments. Addressing systemic and leadership-related barriers is essential to sustain its impact on patient safety improvement.

title: K-SHIELD: An AI-Enabled Statewide Emergency Health Intelligence Platform For Real-Time Hospital Selection And Emergency Resource Coordination in The State of Keralam, India
abstract: Background: Emergency healthcare requires rapid assessment, transport and access to an appropriate treatment facility. The K-SHIELD, Keralam Statewide Health Intelligence for Emergency Incidents, Life Saving and Disaster Response, report identifies limited real-time visibility of ICU beds, trauma facilities, ventilators, specialists, diagnostic services, emergency department capacity and blood availability as an important coordination gap. Methods: K-SHIELD was developed as a conceptual digital-health system design. The proposed architecture integrates Government and private hospitals, ambulance services, emergency control centres, police, fire and rescue services, disaster-management agencies, blood banks and public-health authorities through a secure cloud-based platform. Its AI decision-support engine combines patient, hospital, geographic and operational parameters. Results/Expected Results: The proposed framework is expected to improve real-time resource visibility, support faster hospital selection, facilitate pre-arrival hospital preparedness, reduce avoidable inter-hospital transfers and strengthen disaster coordination. No clinical effectiveness results are claimed because the system remains a proposed framework. Conclusion: K-SHIELD provides a structured framework for integrating real-time health intelligence, AI-assisted decision support and emergency-service coordination. Prospective pilot evaluation is required to establish technical feasibility, safety, recommendation accuracy, acceptability and clinical effectiveness.

title: Safety issues and harms of communication vulnerability for adult patients in critical care: A qualitative descriptive study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Patients, family members, and healthcare providers value and prioritise patient safety in critical care settings. Communication difficulties experienced by patients during critical illness increases their vulnerability to harms and preventable adverse events. Despite their importance, safety issues and harms related to communication vulnerability in adult critical care settings have not yet been described or systematically characterised. OBJECTIVES: The objective of this study was to identify, describe, and understand safety issues and harms related to communication vulnerability as experienced or observed by patients, family members, and healthcare providers in adult ICU settings. METHODS: We used a qualitative descriptive methodology including semistructured interviews which were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Paired content analysis was conducted using an inductive approach. FINDINGS: Between January and April 2024, 22 participants were interviewed including 11 professionally diverse healthcare providers, seven family members, and four patients from a community academic hospital in Toronto, Canada. Participants identified and described actual and potential physical, psychological, social, and self-determination harms related to their understanding of communication vulnerability during critical illness. Physical harms included respiratory distress and failure, unmet care (e.g., treatment of pain), falls, equipment failures, medication errors, and pressure injuries. Psychological harms included emotional distress (e.g., frustration and anxiety). Social harms included isolation and disrespect (e.g., being mislabelled as "difficult"). Self-determination harms were loss of agency and care without consent. CONCLUSIONS: Communication difficulties experienced during critical illness contribute to safety issues and harms across multiple physical, psychological, and social domains. Findings contribute to a growing body of evidence characterising the experiences and perceptions of patient safety in the adult intensive care unit. Findings have multiprofessional clinical implications in critical care settings particularly in relation to patient communication assessment and treatment and the creation of communication accessible and safe critical care settings.

title: Professional Disciplinary Authority, Institutional Independence, and Patient Safety Governance in Indonesia: A Qualitative Policy Analysis
abstract: Introduction: Disciplinary arrangements form part of the way health systems protect patients and hold practitioners accountable. Changes to these arrangements can influence how unsafe practice is identified, how adverse events inform learning, and whether the public trusts professional oversight. This study examines the redistribution of disciplinary authority between profession-based oversight and state-linked administrative governance in Indonesia, with attention to patient safety, professional accountability, and health system legitimacy. Methods: A qualitative policy analysis was conducted using Indonesian legislation, implementing regulations, ministerial regulations, and judicial decisions. Literature on health governance, professional regulation, and patient safety informed the interpretation. Documents were examined deductively for institutional independence, the redistribution of disciplinary authority, transparency, procedural fairness, epistemic adequacy, and accountability that supports learning. Results: The documents indicate a move towards administrative consolidation and closer state-linked oversight of professional discipline. The reform changes both the location of disciplinary authority and how professional conduct is assessed. Better coordination and clearer accountability are possible, although the arrangements also raise questions about independent judgment, profession-specific expertise, and procedural fairness. The analysis identifies a plausible pathway connecting disciplinary design with reporting incentives, professional trust, organisational learning, and safety culture. Transparent and fair procedures that support learning may strengthen patient safety governance. Opaque or predominantly punitive processes may instead inhibit reporting and encourage defensive practice. Conclusion: Professional discipline should be treated as part of public health regulation. In Indonesia, administrative consolidation needs to be accompanied by institutional independence, appropriate technical expertise, and transparent, fair procedures. Incorporating just-culture principles and opportunities for learning into disciplinary practice is a central policy priority for patient protection, professional and public trust, and accountable health system reform in low- and middle-income settings.

title: Analisis Manajemen Risiko pada Pasien di Rumah Sakit Umum Daerah dr. R. Goeteng Taroenadibrata Purbalingga
journal: Protein Jurnal Ilmu Keperawatan dan Kebidanan
abstract: Hospitals as healthcare service providers face various potential risks that may affect patient safety, including both clinical and non-clinical risks. The complexity of inpatient services, the involvement of multiple units, and a low culture of incident reporting make patient safety risk management a critical aspect that requires systematic analysis. This study aimed to analyze the implementation of patient risk management at RSUD (Regional Public Hospital) dr. R. Goeteng Taroenadibrata, Purbalingga. This study employed a mixed-methods approach with a sequential explanatory design. Quantitative data were obtained from patient safety incident reports, visit statistics, and the risk register. Qualitative data were collected through in-depth interviews, observations, and document review. Quantitative data were analyzed using univariate descriptive analysis, while qualitative data were analyzed through coding and thematic analysis. The findings indicated that patient safety risks consisted of both clinical and non-clinical risks. The most frequently occurring clinical risks were patient falls and patient identification errors. Most identified risks were classified as moderate to high based on likelihood and consequence assessments in accordance with SNI ISO 31000:2018. Risk mitigation measures had been implemented through standard operating procedures (SOPs) and incident reporting systems; however, challenges remained regarding compliance and documentation completeness. Patient safety risk management at RSUD dr. R. Goeteng Taroenadibrata, Purbalingga, has been implemented but has not yet reached an optimal level. Strengthening the patient safety culture, improving adherence to SOPs, developing a non-punitive reporting system, and conducting regular risk evaluations are necessary to enhance the effectiveness of patient safety management.

title: Clinical Governance Mechanisms and Contextual Determinants of Healthcare Quality and Patient Safety: A Critical Review
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Bathrooms as a Patient Safety Blind Spot in Emergency Departments: A Narrative Review and Nursing Practice Framework
MEDICAL IOT THREAT MODELING: A LIFECYCLE-BASED FRAMEWORK FOR INTEGRATING CYBERSECURITY RISK AND PATIENT SAFETY
journal: International Journal of Science and Research Archive
abstract: Connected medical devices, including infusion pumps, patient monitors, implantable devices, and remote monitoring platforms, have expanded the attack surface of modern healthcare delivery beyond what traditional IT security practices were designed to address. This paper's objective is to examine threat modeling as a structured, lifecycle-based discipline for identifying and mitigating cybersecurity risks specific to medical Internet of Things (IoMT) devices, and to argue that patient-safety impact must be integrated explicitly into existing threat-modeling methodologies rather than treated as a secondary concern. The methodology consisted of a targeted literature and documentation review covering regulatory guidance, peer-reviewed security research, and documented device vulnerability cases, combined with an applied walkthrough of established threat-modeling methodologies (STRIDE, DREAD, PASTA, and attack-tree analysis) against a representative device scenario. Results show that generic IT threat-modeling approaches underweight safety-critical consequences and do not account for the extended regulatory lifecycles, legacy protocols, and patch constraints characteristic of medical devices, and that documented real-world cases, including confirmed vulnerabilities in implantable cardiac devices, demonstrate that these risks are not theoretical. The paper concludes that threat modeling delivers the most value when applied continuously across a device's full lifecycle, from procurement through post-deployment monitoring, and when existing scoring methodologies are explicitly adapted to weight patient-safety severity. Future work should focus on standardized, patient-safety-weighted scoring extensions and empirical evaluation of threat-modeling programs in real hospital deployments.

title: Awareness of Magnetic Resonance Imaging Safety among Healthcare Workers: A Cross-sectional Study from Pune, Maharashtra, India
journal: JOURNAL OF CLINICAL AND DIAGNOSTIC RESEARCH
abstract: Introduction: The safety of Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a paramount concern in contemporary healthcare, as the strong magnetic fields and radiofrequency energy bring about particular hazards. Healthcare Workers (HCWs) need adequate knowledge, a positive attitude, and consistent safe practices to prevent adverse events related to MRI. Tertiary care hospitals are particularly high-risk environments because of the volume and complexity of imaging performed. Aim: To assess awareness, knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding MRI safety among HCWs. Materials and Methods: A cross-sectional, descriptive study was conducted in the Department of Radiodiagnosis, Dr. D.Y. Patil Medical College, Hospital and Research Centre, Pune, Maharashtra, India, from November 2025 to March 2026. Convenience sampling was used to recruit 47 HCWs who had received MRI safety training. A structured, self-administered questionnaire assessed socio-demographic profiles, knowledge, attitudes, practices, and awareness across zones: Knowledge domain: six questions; Attitude domain: three questions; Practice domain: three questions; MRI Zone Awareness: five questions. Results: Most participants were aged 25-30 years (n=31, 66.0%), and most were physicians (n=29, 61.7%). General knowledge was good, with (n=45, 95.7%) correctly identifying MRI at involving non-ionising radiation and (n=47, 100%) correctly identifying metal objects as the main MRI hazard. However, a significant gap emerged: only (n=19, 40.4%) correctly categorised pacemakers and cochlear implants as unsafe in MRI, while (n=25, 53.2%) incorrectly considered them safe. Attitudes were strongly positive, with (n=43, 91.5%) strongly agreeing that MRI safety is important. Adherence to patient safety practices was 100%. Overall awareness of MRI safety zones was relatively good, although substantial misunderstanding of zone restrictions was observed. Conclusion: HCWs demonstrated high general MRI safety awareness and positive attitudes; however, critical gaps remained in implant safety knowledge and incident-reporting culture.

title: Organisational strategies linked to high influenza vaccination uptake among health workers in Madrid
abstract: Abstract Background Influenza vaccination uptake among healthcare workers (HCWs) remains suboptimal despite its importance for patient safety and workforce protection. Evidence on effective organisational strategies in Spain is limited. This study aimed to identify successful practices in centres with medium–high uptake in Madrid and assess their transferability. Methods A qualitative descriptive study was conducted using semi-structured interviews. Six centres (three hospitals, three primary care) from the Regional Health Service with medium–high uptake (2023–2025) were purposively selected (42.2%–63.8% hospitals; 51.0%–63.8% primary care). Twenty key informants were interviewed (11 hospital-based, 9 primary care). Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed using an inductive–deductive thematic approach supported by Atlas.ti. Results Successful practices were consistently linked to combined organisational strategies rather than isolated actions. Accessibility was central, enabled by walk-in vaccination, mobile teams and flexible schedules. Institutional leadership and visible role modelling reinforced uptake, while local champions facilitated peer influence and informal diffusion. Continuous, peer-based communication contributed to normalising vaccination behaviour, and integration into routine workflows reduced structural barriers. In hospitals, additional factors included multichannel communication (intranet, SMS), real-time feedback (“vaccinometers”) and symbolic incentives. Training and early engagement of residents supported sustainability. Conclusions High influenza vaccination uptake among HCWs is driven by accessibility, organisational culture and leadership. Transferable actions include on-site and mobile vaccination, continuous communication, use of local champions and feedback of coverage data. These findings support system-level interventions to strengthen vaccination programmes. Key messages • High influenza vaccination uptake among healthcare workers is driven by accessibility, leadership, and organisational culture rather than single interventions. • Simple, low-cost organisational strategies can be transferred across settings to improve vaccination coverage in healthcare systems.

title: Approach To Map Health Cost Drivers
abstract: Abstract The WHO universal health coverage cube separates population, service, and cost coverage, yet at the point of care the three arrive as one episode: an entitlement, a service, and a claim met from public funds. That episode needs a unit; hospital cost studies each carry one dimension, in different cost units; this paper proposes the episode-of-care window, with a prespecified index episode and accumulation window, as the unit of analysis. Within the window, each dimension is operationalised as a vector: Entitlement for population (eleven variables, from age to days in hospital), Service Delivery for service (six cost categories, kept separate), and Reimbursement for cost coverage (insurance status, a binary non-cost variable). Because the dimensions arrive together, the three vectors enter one Gamma GLM with a log link to Direct Medical Costs, the episode's total cost. The exponentiated coefficients form the health cost driver map: the weight each variable carries within one episode. Applied to 125 households' episodes, procedure costs carry the largest z, with pharmacy, ICU, test and laboratory costs, disease type, prior disease, days in hospital, and discharge type significant; consultation fee and insurance are not. A separate robust run on the Entitlement and Reimbursement vectors is reported. The map is offered to ministries, insurers, and international bodies as a shared place to stand, informing their conversation without settling it, with each country bringing its own content. Held together at the point of care, the three dimensions of the UHC cube yield one map each institution can draw.

title: Health and Well-being
abstract: From smart wearables, implants, and ingestible electronics to remote physiological monitoring and public health, wireless technology has numerous applications in healthcare.It has the potential to create a pervasive environment for monitoring people's health and well-being while improving how physicians deliver care.It can also boost patient engagement and satisfaction by allowing them to spend more time in the comfort of their homes and interacting with their care centres whenever needed.The End-to-End (E2E) health data connectivity involves the development of technologies that enable reliable and location-agnostic communication between patients and healthcare service providers.The increasing penetration of connected devices in healthcare is a significant driver towards creating an intelligent network that enhances people's quality of life.In recent years, wearable biomedical sensors have experienced remarkable growth; however, there are still many societal challenges, including safety, security, interoperability, and integration with existing wireless infrastructure that need to be addressed.This chapter addresses various cutting-edge scientific problems dealing with communications inside or around the human body, novel antenna designs for wearables and implants, propagation channel characterisation, remote health monitoring, and innovative public health and safety applications.

title: Clinical Costing: the experience of the Italian Healthcare Network (N.I.San.)
abstract: Healthcare systems increasingly require accurate and patient-centered cost information to ensure sustainability and informed decision-making. Clinical Costing, based on Health Activity-Based Costing (HABC), provides a structured methodology to determine full costs, understand cost drivers, and support benchmarking activities. This study describes the Clinical Costing framework and its components—Health Activity Costing, Health Performance Costing, Patient Level Costing, and Health Management Costing—along with the experience of the Italian Healthcare Network (N.I.San.), which annually validates and processes hospital discharge data. N.I.San. has developed one of Europe’s largest databases on hospitalization costs, covering nearly 13 million discharges and offering detailed cost matrices, workload indicators, and standardized reference values. These tools enable precise benchmarking, highlight inefficiencies, and identify resource gaps. Clinical Costing offers a reliable and actionable approach for enhancing transparency, efficiency, and strategic planning, supporting equitable allocation of healthcare resources.

title: Comparative assessment of the cost effectiveness of two molecular biological test systems for CT/NG detection using Time Driven Activity Based Costing
abstract: Aim:Compare the full-process costs of the GeneXpert® CT/NG assay and the Roche cobas® 4800 CT/NG test under different instrument configurations and daily testing volumes, so as to provide a basis for healthcare institutions to select appropriate testing options. Methods:ATime-Driven Activity-Based Costing(TDABC) model was developed, categorizing costs into labor, instrument depreciation and maintenance, consumables, space, and electricity. Cost formulas were derived for different instrument configurations under varying daily testing volumes (n). Results:Cost analysis showed that when the daily testing volume (n) is ≤9, the total cost of the 2 or 4 channel Xpert system is lower than that of the cobas 24. For the cobas 96 system, the Xpert 16 , 48 , and 80 channel systems have a cost advantage when n ≤33, n ≤27, and n ≤24, respectively. Reagents and consumables constitute the largest proportion of total costs. In addition, the Xpert system can complete up to five batches per day, whereas the cobas 24 and 96 complete a maximum of four and three batches per day, respectively, offering faster turnaround time for individual samples. Conclusion:For institutions with a daily testing volume below 9 samples, the Xpert 2 or 4 channel model is recommended for optimal cost-efficiency and reduced patient waiting time. For high-throughput settings (e.g. 100 samples/day), the cobas 96 or higher channel Xpert models (48/80) are suitable alternatives. The choice should be guided by the actual daily testing volume, workflow, and resource constraints.

title: The health economics of physical inactivity and sedentary behaviour: healthcare expenditure and cost-effective interventions
Utilisation profiles and cost drivers in a Portuguese health unit, 2021–2024
abstract: Abstract Background High users (HU) of primary care account for a disproportionate share of health expenditure, yet the magnitude and drivers of cost differences across utilisation profiles remain insufficiently characterised in integrated care settings. Objectives To quantify and compare healthcare costs across utilisation profiles (consistent HU, occasional HU, and non-HU) and assess cost composition and potential savings in a local health unit (ULS) of the Portuguese National Health Service. Methods A retrospective study using an administrative patient-year dataset (110,300 individuals) from ULS Almada-Seixal (2021–2024) was used, linking primary and hospital care, including primary care consultations, diagnostic and therapeutic procedures (MCDTs), prescribed pharmaceuticals, emergency department (ED) episodes, and inpatient admissions. Costs were estimated using a bottom-up micro-costing based on official tariffs and price lists (SNS perspective). Descriptive and stratified analyses were performed across utilisation profiles and cost components. Results Mean cost per patient-year was €1,928, with a clear cost gradient: consistent HU (€4,413), occasional HU (€2,683), and non-HU (€771). MCDTs were the main cost driver, followed by pharmaceuticals and inpatient care, while primary care consultations and ED episodes represented a minor share of total costs. Costs were unevenly distributed, with occasional HU (38.4% of total individuals) accounting for the highest spending, while consistent HU, the smaller proportion (11.6%), exceeded the total costs of non-HU (50.0%). Simulating consistent HU behaving as occasional HU would lower expenditure by 9.6%, and as non-HU, by 61.9%, corresponding to total savings between €81.9 and €526.6 million over 4 years. Conclusions Costs are substantially higher in HU profiles, driven mainly by diagnostic procedures and pharmaceuticals rather than primary care, highlighting the potential savings of targeted interventions in HU. Key messages • Mean patient-year cost for consistent high users of primary care is nearly six times higher than non-high users (€4,413 vs €771), with diagnostic procedures and pharmaceuticals as main cost drivers. • Shifting consistent high users toward occasional or non-user profiles could reduce expenditure by 9.6–61.9%, saving €81.9–526.6 million over 4 years, supporting targeted interventions.

title: [Translated article] Farmastock: A collaborative tool for the reuse of high-cost hospital medications in a public healthcare system
abstract: BACKGROUND: The loss of high-cost hospital medicines due to expiration represents a structural problem affecting the efficiency and sustainability of the public healthcare system. This loss is not solely the result of management inefficiencies; it is frequently driven by unpredictable changes in patient clinical evolution that lead to the suspension of previously planned treatments, particularly in oncological, haematological, and immunological conditions. OBJECTIVE: To describe the economic and operational impact of the Farmastock web-based tool for the inter-hospital redistribution of high-economic impact medicines nearing expiration within the Public Health System of Andalusia (SSPA), and to analyse its evolution, its behaviour by hospital type and the perception of professional users. METHODS: A retrospective observational descriptive study was conducted on transfers registered in Farmastock between July 2019 and June 2025. Descriptive indicators (volume of transfers, cost avoided, most redistributed medicines) and comparative indicators (hospital type, province, efficiency per transfer) were analysed. An anonymous structured survey of professional users was included (Annex 1). RESULTS: A total of 1,462 transfers were registered, avoiding €5,055,822.98 in spending and redistributing 93,741 units. The most frequently transferred ATC group was antineoplastic agents. The average value per transfer was €3,458.16. District hospitals led in volume, while specialised hospitals demonstrated greater efficiency per transfer. The tool was highly valued by users and its use expanded to 27 hospitals. CONCLUSIONS: The descriptive findings suggest that Farmastock is a useful and well-valued tool associated with a positive trend in health system sustainability. Beyond the estimated economic impact, it has enabled the utilisation of medicines in exceptional clinical situations, such as palivizumab administration in paediatric patients. Future integration with artificial intelligence and corporate platforms could further amplify its impact.
