title: Healthcare Cost & Claim Structure (200,000 Episodes)
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This upload contains the data passport and a free evaluation sample (1,000 episodes with 6,093 claim line items) — not the full dataset. The complete dataset — 200,000 episodes, about 1,180,000 claim line items, six reference dictionaries and the coherence-validation script — is available at: https://sentineldata.com.ua/dataset/healthcare-cost-claim-structure Sample contents: File (inside the sample archive)RowsContent sample_episodes.csv1,000Episodes EP-00000001 to EP-00001000, 32 columns, same schema as the full episodes table sample_line_items.csv6,093All claim line items of those 1,000 episodes, 17 columns The sample is the first 1,000 episodes by ID with all of their line items, not a stratified draw. Its mix is close to the full dataset’s nominal mix: encounter types 73.1% inpatient / 18.3% outpatient / 8.6% emergency; payers 36.5% Medicare / 32.7% Commercial / 20.6% Medicaid / 10.2% Self-pay; 931 claims paid, 48 denied and 21 partially denied; 24 claims appealed (8 overturned, 16 upheld). The reference dictionaries and validate_coherence.py are part of the full product and are not included here. We re-checked the sample against every coherence rule that can be computed from the two sample tables (bill arithmetic, DRG and diagnosis presence, adjudication logic, cost logic, date boundaries): 0 violations. Rules that need the reference dictionaries (DRG weight match, length-of-stay ceiling, payer-share range) cannot be checked from the sample alone. Documentation in this upload: the data passport (PDF, English). This sample is released under CC BY-NC 4.0. About the full dataset: Fully synthetic. Contains no real patient data and no PHI. Every medical bill is built line by line and reconciles to the cent. 1. Overview Healthcare Cost & Claim Structure is a synthetic dataset of medical bills and insurance claims with strict internal coherence. Each of the 200,000 episodes is one medical encounter (inpatient, outpatient or emergency) with a fully structured bill: itemized line items, standard coding systems, payer and patient share, payment and denial adjudication, and appeals. Every episode also carries true_episode_cost, a ground-truth internal delivery cost generated from line charges and cost-center cost-to-charge ratios, so cost-estimation models can be scored against a known answer. 2. Dataset Composition FileRecordsDescription episodes.csv200,000One row per encounter episode: clinical, demographic, financial and adjudication fields claim_line_items.csv~1,180,000Itemized bill lines linked to episodes (revenue code, HCPCS, procedure slot, service date, units) icd10_cm_reference.csv140ICD-10-CM codes with descriptions and CCSR mapping categories hcpcs_reference.csv73HCPCS Level II codes with standard descriptors revenue_codes_reference.csv96UB-04 revenue codes with baseline charging rates ms_drg_reference.csv127MS-DRGs with CMS weights, MDCs and average length of stay denial_reason_codes.csv19CARC claim denial reason codes drg_weights_constants.csv38Constants matrix: coverage rates, copay shares, denial likelihoods, cost-to-charge ratios validate_coherence.py—Validation script for the 18 coherence rules (Python 3.8+, pandas, numpy) A free sample of 1,000 episodes with about 6,000 line items is available for evaluation. 3. Schema GroupKey columns Episode & patient (episodes.csv)episode_id, patient_id, age (0–105), sex, encounter_type (inpatient / outpatient / emergency), admission_date, discharge_date, length_of_stay Admission & clinicaladmission_type, admission_source, discharge_disposition, primary_diagnosis_icd10, secondary_diagnoses_icd10, severity_of_illness (Minor / Moderate / Major / Extreme), ms_drg_code, ms_drg_description, ms_drg_weight Payer & chargespayer_type (Medicare / Medicaid / Commercial / Self-pay), payer_plan, total_submitted_charges, total_allowed_amount, payer_paid_amount Patient responsibilitypatient_deductible, patient_copay, patient_coinsurance, patient_total_responsibility Denials & appealsdenial_status (paid / partially_denied / denied), denial_reason_code, denial_reason_description, appeal_status (none / submitted / upheld / overturned) Ground-truth costtrue_episode_cost, cost_to_charge_ratio Line items (claim_line_items.csv)line_item_id, episode_id, sequence_number, revenue_code, revenue_code_description, hcpcs_code, hcpcs_description, procedure_slot, service_date, units, unit_charge, total_charge, covered_amount, payer_share, patient_share, line_denial_flag, line_denial_reason_code DRG, admission type, admission source and discharge disposition are populated for inpatient encounters only and are null for outpatient and emergency encounters. HCPCS codes and procedure slots are populated only on the line items where they apply. 4. Payer Model & Adjudication PayerMarket sharePayer sharePatient shareBase denial rate Medicare35%80%20%5% Medicaid20%95%5%8% Commercial35%80%20%12% Self-pay10%0%100%3% Case mix: inpatient 70%, outpatient 20%, emergency 10%. Sex 48% male / 52% female. Age is lognormal (mode about 65 for inpatient, about 48 for outpatient). Inpatient payment: Medicare is modeled as DRG weight × a fixed base rate; Medicaid, Commercial and Self-pay are adjusted to 55%, 72% and 80% of total charges. Outpatient payment: flat charge-adjustment ratios of 45% (Medicare), 50% (Medicaid), 65% (Commercial) and 80% (Self-pay). Denials: 70% full-claim denials, 30% partial line-item denials. Appeals: 30% of eligible denials are appealed; 40% of appeals are overturned (paid), 60% upheld. Self-pay encounters are excluded from appeal logic. 5. Ground-Truth Cost Generation true_episode_cost = Σ (line_charge × cost-center CCR × noise), with noise uniform in [0.9, 1.1] and CCRs mapped by UB-04 cost center from CMS Hospital Cost Report data. The overall mean cost-to-charge ratio is about 0.42. Cost centerCCR rangeCost centerCCR range Room & Board0.35–0.45Operating Room0.30–0.40 Intensive Care (ICU)0.40–0.50Medical Supplies0.50–0.65 Pharmacy0.55–0.70Emergency Room0.35–0.45 Laboratory0.30–0.40Physical Therapy0.45–0.55 Radiology0.40–0.55Overall mean ~0.42 6. Code Systems & CPT Placeholders The dataset uses curated subsets of public coding systems: ICD-10-CM (CDC NCHS, 140 codes), HCPCS Level II (CMS, 73 public-domain codes), UB-04 revenue codes (NUBC, 96 codes), MS-DRG (CMS IPPS FY2024, 127 DRGs) and CARC (X12, 19 codes). CPT codes are the intellectual property of the AMA and are not included. A structural placeholder, procedure_slot (for example PROC_00001), marks that a procedure occurred on a line item and keeps sequence and linkage intact. Customers who hold an AMA license can map their own CPT hierarchy onto these slots. 7. Quality Assurance The financial model is held together by 18 coherence rules, checked by the included validate_coherence.py (exit code 0 means all rules pass); the data passport records zero violations in the distributed build. The rules cover: Bill arithmetic: line charges sum to total submitted charges; payer paid plus patient responsibility equals the allowed amount; deductible plus copay plus coinsurance equals patient responsibility (all within $0.01); allowed never exceeds billed. Clinical and DRG logic: inpatient episodes carry a valid DRG and primary diagnosis; DRG weight matches the reference table; length of stay is between 1 day and 4× the DRG mean; outpatient episodes carry no DRG; service dates fall between admission and discharge. Adjudication logic: a denied claim pays zero unless overturned; a paid claim has no denial reason and a positive payment (excluding Self-pay); appeals exist only on denied or partially denied claims; an overturned appeal restores payment; payer share falls within the expected range for the payer type. Cost logic: true episode cost is positive and below submitted charges; cost-to-charge ratio equals cost divided by charges (tolerance 0.001). 8. Provenance Parameter categorySource MS-DRG weightsCMS IPPS Final Rule FY2024 (Table 5, public domain) Cost-to-charge ratiosCMS Hospital Cost Report Information System (HCRIS) Commercial deductiblesKFF 2024 Employer Health Benefits Survey Denial and appeal statisticsAHA 2024 claim denial analysis surveys ICD-10-CM / HCPCS / UB-04 / CARCCDC NCHS, CMS HCPCS, NUBC, X12 (public guidelines) 9. Known Limitations Simplified DRG logic: each DRG maps to valid primary diagnoses, but no full MS-DRG or APR-DRG grouping engine is implemented; interactions between procedures, CCs, MCCs and age are abstracted. Curated terminologies: 140 of about 70,000 ICD-10 codes, 73 of about 7,000 HCPCS codes and 127 of 767 DRGs. Generalized cost-to-charge ratios: real CCRs vary widely by region, hospital size and teaching status; the model uses blended national medians. Linear payment modeling: Medicare inpatient payment is DRG weight × a base rate, with no hospital-specific adjustments (IME, DSH, outlier payments). Representative DRG weights: based on CMS FY2024 but may deviate slightly from the final published tables. No CPT codes: see section 6. Synthetic: all IDs, dates and amounts are procedurally generated. 10. Use Cases Suitable for: claim-denial and appeal-outcome prediction, cost-estimation and cost-to-charge modeling against a known ground truth, revenue-cycle analytics prototyping, testing billing and claims-processing pipelines without PHI, and teaching medical billing and health economics. NOT suitable for: benchmarking real payer reimbursement, real-world DRG grouping or clinical decision-making. The data is fully synthetic. 11. License & Distribution Format: CSV (two linked core tables and six reference dictionaries) plus the Python validation script. Delivery: One-time purchase; download link provided after payment. A free sample (1,000 episodes with about 6,000 line items) is available for evaluation before purchase. Usage terms are set out in the data passport.

title: COST RECOVERY RATE OF HOSPITAL TARIFFS AND INA-CBGs REIMBURSEMENT FOR DENGUE HAEMORRHAGIC FEVER (DHF) AT TYPE C HOSPITAL IN INDONESIA
abstract: The implementation of Indonesia's Case-Based Groups (INA-CBGs) payment system aims to improve efficiency in hospital financing. However, discrepancies between reimbursement and actual treatment costs remain a significant challenge for hospital financial sustainability. This study aimed to analyze the Cost Recovery Rate (CRR) by comparing hospital tariffs, INA-CBGs reimbursement, and the actual cost of treating Grade I Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever (DHF) patients while identifying factors contributing to cost discrepancies. A qualitative single embedded case study was conducted at a Type C private hospital in Palembang, Indonesia. Secondary financial and clinical data from 35 Class III inpatients with Grade I DHF were analyzed alongside semi-structured interviews with five key informants representing hospital management, clinical services, finance, and the casemix unit. Data were analyzed through document review, cost comparison, CRR calculation, and thematic analysis. The findings revealed differences between the hospital's internal tariff (Rp82,925,300), INA-CBGs reimbursement (Rp69,730,500), and the actual treatment cost (Rp72,479,198). The resulting Cost Recovery Rate (CRR) of 96.21% indicated that INA-CBGs reimbursement was insufficient to fully recover the actual cost of care. The financing gap was influenced by the interaction of several factors, including the package-based INA-CBGs payment mechanism, length of hospital stay, patients' clinical conditions, diagnosis and procedure coding accuracy, adherence to clinical pathways, laboratory and pharmaceutical utilization, and overall hospital resource efficiency. This study demonstrates that financial sustainability under the INA-CBGs system depends not only on reimbursement policies but also on integrated clinical and operational management. Strengthening clinical pathway adherence, documentation and coding accuracy, resource utilization, and cost monitoring may improve hospital financial performance while maintaining the quality and safety of patient care.

title: Therapeutic Plasma Exchange: A Cost‐Consequence Analysis Using Data From a Tertiary Care Hospital
Cost Burden and Cost-Effectiveness of Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment Repair: A Systematic Review of Economic Evaluations
abstract: Purpose: To review the economic burden and cost-effectiveness analyses of interventions and management of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD). Patients and Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted on Ovid Medline, Embase and Scopus from inception to March 2025 for articles reporting economic burden, cost analyses, cost-effectiveness, or cost-utility outcomes related to RRD repair. Primary outcomes were the cost of RRD adverse events and repair. Secondary outcomes were the incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICER) of RRD repair procedures. Risk of bias was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist for Economic Evaluations. The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42023446301). Results: A total of 46 publications met the inclusion criteria and were included in the study. Most studies were conducted in the United States (48%) and adopted payer or provider analytic perspectives. In 23 studies reporting RRD as an adverse event of another condition or intervention, the mean cost of repair was $3,648±2,986, inflated to 2024 US dollars (USD). Across 22 studies assessing cost comparisons of RRD interventions, the cost of the pneumatic retinopexy (PR), pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) and scleral buckle (SB) surgery ranged from $1,093-$4,761, $5,443-$9,903, and $4,411-$8,131, respectively. Considerable heterogeneity existed across economic models, analytic perspectives, willingness-to-pay (WTP) thresholds, and time horizons used in cost-effectiveness studies. Indirect costs, including caregiver burden and productivity loss, were infrequently reported. Conclusion: Although available evidence suggests that RRD is generally associated with favourable cost-effectiveness outcomes, conclusions are limited by methodological heterogeneity, predominance of evidence from high-income settings, and inconsistent reporting of indirect costs. Broader and more standardized economic evaluations, particularly in non-Western settings, are needed to better characterize the global economic impact of RRD repair.

title: Cost and Morbidity of Three-Dimensional Laparoscopic Living Donor Nephrectomy in Morocco
Health care provider costs of child health services for severe anaemia and malaria in Malawi, Kenya, and Uganda
abstract: Abstract Background Severe anaemia and malaria are among the leading causes of childhood hospital admissions in Africa south of the Sahara. For children being discharged from hospital, readmissions often occur raising the costs for inpatient care. This study aims to estimate healthcare provider costs for children under-five diagnosed with severe anaemia and severe malaria at Zomba and Kamuzu Central Hospitals in Malawi, Kisumu Referral Hospital in Kenya and Jinja Children’s Referral Hospital in Uganda. This is a sub-study of the clinical trial “Dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine and azithromycin for the post-discharge management of children with severe anaemia in Malawi, Kenya and Uganda”. Methods Cost data were collected from January 2024 to October 2024. Using bottom-up costing, we estimated annual economic costs for personnel, supplies and overheads required for a paediatric medical admission, referral, and blood transfusion processes. Individual cost components were identified, measured and valued for the services of in-patient and outpatient care, laboratory processing and ambulance referrals. Results The cost to healthcare providers for one bed-day for a general paediatric medical admission was $18 at Zomba Central Hospital, $50 at Kisumu County Referral Hospital, and $15 at Jinja Children’s Referral Hospital. When accounting for laboratory services, blood transfusions, and malaria medication for the duration of the entire hospital stay, the total costs of care were: $118 in Zomba, $427 in Kisumu and $167 in Jinja. At Kamuzu Central Hospital, a bed-day costs $9 in the main children’s medical ward, and $24 in the High Dependency Unit. The costs of providing for the entire hospital admission were $79 and $310, respectively. Personnel and operational costs were the main cost drivers for admissions costs, while laboratory supplies were the main cost component when providing blood testing services. Conclusion This study demonstrates how the costs of providing health care are influenced by fixed and variable cost components, health service utilization, and country-specific investments in health care. Our findings contribute to an evidence base to inform resource allocation and cost-effectiveness analyses of interventions targeting severe anaemia and malaria in children in Malawi, Kenya, and Uganda. Clinical trial registration Registry: pactr.samrc.ac.za Date of Registration: 8 th March 2023, Trial Registration Number: PACTR202303630742194.

title: Cost-Effectiveness of Hypertension Treatment with Diabetes Mellitus Complications in Hospitalized Patients at Berkah Pandeglang Regional Hospital
journal: PharmaCine Journal of Pharmacy Medical and Health Science
abstract: Hypertension with diabetes mellitus (DM) is a frequent comorbidity that increases clinical complexity and healthcare expenditures. Various antihypertensive and antidiabetic combination therapies are used in hospitalized patients, making pharmacoeconomic evaluation necessary to determine the most cost-effective treatment option. This study aimed to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of hypertension treatment with diabetes mellitus complications in hospitalized patients at Berkah Pandeglang Regional Hospital. This was a non-experimental observational study with a retrospective design using secondary data from medical records and hospital billing data of hospitalized patients diagnosed with hypertension and DM in 2024. Direct medical costs and clinical effectiveness outcomes, including blood pressure control, blood glucose levels, and length of stay (LOS), were analyzed. Cost-effectiveness was assessed using the Average Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ACER) and Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER). A total of 9 patients met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 5 patients received captopril, amlodipine, and metformin, while 4 patients received amlodipine, candesartan, bisoprolol, metformin, and glimepiride. The combination therapy of captopril and amlodipine with metformin showed the lowest ACER value (IDR 25,941), indicating the most cost-effective regimen. Another combination consisting of amlodipine, candesartan, and bisoprolol with metformin and glimepiride had a higher ACER value (IDR 82,621). Both regimens were located in quadrant II of the cost-effectiveness plane, representing lower costs with higher effectiveness. The combination of captopril, amlodipine, and metformin was identified as the most cost-effective therapy for hospitalized patients with hypertension and diabetes mellitus complications at Berkah Pandeglang Regional Hospital.

title: A Single-Number Value Metric Integrating Quality and Cost in Outpatient Physical Therapy
The fiscal cost of 24-hour clinical coverage: Commuted overtime v. shift-based models in a South African regional hospital
abstract: Background. South Africa (SA)’s public health system relies on commuted overtime (COT) to provide 24-hour medical cover in hospitals. Persistent concerns about excessive working hours, fatigue and patient safety have renewed interest in shift-based staffing models. Local evidence on the workforce and fiscal implications of such a transition remains limited. Objectives. To determine the staffing complement required to deliver continuous 24-hour surgical coverage under a shift-based system, and to model the personnel cost implications across three staffing configurations compared with the current COT arrangement. Clinical outcomes and optimal staffing levels were not assessed. Methods. We conducted a retrospective cost analysis from a health-system perspective at a regional hospital in eThekwini District, KwaZulu-Natal Province, SA, using the Department of General Surgery as the case study. Three staffing models were compared: the current COT model; a hybrid model with medical officers (MOs) on 12-hour shifts and specialists retained on COT; and an expanded hybrid model with additional specialist posts. Annual personnel costs were calculated using 2024/25 occupation-specific dispensation salary notches under grade 1 and mixed-grade assumptions. Sensitivity analyses examined variations in specialist salaries, workload estimates and absence allowances. Results. The baseline complement comprised eight MOs and four specialists. Delivering continuous shift-based coverage required scaling the MO complement to 22, a 175% increase. On a base-salary-only comparison, annual costs rose from ZAR13.54 million (all grade 1) to ZAR27.56 million under hybrid model A (+103.7%) and to ZAR31.71 million under hybrid model B (+134.3%). When estimated COT payments are incorporated into the current model baseline – using group 3 parameters and a 1.3 × ordinary hourly rate multiplier applied to 16 contracted overtime hours per week – total estimated annual remuneration rises to ZAR20.58 million (all grade 1) and ZAR23.21 million (mixed grades). Under this COT-inclusive comparison, hybrid model A represents a cost increase of ~48% and hybrid model B ~79%. Shift-based models increase total personnel expenditure under both costing approaches; the COT-inclusive figures are the primary policy- relevant comparator. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness across all scenarios tested. Conclusion. Replacing COT with a 12-hour shift system requires a substantially greater number of MOs, and increases total personnel costs by 48 - 79% when estimated overtime is included in the baseline. Hybrid models reduce but do not eliminate this impact. Any transition should be phased, locally costed using verified payroll data and aligned with national workforce planning priorities.

title: Cost-effectiveness of multidisciplinary care compared with standard neurology care in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: A model-based cost-utility analysis
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of multidisciplinary clinic (MDC) care compared with standard general neurology care for adults with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). METHODS: A cost-utility analysis was conducted using a state-transition Markov model with monthly cycles over a 10-year horizon from the U.S. payer perspective. Health states comprised King's stages 1, 2, 3, 4 A, 4B, and death. Disease progression, mortality, utility, and cost inputs were derived from published literature (2005-2026). Transition probabilities were based on longitudinal data from the Pooled Resource Open-Access ALS Clinical Trials and permitted non-sequential progression. MDC-associated survival benefit was applied to stage-specific mortality across all King's stages. No additional utility benefit was assigned to MDC, while MDC-specific multipliers were applied to outpatient, inpatient, and emergency department costs. Outcomes included quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), costs, cost per life-year gained, and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs). Uncertainty intervals (UIs) were derived from sensitivity analyses. RESULTS: MDC increased costs ($523,170 vs $378,171) and QALYs (0.73 vs 0.60), yielding 0.13 incremental QALYs (95% UI, 0.06-0.20) at an incremental cost of US$144,999 (95% UI, $53,784-$257,504). The ICER was US$1,158,673/QALY and cost per life-year gained was US$149,483. MDC was cost-effective in 0.1% of simulations at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $150,000/QALY. CONCLUSION: MDC improved survival and quality-adjusted survival but at substantially higher cost. Its ICER remained well above commonly used U.S. willingness-to-pay thresholds across sensitivity analyses, including alternative utility valuations. These findings highlight the distinction between clinical benefit and cost-effectiveness and quantify the long-term economic consequences of survival gains associated with multidisciplinary ALS care.

title: Cost estimate for the procurement and preparation of donated corneas for transplantation in an eye bank
abstract: Abstract Corneal diseases are among the leading causes of blindness, and transplantation may be the only treatment option. Studies providing a comprehensive economic analysis of the corneal tissue processing chain, from procurement to release for transplantation by eye banks, are scarce. This study aimed to estimate the cost of preparing donated corneal tissue for transplantation at an Eye Bank. We performed a cost analysis using the Time-Driven Activity-Based Costing (TDABC) method based on data from the stages of corneal tissue preparation. The study population consisted of data from corneal donors collected in 2023. The median cost per donor was estimated at USD 454.65. Supplies (43%), human resources (32%), and operational costs (23%) were the costliest components. Multiple regression analysis identified predictors influencing costs. This study highlighted critical stages in the process and resource consumption. Investing in domestic pharmaceutical production, improving interinstitutional communication, training healthcare professionals, and providing logistical support may reduce costs and contribute to the management and sustainability of Eye Banks.

title: Physical activity and cost of care among adults with diabetes and musculoskeletal disorders in Kaduna State Nigeria
abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are common among adults with diabetes, yet their economic impact in low-resource settings is poorly characterised. This study assessed MSD distribution, examined associations between physical activity and cost of care, and identified factors associated with healthcare expenses among diabetic adults in Kaduna State, Nigeria. A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 409 adults with clinically diagnosed diabetes mellitus and physician-diagnosed MSD at a single tertiary referral centre. Data were collected using structured questionnaires including the International Physical Activity Questionnaire Short Form (IPAQ-SF). Physical activity was measured in MET-minutes/week using the official IPAQ-SF scoring algorithm. The cost of care comprised direct costs (consultation, medication, laboratory tests, imaging, physiotherapy, hospitalisation, transport) and indirect costs (productivity losses from absenteeism and presenteeism), valued using the human-capital approach over the previous three months. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, t-tests with Cohen’s d effect sizes, Spearman correlation with Bonferroni correction (α = 0.0018 for 28 pairwise correlations), and generalised linear models (GLMs) with gamma distribution and log link. Among 409 participants (mean age 59.0 ± 5.9 years; 63.1% female), knee disorders (57.9%) and foot disorders (25.9%) predominated. Participants had a median (IQR) total physical activity of 693 (198–1680) MET-min/week; 68.2% were classified as low, 22.7% moderate, and 9.0% high. The median total cost of care was ₦18,500 (IQR ₦7,200–42,300). Thirty-seven participants (9.0%) reported zero cost. Higher physical activity was associated with lower total cost of care (β = −0.048; 4.7% lower total cost; p = 0.011) and lower direct cost (5.6% lower; p = 0.018). Self-employment was associated with 38% higher indirect costs ( p = 0.004). Effect sizes for low versus high physical activity were Cohen’s d = 0.42 and 0.41, both p < 0.001. Adjustment for education, occupation, diabetes duration, and complications left the physical activity coefficient essentially unchanged (0.048 vs. 0.044–0.046). Higher physical activity was associated with lower cost of care among adults with diabetes and MSDs. The cross-sectional design, same-interview self-report, and selection through clinic attendance preclude causal inference; the findings are presented as hypotheses for longitudinal research.

title: Federal and state cost share compared to private health insurance: a 2022 nationwide analysis of outcomes in patients with acute-on-chronic heart failure

Analysis of the average hospitalization cost for multiple sclerosis in Brazil between 2015 and 2025
Data-Driven Healthcare Management: Predictive Analytics to Improve Access, Quality, and Cost Efficiency
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: ABSTRACT The United States healthcare system is still stuck with a trilemma of access, quality and cost. In 2024, total national healthcare spending was more than $4.9 trillion (17.6% of GDP), but an estimated 25 million Americans are uninsured, Medicare alone spends about $30 billion on avoidable hospitalizations, and there is a wide variation in quality outcomes across the country. In 2020-25, U.S. health systems have accelerated the use of predictive analytics, big data infrastructure, and AI/ML clinical decision support as the operational stack for a data-driven approach to the trilemma. This study conducts an empirical analysis of an integrated model that posits that three technology-capability constructs, along with data governance and staff/organizational capacity, influence two performance outcomes: healthcare access and quality and cost efficiency and utilization. Between February and September 2025, N = 400 healthcare managers and executives from across the United States in eight organization types (academic medical centers, integrated delivery networks, community and specialty hospitals, ambulatory groups, federally qualified health centers, long-term-care facilities, and health-insurance payers) completed cross-sectional survey data. OLS structural-model estimation, moderation and Sobel-tested mediation were employed to test six hypotheses. Measurement-model reliability was strong (Cronbach's α range 0.86–0.91; CR range 0.80–0.88; AVE range 0.50–0.59) and structural-model fit was good (χ²/df = 1.40; CFI = 0.961; TLI = 0.957; RMSEA = 0.033 [0.026, 0.039]; SRMR = 0.041). AI/ML clinical decision support dominates the access-and-quality outcome (β = 0.375, p < .001); big data infrastructure dominates the cost-efficiency outcome (β = 0.364, p < .001); and predictive analytics capability has strong direct effects on both outcomes (β = 0.194, 0.178, p < .001); staff and organizational capacity partially mediates the analytics-to-quality path (Sobel z = 6.65, p < .001; mediation ratio ≈ 35%). Moderation by data-governance of the relationship between analytics and quality was not supported (β_int = 0.002, p = .965). Five of six hypotheses are supported. The final models account for 52.8% and 47.8% of the variance in the two outcomes. Illustrative extrapolation of within-sample association suggests that patient-access target achievement increased from 61% (low-analytics quartile) to 84% (high-analytics quartile), and avoidable-cost reduction increased from 3% to 24%. Implications for the order of investment in health-management and for federal Value-Based Care policy are applied.

title: Hospital Costs of Primary and Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty in Public Health Services in the State of São Paulo: A Multicenter Study
abstract: Objective: To analyze and compare the direct hospital costs of primary and revision total knee arthroplasty (TKA) performed in public hospitals in the state of São Paulo, and to evaluate the economic impact of complicated cases requiring revision surgery. Methods: This multicenter, retrospective observational study included patients who underwent primary TKA between 2008 and 2018 in four tertiary public hospitals. Cost data were obtained from institutional financial records and included hospital stay, surgical materials and implants, medications, and operating room charges. Costs were calculated for uncomplicated primary TKA, revision TKA, and the cumulative cost of complicated cases requiring both procedures. Results: A total of 433 patients (534 procedures) were analyzed. The mean hospital cost of an uncomplicated primary TKA was R$12,402.89, with materials accounting for the largest proportion of expenses (42.2%), followed by operating room charges (27.7%) and hospital stay (26.9%). The mean cost of revision TKA was R$23,655.51, nearly twice that of the primary procedure. In revision surgeries, hospital stay became the main cost driver, representing 42.7% of total expenses. The cumulative cost of a complicated case reached R$36,058.40, corresponding to a 191% increase compared with an uncomplicated primary TKA. Conclusion: Revision total knee arthroplasty imposes a substantial economic burden on the public health system, with costs nearly tripling when complications occur. These findings highlight the importance of strategies focused on preventing prosthetic failure (particularly periprosthetic infection) and optimizing perioperative care to improve sustainability and resource allocation in public hospitals.

title: Cost-effectiveness of differentiated HIV service delivery in North Wollo, Ethiopia: a retrospective study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Differentiated service delivery (DSD) models have been introduced to optimise HIV care by tailoring services to patient needs, but evidence on their cost-effectiveness in Ethiopia is limited. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of DSD models for HIV care compared with standard of care (SOC) in North Wollo, Ethiopia. STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective economic evaluation using bottom-up microcosting from a healthcare provider perspective. SETTING: One hospital and three health centres in North Wollo Zone, Ethiopia, from January 2024 to December 2024. PARTICIPANTS: 786 adults (≥18 years) on antiretroviral therapy, including 393 receiving DSD (across nine models: 6-month multimonth dispensing, 3-month multimonth dispensing, appointment spacing, community antiretroviral therapy (ART) groups (CAG), FastTrack, maternal and child health, peer-led, adolescent groups and key population models) and 393 receiving SOC. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Total annual cost per patient (USD), retention in care at 12 months (%) and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) expressed as cost per additional patient retained. STATISTICAL ANALYSIS: Costs were annualised at a 3% discount rate. ICERs were calculated comparing each DSD model to SOC. Deterministic one-way sensitivity analysis (±20% for medication cost and retention rate) assessed robustness. RESULTS: SOC had the highest annual cost per patient (US$295) and lowest retention (76.6%). All DSD models were dominant (lower cost, higher retention) with negative ICERs. CAG was the most cost-effective (US$199 per patient; 93.0% retention; ICER -5.85), followed by FastTrack (US$212; 92.9%; -5.09) and adolescent groups (US$238; 90.5%; -4.10). Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness; no scenario reversed dominance. CONCLUSION: DSD models, particularly CAG, FastTrack and adolescent groups, provide more cost-effective HIV care than SOC in Ethiopia by achieving higher retention at lower costs. Scaling up these models could optimise resource allocation and reduce health system burden.

title: Working with the Private Sector to Deliver a New Low-Cost Healthcare Card for Somali Bajaj Drivers and Their Families
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: DT Global International Development East Africa Limited
DT Global International Development East Africa Limited
abstract: Introduction and Objectives Private Sector Partnerships in Health (PSPH) is a Market Systems Development (MSD) programme funded by the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC). It aims to improve access to quality and affordable healthcare in Somalia and Somaliland by working with private healthcare providers, which deliver an estimated 60–80% of healthcare services in the region. PSPH provides temporary facilitation and technical assistance to help market actors develop sustainable and scalable healthcare business models. Bajaj drivers and their households generally have low and unpredictable incomes and struggle to afford healthcare. Meanwhile, private hospitals face difficulties attracting patients who cannot pay standard prices. Since 2024, PSPH has facilitated the testing of Bajaj Kaabe, a low-cost healthcare access card designed to address both constraints. The presentation demonstrates how private-sector partnership can generate sustainable and potentially systemic results in a fragile context. Methodology The findings are based on baseline and routinely collected operational and performance data from partner hospitals, card registration and utilization records, partner reports, market observations, and feedback from Bajaj drivers and their households. Data is tracked over time to inform adaptation, decision-making, and reporting and are protected through agreed data-sharing arrangements. PSPH supported Al Caasima Hospital in Mogadishu to design and test the product, determine appropriate costing, establish hospital and driver relationships, and develop outreach mechanisms. PSPH does not finance or deliver healthcare, sell the card, or manage the continuing transaction. Drivers pay USD 3 for household access; the drivers’ union mobilizes members and promotes uptake, and Al Caasima owns and operates the product, sets prices, delivers care, and manages quality and day-to-day operations of its hospital. Results and Discussion More than 6,200 drivers have registered for the Bajaj Kaabe Card, and approximately 77% around 4,800 have used the card. Women account for 67% of users, showing that the benefits extend to drivers’ wives, daughters, and other household members. Cardholders access consultations, diagnostics, medicines, and maternal and child healthcare services at substantially reduced prices. Uptake increased after the drivers’ union began actively promoting the card, demonstrating growing ownership by a trusted market actor. The model has also generated evidence of crowding-in. Siraj Hospital in Somaliland has adapted the Bajaj Kaabe model beyond the original Al Caasima partnership. In Mogadishu, Tiirow Hospital is offering a 50% discount model, while Himilo Eye Hospital has introduced a one-dollar prepayment card. Where their adoption can be linked to Bajaj Kaabe, these developments provide further evidence that private providers recognize the commercial and social value of affordable healthcare products for low-income households. Conclusion Bajaj Kaabe demonstrates that PSPH’s success lies not in directly delivering healthcare, but in enabling permanent market actors to own, finance, deliver, and adapt a viable solution. Driver financing, union-led mobilization, hospital ownership, reduced dependency on PSPH, and adaptation by Siraj Hospital indicate emerging sustainability and systemic change. Continued monitoring should assess whether these models remain operational, expand independently, and stimulate further replication across Somalia and Somaliland.

title: Long-term cost-effectiveness of CKD screening in middle-aged adults
abstract: BACKGROUND AND HYPOTHESIS: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is common in Finland and frequently remains undiagnosed until advanced stages. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) slow CKD progression and reduce cardio-renal events when used in addition to Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System inhibitor (RAASi) treatment. We hypothesized that a one-time CKD screening program using measurements of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), followed by SGLT2i and RAASi treatment for identified CKD, would be cost-effective in Finland. METHODS: We developed a cohort-based Markov model to simulate lifetime CKD progression in a Finnish cohort aged 55 years under two strategies: (1) current practice (no screening) and (2) one-time screening with follow-up and SGLT2i and RAASi treatment for screen-positive CKD (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² and/or UACR ≥3 mg/mmol; confirmed on a repeat sample after ≥ 3 months to establish chronicity). All CKD stages (G1-G5, dialysis, transplant, and death) were included in the model, and screening could detect CKD at any stage, although the incremental detection was concentrated in earlier, previously undiagnosed stages (G1-G3). Outcomes included discounted costs, quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), life years, and clinical outcomes (acute kidney function decline, heart-failure hospital days, dialysis and transplant patient-years, and deaths). Results are reported as means with 95% confidence intervals (CI). RESULTS: Screening increased discounted lifetime costs per person by €907 (95% CI €334-2 553) and QALYs by 0.14 (95% CI 0.07-0.31), yielding an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of €6 478/QALY. Screening increased life years by 0.30. Screening reduced acute kidney function decline (0.88 vs 0.90 events/person), heart-failure hospital days (6.47 vs 6.69 days/person), dialysis exposure (0.29 vs 0.32 patient-years/person) and transplant exposure (0.13 vs 0.14 patient-years/person). CONCLUSIONS: In Finns aged 55 years, one-time CKD screening with eGFR/UACR followed by SGLT2i and RAASi treatment improves long-term outcomes and is likely cost-effective.

title: Educational effectiveness of scenario-based tabletop exercises for disaster preparedness among resident physicians in China
abstract: To evaluate the effects of implementing realistic, scenario-based disaster tabletop exercises(TTX) as a training strategy on a range of outcomes among resident physicians in China. In May 2025, a nationwide, single-group pre–post intervention study was conducted, 151 resident physicians were recruited through convenience and stratified sampling from nine tertiary A(Grade III, Class A) general hospitals located across eight provinces, encompassing the southern, eastern, northern, western, and central regions of China. A disaster-management–focused TTX was implemented. Participants’ perceived disaster management capability, self-confidence, satisfaction with learning, and critical thinking were evaluated both a week before and immediately following the exercise. In addition, instructors independently completed a surge-capacity assessment checklist during the training. Of 151 participants, 133(88.1%) completed both assessments. Previous disaster training and disaster response experience were reported by 7.52% and 0.75% of participants, respectively. Mean perceived disaster management capability increased from 51.06 ± 20.92 to 81.56 ± 11.98(Z = − 9.945, P < 0.001; r = 0.86). Perceived capability, self-confidence, satisfaction, and critical thinking all improved significantly(all P < 0.001). Self-confidence in learning(B = 9.385, β = 0.315, P = 0.003) and critical thinking(B = 4.142, β = 0.303, P = 0.001) were independently and positively associated with post-test perceived capability. Instructors rated a higher overall proportion of fully implemented items during the in-hospital than the prehospital phase(57.9% vs. 36.7%, P = 0.031). Among first-level dimensions, resource requirements remained significantly different after Holm adjustment(adjusted P = 0.047), whereas no second-level dimension remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Resident physicians had limited prior disaster training and response experience. Participation in a realistic, scenario-based TTX was associated with improvements in perceived disaster management capability, self-confidence, satisfaction, and critical thinking. The findings also highlight the need for greater emphasis on prehospital emergency response during disaster preparedness training.

title: Leveraging AI- Driven Predictive Analytics for Early Detection and Risk Assessment in Hospital Disaster Preparedness
journal: International Journal of Energy Research Science and Engineering
abstract: Disaster management in the hospital has become a critical issue especially with the coming of COVID-19 pandemics which caused several losses of lives. Thus, the study presented a conceptual approach to understand how disasters could result into emergencies in the hospital and what measure could be adopted to stop the future occurrence of this menace. Several literatures were consulted and findings revealed that hospital disaster management is inevitable, however, developing measures to avert its occurrence is more important than its occurrence. Therefore, leveraging artificial intelligence driven tools like predictive analytics has the potentials of developing an evacuation concept that will serve as a support system for hospitals or group of hospitals. More so, the approach requires a multidisciplinary team involving the collaboration of several fields. Thus, the study provides a great insight into the improvement of the field to determine its effectiveness and efficiency. .

title: Analysis of Clinical Preparedness in Facing Disasters: A Descriptive Study of 17 Clinics in Makassar City
abstract: Background: Clinics are essential primary healthcare facilities for maintaining lifesaving and routine services during disasters. Preparedness assessment is necessary to identify the capacity and gaps of each facility. Objective: This study analyzed and compared disaster preparedness across 17 clinics. Methods: A quantitative descriptive observational study with a multisite cross-sectional design was conducted in May 2026. Data were obtained through direct observation, interviews, document review, and facility documentation. The instrument included 30 indicators across six domains: policy and management, human resources, infrastructure, logistics, communication, and services. Each indicator was scored from 0 to 2, yielding a maximum score of 60. Results: Mean preparedness was 83.43%, with a median of 88.33%, a standard deviation of 12.42%, and a range of 56.67% to 100%. Thirteen clinics (76.47%) were categorized as highly prepared and four (23.53%) as moderately prepared. Major gaps concerned emergency alarms, evacuation maps, drills, disaster-response teams, emergency procedures, triage, emergency areas, backup power, referral coordination, and mass-casualty management. Conclusion: Most clinics demonstrated high preparedness; however, operational readiness requires stronger infrastructure, standardized procedures, recurring training, and simulation exercises. Addressing these gaps may contribute to SDG 3 by supporting continuity of essential health services, SDG 11 by strengthening urban disaster resilience, and SDG 13 by improving institutional adaptive capacity for disaster-risk management.

title: Disaster preparedness and service continuity in primary healthcare centers: a systematic review and structured contextual evidence synthesis
abstract: Background Primary healthcare centers (PHCs) are a key health-system contact for disaster-affected populations, yet direct PHC evidence remains thin and is frequently conflated with hospital, workforce, policy, and secondary-review literature. Objective To identify factors, barriers, facilitators, capacities, and operational gaps shaping PHC disaster preparedness; contrast component profiles against a structured contextual synthesis; characterize what is operationally distinctive about PHCs; and propose a PHC-derived layered model. Methods A systematic review, supplemented by a structured contextual evidence synthesis, was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement and Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) principles. The primary Scopus search plus preserved supplementary retrieval from PubMed, ProQuest, and OpenAlex, followed by a pre-submission full-text update, duplicate reconciliation, and independent confirmation by two reviewers, yielded 74 unique publications: 15 primary empirical PHC studies and 59 contextual publications. Evidence was mapped descriptively to the 10 World Health Organization Health Emergency and Disaster Risk Management (Health EDRM) components; all 15 primary PHC studies were independently appraised by two reviewers using design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) tools or the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) 2018. Results All 10 Health EDRM components were assessed across the 15 primary PHC studies. The most frequently identified were human resources (14/15, 93.3%), planning and coordination (13/15, 86.7%), information and knowledge management (11/15, 73.3%), followed by health infrastructure and logistics and monitoring and evaluation (each 10/15, 66.7%). Distinctive PHC characteristics included small generalist teams, staff and family-readiness barriers, executable plans, referral dependence, continuity of basic utilities and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services, limited local stocks, community outreach, and regular facility-level monitoring. Conclusion PHC preparedness emerges as an interdependent capacity, with several distinctive PHC characteristics arising from specific Health EDRM components. Community capacities for Health EDRM were reported in only 40% of primary PHC studies, highlighting an under-reported area warranting further exploration. A layered model is proposed for center-level assessment and future instrument development, organizing system support, core preparedness capacity, service and community response, and cross-cutting information, communication, and monitoring as interacting domains linked to continuity of essential services. Systematic review registration Open Science Framework, https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/H8JU7 , Identifier: 10.17605/OSF.IO/H8JU7 .

title: From Campus to Crisis Shelter: A Reflective Case Analysis of Shelter-Based Healthcare and Enacted Disaster Preparedness during the 2025 Hat Yai Flood
journal: Journal of Health Science and Medical Research
abstract: Disaster preparedness is commonly framed around advance planning and formal protocols, yet major emergencies often require institutions to adapt under rapidly changing conditions. This reflective case analysis examines the transformation of Prince of Songkla University Hat Yai Campus into an evacuation shelter during the 2025 Hat Yai flood, when widespread disruption left Songklanagarind Hospital as the principal functioning major hospital in the city. Established through situational necessity rather than prior designation, the shelter expanded rapidly from approximately 2,000 evacuees to a peak occupancy of approximately 7,000 and operated through flexible multidisciplinary staffing, public donations, volunteer mobilization, and cross-sector collaboration. Shelter-based healthcare functioned as an extension of the disrupted health system, integrating triage, medication continuity, referral, transport, and differentiated care for acute, chronic, high-dependency, and psychosocial needs. Social cohesion and adaptive governance enabled resources and personnel to be mobilized despite the absence of predefined shelter governance, while frontline experience generated practical knowledge subsequently translated through an After-Action Review. Viewed through the World Health Organization (WHO) Health Emergency and Disaster Risk Management framework, the experience illustrates preparedness as an enacted capacity spanning preparedness, response, and recovery. The case highlights the potential role of hospitals, universities, and community institutions as complementary operational nodes during health-system disruption and underscores the value of combining formal preparedness with flexible governance, cross-sector coordination, and institutional learning.

title: Disaster preparedness and mental health: understanding psychological responses and support-system demands
abstract: Abstract Purpose: Disasters pose a formidable challenge for mental health support services in terms of resources and timely response. This study evaluates the effects of different types of events on Mexico City population during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, under the assumption that high-resolution time-scale data analysis performed onICT-based and telehealth systems can contribute to understand psychological needs, and toidentifying events with the potential to trigger outburst in support demands, estimate their time of occurrence and the characteristics of calls for service. Methods: The study evaluated the effects of public announcements of quarantine measures, mental health press conferences, festivities during 2020, and earthquakes with public early warnings between 2020 and 2023 reported through national public institutions databases, the “Screening tool for mental health problems” and the “lifeline service”, comprising 138,471 interactions. The analysis uses qualitative and quantitative methods, including principal component analysis, correlations, and one-way ANOVA. Results: The study successfully identified patterns in responses associated with acute stress, depression, and anxiety, as well as possible times of maximum demand associated with different types of events. Complex scenarios with multiple threats pose a high risk to support systems, producing short-term but significant outbursts in demand, with increases as high as 2,651% on a single day. Novelty: The research is novel in its time scope analysis and event-wise approach, providing valuable insights for emergency planning and resource allocation. Additionally, the study proposes evaluation criteria for detecting potential system overloads in telehealth services to enable early countermeasures.

title: A narrative review of CBRN health sector preparedness in Lebanon
abstract: BACKGROUND: As chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) events become increasingly recognised within international and national emergency preparedness efforts, this study aims to provide the first system-level overview of Lebanon's preparedness capacities for CBRN-related health emergencies. METHODS: A narrative review of peer-reviewed and grey literature was conducted using a structured search strategy, with findings thematically synthesised to assess governance and operational CBRN preparedness capacities across eight health system domains in Lebanon. RESULTS: The review identified important advances in Lebanon's preparedness for CBRN health emergencies, including engagement with international preparedness frameworks, development of governance structures, and implementation of coordination, training, and simulation initiatives. However, preparedness remains uneven and constrained by fragmented coordination, legislative gaps, limited surveillance and operational integration, shortages in material and human resources, and dependence on external support. Economic instability and workforce migration further challenge sustainability, while preparedness capacities and readiness levels vary across emergency response and healthcare institutions. Overall, strategic planning and governance capacities appeared stronger than operational response and surveillance functions. CONCLUSION: While major efforts towards CBRN preparedness in Lebanon have been initiated, key aspects remain under-developed. Given Lebanon's continued exposure to recurrent crises and regional instability, strengthening CBRN preparedness should be considered a critical component of broader health system resilience and national disaster risk reduction efforts.

title: THE EFFECTIVENESS OF DISASTER PLANNING MANAGEMENT TRAINING PROGRAM ON NURSE MANAGERS’ PREPAREDNESS, RESPONSE, AND RECOVERY IN MAKKAH CITY, QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL STUDY
abstract: Background: Nurse managers act as the essential link between hospital administration and healthcare providers during disasters, making their preparedness critical to effective crisis response. A structured disaster management training program strengthens this preparedness and supports a more efficient recovery process once a disaster has occurred. Aim: To evaluate the effectiveness of a disaster planning and management training program on nurse managers' preparedness, response, and recovery in Makkah City. Method: A quasi-experimental research design was used, which comprised an intervention group, a control group, and follow-up. The research collected data in three governmental hospitals of Makkah City among 60 nurse managers through the application of two instruments of data collection, namely: the Knowledge Disaster Management Questionnaire and the Disaster Preparation Evaluation Tool. Results: There were statistically significant improvements in the levels of knowledge and disaster preparedness evaluation between the intervention group and the control group at post-test and follow-up after 3 months, while there was no statistical significance between the two groups at pre-intervention. In addition, there was a significant positive correlation between total knowledge and total disaster preparedness evaluation among nurse managers in the intervention group, whereas there was no significant correlation in the intervention group pre-phase and in the control group at all three phases. Conclusion: The training program was effective for improving nurse managers' knowledge of disaster planning and management and disaster preparedness evaluation. Recommendations: Conducting structured and recurring disaster planning management training programs as an integral component of the professional development of nurse managers and considering disaster management training as a must-have element in the hospital policies and strategic workforce development plan for all nurse managers irrespective of their department.

title: Are emergency health systems prepared for rising temperatures?: A mixed methods analysis assessing heatwave vulnerability of four Victorian Metropolitan (Australia) Emergency departments
journal: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
abstract: 1. Abstract Background Temperatures are rising due to anthropogenic climate change, increasing the frequency, duration and magnitude of extreme heat events. Heatwaves remain the deadliest hazards in Australia, with Victoria experiencing a disproportionate number of heat-related deaths. Despite heat plans implemented following the 2009 Black Saturday bushfires, statewide health risk assessments for heatwaves are yet to be developed. Current research focuses on quantitative assessments of mortality and emergency presentations, with no systematic analysis of health system vulnerability. Aims To assess emergency department vulnerability using a modified World Health Organization (WHO) tool and qualitative analysis, identify gaps in hospital preparedness, and inform heat-related health systems policy and resilience strengthening. Method A convergent, parallel mixed-methods approach investigated vulnerability across four metropolitan hospitals, comprising a 72-question checklist covering five domains delivered to emergency management teams, and 21 key-stakeholder interviews with emergency department staff ranging from clinicians to emergency managers. Results Vulnerabilities exist across most categories, with the largest proportion affecting water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), healthcare waste facilities, and patient and workforce capacity. Interviewees identified measures to enhance resilience, including increasing public awareness, improving emergency preparedness protocols, cooling infrastructure, training and surge capacity. Conclusion While emergency departments are equipped to handle sudden mass casualty events, slow-onset disasters like heatwaves present unique challenges that current plans do not adequately address. Victorian health systems are vulnerable to heatwaves and require systematic coordinated responses, robust policy and effective surge capability to manage future extreme temperature events.

title: A mixed method study on simulation based experiential learning through Bhopal Gas Tragedy for disaster risk reduction among health science students
abstract: Abstract The 1984 Bhopal Gas Tragedy remains one of the deadliest industrial disasters in human history, killing thousands instantly and exposing over half a million people to the toxic methyl isocyanate gas. Despite its profound lessons for emergency response, inter-agency coordination, and public health preparedness, a few educational interventions have leveraged this catastrophe as a teaching case for health professionals. We designed, implemented, and evaluated a comprehensive simulation-based educational intervention that recreates key aspects of the Bhopal disaster to prepare the students for disaster risk preparedness in complex emergency scenarios requiring multi-sectoral coordination. We engaged 59 students from two institutions in a five-station simulation exercise. Twenty-two Master of Public Health students served as facilitators following intensive training, while 37 undergraduate Allied Health Sciences students participated as learners. The simulation included personification exercises, role-play scenarios, pre-hospital emergency care, hospital surge management, and multi-sectoral policy response stations. We measured learning outcomes using 15-item pre-post assessments and gathered qualitative feedback through open-ended questions. There was a significant improvement ( p < 0.001) in the competencies measured. The overall mean score for different learning aspects increased from 44.8 at baseline to 61.6 (a 37.4% gain) after the intervention. Qualitative analysis revealed four major themes: nearly all participants (96.6%) valued the experiential learning approach, while most recognized gains in systems thinking (93.2%), empathy (89.8%), and critical problem-solving (81.4%) skills. Both facilitators and participants rated the experience highly satisfying (mean scores 4.4–4.8 on 5-point scales). The study demonstrates that well-planned, historically grounded simulation exercises can powerfully enhance disaster preparedness education among health science students.

title: Transforming pandemic influenza antiviral stockpiling using a capacity-based approach: A modeling study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Pandemic influenza preparedness in high-resource nations has traditionally relied on large antiviral stockpiles, typically targeting coverage for 25% of the population. This inventory-based benchmark focuses on cumulative disease burden but often overlooks the inelastic capacity of healthcare systems to manage acute surges. As multi-billion-dollar inventories reach expiration, we evaluated whether static stockpiles remain a viable strategy for preventing healthcare system collapse during future pandemics. METHODS AND FINDINGS: We projected daily hospital bed demand using three complementary frameworks: a static lower-bound estimation, a dynamic deterministic Susceptible-Infectious-Hospitalized-Recovered transmission model, and historical reconstructions of the 1918, 1957, and 1968 pandemics using mortality data. We evaluated official planning scenarios for the United Kingdom, Japan, and the United States, comparing projected demand against national surge capacities (i.e., staffed beds). To test the theoretical limits of the stockpile strategy, we applied best-case assumptions, including perfect distribution of antivirals to 100% of symptomatic cases and high clinical effectiveness (30% to 60% reduction in hospitalization). Our models identified a critical feasibility gap. While stockpiles successfully suppressed demand to manageable levels in moderate scenarios (analogous to 1957/1968), they were structurally insufficient for severe events. In high-severity scenarios (analogous to 1918 or CDC Very Severe parameters), the daily surge of patients exceeded available hospital capacity by a factor of 5-9. This inundation occurred even under the assumption of 100% treatment coverage, rendering antivirals incapable of preventing transition to crisis standards of care. Although this analysis is subject to the inherent uncertainties of future pandemics, our use of optimistic best-case assumptions suggests that the identified structural failures are a lower-bound estimate. Realistic operational hurdles would only widen the disparity between stockpile targets and system capacity. The main limitations of this study's methodology are its inherent optimistic bias, specifically the use of a conservative 4-day hospital length of stay that underestimates prolonged intensive care needs, the reliance on general hospital beds as a proxy that abstracts away from critical sub-system bottlenecks, and the assumption of guaranteed antiviral efficacy against novel strains. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that large reserves cannot overcome the rigid physical constraints of healthcare systems, even under the optimistic assumption of perfect distribution. Consequently, the conventional 25% coverage target for antiviral stockpiles, a hallmark of legacy planning, presents a critical opportunity for re-evaluation. As global stocks near expiration, policymakers are uniquely positioned to leverage this inflection point by exploring a capacity-based framework. This adaptive paradigm suggests incorporating a synergistic mix of targeted reserves, temporary non-pharmaceutical interventions, and flexible delivery options, such as decentralized home-first care. Together, these integrated measures could serve as a vital temporal bridge, preserving system integrity until vaccine deployment.

title: Magnitude and duration of emergency department shock following the Ukrainian refugee surge in Poland
abstract: Abstract Background Large-scale forced migration can create sudden pressure on emergency departments (EDs), yet the magnitude and duration of these shocks are rarely quantified. Following the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, Poland hosted millions of Ukrainian refugees, with 1 million settling temporarily. Evidence is limited on the duration of refugee-related acute care demand and its return to baseline. This study quantified the size and duration of the refugee-related ED surge in a major Polish city, a key transit-reception hub in Poland. Methods We conducted a retrospective time-series study using ED visit data from a large hospital in Kraków, Poland. Bayesian Structural Time Series analysis estimated the effect of the Russian invasion on ED visits by Ukrainian nationals. The pre-period was March 9, 2020–February 20, 2022, and the post-period was February 21, 2022–December 31, 2023. The control series included ED visits by patients of other nationalities. ED visits excluded suspected COVID-19 (modeled separately as a covariate). Results During the full post-invasion period, mean weekly Ukrainian ED visits were 11.4 vs. 5.0 predicted, corresponding to a 131% relative increase and 619 excess visits (95% CI 500–743). During the acute crisis phase (February–October 2022), mean weekly visits were 24.1 vs. 6.1 predicted, corresponding to a 308% increase and 595 excess visits (95% CI 525–652). ED demand peaked at ∼40 excess visits/week. Utilization returned to the modeled baseline on October 9, 2022, indicating a 7.5-month acute ED shock. Conclusions Ukrainian refugee-related ED demand rose substantially, but excess use was time-limited, concentrated in the first 7.5 months after displacement. Findings support rapid ED surge planning during humanitarian crises, including temporary staffing, interpreters, and flexible bed capacity. Real-time monitoring of nationality-linked utilization may strengthen preparedness and resource allocation during future migration emergencies. Key messages • Ukrainian refugee ED visits surged sharply after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, increasing by over 300% during the acute phase. • The surge was temporary and returned to baseline after 7.5 months, highlighting the need for rapid, flexible ED capacity and real-time monitoring during migration crises.

title: “Existing Disaster Preparedness and Effectiveness of a Disaster Training Module on Knowledge, Perceived Readiness, and Competence Among Nursing Personnel in Primary and Community Health Centres: A Pilot Quasi-Experimental Study”
abstract: Background Primary and Community Health Centres (PHCs and CHCs) form the foundational layer of public-health delivery and frequently serve as frontline response points during disasters. Nursing personnel represent the core workforce responsible for triage, emergency stabilization, and community support. However, structured disaster management training remains limited in primary care settings. Objective To evaluate the feasibility of study procedures and assess the preliminary effectiveness of a structured disaster training module on knowledge, perceived readiness, and competence among nursing personnel in selected health centres in Kollam district, Kerala. Methods A non-equivalent control-group pretest–posttest quasi-experimental design was adopted. Thirty nursing officers were recruited via convenience sampling from one selected taluk, with health-centre clusters allocated to either an Intervention group (n = 16) or a Control group (n = 15 valid participants after data screening). The Intervention group received a 90-minute structured training module ("All-hazard disaster casualty management: a preparedness module for primary care nurses") comprising theoretical foundations, clinical protocols, paper-based triage drills, and tabletop simulations. The Control group received routine facility orientation. Data were collected using a demographic sheet, a 25-item knowledge questionnaire, a 20-item readiness scale, and a 27-item competence scale, and were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics (independent t tests, Mann–Whitney U tests, and Chi-square tests). Results At baseline, participants exhibited moderate levels of knowledge, readiness, and competence. Following the intervention, the Intervention group demonstrated statistically significant and practically large immediate gains compared to the Control group across all three domains: knowledge gain (5.19$vs.0.71, t = -5.97, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 2.19), competence gain (16.13 vs. 0.71, Welch t = -7.69, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 2.66), and readiness gain (13.94 vs. 0.64, Welch t = -6.06, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 2.07). Demographic variables showed no significant associations with baseline or post-test outcomes in this small pilot sample. Conclusion The structured training module demonstrated high feasibility and significant immediate effectiveness in enhancing disaster-related knowledge, readiness, and competence among primary-care nurses, supporting progression to the full-scale main study.

title: Flood Disasters in Nepal (2000-2026): A rapid review of epidemiological trends, health impacts and health system preparedness and response
abstract: Background: Floods are among Nepal’s most frequent climate-sensitive disasters, causing recurrent mortality, displacement, infrastructure damage, and public health emergencies. The objective of this review was to synthesize evidence on the epidemiology, health impacts, health system preparedness and response associated with major floods in Nepal from 2000 to 2026. Methods: A rapid review of flood-related disasters (2000-2026) was conducted using Emergency Events Database EM-DAT, government and humanitarian reports and peer-reviewed literature. Results: Forty major flood disasters were identified, most triggered by intense monsoon rainfall and often accompanied by landslides. The August 2026 floods along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors were the deadliest event, causing 6,342 deaths and affecting over 84,000 people. Other major disasters included nationwide floods and landslides in 2020 (448 deaths), floods in 2003 (300 deaths), the Jure landslide and Sun Koshi disaster in 2014 (294 deaths), and floods in 2024 (268 deaths). The 2024 floods affected the largest population (2.59 million). Common health impacts included waterborne and respiratory diseases, malnutrition, psychosocial distress, and disruption of health services and infrastructure. Conclusions: Floods remain a major public health challenge in Nepal. Strengthening climate-resilient health systems, early warning, preparedness, emergency response, and disease surveillance is essential to reduce future risks and build national resilience.

title: A novel simulation-based early warning model for balancing imaging demand and reporting capacity in radiology departments
journal: The Annals of Clinical and Analytical Medicine

title: Orthopedic Patient Characteristics, Management Patterns, and Clinical Outcomes in a Disaster-Prone Region
journal: Antigen Jurnal Kesehatan Masyarakat dan Ilmu Gizi
abstract: Datu Beru Hospital serves a geographically challenging, disaster-prone region of Central Aceh, where evidence on orthopedic case characteristics and referral practices remains limited. This study aimed to describe orthopedic patient characteristics, injury patterns, management indicators, and referral-based disposition between 2023 and 2025. A retrospective descriptive study analyzed medical records of 766 orthopedic cases using total sampling. Variables included presentation year, sex, anatomical injury location, long-bone involvement, injury mechanism, open or closed classification, and referral status. Frequencies, percentages, and descriptive cross-tabulations were used. The highest number of cases occurred in 2024 (339; 44.3%), and 482 patients (62.9%) were male. Hand injuries were most common (206; 26.9%), followed by leg (119; 15.5%) and foot injuries (89; 11.6%). Tibia-fibula injuries predominated among cases with documented long-bone involvement (116; 31.6%). Road traffic accidents were the leading documented mechanism (394; 57.4%), while closed injuries accounted for 314 cases (76.0%) with available classification data. Overall, 576 patients (75.2%) were managed without interfacility referral, whereas 190 (24.8%) were referred. Referral proportions were highest for spinal (90.9%), wrist (85.7%), and hip injuries (67.9%). These findings highlight the hospital's role in local orthopedic care and identify anatomical presentations requiring more frequent referral. However, incomplete medical records and the use of referral status rather than direct recovery measures limit conclusions about clinical outcomes. The findings support stronger trauma triage, specialized assessment, referral coordination, and disaster-responsive orthopedic preparedness in Central Aceh. Improved documentation of injury severity, treatment interventions, complications, and functional recovery would strengthen future regional evaluations of orthopedic service effectiveness.

title: From Ebola response to adaptable preparedness beyond a single virus
abstract: The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has been an important setting for Ebola innovation, including ring vaccination with recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus-based Ebola vaccine and the integration of clinical research into emergency response. These advances strengthened preparedness for Zaire ebolavirus (EBOV), but the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak highlights a remaining limitation: many preparedness capabilities remain closely linked to individual pathogens. Unlike EBOV, Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) has no licensed vaccine specifically indicated for prevention, and current evidence is insufficient to establish clinically meaningful protection from Ervebo against BVD in humans. Operational constraints documented in the current response, including a temporary Ervebo stock-out, limited mobility for vaccination teams, absent vaccination microplans, shortages of personal protective equipment, and gaps in triage and isolation capacity in the Bas-Uélé province, further illustrate that biomedical tools alone cannot ensure effective outbreak control. We propose extending pathogen-specific preparedness through adaptable, platform-based outbreak infrastructure encompassing four linked domains: scientific readiness, research and regulatory readiness, operational readiness, and community readiness. Such platforms should enable rapid evidence generation while retaining pathogen-specific diagnostics, clinical management, vaccines, and epidemiological knowledge. Global preparedness should therefore support transition from uncertainty to evidence and equitable action before transmission outpaces response capacity.

title: Beyond the COVID-19 Surge: Divergent Postpandemic Trends in Hospitalizations for Anorexia Nervosa at Two Canadian Tertiary Pediatric Hospitals
abstract: PURPOSE: To assess annual number of pediatric hospitalizations with anorexia nervosa (AN) as the most responsible discharge diagnosis before and after the COVID-19 pandemic at two Canadian tertiary pediatric eating disorder programs: Alberta Children's Hospital (ACH; Calgary, Alberta) and the Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids; Toronto, Ontario). METHODS: We conducted a population-based analysis of annual hospitalizations for AN among those aged 7-18 years at ACH and SickKids from March 11, 2014, to March 10, 2025, using Discharge Abstract Database data. Annual discharge counts were analyzed by site using linear regression to compare pre- and post-COVID-19 trends, with outcomes and analyses defined a priori based on early pandemic evidence, before updated data were requested or analyzed. RESULTS: Over the study period, discharges totaled 334 at ACH and 1,101 at SickKids, with no significant differences in age or sex distributions before versus after pandemic onset at either site. At ACH, the best-fitting model showed a significant steep increase in hospitalizations following pandemic onset with no change in prepandemic or postpandemic trends, resulting in elevated discharge counts over time (p < .001). In contrast, SickKids data were best explained by differing prepandemic and postpandemic slopes, reflecting an initial pandemic-associated increase followed by a decline toward prepandemic levels. In the final year, discharge counts at ACH were more than three-fold higher than prepandemic levels, whereas counts at SickKids returned to baseline (p < .001). DISCUSSION: Postpandemic recovery in pediatric AN hospitalizations was not uniform, underscoring the need to consider regional system factors and institutional context when interpreting trends.

title: An elective, theory-informed four-week interprofessional disaster preparedness course using problem-based learning, repeated 3LC exercises and MRMI/MACSIM-informed simulation
abstract: Abstract Background Disasters, and public health emergencies, irrespective of their etiology, require health professionals who can work across clinical, prehospital, public health and organizational boundaries. Although disaster medicine has been advocated in medical and health professions education, curricula remain heterogeneous, variably assessed and often insufficiently interprofessional. Elective courses may offer a feasible route for motivated learners across professions while avoiding overload of already crowded compulsory curricula. Methods We developed a theory-informed elective curriculum using Kern’s six-step model, constructive alignment, problem-based learning, experiential learning, adult learning, interprofessional education, simulation-based education, deliberate practice, reflective practice, communities of practice and prospective evaluation frameworks. Selected disaster medicine education models, competency frameworks, tabletop literature, mass-casualty simulation principles and current postgraduate preparedness programs informed the design.
