Results The proposed course is a four-week intensive elective of approximately 80–100 learning hours for medical and paramedical students, open to other health and emergency-response-related learners. It includes online preparation, seminars, skills workshops, six repeated table-top exercises, structured debriefings, a final major incident simulation and an individual scholarly paper as the written examination. The curriculum is organized around ten previously published competency domains and uses aligned assessments of participation, teamwork, triage, communication, simulation performance, reflection and academic writing. Conclusions The elective model translates established disaster medicine education principles into a feasible, theory-informed and performance-oriented curriculum. Explicit integration of problem-based learning strengthens the role of tabletop exercises as authentic, collaborative and evolving disaster problems. The course may provide an undergraduate and early professional foundation for later postgraduate disaster medicine education and continuing professional development.

title: Research of Emergency Department Spatial Adaptability Measures to COVID-19 Surge: A Study on the Central City Area of Shanghai
abstract: Background : In order to ensure normal operation, the EDs in large-scale hospitals formed certain spatial adaptability measures to accommodate and protect patients and ED staff during the COVID-19 surge. Purpose and Aims : By analysing EDs spatial adaptability measures to the surge, the design strategies for EDs to response to further epidemic should be summarized. Method : Total of 14 EDs in Shanghai were selected as the research objects. By summarizing and analysis data from official websites and news reports, the EDs patient volume before and after surge, the patient spatial distribution and relative spatial adaptability measures were collected, in order to demonstrate the EDs spatial adaptation to the surge. Result : The ED patient volume during COVID-19 surge was far greater than the design capacity, and the observation patients has greater impact on ED overcrowding and spatial occupation. The ED hallway and main corridors were occupied more frequently. Spatial adaptability measures were taken which include existing space requisition, existing patient flows improvement, and the construction of the “Second ED”. Conclusion : The alternative holding area for ED observation patients should be built to avoid ED overcrowding, and the ED hallway and main corridors were the most occupied areas when surge happened. Also, the physical isolated space is necessary to avoid nosocomial infection.

title: Willingness to serve is high, but task expectations diverge in disasters
abstract: Abstract Background Personnel surge capacity is a binding constraint of health systems in situations that exceed routine operations. Students and trainees in the health professions are widely regarded as the obvious personnel reserve; however, they are neither systematically registered, nor qualified, nor integrated into alerting and command structures. The extensive literature on willingness to respond almost exclusively surveys the supply-side. Previous research has begun to examine student and organizational perspectives jointly, but task-level concordance between both perspectives remains insufficiently quantified. Methods Within the KOMPaKT112-MED/ORG study, we conducted two parallel, anonymous, nationwide online cross-sectional surveys in Germany using item-for-item mirrored instruments: one for students and trainees in health professions (MED) and the other among governing and responsible actors in civil protection and disaster response (ORG). The dyad is constructed at the level of items and constructs, rather than individuals. Therefore, all group comparisons were unpaired comparisons of two independent samples. The primary endpoints were the item-wise endorsement proportions for 11 parallel task areas and their differences between populations. Differences were estimated using Newcombe-Wilson hybrid intervals and adjusted for multiplicity within families using the Holm procedure. Ordinal batteries of unequal lengths were compared using Cliff's delta with bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap intervals. Rank profiles were compared using Kendall's tau-b with person-level bootstrap resampling. Predictors of willingness were modelled using a cumulative link model with an a priori fixed predictor set, and preference profiles were characterized using latent class analysis. Robustness was assessed across the analysis populations, aggregation rules, exclusion criteria, and field survey waves. Results The analysis populations comprised 8,133 MED and 1,656 ORG records (completion rates 87.5% and 69.1%, respectively). Stated willingness among MED respondents and perceived relief potential among ORG respondents were both high: 78.7% of MED respondents were willing to be formally recruited and trained, 84.1% would provide spontaneous, specified and 71.3% of ORG respondents saw substantial relief potential. Nevertheless, ten of the eleven task-area differences were significant after Holm adjustment, with a mean absolute difference of 22.7 pp and a range of -44.0 to 41.7 pp. The rank profiles of the two populations were essentially uncorrelated (Kendall's tau-b = 0.02; 95% CI: -0.02–0.09). The discordance followed a single prespecified content axis: patient-facing acute care was endorsed more often by MED (mean difference + 22.1 percentage points) and care-related, nursing, and logistical tasks more often by ORG (-30.4 percentage points), a difference-in-differences of 52.5 percentage points. Insurance coverage was the only framework condition ranked among the two most important by both populations. Concerns about psychological overload were markedly stronger on the organizational side (Cliff's delta = -0.49; 57.2% versus 22.7%). Prior exposure to civil protection structures and practical exercises were the strongest predictors of individual willingness. The direction of all 11 differences was preserved across all specifications examined. Conclusions Both samples broadly supported the integration of additional personnel, but their task expectations diverged along a clearly identifiable content axis. Concepts for integrating additional personnel should start with the tasks on which both sides already agree, explicitly address expectational gaps in the remaining fields, and include insurance coverage as a central framework condition.

title: Ultrasonography in disaster medicine: a narrative review
abstract: This narrative review aimed to critically appraise the diagnostic accuracy, clinical impact, and operational feasibility of ultraportable point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) across the four domains of disaster medicine. A literature search was conducted following the SANRA and PRISMA-trAIce guidelines. Records were identified through an AI-assisted literature-discovery tool (the Undermind Deep-Search platform, interrogating the Semantic Scholar corpus) run on 15 June 2025, rather than through an independent structured multi-database search. Candidate references were screened manually against pre-specified eligibility criteria by a single reviewer, with the search parameters independently verified by the senior author. Of 71 records identified, 63 met the inclusion criteria. The included studies comprised 32 original studies, 10 systematic or scoping reviews, 20 narrative or operational papers, and one guideline. In CBRN scenarios, lung ultrasound demonstrated sensitivities of 90-97% for COVID-19 pneumonia versus 60-69% for chest radiography while minimizing healthcare worker exposure. For blast and ballistic injuries, FAST showed a pooled sensitivity of 92.1% (95% CI: 87.8-95.6) and specificity of 98.7% (95% CI: 96.0-99.9) for intra-abdominal hemorrhage. In natural disasters, ultrasound altered management in up to 44% of patients. Post-disaster applications included vascular access, tube confirmation, and complication monitoring. Ultraportable POCUS demonstrates diagnostic utility and operational feasibility across multiple disaster domains. However, evidence quality varies significantly, and standardized protocols remain lacking. Prospective studies linking ultrasound deployment to improved patient outcomes are needed. KEY POINTS: Question When disasters disable conventional imaging, how does ultraportable point-of-care ultrasonography perform for diagnosis, triage, and procedural guidance across the four domains of disaster medicine? Findings Across 63 studies, FAST reached 92.1% pooled sensitivity for hemoperitoneum, lung ultrasound 90-97% versus 60-69% for radiography; management changed in up to 44%. Critical relevance statement This review critically appraises ultraportable ultrasound across all four disaster domains, showing that radiation-free bedside imaging accelerates triage, conserves scarce CT capacity, and extends radiological expertise through tele-guidance, while exposing an evidence base still lacking prospective outcome data.

title: Complex disaster and conflict-related civil defence – nurses’ role in European civil defence within the context of emerging threats and the European union preparedness union strategy – a scoping review
abstract: Global instability and war in Europe mean that conflict is a significant concern for the European Union (EU). The nature of hybrid warfare leads to complex humanitarian emergencies which also encompass mass casualty events that must be managed by nurses through a civil defence structure. This scoping review investigates the current literature on the role of civilian-based nursing in civil defence in reference to emerging hybrid war threats to Europe and the evolving associated complexity referenced by the EU Preparedness Union Strategy (2025) and the Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP). The aim of this review is to examine the existing literature on the role of nurses in Europe’s civil defence during times of conflict, war, and hybrid threats in reference to the EU’s evolving security and preparedness strategies, with a focus on literature published between 2000 and 2025. The scoping review followed the recommendations of the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews and was registered on the Open Science Framework platform on June 23, 2025. A comprehensive electronic search for relevant articles published between January 2000 and June 2025 was conducted across five databases: MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase (Ovid), CINAHL (EBSCO), PsycINFO, and Web of Science. Supplementary searching of Google Scholar was also undertaken. 836 articles were identified, and after screening, a total of 16 articles were reviewed. Few articles focused specifically on the role of nursing in civil defence within Europe and the current emerging threat landscape. Most literature emanated from the USA and Middle East. It was found that nurses possess essential attributes for civil defence but are under-prepared for conflict scenarios. There is a significant policy-practice gap in disaster nurse workforce planning and training for Europe’s security landscape. Within the EU Preparedness Union Strategy, there is a need to prioritise development and implementation of policies that promote a pan-EU standardized training that integrates the largest professional group within health services - nurses - if a comprehensive civil defence strategy that supports European societal resilience and people’s health needs during conflict is to be effective.

title: Integrating Citizen Perspectives into Table-Top Exercises: A Participatory Approach to Pandemic Preparedness
abstract: Abstract Background The COVID-19 pandemic exposed deep social inequities in health crisis preparedness and response, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations in access to information, healthcare, and decision-making itself. These disparities expose a weakness in preparedness systems: the absence of participatory approaches that actively engage the populations most affected. The PREPSHIELD project ("Preparedness for Society in Health Crises and Disasters," HORIZON-CL3-2023-DRS-01-01) contributes to address this gap by embedding societal perspectives into health crisis preparedness, risk communication, and policy development, through three pilot sites spanning local, regional, and national scales. Methods This contribution presents findings from citizen involvement in a tabletop exercise (TTE) conducted in Piedmont, simulating a novel pandemic Influenza A variant, in which a Crisis Management Team (CMT) and a group of (vulnerable) citizens (MG) interacted through a continuous, facilitator-mediated feedback loop across successive rounds. Data were collected through observation checklists of the MG and CMT discussions, alongside pre- and post-exercise evaluation surveys for the MG and a post-exercise survey for the CMT. Results Citizens did not simply contribute experiential knowledge or a societal perspective on the unfolding scenario: they actively collaborated in shaping the decisions made by the CMT as the simulation progressed. Citizen input fed directly into each round of CMT deliberation, informing more inclusive response measures and shaping how economic support, healthcare access, and communication strategies were designed to reach vulnerable populations facing structural barriers, including vulnerabilities that the CMT had not initially considered. Citizens also surfaced original interpretive contributions, such as diagnosing institutional memory gaps and identifying a pattern of misinformed behaviour, that went beyond simply validating institutional plans. Conclusion This collaborative contribution of citizens moved beyond capturing lived experience toward influence over decision-making, demonstrating that even procedurally modest citizen involvement can generate substantively co-produced knowledge and inform the substance of crisis response. Beyond these findings, this work offers a replicable model, adaptable in duration, group composition, and facilitation structure, for translating citizen perspectives into decision-support processes, making health crisis governance more inclusive, equitable, and socially legitimate.

title: Strategies for Adapting the Public Health System to Future Climate Crises and Pandemics in North Aceh Regency
abstract: Climate change and potential future pandemics pose interconnected and cascading threats to health systems, particularly in disaster-prone regions such as North Aceh Regency, Indonesia. However, empirical evidence on district-level health system preparedness that simultaneously addresses climate and pandemic risks remains limited. Purpose: This study aimed to assess health system preparedness, identify community vulnerabilities, and formulate context-specific adaptation strategies for addressing climate-related risks and potential future pandemics in North Aceh Regency. Method: A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was employed. The quantitative phase assessed health facilities and households across high-, moderate-, and low-risk areas. All primary healthcare facilities were included through total sampling, with facility respondents selected purposively, while households were selected using multistage and systematic random sampling. A total of 27 facility respondents and 230 households were included. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively and using Kruskal–Wallis and Spearman correlation tests. The qualitative phase involved purposively selected stakeholders and used in-depth interviews and focus group discussions, followed by directed content analysis. Results: Overall health system preparedness was moderate, with major weaknesses in disaster-resilient infrastructure, logistics and supply chains, and service continuity. Preparedness differed significantly across risk strata (p=0.008), while higher disaster risk was associated with lower preparedness (ρ=-0.51; p=0.007). Cross-sectoral coordination showed the strongest positive association with preparedness (ρ=0.61; p<0.001). Implications: Adaptation policies should prioritize high-risk areas, integrated surveillance, resilient infrastructure and supply chains, and institutionalized cross-sectoral coordination. Conclusion: Strengthening district health system resilience requires integrated structural and operational adaptation rather than fragmented single-hazard preparedness.

title: 379 CODE BRICK: Exploring the Use of a Novel Table-top Role Playing Game to Train In-Hospital Disaster Medicine Concepts to Emergency Physicians
Beyond Single-Pathogen Forecasts: Predicting Shared Respiratory Hospital Burden from Influenza, COVID-19, and RSV
Barriers and solutions to healthcare access in disaster-affected communities in the Philippines: a convergent parallel mixed-methods study protocol
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The Philippines is among the most disaster-prone countries globally, with recurrent typhoons, earthquakes and volcanic eruptions significantly disrupting healthcare delivery, particularly in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. Despite existing disaster risk reduction frameworks, gaps persist in ensuring equitable and continuous access to healthcare during and after disasters. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This study will employ a convergent parallel mixed-methods design to assess barriers to healthcare access and identify context-specific solutions in disaster-affected communities. The study will be conducted in three purposively selected municipalities with varying hazard profiles: Albay, Leyte and Davao del Sur. The quantitative component will involve a cross-sectional household survey of approximately 422 adult respondents using structured questionnaires. Descriptive and inferential analyses, including logistic regression, will be performed to identify key determinants of healthcare inaccessibility and utilisation of telemedicine. The qualitative component will include key informant interviews and focus group discussions with stakeholders and will be analysed using thematic analysis. A scoping review of digital health systems in the Philippines (2010-2025) will complement primary data collection. Findings from all components will be integrated through triangulation to generate policy-relevant insights. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Ethical approval has been obtained from the De La Salle University Research Ethics Review Committee (2025-369C). Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, policy briefs and stakeholder engagement activities to inform national and local health system strengthening and disaster preparedness efforts.

title: Health and Emergency Preparedness for Mass Gatherings at the 2034 FIFA World Cup in Saudi Arabia: A Systematic Review and Targeted Evidence Update
abstract: The Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) World Cups are complex mass gatherings that place simultaneous demands on public-health surveillance, environmental risk management, emergency medical services, crowd safety, and health-system resilience.Saudi Arabia's selection to host the 2034 tournament creates an opportunity to adapt capabilities developed through decades of Hajj operations to the very different context of a global football event.This review synthesises evidence from major mass gatherings and incorporates post-Qatar 2022 and World Cup 2026 evidence to define practical priorities for 2034.The original review searched PubMed, the Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE), Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for 2000-2025 and retained 43 records according to the documented screening log.A targeted update undertaken in September 2026 searched PubMed/MEDLINE and primary sources from major international, national, and sporting authorities.Because this update was not a complete rerun of the original four-database strategy, newer evidence was synthesised narratively and was not added to the original screening denominator.Post-Qatar studies support dedicated tournament medical services, improved clinician notification, open-source epidemic intelligence, and wastewater surveillance.World Cup 2026 evidence adds cross-jurisdictional dashboards, port-health surveillance, early-warning systems, pathogen-specific risk assessment, and multi-hazard environmental planning.Contemporary Saudi Hajj operations demonstrate large-scale heat prevention, surge care, referral, and emergency logistics.For Saudi Arabia 2034, the evidence favours an all-hazards model built around heat action plans, interoperable multi-layer surveillance, unified incident command, distributed emergency care, crowd-safety intelligence, mental-health pathways, multilingual communication, and predefined post-event evaluation.The central implementation principle is to strengthen routine national systems rather than construct temporary parallel systems for the tournament.

title: Beyond clinical skills: Unlocking the drivers of effective crisis management in operating rooms -a qualitative study
abstract: Abstract Introduction In-hospital crises, particularly in operating rooms, are critical events where human factors significantly influence the quality of crisis management. While clinical guidelines are standardized, the performance of operating room head nurses during crises varies considerably. Traditional quantitative studies often fail to capture the operational and emotional experiences that enhance crisis management. To address this gap, this qualitative study aimed to explore the factors that improve the performance of operating room head nurses in crisis situations. Methods A qualitative content analysis was conducted in western Iran from [April/2025] to [September/2025]. Participants included 17 head nurses from operating rooms of major hospitals in the western region of Iran, selected through purposive sampling with maximum variation. Data were collected through in-depth, semi-structured interviews. Graneheim and Lundman's systematic approach was employed to analyze the data and uncover latent and manifest content. Results The mean age of participants was 39.45 years (range 37–56 years), and most held a bachelor's degree in operating room technology (82.58%). The collected data were categorized into a theme titled "drivers of effective crisis management" and five main categories with 33 subcategories. These categories included professional leadership competencies, emotional leadership and team cohesion, strategic management of reactive capacities, proactive preparedness and crisis operations, and post-crisis support and rehabilitation. Conclusion Professional leadership competencies, emotional leadership, strategic management of reactive capacities, proactive preparedness, and post-crisis support were key drivers of effective crisis management in operating rooms. Empowering head nurses through leadership skills training, strengthening psychological support, ensuring adequate physical space and equipment, providing organizational incentives, and implementing operational training will be effective measures in this regard.

title: A Longitudinal Analysis of Hospital Consumer Evaluation In Virginia
Compound and cascading climate risks in urban infrastructure governance and resilience across North America
abstract: North American cities are increasingly exposed to climate-related hazards that do not occur in isolation. Extreme heat, drought, flooding, hurricanes, wildfires, wildfire smoke, and sea-level rise interact with aging infrastructure, uneven urbanization, social vulnerability, and fragmented governance systems. As a result, an initial climate shock can trigger cascading failures across energy, water, transport, telecommunications, housing, health, and emergency response systems. This article develops a conceptual and comparative framework for understanding compound and cascading climate risks in urban systems, with a focus on cities in Canada, the United States, and Mexico. It argues that urban climate risk cannot be understood through single-hazard or sectoral approaches alone. Instead, cities must be analyzed as socio-technical systems in which infrastructure interdependence, governance arrangements, fiscal capacity, and social inequality shape the scale and distribution of climate impacts. Drawing on selected urban cases, including Los Angeles and New Orleans in the United States, Toronto and Vancouver in Canada, and Mexico City, Monterrey, Acapulco, and Veracruz–Boca del Río in Mexico, the article identifies common patterns and differentiated challenges in North American urban resilience. The reviewed evidence identifies a mismatch between the complexity of cascading risks and the fragmented governance and funding mechanisms available to manage them, although its form and severity vary across national and urban contexts. The article concludes that strengthening urban resilience in North America requires moving from isolated adaptation measures toward integrated risk governance, stable resilience financing, intersectoral metropolitan coordination, and equity-centered infrastructure planning. Stronger disaster-response networks, interagency cooperation, and urban-resilience institutions can support more coordinated preparedness and recovery from climate-related disasters with the potential for severe human, infrastructural, and economic impacts.

title: THE INFLUENCE OF BASIC LIFE SUPPORT TRAINING ON THE LEVEL OF KNOWLEDGE OF THE MEDICINE FACULTY STUDENTS, UNIVERSITAS NEGERI PADANG
journal: Indonesian Journal of Biotechnology (Universitas Gadjah Mada)
abstract: Background: Basic life support training is crucial to enhance the emergency preparedness of healthcare undergraduates at the Faculty of Medicine, Universitas Negeri Padang, Padang, Indonesia, focusing on disaster risk mitigation. The core medical curriculum and the high regional vulnerability to earthquakes and tsunamis in West Sumatra emphasize the strategic urgency of this training. Objective: This study aims to determine the effect of BLS training on the knowledge of UNP Faculty of Medicine students about risk management and disaster mitigation, especially in the West Sumatra region.Method: This pre-post experimental study recruited 150 students (100 general medicine and 50 veterinary medicine) via total population sampling. Cognitive performance was measured using a validated 10-item questionnaire (1 point for correct, 0 for incorrect). The Wilcoxon signed-rank test analyzed paired changes in knowledge scores before and after the intervention.Results: The Basic life support training intervention significantly improved overall cognitive scores from 4.85 ± 1.30 at baseline to 8.37 ± 1.10 post-test (p = .000). General medicine cohorts demonstrated a higher post-test proficiency (8.75 ± 0.85) than veterinary medicine cohorts (7.61 ± 1.20), although both academic programs and genders experienced highly significant knowledge gains (p = .000).Conclusion: Implementing standardized, interdisciplinary BLS instruction is paramount to building regional disaster resilience among future health professionals. Educational institutions must mandate periodic refresher systems to prevent psychomotor skill decay and secure long-term life-saving competencies.

title: Early hospital discharge following delivery during wartime is not associated with increased rates of postpartum hospital referrals
abstract: BACKGROUND: During war, significant adaptations take place in hospitals to improve the treatment of soldiers and civilians. For example, low-risk women were discharged earlier from hospitals following delivery. The aim of the study was to compare the rate of postpartum-visits to the gynecological-emergency-room (GER) between wartime to a similar period in the previous year. METHODS: A retrospective study compared the visits of postpartum-women in the GER to a similar period in the previous year. RESULTS: The study included 801 women who delivered in the first month of the war in 2023 and 913 who delivered in the parallel period in the previous year. There were no significant changes in maternal age, gravidity, parity, mode of delivery, birthweight, meconium, low Apgar scores, and the rate of admissions to the neonatal intensive care unit. There were significantly less elective cesarean sections during wartime (57% vs. 92%; p < 0.0001). The duration of postpartum hospitalization was significantly shorter during wartime [median length of 53.2 [Interquartile-range (IQR] 42.4-72.4) hours vs. 64.1 (IQR 47.4-82.8) in the previous year (p < 0.0001)]. There were no significant differences in the rate of total referrals of postpartum-women to the GER (8.7% vs. 8.8%; p > 0.05), and no differences in referrals due to infections or bleeding. There was no difference in the rate of admission of postpartum-women (17% vs. 14%; p = 0.73). CONCLUSIONS: Shortening of hospitalization following delivery during war is feasible, does not cause increase postpartum visits to the GER, and does not increase GER visits due to infections or bleeding.

title: Crisis project management and business communication strategies as innovations for emergency medical service continuity (literature review)
abstract: This article examined crisis project management and business communication strategies to ensure the uninterrupted operation of emergency medical services during pandemics, natural disasters, armed conflicts, and infrastructure failures. The aim of this study was to develop an integrated “Project management-communications” matrix as a practical decision-support tool for emergency medical services managers across all phases of the “preparednessresponse-recovery” cycle. A narrative theoretical analysis was conducted based on 40 peer-reviewed sources (2018-2026) obtained from the PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus databases. Sources were selected based on their focus on healthcare facilities, the context of crises and emergencies, their emphasis on resilience and resilience management, the presence of an empirical evidence base, and the status of the peer-reviewed publication. Four interrelated areas of effective crisis management in emergency medical services have been identified: adaptive governance and distributed leadership; structured communication architectures, including incident management systems and inter-organisational coalitions; proactive project management mechanisms with reserve capacity; and real-time digital information systems. It has been established that transformational leadership increases staff resilience by 38%, decision-making efficiency by 29%, and recovery speed by 33%. It has been found that proactive investments in preparedness yield a significantly higher return on investment compared to reactive costs associated with mitigating consequences. Crisis project management tools were positioned as organisational innovations that reduce downtime and improve the efficiency of resource allocation. The developed matrix is a structured analytical tool with practical significance for healthcare management and the sustainable development of emergency medical services

title: Advances in Decision-Support Frameworks for Emergency Response and Public Health Resource Allocation

title: Geographies of Dengue Outbreak and Urban Vulnerability in Diphu Town, Northeast India
Human-AI Collaboration for Resilient Infrastructure: A Systematic Review of Artificial Intelligence and Human Factors in Disaster Management
journal: Journal of Safety Science and Resilience
abstract: While artificial intelligence (AI) shows significant potential for enhancing infrastructure disaster management, its practical effectiveness depends on how it interacts with human actors in operational contexts. Despite increasing research, there remains limited synthesis of human-AI collaboration specifically within this domain. This study addresses this gap through a systematic review of studies that explicitly integrate AI capabilities with human roles and human factors. The analysis is structured across five dimensions: AI techniques and functions, human actors and roles, collaboration structures, human factors, and implementation outcomes. The findings indicate that AI is primarily used to support human decision-making, with collaboration structured around cognitive integration rather than full automation. The study also identifies several structural imbalances and common challenges in the current research landscape. In addition, the study proposes a socio-technical framework that conceptualizes human-AI collaboration as the alignment of four interdependent layers: AI capabilities, human decision-making, interaction mechanisms, and organizational context. Overall, the study reframes human-AI collaboration as a structured socio-technical system. It provides both theoretical insights and practical guidance for designing AI systems that effectively support human decision-making in infrastructure disaster management, and outlines key directions for future research toward more robust, context-aware, and operationally integrated solutions.

title: Barriers to prevention and healthcare-seeking in a fragile humanitarian setting: Evidence from Yemen during the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: The healthcare system in Yemen is confronted with substantial challenges, especially during pandemics such as COVID-19. In Aden, the COVID-19 pandemic occurred in the context of prolonged conflict, health-system fragility, resource constraints and other ongoing humanitarian challenges.This study aims to explore the barriers community members in Aden face in adopting COVID-19 preventive measures and seeking healthcare during the pandemic, and to identify implications for future outbreak preparedness in fragile humanitarian settings. A qualitative study involving 25 in-depth interviews was conducted with adult community members in Aden. Participants' perceptions of COVID-19 and reported preventive practices were also explored to contextualise the barriers influencing prevention and healthcare-seeking. Interview data were analysed using inductive qualitative content analysis; the Socio-Ecological Model (SEM) was applied as an interpretive framework to contextualise barriers across five interacting levels: intrapersonal/individual, interpersonal, organisational/institutional, community, and public policy/structural. Participants described barriers across five SEM levels: intrapersonal/individual barriers included denial, fear, perceived ineffectiveness of preventive measures and financial constraints; interpersonal barriers included stigma, mockery and social pressure; organisational/institutional barriers included perceived service refusal, concerns about infection prevention and staff preparedness, long waiting times, limited diagnostic testing, increased treatment costs and shortages of medical supplies; community-level barriers included rumours, misinformation and mistrust; and public policy/structural barriers included limited financial support, inadequate implementation of preventive measures, conflict-related constraints and perceived insufficient preparedness. The findings suggest that barriers to prevention and healthcare-seeking were interconnected across the five levels of the socio-ecological context, with individual perceptions and behaviours occurring within interpersonal, organisational, community and wider public policy and structural conditions. Future outbreak preparedness in fragile settings should therefore combine trusted, culturally appropriate risk communication, community engagement, accessible preventive resources, strengthened infection-prevention capacity, diagnostic and referral pathways, and continuity of essential health services.

title: Standardizing Disaster Health Data Visualization Using Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources in Indonesia: Dashboard Development and Technical Evaluation
abstract: Background: Health data management during disasters enables responders to assess the needs of survivors, efficiently allocate resources, and monitor survivors' health conditions. However, government agencies need to interpret health data in real time during disasters because the volume and complexity of such data can hinder timely decision-making. Objective: In this study, we aimed to develop a visual interface for Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)-based data from various sources, using the daily report form of the World Health Organization (WHO) Emergency Medical Teams Minimum Data Set (EMT MDS) as a template and ensuring compliance with the SATUSEHAT platform. Methods: The proposed solution involves creating a dashboard application within a web-based system to visualize health data using FHIR, leveraging the WHO EMT MDS disaster profile. The interface includes Overview, Location, and Demography pages that display information in tables, graphs, and maps. This application was developed using JavaScript and React. The dataset consisted of 13,300 synthetic patient records generated using Synthea, subsequently modified with GPT-5, and stored on the Health Level 7 (HL7) Application Programming Interface (HAPI) FHIR server. Results: We developed a dashboard application based on the WHO EMT MDS Daily Reporting Form comprising 3 main pages: Overview, Demography, and Location. The Demography page contains several sections, including the total number of patients, health conditions, outcomes, relationships, and protection. The Location page lists all health care facilities, along with their corresponding locations, on a map. Each Location page displays detailed information regarding the organization and demographics of the respective location. Conclusions: The dashboard application demonstrates that health data collected in accordance with FHIR standards can be integrated and presented in a form suitable for disaster response. This dashboard has the potential to support disaster management agencies by enabling real-time, data-driven decision-making during disaster response.

title: A two-stage multi-period multi-objective simulation-based post-disaster response framework for sustainable blood collection
abstract: Blood supply chains face unique challenges in disaster scenarios, where urgency collides with logistical and environmental constraints. The first 48 hours following a major earthquake represent the most critical period for emergency blood collection, during which rapid donor mobilisation and efficient resource allocation can directly influence patient survival. This study proposes a two-stage simulation–optimisation framework that integrates agent-based simulation with p-median optimisation to support emergency blood collection by jointly considering donor accessibility, operational efficiency, and transportation-related environmental impacts. The results indicate that the optimal configuration, comprising two permanent and eighteen mobile collection facilities, increased the expected number of blood donations by 47.9% while achieving 86.4% population coverage within a 1.5 km service radius. Compared with the baseline configuration, the proposed framework reduced total operational costs by 36.5%, while optimisation of the central blood centre location further reduced transportation-related CO2 emissions by 17%. In addition, the proposed normalised scoring framework demonstrated that placing greater emphasis on transportation-related environmental performance could reduce CO2 emissions by up to 25% without compromising emergency blood collection performance. Overall, the proposed framework provides a practical decision-support approach for evaluating alternative emergency blood collection strategies and supporting facility location planning during the critical post-earthquake response period.

title: An Analysis of the Reaction of the Nigerian Governments Against Covid-19 Pandemic in Tarauni Local Government Area of Kano State, Nigeria: 2020-2022 A.D.

title: Performance of the Heatwave ED Forecast Tool in the Emergency Department Network of Ticino Canton, Switzerland
abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives Heatwaves drive surges in acute care demand, yet heat-health action plans (HHAPs) lack tools to scale emergency care responses. This study validated a forecasting tool for heatwave- related emergency department (ED) demand across four clusters comprising the emergency care network of Ticino Canton, Switzerland. Methods This retrospective, ecological, time-series study modeled daily mean temperature and ED presentations using a distributed lag non-linear model framework with autoregressive and calendar adjustment components. The model was trained on summers (June–August) 2016-2024 and tested on summer 2025, defining heatwaves as daily mean temperature >25 °C for ≥3 consecutive days. Results A non-linear temperature–demand association was shown across the clusters, with ED visits increasing at higher temperatures. Model fit varied across clusters (R² 0.389–0.672), and the reference model consistently outperformed naïve baselines. During two heatwaves in 2025, prediction errors remained within acceptable ranges. Baseline demand, heatwave occurrence, and model performance varied substantially within the canton. Conclusions These findings have implications for the design of HHAPs, suggesting that emergency care preparedness should rely on locally calibrated demand forecast rather than standardized activation protocols.

title: Health Service Disruption During the 2024 Floods in Yagoua Health District, Cameroon: A Descriptive Study
abstract: Abstract floods are increasing globally, yet their impact on health service delivery in sub-Saharan Africa remains poorly documented. This descriptive study examined eight essential health indicators in the Yagoua Health District, Cameroon, during the July–September 2024 flood period, using secondary data from the national DHIS2 system. Monthly trends in vaccination, outpatient consultations, hospitalizations, deaths, severe acute malnutrition, community births, malaria cases, and antiretroviral therapy were analyzed. Percentage change and the Kruskal–Wallis test compared flood-period months across 2023, 2024, and 2025. Vaccination declined by 5.5%, while hospitalizations rose 38%, malnutrition cases 51.8%, community births 48.4%, and malaria cases 77.6%. The Kruskal–Wallis test showed no statistically significant differences across years, though community births (p = 0.061) and hospitalizations (p = 0.066) approached significance. Despite non-significant statistical differences, observable trends indicate substantial operational strain on health services during floods. These findings highlight the vulnerability of rural health systems to environmental shocks and underscore the need for targeted disaster preparedness strategies in flood-prone regions of sub-Saharan Africa.

title: High-fidelity simulation as a translational and educational platform for crisis ventilation: quantifying and mitigating tidal volume maldistribution during shared mechanical ventilation
journal: Global Surgical Education - Journal of the Association for Surgical Education
abstract: Background: Shared mechanical ventilation has been proposed during ventilator shortages, but unequal tidal volume delivery remains a major limitation when lung compliance differs. Professional societies have cautioned against this practice, yet the intervention has never been validated clinically, and ethical constraints preclude direct patient testing. Translational simulation-simulation applied beyond education to probe clinical systems, test crisis-driven innovations, and generate actionable safety data-offers a methodological pathway for evaluating interventions that cannot be studied in vivo [1, 2]. In parallel, high-fidelity simulation offers a controlled environment in which clinicians can be taught the physiologic hazards of shared ventilation without risk to patients. Methods: Two high-fidelity patient simulators were connected to one ventilator in volume-control assist-control mode using a parallel circuit. One simulator was set to normal compliance and the other to reduced compliance. Tidal volumes were measured before and after adjustment of the higher-flow limb with inline flowmeters. This study was designed as a translational simulation to evaluate a crisis-care equipment configuration under controlled, reproducible conditions. The objective was to use high-fidelity simulation as a controlled, reproducible experimental platform to (1) empirically quantify the compliance-driven tidal volume reduction predicted by respiratory-mechanics theory during shared ventilation, (2) test whether inline flowmeters with adjustable valves partially mitigate this, and (3) evaluate the feasibility of high-fidelity simulation as a translational and educational platform for crisis-care innovations that cannot ethically or logistically be studied in real patients. We hypothesized that (H1) shared ventilation of two lung units with mismatched compliance would produce clinically relevant tidal volume reduction in the low-compliance limb, and (H2) this would be counteracted by inline flowmeters with adjustable valves. Results: Without adjustment, the low-compliance simulator's delivered volume fell markedly relative to its normal-compliance baseline; after flow regulation, it returned toward baseline at both 900 mL and 1100 mL tidal volume settings. Conclusions: This study demonstrates how high-fidelity simulation can function as a translational research platform for crisis-care innovations that are ethically and logistically impossible to study in clinical practice. Beyond confirming the physiologic limitations of unregulated ventilator sharing, the simulation generated reproducible, condition-specific tidal volume data that can inform crisis preparedness protocols and equipment pre-positioning decisions. This application of simulation as a systems-testing and device-evaluation tool, in addition to translating directly into a crisis-preparedness educational scenario, represents an underutilized but critically important role for simulation science in disaster and pandemic preparedness. Supplementary Information: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s44186-026-00589-1.

title: Telemedicine in Emergencies, High-Risk Zones, and Remote Access Regions: A Review
abstract: Problem: Access to healthcare remains a major challenge during emergencies, disasters, armed conflicts, and in geographically remote or hard-to-reach areas, where inadequate infrastructure, transportation, and healthcare resources frequently delay or prevent timely medical intervention, resulting in increased morbidity, mortality, and adverse physical, psychological, and social outcomes. Objective: To review the scientific evidence on the role of telemedicine in improving healthcare delivery in emergencies and high-risk or difficult-access settings, with emphasis on healthcare accessibility, continuity of care, and health system resilience. Methodology: A narrative literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed scientific publications on telemedicine in emergency care, disaster response, humanitarian crises, and remote healthcare delivery, focusing on the integration of Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) into health services. Results: The evidence shows that telemedicine improves access to healthcare by enabling remote consultation, diagnosis, patient monitoring, and clinical decision-making. It reduces geographical, economic, and logistical barriers, supports timely interventions, ensures continuity of care, optimizes healthcare resource allocation, and strengthens emergency response capacity, particularly where conventional healthcare services are disrupted by disasters, conflicts, poor transportation infrastructure, or shortages of healthcare professionals. Conclusions: Telemedicine is an effective and innovative strategy for healthcare delivery in emergencies and difficult-access areas. ICT integration enhances service accessibility, quality of care, patient outcomes, and health system resilience. Recommendations and Future Work: Expanding telemedicine requires investment in digital infrastructure, telecommunications, regulatory frameworks, and workforce training. Future research should evaluate the long-term effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, implementation challenges, and equity of telemedicine across diverse healthcare settings, especially in low- and middle-income countries.

title: When Winter Comes: Seasonal Patterns in Outcomes After Major Surgery
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Seasonal strain may affect perioperative care, yet national evidence on seasonal variation in outcomes after major surgery remains limited. We evaluated whether postoperative outcomes varied by season among older adults undergoing major surgical procedures. METHODS: Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 y or older undergoing abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, coronary artery bypass grafting, colectomy, lung resection, or pancreaticoduodenectomy from 2016 through 2021 were identified using 100% Medicare Standard Analytic Files. Seasons were defined meteorologically, with spring as the reference. Outcomes included 30-d mortality, 90-d mortality, complications, textbook outcome, failure to rescue, surgical site infection, and length of stay. Multivariable regression models adjusted for patient, procedure, and hospital characteristics and were stratified by elective versus emergency admission. Interactions with the nurse-to-bed ratio and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Hospital Star Rating were assessed. RESULTS: Among 1,165,265 patients, 738,236 underwent elective surgery and 427,029 underwent emergency surgery. Among emergency admissions, winter was associated with higher adjusted odds of 30-d mortality (adjusted odds ratio: 1.10; 95% confidence interval: 1.07-1.13), 90-d mortality (1.10; 1.07-1.13), complications (1.05; 1.03-1.07), and failure to rescue (1.11; 1.07-1.15), as well as lower odds of textbook outcome (0.96; 0.94-0.98) and longer length of stay. Among elective admissions, winter was associated with smaller increases in 30-d and 90-d mortality. No significant interaction was observed by nurse-to-bed ratio or Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Hospital Star Rating. CONCLUSIONS: Winter was associated with worse outcomes after major surgery, particularly among emergency admissions, supporting targeted seasonal preparedness strategies.

title: Frequency and pattern of WHO warning signs among patients with dengue fever admitted to Mufti Mehmood Memorial Teaching Hospital, Dera Ismail Khan, Pakistan: a hospital-based cross-sectional study
abstract: Background: Dengue is an emerging mosquito-borne viral infection. Clinical deterioration is often seen around defervescence, and the World Health Organization (WHO) warning-sign framework is designed to identify the patient who is deteriorating and needs closer monitoring and timely treatment. The study determined the frequency and pattern of recorded WHO warning signs among patients admitted with dengue fever to Mufti Mehmood Memorial Teaching Hospital, Dera Ismail Khan, and explored their distribution across recorded dengue severity categories. Methods: This hospital-based cross-sectional record analysis included 384 admissions aged 15–60 years. Demographic variables, previous dengue exposure, six recorded warning signs, platelet count, hematocrit, WHO classification, and discharge outcome were analyzed. Frequencies were reported with Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: Of 384 records, 270 (70.3%) were classified as dengue with warning signs, 79 (20.6%) as dengue without warning signs, and 35 (9.1%) as severe dengue. At least one recorded warning sign was present in 305 patients (79.4%; 95% CI 75.1–83.2). Persistent vomiting was the most frequent warning sign (197; 51.3%), followed by lethargy (97; 25.3%), hepatomegaly (85; 22.1%), abdominal pain (74; 19.3%), mucosal bleeding (18; 4.7%), and clinical fluid accumulation (16; 4.2%). Patients classified as severe dengue had a median of 3 warning signs (IQR 3–3), compared with 1 (IQR 1–2) among those with dengue with warning signs. Overall, 368 patients (95.8%) were discharged, 14 (3.6%) were referred, and 2 (0.5%) died. Conclusion: Warning signs were recorded in approximately four-fifths of admissions, and persistent vomiting was the predominant manifestation. A structured warning-sign checklist may support triage and serial clinical reassessment, but individual warning signs should not be interpreted in isolation. Prospective validation using verified clinical records, serial hematocrit platelet measurements, and independently adjudicated severe-dengue outcomes is required.

title: Building equitable AI capacity: lessons from continuous education on artificial intelligence as a catalyst for global health and oncology
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming healthcare; however, equitable access to AI training remains limited, particularly in low-and middle-income countries, where digital infrastructure and technical training opportunities are limited.The AI Catalyst for Global Health course was developed as a free, easily accessible, virtual course to provide foundational AI literacy and ethical awareness for a globally diverse audience, with an emphasis on underserved settings.We collected baseline participant demographics using a precourse survey and evaluated participation, engagement and educational impact using weekly post-lecture surveys and a final post-course survey incorporating a retrospective pre-post design.Survey items assessed confidence in explaining core AI concepts and evaluating ethical implications, as well as the perceived feasibility of applying AI approaches, likelihood of future application, perceived barriers and open-ended reflections on course content and impact.A total of 63 participants from 12 countries completed the survey, including healthcare providers (41%), students (24%), researchers or academics (22%) and professionals in technology, policy or other roles (13%).Confidence in explaining AI concepts increased from 2.68 ± 1.22 (retrospective pre-course) to 4.22 ± 0.75 (post-course) (t(62) = 9.84; p < 0.001; d p = 1.24), while confidence in evaluating ethical implications increased from 2.68 ± 1.28 to 4.27 ± 0.70 (t(62) = 9.58; p < 0.001; d p = 1.21).Participants rated the feasibility of applying AI as 3.86 ± 0.93 and the likelihood of applying AI insights within the next 12 months as 4.29 ± 0.87, with strong agreement that AI has the potential to reduce global health inequities (4.40 ± 0.64).The most reported barriers to AI adoption were funding limitations (43%), limited technical capacity (21%) and lack of stakeholder awareness (16%).Qualitative analysis highlighted collaboration, efficiency and the importance of sustained AI education.These findings suggest that accessible virtual education can meaningfully strengthen self-reported AI literacy and ethical awareness, supporting capacity building for global health and oncology in resource-limited settings.

journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Extreme weather events: A practical guide for clinicians
Explainable hybrid deep learning framework for air quality index prediction in Indian cities
abstract: Air pollution constitutes one of the most pressing environmental and public health crises of the twenty-first century, disproportionately affecting rapidly urbanising nations such as India. Accurate prediction of the Air Quality Index (AQI) is essential for enabling timely hospital preparedness, school-closure decisions, and evidence-based policy interventions. AQI prediction remains inherently challenging owing to widespread missing data due to sensor failures (up to 54% missingness in certain pollutant columns), pronounced non-stationarity, nonlinear inter-pollutant interactions, and the limited interpretability of existing predictive models. This paper presents a four-stage Explainable Hybrid Deep Learning Framework validated on 435,742 CPCB India records (1990–2015) to address these challenges. The XAI-Enhanced Ensemble achieves RMSE = 0.3817, MAE = 0.2773, and R 2 = 0.9994 on the held-out test set a 54.7% RMSE and 58.7% MAE reduction over the standalone LSTM baseline. SHAP-guided feature selection reduces input dimensionality by 62% (from 26 to 10 features) while yielding an additional 38% RMSE improvement over the standard ensemble, demonstrating that interpretability and accuracy are complementary rather than competing objectives.

title: Event-Driven Stochastic Regime Shifts in Adaptive Healthcare Systems
A simulation analytics framework for system-level digital twins in hospital operations
abstract: Digital twins in healthcare have predominantly focused on object-level applications, including personalized medicine, organ twins, and wearable-based patient monitoring, whereas system-level digital twins that support the planning and operation of healthcare facilities remain largely unexplored. This study addresses this gap by proposing a revised typology of healthcare digital twins and developing a system-level digital twin for hospital operations. The proposed typology integrates the healthcare facility life cycle with an analytics framework that combines descriptive and diagnostic analytics while introducing a prospective analytics dimension to support simulation-based what-if analyses. The digital twin was developed for a multiservice ambulatory care center within the CIUSSS du Centre-Ouest-de-l'Île-de-Montréal, Canada, integrating blood collection, screening, medical examinations, and vaccination services. A hybrid agent-based and discrete-event simulation model was developed in AnyLogic using service-time and arrival estimates derived from field observations, managerial input, and clinical expert consultation. Six operational scenarios involving alternative staffing levels and service durations were evaluated using 500 simulation replications per scenario. The proposed typology comprises twelve categories, seven of which are represented by previously reported healthcare digital twins, while the presented application occupies the system-level design category. The baseline configuration proved operationally infeasible, with an average patient length of stay of 266 minutes and service completion extending to 01:29. Improving staffing or service durations individually was insufficient to achieve acceptable operational performance. In contrast, jointly optimizing staffing and service durations reduced the mean patient length of stay to 75 minutes and enabled completion of daily operations by 19:14, representing a 3.5-fold improvement over the baseline. These findings demonstrate that system-level digital twins can provide actionable analytics for healthcare facility planning by enabling the evaluation of operational alternatives before implementation, while the proposed typology offers a structured framework for classifying and comparing healthcare digital twins across the healthcare facility life cycle.

title: Hospital selection problem for emergency medical services: a data-driven metamodeling and simulation-based optimization approach
Stochastic reliability modeling of an integrated cloud–fog–IoMT healthcare architecture with VANETs
abstract: The rapid advancement of the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) has transformed healthcare by enabling continuous remote monitoring and timely medical intervention. Although cloud computing, fog computing, and vehicular ad hoc networks (VANETs) have individually supported smart healthcare applications, the reliability assessment of an integrated IoMT–VANET–Fog–Cloud infrastructure remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the need for dependable healthcare services during emergencies and disaster scenarios, this study proposes an integrated cloud–fog-based smart healthcare architecture incorporating IoMT devices and VANET-assisted communication for continuous patient monitoring and real-time healthcare delivery. A stochastic analytical framework based on Reliability Block Diagrams (RBDs) and continuous-time Markov chains is developed to evaluate the reliability of the proposed architecture. The framework models the failure and repair behavior of heterogeneous hardware components and derives analytical expressions for overall system reliability. Extensive numerical investigations under varying operating conditions demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. A comparative reliability analysis with cloud-only and cloud–fog architectures quantifies the benefits of integrating fog computing and VANET technologies. The proposed model achieves a 20% improvement in reliability over the cloud-only architecture and a 23% improvement over the IoMT-enabled cloud–fog architecture. The analytical results are validated through MATLAB-based discrete-event simulation, showing close agreement with analytical results. The findings demonstrate that integrating fog computing and VANET-assisted communication significantly enhances system reliability under the assumed conditions. The proposed stochastic reliability framework provides a systematic tool for evaluating the dependability of next-generation smart healthcare systems and offers insights for designing reliable healthcare infrastructures.

title: Predictive Modeling Techniques for Forecasting Emergency Department Overcrowding and Resource Needs in United States Public Hospitals
journal: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology (IJISRT)

title: A Discrete Choice Experiment to Understand Hospital Discharge Preferences of Populations with Non-English Language Preference
abstract: BACKGROUND: Effective hospital discharge communication is crucial to reducing adverse outcomes and readmissions particularly for patients with non-English language preference (NELP). However, little evidence exists on which specific discharge elements are most valued by this population. OBJECTIVE: To quantify preferences for aspects of hospital discharge among hospitalized patients with NELP and examine how demographic and language-related factors are associated with these preferences. DESIGN: A discrete choice experiment (DCE) was conducted in which participants were presented with pairs of hypothetical discharge scenarios. Each scenario was defined by one level per attribute across four discharge communication attributes: family involvement during teaching (none, by phone, or in person), mode of verbal communication (language-concordant clinician, in-person interpreter, phone interpreter, or video interpreter), record of discharge instructions (written in English, written in preferred language, or audio-recorded in preferred language), and type of post-discharge phone contact (call from primary care nurse, call from hospital nurse, or a number for patients to call). Participants selected their preferred scenario across 20 choice sets. PARTICIPANTS: Hospitalized Spanish- and Haitian Creole-speaking adults at a single urban safety-net hospital (n = 89). MAIN MEASURES: Relative attribute importance and level preferences. Mixed logit models estimated overall and subgroup preferences by language and acculturation measures, with choice simulations generating predicted selection probabilities. KEY RESULTS: Record of discharge instructions held the greatest relative importance (39.9% decision weight; 95% CI 34.0%-44.5%), followed by mode of verbal communication (34.7%; 95% CI 29.0%-39.1%). Overall participants preferred language-concordant providers, audio-recorded and written instructions in their preferred language, and family involvement. Preferences varied within and between demographic and language-related groups. CONCLUSIONS: Hospitalized patients with NELP prioritize language-concordant, multimodal discharge communication, particularly written instructions in their preferred language and discharge teaching from language-concordant staff. Health systems should prioritize implementing these strategies to improve the patient-centeredness of transitional care programs.

title: Hierarchical reinforcement learning with model predictive elevator control for risk-sensitive multi-robot transport scheduling in hospitals
abstract: Hospitals increasingly deploy autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) to move specimens and medicines between wards and laboratories. These fleets must meet clinical deadlines that differ across request classes, which couples two decisions: which request each robot serves, and the order of its stops. Intra-hospital transport is formulated here as a multi-objective Markov game and solved with hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning for transport (HMART). A shared graph-attention encoder feeds a sequential assignment decoder and a route-improvement decoder, a conditional value-at-risk constraint bounds the tail of class-weighted tardiness, and a model predictive control layer coordinates the capacitated elevators. Two instantiations are evaluated: HMART-H, whose decoders are engineered, and HMART-RL, whose assignment decoder is a trained attention network. In a discrete-event simulator of a four-floor hospital with three elevators, at heavy load with twelve robots over twenty paired seeds, HMART-H lowers mean total weighted tardiness from 2359 ± 214 to 29 ± 6 against the strongest dispatching rule, mean work-in-process from 80.1 ± 6.4 to 14.3 ± 1.9, and the ninety-fifth percentile tardiness tail by more than an order of magnitude, while raising the STAT on-time rate from 0.925 ± 0.011 to 0.969 ± 0.007; all differences are significant under Holm-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. HMART-RL reaches 40 ± 8 and transfers across fleet sizes and building configurations without retraining. These gains are obtained in simulation and require confirmation in a live building.

title: An expert-AI co-creation framework for robust health economic simulations
journal: Expert Review of Pharmacoeconomics & Outcomes Research
abstract: BACKGROUND: Health economic (HE) evaluations are essential for healthcare decision-making, yet the rapid pace of innovation demands accelerated HE evaluations. Integrating Generative AI (GenAI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), into HE simulation modeling offers a promising opportunity to enhance model development efficiency and speed. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: We propose a framework for automating HE model development through expert-AI co-creation. This framework enables GenAI to generate simulation models in a structured and transparent manner. The proposed approach is expert-led and incorporates iterative prompt-response cycles. GPT5-mini and GPT-5.2-codex are employed using zero-shot prompting. As LLM results are non-deterministic, we introduced a Prompt Robustness Test (PRT) to assess the stability of LLM-generated outputs, indicating whether a prompt is sufficiently reliable to support automated model development. The methodology is applied to replicate a published discrete-event simulation comparing two post-surgery treatment strategies for colon cancer. The original model is complex and representative of real-world HE practice. RESULTS: Using our framework, we replicated the model in Python, achieving cost and QALY estimates within 2% of the original. While the overall pathway structure was successfully reconstructed, several logic discrepancies remained compared with the original model. CONCLUSIONS: Our framework provides methodological guidance on the expert-AI co-creation of complex HE models, emphasizing that expert oversight is essential throughout the process.

title: Enacting Translational Simulation: A 24-hour Human Biocontainment Simulation Incorporating Patient Participation and Video-Reflexive Ethnography
abstract: Abstract Translational simulation is increasingly used to examine and improve healthcare systems in real-world contexts. This approach is particularly relevant in human biocontainment settings, where opportunities to learn from managing high-consequence infectious diseases (HCIDs) are rare. The aim of this paper is to describe the application of the translational simulation conceptual framing to the design and implementation of a continuous 24-hour in situ simulation in an operational human HCID biocontainment centre, incorporating video-reflexive ethnography (VRE) and a real infectious disease inpatient. The simulation was conducted in a tertiary biocontainment centre using a scenario involving the admission and management of a patient with suspected Ebola disease. A real infectious diseases inpatient (who did not have an HCID), receiving routine care in the hospital, participated in the simulation. The conceptual foundations of the study were grounded in safety and quality improvement within a complex adaptive system, and person-centred care. VRE was used to generate and analyse data. Video data collected during the simulation were used in nine group video-reflexive sessions involving healthcare workers, and a separate reflexive session with the patient. The audio-recorded reflexive sessions were analysed using the Special Pathogen Operational Readiness Self-Assessment (SPORSA) framework. The simulation demonstrated the feasibility of a continuous, time-extended translational simulation embedded within routine healthcare delivery. Implementation required substantial organisational preparation, including governance approvals, workforce coordination, identification of a suitable inpatient participant, and operational support. Inclusion of a real inpatient enabled exploration of both system functioning and lived experience of care. VRE supported collaborative examination of healthcare practices and enabled patient perspectives to inform staff reflexive discussions. The approach generated system-level insights relating to workflow, communication, infection prevention and control, staffing, patient experience, and healthcare worker experience. This paper provides the methodology and a practical example of how translational simulation can be operationalised through explicit consideration of purpose, process, and conceptual foundations. By integrating a continuous 24-hour design, patient participation and VRE, the study extends current methodological approaches to translational simulation. Importantly, it demonstrates how patients can contribute not only to care delivery, but also to the understanding, evaluation, and improvement of healthcare systems.

title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake
Ethics of Medical Students as Embedded Simulation Participants in Ultrasound Education
abstract: Introduction: Medical students are sometimes used as embedded simulation participants (ESP) to facilitate ultrasound training on live volunteers. There is little guidance on how to safeguard the autonomy and dignity of medical student ESPs serving in this role. Based on real student experiences, we used four cases to illustrate the ethical dilemmas that can arise when ESPs are used, including the examination of sensitive body areas, risk for coercion, discovery of incidental findings in a public and professional setting, and social media posting of training events. Through these cases, we explore and articulate the relevant ethical obligations educators have to obtain informed consent, sensitively address incidental findings, and ensure the psychological and physical safety of ESPs. Methods: We developed interventions and procedures at our institution to address the obligation to promote ESP autonomy and bodily dignity, including a comprehensive consent form, ombudsperson role, and restrictions surrounding photography and social media posting of educational events. Results: These interventions were implemented in January 2024 in the emergency department of a large academic medical center affiliated with a medical school. Since implementation, 96 ESPs have participated in 16 discrete educational events. There has been anecdotal positive reception of these interventions. Recruiting and training individuals for the ombudsperson role carried some challenges. Conclusion: Proactive measures are necessary to support the autonomy and safety of medical student ESPs. There are practical challenges associated with recruitment, training, and implementation of the ombudsperson role. We hope that other institutions who use medical student ESPs will consider incorporating similar practices to promote the psychological and bodily safety of their volunteers.

title: A simulation-based framework for chronic disease management to improve health equity
journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society
abstract: Chronic diseases present a formidable global health challenge, with burdens unevenly distributed across populations, disproportionately affecting vulnerable and marginalised groups. A lack of established methods limits policymakers’ ability to design effective and equitable care pathways for individuals with chronic conditions. This study addresses this gap by introducing Chronic-Sim, a simulation-based framework tailored to the complexities of healthcare delivery. Chronic-Sim captures individual patient characteristics, demographics, socio-economic status (SES), and comorbidities. The framework presents a patient flow that is customisable for any chronic disease and supports multimorbidity by simulating multiple chronic conditions simultaneously. A novel hierarchical labelling approach is introduced to classify patients by SES, enabling the generation of outputs by deprivation category. The framework’s adaptability is demonstrated step-by-step within a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) service at a major healthcare provider in the United Kingdom, incorporating cardiovascular disease to model multimorbidity. Interventions targeting access barriers are evaluated across SES categories, with outputs showing cost-effective improvements in patient-related (mortality, quality of life) and service-related metrics (admissions, service usage). Chronic-Sim offers a modular, data-driven decision-support tool adaptable to diverse health systems. Its novel contribution lies in empowering policymakers to test interventions, project inequities, and design fair and effective chronic disease care pathways.

title: SELF-HEALING CYBER DEFENSE FOR CONVERGED HEALTHCARE-FINANCE DATA INFRASTRUCTURES
journal: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
abstract: The convergence of healthcare and financial data infrastructures driven by integrated billing systems, electronic health records (EHR), and digital payment gateways has created unprecedented attack surfaces for adversarial actors. Existing cyber-defense frameworks are predominantly domain-specific, addressing either clinical data protection or financial fraud prevention in isolation, yet failing to address the systemic interdependencies inherent in converged environments. This paper proposes a novel Self-Healing Cyber-Defense Framework (SHCDF) for converged healthcare-finance data infrastructures, drawing upon principles from self-healing networks, cyber-physical systems (CPS) resilience , and Large Language Model (LLM)-powered threat analysis. The framework integrates ML-based anomaly detection, Natural Language Processing (NLP) for cyber-threat intelligence extraction, and an LLM-driven reasoning engine that provides human-interpretable explanations for automated defense decisions. Evaluation across five threat categories ransomware, data exfiltration, phishing, payment fraud, and IoMT device compromise demonstrates an average recall of 89.6% and mean time-to-recovery (MTTR) of 3.3 minutes. Our findings contribute a generalizable architecture for cross-domain cyber resilience and highlight open challenges in regulatory compliance, model interpretability, and deployment scalability.
