Agentic AI-driven human digital twins for personalized healthcare: a comprehensive survey
abstract: Abstract Human Digital Twins (HDTs) are an innovative concept in the field of personalized medicine, relying on real-time models of a human body formed via collection and analysis of physiological, clinical, behavioural, and environmental data. Research on HDTs gives evidence to a considerable promise in terms of disease predictions, patient management, therapy optimization, and clinical decision-making. Nevertheless, existing technologies suffer from incomplete multimodal data integration, low-level of independent intelligence, missing reasoning possibilities, and non-adaptive decision making, which are vital for the development of sophisticated smart healthcare systems. Technological advancements are bringing in a new incorporating idea of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) and Multimodal Foundation Models (MFMs), which may help to solve the outlined limitations and to bring autonomous reasoning, multimodal learning, and intelligent support to clinical practice. This survey aims to review Agentic AI-led HDTs for personalized medicine, concentrating on the interrelation between HDTs and Multimodal Foundation Models, Large Language Models, Vision-Language Models, and autonomous artificial intelligence agents Our study discusses the history, models, supporting technologies, multiple data sources, and clinical uses of HDTs, along with the analysis of Agentic AI approaches that can be applied for flexible decision-making, continuous patient monitoring, and individualized treatment development. Besides, this survey consists of comparative analysis of existing research works where methods, advantages, disadvantages, and research challenges are specified. There are also serious issues discussed, like interoperability, justification, confidentiality ensuring, safety, ethical regulation, clinical testing and legal compliance, etc. And finally, we specify prospects of research within the fields of self-adaptive digital twins, reliable autonomous health agents, federated intelligence, edge AI and multimodal foundations focused on healthcare.

title: Progress in organic nanomaterials mediated healthcare biosensing
abstract: Deteriorating food quality and stress-ridden professional commitments have severely affected the health quality and physical efficacy, making it mandatory to monitor the food quality for cautiously limiting the intake of processed eatables. With exposure to debilitating environmental toxins remaining unabated, regular checkups have emerged as essential for adopting timely cautions. In this context, nanomaterials (NMs) are progressing as current focus for accurate and cost-effective screening of pathogens, environmental and industrial contaminants posing health risks. Progress in functionalization assays and characterization methods has improved the understanding quantum effects and combinatorial functioning in NMs for their biosensing applications. Diversified into organic, inorganic and carbon based textures, NMs provide innovative remedies through their size-morphology graded physicochemical properties and enhanced surface area-enriched chemistry. This article focuses on healthcare-biosensing utilities of organic NMs, with thrust on the structural correlations and comparative aspects for a sustainable future. Illustrations herein comprise the recent use of polymer nanocomposites, dendrimers, hydrogels, thin film-assemblies and molecularly engineered polymers. The discussion on biosensing probe-attributes of these NMs could reinforce their modifications for enhanced accuracy and functionality.

title: Experience of Bi-directional Referral Project between National Taiwan University Hospital Medical Center and Taipei City Hospital, Zhongxiao Campus Community Hospital
abstract: Abstract Background Overcrowding in medical center's emergency departments may threaten quality and safety of health services. The aim of our study is to retrospectively evaluate the practice of bi-directional referral project between National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH) medical center and Taipei City Hospital Zhongxiao Branch community hospital. Methods We retrospectively collected data from 38 electric and paper records of nineteen age- and gender-matched concurrent control patients without bi-directional referral and nineteen case patients who received bi-directional referral between NTUH Medical Center and Zhongxiao Community Hospital from January 1st, 2017 to November 30th, 2017. Patients admitted not due to bidirectional referral during the same period were used as a control group. Mortality rate, rate of transfer back to National Taiwan University Hospital, 11-point satisfaction rating scale are used as key performance indexes of quality improvement of clinical services. Satisfaction of the enrolled patients was evaluated with the questionnaires containing satisfaction rating scale 0-10. An independent samples t test was used to compare the means of variables between the ESI triage level 2 and ESI triage level 3 groups. Results The ESI (emergency severity index) triage level 2 patients were significantly older than the ESI triage level 3 patients with non-significant p value of Levene's test indicating equal variance between the control and case groups, but there was no significant difference of average total satisfaction (TSAT) score of bidirectional referrals between these two ESI groups. Mortality rate is zero. Rate of transfer back to NTUH is zero. The average TSAT score of case group is 8.89± 0.81 while the average TSAT score of the control group is 9.40± 0.31.Both the average TSAT scores of the case and control groups were above 8. Conclusion Early orienting of the admission of elderly patients on bi- directional referral system was demonstrated in this study. The parameters of quality of health care of the case group are comparable to those of the control group. The 0% mortality rate, 0% rate of transfer back to NTUH and good average TSAT score suggest that the referral program is safe and the quality of clinical services of these bi-directional referral patients is good.

Code With Care: A Strategic Blueprint for Nurse‐Led AI in Healthcare
abstract: AIM: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping healthcare delivery. This work aims to explore how nursing expertise can be fully integrated into the development of AI-based health technologies and to assess the implications for clinical practice, education, leadership, industry, policy and research. METHODS: This qualitative expert elicitation study drew on data generated during a structured three-day international think tank hosted by the Brocher Foundation in November 2024. Interdisciplinary experts in nursing, informatics, ethics, philosophy, medicine, computer science and law participated in structured presentations, facilitated subgroup discussions, plenary synthesis activities and collaborative development of recommendations. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to analyse workshop outputs and identify cross-cutting patterns, tensions and implications. RESULTS: Six interrelated thematic findings were generated. Participants framed nursing expertise as a form of sociotechnical governance rather than simply end-user input: (1) nurses were positioned as co-developers who can shape AI problem definition, design and implementation; (2) AI education was viewed as building critical interpretive capacity, not only technical literacy; (3) structural barriers limited nurse participation in innovation; (4) legal and ethical concerns reflected a gap between accountability and authority; (5) nurses were positioned as frontline actors for identifying AI bias and inequity; and (6) competency frameworks were viewed as tools for clarifying role-specific expectations in AI-enabled care. DISCUSSION: The findings suggest that embedding nursing expertise in healthcare AI is a matter of sociotechnical governance, requiring attention to organisational structures, education, legal accountability, professional roles and mechanisms for identifying safety, equity and workflow concerns. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION: This study provides an expert-informed framework for strengthening nursing participation in healthcare AI development. While the recommendations require empirical validation, they indicate priority areas for action, including nurse-led innovation, competence development, cross-sector collaboration, and educational and policy frameworks that recognise nursing expertise in AI development. REPORTING METHOD: The study adhered to the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (SRQR) guidelines.

title: Green Hospital Implementation for Sustainable and Resilient Health Systems in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Scoping Review
journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Health Management
abstract: Introduction. Health care both protects population health and drives environmental harm through energy use, waste, and greenhouse-gas emissions. The Green Hospital concept links environmental sustainability with hospital resilience, but evidence from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) is fragmented. Objective. To map evidence on Green Hospital implementation in LMICs; identify enablers and barriers; characterize measurement approaches; quantify reporting of health, economic, and equity outcomes; and synthesize a conceptual framework of pathways from governance to population health. Methods. Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, registered on the Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/F2BR5). PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and ScienceDirect were searched for English-language peer-reviewed empirical studies published from January 2009 to October 2025 from countries classified by the World Bank (FY2025) as low-, lower-middle-, or upper-middle-income. Screening and charting were performed in duplicate. Results. Twenty-nine studies were included, concentrated in lower-middle-income settings (20/29), Sub-Saharan Africa (11/29), and South Asia (7/29). Implementation clustered in waste management, water and sanitation, energy efficiency, and green infrastructure, with limited resilience integration. Leading enablers were leadership commitment, regulatory support, and institutional awareness; leading barriers were financial constraints, weak technical capacity, fragmented governance, and non-standardized indicators. Life-cycle assessment and multi-criteria decision-making predominated. Three gaps were quantified: one study reported a population health outcome, and only as a cross-sectional association; three reported cost data and none a formal economic evaluation; none disaggregated findings by occupational group, rurality or ownership. Conclusion. The literature maps a Green Hospital agenda concentrated in foundational environmental domains and weakly connected to resilience-oriented governance and performance systems. Because studies were predominantly cross-sectional, pathways from intervention to resilience and health are presented as hypothesized propositions requiring testing. The next priority is to align harmonized environmental key performance indicators with hospital accreditation.

title: Door-to-balloon performance, determinants, and clinical outcomes in low- and middle-income countries: a systematic review
abstract: Abstract Background Door-to-balloon (D2B) time is an important quality indicator in the management of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) treated with primary percutaneous coronary intervention (pPCI). Reperfusion delays remain common in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This systematic review evaluated D2B performance, factors associated with timely or delayed reperfusion and reported clinical outcomes in LMIC settings. Methods PubMed and Embase were searched from inception to 1 st August 2026. Studies reporting D2B time, related reperfusion intervals, target attainment, determinants of delay, or associated outcomes among adults with STEMI undergoing pPCI in LMICs were included. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Because of substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively. Results Twenty-four studies collectively enrolling 29,319 patients with STEMI across 11 LMIC settings were included. Conventional study-level D2B estimates ranged from 34 to 169 min. Among 17 studies with conventional D2B estimates that could be classified relative to the 90 min benchmark, 12 reported values consistently within 90 min and five reported values exceeding 90 min; three additional studies reported subgroup or intervention-period estimates spanning the threshold. Reported facilitators included continuous pPCI availability, single-call catheterisation-laboratory activation, simulation-based team training, direct emergency-department-to-catheterisation-laboratory transfer, regular audit and feedback, ambulance presentation, and organised referral networks. Reported barriers included delayed presentation, interhospital transfer, limited emergency medical service utilisation, reduced out-of-hours capacity, financial or administrative processes, treatment-consent delays, and movement or transport restrictions. Crude in-hospital mortality ranged from 1.0% to 24.3%. Several studies reported associations between longer reperfusion intervals and mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events, or myocardial injury. Conclusions D2B performance varied substantially across LMIC settings. Protocolised activation, continuous pPCI availability, multidisciplinary training, and coordinated referral pathways were reported alongside shorter treatment intervals, whereas prehospital, transfer, financial, and administrative delays remained important barriers. Quality-improvement programmes should address total ischaemic time rather than D2B time alone.

title: Surgical Care of Birth Defects in Low‐ and Middle‐Income Countries: Bangladesh Perspective
Burden, clinical characteristics, management, and outcomes of pediatric acute heart failure in emergency and acute-care settings in low- and middle-income countries: a scoping review
abstract: Pediatric acute heart failure (AHF) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, but its clinical presentation, management, and outcomes in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) remain poorly characterized. This scoping review mapped the available evidence on pediatric AHF in emergency and acute-care settings in LMICs. Following Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews, PubMed/MEDLINE, Global Index Medicus, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception through June 2026. AHF was defined as new or worsening heart failure requiring unplanned acute hospital care, including acute decompensation of chronic heart failure. Primary studies reporting AHF or acute decompensated heart failure among neonates, infants, children, and adolescents receiving unplanned acute hospital care in LMICs were eligible. Data were charted across burden, clinical characteristics, etiology, diagnosis and triage, acute management, outcomes, and health-system and equity domains and results were synthesized narratively. Of 1,124 records identified, 33 studies from 16 LMICs were included​. Most were single-center observational studies; the median sample size was 42 children, and 18 studies enrolled fewer than 50 participants. Infants and preschool-aged children predominated, except in rheumatic disease cohorts. Presentations were typically severe and congestion-dominated, with respiratory distress and hepatomegaly frequently reported; 71%–94% of children were in modified Ross or New York Heart Association class III–IV where severity was graded. In unselected emergency and general pediatric populations, infection and severe anemia commonly precipitated AHF, whereas congenital heart disease, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, and rheumatic disease predominated in cardiology and intensive-care cohorts. Region-specific, potentially reversible causes included cardiac beriberi and epidemic dropsy. Where AHF was ascertained in unselected p​ediatric admissions, it accounted for 4.0%–10.8% of admissions; PICU and disease-specific estimates are reported separately. All-cause in-hospital mortality ranged from 3.2% to 39.7%, with disease-specific cohorts reporting lower case fatality. Late presentation independently predicted mortality in one two-center study. Diagnosis frequently depended on clinical criteria and basic investigations, while access to echocardiography, specialist care, cardiac surgery, and mechanical circulatory support varied markedly. Health-system exposures were formally evaluated in only three studies. Available evidence depicts pediatric AHF in LMIC acute-care settings as a severe condition that presents late, predominantly affecting​ young children, and is often precipitated by conditions that are preventable or treatable. There is an urgent need for prospective multicenter studies at the initial point of contact, utilizing standardized definitions, minimum datasets, and within specified outcome periods.

title: Barriers to quality post-abortion care in low and middle-income countries: a systematic review
journal: International Journal of Community Medicine and Public Health
abstract: Post-abortion care (PAC) is a vital component of reproductive healthcare and essential for reducing abortion-related morbidity and mortality. Despite improvements in service availability, barriers affecting the quality and utilization of PAC services remain common across low-and middle-income countries (LMICs). The review was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, Google scholar and Open search database by following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (PROSPERO registration: CRD420261425414). The peer-reviewed studies published between 2010 and 2026 were screened according to inclusion criteria. Study selection was performed using Rayyan Software, and methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tools. Five major categories of barriers were identified; Knowledge and awareness barriers; Socio-cultural, financial, and geographic barriers; provider-related and quality -of-care barriers; health-system and facility-level barriers; and policy and legal barriers. The common challenges included abortion-related stigma, limited awareness of services, financial hardship, inadequate counselling, shortage of trained providers, weak referral systems, and insufficient infrastructure. Barriers to quality post -abortion care are multidimensional, and addressing these barriers through coordinated interventions may improve access, quality and utilization of post-abortion care services and help bridge the persistent access-quality gap in LMICs.

title: Prescription Patterns in Terminal Cancer Patients: A Prospective Study in a Low- and Middle-Income Country Setting
abstract: Objectives: The objective of the study is to evaluate prescription patterns from admission (Ta) to discharge/death (Td), assess associations between symptom burden and medication use and identify significant co-prescription patterns contributing to polypharmacy. Materials and Methods: A prospective observational cohort study was conducted in an acute palliative care unit of a tertiary cancer hospital (n = 219). Medications were categorised using the World Health Organization anatomical therapeutic chemical codes. Symptom burden was assessed at Ta using the Symptom Assessment Scale. McNemar and Chi-square tests examined changes in prescribing; Pearson correlation assessed relationships between symptom burden and medication use. Results: Polypharmacy was common (mean ~7.5 medications) throughout admission. Opioids (73%), antacids (68%), laxatives (48.9%) and corticosteroids (48.9%) were most frequent at Td. Significant co-prescription patterns included prophylactic combinations (opioid-laxative, corticosteroid-antiulcer, non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs–antiulcer; p < 0.05), symptom cluster management (opioid-anxiolytic, opioid-propulsives; p < 0.001) and potential medication-induced prescribing patterns (gabapentinoid-diuretic; p = 0.035). Individual symptoms predicted the use of relevant medication classes, but overall symptom burden did not predict total medication load at Td (r = 0.056, p = 0.408), indicating cascade-driven rather than symptom-driven polypharmacy. Only 63.6% of medications aligned with the International Association of Hospice and Palliative Care Essential Medicines List. Conclusion: Persistent polypharmacy and identifiable preventive co-prescribing patterns suggest opportunities for targeted interventions, including structured deprescribing, pharmacist-led reviews and development of LMIC-specific essential medicines lists.

title: Leadership and governance mechanisms for routine emergency care service delivery in low- and middle-income countries: a rapid review
abstract: ## Project description Emergency care provides time-sensitive services for people with acute illness or injury across the continuum from care at the scene and prehospital transport to referral, hospital emergency units and early inpatient management. In many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), these services remain fragmented across organisations and levels of the health system. Strengthening emergency care therefore requires more than clinical training, equipment and infrastructure. It also requires appropriate leadership, clear institutional responsibilities, coordination between organisations, regulation, sustainable financing, information systems, accountability and mechanisms for monitoring performance. Although studies have described different leadership and governance arrangements for emergency care in LMICs, the available evidence is diverse and has not been synthesised sufficiently to identify which mechanisms have been used in routine emergency care and what factors affect their implementation. This project is a rapid review of leadership and governance mechanisms used for routine emergency care service delivery in LMICs. The review will address two questions: first, what leadership and governance mechanisms have been used for routine emergency care service delivery in LMICs; and second, what barriers and facilitators affect the implementation of these mechanisms? The corresponding objectives are to identify and describe relevant mechanisms and map them to the ten health-system governance domains proposed by Siddiqi et al.; and to synthesise the factors that hinder or support their introduction, adoption, implementation, operation, scale-up and sustainability. The review will include routine emergency care delivered at community or scene level, through dispatch, ambulance and prehospital services, during emergency transport and interfacility referral, in hospital emergency departments or emergency units, and during initial stabilisation or early inpatient care directly related to an emergency episode. Mechanisms operating at national, subnational, district, inter-organisational, facility or community level will be considered. Eligible mechanisms may include policies and strategic plans, designated leadership structures, emergency-care committees, interagency coordination arrangements, legislation and regulation, service standards, accreditation, stakeholder participation, accountability systems, supervision, audit and feedback, performance monitoring, information systems, registries and referral-governance arrangements. A mechanism will be eligible when it relates to at least one of the Siddiqi governance domains: strategic vision; participation and consensus orientation; rule of law; transparency; responsiveness; equity and inclusiveness; effectiveness and efficiency; accountability; intelligence and information; and ethics. The review will include original qualitative, quantitative and mixed-methods studies; case studies; implementation studies; programme or process evaluations; health-system assessments; and sufficiently detailed government or organisational reports. Eligible publications must concern an LMIC, be available in English, and have been published from January 2005 to the final search date. Studies focusing only on clinical treatment, diagnostic accuracy, clinical triage tools, training, equipment, infrastructure or workforce capacity without a leadership or governance component will be excluded. Studies limited to disaster, pandemic, humanitarian or mass-casualty response will also be excluded because the review focuses on routine emergency care. For the second objective, barriers and facilitators will be included only when they are empirically or clearly linked to an identifiable leadership or governance mechanism. General challenges in emergency care and unsupported author opinions or recommendations will not be treated as implementation findings. The search will use a staged rapid-review approach. Publications included in the scoping review by Phillips et al. covering January 2005 to April 2024 will be obtained and rescreened using the eligibility criteria of the present review. An updated bibliographic search will identify studies published from May 2024 to the final search date. PubMed/MEDLINE will be the primary bibliographic database, with WHO Global Index Medicus used to improve coverage of regional literature. The database search will combine concepts relating to routine emergency care, leadership and governance, organisation and administration, LMIC settings, and barriers and facilitators affecting implementation. Supplementary searching will include predefined Google Scholar queries, backward reference searching, forward citation searching and a separate search for relevant reviews. The search will be validated against known relevant publications and the full search methods, dates, strings and retrieval counts will be documented. Records will be managed using Zotero and Rayyan. Following deduplication, screening will proceed in two stages: title and abstract screening followed by full-text assessment. Reviewers will first complete a calibration exercise using predefined eligibility criteria. After achieving adequate agreement, one reviewer will screen the remaining records, while a second reviewer will verify a random sample of title and abstract exclusions, all uncertain records and all full-text exclusions. One principal reason will be documented for every record excluded after full-text assessment. Multiple publications from the same study or programme will be linked and treated as one study during synthesis. Data will be extracted using a standardised and piloted spreadsheet. Study-level data will include publication characteristics, country, study design, participants, emergency-care setting and governance level. Mechanism-level data will include the name and description of each mechanism, its purpose, responsible actors, stakeholders, scale, duration, implementation status and Siddiqi governance domain. Each distinct barrier or facilitator will be linked to the mechanism it affects, together with its source, implementation stage, level of operation and reported influence on implementation. Where available, reported effects on coordination, decision-making, accountability, service availability, access, timeliness, quality, continuity, responsiveness, equity, efficiency and sustainability will also be extracted. One reviewer will complete extraction, and a second reviewer will verify all key analytical information and a sample of descriptive variables. All included studies and reports will undergo design-appropriate critical appraisal. The Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool will be used for qualitative, quantitative descriptive and mixed-methods studies. RoB 2 will be used if eligible randomised studies are identified, ROBINS-I will be used for non-randomised comparative intervention studies, and the AACODS checklist will be used for grey-literature reports without a clearly defined empirical design. Studies will not be excluded solely because of methodological limitations; instead, appraisal findings will inform interpretation and confidence in the review findings. A structured narrative synthesis will be undertaken because substantial variation is expected in study designs, governance mechanisms, emergency-care settings and reported outcomes. The included studies will first be described by country, income group, study design, emergency-care setting and governance level. Leadership and governance mechanisms will then be mapped to the Siddiqi domains. Barriers and facilitators will be linked to the specific mechanisms whose implementation they affect and grouped into clear subthemes. Similarities and differences will be examined across countries, regions, income groups, emergency-care settings, governance levels, sectors and stakeholder groups. Equity considerations will be examined where studies report differences by rural or urban location, socioeconomic position, sex or gender, disability, geographical access or other underserved population characteristics. Formal meta-analysis is not planned. Where comparable quantitative effect estimates are available, they will be summarised using appropriate methods for synthesis without meta-analysis, and certainty may be assessed using GRADE. Confidence in the principal qualitative findings concerning barriers, facilitators and the operation of governance mechanisms will be assessed using GRADE-CERQual. These assessments will be restricted to the main findings that directly address the review questions. The expected outcome is a structured overview of the leadership and governance mechanisms used for routine emergency care in LMICs, organised according to the Siddiqi governance framework. The review will identify recurring barriers and facilitators, clarify the settings and governance levels in which they operate, describe important differences across contexts and highlight gaps in the available evidence. It is expected to generate findings that can assist policymakers, health-system managers, emergency-care programme managers and service providers in selecting, adapting and implementing governance arrangements for routine emergency care. Planned outputs include a complete rapid-review report or scientific manuscript, summary tables and evidence maps, and a concise policy brief presenting the principal governance mechanisms, implementation considerations and research priorities. As the project is based entirely on published and publicly available evidence, it will not involve recruitment of human participants or collection of identifiable personal information.

title: Cancer outcomes in low and middle-income countries: the role of clinical, sociodemographics, and public funding as drivers
abstract: Abstract Introduction Cancer burden is rising in Uganda, as in many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), with most patients presenting late due to limited access to diagnostic and treatment services. Sustained government investment, strengthened by the Uganda Cancer Institute Act of 2016, has enabled development of a comprehensive cancer care system, including palliative care and population-based cancer registration. This study examines trends in cancer outcomes at the Uganda Cancer Institute (UCI), highlighting the impact of public financing and the role of clinical and sociodemographic factors in shaping cancer care. Methods We reviewed patient records at UCI from January 2020 to December 2024. The study population included all adult patients with confirmed diagnoses of breast, prostate, Kaposi sarcoma (KS), cervix, and esophageal cancer. Descriptive statistics summarized sociodemographic and disease-related variables, while mortality-to-incidence ratios (MIRs) were calculated as a proxy for survival. MIRs were modelled over five years using beta regression with a logit link, adjusting for clinical and sociodemographic factors as well as public funding. Analyses were conducted in Stata (v19) and R (v4.5.0) using anonymized Electronic Medical Records data Results During the study period, 12,438 new cancer patients were registered. Cervix (29.4%), breast (24.5%), prostate (21.4%), esophagus (16.2%), and KS (8.5%) were the most common cancers. Prostate cancer had the lowest MIR (6.3%), followed by KS (11.5%), cervical (14%), breast (23%), and esophageal cancer (33%). Living outside metropolitan Kampala was associated with higher MIR (β = 0.108, p < 0.001), while HIV-positive status increased MIR (β = 0.082, p = 0.012). Diagnosis site type was strongly predictive, and higher government investment was consistently associated with reduced MIRs. Conclusion Sustained public investment in cancer care at UCI has led to improved outcomes, including increased survival and reduced mortality. These findings demonstrate that deliberate investment in cancer care is cost-effective in LMICs and can serve as a model for broader health system strengthening. Expansion through comprehensive cancer control programs integrating prevention, early detection, and referral mechanisms is essential

title: Respectful maternity care in low- and middle-income countries: a narrative review of evidence, implementation challenges, and future directions
abstract: Respectful maternity care (RMC) is increasingly recognized as a fundamental component of quality maternal healthcare and a basic human right. Despite global efforts to maximize facility-based deliveries, widespread institutional mistreatment, abuse, and neglect continue to compromise maternal safety and undermine public trust in healthcare systems. This narrative review offers a timely, comprehensive synthesis of evidence from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) between 2015 and 2026. It provides a critical assessment of the multi-level architecture shaping RMC by mapping how individual provider behaviors, facility infrastructure, systemic health policies, and deep-seated socio-cultural norms intersect to influence childbirth experiences. Methods: A narrative review framework was utilized to evaluate peer-reviewed articles, international agency reports, and national policy documents published from 2015 to 2026. A structured, four-stage screening process was deployed to select and map core clinical and structural literature regarding RMC implementation, barriers, facilitators, and outcomes across diverse LMIC settings. Results: The evidence synthesis was organized into four main areas: defining the dimensions of RMC; examining the consequences of mistreatment; identifying structural and system-level barriers; and describing facilitators of respectful care. Respectful maternity care was associated with greater maternal satisfaction, trust, and utilization of facility-based maternity services; however, implementation was constrained by workforce shortages, professional burnout, inadequate infrastructure, and weak accountability mechanisms. The review also proposes an actionable framework that links interconnected barriers, including facility-level overcrowding and socio-cultural power imbalances, with context-specific, multilevel intervention strategies. This framework provides a practical approach for translating human-rights principles into everyday maternity-care practice. Conclusion: Respectful maternity care is a critical component of quality maternal healthcare and a fundamental human-rights concern. Sustainable improvement requires context-sensitive, multilevel strategies that address provider behavior, facility conditions, health-system constraints, community engagement, and accountability. This review provides a synthesis of evidence that may inform clinicians, policymakers, researchers, and other stakeholders seeking to strengthen respectful maternity care across diverse LMIC settings. The proposed actionable framework may support context-specific implementation planning, although further research is needed to evaluate and refine its feasibility and validity.

title: Privacy-enhancing technologies for next-generation miniaturised biosensors: towards equitable deployment in low- and middle-income countries
abstract: The rapid miniaturisation of biosensors, be it wearable health monitors, point-of-care diagnostics, and community-scale environmental sensing, has enabled health data collection at a rapidly increasing and more distributed scale across Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs). This rise in the scale of adoption in LMICs is due to these technologies becoming more feasible, portable, and orientated toward low-resource deployment. Yet the Privacy-Enhancing Technologies (PETs) developed to protect these data were designed and validated in high-income, high-compute contexts. This Perspective argues that deploying next-generation miniaturised biosensors for LMICs without rethinking the PET design agenda risks compounding existing health inequities. Current PET implementations face three structural mismatches with LMIC biosensor deployment: the computational overhead of secure multiparty computation and homomorphic encryption exceeds the resource envelope of low-power edge devices; differential privacy can disproportionately degrade model utility for underrepresented populations when datasets are small, imbalanced, or hard to model, conditions that are endemic to LMIC biosensor cohorts; and regulatory-technical translation remains underdeveloped in the jurisdictions where biosensor rollout is accelerating fastest. We propose a reorientation around three design principles: computational proportionality (matching PET selection to hardware constraints), equity-aware privacy budgeting (calibrating differential privacy parameters to population representation), and community data sovereignty (architecting local governance into federated biosensor networks). We identify five priority research questions that reframe the field’s open challenges through an LMIC lens. The goal is not to caution against biosensor deployment, but to ensure that privacy-by-design is embedded in the next-generation of sensing systems, while accounting for adoption challenges and broader digital transformation in resource-constrained health systems.

title: Real‐world effectiveness of pain pharmacotherapy for caesarean section in a low‐ and middle‐income setting: A multicentre cross‐sectional study in Ghana
Barriers to rational antibiotic prescription in hospitals: a qualitative study in a developing country
abstract: Abstract Background Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing global threat. Antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs) represent a key strategy to combat AMR and to minimize the adverse effects associated with antibiotic use. Implementing ASPs in hospital settings faces significant challenges and barriers, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This study aims to identify the barriers to the implementation of ASPs in Iranian hospitals. Methods This qualitative study was conducted in 2023–2024, involving 41 stakeholders in antibiotic prescription within five public hospitals in Iran. The participants included physicians, administrators, pharmacologists, pharmacists, the secretary of the stewardship committee, microbiologists, laboratory managers, ICU nurses, nurse managers, quality improvement managers, infection control officers, and information technology managers. Participants were recruited using a convenience sampling method. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using conventional content analysis techniques. Results The barriers to implementing ASPs were categorized into three main categories, nine subcategories as follows: (1) Deficiencies in intelligent surveillance and monitoring of antibiotics prescribing (including inadequate health information technology for ongoing collection, collation and analysis of antibiotic prescribing pattern, and poor audit, and feedback mechanisms in HIS); (2) Deficiencies in health system governance, policies, and regulatory frameworks (including weak policy framework and clinical guidelines, limited policy learning and contextual adaptation and legal and regulatory gaps affecting clinical practice); and (3) Deficiencies in hospital-wide management and support structure (including poor organizational governance and structural capacity, ineffective interprofessional collaboration, weak leadership commitment and low stakeholder engagement, and inadequate professional competencies and limited technical skills). Conclusion The study underscores the multifaceted and heterogeneous nature of barriers to the implementation of ASPs in a LMIC. Enhancing information technology infrastructure, optimizing antibiotic prescribing practices, engaging physicians, strengthening financial and human resource capacity, and fostering supportive management attitudes were identified as potential effective strategies for facilitating successful ASP implementation in hospital settings in a LMIC.

title: Overcoming Barriers in the Treatment of Limited-Stage Small Cell Lung Cancer With a Focus on Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Narrative Review
abstract: Limited-stage small cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC) accounts for a portion of all SCLC cases yet remains associated with a high mortality burden, particularly in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs), where early diagnosis and access to multimodality care are often constrained.This narrative review examines the epidemiology, diagnostic approaches, staging systems, and treatment strategies for LS-SCLC, with a focus on practical solutions suitable for limited-resource settings.Accurate staging through computed tomography (CT), positron emission tomography-CT, brain magnetic resonance imaging, and histopathological confirmation is essential for curative management but remains inconsistently available in many LMICs.Concurrent platinum-based chemotherapy with thoracic radiotherapy continues to form the backbone of treatment.Twice-daily thoracic radiotherapy (45 Gy) remains a preferred reference regimen, whereas once-daily schedules are frequently used when twice-daily treatment is impractical.Prophylactic cranial irradiation can reduce the risk of brain metastases but requires individualised selection to avoid neurocognitive harm; hippocampal-sparing techniques reduce this toxicity.For small, localised tumours, stereotactic body radiotherapy provides high local control and low toxicity.Immunotherapy, which has redefined outcomes in extensive-stage disease, has also changed practice in LS-SCLC.For eligible patients with LS-SCLC without disease progression after concurrent platinum-etoposide chemoradiotherapy (CRT), consolidation durvalumab is now an evidence-based contemporary standard of care, whereas concurrent use of immunotherapy during CRT remains investigational.Persistent barriers, including limited radiotherapy capacity, delayed presentation, and inadequate multidisciplinary coordination, highlight the need for structured referral pathways, registry development, and policy-level collaboration to enhance equity and survival in LS-SCLC worldwide.

title: Regulatory and Accreditation Systems and Their Association With Health Workforce and Healthcare Quality in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review and Policy Analysis
abstract: Purpose: To synthesize evidence on the association between regulatory and accreditation systems and health workforce and healthcare quality in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), and to analyze the policy factors that shape their implementation. Methods: A systematic review reported according to PRISMA 2020. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar were searched for English-language literature published between January 2010 and March 2026. Eligible sources examined regulatory or accreditation mechanisms in at least one LMIC and were analyzed as three separate evidence streams: primary empirical studies, evidence syntheses, and policy or programme analyses. Quality was appraised with design-specific tools (CASP, Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, QuADS, AMSTAR 2 and AACODS). Evidence was synthesized narratively using thematic synthesis, and a literature-based policy analysis applied Walt and Gilson's Policy Triangle. Responsive Regulation Theory and Institutional Theory were used as interpretive lenses. Results: Of 1,243 records, 35 sources met the inclusion criteria (21 primary studies, 7 evidence syntheses and 7 policy or programme analyses). Sources came from the Middle East and North Africa (n = 12, of which 7 were from Iran), sub-Saharan Africa (n = 6), East and South Asia (n = 4) and Latin America (n = 1), with 12 multi-country sources. Thirty-two sources concerned accreditation of health facilities; only two addressed medical education accreditation and one addressed regulation of individual health professionals. Evidence was concentrated at the level of institutional processes (24 sources), where accreditation was associated with standardized procedures, documentation, internal quality assurance and governance structures. Few sources measured workforce-level outcomes (n = 3), and associations with clinical quality were mixed: the two primary impact evaluations reported divergent results. Recurrent barriers included inadequate financing, assessor shortages, fragmented governance, weak enforcement and documentation burden. Conclusion: The available evidence suggests that regulatory and accreditation systems in LMICs are associated with improvements in institutional quality processes, particularly when supportive follow-up accompanies graduated requirements. Evidence that they improve health workforce competence or patient outcomes remains limited. Controlled evaluations of licensing, continuing professional development and education accreditation in LMICs are needed.

title: TSH newborn screening dried blood spot rejection rates: A two-year experience from low-middle income country
abstract: Background: Preanalytical errors in dried blood spot (DBS) sampling delay critical congenital hypothyroidism diagnosis, particularly in resource-limited settings. This study evaluates temporal shifts in DBS rejection rates across East Java, Indonesia (2024 vs. 2025), and identifies evolving clinical patterns of sampling errors to guide targeted quality improvement strategies. Methods: This retrospective study combined aggregated district-level data (38 districts; N = 770,854 screenings) with individual-level data from a subset of rejected samples (N = 931). Wilcoxon signed-rank tests compared paired programmatic outcomes; Mann-Whitney U and Chi-square tests analyzed individual-level data using IBM SPSS statistics version 29.0 for Windows. Results: Total screenings increased 7.0% from 2024 (N = 372,454) to 2025 (N = 398,400). Median rejected samples per district decreased significantly from 373.0 to 359.5 (p = 0.004), but rejection rates did not change significantly (4.07% to 3.61%; p = 0.243). Extreme inter-district disparity persisted (0.44%-25.20%). Monthly analysis revealed significant improvements in January (p = 0.003), February (p < 0.001), and June (p = 0.023). A total of 931 DBS samples were rejected, with the distribution of rejection causes shifting significantly (p < 0.001). The rejection type of “small sample” decreased from 16.8% to 7.9%, while samples with “hemolysis” increased from 20.0% to 29.2%. Conclusion: While overall rejection rates remained stable, the newborn screening (NBS) program drove a significant structural transition in preanalytical error patterns—successfully reducing basic collection errors while encountering an emerging vulnerability in specimen handling (hemolysis). These novel insights demonstrate that scaling up NBS in low- and middle-income countries requires a strategic evolution from universal training to data-driven, precision quality interventions.

title: Equity effects of digital primary care interventions in low-and middle-income countries: A systematic review using the PROGRESS-Plus framework

title: Reframing Trisomy 13 and 18 Care: Moving Beyond the Myth of “Incompatibility With Life” in a South African and Low‐and Middle‐Income Country Context
journal: American Journal of Medical Genetics Part A
abstract: Trisomy 13 (T13) and trisomy 18 (T18) have historically been described as "lethal" or "incompatible with life," contributing to diagnosis-based limitations of care. Contemporary evidence demonstrates greater heterogeneity in survival and outcomes than previously recognized, including among selected children receiving intensive care or cardiac surgery. Parental perspectives further challenge assumptions that quality of life and benefit can be inferred from diagnosis alone. This Commentary draws on contemporary evidence and multidisciplinary stakeholder discussions convened in Johannesburg in August 2025 to consider the implications for South Africa and comparable resource-constrained settings. South African pathways are shaped by inequities between public and private healthcare, uneven access to prenatal screening and diagnosis, limited specialist capacity, variable referral and care coordination, and the absence of nationally standardized T13/T18-specific guidance. Published local evidence on survival, intervention and family experiences remains limited. We argue that T13/T18 should be approached as medically complex and potentially life-limiting conditions requiring transparent, individualized and proportionate decision-making rather than predetermined non-intervention. Priorities include strengthened professional training, coordinated multidisciplinary referral pathways, balanced counselling and shared decision-making, integration of palliative care alongside disease-directed care, regional centers of expertise, improved data generation, rights-aligned governance and contextually appropriate adaptation of international guidance.

title: Impact of a Capillary Refill Time–Guided Personalised Hemodynamic Resuscitation Protocol in Septic Shock in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Post Hoc Analysis of the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 Trial
abstract: Abstract PURPOSE: To assess the treatment effect of capillary refill time–guided personalised hemodynamic resuscitation (CRT-PHR) in patients with early septic shock in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). METHODS: Post hoc analysis of the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 randomised clinical trial, conducted in 86 ICUs across 19 countries. Centres were classified according to World Bank income groups as LMICs or high-income countries (HICs). The primary outcome was a hierarchical composite of 28-day mortality, duration of vital organ support, and hospital length of stay, analysed using a stratified win ratio. RESULTS: Among 1,467 patients, 652 (44.4%) were treated in LMIC centres and 815 (55.6%) in HIC centres. Patients enrolled in LMICs were younger, had higher lactate levels, more frequent abnormal CRT, and greater baseline vasopressin use (59.4% vs 29.5%). Treatment-effect estimates were similar across income groups, with win ratios of 1.16 (95% CI 1.14–1.18) in LMICs and 1.18 (95% CI 1.17–1.20) in HICs, with no evidence of treatment-effect modification by country income level. Within LMICs, baseline lactate >4 mmol/L showed the strongest exploratory signal of heterogeneity (win ratio 1.57 vs 0.93; interaction p =0.002). Vasopressin use was associated with a numerically larger treatment-effect estimate (1.39 vs 1.12), but was not statistically significant. Centre-level analyses suggested heterogeneity by hospital and ICU size (interaction p =0.081 for both). CONCLUSION: Despite the marked differences in baseline severity, vasopressor use, and resuscitation practice, CRT-PHR produced consistent and significant treatment effects in both LMIC and HIC settings. Within LMICs, hyperlactatemia a centre-level heterogeneity identified contexts of differential benefit, underscoring limitations of national income classification as a proxy for local critical-care capacity.

title: Anti-Amyloid Monoclonal Antibodies in Alzheimer Disease: Weighing Modest Clinical Benefit Against ARIA Risk, Cost and Health System Readiness in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
abstract: Lecanemab and donanemab are the first drugs shown in phase 3 trials to slow clinical decline in early symptomatic Alzheimer disease by removing cerebral amyloid. Over roughly 18 months, lecanemab reduced progression on the Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) by 0.45 points, and donanemab by 0.67 points in its primary low/medium tau population. These are relative slowings of about a quarter to a third, yet neither difference reaches published thresholds for a minimal clinically important difference. The cost of that benefit is amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA). Oedema or effusion developed in 12.6% of lecanemab and 24.0% of donanemab recipients, rose to about one in three among APOE ε4 homozygotes, and was occasionally fatal. Safe prescribing therefore depends on biomarker confirmation of amyloid, APOE genotyping, repeated MRI, infusion capacity and clinicians able to recognise ARIA. This review appraises the efficacy and safety evidence and then tests it against conditions in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), home to more than 60% of people with dementia and to most of the projected rise from 57.4 million cases in 2019 to 152.8 million in 2050. Low-income countries have fewer than one CT scanner and 1.9 radiologists per million people, and one year of donanemab in India costs about 17 times national per capita gross domestic product in drug acquisition alone. At current prices and capacity, population-wide use is neither affordable nor safe in most LMICs. A staged model is proposed: timely diagnosis and risk-factor control for everyone, locally validated blood-biomarker triage at referral hubs, and antibody treatment confined to accredited centres with mandatory registries and prices negotiated against demonstrated value.

title: Unpaid Clinical "Volunteer” Roles in Low- and Middle-Income Health Systems: A Narrative Review of Workforce Governance and Patient Safety
abstract: Unpaid or unsalaried clinical "volunteer" roles are an underexamined workforce-governance issue in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This narrative review synthesized evidence on unpaid and unsalaried clinical work, labour-market transition, health-system governance, health-worker wellbeing, and patient safety. Targeted searches of PubMed, Google Scholar, World Health Organization (WHO), International Labour Organization (ILO), Cochrane, and grey-literature sources from 2000 to 2026 yielded 22 substantive sources: seven empirical or context-specific studies, six evidence reviews, and nine policy, technical, or country documents. Eight sources directly or closely described unpaid, unsalaried, volunteer, or transition-to-employment clinical roles. Evidence from Somalia, Sierra Leone, Nigeria, and Kenya confirms that such arrangements occur in several LMIC settings, although their prevalence and forms in private facilities remain poorly characterized. Across the wider evidence base, constrained employment absorption, weak supervision, poor working conditions, burnout, turnover, and limited reporting capacity are associated with workforce instability and patient-safety risk. The review develops a cautious framework linking enabling labour-market and governance conditions to workforce harms and plausible safety pathways, while distinguishing directly observed findings from contextual evidence. Clear role definitions, written documentation, supervision, worker protection, accountability, and setting-specific empirical research are priorities for healthcare leaders and regulators.

title: Community-Based Preeclampsia Screening by Midwives and Community Health Workers in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Scoping Review and Evidence-Informed Framework for Indonesia
abstract: Purpose: This scoping review mapped evidence on community-based preeclampsia screening delivered by midwives and community health workers (CHWs) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), identified implementation barriers and facilitators, and developed evidence-informed design requirements for an Indonesian community screening framework. Design and Methods: Guided by the Population-Concept-Context framework and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR, we searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for English-language studies published from 2016 to February 2026. A total of 133 records were identified across the databases. After deduplication and screening against prespecified eligibility criteria, nine studies were included in the scoping review. A structured data-charting form, informed by the review questions and Joanna Briggs Institute scoping-review guidance, was piloted using two purposefully selected studies before full extraction. Included evidence was mapped descriptively and synthesized thematically. Results: The included studies were conducted in Indonesia, Mozambique, Nigeria, India, Ecuador, South Africa, and other LMIC settings. The evidence, which was predominantly qualitative and mixed methods, suggested that community-level blood-pressure measurement, danger-sign assessment, simple decision support, and linkage to referral may be feasible and acceptable when supported by training, supervision, appropriate equipment, defined roles, documentation, and functional referral pathways. The evidence did not permit definitive conclusions about clinical effectiveness or safety across settings. Five implementation domains informed the proposed COMPREP Screen framework: workforce capability; tools and supplies; role clarity and accountability; documentation and data use; and referral-system functioning. Conclusion: Community-based screening led by midwives and CHWs may support earlier recognition of preeclampsia risk and timely linkage to facility-based assessment and care. Because the evidence base is limited and heterogeneous, COMPREP Screen should be regarded as an evidence-informed, context-sensitive framework that requires stakeholder validation and prospective implementation evaluation in Indonesia. Keywords: preeclampsia, community health workers, midwives, scoping review, antenatal care, low- and middle-income countries, referral

title: Traumatic brain injury from a developing country in the CT-scan era: a 13-year prospective in-hospital cohort study
abstract: Introduction Most previous reports from Africa and other low middle-income countries (LMIC) on cranial neurotrauma address a more loosely defined subject of head injury (HI), rather than traumatic brain injury (TBI), and lack deployment of standardized scoring systems. We present a prospective TBI cohort from an academic neurosurgery practice at Ibadan, Nigeria, the nation's foremost university teaching hospital where TBI constitutes a core component of our clinical activity. Materials and methods This was a prospective cohort study of patients enrolled in a TBI registry over 13 years. We analyzed the clinical epidemiology of TBI, defined as cranial trauma with definite perturbation of brain function, qualified/quantified using relevant clinical features, the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), the Abbreviated Injury Scale-Head (AIS-Head), and Injury Severity Score (ISS). Brain imaging was graded using the Rotterdam CT scoring system. In-hospital outcome was assessed with Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS), dichotomized for analysis. Results There were 1,440 TBI cases, 1,110 (77.1%) males, mean age [32.2 Standard deviation (SD), 19] years. Most (76%) were referrals, with delayed presentation from outlying health facilities, median duration 13 [interquartile range (IQR) 5, 48] hours. Road trauma accounted for 1,173 (82%), even in the elderly, predominantly by two- and three-wheelers (57%); fall for 136 (9.4%), this mainly in childhood. Clinically, loss of consciousness (LOC) occurred in 89%, median duration 11.0 (IQR 2, 48) hours, vomiting 25%, seizures 16%, and anisocoria in 27%. In 86% the AIS-head was >2; the TBI was moderate-severe, GCS 3–12, in 47.0%. Brain CT was obtained in 1,046/1,440 (72.6%), while 13% received acute operative treatment. In-hospital mortality was 21%, mostly among the young and the severely injured. Good outcome (GOS: good recovery/moderate deficit) was 75%. The outcomes were significantly associated with the TBI severity per the GCS scores and brain CT severity. Conclusions The clinical epidemiology of TBI from this single-institution LMIC series differs substantially from that of high-income countries. A 21% mortality predominantly affecting young economically productive adults represents a serious public health burden. Substantial gaps persist across many aspects of the TBI-management continuum, presenting clear opportunities to improve the current sub-optimal outcome-metrics in sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Home visits following hospital discharge for families with preterm and low-birthweight infants
abstract: RATIONALE: Home visiting programmes are widely used to support families of preterm and low-birthweight (LBW) infants after hospital discharge, yet evidence on their effectiveness is limited and of variable quality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). A comprehensive, up-to-date review was needed to inform healthcare decisions. OBJECTIVES: To assess the effectiveness of home visits following hospital discharge compared to standard of care or no home visits, for families/caregivers of preterm or LBW infants to reduce morbidity and mortality and enhance health and well-being. SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO ICTRP, together with reference checking, to identify eligible studies. The latest search date was April 2026. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of preterm and LBW infants and their caregivers comparing home visits after discharge from hospital with no home visits or standard of care including home visits. There were no restrictions on language or publication status. OUTCOMES: Our critical outcomes included all-cause mortality, neurodevelopment, morbidity, growth, breastfeeding rates, exclusive breastfeeding, and emergency hospital visits. Important outcomes were hospital readmission rates, maternal/parental emotional well-being, and maternal-infant interaction. RISK OF BIAS: We used Cochrane's RoB 2 tool to assess the risk of bias. SYNTHESIS METHODS: We synthesised results for each outcome in meta-analysis where possible, using random-effects models to calculate risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes, mean differences (MDs) or standardised mean differences (SMDs) for continuous outcomes, and hazard ratios (HRs) for time-to-event outcomes, along with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We used GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence for each outcome. INCLUDED STUDIES: We included 35 RCTs, of which 28 (12,021 infants and 10,056 mothers/caregivers) contributed data to our prespecified outcomes. Most studies were from high-income countries; however, approximately 70% of participants were from a large study in India contributing data to comparison 2. The content, timing, duration, and frequency of home visits varied widely. Twenty-one studies contributed data to meta-analyses. SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Home visits versus no home visits The effects of home visits on all-cause mortality at one year are very uncertain (RR 3.08, 95% CI 0.13 to 73.27; 1 study, 79 participants). Home visits may have little to no effect on cognitive development (SMD 0.06, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.29; 3 studies, 287 participants), and likely have little to no effect on motor development (SMD -0.02, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.33; 1 study, 127 participants). The effect on morbidity, specifically on diarrhoea at six months, is very uncertain (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.19; 1 study, 179 participants). Home visits likely have little to no effect on growth, specifically weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ) at six months (MD -0.09, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.18; 1 study, 179 participants). Home visits likely increase the proportion of infants breastfeeding at six months (RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.37; I² = 0%; 4 studies, 1217 participants) and may result in a large increase in exclusive breastfeeding at six months (RR 2.31, 95% CI 0.85 to 6.29; 3 studies, 1129 participants). The certainty of the evidence ranged from moderate to very low due to risk of bias and imprecision. More intensive home visits versus less intensive home visits (part of standard of care) Home visits with community-initiated kangaroo mother care likely reduce all-cause mortality at 6 months (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.93; 1 study, 8402 participants), likely have little to no effect on cognitive (MD 0.21, 95% CI -1.77 to 2.19; 1 study, 552 participants) or motor development (MD -0.85 95% CI -2.59 to 0.89; 1 trial, 552 participants) at 12 months, and likely reduce morbidity, specifically rates of diarrhoea slightly at 3 months (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.04; 1 study, 7654 participants) and the risk of possible serious bacterial infections slightly at 28 days (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.82 to 0.97; 1 study, 8384 participants). They likely have little to no effect on WAZ at six months (MD -0.01, 95% CI -0.06 to 0.04; 1 study, 7086 participants) and likely reduce the proportion of infants who are severely underweight at six months slightly (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.04; 1 study, 6641 participants). More intensive home visits may have little to no effect on breastfeeding at six months (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.59; 1 study, 308 participants), and their effect on exclusive breastfeeding at six months is very uncertain (RR 1.97, 95% CI 0.19 to 20.62; I² = 84%; 3 studies, 7091 participants). The certainty of the evidence was moderate for all outcomes except for breastfeeding and exclusive breastfeeding, for which it was low and very low, respectively. The certainty of evidence was downgraded for risk of bias, imprecision, and indirectness. No study in either comparison reported on emergency hospital visits. AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Home visits likely improve breastfeeding and may improve exclusive breastfeeding compared to no home visits. They may have little to no effect on cognitive development, and likely have little to no effect on motor development or growth. The effects on mortality or diarrhoea are very uncertain. In places where home visits are already implemented, enhancing them so that they are more intensive than the standard of care (i.e. more frequent, longer, delivered by specialised personnel, with kangaroo mother care, etc.) likely reduces mortality, morbidity, and the risk of underweight. However, they likely have little to no effect on cognitive and motor development or WAZ, and may have little to no effect on breastfeeding rates. The effects on exclusive breastfeeding are very uncertain. Better-quality studies are needed, particularly in LMICs. There is a need for studies reporting on the critical outcome of emergency hospital visits, and to standardise outcome measures reported in this area of research, particularly for mental health and neurodevelopment outcomes. FUNDING: This review was conducted for the GELA project (africa.cochrane.org/projects/GELA) which is funded as part of the EDCTP2 programme (grant number RIA2020S-3303-GELA) supported by the European Union. REGISTRATION: Protocol: CRD42024496298 registered on 15 January 2024 (PROSPERO), available at https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024496298.

title: Psychological Stress and Acute Myocardial Infarction among Cardiac Patients at Khwaja Yunus Ali Medical College Hospital, Sirajganj
abstract: Background: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Psychological stress has been increasingly recognized as an important factor among cardiac patients, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Understanding the distribution of stress levels alongside clinical characteristics of AMI patients is essential for comprehensive cardiac care. Objective(s): To describe the sociodemographic characteristics, psychological stress levels, risk factors, severity, and outcomes of acute myocardial infarction among cardiac patients admitted to Khwaja Yunus Ali Medical College Hospital, Sirajganj. Materials and methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 300 cardiac patients diagnosed with acute myocardial infarction at Khwaja Yunus Ali Medical College Hospital, Sirajganj. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire covering sociodemographic variables, psychological stress levels, and established risk factors of AMI. Clinical information regarding AMI severity and patient outcomes was obtained from medical records. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and presented in tables and figures. Results: The age of the participants ranged from 35 to 73 years, with a mean age of 50.95 ± 10.43 years. The largest proportion belonged to the 35–45-year age group (37.3%). Males constituted 72.0% of the study population, and 85.3% were married. Regarding education, 38.0% had secondary-level education, while 20.7% had no formal education. Salaried employment was the most common occupation (32.7%). In terms of psychological stress, 61.3% of the patients experienced moderate stress, while 25.6% had high stress levels. Hypertension was the most prevalent risk factor (61.3%), followed by smoking (53.3%) and diabetes mellitus (52.0%). Moderate AMI severity was observed in 58.7% of patients, whereas 26.7% had severe AMI. Regarding outcomes, 73.3% of patients showed clinical improvement, while mortality was recorded in 26.7% of cases. Conclusion: The study findings reveal that the majority of AMI patients were middle-aged males with moderate psychological stress and multiple conventional cardiovascular risk factors. Moderate severity of AMI and favorable clinical outcomes were observed in most patients. These findings highlight the importance of comprehensive assessment, including psychological stress, in the management of patients with acute myocardial infarction. KYANCJ 2026; 07 (01): 1-5

title: Assessment of nutritional status of critically Ill pediatric patients and its impact on outcome in a low-and middle-income settings
abstract: Malnutrition among children is a crucial public health issue. Children in critical care units may suffer from nutritional vulnerability due to their underlying disease or barriers to nutrient delivery. Early detection and management of malnutrition may improve clinical outcomes. To evaluate the nutritional status of critically ill children admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) and its prognostic outcome. This observational prospective cohort research entailed 250 children admitted to the PICU. All participants were assessed at admission and weekly thereafter for 28 days. Nutritional status was evaluated using anthropometric measurements and the PYMS and STRONGkids scores. The PRISM score was used to assess illness severity on the day of admission. 59.2% of patients were underweight and/or stunted at admission and 59% at day 28 of follow-up. PYMS, and STRONGkids scores were significantly higher among underweight and/or stunted on day 1 and during follow-up (p < 0.05). Multivariable regression analysis demonstrated that admission PRISM score was an independent predictor of mortality (aOR 1.50, 95% CI 1.19-1.88, p = 0.001), mechanical ventilation requirement (aOR 1.18, 95% CI 1.07-1.31, p = 0.001), and feeding interruptions (aOR 1.29, 95% CI 1.16-1.45, p < 0.001). Socioeconomic status was independently associated with feeding interruptions and length of stay. CONCLUSION: Underweight and/or stunting was common among PICU patients. PYMS and STRONGkids were effective in identifying nutritional risk. After adjustment for confounding variables, clinical severity rather than baseline malnutrition independently predicted adverse clinical outcomes. WHAT IS KNOWN: • Underweight and/or stunting were prevalent among children admitted to the PICU and this represent a crucial public health problem. • Both PYMS and STRONGkids were useful screening tools for identifying children at risk of malnutrition. WHAT IS NEW: • This study demonstrated that clinical severity and the need for inotropic support were the primary independent predictors of adverse outcomes. • The baseline malnutrition was not independently associated with mortality, mechanical ventilation, feeding interruptions, or length of PICU stay.

title: Development of a Resource-Adaptive Acute Care Architecture for Low-Resource Hospitals: A Yemen-Informed Clinical and Operational Framework
abstract: Background: Acute-care delivery in resource-constrained hospitals requires two distinct judgments: what the patient clinically requires and what the facility can safely deliver at the present time. Existing triage, severity, early-warning, and syndrome-specific tools address important components of this problem but do not constitute a single operational architecture for capability matching, escalation, referral, and reassessment. Objective: To develop a testable Resource-Adaptive Acute Care Architecture (RAACA) that integrates established clinical assessment functions with a time-stamped representation of facility capability while preserving the independence of clinical risk assessment. Methods: This conceptual framework was developed through targeted evidence mapping of WHO emergency-care resources and peer-reviewed literature on emergency care, triage, deterioration assessment, and prehospital systems in low- and middle-income countries. Requirements were extracted, mapped to a seven-layer patient journey, and synthesized into explicit constructs, decision rules, operational states, and a prospective validation pathway. RAACA does not introduce a composite clinical score. Instead, it proposes a four-state operational capability taxonomy (R0–R3) and a structured capability-mismatch process. Results: RAACA comprises seven linked layers: (1) acuity/triage, (2) immediate physiologic threat, (3) severity and deterioration, (4) syndrome-specific risk, (5) required and available capability, (6) operational disposition and referral, and (7) reassessment and quality feedback. The architecture separates patient state, system state, and operational decision, and treats referral/transfer as a clinical risk-control process. R0–R3 is explicitly defined as an unvalidated operational construct rather than a severity or mortality score. Conclusions: RAACA provides a testable architecture for coordinating validated clinical tools with changing facility capability. Its principal research question is whether resource-state classification can be assigned reproducibly, represent actual capability, and improve predefined process measures without altering clinical risk classification. Prospective multicentre validation is required before clinical effectiveness can be inferred.

title: Microsurgical Reconstruction in Central America: Experience With Free Latissimus Dorsi Flaps at a Public Tertiary Referral Hospital in Costa Rica
abstract: The latissimus dorsi muscle flap is a versatile and dynamic reconstructive option widely used in the management of a variety of oncologic and traumatic injuries and defects.Although microsurgical reconstruction has proven to be highly effective and associated with low complication rates, its implementation in low-and middle-income countries like Costa Rica remains challenging due to technical complexity, limited infrastructure, and a shortage of adequately trained personnel.This case series presents data from five patients with oncologic or traumatic defects managed by the Plastic Surgery Service at Hospital San Juan de Dios, Costa Rican Social Security Fund (CCSS).Reconstruction of these conditions required coverage using free latissimus dorsi microsurgical flaps.Only one infectious complication was reported, which was successfully treated with medical management without compromising flap viability.Successful functional and aesthetic outcomes were observed in all cases, with results remaining satisfactory throughout five years of follow-up.

title: Cost-utility analysis on the inclusion of pneumococcal vaccines in the national immunization program for older adults in the Philippines – Evidence from a middle-income country in Asia
abstract: Abstract Background Pneumococcal disease remains a substantial cause of morbidity and mortality among older adults. This study evaluated the cost-effectiveness and budget impact of four pneumococcal vaccination strategies among adults aged 60 years and older in the Philippines. Methods A Markov model with seven health states (healthy, meningitis, bacteremia with pneumonia, bacteremia without pneumonia, non-bacteremic pneumococcal pneumonia [NBPP], disability/sequelae, death) was used to simulate a 15-year time horizon under annual cycles. Four strategies were compared: no vaccination, PPV23 alone, sequential PCV13 followed by PPV23, and sequential PCV15 followed by PPV23. The analysis used a healthcare system perspective, with costs and outcomes discounted at 7% annually. The willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold was set at PHP 173,742.26 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY), equivalent to 75% of the 2024 GDP per capita. Epidemiologic parameters, vaccine effectiveness, waning rates, utility values, and cost inputs were derived from local and international sources. One-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses (PSA) were performed, and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves (CEACs) were generated. A budget impact analysis (BIA) estimated financial implications over a five-year period (2025–2029) at 95% vaccination coverage. Results Compared with no vaccination, PPV23 alone had the lowest incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER: PHP 3,705.50 per QALY) and the highest net monetary benefit (NMB: approximately PHP 1.31 million). PCV13 followed by PPV23 and PCV15 followed by PPV23 had ICERs of PHP 19,289.21 and PHP 23,453.88 per QALY, respectively. Vaccine coverage against IPD was the most influential parameter in sensitivity analyses. PSA indicated PPV23 was cost-effective in nearly all simulations at the specified WTP threshold, with a CEAC-derived probability exceeding 90%. In the BIA, only PPV23 was associated with net cost savings relative to no vaccination after accounting for vaccine procurement, wastage and storage. PCV13 plus PPV23 was projected to cost PHP 16.69 billion more than PPV23 alone, and PCV15 plus PPV23 was projected to cost PHP 20.9 billion more than PPV23 alone and PHP 4.21 billion more than PCV13 plus PPV23. Conclusion Among the four strategies evaluated, PPV23 alone was associated with the lowest ICER and lowest impact on budget. Sequential PCV13/PPV23 and PCV15/PPV23 strategies were associated with additional health gains but at a higher cost.
